en: Continuation of the *Huayan lüeshu kandeng ji*, Scroll One (Combined Original and Commentary;
End of the Ninth of the Ten Gates within the Text).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Huìyuàn of Jingfasi Temple in Jīngzhào.
Regarding the editor of this publication: I, Yuan, being of meager merit, saw my Preceptor suddenly pass away to his place of rebirth.
I have composed this brief commentary, which covers only one-quarter of the scripture, beginning from the "Wondrous Adornment" chapter and ending at the twentieth line of the twentieth chapter.

Furthermore, it includes the nine preceding concentrations from the *Commentary on the Ten Concentrations* (composed by the same author), while the introductory discourse, the intermediate sections, and the commentary following the ten concentrations have not yet been included.

I have repaired and restored it. As for those portions already composed, I have had no leisure to edit or prune them. Now, therefore, I have gathered together both extensive and concise texts, synthesizing the doctrines of both ancient and recent traditions.

I have re-examined the Sanskrit manuscripts to collate their variations and discrepancies. I have harmonized the teachings according to the Imperial Edict of the Xuanzong Emperor, preserving them as a means of reaching a balanced judgment.
With concise language and clear meaning, I have annotated this work through the process of revision and refinement. Thus it is said.
In order to explain this sutra, I shall briefly open ten gates: first, the causes for the arising of the teaching; second, the collection and school to which it belongs;

third, the distinctions within the teaching; fourth, the identification of the intended audience; fifth, the essence of the expressive teaching; sixth, the fundamental tenets and purpose expressed therein; seventh, the scope of the meaning revealed;
eighth, the categories of the text and its translation history; ninth, a detailed explanation of the title; and tenth, the formal exegesis according to the text.

The beginning and middle [of this section] consist of two parts. First, a general explanation of the names and their intent; second, the formal exposition of the arising of the teaching. Regarding the general explanation of the names and their intent:
observe that the Great Image has no fixed form, yet it assumes form according to the response to stimuli, being infinite in its manifestations.

The Great Sound has no speech, yet it speaks according to the capacity of the vessel, being inexhaustible in its discourse. Thus, one knows that form does not form itself—it forms through the response to stimuli; speech does not speak itself—it speaks through the vessel.
It speaks in response; it possesses form though it is formless. It pervades the ten directions without expanding, and reaches the infinite without wearying.
It speaks without speaking; it traverses the nine periods of time without delay, responding to the inexhaustible without ever tiring.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vaipulya Buddha—is truly what may be called the inconceivable secret treasury and the unfathomable ocean of teaching. Thus say the words and phrases.
Vast and expansive, it takes all the various scriptures as its source. Its principles are profound and mysterious; though paths differ, they converge toward the same goal.
As for its essence (*tattva*), it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent. It takes non-ceasing as non-arising, and non-arising as non-ceasing.

In phenomena, it encompasses the myriad categories; in principle, it reaches the ultimate unity (*ekayāna*). There is no phenomenon that is not integrated with principle, and there is no principle that is not [manifested] in phenomena.

Yet it does not flow away. Thus, by touching upon various categories, it forms the teachings; yet within the teachings, words vanish. It blends the ultimate and the conventional at the dual limits, and transcends both emptiness and existence within the Middle Way.
The fish-trap and rabbit-snare lose their point of reliance; the net of teachings is cast ever wider. Fish and hares have no place to depend; the mountain of meaning becomes ever more precipitous.
As for its virtue: when it accords with the distinct bodies of different categories, it subtly and minutely contains and sustains them;

when it accords with the separate forms of different categories, it manifests repeatedly and successively. The subtle and minute realm is difficult to believe, so it is explained by the analogy of the mustard seed and the jar;

the phenomenon of successive manifestation is easy to doubt, so it is illustrated by the metaphor of Indra’s net. As for its function: it is all-pervasive without being divided, and it reaches everywhere without departing.

They reach a state where the one and the many, the large and the small, mutually extend and contract; stillness and turbulence encompass one another. Many kalpas enter into a single thought-moment, neither contracted nor expanded;

a single mote of dust contains a world-system, without increase or decrease. Thus, the lands encompass both the pure and the defiled: as the Sahā world trembles, the Flower Treasury (Puṣpasaṃcaya) quakes.
The primary and retributive bodies merge with the transformation body; by beholding Vairocana, one perceives Śākyamuni. This encompasses all...
The second seven-day period of the three intervals is the time for proclamation.
Taking the one-many bodies of the five stages as the perfection of assistance, the essence and function of "this" and "that" ascend to the four heavens without arising.

As lords and attendants who mutually conceal and manifest each other, they respond to the ten lands without consultation, manifesting the Sea-Seal Samādhi of the Muni, clearly revealed in seven locations.

Manifesting the lotus flowers of those to be transformed, the nine assemblies shine with brilliant splendor. Thus, those possessing the Vajra lineage may hear the sutras even amidst the eight difficulties;

yet those lacking the cause of the eye of wisdom cannot behold the ten bodies, despite being face-to-face with them. Sudhana inquired of his spiritual friends, symbolizing his southward journey in accordance with the Dharma;
Samantabhadra followed the capacities of beings, revealing the initial source of the teaching at the Eastern Temple. Such is the Great [Vehicle], which encompasses all through its essential nature.

"Containing" means that its vast and extensive karmic functions are all-pervasive. "Buddha" refers to the two-fold awakening that is perfectly consummate. "Flower" is a metaphor for the myriad practices in full bloom.
"Adornment" refers to both the subject and the object of adornment. "Sūtra" means that which threads together and gathers. Therefore, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Regarding the first chapter, "The Sublime Array of the Lords of the World" (*Lokendra-vyuha*): "World" (*loka*) refers to the mundane world, which is another designation for sentient beings.

"Lord" (*indra*) refers to a sovereign, which is a synonym for various kings. "Sublime" (*praṇīta*) signifies the profound and wondrous nature of the Dharma-gates. "Array" (*vyuha*) denotes majestic virtue and adornment.
"Chapter" (*pin*) refers to a category; "first" (*di-yi*) refers to sequence. "One" (*yi*) is the initial designation, the head of the numbering.
This sutra contains thirty-nine chapters; as this chapter stands at the beginning, it is called the "First. Thus, it is titled: *The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sutra, Chapter One:
The Sublime Array of the World Rulers*. According to the Sanskrit manuscript, the full title of this chapter is *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*.
*Upāya-pratīhāra-naya-parivarta-maṇḍala-vibhūti-nāma*. This is translated as "The Chapter on the Majestic Power of the Dharma Gate Adorned by All Worldly Lords.

The commentary states: Although this chapter also explains the dharma gate of adornment for the *sahaja-sattva* (co-arisen assembly) to manifest the Buddha’s majestic power, it is so named because there are thirty-nine assemblies of *pṛthagjana* (ordinary beings) among the co-arisen ones.

It is singular, yet it is designated as plural for the sake of conventional expression. Furthermore, this chapter also merely reveals the characteristics of the World-Honored One’s virtues, benefits, and so forth.
Regarding the term "majestic power" (*mahānubhāva*), it is used to manifest the Buddha; as the *Prajñāpāramitāśāstra* by Guṇaprabha states:
"The listing of the assembly at the beginning of all sūtras is to demonstrate the great majestic power of the Tathāgata."
In the subsequent section, which correctly analyzes the causes for the arising of the teaching, there are three parts: first, the cause of past conditions; second, the cause of present conditions;

and third, the purpose for which it is taught. Regarding the first [the cause of past conditions], there are two types: first, the power of vows; this further has two types: first, the vow of the transformer (the principal teacher);

and second, the vow of those who assist the transformation. Therefore, the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra" states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying: 'By means of the *vīrya*...'"

By the power of the original vows of Vairocana Tathāgata, and also by the power of your cultivation of the practices and vows of all Buddhas—namely, the ability to turn all wheels of Dharma—the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Ten Stages Chapter) states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
'Furthermore, this is due to the power of the past vows of Vairocana Tathāgata,' and so on, until it says: 'causing..."
"You preach the Dharma. The chapters on the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Ten Stages all speak in this same manner. A verse in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" says:
"The Buddha Vairocana, through the power of his vows, pervades the entire Dharma realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel."
It is further said: "Throughout all the great oceans of worlds in the ten directions, by the power of the Buddha’s supernormal knowledges and vows, the wheel of Dharma is turned everywhere.
It is also said: "By the great majestic power of the Tathāgata and the vows accomplished by Samantabhadra, his wondrous voice reaches every land.
Because of these two roots of goodness, there are also two kinds: first, the Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma through his own goodness; [the second is the power of the Buddha’s grace].

The power of the faculties and the power of the roots of goodness of the assembly of bodhisattvas who have gathered together. Herein, "roots of goodness" refers to all roots of goodness except for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes": At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
And by the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, may you enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma.

In the "Ten Practices" chapter, the Buddhas of the ten directions say to Bodhisattva Guṇakara: "And by the power of the roots of goodness of the assembly of bodhisattvas, may you enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma.
In the "Dedication" chapter, it says: The Buddhas of the ten directions say to [Bodhisattva] Jina...
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhaketu said: "Because the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas have increased and become preeminent, they cause you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma.
There are four factors for the manifestation of conditions in the second [case]: first, wisdom; second, empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna); third, exhortation; and fourth..."
Because of samādhi. Regarding "initial wisdom," the *Parivarta on Dedication* states: "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, saying:
'...and because your wisdom is pure,' and so forth, until it says: 'causing you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma.
In the *Daśabhūmika-parivarta*, at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
It is said: "This is also because of your superior power of wisdom; it is because you wish to cause all bodhisattvas to hear the light of the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas.
Regarding the two types of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there are two kinds: first, the empowerment of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
second, the empowerment of the Buddhas of the present assembly. As the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi" states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra..."
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, these are the common empowerments bestowed upon you by all the Buddhas of the ten directions," and so on, up to:
"namely, because you are able to turn the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas. The *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* states: "At that time, the Buddhas addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
'All the Buddhas, numbering as many as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, together empower you through their spiritual powers. Furthermore...
This is due to the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana Tathāgata. It continues until it says: "He causes you to preach the Dharma.
This same explanation applies to all chapters such as the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Ten Stages.

Furthermore, throughout the preceding and following passages, whenever it is stated that various Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma or offer praises to the Buddha, saying they do so "by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power," these are all instances of this same category. Third, the Request.

This refers to the requests made by the various bodhisattvas in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," the requests made in verse by the various bodhisattvas in the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra," the requests made by the various bodhisattvas in the "Chapter on Names and Titles," and Mañjuśrī’s exhortation to teach in the "Chapter on Worthy Leader."
The chapters on the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and so forth, were all exhorted by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within the "Ten Grounds" chapter, there are exhortations from the three families [of bodhisattvas], and likewise in the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter and others;

the details of these exhortations should be understood according to the text, though they are not recorded here for fear of being too prolix. Regarding the four samādhis: throughout the nine assemblies, whenever the bodhisattvas were about to preach the Dharma, they first...
"Entering meditative concentration and then preaching by virtue of the Buddha's power" refers to the conditions for the arising of his teaching.
Within the third category—those for whom [the teaching is intended]—there are immeasurable varieties; here, ten types are briefly indicated. First is "due to the resonance of the capacity.
Regarding this, there are two kinds of resonance of capacity: first, resonance of capacity in the present; second, resonance of capacity in the future. Thus, at the initial arousal of the mind...

The "Chapter on Merit" states: At that time, Buddhas named Dharma Wisdom, as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, praised the Bodhisattva Dharma Wisdom, saying:
"You are now able to expound this Dharma. When you expounded this Dharma, there were Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields who resolved their minds upon Bodhi.
We now bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them all, that in a future age, beyond..."

It cannot be said that they attain Buddhahood within the same kalpa across incalculable, boundless kalpas; rather, they all attain it within a single kalpa, and all are named Pure Mind (*viśuddhacitta*).

The worlds in which they dwell are each distinct. We Buddhas protect and uphold this Dharma so that all Bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may hear it in its entirety. As the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: At that time, in each of the ten directions...
There were as many Buddhas named Samantabhadra as there are atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
They praised the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying: "Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound this Dharma.

Now, within this assembly, there are as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions who have attained the samādhi of the supernormal powers of all Bodhisattvas; we all grant [our approval]."

I bestowed upon them the prediction that in one lifetime they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field who resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

I likewise bestowed predictions upon them that in the future, after an incalculable number of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, they shall all attain Buddhahood, sharing the common name "Exquisite Realm" (Vishistaviṣaya). We did this so that all Bodhisattvas of the future might hear this.

Therefore, all together protect and uphold it. The "Chapter on Departing from the World" states: The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying, "We Buddhas, with one mind, shall all together protect and uphold this sutra, so that the assemblies of bodhisattvas of the present and future who have not yet heard it shall all be able to hear it.
The "Chapter on Worthy Leader" states that Worthy Leader Bodhisattva spoke this...

The verse concludes: "The evil realms are brought to rest. The commentary explains: These sentient beings in the evil realms possess a karmic affinity with the Dharma from previous lives and ought to receive the power of the Dharma;

it is because they have evoked this teaching that it arises. Furthermore, just as among the various assemblies in the heavens, the celestial maidens and others are all present vessels for the teaching who cause this teaching to arise.
Moreover, all the Buddha-teachings throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions are nothing other than responses to such karmic conditions.

Why is this? Because apart from the capacity of the recipient (*karman*), the Buddha has nothing to teach. Question: Since the resonance between the capacity and the stimulus (*karman*) extends to both the present and the future, why is it not subsumed within the category of present conditions?
Answer: It is precisely because it extends to both the present and the future, and not merely to present conditions, that it is not so subsumed.
Question: In the preceding section on the "Mind of Induction" (*āvāhaka-citta*) and other chapters, it was stated that all Buddhas provide protection and support for future bodhisattvas.
Regarding this sutra: how could other sentient beings be entirely excluded from its scope? Answer:

If one considers both the primary and secondary audiences, it universally encompasses all four classes of beings, as explained below in the section on "the intended audience. However, in terms of the primary audience, it speaks exclusively of bodhisattvas.

The second [purpose] is to manifest the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). This has two types: first, the sequential stages of practice (*paryāya-caryā-bhūmi*), as explained in the *Three Degrees of Worthiness* (*tri-satkṛti*) and the *Ten Stages* (*daśa-bhūmi*);

second, the mutually inclusive and perfectly integrated stages of practice (*yuganaddha-paraspara-saṃgraha-caryā-bhūmi*), as explained in the "Universal Good Conduct" (*Samantabhadra-caryā*) chapter and others.
Nevertheless, these two gates do not obstruct one another. Why is this? Sequential practice is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) of the teachings, whereas perfect integration is...

The rational nature, its qualities, and its functions are mutually identical because the characteristics [of phenomena] are the characteristics of the nature; thus, while they are distinct in their sequential arrangement (*pratipatti*), they do not obstruct their perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).

Because the nature is identical to the characteristics, while they are perfectly fused, they do not obstruct their sequential arrangement. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu employs the gate of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) to perfectly fuse these ten phrases.

Third, it is for the purpose of manifesting the qualities of the fruit (*phala-guṇa*). This also has two types: first, the fruit as result (*niṣyanda-phala*), which refers to the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*);
second, the actual fruit (*maula-phala*), which refers to the ten bodies of the Buddha pervading the three worlds.

This includes the qualities of the Buddha praised by the remaining assemblies—excluding those seated within the central assembly—as found in the first assembly among the forty-three groups, as well as the qualities of the Buddha’s light and names in the second assembly.

In the sixth assembly, there are the virtues of the fruit-stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). In the seventh assembly, there are the virtues such as the ocean of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), and the inconceivable Dharma.
In the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prakāśana-parivarta*), there are the ten kinds of virtues that manifest in the world. Within the two thousand phrases of the eighth assembly:

The final one hundred and ninety phrases concern the virtue of transformative function. Within the two thousand answers of the *Dushi jing* (Sutra on Delivering the World), they are divided into six sections.
Among these, the sixth section contains five hundred and ten phrases;

of these, the first three hundred and twenty clarify the perfection of the cause, while the final one hundred and ninety clarify the fulfillment of the fruit. In the ninth assembly, the Buddha enters samādhi.
He emits light from between his eyebrows, manifesting clouds of bodies of the Dharma-realm so that all beings may behold them; this is the virtue of his sovereign mastery.
Fourth, it is to reveal that the merit produced in the field of the Buddha is supreme. As the "Appearance Chapter" states:

"Whatever roots of goodness are planted by seeing, hearing, or drawing near to the Tathāgata, none of them are in vain. Why is this? Because these small roots of goodness do not conform to the conditioned."
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) coexist with afflictions (*kleśa*), it is like a man who swallows a small diamond;

or like a small fire that can burn a stack of dry grass as large as Mount Sumeru; or like the great medicinal king-tree, *Sudhana*, through which all who see, hear, perceive, or know it obtain benefit without it being in vain, and so forth, as explained in detail below.
The fifth [point] is for the purpose of manifesting the attainment of supreme benefit regarding the Dharma; this is of two kinds.

First, attaining benefit by hearing the Dharma while the Buddha is present, as described previously in the section on the "responsive capacity" (*indriya*). Second, attaining benefit by hearing the Dharma during the period of the Buddha’s bequeathed teachings.
This latter case encompasses the ten dharma-practices. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, chapter seven, states: "Transcribing, making offerings, bestowing, listening, reading, and upholding."

It involves exposition, recitation, contemplation, and cultivation. In other treatises, the beginning is termed "faith and aspiration" and the end is termed "cultivation," while the middle is largely the same.

In the *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*), the seventh [chapter], the beginning is "transcribing" and the end is "cultivation," with the middle also being abbreviated.
The *Bhadramukha-parivarta* states: "To enter the Great Vehicle is still considered easy; to be able to believe in this Dharma is twice as difficult.
How much more so to be able to recite and uphold it, to explain it for others, to practice according to the Dharma, and to attain true understanding. It continues:

"Even if one were to bestow all manner of pleasant requisites upon sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, that merit would not be superior to that of one who believes in this Dharma."

It is most excellent. Even if one were to serve as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire kalpa, if one is able to recite and uphold this chapter, its merit will be far more supreme than that. The "Chapter on Manifestation" states:
"All those of the two vehicles do not even hear this sutra, let alone receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain it; only bodhisattvas are able to do so."
It is so. For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this Dharma-gate, they should rejoice greatly and receive it with reverence, respect, and upon the crown of their head.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has faith in and delights in this sutra will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās...

Honey. One cultivates and accumulates the various dharmas of enlightenment; yet, if one has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majesty of the Tathāgata, or if having heard it at some time, one does not believe, understand, follow, or enter into it, such a person cannot be called a true Bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
However, if one hears this sutra, believes, understands, follows, and awakens to its entry, [they are a true Bodhisattva].
One should know that this person is born into the family of the Tathāgata. It continues, saying: "They enter deeply into the realm of the Tathāgata’s non-attainment. Furthermore, it says:
"Once a bodhisattva has heard this Dharma, they are able, by means of the wisdom of equality, to know immeasurable dharmas," and so forth.

By constantly contemplating all phenomena through a single dharma, one accomplishes such merit that, with little exertion, one attains teacherless wisdom and spontaneous wisdom, as explained at length therein.
Furthermore, a verse says: "If, upon hearing this sutra, one gives rise to joy and celebration..."
He has made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past and is sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas; praised by humans and devas, he constantly makes offerings.
Sixth, in order to manifest the principle of the complete aspect of *vijñapti-mātra*, there is the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven" by the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.

It says: "For example, like a skilled painter who distributes various pigments, falsely perceiving different colors [where there is none], while the great elements (mahābhūta) themselves have no differentiation...
and so on, until it says: "If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu):
everything is created by mind alone. These ten verses all clarify *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only); one should know that this is explained at length. The *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* says:
The Bodhisattva further reflects: "All that exists within the three realms is created by the single mind alone. As Vasubandhu’s Commentary explains:

"'Created by the single mind alone' means that all of the three realms are merely the transformation of mind. How does one observe conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in accordance with its distinctions and thereby enter ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
All that is elucidated as "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) throughout the preceding and following sections is subsumed under this gate.
The seventh is for the purpose of manifesting the vast bodhicitta. Within this, there are three aspects: essence, characteristics, and qualities.
The first is the wisdom of great compassion, aspiration, and power. As stated in the seventy-eighth fascicle of the [Avataṃsaka] Sūtra:

"The lamp of bodhicitta has great compassion as its oil, great vows as its wick, and its light illumines the entire dharma-realm. The commentary explains that "light" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Second, the characteristics refer to the aforementioned three.
The modes of conduct inherent in the Dharma are all limitless. As stated in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Initial Resolve":

"Not only does one offer all articles of pleasure to sentient beings throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the ten directions for hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* kalpas, but also causes them to cultivate the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, and teaches them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments."
It is certain. Because they have attained the four fruits and the state of a pratyekabuddha through the teaching, they resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It continues, saying:
"One does not resolve upon bodhicitta merely by limiting oneself to making offerings to such-and-such a number of Buddhas;

rather, it is for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed, for the sake of thoroughly understanding the worlds of the ten directions, and for the sake of fully knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds."
Because they fully know the various inclinations, various faculties, various skillful means, various minds, various karmas,
and various afflictions of all sentient beings in all worlds; and in order to make offerings to the unspeakably unspeakable number of Buddhas of the past,
future, and present throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space...

Because there are Buddhas, one generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, as revealed in the seventy-eighth [chapter], the characteristics of the two-fold benefit of the bodhicitta—namely, benefiting others and bringing peace and happiness to oneself—are explained in detail therein, including the abandonment of faults and the progression toward excellence.

Regarding the "three virtues," they refer to meritorious qualities (*guṇa*). As stated in the "Chapter on the Wise Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*): "If there is a bodhisattva who, having first generated the mind, vows to seek..."
They realize the *buddhabodhi*. Their merit is boundless; it cannot be measured and has no equal.

These and other verses, numbering more than three hundred, manifest the virtues of the bodhicitta. Furthermore, within the "Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving Mind," there are ten successive comparisons, each stating that [the merit of other practices] does not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, when compared to a Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind.

Even one part in a hundred thousand does not equal it; this extends even to one part in a hundred thousand billion, one part in a hundred thousand *nayuta*, a numerical fraction, a *kalā* fraction, a calculable fraction, a metaphorical fraction, or even a *upaniṣad* fraction—it does not equal even one of these.

Furthermore, among the two hundred and twenty-one questions within the seventy-eight [sections], there are those that praise the bodhicitta, some of which extol its essential nature and its endowments.

Regarding "superiority" (*viśeṣa*): either inferior form reveals superiority, or it refers to merit or wisdom that gives rise to the wholesome, extinguishes evil, subdues malevolent spirits and demons, and ultimately encompasses the fruit of Buddhahood, as explained extensively in those [scriptures].
Furthermore, throughout the preceding and following sections, wherever the bodhicitta is elucidated, all such instances are subsumed under this category.
The eighth is for the purpose of revealing the principle that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The *Gāthā-stava-parivarta* at the summit of Mount Sumeru states:
"To thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and non-existent—thus understanding the nature of phenomena, one beholds Vairocana. It further states:
"All phenomena lack true reality, yet they falsely grasp at the appearance of true reality; therefore, all ordinary beings wander in the prison of birth and death. Furthermore...
It is said: "The present is not produced by the conjunction of conditions; the past and future are likewise so. All phenomena are without marks (*animitta*);
this is the true essence of the Buddha. If one can contemplate the profound meaning of all phenomena in this way, then one sees the true mark of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
The *Gāthā-stava-parivarta* of the *Yāma-deva-sabhā* says: "All phenomena have no coming; therefore, there is no birth."
Because arising does not exist, cessation is likewise unattainable. All phenomena are without arising, and they are likewise without cessation.
One who can understand in this way sees the Tathāgata. Because phenomena are without arising, they lack intrinsic nature and are non-existent.
One who understands through such analytical discernment has realized the profound meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "How are the aggregates (skandhas) described?

What is the nature of the aggregates? The nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished; therefore, they are said to be unarisen. When one analyzes these aggregates, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished; this is the meaning of 'unarisen. Since sentient beings are thus, so too are all Buddhas."
It is likewise so. "The Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature"—passages such as these appear throughout every section of the nine assemblies;
they cannot be cited in full for fear of prolixity.

The ninth is for the purpose of revealing that the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is devoid of attainment regarding both principle and phenomena. The *Gāthā-stava-parivarta* (Chapter on Verses of Praise) in the *Yāma-deva-palace* states:
"Just as gold and the color of gold are in their nature without distinction, so too are dharma and non-dharma; their essential nature is no different.

Furthermore, the fourth dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) states: "The Bodhisattva understands that the world is entirely like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and clearly realizes that sentient beings are merely..."

There is one dharma; it possesses no dual nature. Without abandoning the sphere of karma, through skillful means, it manifests unconditioned dharmas within the conditioned realm without destroying the characteristics of the conditioned.
Within the unconditioned realm, it manifests conditioned dharmas without conceptualizing the characteristics of the unconditioned.
As stated in the fourth of the eight dedications: "For example, True Suchness has reality as its very nature."
The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: it understands that all phenomena have reality as their nature.
Just as true thusness (tathatā) has the absence of nature in all phenomena as its nature, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:
it understands that all phenomena have the absence of nature as their nature. Just as true thusness has no marks as its mark, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
To understand that all phenomena have "signlessness" as their characteristic is like true thusness (tathatā) arising and sharing the same essential nature as all phenomena.
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise: it shares the same essential nature as the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Such are the passages [of the scripture].
These [features] appear throughout the nine assemblies of the sutra and cannot be described in full detail.
The tenth is for the purpose of manifesting the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in which every phenomenon is non-obstructive; herein, there are briefly ten types, namely:

principal and attendant, hidden and manifest, subtle, and the layering of the profound. These are explained extensively in the ninth section on the "Manifestation of Meaning" in the lower fascicle. The above are the various gates.
Regarding the statement "spoken for the sake of manifestation," this means that the Sage’s intention was to manifest these matters so that the world might know and see them;

thus, he gave rise to this teaching. Furthermore, there are ten causes for the arising of the teaching. As stated in the *Bodhicittotpāda-parivarta*: "All [is] by the spiritual power of the Buddha," and so forth, up to the tenth:
"Because the dharma-realm is understood to be non-dual, such a Dharma is taught. The detailed explanation is as found therein. Regarding the causes for its arising...
The section on the Gate of Causes is concluded.

Regarding the second part, that which is subsumed within the Piṭakas and the divisions (nikāya), there are two sections: first, the explanation of the Piṭakas and the divisions; second, the analysis of what is subsumed therein.

Within the first of these, "Piṭaka" refers to the Three Piṭakas and the Two Piṭakas, while "divisions" refers to the twelvefold division of the Sūtras. Among these, the Three Piṭakas are explained first, and they are divided into three parts.
Regarding the first, the Sūtra-piṭaka—also called *sūtranta*—there are two parts: first, explaining the general name; second, interpreting the specific titles.
First, concerning the general name "Three Piṭakas," this is found in the first chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* and the fourth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.

Everyone asks this question: "What is meant by 'pitaka' (collection) regarding those three and those two? The answer is: "Because of inclusion. That is to say, it includes all meanings that ought to be known.
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two interpretations, or alternatively, three meanings.
The two meanings are: first, solidity; second, production. Within the meaning of production, one further derives the sense of containment, like a fetus within a womb.
This is because there are two meanings. Thus, the first [treatise] states: "The *piṭaka* (store) is called 'firm' (*dṛḍha*). It is like the core of a tree, or like a fetus dwelling within a womb.
These roots of goodness possess the most supreme power among all other roots of goodness, being like a diamond (*vajra*);

they are also capable of producing the practices leading to the realms of humans and devas. Now, the meaning of these three *piṭakas* is likewise: they are able to express that which is to be expressed."
1. Because it explains that which is indestructible; for by means of this, one is able to destroy afflictions that are otherwise difficult to destroy. 2.

Within the expressive [words], because they accumulate the various meanings and principles to be expressed. 3. Because the relationship between the expresser and the expressed constitutes profound and non-virtuous causes and effects.

"Three" is a numerical term, specifically a *saṃkhyā* (numeral) compound. Within the second section, the individual explanation, there are three parts: first, the definition of the names; second, the explanation of their characteristics; third, the alternative names.
Regarding the *sūtra* at the beginning: this is translated as "Kie-king" (契經). "Kie" (契) means to accord with principle (*dharma*) and to accord with the capacity of the audience (*yoga*).
"King" (經) means to string together and to gather and transform. This may refer to a sūtra that accords with principle and fits the capacity;

or "kie" itself is the sūtra. Furthermore, the *kie-king* is the *piṭaka*. Traditionally, many have offered this interpretation. However, upon careful examination of various treatises and the Sanskrit terminology, it is likely not so. As for...

Why is this? Because herein we comprehensively examine three types of errors. First, the error of translating by reversing the meaning of the term; second, the error of translating the meaning as the name;
and third, the error of failing to distinguish between the general and the specific. Regarding the first error, ancient masters explained that *sūtra* means:
This is translated as "thread" (sūtra). In this region, the term for thread is not highly esteemed; thus, the word for thread has been abandoned in favor of "sūtra.
According to the five regions of India, the terms *sūtra*, *śīkṣā*, *sūtra*, and *rajju* are all called *sūtra* within the holy teachings.

Ancient scholars did not realize that the sound of *sūtra* encompasses these various meanings, and so they insisted that "thread" was the correct translation, while "sūtra" was not its direct equivalent. However, in this country, the sages...
First, regarding the title "Jing" (Sūtra): Since it is already designated as a "Jing," and the Buddha expounded the *sūtras*, how could one employ a different designation?

To translate it by using a term that stands in direct opposition [to its original] would be incorrect; it is precisely appropriate to call it a "Jing. Second, regarding the error of naming according to the meaning:

Translators have their own established standards. If a name exists in both Sanskrit and Chinese, then one translates it by using the corresponding term. However, if a term exists in the former but not in the latter, one should simply retain the Sanskrit word.
Alternatively, there are cases where meanings are borrowed to serve as names. Whatever is absent from this region [of China] and is thus translated into a Chinese term belongs to this category.
As for the translation of *sūtra* as "契經" (*qìjīng*), this is half meaning and half name; it is not a purely borrowed term.
If both characters of the term *sūtra* were names (*nāman*), why would the Sanskrit original not say *yukti-sūtra*?

(*Yukti* has three meanings when translated in full: first, "conformity" (*yoga*); second, "in accordance with what has been practiced since antiquity"; third, "acting according to correct principle. Here, we take the sense of "conformity. Some superficial scholars claim that *yukti* is merely a word for "principle."
This is erroneous. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, and other texts all state that they are called "sūtras" because they are able to penetrate and encompass [the meaning].
They do not say that penetration and encompassing are themselves the title of the sūtra. Rather, it is understood that the sūtra possesses the functional activity of penetrating and encompassing;

in this sense, "penetration" corresponds to "conforming to the principle" (*li*), and "encompassing" corresponds to "meeting the capacity" (*ji*). For this reason, the translators, following the principle of editorial revision (*pi-xiue*), [applied these terms].
Seizing upon the opportunity for invocation, they borrowed meanings to assist in the nomenclature of the *Sūtra of the Seal* (*Yiqie jing yinyi*).

This refers to those who compiled the *Ekottarika-āgama* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, placing ancient materials first and taking the translations of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras as their models later on.

Thus, they followed one another in succession like ancestral lineages, no longer subjecting these works to critical examination. Although Master Huiyuan also pointed out contradictions, he did not exhaust their source. Now, I rely upon...
Although they are opposed [in meaning], one may still refer to them as "sūtras. Therefore, in the second chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Sūtra-piṭaka is called the "Sūtra-piṭaka.
Even this single character "sūtra" (經) is not subsumed under any of the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*); how much less could it be a *karmadhāraya* or a *tatpuruṣa*?

If it were to include the name of the "Piṭaka" (藏), it might potentially be a *karmadhāraya*. One should understand that when various treatises explain the term "siddha" (契), they are themselves providing an interpretation of the "sūtra" (經) within the term "siddha-sūtra" (契經).

The meaning [of the title] is not an explanation of the name of this sūtra. If it were otherwise, then since the five meanings of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* are also the meaning of the sūtra, why would they not be translated as the names of sūtras—such as the *Udaka-utsaya-sūtra* (Fountain Sūtra) and so forth?

Furthermore, for example, while "many substances" (*bahudravya*) has "arising together" (*samudaya*) as its meaning, why would "arising together" also be translated as the name [of the sūtra]? One should know that all names and their meanings are like this. Question:

Names are established based on their referents; how could a name be different from its referent? The answer is: while the referent is fixed, the name is not fixed, as names vary according to region and differ in their various forms;

the referent, however, is not like this. Regarding the third point, the loss of the distinction between the general and the specific: when the various schools (nikāyas) establish names, each has two levels of general and specific.
First, the "Three Piṭakas" and the "Twelve Divisions" constitute the general names, while the *Sūtra* and so forth constitute the specific names.
Regarding the term "Sūtra": first, it refers to the general designation; second, it refers to the specific titles such as the Vinaya and the Geya.
According to tradition handed down from antiquity, only the former category has been analyzed, while the latter has not been discussed.

Following Master Fayuan, although he speaks of three types—the general, the specific, and the abbreviated Sūtras—his first point conforms to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, his second lacks scriptural authority and contradicts correct reasoning, and his third violates the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which states: [text omitted].
The *Saṃyukta-sūtra* (Miscellaneous Sūtras) refers to prose compositions that collect and arrange the meanings that ought to be briefly explained. The commentary states:
these meanings that ought to be briefly explained are precisely those prose compositions that have never previously appeared as a brief summary followed by an extensive explanation.
One should know that "brief" (*saṃkṣipta*) is a synonym for "general" (*piṇḍita*); that is, one part of the *Sūtra* is general, while the remaining ten are [specific].
One part is distinct. Therefore, what is now called *sūtra* establishes its name based on the general characteristics and functions within its respective *nikāya*.
The names of the other *piṭakas* and *nikāyas* are established based on their specific characteristics and functions within those [respective] *nikāyas*. Why is this?

Because the function of the *sūtra* is able to penetrate and encompass; thus, that which is explained and that which is converted by the other *piṭakas* and other *nikāyas* are only then [fully realized] through this penetration and encompassing.

Because it is established as such. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 15, states: "From the beginning with 'Thus have I heard' down to the end with 'Rejoicing and practicing accordingly,' all are termed *sūtra*.
Furthermore, in the "Two Truths" chapter of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, the *sūtra* is designated as the "Root of the Dharma" (*dharmamūla*).
Therefore, one knows that this [term] is a general designation. Were it not so, other *piṭakas* and other sections might not all be capable of conforming to the capacities of sentient beings.

It accords with the principle. Alternatively, each [of the five] should individually be called *sūtra*, as there is no other designation [for them]. This is because they do not exist through mutual dependence as either general or specific categories.
As for the remaining names established based on their distinct characteristics: the *Vinaya Piṭaka* is so named in reliance upon the function of discipline (*vinaya*);

the *Abhidharma Piṭaka* is so named in reliance upon the function of analytical knowledge (*jñāna*). The five others—the *Itivṛttaka*, *Jātaka*, *Vaipulya*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and *Adbhutadharma*—are likewise established.

Based on the activity of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-artha*), it is the "self-proclamation" (*svavāda*) that constitutes the activity of the cause for the arising of the teaching. Based on the characteristics of the instruction, the "recitation" (*uddeśa*) and "chanting" (*pāṭha*) constitute the activity of the teaching.

Based on skillfulness (*kauśalya*), the "parables" (*avadāna*) and "discussions" (*upadeśa*) constitute the activity. This is because the specific (*viśeṣa*) necessarily depends upon the general (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, the *geya* (verses in response) and so forth are also designated as *sūtra* (discourses) because they depend upon the general; however, since the general is that which sustains and does not depend upon the specific, it does not include [the specific categories].

Regarding the titles such as *Geya* (Verses), it is asked: If the cultivation of many [factors] constitutes the general [category] and the others constitute the specific, why does the fourteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state:
"From the cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes butter; from butter comes clarified butter (*ghṛta*); and from clarified butter comes refined clarified butter (*sarpis*)"?
From refined butter comes *ghṛta* (clarified butter). The Buddha is also like this: from the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
from the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerges the *sūtra*; from the *sūtra* emerges the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) sūtras;
and from the Vaipulya sūtras emerges the Great Parinirvāṇa. The Great Parinirvāṇa is like *ghṛta*. *Ghṛta* is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The Buddha-nature...
This is precisely the Tathāgata. The answer to this passage clarifies that *Sūtra* (修多) is the general category. However, there are two interpretations. One says:
"That which emerges from the Buddha as the twelve divisions" refers to the twelve divisions of the teaching as the primary reality (*bimba*).

"That which emerges from the twelve divisions as *Sūtra*" refers to the twelve divisions of the teaching as a reflection (*pratibimba*). *Sūtra* is the general category; it is simply cited here as *Sūtra*.

It is extensive. Regarding "emerging from the *sūtras* into the Vaipulya": Vaipulya is the specific [teaching] that relies upon the general. Regarding "emerging from the Vaipulya sūtras into the *Nirvāṇa*":
this is because the *Nirvāṇa* reveals its intended meaning by relying on the Vaipulya teachings. One interpretation states that these two passages cite each other reciprocally.
This clarifies the principle of the relationship between the general and the specific. For there is no general category without which the specific cannot be established;

and there are no twelve [divisions] without which the general cannot be manifested. Thus, the *sūtra* emerges from the twelve. To say "from the twelve divisions" is a statement made in terms of their common characteristics.
Regarding the explanation of their characteristics through pairs, various treatises differ in how they assign and subsume them; some possess both meanings.

Each is assigned individually; alternatively, they may be subsumed by a single thread and applied to both functions collectively; or, despite possessing both, there may be no distinct allocation between them.
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states: "Because it can penetrate and because it can encompass, it is called 'sūtra' (*sūtra*);

for the holy teachings of the Buddha penetrate and sustain the meanings that ought to be explained for those beings to be converted. Furthermore, Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Sūtra..."

There are four meanings: namely, the ability to penetrate [the teaching] by way of basis, characteristic, phenomenon, and meaning. "Basis" refers to that location, that cause, or that purpose for which something is taught.
"Characteristic" refers to the characteristic of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Dharma" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika*), non-contention (*araṇā*), and so forth. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is taught according to the underlying intention (*saṃdhi*).
Furthermore, both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (25) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (20) state: "Sūtra" refers to that which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [spoke] therein..."

Regarding the locations: for the sake of those sentient beings, in accordance with the various distinctions of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be transformed, he proclaimed immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth, up to the extensive explanations.
The compilers of the Dharma, having adopted the noble language so that the Dharma might endure for a long time, compiled it in succession using exquisite words;
they wove it together and stitched it into a whole, capable of leading to meaningful benefit and capable of leading to the true holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"Excellent and subtle meaning"—this is what is called a *sūtra*. There are three alternative names for it; the first is "Dharma-Root" (*dharmamūla*) as found in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
According to Master Suiyuan’s commentary, there are five meanings: first, the teaching is the root of principle; second, the sūtra is the root of the śāstra;
third, the general is the root of the specific—meaning that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the first is the general *sūtra*, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It is said: From the beginning with "Thus have I heard" down to the end with "rejoicing and practicing accordingly," all are termed *sūtra*.
Thus, within the aforementioned general category, eleven divisions are distinguished; those not included elsewhere are subsumed back into the *sūtra*, which is termed the "particular.
The former serves as the basis for the latter, meaning that the aforementioned particular *sūtras* are, in relation to [the general category]...
The *geya* (repeated verses), *avadāna* (parables), *upadeśa* (treatises), and so forth, are the detailed expansions of these [sūtras], as they are based upon them.

That is to say, among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the first briefly sets forth the general name for all of them, "Sūtra," while the latter provides extensive explanations, resulting in the twelve divisions.
For example, the word "form" (*rūpa*) is the fundamental, brief sūtra; what follows, such as "blue, yellow," and so on, constitutes the detailed explanation.

This refers to the extensive *sūtras*. Now, the explanation is not so; it should follow the meaning of the "total" (*samasta*) and "particular" (*vyasta*) categories within the two layers previously described.
The total serves as the basis for the particular, and is thus called the "Dharma-basis" (*dharmamūla*).

If one were to explain the name "Dharma-basis" according to the five meanings following the distant [tradition], then the remaining eleven divisions [of the canon] would not be the basis of reason, would not be explained by this treatise, and would not be...

They accord with both the principle and the capacity [of the audience]. Since there is nothing that does not accord with the principle and the capacity, there is no *sūtra* that is not subsumed within the eleven categories.

It would follow that only the *sūtra* category contains the *geya* (repetitive verses), yet the *geya* should also be included within the *sūtra*. With the exception of the *udāna* (inspired utterances) and the *geya*, the remaining nine categories should all lack repetitive verses.
With the exception of the *upadeśa* (treatises) and the *avadāna* (narratives), the remaining nine categories should all lack treatises and narratives. Since these [categories] are all...

There are [such cases]. They should all be called *dharmamūla* (bases of the Dharma). Since this is so for the classification of the teachings (*śāsana*), it should likewise be so for the Piṭakas. A brief version serves as the extensive original, and thus it pervades everything;
indeed, all that constitutes the Piṭaka teachings possesses both a title and an explanation. If this is the case, then everything is a *dharmamūla*; why then would it apply exclusively to the Sūtras?
Since this reasoning is not tenable, the distant interpretation is incorrect. Second, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is called "directly spoken language."
This refers to the Venerable Harivarman. Speaking in terms of general characteristics according to the Buddha’s words, it is called "direct exposition" (*ṛju-nirdeśa*).

When each individual expression is analyzed according to its many meanings, it is called "non-direct exposition. Third, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, among the three baskets (*piṭaka*), this is designated as the Sūtra-piṭaka;
this is precisely the name translated through the method of "opposing correspondence," as explained in detail previously.
Within the second [category], the Vinaya Piṭaka, there are three parts: first, the definition of the name; second, the explanation of its characteristics; and third, its alternative names.

Regarding the first, the definition of the name: the meaning of *vinaya* is translated as "subduing" (*zhàofú*). If translated according to its direct correspondence, it is properly called "discipline" (*lǜ*).

However, it disciplines and refines the three types of action (*trikarma*), and "subduing" refers to the restraint of transgressions and faults. "Disciplining" is the essence of the practice, while "subduing" is its function. Thus, disciplining is itself subduing; it maintains [the precepts].

This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound: "the discipline (*vinaya*) that is the activity (*karman*) of training. However, both the essence and the function of this practice are what is expressed by the term "Basket" (*piṭaka*).

Thus, it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*: "the Basket which is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of this discipline. Alternatively, it is a *matup-bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound): "the Basket which possesses the functional activity of this training.

Regarding its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The *vinaya* has four meanings: namely, transgression (*āpatti*), motivation (*samutthāna*), purification (*vyutthāna*), and [the nature of] the training (*śikṣā*)."
Regarding "emergence" (*naiṣkramya*): it refers to the five classes of offenses. Regarding "origination" (*samutthāna*):
it refers to committing various offenses due to ignorance, negligence, the intensity of afflictions, and a lack of respect. Regarding "purification" (*viśuddhi*):

it refers to restoration through one's intention (*āśaya*), not through punitive measures, as is the case with the undertaking of vows. There are seven types of emergence: first, confession by addressing each individual.
1. That which is transgressed; 2. Undertaking punishment through a vow, such as undertaking the training (*śikṣā*) and so forth; 3.

If there is an obstruction to a previously established rule of training (*śikṣāpada*), it is later permitted again by way of another method; 4. Cessation in a specific location, meaning that when the Saṃgha is in harmony, they rescind what was established;
5. Transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), meaning that because a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī undergoes a change of gender, they relinquish the offenses unique to that class.
Sixth, by means of contemplation of reality (*tattvadarśana*); that is, the contemplation of the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being the supreme *dharmodāna*.

Seventh, by means of obtaining through the nature of things (*dharmatāpratilambha*); that is, by seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*), one obtains [the state] where there are no minor or secondary offenses (*anāpatti*).

Regarding the *Vyākhyāyukti*, there are two interpretations concerning the absence of minor and secondary offenses: first, some say that "minor" refers to offenses of the second category (*dvitīya-pārājika*), and "secondary" refers to the two types of methods...
[This constitutes] an offense. "Minor" refers to natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); "concomitant with the minor" refers to the proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) among the various precepts.
As for the statement "one who has already seen the truths," it is because such a person naturally attains liberation from those various offenses by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*). Question:

Now that you are elucidating the Tripiṭaka of the Mahāyāna, why is it that here the characteristics of the Vinaya are revealed based on the teachings of the Śrāvakas? Answer: In truth, the three collections (*tri-piṭaka*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.
However, for now, let us proceed according to the teachings that guide and introduce [the path]. This has been the case since antiquity. There are six names for the three [categories].

The first is called *prātimokṣa*, which is translated here as "individual liberation" (*bie jie tuo*). Yet, there are two aspects to it: first, regarding the cause, it is named "individual liberation."

There are two meanings for this: first, it is called "distinct" (*prātimokṣa*) because it distinguishes itself from that which arises simultaneously with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or the Path (*mārga*).

Second, it is called "distinct" because each of the three types of action and ten branches individually prevents wrongdoing and abandons faults. The former [explanation] relies on the sense of distinguishing and maintaining, while the latter concerns the abandonment of faults.

If there were no such distinction and maintenance, then meditative concentration and the Path would also have to be called "distinct liberation," as they all possess the meaning of individually abandoning faults. Alternatively, [the term may be explained as follows:]...
There would otherwise be no such liberation free from faults. Second, based on the fruit, it is called "conducive to liberation" (*anuloma-vimukti*);

that is, it refers to the purification of the means (*upāya*) and nirvāṇa as manifested through the removal of hindrances. Since ethical discipline (*śīla*) can accord with these, this name is established. The *Commentary on the Saṃtati-vimukti-sūtra* states:
The fivefold Dharma-body is called liberation (*vimukti*). In Sanskrit, it is *vimokṣa*. Nirvāṇa-liberation is called *mokṣa* in Sanskrit. Master Huiyuan said:
"Nirvāṇa is unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*); the fivefold Dharma-body is conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*)."

Now, this interpretation is not correct. Freedom from faults and the absence of obstruction is called *vimukti* (liberation). The activity that is free from attainment is called *vibhūti-vimukti* (analytical liberation).

Regarding the commentary on the Sūtra concerning the fivefold *dharma-kāya*, the intention is to take up liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), rather than to cause one to grasp the five [aggregates].
Because mastery over objects is termed liberation, the definitive discernment of the matter of liberation is called liberation.
Because of knowledge and vision. Second is *śīla*. Its meaning is derived from *śītala*. *Śītala* here means "cooling" (*qingliang*). This also has two meanings:
because it is free from the causes of feverish affliction, and because it attains the fruit of cooling.

Third is *upavāsa*, which is the name for the discipline (*vinaya*) of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions; it is also called *mañca*. Fourth is *vārṣika*; the sound of *di* is pronounced as *tian-yi*.
Conversely, this is the name for the laws and regulations of the kings of the Western Regions. Fifth is "keeping one's word," which means that as originally promised, there is no violation.
Sixth is "good nature," because among the three natures, it is comprised solely of the wholesome.

Within the three Piṭakas of Abhidharma, there are three [sections]: first, the definition of the name; second, the explanation of its characteristics; and third, its alternative names. Regarding the first: *Abhidharma* is translated as "Counter-Dharma" (*Duifa*).
If translated according to the sense of opposition, it might instead be called "Tradition" (*Chuan*), such as in the *Gongyang* [Commentary] and other works;
however, this is not superior [to the former], and thus it is not so used. Now, *abhi* signifies "counter" (*dui*) and *dharma* is termed "Dharma" (*fa*). The old [translation] says...
*Abhidharma* is translated as "The Peerless" (*Anuttara*), because it elucidates the excellence of wisdom. Now, according to various schools, there are three further explanations.

First, some say that "counter" (*prati*) refers to that which is countered, namely *nirvāṇa*; and "dharma" refers to the "store" (*piṭaka*). Because this store of dharmas enables practitioners to proceed toward *nirvāṇa*, it is the dharma that is countered;
thus, it is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Second, some say that "counter" refers to wisdom.

"Function. Since the dharma is the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*), the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated it with two meanings: first, the aspect of "tending toward attainment," meaning that the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) tends toward *nirvāṇa*;
second, the aspect of "knowing reality as it is," meaning that the untainted faculty of wisdom takes the principle of the truths (*satya-tattva*) as its object.
The commentary states: these are merely two divisions of a single essence of untainted wisdom according to its functions, based on its objects.
Because there is a distinction between the fruit and its causal principle. Question: How is it that the *piṭaka* (the treasury) is distinguished and yet explained as being wisdom (*jñāna*)?

Answer: There are two senses to this: first, based on the wisdom that is the subject matter expressed; second, based on the wisdom of the author of the treatise. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:
"The 'expositor' (*vādī*) refers to one who repeatedly investigates and examines the various sūtras and the *mātṛkā*, and so forth, up to the noble disciples..."
The son [the disciple] has already seen the traces of the Truths; relying on his own realization, he correctly discriminates the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*dharma*).

This, too, is called Abhidharma. The commentary states: according to this very text, the expositions composed by the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and those at the stage of the Seven Preparations (*sapta-prayoga*) are not included within the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Thirdly, it is because they are named as commentaries based upon the Piṭakas and in accordance with the Piṭakas. (From the *Nyāyānusāra*).
The principle states: "Sūtras are called *dharma*; the treatises (*śāstra*) that can definitively discern them are called *Abhidharma*.

Since this [treatise] is the counterpart (*pratipakṣa*) to *dharma*, it is interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Regarding the characteristics of these two interpretations, Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "There are four meanings of *Abhidharma*."
It is called "Abhidharma" because it is confrontational (*abhimukha*), enumerative (*abhisaṃkhyāna*), subduing (*abhibhava*), and penetrating (*abhiprāya*).

That is to say, Abhidharma is named "Confrontational Dharma" (*abhidharma*) because this dharma confronts (*abhimukha*) non-abiding nirvāṇa and is able to explain the truths, the factors of enlightenment, the doors of liberation, and so forth.

It is also called "Enumerative Dharma" (*abhisaṃkhyāna-dharma*) because, regarding each and every phenomenon, it repeatedly explains its etymological definitions, specific characteristics, general characteristics, and immeasurable distinctions.

Because it is distinct [from other categories], it is also called the "subduing dharma" (*vibhāṣā-dharma*), for by means of its complete treatment of the locus of the treatise and so forth, it is able to subdue the arguments of others.
It is also called the "pervasive dharma" (*vyākhyā-dharma*), because it is able to pervasively explain the meaning of the *sūtras*.

Among the three alternative names, the first is *upadeśa*, which is translated as "treatise" (*lun-yi*); the second is *mātṛkā*, which is translated as "matrix" (*benmu*). This refers to the *piṭaka*.
The *mūla* (root) is called the "mother" because it is capable of producing understanding; thus, the root itself is the mother, which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Third, it is named *mātṛkā*, which here means "mother of practice. This signifies that understanding arises based on the *piṭaka* (scriptural collection), and practice is accomplished based on that understanding.
It is named after its source, hence it is called the "mother of practice" or the "mother that gives birth to practice," which is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. The Three Piṭakas are concluded.
Regarding the second [classification], the two piṭakas: first, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; second, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. However, the essence of these two piṭakas is not different from the three;
they are divided into two based on the difference in their intended recipients. The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, chapter four, states:
"These three piṭakas, due to the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles, are further described as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "As..."
Because there is a distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna within these three piṭakas, they constitute two collections: first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Regarding the term "Bodhisattva," because there are three masters who provide distinct explanations in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the second [master] states:
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to those *sattvas* who seek *bodhi*; this term applies generally to all three vehicles (*yāna*).

To specifically distinguish and select for the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), the word "Mahāsattva" is further added. Furthermore, they are called "Bodhisattvas" because they take *bodhisattva* as their object of focus.
They are fully endowed with the great vows for self-benefit and the benefit of others; they seek great *bodhi* for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Moreover, *sa*...
*Bodhi* (埵) has the meaning of "valiant" (*vīrya*), signifying that one is called a *bodhisattva* because they are able to valiantly seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Regarding the compound [analysis] of the first and last terms, in the case of *bodhisattva*, it is either a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) or a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive adjective). As for the term *śrāvaka* (聲聞), the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "One who attains awakening by hearing the Dharma."
It is said they are "śrāvakas" (voice-hearers). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because they enter the noble path by hearing the sound of the Buddha’s voice, they are called śrāvakas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 82, says: "Because they hear the sound of the true Dharma from others, and can also cause others to hear the sound of the true Dharma, they are called śrāvakas.
The second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, it causes all to hear."

They are called "Śrāvaka" (Hearer). Regarding the various explanations above: whether one hears for oneself based on the voice of another, or causes others to hear based on one's own voice, these are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds.

However, regarding these two Piṭakas, if they are named according to what they express—namely, the principles, practices, and fruits of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas—they are all *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds.
If, however, the names of the Piṭakas are established based on the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas themselves, [they are likewise *tatpuruṣa*].
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound). The section on the two *piṭakas* is concluded. Question:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* both state that the three *piṭakas* are divided into two *piṭakas* based on the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles (*yāna*).

Why, then, do the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra*, the *Lalitavistarasūtra*, the *Rājāvavādakasūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra*, and the *Mahāyānāvatāraśāstra* all explain that the three vehicles constitute the three *piṭakas*? Answer: The former [texts] rely upon the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).

Because the principle and the fruit are the same; because the teachings and practices of the Śrāvakas are manifold; and because Pratyekabuddhas for the most part do not rely on formal teaching, the Piṭakas are combined according to the Vehicles.

Later, because the teachings and practices of the two vehicles differ, the Piṭakas are differentiated according to the Vehicles. Although each has its own justification, [the former approach is adopted].
The former [section] possesses three meanings, while the latter possesses only one; since the meaning with more aspects is superior, it is now explained according to that superiority.

The details are as set forth in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicles 25, 38, 81, and 85), the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (fascicle 11), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (fascicle 6), and so forth.
The thirty-second division of the scriptures is also called the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*). Within this, there are two aspects: first, the general, and second, the specific.

Regarding the general: "twelve" is the number; "division" (*piṭaka*) refers to the categories; and "sūtra" (scripture) refers to the teaching itself. The term "twelvefold," etc., is explained as a *saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa* (an adjective indicating a number).

However, the name of these divisions may be confused with the *piṭakas*, and the term "sūtra" may overlap with the physical scrolls or volumes. Otherwise, it would be like saying "if... [and so forth].

Regarding "a certain number of fascicles of sūtras," one should say "teachings consisting of a certain number of fascicles" in order to prevent erroneous interpretations; thus, the new term is "divided teachings. Within this category, there are three parts:
first, listing the names; second, explaining the names; and third, discerning their characteristics. First, as for the listing: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 15, states:
"One who knows the Dharma is a bodhisattva who knows the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*), namely: *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*..."
Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa;
the Vyākaraṇa (in Sanskrit called *vyākaraṇa*)—the third chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* asks:
"How does a bodhisattva rely upon these four kinds of śamatha? and so on, up to: "is able to skillfully [discern]..."
Regarding *vipaśyanā*, the Buddha said: "It is as I have provisionally established for the sake of the bodhisattvas, namely:

the sūtras (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), stanzas (*gāthā*), spontaneous utterances (*udāna*), causal narratives (*nidāna*), parables (*avadāna*), past events (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), extensive teachings (*vaipulya*), and marvelous accounts (*adbhutadharma*)."
Discourse (Upadeśa). Second, regarding the explanation of the names: first, the analysis of the *sūtra* (契經) is as extensively explained previously.
As for the *geya* (應頌): "should" (*ying*) means "correspondence" (*xiangying*); it refers to verses that correspond to the prose (*gadya*), or because they are to be recited again later.
This is an *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the *vyākaraṇa* (記別): the *Yupian* states it means "to record"; the *Shuowen* states it means "to explain separately. It refers to recording those fruits.
It is shown so as to bring about understanding and knowledge. "Recording" (*jì*) constitutes the essence of the teaching, while "bringing about understanding" constitutes its function.

"Recording" (*jì*) is thus a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Some say that the consciousness which records distinctions is called "recording-distinction" (*jibie*). Are not the *Vastusamgrahaṇī* and *Jātaka* sections not themselves consciousnesses that record distinctions?

As for "reciting" (*fèngsòng*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To recite by intoning. Since "intoning" (*fèng*) is identical to "reciting" (*sòng*), this is also a *karmadhāraya* compound. From here on...

Regarding "explanation" (*nirdeśa*): it is understood as both *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), meaning "based upon one's own explanation" and "that which has something to be explained.

Regarding "causal condition" (*nidāna*): the cause (*hetu*) is itself the condition (*pratyaya*). Regarding "parable" (*avadāna*): the illustration (*apadāna*) is itself the metaphor (*upamā*). Regarding "past events" (*itivṛttaka*) and "birth stories" (*jātaka*): [the former refers to] what actually occurred, and [the latter refers to] previous births.
"Causes" (nidāna) refers to events according to the time and births according to the time; it means there are circumstances.
"Vaipulya" (Extensive) means that its karmic function is vast and expansive, like empty space, filling the ten directions, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This term "fang" (方) signifies "extensive"; because correct principles are extensively set forth, it is called Vaipulya. "Adbhuta-dharma" (Marvelous Teachings) refers to extraordinary and rare phenomena.
The term "discourse" (*lunyi*) refers to circular investigation and examination; "discourse" (*lun*) is itself the "discussion" (*yi*).

If these twelve [divisions] each carry the two-character designation "division of teaching" (*fenjiao*), they are all *dharmadhāraya* (explanatory) compounds, meaning that the *sūtra*-division is itself the teaching, and so on up to the final one.
Third, regarding the differentiation of their characteristics: each of the twelve divisions of teaching has two meanings. First, concerning the *sūtra*: the first is general...

Regarding the characteristics: there are two types of concise characteristics. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* (XI) states: "The Sūtra refers to prose compositions that briefly explain the meanings that ought to be explained.
