Secondly, because it was heard successively from others, it is called "thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*); this also avoids the aforementioned difficulty.
Thus, the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), fascicle six, states: "Ānanda heard it from the various bhikṣus, or some devas spoke to Ānanda."
Third, it is said that because Ānanda heard [the teachings] directly from [the Buddha], he declared, "I have heard.
Regarding this, there are four explanations. First, as stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, there are three types of Ānanda:
namely, Ānanda who upholds the Śrāvaka-dharma, Ānanda-bhadra who upholds the Pratyekabuddha-dharma, and Ānanda-vaktra who upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, in the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*...
The *Tattvārtha-prajñā-paryāya-ṭīkā* cites the *Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru’s Repentance* and other texts, all of which agree with this explanation.
Since these various sūtras and śāstras state that there are three types of Ānanda, if [the narrator] is the Ānanda who says "I have heard," then the aforementioned objection is avoided.

Second, if it refers to the Ānanda who had not previously heard the sūtra and the Buddha spoke it again for him, he likewise says "I have heard," and thus the aforementioned objection is also avoided. Therefore, the *Bao’en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states:
For twenty years before Ānanda became the Buddha’s attendant, the Dharma taught by the Buddha was restated in its entirety at Ānanda’s request.
This was because Ānanda had attained supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), dhāraṇī, and other such qualities. As the *Vajrapuṣpa Sūtra* states:

"Because Ānanda has attained the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Awakening to the Nature of Phenomena (*dharmatā-avabodha-viśeṣa-rāja-samādhi*), he is able to remember and maintain all the sūtras previously spoken by the Tathāgata."

"I heard it directly and there is no difference. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Ānanda, the man of much learning, whether present or absent, will naturally be able to understand the meaning of the permanent and the impermanent.
This is because the four Ānandas were great bodhisattvas; thus, they were able to hear [the teachings] directly.
The *Acintyavimokṣa Sūtra* states: "At that time, there were again ten billion bodhisattvas who manifested in the forms of śrāvakas and also came to the assembly."
They were seated, with Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana as their leaders, down to Ānanda, Devadatta, Upananda, and others.
All of them had long practiced the six pāramitās and were close to the Buddha’s bodhi;

yet, in order to transform sentient beings, they manifested in the forms of śrāvakas within the defiled lands. The commentary states: according to this scriptural passage, [this refers to] the ultimate [state].
[The text] says: "As for the various [previous] exponents, all were merely skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the three questions concerning those who transmit the Buddha’s teachings: why do they not state their names, but simply say 'I have heard'? Answer: It is because one fears the error of confusion with others who share the same name.

[Objection: Others also possess the designation "I"; how could there not be confusion? [Response: When one refers to oneself as "I," it is definitively restricted to one's own self; therefore, there is no confusion.

[This is] an erroneous omission. Fourth, regarding the question: "All Buddhist teachings speak of the non-existence of a self (anātman) or a person (pudgala); for what reason, then, is the term 'I' used at the beginning of the sūtras?
The answer has two explanations. First, according to the second chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is briefly due to five reasons. First, although the disciples of the Buddha...
One knows that there is no self; yet, following worldly convention, one speaks of a "self," though this is not a real self. There are three roots to the linguistic conventions of the two worlds:
first, falsehood; second, pride; and third, mere names. The first two are impure, while the last is pure.

All ordinary worldlings possess all three types of speech. Those who have realized the Path still possess pride and names. As for noble ones beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they possess only names. Internally...

Because the mind does not accord with unreal dharmas but follows worldly people, this teaching is transmitted together [with them]. Third, it eliminates worldly wrong views; fourth, it accords with worldly convention and is free from dispute.
Fifth, if a disciple of the Buddha were to cling to the mark of selflessness, they might be subject to refutation; yet, once selflessness is truly known, [such clinging no longer arises].
For what reason is it said, "Thus have I heard"? One does not even cling to all phenomena; how much less would one cling to non-self?

According to the sixth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is briefly stated that there are four reasons for saying "Thus have I heard": first, for the sake of conforming to worldly linguistic convention;
second, for the sake of following along with worldly norms; third, for the sake of eliminating the fear of those who are certain that there is no self; and fourth, for the sake of...
This is taught in order to proclaim the gains and losses for oneself and others, thereby causing the arising of a mind of resolute faith and understanding.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Chapter 9) and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Section 13) both state this in the same way. The questions and answers are concluded.
Regarding the four sections within the accomplishment of the third period: first, a general indication of the time; second, a specific explanation of "one time";

third, the analysis of the essence; and fourth, the questions and answers. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the citation of ancient masters; second, the explanation based on the treatise. Within the former, there are three accounts. First, Bodhiruci says: "Time is of many kinds, namely:
the time of a single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), the time of day and night, the time of a hundred years, and the time of one eon (*kalpa*)."
"Time" refers here to the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—but the "one time" mentioned now does not refer to these. It is precisely the time when the Tathāgata preached this sutra.
Second, Chang-er (Long-Ear) said: "There are two kinds of time: first, the *ardha-nirghoṣa* (half-sound) time, which does not reach all objects;
second, the *pari-nirghoṣa* (full-sound) time, which reaches all objects. He further stated: "The *brahma-svara-kalpa* (Brahma-voice aeon) itself has three types: first, *kāla*..."
At that time, this refers to the "time of specific characteristics. For example, when the precepts are being recited, one may hear them during the Great Precepts but not during the Minor Precepts;
one may hear them when they concern those who have left the household life but not when they concern those living at home; and a king may hear them while others do not.

The second *samaya* (time) is here called "the time for destroying false views. This refers to the five collections of the Āgamas and the nine divisions of the Dharma, which are accessible to all without distinction between the ordained and the laity.

Regarding the five collections: they consist of the Long, Medium, Mixed, Increased, and Ekottarika Āgamas, totaling one hundred sections. Regarding the nine divisions: first, the Vinaya-vibhaṅga (Analysis of the Precepts); second, the Lokāyata (Worldly Matters); third, the Nidāna (Causes and Conditions); fourth, the Dhātu (Elements);

fifth, the Samyukta (Connected Discourses); sixth, the Ekottara (Numerically Increasing Discourses); seventh, the Jātaka (Birth Stories); eighth, the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings); and ninth, the Upadeśa (Instructional Treatises). It was obtained at the same time [as the previous].

Sixth, names, phrases, and syllables; seventh, the collection of meditative concentrations; eighth, the collection of karma; ninth, the various aggregates. Each of these six sections contains six thousand verses.
Six times nine is fifty-four; thus, there are fifty-four thousand verses in total. This is as stated in the first volume of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra-vibhāṣā* and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the time of its circulation throughout the three periods [of past, present, and future], it is as stated: "At one time, the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Ganges River. One.

Regarding the phrase "at that time" (*tadā*) in the Śiṃśapā Grove and other locations, the present expression "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) relies on the latter two of the three explanations, or perhaps the third.
As Sengzhendi (三真諦) states, there are ten kinds of "time": first, the time when a Buddha appears in the world; second, the time when the True Dharma is preached; and third, the time of listening.

Fourth, the stage of upholding; fifth, the stage of reflection; sixth, the stage of cultivation; seventh, the stage of planting the roots of goodness; eighth, the stage of perfecting the roots of goodness; ninth, the stage of liberation through the roots of goodness;

tenth, the stage of equanimity (which refers to the mind being free from regression, agitation, and abandonment; having extracted both sinking and floating, it attains balance and achieves the equanimity of mindful relinquishment, thereby entering the True Dharma—this present [stage] encompasses all four).

Regarding the second point, the explanation according to the treatises, there are two interpretations. First, the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "There are three kinds of time."
First, the time of equality (*samatā-kāla*), meaning there is no sinking, floating, or inversion. Second, the time of harmony (*saṃnipāta-kāla*), meaning it causes the listener to hear correctly.

Third, the time of turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana-kāla*), meaning correct preaching and correct reception. The present phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) encompasses these three types.
Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of time: first, *kāla*-time, which applies to both the conventional (*prajñapti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Internally...

This applies generally to external [explanations]. Regarding the second point, the time of the *samaya*, it is merely provisional and not real. As for the present term "one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), it is subsumed under the latter [category].
Second, regarding the specific explanation of "one time," there are three parts: first, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by Guṇadatta, "one time" refers to the time of preaching.
Regarding the phrase "at this time": since other sūtras are also taught at other times, and because there are three interpretations in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the first states:

"The term 'at one time' refers to the time of speaking and listening. This is designated as 'one time' because the speaking and listening reach their conclusion through a continuous succession of moments without interruption.
If it were not so, then the letters, names, and phrases [would not constitute a single discourse]. Regarding the speaking and listening of the letters, names, and so forth:

The times differ; how can they be said to be one? Second, it may be that the speaker has attained *dhāraṇī*, such that within a single syllable and in a single moment, he is able to uphold and expound all dharma-gates; or it may be that the listener has attained the purity of the ear-faculty.
In a single *kṣaṇa*, at the moment of a single syllable, there is no obstruction regarding all other things; they can all be fully received.
Therefore, it is called "at one time. Third, it may mean that because the temporal divisions of their mutual encounter are indistinguishable, it is called "at one time.
Third, according to this sutra, at the moment of first attaining perfect enlightenment, a single *kṣaṇa* and immeasurable eons are fused without obstruction. Thus...
When it reaches the point of encompassing the entire dharma-dhātu without exception, only then is it called "one moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*).
Third, regarding the analysis of its essence: first, it is said that within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools, there are four general explanations.

First, according to the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika schools, in the context of the *skandha* (aggregates) gate, both take the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature. In the context of the *dhātu* (elements) and *āyatana* (bases) gates, [the conditioned] is...
Regarding its nature: according to the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa, it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) within the framework of the five aggregates;

and within the framework of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), it is the object of the mental base (*manāyatana*), the mental element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Time is that which exists upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)."

It is a provisional designation of a state (*avasthā-prajñapti*). Alternatively, because it is a provisional designation applied collectively upon the mental states, images, form, mind, and so forth, it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
Regarding the third point, "relying on the signless," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:
Question: In the Buddha-dharma, dharmas such as number and time do not truly exist, because they are not subsumed within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), or sense-bases (āyatanas).
It is even said that various things such as these are not called *kāla* (time) but are called *samaya* (occasion) in order to eliminate false views.
Answer: One perceives the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases and conventionally designates this as "time. There is no separate time apart from this; that is to say:

At that time, names such as separation, conjunction, identity, difference, long, and short are merely conventional designations to which the minds of ordinary people become attached, asserting them to be real dharmas.

For this reason, one must discard these worldly names, linguistic conventions, and dharmas. The commentary states: "This takes the absence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."

Regarding the fourth [aspect], the non-obstruction between the numerical and the temporal: this means that both "one" and "time" are aspects of virtue and the instruments for responding to capacities.
Therefore, "one" encompasses all numbers, such that they are entirely the substance of the One; "time" subsumes all past and future kalpas, such that they are entirely the substance of time.
Ultimately, each possesses the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, which is boundless and inexhaustible.
This is considered its nature. Why is this so? Because all dharmas do not depart from this. The defiled realm and the deluded mind manifest simultaneously;
at that very moment, they are both identical to and different from it.

Regarding the fourth question and answer: The question asks, "Since the location, city, and country have already been specified by name, why are the day, month, and year of the teaching not specifically indicated?

The answer is: For now, based on the general designation, it is stated simply as "at one time" due to two reasons. If one were to specify them individually, there would be no fault in doing so. As for the two reasons:
first, because the meaning is concise and identical, it is said to be "at one time. This means that when the Buddha preached the Dharma...

Whether it be a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or even many eons (*kalpa*), because the entire duration from beginning to end is collectively termed "one time," and because it facilitates ease of linguistic expression, there is no fault in speaking of them individually. This is as stated in the text of this very passage: "Just having attained perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that it was not long after his attainment of enlightenment—specifically during the second seven-day period.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that it was on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the time he was about to enter nirvāṇa. The *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states that it was on the eighth day of the first month of the year when he finally sat upon the tenth bhūmi.
Such passages exist everywhere; they cannot be cited exhaustively here. Thus concludes the third section: the Attainment [of Buddhahood] at the Third Time.

The conclusion [of the preceding section]. Within the fourth [section], the "Principal Accomplishment," there are three parts: first, the naming; second, the definition of its essence; and third, the questions and answers. Regarding the first [of these three], there are three [subdivisions]: first, the Buddha, namely *buddha*.
This is translated as "Awakened" (*jue*), which refers to the illuminating function of perfected great wisdom. That which is illuminated is...
What is it? It refers to the Dharma of Bodhi; that is, the realm of the dharmadhātu where the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual and unobstructed.

Second, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 1: "Possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), being free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one is able to awaken to oneself regarding all phenomena in all their aspects, and is also able to awaken all sentient beings."
Sentient beings are like awakening from a dream or like the blooming of a lotus; for this reason, they are called Buddhas.

Third, according to the central tenet of this sutra, the wisdom in which the beginning and the fundamental are non-different illumines the phenomena of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without any distinction; this is termed "Buddha. As the subsequent text states:

"Because one has attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena, one universally illumines the objective realm, wherein all share the same dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the beginning and the fundamental are in profound union."
The non-duality of object and wisdom is termed "Buddha. Regarding the two aspects of its essence (*svabhāva*):
according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the ground of great enlightenment is subsumed within five factors, namely the four wisdoms and the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

According to the tenet of this sutra, it fully encompasses all phenomena of the infinite and unobstructed dharma-realm, even including the three kinds of worlds, which are collectively taken as its essence. Three questions [follow].

The answer consists of three parts. First, regarding the question as to who speaks this sutra: is it spoken by the Buddha himself, or by a bodhisattva, or within the light of the Buddha and bodhisattvas, or by various kinds of deities and spirits? Why, then, is it here designated solely as "spoken by the Buddha"? The answer is:
although there are many types of speakers, none do so without relying upon the power of the Buddha. Because the Buddha is the sovereign, and because his testimony is supreme for inspiring faith.
It merely designates the Buddha. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one does not trace [the teaching] back to what was heard from the Buddha, then disputes will arise.
Second question: The Great Master possesses ten titles; why, then, is only the appellation "Buddha" indicated at the beginning of the sutra? Answer:

According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the Buddha possesses ten meanings, whereas the other titles do not. Therefore, only "Buddha" is mentioned. These ten meanings have been fully explained previously in the detailed commentary on the title.

It is stated in the *Madhyamaka-hṛdaya-vṛtti-tarkajvālā*: "Regarding the three questions concerning the Buddha who taught this sutra: is he the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) for others, or is he the coarse Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
Even if [one of these] were the case, what would be the fault? Both positions entail errors. If it were the Enjoyment Body, then he should not be in the kingdom of Magadha.
Furthermore, it would contradict the verses of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which say: 'The most excellent among humans, the supreme in the world, the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas...'"
Regarding that, if it were a coarse transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it should not be called Vairocana. As stated in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs":
"The ocean-like surface of the great wisdom of Vairocana emits light from its gate of the face; there is nowhere it does not reach. Passages such as these appear in every assembly [of the sutra].

How is this to be explained? The answer is: when this sutra speaks of the Buddha, it refers not only to the *paranirmāṇakāya* (transformation body for others), nor does it refer solely to the coarse emanation body.

Why is this so? Because it speaks of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*). That is to say, the Tathāgata’s bodies manifest in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, and these capacities are inexhaustible.

The Buddha’s body is likewise so; therefore, ten bodies are taught to manifest its inexhaustibility. Yet, the single body of the Buddha and his inexhaustible bodies are neither identical nor different.

Why? Because it is by virtue of being the Buddha that the various chapters on entering the *dharmadhātu*, such as those concerning names and titles, all speak of a single body—sometimes called Śākyamuni, sometimes called Vairocana, and sometimes called Siddhārtha, and so forth.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. As for the "ten bodies," they are as explained in the *Bie xing zhang* (Chapter on Separate Practices). The above concludes the fourth section, the Accomplishment of the Lord.
Within the fifth section, the Accomplishment of the Location, the general designation of "Magadha" is used because the six explanations of the Buddhas of the Western regions differ.

First, it is said that *Magadha* is a name based on its general characteristics, meaning "Excellent Victory" (*śubha-vijaya*), because it is the most excellent among the good, or because the good itself is victorious.
Second, it is said that *ma* means "not," *gadha* means "evil," and *dha* means "place"; thus, it is so called because there are no evil dharmas in this location.
Third, it is said that *ma* means "not," *gadha* means "harming," and *dha* means "place"; thus, it is so called because there is no execution by punishment in this country.
1. It is said that those who committed capital offenses were placed there in the *śmaśāna* (cold forest). 2. It is said that *Magadha* means "pervasive" (*mā-vyāpti*). *Gadha* means "intelligence.
This refers to a person of comprehensive wisdom who pervades the entire kingdom. 3. It is said that *Magadha* is the name of a constellation (*nakṣatra*), and *gadha* means "place.

Because the boundaries of this country belong to that constellation. 4. It is said that *Maga* means "great" (*mahat*) and *dha* means "essence" (*tattva*). This refers to the fact that this country... [is great in essence].
Among the various kingdoms of the five regions of India, this one possesses the greatest territory;

therefore, among the six aforementioned explanations, the sixth is now employed to represent the Dharma, as it is preeminent because the Dharma-realm it elucidates is vast and all-encompassing. Alternatively, it may also apply to the first four [explanations], as there is no logical contradiction in this.

From here below is the second section, which specifically elucidates the fourfold accomplishment. First, the specific elucidation of the profundity of the location; second, the specific elucidation of the pervasiveness of time at the commencement of the accomplishment;
third, the specific elucidation of the adornment of the location; and fourth, the specific elucidation of the virtues of the Lord, beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One...

Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts: first, the explanation of the text; second, the questions and answers. Within the former, it says: "The dharma of the araṇya is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)."

Regarding the middle [term]: consulting the Sanskrit original now, it is correctly *dharmāraṇya*. This is translated as "the tranquility of the Dharma" (*dharma-śānti*) and is also called "the Dharma without clamor or contention.

This name distinguishes it from "the non-clamor and non-contention of phenomena" (*vastu-aśabda-vivāda*), wherein the stillness of phenomena and the clamor of phenomena must necessarily differ in terms of time and place.
In "the Dharma without clamor and contention," clamor itself is non-clamor; therefore, it is called *dharmāraṇya*. It is precisely because of this...
Regarding this principle: when translating Sanskrit terms, it is not always necessary to employ literal calques. Thus, there are three types of *araṇya*:
first, the *tāndaka-araṇya*, which refers to a place of sand and gravel; second, the *maṇḍaga-araṇya*, which refers to the vicinity of cemeteries at a distance of one *krośa* from a village.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 136, four *catur-aṅgula* [are the measure of a *hasta*].
One *dhanus* (bow-length). Five hundred *dhanus* constitute one *krośa*. Calculating by the current standard where two *chi* make one *hasta* (cubit), four *hastas* equal eight *chi*.
Thus, there are a total of four thousand *chi*. According to the Saṃmitīya school, one *krośa* measures one thousand *dhanus*.
With eight *chi* constituting a *dhanus*, this amounts to approximately eight thousand paces, which corresponds here to slightly less than four *li*. Paramārtha’s commentary states: "A..."
"Āraṇya" means a place free from sound; that is to say, because it is devoid of the sounds of villages, the sounds of cutting and chopping, and the sounds of strife and contention.
The third *dharmāraṇya* is precisely what is being explained here, as fully interpreted as before. As for "bodhi":

This refers to the "Dharma to be realized," which is the unimpeded *dharmadhātu* where the ultimate and conventional truths are seamlessly fused. Because one realizes and attains this therein, it is called a "field" (*maṇḍala*).

This is a metaphorical designation; just as worldly sacrificial grounds (*maṇḍala*) are places where spirits and deities dwell, the Buddha is the supreme among all sentient beings and spirits, and thus the name is applied to the site upon which he relies. According to the *Xiyuji*, the kingdom of Magadha is located... [text continues].
Within the realm of Central India lies the city of Rājagṛha. To the west of this city, at a distance of more than two hundred *li*, there is a mountain named Gayā.
On the southern side of the mountain stands a tree called Pippala; because the Buddha attained *bodhi* beneath it, it was renamed the Bodhi Tree.
Regarding the subsequent question and answer: the question concerns whether the place where this sutra was preached is pure or defiled.
What would be the fault in either case? Both positions entail errors. If it were defiled, one should not speak of jeweled trees and jeweled ponds;

furthermore, at the end of this chapter, it should not be said that "at that time, the ground of the Flower Treasury World shook in six ways. If, on the other hand, it were pure, why would it be described as the location of the nine assemblies?
Therefore, they all reside among the humans and devas of the Sahā world. The answer follows from the preceding and following contexts:

while the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) and the Sahā World are described as distinct in terms of their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), when these characteristics are traced back to their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), they are unimpeded and perfectly interfused. Thus, it is based on such a place that such a Dharma is taught.
Question: Since this first assembly was preached in the kingdom of Magadha, were there sentient beings from that country who participated in the gathering?
If so, what is the fault? If both cases are problematic—if there were participants, why does the sutra not mention them? And if there were none, why was it necessary to preach this?
Answer: There are two meanings here: first, to manifest the Dharma; second, to respond to the capacities of the audience. Regarding "manifesting the Dharma," it means:
The kingdom of Magadha is the foremost among all nations; this assembly is the first of the nine assemblies, and for these reasons it is spoken of in this way.

Regarding the phrase "responding to capacities": among those in the assembly, with the exception of the newly arrived bodhisattvas from the ten directions, all others were born in this land in accordance with their vows.
This is precisely what it means to respond to capacities. Why must one necessarily list ordinary worldly people to constitute the audience being transformed?
Second, regarding the detailed exposition of the pervasiveness of time, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the text; second, the questions and answers.

Within the former, "initially attaining perfect enlightenment" means that while previously it was only stated in general terms that the period of hearing the Dharma reaches its ultimate conclusion, it had not yet been specifically identified as occurring at a particular time;
therefore, this is specifically named the time of initially attaining perfect enlightenment. This refers to the initial accomplishment of the wisdom of true and correct awakening. However, this...
Regarding the provisional teachings, there are five general explanations. First, according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) school:

when a bodhisattva has cultivated the thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree and attains enlightenment, it is called the initial attainment of perfect awakening. This is as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 82.
Second, regarding the Mahāyāna according to the provisional teachings, there are two explanations. First, with respect to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) of the eight aspects:

when, beneath the Bodhi tree, having manifested the subduing of Māra, it displays the attainment of perfect enlightenment, this is called "initially attaining perfect enlightenment. Second, with respect to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body):

after three incalculable eons of fully cultivating the myriad practices and fulfilling the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), at the moment the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are first perfected following the path of non-interruption (*ānantaryamārga*), this is called [the initial attainment].
First, regarding the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), there are two interpretations based on the Mahāyāna of the True Teaching (*saddharma*).

First, it is called the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment when the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*) becomes identical to the wisdom of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*), at which time the distinction between the beginningless and the original no longer exists.

Second, it is so called when the cloud-like bodies of the Buddhas’ Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya-megha*) pervade the entire Dharma-realm, such that there is no place or time where they do not manifest anew.

He attains Buddhahood; this is called "initially attaining perfect enlightenment. This refers to the aforementioned phase of manifested transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which is also identical to this [present case]. Why is this so?

Because sentient beings require that he attain it for the first time, and there is nothing that would not be appropriate [if it were otherwise]. What is elucidated here, however, is the final [attainment].

In the second question and answer, there are five points. First: although this [passage] specifically clarifies the time when the teaching arose, it states that he "first attained perfect enlightenment.
However, it has not yet been definitively stated how many days after his attainment of the Way he preached this sūtra. Answer:

According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, based on the scriptural account, the Buddha preached this sūtra on the second seventh-day period (the fourteenth day) after his attainment of the Way. If that is so, why does the Buddha...
As stated in the "Chapter on the Inconceivable": because all Buddhas manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma, pervading the entire Dharma-realm at all times and in all places, it says therein:
"All Buddhas are able, within a single body, to magically manifest as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands.
From each head, they produce a certain number of tongues; from each tongue, they produce..."
They produce various distinct sounds, and each sound expounds various sūtras, even to the point of saying:
"Even until the end of future kalpas, they may be exhausted; yet the wheel of Dharma turned by the emanation bodies of the Tathāgata has no end.
Furthermore, it says: "All sounds, letters, phrases, and meanings, each and every one, completely fill all things."
Within the dharma-realm, all sentient beings therein attain understanding; yet the Buddha’s vocal resonance undergoes no change, suffers no interruption, and is without end.
The answer to this is that the "second seven-day period" mentioned here subsumes the second seven-day period of the nine or ten periods of time.
Therefore, what is taught on this day is identical to what is taught at all times; thus, there is no contradiction.
Question: If that is so, since the power of mutual inclusion among all the times is equal, why must it be here and not at other times?
Answer: This very [time] is the "other"; one cannot speak of it as something else. Furthermore, this does not obstruct the initial statement, because its characteristics are not held [as distinct].
Question: The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in his commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, says: "Because this dharma is supreme, it is placed at the beginning. And...

Regarding the explanation of the *Abhibhvāyatana* (Stages of Mastery): could it be that the Buddha-fruit taught in the first two assemblies, as well as the seventh, eighth, and ninth assemblies, is not equal to that taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*?
Furthermore, both the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* and the *Lalitavistara-sūtra* state in common that, on the second seventh-day period after attaining enlightenment, [the Buddha] was at the Deer Park.

He taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. As for the *Samantaprabhāsa* stating that the teaching of the twelve links of dependent origination benefits all three vehicles, this is because the twelve links of dependent origination are common to all three vehicles.
If it were the case that what was taught first is necessarily superior, then this teaching of the Three Vehicles should also be superior [to the teaching of the One Vehicle].
Answer: Vasubandhu made this statement based on a single aspect, namely, within the mind of nirvāṇa.

The tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is supreme; among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Heaven of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is supreme; within a single lifetime of teaching, this day is supreme.

This does not mean that it is so for all things. Question: Since Vasubandhu stated that "because this Dharma is supreme, it was taught at the beginning," and since "the beginning" refers to the second seven-day period, why do various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras state that the Wheel of Dharma was first turned [at the end of the first seven days]? Answer: It is because... [this] with that.
Regarding the differences and similarities: as previously cited from the *Guhyakapada* and the *Lalitavistara*, the accounts of the turning of the wheel [of Dharma] are consistent with this sutra.

If one follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is the fourth seven-day period; according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is the sixth seven-day period; the *Xingxianxing jing* (Sutra on the Manifestation of Practice) says the seventh seven-day period;
the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* says the eighth seven-day period; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says fifty-seven days; and the *Shier you jing* (Sutra of the Twelve Wanderings) says one [year].
Regarding the various accounts: some say that the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught during fifty periods of seven days, which is the same as the one-year teaching mentioned in the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*.
How should such differing explanations be reconciled? Answer: This is due to differences in the faculties and capacities of sentient beings, such that what is appropriate for them to hear varies.

From the perspective of the Buddha responding to their needs, there is no time when he does not teach. Yet, from the perspective of the lack of resonance in their faculties, he has never taught. Therefore, [the discrepancies arise].
The assembly of bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages do not perceive a distinction between the Tathāgata’s initial teaching and his subsequent teachings;

at all times and in all places, they constantly perceive the Tathāgata as always preaching exclusively the single flavor of the Mahāyāna, the inconceivable Dharma. This is established according to this passage within the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma."
Third, regarding the specific explanation of the adornments of the site: from this point onward, one may also discern the adornments of the three worlds.
Furthermore, although the *āraṇya* (hermitage) and other locations were previously explained individually, they did not fully clarify everything contained within the precincts;

therefore, this is explained specifically. Within this, there are four parts: first, the adornment of the ground of the site; second, the adornment of the Bodhi tree, beginning with "beneath that Bodhi [tree]"; third, [the adornment of] where the Tathāgata...

The lower part clarifies the palace and its majestic towers. Regarding the fourth point, the lion throne beneath the lions, within the first section on the majesty of the ground, there are ten items divided into four parts.
The first is the majesty of the essence of the ground; this refers to designating it as "firm" and explaining it as "vajra.
This is the general statement. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter eleven, states: "Only in this continent [Jambudvīpa] is there a vajra-throne. Above...

It reaches the very limits of the earth and rests below upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḍa*). All Bodhisattvas who are about to ascend to perfect enlightenment sit upon this seat and give rise to the *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like concentration).
This is because there is no other basis or location that possesses the firm strength capable of supporting it.
Reflect upon how these share both similarities and differences with that [previous description]. Next, regarding the four matters concerning the adornment of the ground:

first, the jewel wheel, which is the ultimate transcendence of signs; second, the jewel flowers; third, the pure jewels; and fourth, the manifestation of various colors and forms, as vast and numerous as the ocean.

Next are the four matters concerning the adornments of the ground. First, the jeweled banner (*ratnadhvaja*). Within this, there are five aspects: first, its substance is *maṇi*; second, because its luminous activity is unceasing, it is called "constant" (*nitya*);
third, because its preaching of the Dharma is uninterrupted, it is called "perpetual" (*dhruva*); fourth, it is adorned by jewel nets that appear and disappear;

fifth, flower tassels—whose substance is fragrant and which are named "fragrant flower tassels"—hang down in profusion and clarity, serving as auxiliary adornments for the banner. Second, the jewels...

Because they are able to manifest physical supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they are called "transformative manifestations" (*nirmāṇa*). First, they can rain down jewels to preach the Dharma; second, they can rain down flowers to perfect the practices (*caryā*).

Both are able to respond to the capacities of beings as they arise, and thus are called "sovereign" (*vaśitā*). Third, the flowers born of the *dharmatā* are magnificent and universal, melting together the stages and positions of practice (*bhūmi-vinyāsa*).
Fourth, the jeweled trees surrounding the victory banner form a retinue of ranks, their branches and leaves lush and dense. All of these—
Because it emits light, it is called "Radiant and Flourishing" (Guangmao). Subsequently, the Buddha’s power added further adornment;
that is to say, all objects within the ritual arena manifested their reflections upon the surface of the ground.
Regarding the second section, the Adornments of the Bodhi Tree, there are nine matters divided into four parts. The first concerns the adornment of the tree’s form:
it is called "extraordinary" because its height is peerless; this is the general statement. The next three matters concern the adornment of the tree’s substance: first, its body is of vajra.
The two trunks are of lapis lazuli; the three branches are composed of various jewels. Next, four aspects are adorned by essence (*tattva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*):

first, that which is adorned solely by function, namely, the dense foliage providing cooling shade; second, that which is adorned solely by characteristic, namely, the flowers of various colors interspersed among the branches;

third, that which is adorned by both essence, function, and characteristic, namely, the mani-jewels whose essence emits flames while their function adorns the characteristics; fourth, that which is adorned by all three simultaneously, namely, the flowers and fruits appearing together.

There are two meanings: first, because it arises from the practice of simultaneous cause and effect as observed; second, because it originates from the conduct of the Buddha. The Buddha’s conduct is as explained in the "Chapter on Manifestation.
Fourth is the mutual adornment through successive application, which consists of three parts: first, the pervasive planting of light; second, the rain of jewels from the light;

third, the emergence of Bodhisattvas from the jewels. This reveals the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and the *adhiṣṭhāna*), as well as the fact that these Bodhisattvas are not original [beings].

Because they constitute a single act of solemn service, they are collectively treated as one. Even if they were divided into three, there would be no harm. The latter [set] is adorned by the power of the Buddha;
it is called "constant" because the preaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible.

Regarding the third palace, the Array of Towers, there are eleven matters divided into five sections. The first concerns its dimensions and the adornment of its characteristics, meaning it is both vast and magnificent.
Within this, there are four phrases: the first indicates the subject; the next two cite the vastness and magnificence of the phenomena; and the final phrase explains the term "vast."
This is the general statement. Next is the adornment of the single essence (*ekātma-vyūha*), meaning it is formed from *maṇi* jewels of manifold colors.

Next is the adornment of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-vyūha*), meaning it is adorned with precious flowers. Next are the seven adornments of superior function (*saptaprakāra-prakarṣa-kriyā-vyūha*): First, the adornment of its emission of light:

like clouds surging forth, its application has no coming, and when its function ceases, there is no going. Second, the shadow between the palaces forms banners; regarding the character for "shadow" (*ying*), in Sanskrit it is *ava-* (or *ābhāsa*).

(*Mu-he*) *pō* (*pu-he*) *sā*. This is translated as "illuminating," also as "shadow," and also as "light. Although it encompasses these three meanings, one should employ whichever is appropriate for the context.
In this case, it should be rendered as "a banner formed of radiant splendor. It is where the ocean-like assembly of the three groups gathers.
According to the Sanskrit manuscript, it says: *ānanda-raṅga-bodhisattva-maṇḍala-saṃketa-samāvasaraṇa-kaṭabhi*.
This is called the treasury into which the ocean-like assemblies of the various classes of infinite bodhisattvas converge. The term *maṇḍala* (mandara) conveys five meanings:
the site (*sthāna*), the sun-disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*), the perfected sphere (*pariniṣpanna-viṣaya*), the internal [deities], and the classes (*varga*).
Here, it corresponds to the meaning of "classes," as the assemblies of the ritual site (*maṇḍalagṛha*) are completely filled by infinite varieties of beings, not merely gathered within the palace.
Because it is at the side of the Hall, the palace is praised as a "repository" (*kośa*), for it encompasses the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

There are two kinds of sounds that emerge from the Buddha’s light: first, sounds emerging from the Buddha’s light; second, sounds distinct from the light. Nevertheless, these are both the substance and the phenomena of the *dharmadhātu*.

Furthermore, it can expound the gateway of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is called "inconceivable. Five: jeweled nets hang down all around. Six: it manifests the sphere of the Buddha’s power. Seven: it manifests defiled images. Question:
Since defilement and purity do not coexist, how can defilement appear within purity? Answer: Defilement takes the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as its very nature;
yet, because it does not destroy its own characteristics, purity—having realized the absence of intrinsic nature—becomes the essence for defilement. It does not... [The text ends here].

Because their nature is that of the destruction of impurities, when defilement and purity are compared, they are neither identical nor separate. The final one is adorned by the empowerment of the Buddha’s power;
that is to say, regarding time, place, substance, and phenomena, he manifests the karmic functions of vastness and brevity, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment.

Regarding this "single thought-moment," the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness," states: "One thought-moment contains ninety *kṣaṇas*; within one *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred arisings and ceasings."
The following text speaks of mindfulness; based on this, it should be understood accordingly.

Among the four matters concerning the adornment of the fourth lion throne, the first is the adornment of its dimensions and characteristics. This means it is both lofty and vast, yet exquisitely beautiful.

It is "lofty" because there is nothing superior above it; it is "vast" because there is nothing external beyond it; and it is "exquisite" because it is the principle within the phenomenon, and the phenomenon within the principle.
"And thus the matters are excellent" is the general statement. Next, four matters concern the adornment of the substance: first, the platform is made of *maṇi*; second, the nets are lotus flowers;
third, the wheels are exquisite jewels; and fourth, the tassels are various flowers. Next, four matters concern the adornment of the characteristics:

first, all the elements are refined and adorned; second, they are interspersed with artistic fruits; third, the jewel-lights mutually illuminate one another; and fourth, the central jewels are accompanied by their satellites. All are present.
The radiance is released and purified. Subsequently, one matter is further adorned by the power of the Buddha’s majesty; that is, the teaching on the realm of the Buddha.

The four preceding sections constitute the third part, which specifically reveals the adornment of the place; this concludes the description of the adornment of the *bhājana-loka* (receptacle world) among the three types of worlds.

The fourth section specifically elucidates the virtues of the Lord. Although the Buddha was previously designated as the Lord in general terms, his specific virtuous functions have not yet been fully explained;

therefore, they are clarified here. This section contains two parts: first, a general reference to the seat upon which he sits; second, beginning with "In all... and so forth, a specific explanation of his virtues.
Within these virtues, there are five aspects: first, the universal pervasiveness of the three karmas; second, the body is constant...

The following clarifies the universal response to the capacities of all beings. 1. "Each of the three hundred and sixty thousand hairs... and below clarifies that the tip of a single hair can contain worlds.

2. "His body pervades... and below clarifies that his body and wisdom return to quiescence. 3. "Throughout the three periods of time... and below clarifies the manifestation of Buddha-activities through light. Regarding the first [section], there are two parts: first, the principle (*dharma*); second, the analogy (*upamā*).

Within the principle, the three types of action (*karman*) constitute three sections. Regarding the first, the mental action (*manas-karman*), there are two parts: first, the heading; second, "Wisdom enters... and below, which provides the explanation.

Regarding the phrase "in all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) in the heading: this refers to the phenomena of the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional. "Attaining perfect enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*):

"attaining" (*siddha*) means to have acquired; "supreme" (*samyak*) means reaching the pinnacle; "correct" (*samyak*) means being free from inversion; and "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means awakening. What is it that is awakened to?

It is precisely the aforementioned all phenomena. How is one awakened? There are three explanations for this: first, it is said that one realizes [the truth] within the sphere of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the "limit of nature" (*dharmatā-koti*): within the sphere of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one exhausts all differentiated characteristics. Second, it is said that because the sphere of the differentiation of phenomena is itself non-differentiated;

as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states: "Because one awakens to all phenomena according to their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is called 'Perfectly Complete Awakening' (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The subsequent commentary explains this as "wisdom entering into equality. Third, it is said that realizing the true is precisely the conventional, yet without destroying the true.

Realizing the conventional as the ultimate, yet without destroying the conventional, the two realms of the ultimate and the conventional, as well as their corresponding wisdoms, are fused into a single unity. They are non-dual yet dual;
dual yet non-dual. To awaken in this manner is the pinnacle of correct awakening; therefore, it is called "Supreme Perfect Enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Regarding the statement "the entry of wisdom" (*jñānapraveśa*) and so forth in the subsequent commentary, this explains the aforementioned "perfect awakening to all phenomena. These two phrases share a single meaning.

The former concerns the term "entry" (*praveśa*) in terms of conventional discourse; it refers to "penetration" (*prativedha*), meaning that one penetrates past and future events with such clarity and distinctness that they are no different from the present;
hence, it is called "equality" (*samatā*). The latter concerns the term "entry" in terms of realizing the nature (*dharmatā*); it refers to "realization" (*adhigama*).

The essence of the dharmas of the three periods of time is one and the same *dharmatā*; therefore, it is called "equality. Regarding the phrase "his body is equal" within the context of the two types of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), there are two meanings.
First, at the very moment he sits upon this seat, he immediately fills the space before all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*.
The two Buddha-bodies fully encompass the three kinds of worlds; therefore, it is said they are "pervasive. Regarding the third [category], vocal action (*vākkarman*):
the phrase "its sound," etc., applies to all three—first, sound itself; second, the sounds of speech; and third, the dharmas signified by those words.

Although the text encompasses all three, the underlying intent concerns the preaching of the Dharma, as it accords with the ten directions. Among the two similes in the subsequent section, the first simile illustrates the aforementioned meaning.

The "karma" [of the preceding analogy] refers to the two types of karma—body and speech—of the former [analogy]. In the first analogy, there are two phrases: first, the sense of "containing," which illustrates how the wisdom of *pramāṇa* (valid cognition) illuminates the conventional without being obstructed by the myriad phenomena;

second, the sense of "equality," which illustrates how the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) illuminates the ultimate truth such that the myriad phenomena are of one single nature, yet without obstructing the myriad phenomena.
In the latter analogy, there are also two phrases: the first phrase conveys the sense of "pervasiveness," illustrating how the bodily karma of the former fills the three [realms].

Regarding "the world": the latter phrase has the meaning of universal penetration (*praveśa*). It is a metaphor for verbal action that universally expounds [the Dharma] to suit the capacities of beings; hence it is said to "equally follow and enter.

Alternatively, it refers to the perfect voice (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*) which accords with the capacities of beings, such that each understands according to their own reflection; therefore, it is called "entry" (*praveśa*).

In the second section, regarding the virtues that respond to the various capacities of sentient beings, there are two parts: first, the physical action (*kāyakarman*); second, the verbal action (*vākkarman*), beginning with the phrase "expounding all...

Within the former, there are three sections. First is the elucidation of the virtue of universal and transcendent excellence. This consists of first elucidating universality and subsequently elucidating transcendence.

Regarding the former, the statement "universally seated in all sites of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) refers to five categories; therefore, it is called "all. That is to say, first, all [beings] who are identical...
1. The site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) within all similar world-systems, as described in the "Chapter on Names" (*Nāmanirdeśa-parivarta*) and elsewhere. 2.
The site of enlightenment within all dissimilar world-systems, such as those shaped like trees, as described in the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds" (*Lokadhātusaṃbhava-parivarta*).

3. The site of enlightenment within all seeds of world-systems. 4. The site of enlightenment within all oceans of world-systems; both are as described in the "Chapter on the Treasury of Flowers" (*Puṣpakūṭa-parivarta*). 5. All... [text truncated]
Within the world-systems inside each atom, there are dharma-assembly halls, extending even in infinite layers; in these five categories of realms, the Buddha sits pervasively everywhere.

As for the subsequent mention of "surpassing excellence," this demonstrates that excelling the inferior is not considered extraordinary; thus it is said that among the assembly of bodhisattvas, he is like the sun shining amidst the stars.

The third section, following the two preceding sections, clarifies the virtue of the fulfillment of the fruit and the cultivation of the cause, as well as the virtue of the mutual manifestation between the principal and the retinue. Three.

The quality of the infinite, downward-shining light pervading the dharma-realm consists of two phrases within the section on verbal activity: the first is the principle (*dharma*), and the second is the analogy (*upamā*);
their correspondence can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the third quality, that of containing world-systems within a single hair-tip, there are two parts. First, it clarifies the unimpeded containment of world-systems; however, this involves two meanings. The first is...

First, that many lands exist upon a single hair-tip illustrates the non-obstruction between the small and the large. Second, that many lands mutually contain one another without losing their own characteristics illustrates the non-obstruction of characteristics within existence.
Following this, each manifests individually below, clarifying the sovereign mastery in taming and transforming beings within all those lands.
Regarding the fourth [section], the virtue of the body and wisdom being quiescent, there are two parts. First, it clarifies that while the body is immovable, it is omnipresent;
this has two meanings. First, although it functions, it is eternally quiescent: because the body responds to the ten directions while remaining eternally quiescent, there is no coming or going.

Second, the Buddha-body is perfectly pervasive of all things according to the principle (*tathatā*); since it is already present therein, it does not depend upon coming or going. Next, the entry of wisdom [into the lower realms] is clarified below.
"Wisdom is non-quiescent" means that because it realizes characteristics without dependence, it is called "entering.

Within the fifth section on the virtue of manifesting Buddha-activities through light, there are two parts: first, the manifestation of the supernatural transformations of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
