Within the latter two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the first is the manifestation of supernormal power through the body of eight marks, and the second is the manifestation of supernormal power through the repeated transformation of bodies.
The third section, "Ten Verses Praising the Buddha’s Virtues of Quiescence and Activity Responding to Capacities," is divided into four parts.

First, three verses clarify the virtues of the Buddha’s body and speech responding to capacities. Second, one verse clarifies the extensive response of the three karmas. Third, three verses clarify mastery over quiescence and activity.
First, quiescence and function are unimpeded and non-arising; second, it is quiescent yet constantly functioning; third, it brings function back to quiescence.

The latter three are the inexhaustible virtues that respond to capacities: first, the inexhaustibility of the Dharma-cloud; second, the inexhaustibility of the assemblies; third, the inexhaustibility of the bodily marks.
The fourth section, consisting of ten verses on the Bodhisattva Gandhavabhāsa, praises the virtues of the bodhisattvas in this assembly regarding their own stage and their further advancement.

This is divided into four parts: the first three verses praise the activities of their own stage, namely seeing Buddhas throughout all lands; the next two verses show their activities equaling those of Samantabhadra;

the following three verses concern their further advancement equaling that of the Buddhas; and the final two verses concern mastery over meditative concentration and its functions—all of which may be understood accordingly.
The fifth section, "Ten Verses Praising the Buddha’s Virtue of Turning the Wheel of Dharma by the Bodhisattva Siṃha," is divided into eight parts.
The first two verses praise the turning of the true wheel of dharma as it pervades all places; the former verse clarifies the fruit of turning the wheel, while the latter verse sets forth its cause.
The next two verses clarify the turning of the wheel of dharma through various names and epithets; the former verse clarifies the fruit of the wheel, while the latter verse sets forth [its cause].
The cause. Next, one verse clarifies the turning of the wheel of the Dharma of the equality of non-arising. Next, one verse clarifies the turning of the wheel of the Dharma of original practice.

Next, one verse clarifies the turning of the wheel of the Buddha-dharma through transformation. Next, one verse clarifies the turning of the wheel of the Dharma by manifesting diverse physical bodies within an undifferentiated body.
Finally, one verse [clarifies] the turning of the wheel of the Dharma of the names and titles of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Hereafter...
One verse provides a summary: all the wheels of Dharma taught throughout the three periods of time were spoken at this very place.

Regarding the sixth section, the ten verses of the Bodhisattva Dharmasāgara praise the virtues of the bodhisattvas in the assembly who assist the Buddha in propagating his transformational teachings. Within this:
First, the fulfillment of wisdom and the attainment of the Dharma; that is to say, because one has attained such profound and vast skillful means (*upāya*).
This refers to each individual realm and so forth in their entirety; this is also a general heading, which will subsequently be explained in detail.

Therefore, it says, "one is able to enter such skillful means," which points to the detailed explanation that follows. Second, the extensiveness of transformation in all places; third, the contemplation of reality at all times.
Fourth, the Buddha’s internal practice is supreme at all times; that is to say, he constantly emerges from within his own body through the space between his eyebrows.

Fifth, his activity is unimpeded throughout all atoms. Sixth, he manifests the sovereign mastery of the Buddha within all lands. Seventh, he reveals the Buddha’s pervasive dharma-realm and perfect voice.
Eighth, he enters the ground of wisdom of the sublime, equalizing sound. Ninth, he attains the consciousness that penetrates both the ordinary and the sagely.
The Wisdom of Sound. This is fulfilled on the tenth stage.

The seventh [chapter], "The Lamp of Wisdom Bodhisattva," consists of ten verses praising the Bodhisattva’s realization and entry into the Buddha’s profound and vast virtues. It is divided into four parts.
The first two verses praise the Bodhisattva’s vision of the Buddha’s true essence: (1) the wisdom that perceives the Buddha as free from marks; (2) the perception of the Buddha’s own...
Regarding the essence: next, the four [verses] clarify the subject who awakens and the Dharma. First, the Dharma of realizing the profound principle and receiving a body through the power of vows.

Second, contemplating the profound Dharma and practicing formal conduct; this is called the "Supreme Practice," by which one attains the fruit. This is the stage of wisdom where merit arises and abides.

Third, the continuity of the essence of the fruit-Dharma. Fourth, obtaining a vast fruit through extensive causes. Next, the two [verses] praise the Buddha-body’s ability to respond universally: first, its profundity; second, its...

Broadly speaking, the latter two [verses] praise the attainment of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which enables bodhisattvas to see all Buddhas. First, one should long for the Buddha’s empowerment;
second, [one sees] all other Buddhas.

The eighth section, consisting of ten verses, praises the Buddha’s sovereign virtue in gathering and sustaining sentient beings through the "Flame-Topknot" Bodhisattva. This section is divided into four parts.

The first two [verses] clarify how the Buddha’s body and speech are vast in gathering and sustaining sentient beings. In the preceding verse, the first and last lines clarify the locus where the wheel of activity gathers and sustains beings;
the middle two lines explicitly reveal the function of gathering and sustaining beings. In the subsequent verse, the upper half refers to the essence and the lower half to the function. Next...

The fourth section clarifies the gradual manifestation of profundity for those who are to be guided. First, regarding bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*): internally, they possess deep faith and joy;
externally, through the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, they are then able to give birth to the actual wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*), thereby illuminating and realizing the true essence.

Second, distinguishing the inferior from the superior: it means that the wisdom of the two vehicles is inferior and cannot perceive the true essence, whereas the eye of the bodhisattva is pure and can see it.
Regarding the True Body (*dharmakāya*): Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) who have attained the three knowledges (*trividyā*) observe it by means of its power;

throughout all the stages, they clearly perceive the reality (*tattva*) during their entry, abiding, and emergence. The fourth knowledge clarifies that upon the fulfillment of the tenth stage, one attains omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and is finally able to realize and enter the ocean of the Buddha-fruit.
The subsequent two clarify the Buddha’s virtue of unimpededness between quiescence and activity: first, that activity is itself eternal quiescence; second, that quiescence is itself eternal activity.
The latter two clarify that the great function is boundless: first, what is manifested within a single pore can only be fully perceived by the Universal Eye;
second, each and every body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, constantly turning the wheel of the Dharma in all places, overlapping without end and immeasurable.
The ninth section, "The Ten Verses Praising the Virtue of the Buddha’s Body and Speech Universally Responding," consists of four parts.

First, three verses clarify the universal pervasiveness of the body’s light: (1) the body pervades the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); (2) the light responds to the various capacities of sentient beings; and (3) it reveals lands within atoms.
Next, two verses clarify the diverse forms of the oceans of lands as they are enjoyed, which are also the places where the wheel of Dharma is turned. The subsequent verse [provides] the formal...

This clarifies the universal manifestation: first, it manifests universally within all lands, both inside and outside of sensory objects; second, it manifests universally within all lands inside the Buddha’s body;
third, it manifests within the signless Dharma while expounding the characteristics of phenomena; fourth, it proclaims inexhaustible teachings with a perfect voice.
The final point clarifies that the Buddha’s body universally responds to beings without ever arising or ceasing.

The tenth chapter, "Ten Verses Praising the Supreme Qualities of the Buddha," is that which Bodhisattvas are able to enter. It is divided into two parts. The first three verses manifest the Buddha’s supreme qualities:
(1) his exquisite form that inspires joy; (2) the manifestation of the Buddha within all signs, pervading the interior of every atom;

and (3) the manifestation of many bodies everywhere, eternally continuous and uninterrupted. The latter seven verses clarify how Bodhisattvas are able to enter the Buddha’s realm. Within these, the first...

The fourth [verse] clarifies entering the Buddha’s realm. First, internally possessing realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) and externally being sustained by the Buddha’s power, one knows the Buddha’s supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and skillful means (*upāya*), manifesting bodies pervading all atoms.
Second, one beholds [the Buddha] only when endowed with universal conduct and vows. Regarding the third and fourth verses:

it is by virtue of possessing faith, correct understanding, great vows, and realized wisdom that one dwells in the true *dharmadhātu* and only then realizes the Buddha’s sovereign realm of form and sound. The former...
One possesses four dharmas, beginning with faith. The last [of these] involves contemplating the Buddha’s form and voice without obstruction. The final three clarify the benefits obtained:
first, by realizing the conduct of the Buddhas, one can swiftly enter the stage of Buddhahood and universally encompass the dharma-realm;
second, one can manifest lands within a single atom; third, one can manifest many lands within a single land and attain spiritual powers.
The eleventh section, "The Ten Verses on the Bodhisattva Vīrya Praising the Buddha’s Perfect Voice, Sublime Form, and Sovereign Reality," is divided into four parts.

The first three verses clarify the Buddha’s perfect voice preaching the Dharma: (1) how within a single sound all sounds are contained, and how that sound is heard throughout the ten directions as he preaches the Dharma;
(2) how he preaches the Dharma in all buddha-fields using sounds that accord with the various classes of beings; (3) [and so forth].
In all lands, one sees the Buddha’s spiritual transformations and his preaching of the Dharma as he proceeds toward Bodhi.

Next, by means of the power of the Buddha’s liberation, he manifests his body within every atom of all lands. Next, three aspects demonstrate the non-obstruction between essence and function: first, the Dharma-body is like space, unobstructed;

there is no separate form-body, which appears in various distinct ways according to the types of beings, like a shadow or a reflection. Second, this further clarifies the preceding gate, manifesting both simultaneously.

Regarding "one who is able to comprehend": the first three insights [of the *vidyā*] reveal that the essence and function of the preceding [state] are non-dual, like space. The latter three insights reveal the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the power of his vows:
namely, first, that the Vairocana Buddha enters a single pore of a *cakra-vartin* king, which can only be seen by those with the eye of wisdom who manifest supernormal powers;

second, that through the former vows of Vairocana, he now preaches the Dharma throughout all lands pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*; and third, the divine transformations of all Buddhas within a single pore.
All Buddhas speak in unison; were one to seek their ultimate limit, one would not find it even after many kalpas.
The preceding section has separately clarified how each of the eleven bodhisattvas spoke verses in praise of his virtues. This concludes the seventh section.

The eighth section consists of two parts concerning the pervasive and universal [assembly]: first, the gathering of bodhisattvas like clouds within the precincts of the four continents of this world-system, specifically Jambudvīpa, through the miraculous transformations of the Buddha;

second, the subsequent connection to the pervasive and universal [assembly], indicated by the phrase "it should be known," which is omitted and abbreviated in this text. According to the Sanskrit original, it should read:

"In this manner, within the precincts of Jambudvīpa among the four continents of this world-system, through the miraculous transformations of the Buddha, there was in each of the ten directions one person of faith..."
In oceans of worlds as numerous as the atoms within a world-system, clouds of bodhisattvas gathered to reveal and manifest the Dharma-gates.
Likewise, in every one of these four-continent systems, within each Jambudvīpa at the site of enlightenment, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations,
clouds of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten billion world-oceans gathered from each of the ten directions to reveal and manifest the Dharma-gates.
It is also thus. Regarding the third chapter, "The Samādhi of Samantabhadra," which is now to be explained, the four gates are the same as before. First, regarding the explanation of the title:

"Universal" (*samanta*) means that one's virtues pervade the dharma-realm; "Worthy" (*bhadra*) means being supple, compliant, harmonious, and good. If one explains this according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya*, one attains...
The wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*. Because it universally realizes that its own essence is suchness (*tathatā*), it is said: "Because the essence of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is all-pervasive.
The name of the samādhi is explained as before. Samantabhadra is the person; the samādhi is the dharma. The person is that which enters; the dharma is that which is entered.
The union of the subject and object constitutes the title; thus it is called the "Samantabhadra Samādhi. This is how the name is derived. (6)

Regarding the analysis of the compound, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) because Samantabhadra enters by relying on the Buddha’s samādhi; alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive determinative) because this samādhi belongs to Samantabhadra.

If one relies on the meaning that the subject and object of realization are neither identical nor separate, both the *tatpuruṣa* and *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) analyses may be understood.
Now, consulting the Sanskrit original, the full title is "The Chapter on the Miraculous Manifestations of the Majestic Power of the Samādhi of Samantabhadra."
The Samādhi of Samantabhadra refers to invoking the essence by means of its name; its majestic power and spiritual transformations constitute the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because the function is subsumed within the essence, it is simply called the "Samādhi of Samantabhadra."

Second, regarding the intent of this section: The preceding chapter clarified the assembly of the multitude; next, the Dharma should be preached. Since the Dharma is profound and subtle, it cannot be proclaimed without meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, the preceding chapter served as the distant preparatory means (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the formal teaching, whereas the present chapter constitutes the proximate preparatory means; therefore, it follows immediately after.
Regarding the three points of essential purpose (*piṇḍārtha*): entering meditative concentration and receiving empowerment is the purpose;

expounding the ocean of lands is the goal. Fourth, the explanation of the text has two parts: first, a general analysis of the meditative concentrations within the nine assemblies; second, the formal explanation of the text. Within the first part, regarding presence or absence:
only the second assembly does not enter concentration, to signify that the stage of faith has not yet been perfected among the causal practices.

This is because it is the coarsest. Regarding the second point, as for those that appear and those that do not: only the seventh and ninth assemblies do not appear. The seventh reveals that this is exclusively for the sake of superior progress;
the ninth reveals that the realization of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is singular and without regression. Third, regarding cause and effect:

the first, seventh, eighth, and ninth assemblies are all assemblies of the fruition-dhyāna (*phala-samādhi*), because the fruition is universally present throughout these four. As for the remaining five assemblies...

These are all due to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because they all manifest the practices of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). As for the fourth point, those who are able to enter [the assembly]:
in the seventh, ninth, and second assemblies, the Buddha himself enters meditative concentration to manifest the function of the fruition (*phala*).
Second, regarding the formal explanation of the text: this chapter is divided into six sections: first, samādhi; second, empowerment; third, emergence;
fourth, the rain of jewels from the various lands; fifth, the praise of virtues through light from the pores; and sixth, the repeated request of the great assembly.
Within the first section, there are two parts. First, it clarifies that at this location, Samantabhadra enters meditative absorption before the Buddha.

Second, from the phrase "as in this world" onwards, it extends this to all ten directions and the paths of all atoms. Within the latter, there are four points: first, the location where the Lord of Dharma resides is also the place where he enters meditative absorption;
this means he is personally facing the Buddha, for he realizes and expounds the truth. Second, it signifies that the Buddha’s power is added [to him], as he possesses no wisdom of his own. Third...

This reveals the name of the samādhi. It is called "All Buddhas" because it encompasses all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm. A "Buddha" is so called because they expound the dharmas of fruition.
"Vairocana" means that the light of wisdom shines universally; where does it shine? It is said to be upon the body of the Tathāgata-garbha.
This refers to the fact that the wisdom of all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm equally and universally illumines the dharma-nature, for that nature is in every respect the Tathāgata.

Therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*). Furthermore, because it is that upon which [all things] rely, it is called a "Body" (*kāya*). This is the treasury of the light-illumination of all Buddhas; the treasury is itself the body.
This refers to the function of emerging from meditative absorption, named after that function. For what reason does one enter this absorption?

It is to reveal that the Flower Treasury World-realm (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*) and so forth, as described, have no separate intrinsic nature apart from the Tathāgata-garbha. Fourth, the section on "Universal Entry" below clarifies the three...

Regarding the obscured function (*karmopayoga*), there are thirteen phrases that subsume the sixth pair. The first two clarify the pair of essence and function (*tattva-upayoga*), which is also the pair of principle and phenomenon (*li-shi*).
This refers to the nature of equality (*samatā-svabhāva*); since "nature" is the essence, and "manifesting as reflections throughout the *dharmadhātu*" is the function.
Next, the second pair clarifies the pair of profundity and vastness, which is likewise essence and function; that is to say, the fixed essence is vast and pervasive throughout space, causing...

Wisdom penetrates deeply into the profound mysteries of principle; because the waters of the ocean are exceedingly deep, it is named "The Ocean of Giving," and because the ocean of Dharma is exceedingly deep, it is named accordingly.

The third pair consists of two [aspects] emerging from one: this is also concentration and wisdom, meaning that many concentrations are produced, causing the concentrated mind to encompass the net of the Dharma-realm.
The fourth pair consists of two [aspects] based on one: this is also object and wisdom, meaning that the illuminating function of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods arises therefrom.

All things existing within the ocean of lands in the ten directions arise from this samādhi; they appear by relying upon this samādhi. The fifth pair, consisting of the two bases of mutual containment, also refers to the internal and external.
That is to say, because this samādhi internally contains the ten powers, liberations, and the wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is called "containing" (saṃgraha).
Externally, it causes the vast phenomena of the *dharmadhātu* to be contained within a single atom of a land. This refers to the third... [text fragment].
This is the planting of the seeds for worldly existence. The latter three [verses] constitute a pair concerning the attainment of Buddhahood and the upholding of the Dharma;

that is to say, by means of this meditative concentration, one attains the ocean of Buddha-virtues, manifests the ocean of Buddha-vows, and protects and maintains the bequeathed Dharma so that the service and transformation of beings continue without interruption. This constitutes the upholding of the True Dharma.

Furthermore, these may be categorized as "practice" and "teaching," because the former two lines refer to practice and the latter line refers to teaching. Within the two categories of pervasiveness, there are two [points].

First, this realm is raised; subsequently, such lower categories pervade the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Within these pervasive categories, there are two types: first, a single-layered pervasion;

second, a layered pervasion of both that and the preceding lower category. Among the eleven phrases in the former [section], the first phrase generally reveals the phenomena that are identical with principle (*tattva*) because they exist within the dharma-realm. As for the ten specific phrases: first, pervading space; second, pervading the directions; third, pervading time.
4. The pervasive subtle form-spheres; 5. the small space-sphere; 6. the vast form and space-spheres; 7.

the spheres of the sun, moon, stars, and so forth; 8. the spheres seen by the Buddha-eye to their limit; 9. the spheres reached by the limit of supernatural power; 10. the spheres manifested by the limit of the Buddha-body.
Regarding the four within the second pervasive "layered" sphere: the first and the dust of this land [are mentioned] as a general summary of all the aforementioned lands.

There are indeed such objects. Regarding the terminology of "all lands," if one follows the interpretation that these are manifested by the Buddha’s own body and thus do not apply to the former case, then this power of meditative concentration can pervade the successive layers within the internal body, but cannot pervade the successive layers externally.
Furthermore, in the former case, which includes subtle and minute locations, Samantabhadra is present before the Buddha entering samādhi; yet even there, he does not exist in the world.
1. Within this realm, is there such an assembly? 2. Within each and every atom, there are as many lands as there are atoms. 3.
Within each and every land, there are as many Buddhas as there are atoms. 4. Before each and every Buddha, there is a Samantabhadra as numerous as atoms.
In the second section on the "Augmentation of Power" (*anugraha*), there are three parts. First is the augmentation by speech; next, from "At that time, in the ten directions...

onwards, is the augmentation by mind; third is the augmentation by body, from "At that time, in the ten directions... onwards. Within the first [the augmentation by speech], there are four sections. The first is the manifestation of the bodies of all Buddhas:

this means that within each of the preceding instances of time and place—the layers upon layers before Samantabhadra—there are manifestations of Buddhas filling the ten directions. Through this augmentation by speech, there is again no end to their pervasiveness.

Therefore, this [section] "Hence" generally enumerates each instance prior to Samantabhadra. Second, from "Those various [beings]" onwards, they collectively praise the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Although this is a resultant concentration, because Samantabhadra is a Buddha-Bodhisattva, it is termed the "Buddha-Bodhisattva Concentration. Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies the cause for attaining this concentration; herein there are two parts.
First, a general manifestation, meaning that all Buddhas collectively bestow empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that he attains concentration. Following this, by means of Vairocana...

The following section clarifies that there are two causes for this shared reception of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): first, the empowerment of Samantabhadra by all Buddhas through the original vows of Vairocana;
second, the capacity of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows to receive the empowerment of all Buddhas. Because these causes and conditions are mutually dependent, the word "also" (*api*) is used.
Regarding the four points below, which clarify the purpose of the empowerment, there are eleven phrases. The first one is general, meaning it refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because it turns the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas, the ten distinct phrases are subsumed into five pairs. The first is the pair of object and wisdom;
this refers to the manifestation and clarification of the Buddha-wisdom that fully knows the oceans of the established realms throughout the ten directions. Why is this done?
It is because one wishes to explain this very point—namely, what is taught in the "Chapter on the Achievement of Worlds" regarding the causes and conditions for the achievement of all world-oceans.

Second is the pair of practice and its fruit: that is, to cause sentient beings to hear of the fruit of the pure reliance, they engage in the practice of leaving behind defiled lands and cultivate the practices for a pure land, thereby encompassing the untainted realm. Third is the pair of being able to enter and being able to manifest:

that is, to cause Samantabhadra to enter the ocean of Buddha-fields known to the Buddhas without obstruction, thereby manifesting their majestic adornments. Fourth is the pair of meaning and principle: that is, to cause...

Samantabhadra attains the wisdom that realizes the true nature of the Buddha’s awakening because he perceives the characteristics of all phenomena. This constitutes the correspondence between the five capacities and the single teaching;

that is, it causes Samantabhadra to understand the specific capacities for whom this dharma-gate is intended, thereby ensuring that the teaching capable of responding to those capacities is maintained for a long duration.

In the Sanskrit original, the word for "teaching" (*deśanā*) refers to sound; "text" (*vyañjana*) refers to the written characters. By citing the text, one encompasses both phrases and names, which together constitute the expressive medium.

Regarding the two types of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), first the characteristics of the empowerment are clarified, and subsequently, the phrase "Why is this... explains the cause. Within the former section, there are two parts: first, the manifestation in this world;
second, the extension of this to all ten directions, beginning with the words "Just as in this world. Within the former of these, [the Buddha and Samantabhadra]... ten.

Regarding the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*): the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. Within the general category, it is called a "power" (*bala*) because it is the wisdom capable of entering the ocean of the Buddha-fruit's wisdom;

thus, it is named by its capacity to enter the wisdom of the fruit. Within the specific category, one [of the powers] corresponds to the wisdom that universally knows both the principle (*tattva*) and the phenomena (*dharma*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Second, it is called "vast" because it is endowed with the knowledge of the Buddha’s pure lands. Third, it is called "vast" because it is endowed with the knowledge that the contaminated lands (*sāsrava-bhūmi*) are subject to decay.

Fourth, it is called "vast" because it is endowed with the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), which is manifold. Fifth, it is called "profound" because it is endowed with the knowledge of the activities of the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mukha*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*) of a Buddha;

this is profound because it is not within the scope of knowledge during the stage of a causal practitioner. In the Sanskrit original, the word for "abiding" (*sthita*) also means "practice," signifying that which is capable of being practiced.
Regarding its great function: (6) the wisdom that knows those who are suitable vessels for this Dharma; (7) the wisdom of eloquence in speech according to their faculties;
(8) the wisdom of the pervasive cloud-like body; and (9) the wisdom of the universally responsive perfect voice. These two categories can be understood through the general principle.

Regarding the second [section], the explanation of the causes, there are two parts. First, the underlying intention is as follows: the Buddhas possess the power to bestow [this wisdom] and the compassion to do so universally. Why is this? [Because...]
Regarding the ten kinds of wisdom: they are granted only to Samantabhadra and not to other bodhisattvas. The subsequent commentary states that this is because Samantabhadra has attained that samādhi;
thus, the Dharma is bestowed [upon him] accordingly. Furthermore, it is asked: for what reason do other bodhisattvas not enter this meditative concentration?

Answer: It is for the sake of expounding the Universal Dharma; it is due to the original vows of Samantabhadra. Within the empowerment of the three bodies, two are first presented here in this land, and furthermore, these same types extend throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the first of these two, it first clarifies the hands stroking the crown of the head, followed by the manifestation of the hand’s characteristics and functions below that.
Within the former, the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions stroke the crown of Samantabhadra’s head, clarifying the conferral of empowerment and power.

Regarding the signs of his seal of approval: when the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously touch his head, his body is not merely unbreakable, but even if it were to shatter, he would not regress.
Each [Buddha] touches his crown personally, yet their hands do not obstruct one another. Second, within the application of the characteristics of his hands, there are briefly ten meanings:

the first five concern the perfection of the virtues of his marks, and the latter five concern the mastery of his wondrous functions. Within the former, regarding the category of his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they are described as being "perfectly round and symmetrical."
1. His ten fingers are slender and straight, each tip bearing the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra-cakra*). 2.
On the surfaces of all the joints of his ten fingers, there is the *nāgakesara* mark on one and the *kuntala* mark on the other, thus adorned in alternating fashion.
3. The webbed membrane (*jālāvanaddha*) exists between his fingers. 4. A golden hand-radiance is constantly extended. 5. Fragrant scents waft forth, and he emits blazing rays of light.

This is the emission of light. Among the latter five [verses], the first two lines constantly manifest two matters: namely, the two medicines of body and speech, and the supernatural power of wondrous sound.

The latter three lines reveal the manifestation of three matters. First, "manifesting the ocean of the vows of Samantabhadra of the bodhisattvas of the three periods" means that the persons who give rise to vows throughout the three periods and the matters for which those vows are made are all brought forth by the hands of the Buddhas appearing in the world.

Second, all Buddhas and the wheels of Dharma they turn also appear therein. Third, the bodily forms and radiance of the Buddhas of the three periods of time likewise manifest their reflections therein.
For this reason, this hand spans the ten directions, encompasses the three periods of time, subsumes cause and effect, and gathers both persons and dharmas.
Its essence and function are profoundly vast, sovereign and boundless; by reflecting upon its categories, one may understand that it is omnipresent.
In the third section on "Arising," there are two parts. First, this world-system; second, how such lower classes as in this world pervade the ten directions.

Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, arising from meditative concentration; second, the benefit for the assembly as shown by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva starting from the phrase "from such [a state] below.

Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, arising from this one concentration; second, arising from all concentrations starting from the phrase "when arising from this samādhi" below. Within the first of these...

According to the Sanskrit original, immediately after [the Buddha] had touched [Samantabhadra’s] head, he arose from that samādhi. At that time, there was neither the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra nor these syllables.
Regarding the arising from all samādhis, the ten phrases are divided into two parts: first, one phrase which generally reveals the arising of all through a single arising;
second, the nine subsequent phrases beginning with "That is to say," which specifically distinguish the names of all the samādhis. Within the former:
Because this concentration is one with the entire ocean of all samādhis, therefore, by arising as one, one arises as all.
Within the particulars: first is named the wisdom that skillfully knows the equality of every moment throughout the three periods of time;

second is named the knowledge of all phenomena within the three periods of time, numbering as many as the atoms of the dharma-realm; third is named the manifestation of all buddha-lands within the three periods of time, which are identical.
1. Named "Extensively Manifested Among Sentient Beings in All Defiled Realms. 2. Named "Knowing the Ocean of Sentient Beings' Minds.
3. Named "Knowing the Names of Sentient Beings. 4. Named "Knowing the Distinctions of Names for Dharmadhātu Affairs in the Ten Directions. 5.
Named "Knowing that Within Every Atom Throughout the Entire Dharmadhātu There Are Boundless Clouds of Buddhas’ Bodies. 6. Named "Expounding All Dharmas."

The Ocean of Gates. These names for the higher meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are all designated according to their functional activities, namely, the ability to know, to manifest, to expound, and so forth.
Second, regarding the benefits for the assembly, there are two parts: first, explaining the benefits obtained when Samantabhadra emerges from concentration at this stage;

second, [explaining] how such worlds and so forth extend throughout the ten directions. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a general indication of the time when the benefits are obtained, which also serves to distinguish those benefits.
The cause can be understood. What follows clarifies the characteristics of the benefits obtained; herein, the nine phrases are divided into two parts.

The first five concern the attainment of the various gateways of benefit for Bodhisattvas—namely, the dharmas of samādhi, dhāraṇī, skillful means, eloquence, and practice—each numbering as many as the atoms in an ocean of lands.
What one person attains, all others likewise do; therefore, it is said that "each and every Bodhisattva individually attains them."

Therefore, the latter four [verses] concern the benefits of attaining the dharmas of fruition: first, attaining the light of wisdom from the Buddha’s treasury of merit; second, attaining the skillful joy of the Buddha’s ten powers and so forth;
third, each pore manifesting oceans of many buddha-fields; and fourth, attaining the benefit of the karmic function capable of manifesting the eight phases of enlightenment.
The two categories can be understood universally.
Regarding the fourth category, within the section on the rain of jewels from the lands, there are four points: first, the oceans of lands in the ten directions tremble subtly;

this is due to two causes, and it is "subtle" because it is a manifestation of light. Second, the adornment of the lands with jewels. Third, the emergence of sound to preach the Dharma. Fourth, the assemblies of Buddhas.
The rain of jewels is briefly discussed as being of ten kinds, for their varieties are inexhaustible. The first four concern the physical manifestations of various jewels;
the latter six concern the transmission and realization of the Dharma-transformation. These jewels are all pure, untainted, and correspond to the essential nature of sentient beings.
The fifth section, "Praising the Virtues of the Light of Body Hairs," consists of two parts: first, the prose introduction; second, the formal presentation of the verses.

Within the ten verses, all praise the profound, vast, and inexhaustible virtues of Samantabhadra. Among them: first, it describes how the aforementioned Samantabhadra pervades all lands, enters meditative absorption, and manifests his universal presence;

second, it describes how his body fills the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and how his meditative powers, supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and perfect voice are likewise so.

Third, it describes the karmic functions of the aforementioned Samādhi that pervades all Buddhas through Samantabhadra. Fourth, it describes how the aforementioned Samantabhadra, while within the realms of the mundane dust, enters meditative absorption and manifests the power of his vows to appear universally among all Buddhas.
Fifth, it praises the non-dual integration of the universal body and its land as the support and supported. This consists of four points:

namely, the form-body (rūpakāya) relies upon the land of phenomenal characteristics (lakṣaṇabhūmi), and the dharma-body (dharmakāya) relies upon the land of the nature of phenomena (dharmatābhūmi). As for the form-body...

According to the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature land), the *dharmakāya* relies upon the land of form and appearance. This passage states that "the bodily marks are like space" to manifest the meaning of non-obstruction.
Since there are the preceding phrases stating that "all great earths rely on space, and space relies on form for its manifestation," the correspondence with the Dharma can be understood.
Regarding the phrase "The Dharma-cloud [Bodhisattva] abides in reliance upon the True" (*tathatā*), this cites the form-body (*rūpakāya*) as abiding in the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).

This is stated in response to an objection to highlight a specific point; the rest may be understood by analogy. The latter half clarifies that this [Bodhisattva] can manifest bodies that respond universally to all capacities, even where those capacities have been severed.

According to the Sanskrit original, the second line reads: "Abiding in reliance upon suchness (*tathatā*), not in reliance upon a realm (*kṣetra*). The fourth line reads: "Universally manifesting the appearance of bodies."

[He] is equal to all [of them]. Sixth is the Great Vow of Samantabhadra’s Abiding. He attains manifold pervasiveness as one, constantly remaining within the bodies of all Buddhas and within all lands.
The first phrase in the Sanskrit original says, "Abiding in the Great Vows of Samantabhadra.
The fourth phrase says, "Completely entering therein to infinite limits. Seventh, his body is able to universally enter the boundless oceans of assemblies, manifesting pure lands and kṣetras.
That manifests for many kalpas. The second phrase, according to the Sanskrit manuscript, states: "By means of immeasurable bodies, they universally enter [all realms].

The character "jian" (see) in the fourth phrase is also the character "xian" (manifest). Eighth, they cause sentient beings to personally awaken to the Dharma and attain the fruit by shaking the lands. Ninth, by the power of samādhi.
It manifests the virtues of the Buddha-fruit and its past causes. The tenth section summarizes the difficult points. Furthermore, within the supramundane samādhi, light and sound are manifested;
this concludes by identifying the source from which they emerge.

Regarding the sixth section, "The Great Assembly’s Repeated Request": Question: What is the distinction between this and the request made by the assembly in the preceding chapter? Answer: There are four distinctions.

First, although they were previously instructed to request [the teaching], they had not yet spoken; therefore, here they formally make their request. Second, whereas previously only the original assembly requested it, here both the original and the newly arrived assembly are shown to do so.

Third, previously they requested the primary teacher of transformation (*pariṇāyaka*), whereas now they request those who assist in the transformation. Fourth, previously they made their request by truly citing the Dharma.

Now, this praises the virtue of the Master of the Seat (Ācārya) while simultaneously presenting the request for the Dharma to be taught. Since the subject matter requested is the same as that in the preceding chapter, these ten verses are briefly divided into three parts:
the first eight praise the Master and present the request; the next one presents the request for the Dharma; and the final one praises the assembly and presents the request.
The first two [sections] consist of five verses praising the profound and vast virtues of Samantabhadra’s cause and fruit. The first [five] clarify the existence of the cause of teaching;

the latter three praise Samantabhadra’s ability to rain down the Dharma throughout all pervasive lands, clarifying the existence of the fruit of teaching. Within the former [section], the first [verse] praises three kinds of merit of Samantabhadra:
first, arising from the fruit of Buddhahood; second, being produced by great vows; and third, the purity of the *dharmakāya*. Second...
The middle three virtues are: first, universally responding to the Buddha assemblies; second, the vastness of the ocean of merit; third, the equal illumination of the light of wisdom.

Within the third [set], there are three: first, the vastness of the ocean of virtue; second, being near to all Buddhas; third, the lands within all atoms. Within the fourth [set], there are four: first, being near to all Buddhas.

Second, abiding in the state of meditative concentration; third, abiding in all lands; fourth, abiding for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; fifth, the middle three [aspects]: first, manifesting the universal body to reach the ten directions;

second, delivering the ocean of sentient beings; third, entering within the lands and motes of the dharma-realm. The final three [aspects] praise Samantabhadra’s ability to rain down the teaching of the Dharma:
first, his single body pervading within every mote of dust to preach the vast Dharma of the Buddhas; second, pervading the ocean of sentient beings to preach the supreme Dharma of the Buddhas.
[The Buddha] acts. Having accumulated practice over many eons, he proclaims the Dharma with a great voice. Next, one verse raises the request regarding the Dharma;

although there were many inquiries in the preceding chapter, they do not exceed three types of worlds when summarized. Thus, the first three lines now manifest this in general, while the final line concludes the request.
In the subsequent verse, which praises the assembly and makes the request, the phrase "the World-Honored One, previously honored" clarifies that the assembly is desirous [of hearing the teaching].
With body dwelling [in reverence] and mind full of respect, you are fit to be a vessel for the Dharma; please preach it for them. This is what the Buddha rejoices in.
Regarding the fourth chapter, "The Accomplishment of the World," its four sections are the same as those previously mentioned.
First, regarding the explanation of the name: "world" (*loka*) refers to that which is concealed or covered; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to a boundary or limit.

This means that the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), which is subject to destruction, conceals the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) indestructible dharma. Furthermore, that which arises from true nature and is identical to unconditioned dharmas conceals the conditioned world subject to destruction.
These do not intermingle with one another; this is their respective boundary. Therefore, it is perceived as the Sahā world.
These [realms] differ from one another in relation to the Flower Treasury (Huazang). Those who are moved by the Flower Treasury see the Flower Treasury;
those who are moved to see the Flower Treasury dwell in the Sahā world and thus differ from one another. Those who are moved by the Sahā world see the Sahā world.

Now, the world is that which is accomplished (*sādhyam*), while the act of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is that which brings it about. In this present chapter, however, only the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) is examined; yet the means of accomplishment is not identical [to the result].
"World" (*loka*) is established as a name based on that which is formed; "world-formation" (*lokadhātu*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
According to the Sanskrit original, it says: *lokadhātu-samudra-nirdeśa-vyūha-tantra-samuccaya-nāma-parivarta*.
Following the literal text, it is generally called: [The Chapter on the Collection of the Tantra of the Array of the Ocean-like Exposition of the World-Spheres]

The title "Chapter on the Combined Exposition of Observing the Ocean-like Worlds of the Ten Directions" has now been abbreviated by the translator to merely "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World.
This abbreviation is excessive. Furthermore, *vibhūta* also carries the meaning of "illumination"; that is, the wisdom illuminating the object is equivalent to observation.
*Saṃbhāra* refers to accomplishment through the gathering together of various conditions; it means that the collection of all conditions is able to bring about accomplishment.
Regarding the worldly matters:

second, as for "the accomplishment of the intent of accomplishment," the former section clarified the skillful means (*upāya*), while the present section distinguishes the correct teaching; therefore, this constitutes the accomplishment.

Third, regarding the essential tenet (*siddhānta*): the general teaching that the entire ocean of lands throughout the ten directions can accomplish both the fundamental and the derivative constitutes the tenet. For...

The purpose is to clarify the ocean of *kṣetra* (buddha-fields) within the *garbhadhātu*. Alternatively, one may observe that the ten oceans are taught as the ten wisdoms (*jñāna*), taking these as the central doctrine;
the purpose is to explain the fundamental and derivative aspects of the accomplishment of the ocean of *kṣetra*.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: the three chapters from here on clarify the formal teaching of the assembly.

Among them, the first two chapters comprehensively answer the thirty phrases concerning the characteristics of the fruit in the preceding questions; the final chapter clarifies the Buddha’s past causes, comprehensively answering the ten phrases concerning the characteristics of the cause in the preceding questions.
Question: Since this section also clarifies the cause, why is it titled "Exhorting Delight by Citing the Fruit"? Answer:

Because it primarily explains the fruit, and because it explains the cause in order to manifest that fruit. Within the preceding two chapters, the first chapter generally elucidates the causes and conditions capable of establishing the ocean of Buddha-lands;
the subsequent chapter specifically reveals the ocean of lands established by Vairocana.

Within the former chapter, there are two parts: first, a general presentation of the essential framework, which constitutes the "Fundamental Section"; second, [the section beginning with] "At that time, Samantabhadra..."

The Bodhisattva addresses the Bodhisattvas, saying, "O Sons of the Buddha," and so forth. This section correctly presents the fundamental meaning; it constitutes the *vibhāga* (the section of exposition).

Within this, there are two parts: first, a general restatement of the preceding questions; second, from "At that time" onwards, an exhortation for the assembly to listen and receive the teaching. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a formal citation of the preceding questions;

second, from "In order to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha... onwards, the revelation of the purpose of the answer. Within the first of these, there is first the citation of the preceding questions.
Following this, the text below correctly clarifies the granting of the teaching. Within the preceding section, there are forty phrases;
these are a summary and praise derived from the latter part of the thirty phrases within the previous inquiry regarding the fruits [of practice].

Among these, the first twenty phrases correspond to the final ten inquiries among the questions concerning the oceans of worlds and so forth in the prior inquiry. Within those, the first ten inquiries concern the profundity of the objects of observation.

Extensive. Regarding the ninth phrase therein, the Sanskrit original adds the two characters "accumulated" (*saṃcita*). The remaining phrases may be understood by analogy with the preceding and following explanations.
Next, the ten phrases praise the inconceivability of the Buddha’s wisdom capable of knowing, based on the prior inquiry and contemplation which spoke only of "oceans of worlds.
That this section additionally distinguishes between their formation and destruction is a brief explanation. [He] knows that there is none...
Because it is not clearly understood, it is called "pure wisdom. Because it is vast, manifold, profound, and subtle, it is difficult to comprehend even when layered;
since its knowledge is beyond the reach of the thoughts and speech of those in lower stages, it is all termed "inconceivable.

The same applies to the rest. Question: Can world-oceans undergo formation and destruction? Answer: This is a case where the words are general while the meaning is specific; that is, the intent refers to the *kṣetra* (buddha-field).
Regarding the world-systems sustained by the oceans: for now, we shall speak of them collectively as "oceans of lands" (*kṣetra-samudra*).

According to the Sanskrit original, within each of the ten phrases, the character "wisdom" (*jñāna*) appears below [the compound], while the character "knowledge" (*jñā*) does not appear above it; the translator has added it based on the meaning.

Second, concerning the distinctions among the types of retributive bodies of sentient beings therein, and the distinctions among the oceans of karmic actions performed by those sentient beings—the Sanskrit original states: "all sentient beings."
1. Wisdom of the ocean of the manifestation of karma. This explains that "manifestation" refers to the stage of fruition produced by karma.

2. Wisdom of the ocean of the establishment of all dharma-realms. In the Sanskrit original, it is stated as "wisdom of the established dharma-realm of all dharma-realms" or "ocean of wisdom," which differs from the previous explanation;
it is another name for the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*), termed the "Ocean of Establishment. 3. The number of Buddhas who can manifest emanations is boundless.
The faculties, inclinations, and desires of those to be transformed are likewise manifold and difficult to know. In the previous inquiry, they were called the "ocean of *pāramitās*";
this is because the various aspects of the practices of the perfections correspond to the faculties, understandings, and desires [of beings], and thus they are mentioned interchangeably.

Sixth, regarding the previous contemplation of the ocean of the three periods of time, the statement here that "in a single thought-moment one universally knows all things of the three periods" is a brief explanation of the excellence of wisdom. In the inquiry, these were called the "ocean of the Buddha’s liberation."
This is because a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is the inconceivable liberation-dharma of the Buddha, wherein the three periods of time are identical.

According to the Sanskrit original, this is the liberation that is free from obstructions (*āvaraṇavimukti*). The Sanskrit text states: "In a single thought-moment, one equally awakens to all the immeasurable wisdoms of the three periods of time.

These seven great vows in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) serve as the cause for manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma. In the preceding inquiry, [the Buddha] was referred to by the title "Ocean of Lifespan" (*Sāgarāyuṣpramāṇa*).
The ocean [of vows]. This is entirely due to the power of his vows; in the Sanskrit original, it is called "the wisdom that gathers the oceans of the immeasurable vows of all Buddhas.
Eighth, the boundless spiritual transformations that act in accordance with the capacities of beings. Ninth, the ocean of the wheel of Dharma that transforms natures.

Regarding the previous question, the turning of the wheel of Dharma was subsumed within "expounding"; regarding the contemplation, expounding was subsumed within the turning of the wheel of Dharma. These are different ways of dividing the text.

The ten distinctions of vocal expressions established according to various regions are also the Dharma wheel’s differentiation according to the capacities of sentient beings; hence, it is called the "Ocean of Exposition.
The second section, consisting of ten phrases beginning with "the Buddha-body," restates the ten questions concerning the six retributions and the three karmas of the Buddha mentioned above.

Within this, the fact that only the body, light, and so forth are extensively described is for the purpose of subsuming the particulars within the general. First, the bodies that respond to the capacities of beings are immeasurable in their height and breadth;
second, they manifest the colors of various jewels, gold, silver, and so on, each color radiating brilliantly and all being infinite;
third, there are the Śrī-vatsa and others, numbering as many as the atoms in the oceans of Flower Treasury lands, such as the King of Perfectly Complete Marks.
Excellent. These [lights] are several times more numerous. Fourth, the four circular halos pervade his body and its physical marks, appearing in various ways according to what is seen.
Fifth, he emits superior light that rises like surging clouds; the physical marks are even more numerous. Sixth, from the locations of his constant radiance, flames further burst forth.
1. His physical form is like a multitude of jewels, and his shape is like a flame that blazes without ceasing; the colors of these flames are manifold. 2.

His seven types of perfect sounds (*saptasvarāḥ*) are inexhaustible, each one profound and vast, difficult to fathom. 3. He gathers and transforms beings through the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), namely: the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), the wheel of majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), and the wheel of knowing the minds [of others] (*cetaḥparyāya*).

Those who are not yet matured, he disciplines and brings to maturity. 4. For those whose faculties (*indriya*) are already matured, he urges them on so that they may attain fierce [insight] even in their dreams.
Because one practices and accordingly attains the fruits [of that practice], it is called "not empty. The nine phrases above each possess qualities that are profound and vast;
therefore, they are all called "oceans. Because they are difficult to measure, they are termed "inconceivable. This, then, is a reduction of ten [from the original count].
The third section, "Abiding on the Buddha-ground," consists of ten phrases that recapitulate the first ten phrases from the preceding inquiry into the fruits.

In the prior inquiry, two phrases—"transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) and "mastery" (*vaśitā*)—were omitted, as they are subsumed within the phrases "not subject to destruction" and "the inability of others to surpass.
Spiritual transformations reside in the body; mastery belongs to wisdom. This is because there is no other path and because of the [absence of] the two vehicles.
Because the power of the Bodhisattva is able to subdue, crush, and restrain [them], it is said that they "cannot be destroyed," and so forth. The remaining meanings should be explained accordingly.
This concludes the brief praise following the restatement of the question.
Regarding the second section on the two types of teaching, there are three parts. First, the summary of the preceding inquiry. Second, "I shall now...

clarifies that [the Buddha] relies upon two powers—namely, those of his own realm and those of other regions—in order to manifest the absence of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), to manifest the teaching of many Buddhas, and to manifest the perfection of what is taught. Third, the actual explanation of the teaching.

Later, he fully proclaimed a single phrase, explaining it with complete clarity and without omission. Question: Since it is said that he "fully proclaimed" it, why does the subsequent text speak only of the "ocean of worlds"?
Answer: There are two explanations for this. First, because the sūtra of this assembly has not yet reached its conclusion.
Second, although the subsequent text speaks only of a single ocean of lands, within it are universally contained all thirty points of meaning previously inquired about.
Second, regarding the ten points that clarify the benefits for those to be benefited, these are subsumed into five pairs. The first two constitute the pair of merit and wisdom.
That is to say, it causes [beings] to enter the ocean of Buddha-wisdom and abide in the ocean of Buddha-blessings.
Next is the pair of "all times" and "all places," which means that all oceans of lands are entirely adorned and purified, and the lineage of the Buddhas is perpetually sustained at all times.

Next is the pair of "principle" and "adornment," which means manifesting the true nature of all phenomena and establishing verbal adornments according to various understandings and inclinations. Next is the pair of "arising" and "ceasing," which refers to wisdom— *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "智" (wisdom), suggesting the source material was cut off.*

The first pair concerns severance: that is, causing the Buddha-wisdom to arise in accordance with the faculties, and causing the mountains of obstructions to be crushed in accordance with one's aspirations.
The latter pair concerns practice and vows: that is, cultivating practices of remediation and abiding within the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows.
These ten phrases above are also the "gate of purpose" among the causes for the arising of the adornments of this assembly.

Second, the explanation of admonishing the assembly to listen and receive [the teaching] has two parts: first, the prose section clarifies the intent; second, the verse section explicitly reveals it. Within the former, there are eleven phrases.
The first is a general heading, meaning that one must cause them to hear the Dharma, thereby generating joy. The remaining ten phrases specifically reveal the meaning of this joy.
The first two constitute a pair concerning delighting in the Dharma and generating faith; the next two constitute a pair concerning manifesting nature and establishing [it]; the next two...
The first pair [of verses] concerns the realization of the ultimate state; the next two concern the support of the Dharma and the manifestation of the Buddha’s realm;
and the final two concern the elucidation of the Dharma and the increase of wisdom. Within the ten verses that correctly manifest this, there are three sections.

The first two clarify the purpose of the Buddha’s appearance—namely, manifesting his body, preaching the Dharma, adorning the lands, and harmonizing sentient beings. The next six distinguish and sustain those who are vessels for the Dharma. First, the distinction...

"Not a vessel" means that the Buddha universally reveals the realm he himself has realized in order to lead others to enter it, yet this is beyond the reach of the power of those of the Two Vehicles or ordinary fools;

hence it is said they "delight in the small" and "are attached to existence. Next, the five [verses] reveal who are vessels for the Dharma. The first [verse] shows one who possesses four powers and is capable of hearing:
first, having pure faith; second, firming the mind; third, being inspired by proximity to the virtuous; and fourth, being empowered by the Buddha's strength. The next one...

To render the eight types of mind capable of hearing [the Dharma]: first, being free from hypocritical pretension and flattery; second, being free from guile, deception, and delusive confusion; third, being free from a mind seeking ulterior motives;
fourth, a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); fifth, a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*); sixth, a virtuous mind, because it is universally free from enmity, jealousy, and contention;
seventh, a vast mind, because it encompasses all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*; eighth, a mind of profound faith, which is free from hesitation regarding the inconceivable Dharma.
Because they were prepared in advance, having fulfilled all the aforementioned prerequisites, they were now fit to serve as vessels for this Dharma.

Next, a single list enumerates the vessels for Samantabhadra, meaning those who possess four virtues and are capable of knowing the realm realized by the Buddha himself: first, possessing the vows of Samantabhadra; second, dwelling on the stages of Samantabhadra;

third, cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra; and fourth, contemplating the dharma-realm of true emptiness. Finally, a single line concludes by praising this assembly for possessing these universal qualities.
Worthy Conduct. First, he attains the direct vision of the Buddha’s supernormal transformations;

next, he universally binds all sentient beings so that they may merely hear the Dharma—this is entirely due to the power of the Buddha’s protective mindfulness. The final two [verses] cite the Dharma being taught and exhort the assembly to observe and listen.

This is because the lands and Buddhas about to be described are all manifested within his own body; furthermore, as he wishes to proclaim them, he exhorts them first to observe and again warns them to listen.
The second major section. Within the formal presentation of the primary meaning, this is one of the thirty questions previously cited;

specifically, it concerns the "ocean of worlds," wherein all others are subsumed. Upon careful examination, they are all present therein, though perhaps some were omitted from this translation because the sūtra has not yet been fully transmitted.
As for those omissions, they exist within that [original source]. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the general announcement.
"Know. From "Those sons of the Buddha below," the actual exposition of what is taught begins. Within this exposition, there are two parts: first, a brief indication of the ten chapters;

second, from "Sons of the Buddha, briefly explained by means of the ten below," the detailed explanation according to those chapters. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a general indication and citation of proof; second, from "What are they?

onwards, an inquiry into the headings followed by their individual listing; third, from "Sons of the Buddha" onwards, the conclusion of the brief and the expansion. Regarding the first of these, it says: "The world."
Regarding the ten matters concerning the oceans: because all worlds and their types are subsumed within the oceans, they are collectively termed "oceans.

In reality, however, these ten matters exist in some locations and do not exist in others across the lands (*kṣetra*) and their types; they are not universally present everywhere. The same principle applies to the following sections.

As for why the three periods [of time] are all mentioned: there are two meanings to this. First, it clarifies that what is being explained here is as it truly is, without any discrepancy. Second, it reveals...
This essential and supreme teaching is not taught by anyone other than a Buddha. Within the second section, the detailed enumeration, there are two parts:

first, the inquiry; second, the enumeration. Within the enumeration, there are ten types. First is "that which gives rise to and possesses causal conditions. This refers to that which can give rise to the lands and the causal conditions possessed therein.

Here, "giving rise" is itself the possession of causal conditions. Alternatively, "giving rise" is that which is produced, while the ocean of lands possessing the causal conditions is that which gives rise; this is the possession of the arising.
"Cause and condition" (hetu-pratyaya) applies to both explanations. Second, "that which is the basis of abiding" refers to what the seeds and so forth rely upon as their support.
Third, "shape" refers to the external characteristics of the seeds and so forth. Fourth, "essential nature" refers to the substance of the seeds and so forth.

Fifth, "ornamentation" refers to the superior dharmas of practitioners within the seeds and so forth, as well as various superior objects. Sixth, "purity" refers to [the purity] within the seeds and so forth...
Regarding "people cultivating pure karma": this refers to the manifestation of the Buddha's deeds by the Buddhas who appear within the [seven] lineages (*gotra*). Regarding "the kalpas of abiding":
this refers to the duration of time that remains after the lineages and so forth have been formed. Regarding "the distinctions of the transformation of kalpas":

this refers to how the lands (*kṣetra*) of the lineages and so forth are transformed, either through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or through the cultivation of outflows (*āsrava*) or the absence thereof by the inhabitants.

The transformation of the kalpa refers to the transformation of the realms inhabited and their constituent substances, as well as the intense karmic activities—whether tainted or untainted—that cause differences between preceding and succeeding time periods;

this is explained in detail in the commentary. Regarding the tenth point, "absence of distinction," it means that within the categories such as the "seeds" (gotra) and so forth, those things common to all realms are being described. This is the third [point], which is presented briefly for clarity.
Regarding the "Extensive" [section]: the statement that there are "ocean-like lands as numerous as the atoms of a broad field" should be understood as a general description.

Second, within the detailed explanation according to the chapters, there are ten sections based on ten topical gateways. Each section has two parts: first, the prose (long-form), and second, the verse.
Within the first section’s prose, there are three parts: namely, the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, within the heading, there are six [points]. By means of...

Regarding the phrase "by way of ten kinds," this refers to the causes that give rise [to the lands]. This section discusses both the defiled and the pure universally. As for the expression "already established" and so forth, it refers to the lands that have arisen;

this is because the causes of the lands throughout the three times are all identical to this. Within the two explanations, there are two parts: first, the inquiry and the heading; second, the formal explanation.

In the formal explanation, there are two points: first, the power of the Buddha’s universal wisdom; second, "the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus. According to the Sanskrit manuscript, *dharma* [is used].

"Much. This is called *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and it is also termed *dharmatā-prakṛti* (the natural state of phenomena); that is to say, "thusness. If one explains this according to *dharmatā*, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the originating cause.
How then can rational nature (*rig-pa'i chos-nyid*) be the causal condition? The commentary states: How could the causal condition not be rational nature?
If one understands this according to *dharmatā-prakṛti*, then the establishment of the ocean of lands is naturally so; such is the turning of the wheel.

Although the two meanings of "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) differ, both are universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu). Third, they are mostly contaminated (*sāsrava*) because pleasure and pain are intermingled;

this is because it is said that karmic actions encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome. Fourth, they are taught in relation to the self-enjoyment realm or the other-enjoyment realm at the time one attains *bodhi* after the path of the diamond-like samādhi has reached its full completion.
Fifth, they consist mostly of defiled [causes] and only a few pure ones, because ordinary beings...
1. The two types of noble causes possess mutual dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as they do not obstruct one another while occupying the same location. 2.
The purely pure, untainted cause, such as the vow to purify Buddha-fields among the ten great vows of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
3. The cause for the non-retrogressive practice of effort by Bodhisattvas in the eighth stage. 4. Within the state of mastery, by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*).
As for the causes: either by the power of this [cause], one transforms defilement into purity and manifests in a pure land;

or, through roots of goodness that respond to the needs of others, one goes to Buddha-less realms or to one's own realm—these two cases are both explained in terms of coarse transformation lands and serve as the cause for a predominance of defilement with a small measure of purity.
Tenth, taking universal vows as the cause, within the substance of the environment and its inhabitants, one manifests subtle and minute lands such as Indra’s net.
If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it is fully contained in a separate chapter.
Regarding the brief indication within the extensive explanation that there are "as many worlds as there are atoms in an ocean of lands," there are two interpretations. The first states:
this refers to the total number of individual causes for each and every land within the ocean of lands; it does not rely on [the number of lands themselves].

Because of the multiple causes and because of the exclusion of the term "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*), since within a single ocean of lands there are as many lands as there are atoms in an ocean of lands, it is stated in this section and in other sections—specifically in the tenth section on "Non-differentiation"—that the total number is established.
If the term "homogeneous" were excluded, the enumeration of sounds would be deficient; if one were to rely solely on the multiple causes, the total count would be excessive. Its...

Regarding the five [aspects] beginning with causes and conditions, physical forms, bases of reliance, kalpas, and so forth: one may only exclude commonalities or deficiencies; there can be no additions, because the fruit is one.
As for the five [aspects] beginning with adornment, purity, the appearance of Buddhas, transformations, and non-differentiation:

these not only exclude commonalities or deficiencies, but are also innumerable and inexhaustible. Why is this? Because pure lands have many adornments, while impure ones may consist of gold or other elements.
Because there is no such reason; because the pure lands are exclusively and consistently pure; because the Buddha-activities manifest or do not manifest according to the capacities of beings;

and because transformation applies only to cases involving the pure and the defiled, or the defiled and the pure—specifically within impure lands—whereas in the purely untainted lands (*anāsrava-kṣetra*), this category does not exist.

Furthermore, the creation of good and evil cannot be analogized [to these transformations], so there is no discrepancy; it is spoken of only in reference to what is common to all, and not to every case. One interpretation states:
The enumeration of the total number herein, both in its initial presentation and its concluding summary, is based entirely upon actual reality; there is neither deficiency nor redundancy.

Although some buddha-fields may be composed of many causes, they nonetheless share the same cause for a single effect. Furthermore, although the causes and effects of many fields may be of a similar type, their respective entities are distinct.

There are nine verses in this hymn. The first verse concerns the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). The second [verse] skips ahead to praise the fifth [topic]: the common accumulation of roots of goodness by sentient beings and bodhisattvas.
The third [verse] skips ahead to praise the fourth [topic]: bodhisattvas attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). The fourth [verse] skips ahead to praise the sixth [topic]:
the bodhisattvas’ vows to adorn the buddha-fields. The previous [verse] cited the power of their vows; this one clarifies the practice arising from those vows.
Therefore, it is said "immeasurable kalpas. The fifth single verse in sequence praises the third [topic], the karmic actions of sentient beings;
herein, afflictions and desires are also distinguished. The sixth single verse in sequence praises the eighth, the power of the Bodhisattva’s resolute belief (*adhimukti*).

The seventh two verses in sequence praise the tenth, the power of Samantabhadra’s vows, which includes the power of practice; [the Bodhisattva] manifests before all Buddhas, his body encompassing the ocean of lands. Eighth.
The final verse praises the ninth [topic]: the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and the sovereign power of his attainment of enlightenment.
The second dharma, which is the cause [of these], as well as the seventh, the cause of non-retrogression, are both omitted from this verse;
they are either subsumed within the fourth verse or included in the single verse that follows.
Regarding the second point, the basis of the lands (*kṣetra*), this encompasses both defiled and pure lands. Within this, the three sections of the prose text are the same as before.
First, in the introductory heading, it says: "In each ocean of lands, there are bases as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of lands.
This is because within a single ocean of lands, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of lands, and each individual basis is distinct. Second...
The ten types [of bases] within the explanation are as follows: first, based on various jewel ornaments; second, based on the sky like clouds;

third, based on the "Treasury of Light" (*prabhā-kośa*), which is the place where light emerges from the ocean of jewels—this serves as the basis for the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) because it is the constant substance of the fruit of outflow (*anāsrava-niṣyanda-phala*);

the subsequent categories, such as sound and light, are all to be explained according to this principle. Fourth, based on the light of the Buddha; fifth, based on that which has the color of various jewels...
1. Radiance. 2. The sound of the Buddha’s perfect voice preaching the Dharma; this also sustains the abiding of the world-system through the preaching of the Dharma within it. 3.
Those born from the illusory karma of the vajra-palm, who contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions;

these are produced by the power of dedication toward the cause of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). 4. Those based on the bodies of all world-protectors; this refers to the Chapter on World-Protectors.
It is said that there are thirty-nine types of forms for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). How can it be that the world, as a vast entity, subsists upon the small bodies of sentient beings?
There are four reasons for this. First, because the external is induced by the internal, it is said to depend on the body. This, moreover, is of two kinds.
1. The power of past causes: as stated in the verse, "because it is sustained by the power of karma. 2. The power of present transformation: as explained below.

Second, because it is appropriated and belongs to oneself, it is called the "basis-body" (*āśraya*). Just as objects such as gardens, houses, or dwellings, though located elsewhere, are called the "basis-body" because they are included within one's own possession;
this does not necessarily imply being physically carried. 3. By the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the World-Ruler (*lokapāla*).
Because power sustains and causes [the body] to abide; because the power of supernormal faculties resides in the body, it is said to be "dependent on the body. Thus, a verse in the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"The various defiled and pure, immeasurable types of buddha-fields arise according to the minds of sentient beings; they are sustained by the Bodhisattvas.

Fourth, it is because the undefiled support (āśraya) and the supported phenomena (pratiṣṭhita-vastu) abide in mutual dependence through the virtue of the non-obstruction between the large and the small. Alternatively, this may also be understood in terms of their functional activity.

Because there is no attainment (*anupalabdhi*), although it encompasses all four meanings, it primarily relies on the latter two. Regarding the ninth point, which relies on the bodies of bodhisattvas in the five stages, this is explained in the same manner as the previous assembly.
As appropriate to each case, the tenth point relies on the various adornments produced by the vows of Samantabhadra;
these refer to the outflowing fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the untainted realm, which are as numerous as the ocean and arise from the vows of Samantabhadra, for he freely sustains the buddha-fields.
The twenty-two verses in this hymn are divided into two parts. The first verse provides a general summary, exhorting the assembly to contemplate; in the Sanskrit original it says:

"O you, behold these oceans of lands, all manifested through the spiritual powers of the Buddha. By means of this, the lands throughout the space of the ten directions—all worlds—are clearly perceived.
