The subsequent twenty-one verses correctly versify the preceding prose. Within them, there is a general...
This is divided into thirteen sections. The first verse praises the previous dwelling supported by all adornments, because those ornaments are all composed of various jewels.
The next two and a half verses praise the previous dwelling supported by space. The following three and a half verses praise the previous dwelling supported by the radiance of all jewels;
among these, the upper line lacks a prose commentary, or rather, two lines are praised together, namely the *maṇi*.

Because within the ocean there is subsequently the light-treasury (*prabhā-kośa*) which serves as the support for the *kṣetra*, the fourth [verse] consists of two lines that skip ahead to praise the sixth support:
the Buddha’s voice. Within this, the first line correctly praises the supported, while the latter line clarifies the supporting *kṣetra*, including its shape, adornments, and canopy.

In the prose section, four or five [verses] lack verses; in the fifth [section], two lack prose. Among these, the former consists purely of the Flower-Ocean of Pure Abodes, while the latter abides in the Perfect Ocean.
Regarding the first phrase of the subsequent verses, the Sanskrit original states: "The buddha-fields follow the oceanic wheels."

This reveals that the shape of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) is circular like an ocean of fragrance. Regarding the two words "circular" (*maṇḍala*) and "wheel" (*cakra*), they are pronounced identically in the Sanskrit sound as *maṇḍala*.
Sixth, one verse concerns the first two [points], the basis and its location. Within this, the first half of the verse correctly praises the basis upon which one dwells:
the upper line praises Vajrapāṇi, and the lower line praises the body of the World Lord. The second half [of the verse] concerns the Buddha preaching the Dharma therein. Seventh, two... [verses].
There is no prose. All [verses] rely on the Buddha’s spiritual power. The eighth section consists of alternating half-verses;

the ninth relies on the adornments produced by the vows of Samantabhadra. The prose for the eighth section contains no verses. The tenth section consists of one full verse that extensively praises the preceding reliance on space.
The eleventh section consists of one half-verse with no prose, relying on the Bodhisattva’s crown. The interpretation of these is as in the latter two of the four meanings previously mentioned. Ten.

The first [section] consists of one and a half verses based on abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as extensively praised previously. The twelfth [section] consists of four and a half verses based on abiding in atoms (*paramāṇu*);

there is no prose commentary for this either, as it is manifested through the power of the Buddha. This is the section on karmic activity (*karmakriyā*). The thirteenth [section] consists of two verses based on abiding through the power of karma.
There is also no prose commentary.
Third, regarding the explanation of the shapes of the buddha-fields (*kṣetra*), this applies generally to both defiled and pure fields. Within this, the prose section has three parts, as before.
The first, the heading, is self-evident. Second, in the explanation, there are three types: first, circular; second, universally square; and third, those with proportional length and breadth. And...
The eight facets are not circular; the three corners are not square. Alternatively, they share a single name because they are neither square nor circular. The rest is easily understood.

Among the ten verses in the *kārikā*, the first two briefly summarize the preceding text while also adorning the basis (*āśraya*) and so forth. The next two [verses] describe the shapes of the two lands (*kṣetra*).
1. "Pure and Adorned," etc.: These three verses collectively reveal the causes and effects of defiled and pure lands.
2. The fourth verse: One Buddha preaches the Dharma within a land inside a pore. 3. The fifth verse: Two Buddhas preach the Dharma within a land inside a mote of dust;
that is, first taking up one mote of dust as an example of preaching the Dharma within a land therein, and subsequently applying this analogy to all such motes. 4. The final verse: The sixth [verse].
This concludes the Buddha’s great activity (the latter four [sections] mostly manifest the adornments of the lands).
Within the fourth section on the essence of the land (*kṣetra-tattva*), only pure lands are clarified; the commentary briefly distinguishes twenty types among them.

Regarding the statement that "various fragrances constitute its essence," this mostly refers to substances that are not inherently fragrant, or those that may possess fragrance, as they are objective realms manifested by the mind.

As for its essence: it refers to the various objects such as jewels manifested by the concentrated mind of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or manifested through clarity (*prabhāsvara*) or resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which will be understood in detail in the *Avataṃsaka* verses. Regarding its essence being the Buddha’s vocal sound:
this means that the Buddha, through his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), manifests sound as a pure land; or it refers to the Bodhisattvas who, hearing the Buddha’s vocal sound, practice...
This is the practice of the Pure Land, for it is by this that the buddha-field is manifested. Thus, it is said that words and forms constitute its essence;

as it is said, "The sons of the Buddha are born from the Buddha’s mouth," and likewise, [the field arises] from the power of meditative concentration and so forth. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Within the verses, in the first verse: the first two [lines] and the sixth refer to all jewels, the single jewel, the indestructible vajra, and so forth.
The second single verse refers to the third and fourth [lines] of the previous section: the light of all jewels and various lights.
The third single verse refers to the fifth [line]: the light of all adornments. The fourth single verse skips ahead.
Verse 10: The Jewel Image (Ratna-bimba). First, one verse on the *maṇi-cakra* from the previous [section]. Second, one verse on the Jewel Flame (*ratna-jvāla*) and Jewel Light (*ratna-prabhā*).
Third, one verse on the previously mentioned Auspicious Jewel Mark (*ratna-lakṣaṇa*), the Flower Crown (*puṣpa-mukuṭa*), and the Buddha’s transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
The eighth section, consisting of one verse, describes the preceding state in which a single thought-moment universally manifests all realms.
The statement "all are conceptual constructions" means that the various realms manifested by the Buddha's mind all become differentiated according to the conceptualizations of sentient beings.

The ninth section, consisting of one verse, describes the preceding power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace and the universal inclusion of the Buddha’s speech and sound. The tenth and final section, consisting of one verse, concerns the Bodhisattva-jewel.
Regarding the fifth, the adornment of the land: it is solely a luminously pure land. Within it, there are ten types of adornments described in prose:

first, the adornment of clouds of various ornaments emerging; second, the adornment of the preaching of the Great Dharma within the land; third, the adornment of the preaching of karmic cause and effect within the land.
1. Proclaiming the bodhisattva vows as an adornment. 2. Manifesting the reflections of the Buddhas of the three periods of time as an adornment.
3. Recollecting the manifestation of kalpas as an adornment. 4. Manifesting the Buddhas and their retinues as an adornment. 5. Adorning with clouds of precious incense. 6.
Adorning by emitting light from precious jewels and other objects at the sites where Buddhas attain enlightenment. 7. Proclaiming the practices and vows of Samantabhadra as an adornment.

In these verses, the first one provides a general summary of the ocean of lands that are adorned. The subsequent nine verses correspond to the preceding prose. Among them: one verse praises the first [array], the "Exquisite Cloud";
one verse praises the second [array], the "Bodhisattva’s Merits," as well as the fourth, the "Ocean of Bodhisattva Vows.

Next, one verse describes the karmic retribution of sentient beings; next, one verse describes the reflections of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; and finally, one verse describes the manifestation of eons within a single thought-moment.
The next verse manifests all Buddhas; the next verse [describes] clouds of precious incense; the next verse [describes] the adornment of light from the sublime objects of all sites of enlightenment;
and the final verse [describes] the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the sixth [topic], the skillful means for purifying buddha-fields (*kṣetra-pariśuddhi-upāya*), this refers exclusively to the purification of the field.
Skillful means (*upāya*) are the causes and conditions for the manifestation of various fields through all manner of skillful methods;

since there are skillful means for purification in accordance with every gateway of practice (*caryā-mukha*), the verse clarifies the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*), while the prose commentary distinguishes the "concordant fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*) and so forth. As it says: "By long-term cultivation and thorough knowledge..."
Because of this consciousness, one is born in a realm of virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The rest should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is identical to the place of adornment, it is because they differ when viewed from the perspective of their respective gates. Within the prose commentary on the "Ten Purities," the first is the purity of proximity, which is easily understood.

The second is the purity of increase, because it is the cause for cultivating supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The third is the purity of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). The fourth is the purity of abiding in the objective sphere.

1. It is because they abide solely in the sphere of the bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom. 2. The purity of the five perfections (*pāramitā*), through the purification of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*). 3.

The purity of contemplating the bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*), being skillful in entering, abiding in, and emerging from them. 4. The purity of aspiration, by constantly making vows to purify buddha-fields.
5. The purity of the antidote, through liberation from bondage. The Sanskrit original for this phrase reads: "observing the production of a single eon."
The Ocean of Conducts. According to the verse and this text, this phrase serves as the antidote to self-interest;

that is, by observing what is appropriate for sentient beings, one gives rise to all modes of conduct as antidotes, causing them to cultivate the path of transcendence. Ninth is the purity of skillful wisdom, through which one enters the ocean of the Buddha’s virtues by means of one’s own cultivation.
Tenth is the purity of the ten powers, because of benefiting sentient beings and making offerings to the Buddhas.
There are nine verses in this section. The first verse provides a general explanation of the ocean of buddha-fields to be purified. The remaining eight verses correspond to the preceding text:

one verse on the purification through proximity; two verses on the purification through increase; one verse on the purification through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); one verse on the purification of the objective sphere;
one verse on the purification of the perfections (*pāramitā*), which also transcends the purification of vows; and one verse on the antidotes.

Above this, passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms in seven Buddha-fields, one reaches the very top of this system of worlds (*kṣetradhātu*).

There are worlds that are equal [in number]. Since the system of worlds has reached its ultimate limit, there is no concern regarding the loss of sequential order; therefore, the names of the equal worlds are not mentioned.

Furthermore, the three sections herein are presented in abbreviated form, all stating "passing above this. According to the Sanskrit original, this is a term meaning "transcending to" (*atikramya*), which means: from... [the passage continues].

The six verses from "The limits of all lands" (*sarva-kṣetra-anta*) clarify the characteristics of the defilement and purity of worlds. First, there are two verses that generally enumerate the characteristics of purity; next, one verse [describes] only the characteristic of defilement;

next, three [verses] [describe] characteristics common to both defilement and purity; finally, one [verse] [describes] only the characteristic of purity. III. Each individual land-seed (*kṣetra-jāti*).
The following four verses clarify the preservation and destruction of the *kṣetra* (buddha-fields). First, while the coarse is destroyed, the subtle remains.

The first verse states that within each and every *kṣetra-vyañjana* (seed of a field), for the sake of defiled sentient beings, inconceivable kalpas of the burning of the *kṣetra*-wheel are manifested, yet it remains eternally firm.

Second, it is established as the locus where karma persists. Third, its nature is without arising or ceasing. Fourth, it is constantly manifested through the power of the Buddha. Regarding the fourth point—that there are *kṣetras* made of earth and so forth—the following ten verses follow.
This clarifies the matters of suffering and pleasure within the world. Among these, the first six [verses] clarify the suffering of the evil realms;
the second verse’s first two lines—stating in the Sanskrit original that "some lands are made of iron, or some are made of red copper"—clarify the karma of humans and devas.
Next, one verse clarifies the subtle realm of the body; this consists solely of pure bliss. The final verse summarizes that suffering and pleasure arise from karma.

The ten verses beginning with "The lands possess various jewels" clarify the essential nature of the buddha-fields (*kṣetra*), along with other meanings, which may be understood through their respective explanations.
The ten verses beginning with "Visible purity" clarify the adornments of the buddha-fields. Within these, the first five clarify the mutual adornment of the one and the many.

The final five verses universally encompass the adornments of the three periods of time. Section Seven, consisting of ten verses beginning with "There may be many," clarifies the differences in the forms of the buddha-fields (*kṣetra*).

Section Eight, consisting of ten verses beginning with "There are fields that abide for one eon," clarifies the duration of the fields' abiding as well as the presence or absence and the number of Buddhas appearing therein.
Within this [Section Eight], the first two verses clarify the duration of their abiding, while the latter eight clarify the presence or absence and the number of Buddhas appearing. Section Nine...

The ten verses beginning with "There are lands without light" clarify that within these lands there are both those with light and those without. Among them, the first one concerns the absence of light, while the subsequent nine concern the presence of light.
The eleven verses beginning with "There are lands most terrifying" clarify the nature of the sounds—good or evil—within these lands.
Among them, the first two concern the sounds of the evil realms; the next three concern the sounds of humans and devas; and the final six concern the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The "Wheel-Sound" (Cakravākya) [chapter] shall be explained accordingly. The preceding section on the "Flower Treasury World" (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu-parivarta) is concluded.
Regarding the sixth chapter, the "Vairocana" (Vairocanaparivarta), it will now be explained; its four topical gates are the same as those previously mentioned.
First, regarding the explanation of the name: *Vairocana*—*vi* here means "pervasive," and *rocanā* means "illuminating radiance.

This refers to the two lights of body and wisdom awakening sentient beings and illuminating the Dharma, as explained in detail at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Sublime Array" in the section discussing the Bodhisattva’s merits.

Second, regarding the intent of this section: previously, the results of the investigation of logic (*hetuvidyā*) were explained; now, the causes of those aforementioned results are being analyzed. Therefore, this section follows.
Furthermore, it is introduced to answer the previous question concerning the cause. Question: If this section clarifies the cause, why does the title of the chapter use the term for the result?
Answer: If the fruit were not indicated, whose cause would the cause be?

Regarding the three points of the thesis (*siddhānta*): the Buddha’s past causes are clarified as the thesis (*pakṣa*), and their function is to establish the aforementioned fruit so that it may be believed (*gati*).
The commentary on the text has two parts. First, it clarifies the setting of the Tathāgata’s past deeds. Second, from "O sons of the Buddha, that Victorious One...

onwards, it clarifies the time of the Buddha’s past deeds. Within the first part, there are three sections: 1. A general explanation of the distance between what was taught and the present, which is as many eons as atoms in two buddha-fields.
2. From "There is a world... onwards, it clarifies that the names of the oceans of lands depend upon the light of pure wisdom, and [the Buddha] cultivated universal...

The name "Virtue of Gate-Practice" is so called because it is perfected through being adorned and purified. Third, from the passage "In this ocean of world-systems" onwards, it clarifies that there are worlds based upon the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*).
Herein, one should explain that there are land-clusters (*kṣetra-vyuha*) based upon the ocean of lands, and that there are worlds based upon the land-clusters;

however, the clusters are not mentioned here for the sake of brevity. Within the section on the worlds, there are seventeen passages. First, regarding the land named "Victorious Sound" (*Jayaśabda*), many Buddhas...

Because the Dharma-sound that issues forth is supreme; second, the basis of the lands; third, the retinues of the lands; fourth, the shapes of the lands; fifth, the adornments of the substance of the lands;
sixth, the surrounding mountain-ranges; seventh, the canopies covering the crowns of the lands; eighth, the purity within the lands; ninth, the height of the cities and palaces;

tenth, food and clothing appearing according to thought; eleventh, the names of the eons—because these three types of worlds are all fully endowed with excellence, they are called "variously adorned."
Within the twelve lands there is a sea of fragrance. Within the thirteen seas there is Mount Sumeru; regarding this, there are three points:

first, the shape of the mountain resembles a flower; second, its name; third, that it is encircled by a railing of the three jewels. On the summit of the fourteenth mountain there is a forest; regarding this, there are eleven phrases.
1. The name of the grove; 2. Flowered towers; 3. Jewel terraces; 4. Fragrant banners; 5. Mountain banners; 6. Self-arisen lotuses; 7. Jewel nets; 8. Musical sounds; 9.

Light forming fragrant clouds; 10. Encircled by many cities; 11. The inhabitants dwelling within the cities. Regarding the fifth [point], the grove to the east of the trees, there are two parts in the text:
first, a brief indication of three matters; second, a detailed exposition of these three, beginning with "Furthermore, it is pure and... and so forth.
Regarding the matter: in the preceding section, first, one item designates the name of the principal city; second, from "the human king" downward, it designates the classes of inhabitants;

third, from "three million" downward, it designates the number of attendant cities. In the subsequent detailed exposition, there are likewise three parts. First is the detailed exposition of the principal city, which contains eleven sub-sections within the text.
1. The body of the city; 2. its dimensions; 3. the three types of external adornments such as the walls; 4. the precious moats adorned with fragrant waters and flowers;
5. the precious trees; 6. the palaces and pavilions; 7. the nets; 8. the ointment-scented powders and scattered flowers; 9. the precious gates; 10. the precious banners before the gates;
11. the groves and gardens. Within the gardens are two types: namely, the fragrant precious [trees] and the birds singing in harmony; when subdivided, there are ten.

There are nine matters; they should be understood according to the text. Second, the detailed exposition of the splendors of the dwelling has three parts: first, the accomplishment of supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaja-ṛddhi*);

second, conduct identical to that of the gods, free from deceit; third, responding to wishes according to thought. Third, the detailed exposition of the retinue and the city has two sections: first, the specific explanation of the city’s name and the splendors of its dwelling;
second, the general manifestation of the adornments, beginning with the phrase "this one... and so forth. Within the former [section], there are two parts; first—

Briefly distinguishing seven cities: the passage beginning with "Later, such as these... and below summarizes them collectively, following the same principle as the large number of cities indicated previously.
The sixteenth [city] reveals that within the grove on the fourteenth mountain peak there is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); eight matters can be known from the text.

Seventeenth: In front of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) there is a great ocean. Within this ocean there are seven matters: first, the name of the ocean; second, the flowers that emerge from within the ocean; third, the dimensions of the flowers;
fourth, the fact that the stalks and other parts of the flowers are all made of jewels; fifth, the retinue of the flowers; sixth, the constant emission of light by the flowers.
The seven flowers constantly emit sounds; these are all explained according to their respective contexts.
The second major section, which clarifies the period of the Buddha’s past lives (*pūrvayoga*), has two parts: first, a general enumeration of the many Buddhas of the initial eon;

second, from "Of those, the first... onwards, a specific clarification of the Buddhas encountered by Weiguang (*Vairocana*). Regarding the former, the phrase "the initial eon" refers to the aforementioned...
This is the Kalpa of Various Adornments (*Vicitravyūha-kalpa*). It is also subsequently called the Great Adornment Kalpa (*Mahāvyūha-kalpa*).

Regarding the phrase "ten Mount Sumerus," this first presents the general overview before intending to explain the particulars. However, according to the subsequent text, within this great kalpa there are as many intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
the human lifespan lasts for two intermediate kalpas. The first Buddha’s lifespan was five billion years, and his majestic radiance served three Buddhas throughout his career.
Having changed his faculties, he was reborn in heaven. Now, regarding the statement that during the first kalpa there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of ten Mount Sumerus:
does this refer to the first of several great kalpas within that world-system, or does it refer to a small kalpa among the various small kalpas?
If it refers to a small kalpa, it would be inconsistent for a single lifetime of majestic radiance to encounter only three Buddhas. If it refers to a great kalpa...

Within a single *kṣetra*, how could there be so much space? Therefore, one should know that the three characters "initial kalpa" (*ādikalpa*) in this text should be transposed to read "kalpa initial" (*kalpādi*).
Furthermore, these three characters should be moved to appear beneath the characters "arising in the world" (*loke prādurbhūtaḥ*) in the following line.
There is no fault here. In the subsequent section that correctly elucidates the matters encountered by the majestic light, four Buddhas are explained individually, forming four distinct segments:

first, encountering the Buddha Sarvaguṇasumeruśrīmegha; second, from "After that Buddha passed into extinction" onwards, elucidating the encounter with the second Buddha, Paramapāramitakuśalamūlavyūha;
third, from "O sons of the Buddha, regarding the pāramitās... onwards, elucidating the encounter with the third... [text continues].
Third is the Buddha Ocean of Supreme Merits; fourth, beneath the *maṇi* jewel of all the Buddha-sons, it clarifies that he encountered the fourth Buddha, Padmavimaladhvaja of Universal Renown.

Within the first section, there are seven parts: first, the preliminary auspicious signs ripen the capacity of the disciples; second, at that time, beneath the mountain of all merits, the Buddha appears within the flowers;

third, from the phrase "at that time, that Buddha" onwards, the Buddha’s light awakens the capacity of the disciples; fourth, from the phrase "at that time, the lords of all worlds" onwards, those whose capacity has awakened gather together;
fifth, from the phrase "at that time, that Tathāgata" onwards, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them; sixth, at that time... [the text continues].
"Great Majestic Radiance" (Mahātejas): below this, the majestic radiance attains benefit. "O sons of the Buddha, you all... and so forth: the Buddha manifests *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the first three [sections], the first is the designation of the Buddha’s name: that is, his manifold virtues are perfected, he rises high above the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and from here he is a mountain of virtue.
It is named because clouds of supreme bodies appear, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Second, from "O sons of the Buddha" onwards, it describes the Buddha’s prior manifestation;
herein there are two parts. First, the general indication of the time: a hundred years ago, the grove was universally adorned and purified.

Second, from "That is to say" onwards, the ten kinds of auspicious omens are revealed, as may be understood. Third, from "In that world" onwards, all the kings behold the omens; their faculties are matured and they desire to go [to the Buddha].
Buddha. Regarding the two Buddhas appearing within the lotuses, there are two parts: first, specifically revealing the superior places and manifesting the bodies of superior virtues;
second, as below, concluding by showing that these manifested bodies pervade those worlds. Within the former, ten kinds of superior virtues are briefly revealed. First, they are identical to reality.

Just as it is entirely present within each and every phenomenon of the mundane and supramundane realm throughout all worlds, extending even to infinite layers of multiplicity, it is therefore called "equal" (*sama*).
Second, the universal manifestation of birth: this means that by means of a body that is perfectly pervasive, [the Buddha] appears in all lands.
1. Manifesting the perfect body; 2. Pervading all places of practice (maṇḍalas) three times over, whether as principal or as attendant; 3. The form-body (rūpakāya) being perfectly pure;
4. Power being incapable of being usurped; 5. The various marks being clearly manifest; 6. Manifesting images that are universal; 7. Responding such that there is nowhere it is not seen; 8.
Transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) being inexhaustible; 9. Various lights filling the lands. The subsequent concluding summary may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the third section, "Emitting Light to Awaken Sentient Beings," there are three parts: 1. Revealing the name of the light: This means that when the time for those to be converted has arrived, they must await conditions to attain awakening;

therefore, this light is emitted as a sound to initiate their roots of goodness. 2. "The Buddhas below": This clarifies that the primary light and its accompanying manifestations pervade everywhere together.

3. "If there are... and so forth: This distinguishes the superior efficacy of the light. There are two kinds of superior efficacy: first, touching objects to bring them benefit; second, [touching sentient beings to bring them benefit].

It awakens and causes them to assemble, providing ten kinds of benefit: first, the opening of self-awakened wisdom; second, the cessation of active afflictions (*kleśa*); third, the destruction of the net of the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);
fourth, the subduing of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); fifth, the purification of the seeds of affliction; sixth, the arousal of faith and understanding prior to the stages (*bhūmi*);

seventh, the production of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) on the stages; eighth, the departure from the eight difficulties and five fears; ninth, the relinquishing of the suffering of limited rebirth (*paricchinna-vedanīya-karma*); and tenth, seeing the Buddha and seeking [his path]. This...
These ten kinds of benefits are the power of this light; they are obtained merely by being touched by it, and do not depend on the circumstances of the time.
Regarding the gathering of the four types of assemblies, there are two parts: first, the various retinues, the lords of the cities, and their followers gather through the awakening of the light;
second, the various sons of the Buddha, King Vimalaprabhāsa (Clear Joyful Vision) and his retinue, gather beneath that flame-light through the awakening of the light.
Within this, there are five sections: first, an account of King Priyadarśana and his internal and external retinues; second, from "At that time, Mahātejas...

onwards, clarifying how Mahātejas saw the light and obtained benefit; third, from "At that time, Mahātejas... onwards, clarifying how Mahātejas spoke verses in praise of the Buddha; fourth, from "O sons of the Buddhas, that Mahā...
onwards, clarifying how Priyadarśana heard the sound of Mahātejas’s verses and also spoke verses to command his retinue to go [to him]; [fifth, the conclusion].
The Buddha. At that time, the King of Joyful Vision descended; the King and his inner and outer retinues went to the Buddha. This section has three parts:
first, identifying the majestic splendor and the name of the father-king; second, "ruling over" and below, clarifying the inclusion of the outer retinue;
third, "the queen" and below, clarifying the inclusion of the inner retinue. Regarding the statement that there were five hundred princes, an alternative version says there were twenty-five thousand.

According to the first fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Garland* (*Śrī-mālā-deśanā-sūtra*): "O Son of the Buddha, regarding the worldly retributions, these refer to the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).

[At this stage, one is] a Copper-Treasure-Garlanded Copper-Wheel-Turning King, with a hundred sons of merit as his retinue; he is born in a single Buddha-field, receives the Buddha’s teachings and practices, and transforms two worlds.
At the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), [one is] a Silver-Treasure-Garlanded Silver-Wheel-Turning King, with five sons of merit as [his retinue]..."
Retinue: Born in the lands of two Buddhas, they receive the Buddha’s teachings and practice them, transforming the three continents.

At the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī pariṇāmanā*), they become a Golden Wheel-Turning King adorned with a necklace of vajra-jewels, with a thousand meritorious sons as retinue. They enter the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions to transform all sentient beings, dwelling within the four continents.
At the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they possess necklaces of a hundred jewels and a seven-jeweled state-wheel (*cakravarti-cakra*). [They dwell in] the four heavens.
The King of the Lower [Heaven] has ten thousand sons as his retinue; in a hundred dharma-bodies and a hundred Buddha-lands, he transforms the sons of the gods throughout the ten directions.
The King of the Second Stage (Dvitiyā-bhūmi) wears a jeweled necklace and an eight-jeweled *cakra*; the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has twenty thousand sons as his retinue.

This continues up to the Kings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens from the Third Stage upward, and even the Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Stage all have twenty thousand sons. The commentary states: "The [Tenth] Stage..."
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages manifest as kings; there should be twenty-five thousand [of them].

According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* and the *Aparimitāyur-jñāna-sūtra*, prior to the presence of the Buddha Bhadra-akṣi, they have not yet reached the Second Stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*). It is feared that "twenty-five thousand" may be an error.

Alternatively, it may be explained differently according to the specific teaching (*śāsana*), and there would be no logical fault in this. The rest of the text is clear. Second, the Radiance of Majesty (*Vaiśvānara-prabhāsa*).

Within the section on "seeing the light and obtaining benefit," there are two parts. First, it clarifies that due to past causes, one encounters conditions and attains ten kinds of wholesome benefits;

thus it says, "by means of the former [causes]," and so forth. Second, it correctly clarifies the benefits themselves, which also has two parts: first, an inquiry; second, a revelation. Within the revelation, the phrase "realizing all...
and so forth means that this samādhi can enable one to see the ocean of perfect virtues of all Buddha-lands. This merit is itself the wheel.
Second, "all-encompassing" means that this dhāraṇī contains all the teachings of the Buddha-dharma.
Third, "vast" refers to the wisdom of skillful transformation throughout the entire dharma-realm, which is called vast skillful means (*upāya*).

Since skillful means arise from wisdom, and wisdom gives rise to [this] treasury, it is named a "treasury. Fourth, "subduing" means that compassion serves as the treasury to discipline sentient beings.
Therefore, the fifth is called "the sound that names [beings] to rescue them from suffering," which is like clouds providing shade to alleviate the affliction of scorching heat;
this compassion is called "universal" because it is not limited by time or place. The sixth is "joy," because one sees that all sentient beings are benefited and brought to liberation.

The seventh is "equanimity," because one awakens to dharmas such as equality and does not grasp at them. The eighth is called "great equality," because one gives rise to supernormal powers based on effortless mental application.

Skillful means arise universally from skillful means; "skillful means" is the name for the treasury. Ninth, because one attains the realization of true faith, understanding, and vows upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Tenth, because one realizes the Buddha’s analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and the wisdom of what is to be done. That all ten [stages] are called "realization" is because, in each of them, one attains thorough penetration (*prativedha*);
otherwise, as in the case of the "majestic light," this would already constitute becoming a Buddha. The realization of the first two and the tenth is identical.
Because it is the Buddha. However, this character for "realization" (zhèng) is, in Sanskrit, *pratividdha*, which here means "pervasive penetration" (*guānchè*).
It also carries the sense of "thoroughly penetrating. It does not necessarily mean that one has realized the true nature (*tathatā*) in its entirety.
Later, in the second section on what is seen by the Buddha and the resulting benefits, it is stated that this is "penetration. Third, in the verses of praise to the Buddha by Guṇaprabha, first—

This concludes the preceding section. What follows is the formal exposition in verse. The ten stanzas therein are divided into four parts: first, seven stanzas praising the Buddha and exhorting the assembly to contemplate him.
These are: (1) the Buddha seated at the site of enlightenment; (2) the rarity of encountering a Buddha; (3) his manifestation in many places; and (4) his mastery of supernormal powers.
Five: his bodies appear universally and perfectly. Six: his perfect voice responds universally. Seven: his light shines to extinguish suffering. Next, one verse praises the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Next, one verse praises the wondrous sounds emerging from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Finally, one verse praises the gathered multitude who joyfully behold the Buddha without weariness.
Fourth, King Priyadarśana speaks a verse to command his retinue; of these two parts, first he presents the king’s speech.
This is the introduction to the verses; the verses themselves follow. Within the verses, the eleven stanzas are divided into three parts:

the first three admonish the assembled multitude to proceed to the Buddha’s presence; the next seven exhort them to prepare offerings; and the final one urges them to go to the Buddha together with him. This may be understood generally.

Regarding the second part, concerning the five kings and their internal and external retinues proceeding to the Buddha, there are two sections: the first clarifies how the people of the city of Jvālāprabha, by the power of the king, travel through the air.

The Buddha [is here]. These are his inner retinue. Furthermore, there were the lords and their attendants of the nine cities, such as the devas and nāgas of the city of Supuṣpita, and so forth, up to a million billion nayutas of great cities, including their lords and attendants, who approached the Buddha;
these are all his outer retinue.
Among the five categories of the Buddha’s teachings, this belongs to four of them. First, regarding the purpose of the discourse, it says, "In order to... and so forth.

Second, regarding the name of the principal scripture, "The Universal Collection" (*Samantasaṃgraha*) and so forth, this means that all the dharmas of sovereign fruition possessed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time are gathered therein.
3. Because the retinue follows and turns [with him]; 4. because he acts according to their inclinations and desires to ensure they obtain benefit; 6.

regarding the four [sections] within the context of obtaining benefit through majestic light and hearing the Dharma: 1. obtaining benefit from hearing the sutra; 2. "At that time, with great majesty... and so forth.
I. Praising by means of verses. II. "The sons of the Buddhas" and below: transmitting and showing it to sentient beings. III. At the point "At that time, all merits," and below:

the Buddha praises his majestic radiance. This section has two parts: first, a general clarification of how he attained the light of wisdom from the ocean of dharmas throughout the Buddhas' past lives;
second, a specific manifestation of the eleven kinds of light of wisdom, which—regarding the ten objects of knowledge—[is as follows].
It is a single object. It is called "light" (*āloka*) because it is designated by the name of the distinct wisdom that knows it, yet all of them thoroughly illuminate and penetrate [the object];
thus, this is a name for the function of wisdom. Within the eleven [stages], the Great Samādhi gives rise to wisdom that illuminates the essence of all phenomena as being perfectly equal and uniform.
Second, it illuminates the Bodhi-mind, which clearly encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena;
this is because the True Mind is the essence within both gates of all minds, wherein the Gate of True Suchness (Tathatā) subsumes all phenomena.

Third, it illuminates the phenomenal realm of the ten directions, which is the illumination of the Tathāgatagarbha and the pure eye. Sixth, it illuminates the effortless progression toward enlightenment.

It is called a "Treasury" (*kośa*) because it brings together all practices from within the two types of practice. It is "Great" (*mahā*) because it is not subject to regression through effort and is accomplished without exertion.

It is "Swift" because it is undifferentiated and pervasive. The seventh illumination is the "Manifestation of the Wheel of Dharma. Among the three wheels, this refers to the wheel of the correct teaching;

it is called "manifestation" because it causes sentient beings to follow its transformation, rather than referring to the manifestation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). The eighth illumination is that of the Buddha.
1. The illumination that thoroughly fathoms the depths of the ocean of perfected virtues; 2. The illumination that decisively enters the words [of the Buddha] and reaches their source;

3. The illumination that is ultimately endowed with the supreme resolve of the Buddhas; 4. The illumination that manifests before sentient beings according to their capacities throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Eleventh is the illumination of the Buddha’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses. Second, regarding the majestic light, within the section on praising with verses, there are two parts:

first, revealing the causes for the verses; second, the actual recitation of the verses. Within the verses, there are ten stanzas divided into four sections. The first describes the benefit of hearing the Dharma oneself.

The second consists of seven stanzas concerning the past causes for seeing the Buddha due to having obtained such benefits. Among these, the first six are explained through the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).

Regarding the final simile: in the section on the Dharma-explanation, the first two [verses] concern the practice of service; the next two concern the practice of giving; and the final two concern the practice of adorning the buddha-field. These can be understood from the similes.
Third, one verse [explains] how, by virtue of benefiting others, one perceives mastery over the primary and secondary environments. Fourth, the final verse has two meanings:

first, it expresses the aspiration to rely upon the power of the Buddha, returning to the cultivation of the two practices of adorning the primary and secondary environments as when attaining Buddhahood; second, [it concerns the practice of...]
Just as the Buddha, during his causal stage, made vows, cultivated two practices, and attained two fruits, so too does he now transmit [the teaching] to sentient beings.

Of these two, the first clarifies the transmission of the robe and the Buddha’s virtues; the latter, as follows, distinguishes the benefit to beings. Within the former, [he transmits] the Dharma which he himself has realized.
He speaks for the sake of sentient beings so that they may obtain benefit. These ten, together with the ten previously attained by oneself, make eleven;

some are the same, while others are different. First, the general practice of the ocean of conduct; second, the skillful means of cultivation; third, the ocean of perfected virtues; fourth, the realization of the pure dharma-realm;
fifth, the manifestation of perfect enlightenment; sixth, the non-distinction of merit; seventh, the universal response through clouds of bodies; eighth, the mastery that is difficult to fathom.
The deliberations: nine, the purification of oceans of buddha-fields; ten, the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. Within the two verses on benefiting sentient beings:

first, causing them to resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta); second, causing them to cultivate the pure and correct practices. Within the eleven verses on the Buddha praising his majestic radiance: the first praises the resolution of the mind;
the second and third praise the certainty of the fulfillment of the fruit; the fourth praises surpassing a mustard seed; the fifth praises the cultivation of vigor; the sixth praises...
1. Profound Compassion; 2. Sevenfold Offerings; 3. Fulfillment of Vows; 4. Knowledge of Skillful Means; 5. Praise of the Two Benefits; 6. Universal Practice—all of these may be understood.

Seventh, clarifying three aspects within the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: first, clarifying that within a great kalpa there are many intermediate and small kalpas, and the intention to speak of one among them.
Because it refers to the number of persons and their lifespans, this "Great Kalpa" (mahākalpa) is simply another name for the previously mentioned "Kalpa of Planting Adornments" (vibhūṣaṇakalpa).

Second, it reveals that the lifespan of sentient beings is long; third, it distinguishes the Buddha’s lifespan according to his intention, in order to resolve the doubt regarding how [the Bodhisattva] could have served three Buddhas during the period of "Majestic Radiance" (tejasprabha).
The remainder of the text is easy to understand.

The second section clarifies the encounter with and service to the majestic light. This section on the second Buddha consists of four parts: first, it clarifies the appearance of the Buddha in the world;

second, from "At that time, during a great period" onwards, it clarifies how the youth saw the Buddha and obtained benefit; third, from "At that time, Great Majestic Light" onwards, it describes how Majestic Light spoke a verse to exhort the assembly to go to the Buddha;
fourth, from "At that time, Prince Majestic Light" onwards, it describes how Majestic Light set out with his retinue and others to visit [the Buddha].
Regarding "Buddha": At the beginning, the name "Buddha" is used because he has reached the ultimate adornment of all practices through the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-jñāna*).
Since the place of his appearance is no different from that of the previous Buddha, it is also there.

Second is the section on the benefits gained by seeing the Buddha through majestic light. Within this, there are four points: first, because he manifests vast numbers of Buddhas within the meditative concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha, he is named "Ocean Treasury" (Sāgaragarbha).

Second, because his power of wisdom upholds the profound meaning of the teachings, he is named "Great" (Mahā). Third, because he prioritizes bestowing happiness, he is named "Conforming to Discipline" (Anuvartana-vinaya).

Fourth, because he ultimately brings about liberation, he is named "Deliverance" (Vimukti). Fourth [of the four], his manifested body is like a cloud that provides shade and cover, appearing as if it were present within the objective realm.

The realm (*dhātu*). Because it is that which is rescued by compassion. The fifth is *muditā* (joy), which refers to all benefit and happiness for sentient beings that brings them celebration and delight.
The Buddha has already fully perfected this ocean of the merit of joy; from this, there emerges the supreme realm of birth within the *kṣetra*, named "Treasury of Majestic Power" (*vīryagarbha*).
Because his majestic light penetrates this, it is called "Attained. The sixth is the penetration of all phenomena as being like space—pure and non-dual.

It is called equanimity (*upekṣā*) because characteristics are non-dual and because they are perfectly equal. Seventh, it is the wisdom that penetrates the nature of intrinsic purity; "body" (*kāya*) refers to its essential nature.
Eighth, it is the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of manifesting in response to conditions. Ninth, it is the concise explanation of profound and subtle dharmas that is easy to understand.
Tenth, it is the treasury of outflow-free teachings (*anāsrava-śāsana*) illuminated by wisdom. This concludes the summary: ten thousand [beings] all attain these supernormal powers.

"Attainment" (prativedha) explains the term "immediately attained" (*pratilabdha*) from the preceding section. By this analogy, one should understand that the previous instance—where one perceives the light of the first Buddha and realizes the ten dharma-gates—is likewise nothing other than this very term, "attainment."

Regarding the third section, "Prabhāsa’s Verses Exhorting the Assembly to Approach the Buddha," there are two parts. First, Prabhāsa speaks the verses; second, from "Thereafter, the Sons of the Buddhas...

onwards, it clarifies how the sound of these verses benefits sentient beings. Within the first part, the ten stanzas are divided into two sections: the first eight praise the Buddha, and the final two exhort the assembly to go together to him.
Within the first of these, there are four sub-sections: the first clarifies that a Buddha is difficult to encounter; the next three praise the mastery of the Buddha’s physical actions (*kāyakarman*).
The next three [verses] praise the Buddha’s mastery over the activity of speech; the final one praises the Buddha’s mastery over the activity of mind.

The final two [verses] exhort the assembly to go together to his presence. Of these, the first three lines exhort them to see the Buddha, while the subsequent five lines clarify the benefits of such a vision.
Regarding the second verse on the benefit of sound for sentient beings: by the power of the Buddha, his voice pervades all lands, and those who hear it all resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Regarding the fourth section, "Vigorous Radiance and his Retinue Approach the Buddha," there are four parts: first, the great assembly approaches the Buddha;

second, that Buddha descends and the Buddha expounds the sutra for them; third, those in the assembly hear the Dharma and receive benefit; fourth, at that time, that Buddha praises Vigorous Radiance with verses. The first part may be understood as it stands.
Regarding the second part, the exposition of the sutra, the primary title of the sutra is *The Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu*.
"Purity" refers to the principle that is explained; "adornment" refers to the practice and fruit that are explained, which are established based upon that principle.

"Extensive" refers to the teaching that explains [the former], so it is said because it is established from what is explained. The "associated sutras" are intended for those of inferior capacity who follow in succession.

While the response occurs simultaneously, it varies according to what is heard. Among the ten kinds of benefits derived from hearing the Dharma by the three assemblies, these are explained in general terms;
it is not necessarily the case that every individual obtains all ten benefits. Some may obtain the first two, while others may obtain up to the tenth benefit.

Regarding those who first obtain pure wisdom: this refers to the arising of faith upon hearing the Dharma, thereby accomplishing the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which serves as the cause for [subsequent] wisdom.

Because one attains faith, it is called "Pure Expedient Means. Second, regarding "attaining the stages": upon hearing the Dharma, one gives rise to correct understanding; as the ten understandings establish their positions, these positions are themselves the stages.

Because the wisdom of understanding shines through with clarity, it is called "Stainless Light. Third, regarding "attaining the wheel of the pāramitās": upon hearing the Dharma, one transcends practice;
this practice, being free from signs, serves as the cause for reaching the other shore. This cause shall become manifest throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Because it is the fruit of the adornment of love (*vatsalya*), it is named after its fruit. Regarding the fourth, the "Expansive Practice" (*vaipulya-caryā*): this is also the same as before, in that one attains the ten benefits of practice;

however, whereas the former was based on one's own practice of hearing the Dharma, this consists of practices for the benefit of others, and is therefore called "Universally Entering All Buddha-fields."

Boundless light shines forth, causing pure vision to be attained. Fifth, those who proceed toward practice: there are those who, upon hearing the Dharma, accomplish the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This is spoken with reference to turning from the outflows (*āsrava*) toward the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); therefore, it is called the "Stainless Merit Banner.

A "banner" (*dhvaja*) has the meaning of "turning toward" or "relying upon," just as the banner of a fierce general is explained in the same way as the Vajra-banner. Regarding the four mentioned above, they are all called "wheels" (*cakra*) because of their practice.
6. Regarding "attaining entry into realization": "entry" (anupraveśa) has the sense of being inseparable from it;
that is to say, having heard the teaching on the *dharmatā-tathatā*, one realizes it without interval and enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).

It is called the "Ocean of Dharma" (*dharmasāgara*) and so forth because the light of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) illuminates the ocean of the *dharmatā*. 7. Regarding "attaining a deeper engagement in practice": there are many such persons, or...

One attains the second, third, and even up to the seventh bhūmi. Now, when these are considered individually or collectively in relation to the stages prior to the bhūmis (*pūrvabhūmi*), they constitute "progressively deeper practice.

When considered in relation to the eighth bhūmi and above, they are "practices of setting forth" (*abhinirhāra-caryā*). "Setting forth" is a synonym for *prayoga*, *upāya*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "named great wisdom" and so on:

this is because it is in relation to the stages prior to the bhūmis, because it draws forth the practices of the six *pāramitās*, and because on the eighth [bhūmi] one obtains the wisdom of consecration (*abhiṣeka-jñāna*).

As for "Ocean": because one has eliminated the habitual tendencies conditioned by ignorance together with the Bodhisattvas who have received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one takes on the name "Consecrated" (according to the *Benevolent Kings Record*).

Because within this stage one attains the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), one is called the "Inconceivable Wisdom One," the "Immeasurable Wisdom One," the "Vast Wisdom One," and the "Wisdom One Beyond Comprehension. Due to the predominance of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is called the "Wisdom Ocean."
Furthermore, this stage is identical to that of the Bodhisattvas who have received empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) in its lack of effort (*anābhoga*).
However, this [stage] is the foremost; speaking in terms of the ultimate limit, the rest is as previously explained. Regarding the ninth [stage], "attaining the manifest light of great wisdom":

this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the preceding stages who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, attain entry into the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). In the preceding stages, they likewise, in accordance with the principle, produce the medicinal Dharma, recognizing the diseases of the faculties. Following...
One should explain it thus: it is not merely because the great light of wisdom clearly illuminates this stage;
rather, because one teaches with mastery through the forty kinds of unhindered analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), one attains the name "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī*).

Herein, the phrase "the pervasive illumination of the reflected light of the ocean of the Tathāgata’s qualities" means that the medicinal herb of the faculties is universally illuminated, manifesting a body of reflected light that brings about benefit through discernment and exposition, equal to that of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, regarding the tenth attainment, the power of the birth of vows: there are those who, having heard the Dharma, attain this stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi) by means of their previous practice.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage, through the power of their own vows, raise the clouds of compassion, thunder the roar of the Dharma, and flash the lightning of penetrating wisdom and fearlessness.

The body of the Secret Cloud of Merit and Wisdom traverses in a single thought-moment hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* worlds, as numerous as the atoms within them, and even beyond that number of lands, according to the inclinations of beings' minds.
It rains down the rain of Dharma, extinguishing the flames of the dust of delusion for those of pure wisdom.
Because they have attained mastery over wisdom by relying upon the *dharmadhātu*, they are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth.

This is precisely what is accomplished through the power of the previously mentioned vows, causing immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to faith and understanding; thus, it is called the "Treasury" (*kośa*).

Within the verses of praise for the Majestic Splendor (*tejaḥprabha*) by the four Buddhas, there are ten stanzas divided into two parts: the first six praise the practices accomplished by oneself, and the latter four praise the cultivation [of those practices].

These practices form the roots of goodness that constitute the mutual relationship between the Bodhisattva and the Buddha as principal and attendant. Of the six verses, the first two praise the virtue of great wisdom:

the first concerns wisdom tending toward Bodhi, and the second concerns wisdom entering the realm of the Buddha. The latter four verses conclude the practices and exhort progress; in each, the first half concludes the practice accomplished.
The second half clarifies the fruits obtained. Among the latter four [points], first, [the bodhisattva’s] practice of antidotes forms a primary-and-retinue relationship with that of the Buddha;

second, his practice of making offerings forms a primary-and-retinue relationship with that of the Buddha; third, his vow forms a primary-and-retinue relationship with that of the Buddha; and fourth, his practice of adorning the buddha-field forms a primary-and-retinue relationship with that of the Buddha.
Third, the clarification of the encounter with and service of the third Buddha, which consists of four parts: first, clarifying the parinirvāṇa of the preceding Buddha;

second, from "Joyful Vision" (*Priyadarśana*) onwards, clarifying the passing away of the father-king; third, from "Great Power" (*Mahātejas*) onwards, clarifying the prince’s accession to the throne;

fourth, from "Brahma-mani" onwards, formally establishing the appearance of the Buddha. The first three are understandable. Within the fourth section on the appearance of the Buddha, there are five sub-sections; the first is the manifestation of the time of the Buddha’s emergence.
Regarding the phrase "and the title 'Most Victorious' (*jina*)": this refers to the name given because the ocean of the Buddha’s merits is full and there is nothing that can surpass it.

Second, regarding "at that time, those of great majesty" and below: this clarifies that the majestic light and the assembly went to the Buddha to make offerings; this is easily understood. Third, regarding "at that time, he" and below:

this clarifies that the Buddha preached the sutra, and that the Bodhisattvas and others therein are called "in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānugata*), meaning that within this sutra, the Bodhisattvas are explained and manifested as being in conformity with the Dharma.
The practice of the realms (*dhātu*). Because each and every wisdom-light of this practice illuminates cultivation in accordance with the *dharmatā*, the one is all and the all is one;
they are fused without obstruction. Therefore, it is called the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Practice of Universal Eye Radiance*. Its inclusion of retinues may be understood [from the context].

Fourth, from "At that time, Great Majesty" (*atha khalu mahātejas*) onwards, it clarifies how Mahātejas heard the Dharma and obtained benefit. Within this, first the name is designated, and afterwards...
Discriminating Function (*vibhāga-vṛtti*). This refers to the power of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is able to universally illuminate the merit and demerit of all sentient beings;

thus, it is named after its function. The function may be understood by analogy. Below that, in five sections, it clarifies how the Buddha praises his majestic light with verses. Within these, the eleven stanzas are divided into two parts:
the first four clarify the practice he has perfected himself, and the latter seven manifest his relationship as principal and attendant with the Buddhas. The former...

In the middle [section]: 1. the practice of generating the resolve; 2. the practice of great compassion; 3. the practice of diligent application; 4. the practice of great vows. Within the latter seven [practices]: 1.
using the vow to turn the preceding practices so that they become the primary and its attendants; 2. seeing all Buddhas as having the same roots and joints as the primary and its attendants;
3. following all Buddhas in practicing the primary and attendant deeds; 4. forming the primary and attendant practices for adorning the Buddha-fields; 5. causing those in the intermediate [stages]...
Regarding the explanation of the vows of majestic light (*vairocana-praṇidhāna*), these likewise all equally constitute the primary and auxiliary roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The universal practices (*samantacaryā*) cultivated in many places and over long periods of time all achieve the status of primary and auxiliary through the fulfillment of these vows.
The fourth section clarifies the six matters concerning the encounter with and service of the fourth Buddha. First, it clarifies the appearance of the Buddha:

because his body does not conform to the three realms yet perceives the three realms, he is named Padmaprabha (Lotus Radiance). His virtues are praised throughout the ten directions, and his fame is universally heard;

all who hear it turn toward him in devotion, and thus he is called Dhvaja (the Banner). Second, regarding the exhaustion of the lifespan of Tejaprabha (Flame Radiance) and the acquisition of the merit of the Lord of Heaven through the transformation of retribution...
In the vicinity of the celestial city of Prabhāketu, the three [kings] together with their subordinates and the multitude went to the Buddha to present offerings.
At that time, the Buddha preached for them a sutra titled "The Vast and Equal" (*Vaipulya-samāna*).

This means that within this sutra, the method of universally illuminating the vast essence of the Dharma-realm through the wisdom of the universal gate (*samantamukha-jñāna*) is elucidated; it is named after that which is thus expressed. It encompasses its retinue.

This may be understood accordingly. Following the section on the Heavenly Kings of the Five Periods, there is the clarification of the benefits of hearing the Dharma. Within these benefits, first is the name of the concentration, and subsequently is its function. Regarding the term "Universal Equality" (*pumen*):

it means that the myriad phenomena are devoid of distinction, as there is nothing that is not the *dharmatā*. Since their essence is one and the same, each and every phenomenon encompasses all others;
based upon this, the fused *dharmadhātu* is called the "Universal Gate. One who is able to know this is [the practitioner of] the Universal Gate.
Wisdom. Thus, when universal wisdom accords with the universal banner, it is named "Joy. Joy arises from the object; the object is precisely what is called the "Treasury.
Regarding the phrase "by means of its function, one can enter [equality]," this refers to universal wisdom acceding with the universal object.

This is because the following matters are explained below, and because the sūtra text here is not yet exhaustive; thus, there is no formal conclusion regarding past and present. Furthermore, since there are ten Mount Sumerus within that world-system...
Buddhas as numerous as atoms appeared; his majestic radiance served four Buddhas from the very beginning, and it would not be sufficient to describe this merely as such.

This immediately reveals the completion of the causes for the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*). Thus far, this chapter has answered the preceding questions regarding causes according to its capacity. With this, the first assembly, comprising five chapters in total, is concluded.
[Note: It is feared that the records for the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata" and the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths" have not survived.
*Continued Abridged Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra: A Critical Record*, Fascicle 4 (Combined Main and Supplements;
ending with the "Chapter on the Virtuous Leader"), composed by the Śramaṇa Huìyuàn of Jìngfǎ Monastery.
Chapter Nine: The Awakening through Radiance. In explaining this chapter, the four gates are the same as before.

First, regarding the explanation of the title, there are two parts: first, revealing how it is named; second, analyzing the meaning of the name. Regarding the first, the title in the Sanskrit original is *Tathāgata-prabhā-jāla-bodhana-parivarta*, which means "The Chapter on the Awakening by the Tathāgata’s Net of Light.
This refers to the light emitted from the wheel-mark and webbed fingers (*cakrāṅka-pāda*) beneath the Buddha’s feet.
It is further named the "Luminous Net" because it illuminates the assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions, awakening the bodhisattvas and causing them to resolve to come here.
Regarding the etymology: the Tathāgata is the master who emits the light; the "luminous net" is the substance of the light emitted; and "awakening" is the functional activity of that light.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound based on the Tathāgata’s luminous net, or a *bahuvrīhi* [possessive] compound. This serves to distinguish it from [the term used for] bodhisattvas.
Because it is equal to the *sattva* (sentient beings) and because it belongs to the Buddha, the "Awakening by the Net of Light" (*prabhā-jāla-bodhana*) admits of both interpretations:

because it awakens through sounds and so forth, and because the light possesses this function of awakening. If one speaks generally of the category of the Tathāgata’s awakening by the net of light, it is solely a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative compound).
Regarding the second reason for its coming, it is briefly due to two meanings. First, it comes because it answers the previous eight questions. That is to say:
first, a Buddha emits light that illuminates the entire Dharma-realm; this answers the point regarding majesty and power being like the radiant light of the sun.

Second, the single act [of emitting light] is able to manifest all things; this answers the intent of the opening statement that the light universally traverses all phrases. Third, within the lands manifested by the light...
1. There are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this answers the adornment of the lands (*kṣetra-vyūha*). 2. Mañjuśrī’s fourfold preaching of the Dharma reveals the Buddha’s merits and the true principle;
this answers the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). 3. The various Bodhisattvas who have come, awakened by the five lights, each cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) in their own original lands;
this answers the purity of the Buddha-lands (*buddhakṣetra-pariśuddhi*). 4. The original lands of the various Bodhisattvas who have come are golden in color, even unto the color of equality.
Among these, those that establish their names based on their substance refer to the essential nature of the *kṣetra*.

For example, when gold is the substance, it is named "golden color," and when a diamond is the substance, it is named "diamond color," and so forth. Seventh, the original lands from which the visiting bodhisattvas come are each distinct and separate;
thus, both their names and substances differ. This answers the question regarding the accomplishment of the *kṣetra*. Eighth, within all the lands illuminated by the light, there are...
"Billion Tathāgatas have attained perfect enlightenment"—this answers the Buddha’s great *bodhi*.
"Furthermore, the multitude may see the World-Honored One pervading the world-systems of empty space, all seated upon lion thrones within the Lotus Treasury"—this answers the Buddha’s dwelling.

Having known the thoughts and requests of the great assembly, the Buddha manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) for each according to their kind, causing the multitude to see them all; this answers the Buddha’s majestic power (*anubhāva*).

The virtue is as previously explained. Second, it is to manifest that while the names of the preceding two chapters were distinct and partial regarding the truths (*satya*), this chapter comes because it integrates and pervades them all.

That is to say, what was clarified previously—namely, that the "truths" and "all" pervade all directions and all things—is now shown in this chapter through the Buddha and the assembly, wherein one is all, and the preceding and succeeding [chapters] together reveal this. For this reason, it follows.
Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental purpose (*abhiprāya*): the fundamental principle (*mūla*) is that the Buddha’s light illuminates all lands so as to [reach] the bodhisattvas therein;

the objective (*prayojana*) is to awaken those bodhisattvas and cause them to come here. Within this gate of fundamental purpose, only the fundamental principle and the objective are explained; there is no need for the cumbersome explanation of other dharmas.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: herein, the sections concerning the illumination of the various realms number twenty-six in total.

Among these, the first nine are explained individually, while the latter seventeen are treated collectively; thus, there are ten segments. This does not refer to the emission of light on twenty-six occasions.

Nor is it that the light is emitted only once and then shines sequentially; rather, with a single emission of light, it simultaneously and instantaneously illuminates the entirety of the world-systems throughout space.

However, because words cannot manifest all at once, the teaching is presented as having a sequence of before and after. Furthermore, in order to guide sentient beings according to their capacities and lead them into the Dharma so that they may gradually behold it, the teaching is divided into twenty-six sections.

Within the first section, there are two parts. First, it clarifies how the Buddha uses the light of his body to manifest the sphere of phenomena, enabling the assembly to behold it with their own eyes.
Second, from the passage "At that time, in all places, Mañjuśrī... onwards, it describes the praise of the light of wisdom, causing the assembly to realize the Dharma.

Alternatively, the term "light of wisdom" (*jñānāloka*) here may merely be a textual division and does not indicate the title of the sutra; for the name of the sutra is "The Light of the Tathāgata. Now, as for Mañjuśrī...

Because this is the gateway of the Bodhisattva, there are two parts to the preceding section. First, it reveals the light that is capable of illuminating; second, from "illuminating this" onwards, it clarifies the realm that is illuminated.

Regarding the phrase in the preceding text, "beneath the wheel-marks on the soles," this refers to the center of the wheel-marks on the soles of the feet. Light is emitted from beneath the feet to symbolize three meanings:

first, that the cause for reaching [enlightenment] originates from beneath the feet; second, that when practicing the myriad practices, faith is the ultimate [foundation]; [and third, that the light reaches all places].
First, this light is emitted to signify the teaching of faith. Second, compared to the subsequent stages, faith is the most inferior;

among the parts of the body, the soles of the feet are uniquely the lowest. This light is emitted to signify the gate of inferiority. Third, it signifies the meaning of being the basis for what is fundamental;
that is, the body is able to walk and travel because it relies on the soles of the feet as its foundation, and faith is likewise the root for attaining Bodhi.
This is the fundamental reason for this emission. As the subsequent text states: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit.

The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle nine, says that the light emitted from the soles of the feet is because the body finds its place of abiding through the feet; it is obtained in this manner.
Regarding the phrase "ten billion rays of light," this indicates the number of the lights. Although the worlds illuminated by them are without limit, they are all [included therein].
The Sahā world, the Guhyavidyā world, and so forth—these categorized lands all have ten billion four-continent systems as their illuminated realms.
For this reason, the light rays are also emitted in numbers of ten billion. Regarding the two types of illuminated realms, there are two [aspects]:
first, it illuminates the present fundamental lands and their various phenomena, both defiled and pure; second, it manifests here below the universal assembly of its own Dharma teachings.

Regarding the characteristics, there are three parts to the preceding section: first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition beginning with "ten billion Jambudvīpas" and below; and third, a comprehensive conclusion beginning with "within which... and below.

In the first part, "illumination" refers to the light that illuminates, while "this trichiliocosm and so forth" refers to the objects illuminated. However, there are differing explanations regarding the dimensions of this world-system.
According to the *Heterodox Tenets Record* (I-chih chi) of the Satyasiddhi school, one four-continent world-system constitutes a single [great chiliocosm].
Numeration: Counting from one up to ten, ten to a hundred, and a hundred to a thousand constitutes a *sāhasra-cūḍika* (small thousand) world system.

Three times a small thousand makes three thousand; that is, one set of ten small thousands, two sets of a hundred thousand, and three sets of a thousand thousands—this is the *trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu* (trichiliocosm).
Furthermore, by multiplying this threefold, it becomes a great trichiliocosm; that is, one...

Twice that amount reaches three thousand; twice again reaches one hundred thousand three thousand; thrice again reaches one thousand three thousand. This constitutes a Great Trichiliocosm (Mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu).

According to the eighteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, one thousand suns and moons, one thousand Mount Sumerus, one thousand sets of four continents and six heavens of the desire realm, and one thousand Brahmā heavens—this is called a Small Thousandfold World (*Sāhasracūdika-lokadhātu*). One thousand Small Thousandfold Worlds is called a Middle [Thousandfold World].
A thousand worlds. A thousand times a thousand worlds is called a trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu).
This is also stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*, fascicle 16. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 11, there are two interpretations. The first clarifies the dimensions of the physical basis.

Next, the three-thousandfold world system is correctly elucidated. Regarding the measurement of the abodes, it is asked: what is the extent of the supporting bases for the celestial palaces of the Yāma and other heavens?
Some masters say that the extent of the supporting bases for these four higher heavens is equal to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Other masters say that they increase twofold at each successive level. Still others say that the supporting bases for the palaces of the first dhyāna stage are equal in extent to [the entire earth].
The four continents are equal to the second dhyāna; the small chiliocosm is equal to the third dhyāna; the middle chiliocosm is equal to the fourth dhyāna;

and the great trichiliocosm is equal to the fourth dhyāna. Other masters say that the three lower dhyānas are respectively equal in extent to the small, middle, and great chiliocosms, while the extent of the fourth dhyāna is limitless. As for the term "trichiliocosm," they ask: up to what extent is it considered "small"?

The intermediate great chiliocosm. The verse says: One thousand sets of the four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds, is called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. One thousand times this [medium chiliocosm] is the great chiliocosm.

All [world systems] undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. This is largely consistent with the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury), though it differs slightly in that it states the trichiliocosm extends only as far as the Brahma Heaven.
As it says: "The Noble Teaching speaks only of reaching the Brahma world. This is according to the Mahāyāna perspective.
There are also various differences. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Sixth), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* (Sixth), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Second), and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* all agree with this.
The previously cited *Dīrgha Āgama* and other texts are similar. However, according to the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the general meaning is the same as before;

yet it states that the three thousandfold world-system is destroyed by the three calamities. Therefore, we know that the first dhyāna corresponds to the small thousandfold world-system, the second dhyāna to the intermediate thousandfold world-system, and the third dhyāna to the great thousandfold world-system. If...

Relying on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, throughout the three thousandfold world-system up to the formless realm, those so-called Benevolent Kings held incense burners in their hands to make offerings while the sutra was being recited.

At that moment, the fragrance spread everywhere, reaching in a single thought-instant across the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, including ten billion suns and moons, and even up to ten billion heavens of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. If one relies on this sutra...
It reaches only as far as the fourth dhyāna; therefore, it is stated below that it illuminates ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens. Question:
Among these various explanations above, which one is definitive? Answer: If one relies on the authority of the authentic scriptures (āptāgama), then this sutra is definitive.
If one follows the principle of teaching according to the specific capacities of beings, then all of them are definitive.

Within the second section, which specifically elucidates [the manifestations], there are three parts. First, the analysis of the manifestation within the human realm; second, from "ten billion bodhisattvas" onwards, the clarification of the manifestation of the eight perceptions;
third, from "there are ten billion Sumerus" onwards, the manifestation of the desire and form realms. Within the first of these, there are three subsections: the first concerns the four continents.

Regarding the two great oceans, the triple Cakravāḍa mountains, and the four continents: according to the explanations in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises, Central India is situated in the center of Jambudvīpa.
From that center toward the north, there are three sets of triple Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇaparvata*), and to the north of these Black Mountains lies the Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*).
To the north of the Snowy Mountains lies Mount Gandhamādana. Between the fragrant mountains and the snow lies Lake Anavatapta. Beside the lake is a forest called Jambū;
its trees are massive and tall, producing sweet and delicious fruit. The continent is named after this forest, and it is also designated by the name of the fruit.
It is called Jambudvīpa; "dvīpa" here means "continent. As for the literary style and ancient usage, it is still called Jambū.
