In verse ten, "seeing the great river" refers to those who have entered the stream of the Dharma, realizing the water of the fully manifest *dharmatā*.
Entering the stream of noble practice, they reach the ocean of nature realized by true resultant wisdom, where object and wisdom are one in profound stillness.

Regarding the wisdom of the same fruit: would it not be the case that the stream of dharmas realized by those of provisional capacity in the Lesser Vehicle enters the ocean of fruition only through successive stages?

If it were not for this great river, it would be like a small stream, unable to enter directly into the great ocean; yet because all successively flowing streams likewise enter the sea, [the analogy holds].
11. *Tāpasa* refers merely to the auspicious waters of that specific location; it is not like rivers, oceans, and other flowing streams which are a mixture of various currents.
12. Regarding ponds (*puṣkariṇī*): they are obtained by being dug near a source and filled by the drawing of water.

This can be compared to the perfection of analytical explanation through the skillful digging of shallow and deep [levels] via investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*). 13. Seeing the waves, one further seeks them out to investigate the taking of water.
[The preceding section] concludes. This may be compared to attaining the analytical knowledge of non-interruption (*anantarya-pratisaṃvid*) to fully expound all phenomena.

The fourteenth, "Fountain," does not depend on expedient means (*upāya*), yet it reveals expedient means through its inversion. The fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth can be understood universally.

However, clear flowing water can wash away the filth of the body; the dharma of craving and desire is like water. May others use the water of the dharma of wholesome desire to dispel the afflictions of the mind.
The defilements of delusion are like a forest named Aśoka; in the Western Regions it is called Heshoujia.
Although this region lacks such a tree, it may be known by the presence of flowers and fruits within its gardens.

The seventh section contains twenty-four vows. The first, second, third, fourth, and fifth are easily understood. The sixth vow concerns the attainment of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which extinguishes the root of all suffering.
Wisdom is of two kinds: first, the non-conceptual wisdom of the true essence (*svabhāva-jñāna*), which is termed "fundamental" in relation to preparatory and subsequently attained wisdom;

second, the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibodha-jñāna*), which is termed "fundamental" because it serves as the basis for initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). [The vow] concerns the attainment of...
This refers to "attainment. One attains the fundamental wisdom of the true essence (*mūla-jñāna*), which severs delusions and extinguishes suffering.

Although this wisdom is present throughout all stages, including those of both insight (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it is most manifest in two locations: namely, the path of insight and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Although the outflowing wholesome dharmas associated with the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) exist simultaneously with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in a single moment, they do not constitute a distinct category. Speaking in terms of the path of insight, one acquires the fundamental [wisdom].
"Wisdom that extinguishes all suffering": all suffering does not exceed the three or eight [categories]. Because one attains this wisdom, one severs the karma of the evil realms and ignorance;

thus, the suffering of the three miserable states (trāya) is extinguished, and the sufferings of birth, old age, and sickness likewise perish. By severing these delusions, one does not create the ten unwholesome karmas;
therefore, no enemies or those one hates will come together with one. By severing discriminative desire and greed, there is no seeking.
One encounters acquisition and separation from what is loved; from this point on, there remain only enmity and the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*).

Upon reaching the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains the Vajra-like Mind, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and severs those two types of suffering. Although wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-kuśala-dharma*) still persist at this time, they are already illuminated by supreme wisdom as being identical to the *dharmatā*.
On the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cannot be further extinguished. This should be understood by correlating it with the three sufferings and the eight sufferings.

It is known that one who attains the fundamental wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-ādi-bodhi*) and thereby extinguishes suffering does so only at the moment of realizing the principle through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

At that time, the original and the fundamental merge in darkness; this is what is called "attaining the fundamental original enlightenment. From this point on, there is forever no death nor the aggregates (*skandha*).

Although the names of two paths—the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) regarding the severance of delusions and the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*) regarding the realization of the principle—are established, they occur in a single moment. The attainment of wisdom is likewise so. Therefore, there is none.
The moment when the seeds of both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations are suddenly severed is precisely the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Seventh, the aspiration that others may enter true wisdom and be forever free from illness and affliction has two aspects. First, regarding the wisdom that enters the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it severs the suffering of illness and the disease of the afflictions;
that is to say, [it severs] all categories of afflictions belonging to the various miserable realms.
There is a state of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that arises from conceptual discrimination; it is also the remote cause of physical illness.

Within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it is severed in a single instant. One suddenly realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Four Truths of the three realms, and both physical illness and afflictions will never arise again.

Second, by means of the wisdom of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), one suddenly severs all illnesses of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Having realized the most perfect, true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), all afflictions are eternally extinguished; thus, regarding the physical illness caused by the eight great adversities, one prays that others may realize the essence of these adversities is empty and quiescent, thereby attaining liberation from them.
Ninth, one prays that others may have faith in the sublime beauty of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whether through patience or faith, this is a profound aspiration for patience. This patience is the Dharma; it is called the cause of true uprightness.

(10) One vows that others shall not find pleasure in or tolerate [one's faults]. (11) According to the Sanskrit manuscript, one vows that others shall always remember the kindness and virtue of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
(12) According to the Sanskrit manuscript, one vows not to retaliate against those who harbor enmity. (13)
"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "cessation. Now, one wishes for others to attain the foremost state within cessation—that which is neither disciplined nor tranquil—namely, Great Parinirvāṇa.
The fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth [aspirations] may be understood accordingly. The seventeenth is seeing the excellence of others.
May others practice the diligence of donning the armor; for according to the Sanskrit original, there are also two types: preparatory application (*prayoga*) and lack of timidity (*anavalīna*).
In the Sanskrit original, the word "striving" (*qù*, 趣) in the following line means "heroic seeking. As for "without a teacher," the Sanskrit original says "spontaneously" (*svayam*).

This is an alternative designation for the Buddha. It means that one vows for sentient beings to courageously seek the fruit of Buddhahood, like donning armor to enter battle in pursuit of merit and reward.
The eighteen types of armor and staffs are instruments of inauspiciousness; because one has not seen the Buddha oneself, one does not act for others.

The nineteenth [point] is easy to understand. The twentieth is right livelihood as right action, because it is by means of this that one sustains one’s life. There are five types of wrong livelihood for sustaining one’s life:

first, manifesting wonders; second, speaking of one’s own virtues; third, divining good or bad fortune through signs; fourth, raising one's voice to display authority so as to inspire fear and respect in others;
and fifth, preaching the Dharma to others for the sake of gain. Practicing these five things is entirely for the sake of profit and sustenance, and thus one falls [into wrong livelihood].
Regarding wrong livelihood: here, the third phrase generally includes the aspiration for others to be free from it, while the fourth phrase only encompasses the first four [types].
The twenty-first, twenty-second, twenty-third, and twenty-fourth [categories] may likewise be understood. However, because the elder was advanced in years...
Because he excels all others in every matter, he is able to discern and resolve them clearly. The eighth section contains twenty-three vows:

First, that the city walls may be firm enough to prevent calamities and protect life; therefore, he vows that others may obtain a body not subject to transformation by the four marks, and a mind that cannot be bent by even supreme wisdom.
Second, that the royal capital be a place of abundant superior merit, where wise people gather and rejoice.
Because of this joy, one wishes that others may meet with those endowed with supreme merit and constantly obtain the bliss of the Dharma;

or that they may skillfully accumulate all roots of goodness, so that body and mind are at ease and delighted. Third, dwelling in seclusion within the forest of the three bases for views is praiseworthy;

one wishes that others may attain Buddhahood and reside in the tranquil forest of the Dharma, where humans and devas look up in admiration—these four or five points are thus to be understood. Sixth, before entering their homes, then...

Regarding the distinctions between various schools: once one has entered a single school, there is only one and no plurality. Therefore, I vow that others may enter the One Buddha Vehicle, realizing that the three vehicles are non-different and no distinct from what was taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This applies equally to the seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth [stages], all of which can be understood accordingly.
In the thirteenth stage, one perceives that by relying on the power of one's own Dharma, one honors the worthy and values the wholesome teachings, feeling shame at not practicing them.

13. Regarding the wicked: one vows that sentient beings may likewise conceal and guard their sense faculties, such as the eyes, so as not to become heedless—just as one hides and protects a cat to prevent it from killing mice, or as one covers and protects the unattractive forms of men and women with clothing. 14.
Seeing oneself devoid of shame and lacking benevolence, one vows that others may practice objectless compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) to rescue all beings. 15. Oneself...

Regarding the food of meaning (*arthāhāra*), one hopes for the fulfillment of one's own aspirations; one vows that others may have their hopes fulfilled regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, having no further desires themselves.

(16) Because one has personally experienced the savoring of attachment within the intermediate state, one reverses this and vows that others may obtain the flavor of the meditative joy (*dhyānāsvāda*) of non-arising and so forth.
Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-two, and twenty-three can likewise be understood. However—
Regarding the phrases concerning the aspirations for others: the first three pertain to both cause and fruit, while the latter four pertain solely to the fruit of Buddhahood.

This is because those who enter Buddhahood have reached the ultimate realization of wisdom regarding great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). The Sanskrit original states that they have "thoroughly pervaded the Buddha-wisdom."

The ninth section contains fourteen vows. First, because water is equal in nature and can penetrate [all things], he vows that others may attain mastery over the objects known by the Buddha’s wisdom—namely, knowing past and future events as if they were present. In the Sanskrit original, this is expressed as "entering the knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Second, because he has washed his own body, he vows that the bodies and minds of others shall be pure, both physically radiant and mentally luminous. Third, according to... [text continues].

In the Sanskrit original, the first line says *uṣṇam*, which means "whatever heat is experienced. The current rendering as "intense summer heat and toxic miasma" refers only to the specific phrase concerning mutual heat;
it should rather be stated as "separated from the heat of afflictions, forever extinguished without remainder.
Among the four [lines], the third is *bodhi* (enlightenment) and the fourth is *nirvāṇa*. This is because one recites them in accordance with the text and maintains them in mind.
May others follow what the Buddha has taught and attain *dhāraṇī*. [The numbers] six, seven, eight, nine, and ten may all be understood accordingly.

At eleven, one circumambulates with one’s own [right side]. This is the wish that the actions of others may not be contrary [to the Dharma]. In Sanskrit this is called *dakṣiṇī*; here it is translated as "right" (*yǒu*).
Since "right" carries the meaning of "conformity," the "Chapter on Leaving the World" states: "By treading upon the right foot, one does not contradict what all Buddhas have taught. Universally...
The second *Yao* (chapter) says: The Bodhisattva then descended from Tuṣita Heaven and proceeded toward the right side [of his mother’s womb].
The reason the Bodhisattva stayed on the right is that his conduct is without reversal; it is because he acts with repeated gravity twelve times over, wishing others to seek diligently.
The thirteenth and fourteenth [sections] may be understood.

In the tenth section, there are three vows. The first and second may be understood. Regarding the third, which says "surveying the ten directions," it means that he vows for others to achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
At the time of birth, he surveys the ten directions, encompassing me as his sole honored one and manifesting that there is no equal to him.

The above constitutes the initial general analysis of the four propositions regarding the various vows. Following this is the comprehensive categorization and individual explanation. This concludes the second section, which provides a general clarification and specifically reveals the characteristics of the application of the mind in practice.

The third section, which summarizes how the application of the mind can accomplish supreme virtues, consists of two parts. First, the summary of the preceding application of the mind is understandable [from the context].
Second, "then one obtains" and below, which demonstrates its supreme efficacy. This part also has two sections:

first, demonstrating the excellence of the resulting fruit, which refers to the one hundred and ten phrases in the preceding question and the ten phrases in the answer; second, "all worlds" and below, which demonstrates the praise.
Victorious. Within this, there are two parts: first, that which cannot be moved by worldly multitudes, briefly cited as seven categories;
second, that which cannot be moved by lower supramundane multitudes, briefly indicated as two categories. Regarding the term "unmoved," it has two meanings.

First, at the time of correctly cultivating the vow, those worldly and supramundane multitudes may praise or disparage its formation and destruction, yet they are unable [to cause wavering]. Why is this? Because the mind is single-mindedly focused.
Because it is thus annotated; because it does not abide in signs (*animitta*). This is because the mind transforms the activity, rather than the activity transforming the mind.

Second, these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the vow bring about a definite fruition, just like immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*). This is because the immovable fruit cannot be induced by other intense karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
Thus far there have been three [sections]: first, a general inquiry into the mental application that accomplishes virtue; second, the specific manifestation of that application.

The mental mode of activity. Third, the summary of the superior efficacy of the mind’s application. This concludes the general explanation of the second [section], the causal practices that constitute the means of accomplishment.

Above, there were two parts: first, the preliminary indication of the qualities of the fruit to be accomplished; second, the manifestation of the causal practices that constitute the means of accomplishment.

This concludes the general and specific clarifications. Above, there were two parts: first, the general response; second, the specific manifestation. This concludes the general and direct response. Above...

The second part consists of: first, the initial inquiry; and second, the formal response. This concludes the general explanation of Mañjuśrī’s reply. Above, the two [sections] consist of: first, the question by Jñānaśrī; and second, the answer by Mañjuśrī.

This concludes the general explanation of the fourth [section], the "Explanation of the Text. Above, there were four [parts]: first, the explanation of the title; and second, the purpose of the coming.
Third, the essential purport; fourth, the explanation of the text. This concludes the general exposition of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct.
Regarding the upcoming explanation of the twelfth chapter, "The Chapter of Worthy Leaders" (Bhadrapāla), there are four sections, the same as before.

First, regarding the explanation of the name: "Worthy" (*bhadra*) means virtuous; "Head" (*mukha*) means preeminent. Because his nature is virtuous and his qualities are preeminent, he is called "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*).
Since he is the head of the worthy, this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. This chapter is named the "Chapter of Worthy Head" because the Bodhisattva Worthy Head expounds it;
since it is the chapter of Worthy Head, this is also a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Second, regarding the intent of this section: the preceding chapter clarified the vows and practices within faith; this chapter now clarifies the virtues and activities within faith. Thus, it follows in sequence.
Third, regarding the central theme and objective: the central theme is the functional power of the virtues of faith, and the objective is the subsequent attainment of the stages of realization.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: Now, this chapter is divided into four sections in total. First, the section where the Sūtra narrator describes Mañjuśrī’s prior discourse;

second, the section where I now [speak] as Mañjuśrī exhorts me to speak below; third, the section from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha" onwards, which elaborates on the teaching according to the exhortation;
and fourth, the section from "At that time, Bhadramukha" onwards, which reveals the realization of the ultimate truth. Regarding the first, it concludes the preceding [section].

This has already been explained; namely, in a separate chapter, it was clarified that by employing the mind skillfully, the six sense faculties and the three types of action become entirely pure, untainted, and undisturbed regarding their respective objects.

Subsequently, wishing to manifest what follows and set forth what comes after—specifically, desiring to have the Honored One explain the great function of the merit of the bodhicitta perfected through faith—the verse is spoken.
The first verse within the second section, "Exhortation," is divided into two parts. The first half concludes the previous chapter by stating that the purity of conduct has already been explained;

by analogy, it should also be said that the practices and qualities have been explained, though the verse is most concise. The second half properly exhorts one to explain the function of the superior qualities accomplished through the practice of the preceding chapter.
The third section, based on the exhortation to expound, consists of two parts. First, the introductory remarks by the narrator identifying the speaker can be understood.

Second, from "Excellent! (*sādhu*) onwards, the actual verses are clearly presented. Within this, there are three hundred and fifty-seven and a half verses in total, which are divided into seven sections:
1. Praising the extensive teaching as being concise; 2. From "The Bodhisattva’s Resolve" (*bodhicitta*) onwards, a brief exposition of the aspects of practice; 3. Faith as the Path.

1. The first section, "The Original [Exposition]," briefly demonstrates the superior efficacy. 2. The second section, "If one constantly and faithfully believes," details the practices and stages possessed.
3. The third section, "There may be a buddha-field," describes the boundless great function. 4. The fourth section, "All Tathāgatas," provides metaphors to illustrate the profound intent. 5.
The fifth section, "The foremost wisdom," involves comparative evaluation and exhortation to uphold.

Within the first section, the four verses are divided into two parts. The first verse provides a general summary of the vastness and immeasurability of the virtues, of which only a small portion is described herein.

The first line praises the questioner and the listeners; the next line indicates the vastness of the virtues; the following line indicates that only a small portion is being described; and the final line clarifies this through a simile.

The subsequent three verses specifically distinguish the difficulty of measuring and the difficulty of explaining these virtues. Within these, the first two verses further elucidate the virtues previously mentioned.
Broad. Next, half a verse reiterates the previous brief explanation; the latter half of the verse specifically clarifies the preceding metaphor. Within the first two verses, there are two parts:
the first one and a half verses clarify that because the qualities to be measured are vast, those qualities are difficult to measure;

the latter half of the verse clarifies that because the persons who measure them are great, the qualities are difficult to measure. Regarding the vastness of the qualities to be measured, this is the first verse.
The first half of the verse clarifies that even for a beginner, the merit of a small amount of practice over a short period is already immeasurable.
The latter half of the verse clarifies the stage of practicing extensively over a long period; it uses the preceding "small" as a comparison to demonstrate its immeasurability.

Subsequently, it cites the "measuring persons"—ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and all bodhisattvas—to show that they are insufficient to be considered "vast" when facing this immeasurability. As for "one Buddha" or "two Buddhas," [it refers to...]
Even if all Buddhas were to speak together, they could not fully measure it, nor would it be exhausted;
this is because it reaches the ultimate limit of being difficult to measure. Within the two and a half verses that clarify the teaching of only a small portion:
the first line clarifies the vast virtue of the initial resolve for enlightenment, while the [subsequent] five lines manifest that it is immeasurable and therefore only a small portion is taught.
The latter half-verse of the third section clarifies and expands upon the preceding analogy; the text is explicit and thus easily understood. Question:

What is the distinction between the "arousing of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) discussed here and that taught in the context of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and the chapter on the "Arousing of the Mind"? Answer: They are essentially one and the same, but they differ according to their respective points of reference.

Specifically, the "arousing of the mind" mentioned here refers to the arousal of the mind at the conclusion of the preceding stages. This is what is termed "Faith" (*śraddhā*) among the three types of arousing the mind described in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
This is the fulfillment of the arousal of the bodhicitta. The arousal of the mind in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is entirely [the fulfillment].

This is subsequently called the "Stage of the First Arousing of the Mind" (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), as it reveals that mind by way of its stages. As stated in the "Chapter on the Arousing of the Mind" (*Cittotpāda-paṭala*), this refers to the vastness of the mental activity;

thus, metaphors are employed to illustrate its virtues. Question: Is there not an arousal of the mind at the beginning of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)? Answer: Although there is an arousal of the mind, it is not the primary one.
It is "arising. Why is this so? Because it is like light down, and because it is called the "faculty of faith" (*śraddhendriya*) in such texts as the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing).

Question: Since this is the beginning, how can it possess all subsequent stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*)? Answer: Because it is the practice of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is explained at length in the seventh section of the "Hanging Discussion" (*xuántán*). Question:
Based on the nature of phenomena, it is plausible that its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) may contract and expand; however, regarding the cultivation by a person, how could the ten [stages]...
"Is it then that one attains [enlightenment] immediately upon a thousand kalpas? Answer: "The person has no separate substance; it is formed by gathering together dharmas.

Since the dharmas are already fused and integrated, the person is likewise without obstruction. Between ten thousand kalpas and a single thought-moment, or between a single thought-moment and many kalpas—herein there is no fixed limit to be found.

Time has no separate substance; it is established in dependence upon form and mind (rūpa-citta). Since form and mind arise from the fundamental nature (prakṛti) and are without [substance], [time is likewise without substance]."

Because of these obstructions, even the recollection of sounds is integrated with principle according to the logic [of the situation], as seen in the practices and attainments of Sudhana, the devaputra of Tuṣita, and others;
in each case, the person and the method differ.

Within the second section, the "Brief Exposition of the Aspects of Practice," there are five verses divided into two parts. The first half-verse provides a general heading, while the remainder of the text provides a detailed exposition.
Within the heading, there are three points: first, the generation of the bodhicitta; second, the cause for generating the mind; and third, the conditions for generating the mind.

*Bodhi* refers to the *dharmadhātu*, the reality realized by the great wisdom of the Buddha’s fruition. To "generate the intent to seek" means to initiate, for the first time, [the aspiration] toward that *dharmadhātu*. It is certain that...

Because one will certainly attain the mind, there are many kinds of causes and conditions. Some say that abiding in one's own nature (*svabhāva-vihāra*) is the cause, while that which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-samudāgata*) is the condition.
Others say that the two natures are the cause, while virtuous friends and various objects such as what is seen and heard are the conditions.
Now, this is not so, as will be understood later. To explain the causes and conditions in detail, it is as in the Chapter on the Bodhicitta.
Regarding the subsequent specific explanations, there are many types of causes and conditions herein. In the first half-verse, pure faith is the cause and the Three Jewels are the conditions.
In the following five phrases, great compassion and great wisdom together constitute the causes and conditions; therein, compassion is the cause and wisdom is [the condition].

The conditions consist of eight dharmas in total. Five are explained by way of contrast (vyatireka), while three are explained by way of agreement (anvaya). Alternatively, the first five may be understood as the objects of wisdom (*jñāna*), and the latter three as the causes of compassion (*karuṇā*).

The "five" refer to not seeking the five desires, royal status, profit, self-comfort, or fame. The "three" refer to the cessation of suffering, the provision of benefit and happiness, and the adornment of the buddha-field.

Since the adornment of the field is for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, it is subsumed under the category of compassion. Next, three and a half verses explain that wisdom serves as the cause.
The Buddha-dharma and the dharma-realm serve as conditions (*pratyaya*). This is because revering, supporting, upholding, and seeking realization of the Dharma are all acts of wisdom.

The next verse identifies faith and knowledge as the causes (*hetu*) and the Three Jewels as the conditions. The former refers to faith alone; the latter refers to knowledge alone; and the subsequent one refers to both faith and knowledge.

The following verse identifies faith as the cause and the Buddha-dharma, the bodhisattva practices, and the dharma-realm as the conditions. Thus far, the causes and conditions have been profound and weighty.

The reality consists of three causes: namely, faith, compassion, and wisdom. The conditions consist of thirteen: namely, the Three Jewels, the eight dharmas, the dharma-realm, and the bodhisattva practices.
Among these, one should reflect according to principle on how they differ from those of ordinary beings and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle.

Within the third section, "A Brief Demonstration of Superior Capabilities," the seven verses are divided into three parts: first, two lines provide a general heading; second, five and a half verses provide a detailed explanation; and third, one verse provides a summary. Within the first part, there are two sections and four meanings. "Path" (*mārga*) refers to the myriad practices of a bodhisattva. "Origin" (*mūla*) means the beginning. Because faith is the origin, the myriad practices arise accordingly. The Sanskrit term is *prabhava* (rendered as *pu-han-ga* in the Chinese transliteration). It signifies that which has been produced. Thus, it is said: "Faith is the origin of all dharmas. This is the first meaning. The second meaning is that faith is the root of the path. As stated in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*: "Faith is the root of the path. This is because the path arises from faith. The third meaning is that faith is the precursor to the path. As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "Faith is the precursor to the path. This is because the path arises following faith. The fourth meaning is that faith is the support of the path. As stated in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*: "Faith is the support of the path. This is because the path relies upon faith. These are the four meanings. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "faith is the origin": the word "origin" (*mūla*) is synonymous with "root" (*mūla*). It is called "origin" because it is the source from which all dharmas arise. It is called "root" because it is the foundation upon which all dharmas depend. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The roots are so named because they are the basis for all conditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is known that faith is the origin of all dharmas. Regarding the statement that faith is the root of the path: this is because the path arises from faith. Regarding the statement that faith is the precursor to the path: this is because the path arises following faith. Regarding the statement that faith is the support of the path: this is because the path relies upon faith. These are the four meanings. Each line constitutes a distinct excellence. First, it clarifies that the substance of faith is pure;

now, the mind-king is purified because one has faith in the Truths and the Jewels, thereby extinguishing pride toward sentient beings and the Triple Gem. Third, among the seven noble riches, faith is the foremost.

Because one cultivates goodness through faith and thereby gives rise to virtues, it is subsequently called a "treasury" (*kośa*); this refers specifically to the "Treasury of Faith" (*śraddhā-kośa*) among the ten treasuries.

Fourth, one practices all correct conducts by means of accepting and practicing them through faith. Fifth, it is through faith that one is able to relinquish [attachments] regarding the merit of giving.

Because wisdom is able to cross over; seventh, through faith one knows that the pāramitās increase, and the eighty thousand practices of the virtues he cultivates are accomplished;
because faith is the root, he reaches the stage of Buddhahood; ninth, among the five faculties, faith is the foremost.

Because one attains clarity and sharpness through understanding causes and following habitual practice, faith is also foremost among the fifteen powers (*bala*). The rest are as explained regarding the faculties (*indriya*).

Eleventh: regarding that which is to be countered, one understands that false inversion has no substantial reality; regarding the path that counteracts it, one has faith in both the path itself and that which is realized through it.
The essence is neither identical to nor separate [from phenomena]. Thus one abandons delusions and thus realizes the principle; all of this has faith as its foundation.

Faith. Fifteenth, by believing in the ten powers of the Buddha and not being deceived by the four [māras], one transcends the path of celestial Māras.

Twentieth, there are two meanings: first, all Buddhas attain Buddhahood and appear in the world with faith as their fundamental basis; second, [all Buddhas]...
This occurs because the Buddha appears only when the faculty of faith has matured in those who are suitable vessels. In the threefold summary, there are two parts;

the first half-verse provides the explanation in terms of the Dharma. This refers to the fact that within the practices of the five stages, such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), the culmination of this practice of faith (*śraddhā-caryā*) constitutes abiding in the initial mind.

Because it is subsumed within the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*), among the successive stages of practice, faith (*śraddhā*) is at the very beginning; it is the foundation for what follows. Because it is the foundation, it is preeminent.
If this beginning were absent, nothing subsequent would exist; therefore, it is called "supreme" (*agra*). This refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and above.
To have faith in the unimpeded realm is not difficult; however, to be able to believe and incline toward it while still bound by all fetters is what makes it difficult to attain.

The latter half of the verse provides an analogy: "In the world" is a general term with a specific intended meaning. Although it says "in the world," the intent refers specifically to the human realm.
Just as the *maṇi* jewel is difficult to find and appears only when a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) manifests, so too is the practice [of this faith] difficult to attain.
According to the Sanskrit original, there is one additional line to this verse: "Like the *kimpuruṣa*, like the lion king, and like the mani jewel, difficult to find in the world.
The commentary explains: as for the *kimpuruṣa*, it refers to those who merely possess the curled hair on the crown of their heads shaped like a whorl of flowers;
such individuals are already rare, let alone those who are subsequently kings—these are even more exceedingly rare.
The fourth section, "The Stage of Possessing the Practices," consists of fifty and a half verses and is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the practices possessed;

second, from "If for the sake of all Buddhas... onwards, the explanation of the stages possessed; and third, from "The Bodhisattva diligently cultivates... onwards, the concluding praise of its merits.

Within the first part, there are eight and a half verses divided into two sections: first, four and a half verses explaining how the Three Jewels perfect the various practices; second, the remaining four...

The verse clarifies how various practices are accomplished through the progressive development of faith. Within the preceding section, the first two verses explain how the practice of training in the precepts is accomplished by virtue of faith in the Buddha.

Among these, the former verse generally elucidates how training in the precepts enables one to possess all virtues, while the latter verse specifically reveals the distinct ways in which the precepts and the points of training (śikṣāpada) each bring about specific virtues.
Furthermore, there are two types of names for the points of training: the general and the particular.

In general, "training" (*śikṣā*) refers to the simultaneous inclusion of all three—precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Specifically, however, it is restricted solely to the preliminary application of upholding the precepts;

that is, first practicing and studying the characteristics of what constitutes an offense and what does not is called "cultivating training," while acting in accordance with that understanding is called "upholding the precepts.

Thus, here the stages (*bhūmi*) serve as a metaphor for the points of training (*śikṣāpada*), and the root serves to clarify the upholding of the precepts. The distinction between understanding and practice is like the difference between a path marked by ink and a path through ore.

Next, one verse clarifies that through faith in the Buddha, one accomplishes the practice of making offerings. Next, one verse clarifies that through faith in the Dharma, one accomplishes the practice of seeking the Dharma without weariness.

first, accomplishing the practice of firm and clear faculties and powers; second, the practice of distancing oneself from evil and drawing near to the good; third, the vast and great...
The practice of virtuous causes and the practice of guarding based on the four types of resolute belief each possess two aspects; thus, it should be understood that these constitute eight practices.

Second, regarding the clarification of the stages possessed [by these practices], thirty-nine verses are divided into four parts. The first three verses clarify the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

That is to say, "generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*) is the name for the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and so forth refer to the practice of the stage of purification (*viśuddhi-bhūmi*).
"Birth" refers to the second stage, the Stage of Noble Birth (*jāti-garbha-vihāra*). "Skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the Stage Endowed with Skillful Means (*upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra*).

"Purity of the mind through faith and aspiration" is the Stage of Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*). "Supremacy" is the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-vihāra*). "The most excellent mind" refers to the final three stages. This may be understood according to the explanation.

[The text] understands this. Second, if one attains increase, the two verses and a half above clarify the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*). *Pāramitā* is the general name for these ten practices.

*Mahāyāna* refers to the practice that distinguishes it from the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Thus, the first two practices comprise the offering of the Dharma (*dharmapūjā*), which is the practice of conforming to principle;

The practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*) is subsumed within the latter six stages of practice; its characteristics can be understood through this explanation. Eloquence in expounding the Dharma and so forth refers to the protection of sentient beings while remaining free from the marks of sentient beings (*sattvanimitta-vivikta*).
The first five dedications—beginning with compassion and so forth—are dedications that accord with sentient beings through an impartial mind.
"Firm great compassion" is the sixth dedication, which accords with firm roots of goodness, because it bestows extensively through universal pity.

Within the first section, the initial verse clarifies the manifestation of Buddhas preaching the Dharma; the second verse clarifies the sovereignty of essence and function, within which there are four [points].

The meaning [of this] is as follows: first, there is no conceptualization or discursive thought; second, there is no effort on the part of the Buddha’s activity; third, a single thought-moment pervades the ten directions; and fourth, there are many gates of skillful means.

Therefore, by encompassing the immeasurable and the non-beneficial, it is called "transforming all living beings. The four meanings are illustrated by the metaphor of the sun; one should understand them according to the Dharma.
Thirdly, in each instance, he manifests the eight phases of enlightenment. Regarding what was previously called "immeasurable skillful means," these eight are briefly indicated.

This is the manifestation. The fourth [instance] appears once to gather and transform beings through the three vehicles; the fifth appears once with various manifestations to correspond to their capacities.
The final one concludes the function by returning to the source. Within this, the first two lines summarize that the various types manifested are so vast and numerous they cannot be fully described;
the latter two lines conclude by returning to the source. As for "the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal," it is named after a metaphor, like the fourfold army of the asuras.
They are arrayed in the sky; within the great ocean, their images are manifested as seals (*mudrā*). The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, chapter fourteen, states:
"Just as the bodies of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, as well as other external forms—such forms as these all exist as seal-images within the ocean.
For this reason, the great ocean is called 'the Seal. The Bodhisattva is likewise; he attains the Samādhi of the Great Ocean Seal."

Therefore, one clearly perceives the mental activities of all sentient beings; having attained the illumination of wisdom regarding all dharma-gates, this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) through which one perceives the destinations of the mental activities of all sentient beings. The commentary states:

That sutra merely speaks of the manifestation of the mental activities of sentient beings within meditative concentration for the purpose of what is appropriate for their transformation. Now, here we briefly cite ten [examples].

The types are as follows: first, manifesting as a Buddha; second, preaching the Dharma; third, manifesting supernatural powers; fourth, manifesting śarīra relics; fifth, attaining the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; sixth, manifesting many kalpas;
seventh, the physical forms and appearances of sentient beings; eighth, manifesting the inclinations of the mind; ninth, karmic actions; and tenth, vocal sounds.

The second section, concerning the *Avataṃsaka-samādhi*, consists of two and a half verses divided into two parts. The first two [verses] clarify the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), while the latter half concludes by returning to the basis of reliance.

Within the former, the application of practice is briefly distinguished as being of seven kinds: first, the practice of adorning the buddha-fields; second, the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas.
Third is the practice of luminosity; fourth is the practice of delivering sentient beings; fifth is the practice of wisdom; sixth is the practice of preaching the Dharma;

seventh is the practice of the ten perfections. Within the latter half [of the verse], the upper line—“all-pervading mastery”—summarizes the unimpeded accomplishment of the practices formed through various gateways.

The lower line—“returning to the source”—concludes by showing that the myriad practices are like flowers used to adorn the ten bodies; thus, it concludes the practices by returning them to their origin.

the latter half-verse clarifies the cause of that concentration’s function. Within the former [part], there are two [subdivisions]. The first three lines clarify that the objects and the mind within the concentration are neither one nor many.

Obstruction. The latter two verses and three lines clarify that within the meditative state (*samādhi*), one manifests as all. This consists of two parts; the first two lines clarify that "one is all.

That is to say, by the power of *samādhi* and so forth, one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) upon a single atom (*paramāṇu*), and thereby immediately accomplishes meditative absorption upon all atoms.

The final line clarifies that all is one. This means that at the very moment when the former is one, it is all; because this non-differentiation is not destroyed, it is said that "there is no increase.
The latter part clarifies that within the fixed realm, a single atom manifests many lands. This consists of two sections: first, clarifying how many lands manifest within a single atom;
second, the latter half of the verse generalizes this to show how lands manifest within all atoms. Within the first section, there are two parts, the first being seven lines.
The first part is the direct teaching (*dharmadeśanā*); the latter two lines are the illustrative metaphor. Within the former, there are two sections:

the first line provides a general designation of the manifested lands, while the subsequent six lines clarify the characteristics of the various manifested lands. Briefly, ten types are shown in five pairs: (1) the presence or absence of Buddhas;

(2) defilement or purity; (3) small or large; (4) formation or destruction; (5) upright or lateral. Regarding the subsequent illustrative metaphor: they appear to exist through conditions, yet in reality...

It is not existent; therefore, it is like a mirage. All objects appear to one another as each being the totality of all, yet they do not become confused or disordered, but are arrayed in their respective positions without ever obstructing one another;
thus, it is like Indra’s net. Regarding the subsequent category of "pervasion," just as it is when a single atom manifests a buddha-field within meditative concentration, so it is for all others.
Within the three [points] concerning the causes of the latter, the first concerns the power of samādhi; this is attained—

In the summary: second, the power of liberation (*vimukti-bala*) refers to the inconceivable power of liberation, which manifests these karmic functions as explained in the "Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas" (*Acintya-dharma-paṭala*) below—such as manifesting the buddha-fields of the three periods of time within a single atom.
Third, the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-bala*) refers to mastery over the superknowledges, all of which are explained as follows.
In the fourth [section], the Samādhi of Manifest Offering, there are eighteen verses divided into three parts. First, one verse provides a general heading.

Second, sixteen verses manifest the specific offerings intended for all [beings] as indicated by the heading. Third, one verse provides a general conclusion. Within the first part, there are two sections:

the first half-verse provides a general definition of the samādhi, and the second half-verse clarifies that the universal offering to all is based upon the objects of offering; this is easily understood. Next, regarding the specific manifestation:

To manifest the excellence of his power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he offers to each Buddha with only one hand; this clearly indicates that he is making offerings to as many Buddhas as there are hands.

Within this, the first five verses clarify the offerings emerging from within the hands: the first three concern form (*rūpa*) and the latter two concern sound (*śabda*). The subsequent eleven verses clarify the offerings manifested by the light of the hands.

Finally, the four concluding verses summarize the preceding sections. First, they conclude the brief presentation by revealing its extensive implications. What has been discussed above constitutes the "brief and extensive" [explanation], which addresses potential difficulties.

Contemplation. Second, by concluding the extensive offerings, one makes offerings to a single Buddha; third, making offerings to all Buddhas is likewise; fourth, the application of what is used may be understood from the context.
Within the fifth section, the Samādhi of the Present Dharma, the eight verses are divided into four parts: first, one verse provides a general outline of the many gateways; second...
The five verses separately manifest twenty kinds of dharma-gates in brief for the purpose of gathering and transforming sentient beings.
Three verses and one line manifest their manifold applications; the final verse concludes that their functions are unfathomable. Regarding the sixth, the samādhi that gathers sentient beings:

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) integrate sentient beings. Within this, the sixteen verses are divided into two parts: the first verse provides a general indication of their names and functions, while the subsequent fifteen verses specifically manifest their activities.
Within the section on the specific manifestations, there are four parts; the first four verses clarify the integration through generosity (*dāna*).
Among these, the first two are subsumed under that which brings peace and happiness to the body; the latter two are subsumed under that which gladdens one's own mind.

The next two verses clarify their inclusion within the bond of affection (*anunaya*). As the *Mahāvaipulya* states: "To preach the six *pāramitās* for the sake of sentient beings is subsumed under pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).
Regarding "various Brahma-voices," this refers to the eight kinds of Brahma-voices, or alternatively, sixty kinds; the meaning is as explained elsewhere.

Chapter. The three sets of four verses clarify the inclusion through "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*). Among these, the first two verses correctly demonstrate the performance of common activities by acting as a close acquaintance through the eight dharmas.

The latter two verses clarify the meaning of inclusion; that is, because one already possesses a karmic connection with them, one includes them through the monastic life and causes them to clearly understand and explain [the Dharma].
The four sets of five verses clarify the inclusion through "beneficial conduct" (*hitacaryā*). Among these, the first verse provides a general summary.
"Discrimination" refers to the ten practices; these are the Buddha’s ten perfections (*pāramitās*).

"The Dharma of Great Beings" refers to the conduct of all Buddhas and their equals—namely, Bodhisattvas, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), or those with the five mundane supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The following two verses demonstrate the faults and the means of gathering [beings].

Within them, the former verse reveals that for long-lived beings whose afflictions are slight but who are attached to pleasure, one should show the four signs to induce weariness [with cyclic existence]. The latter verse reveals...

For those whose afflictions are heavy, four aspects are manifested to induce weariness [with cyclic existence]. The latter two verses demonstrate the Buddha’s qualities to inspire a joyful desire for them.
Within these, the former verse briefly enumerates the three ways of gathering beings, while the latter verse generally concludes the gathering of beings by means of the three wheels.
Within the seventh section, "Attaining the Worldly Samādhi," the eighteen verses are divided into two parts. The first verse provides a general indication;
the subsequent seventeen verses specifically manifest its great functions. Within this, there are three sections. The first six clarify how the body attains worldly benefit for sentient beings.
The first prepares one with various arts; the next serves as a leader and savior; the next provides external vessels and requisites; the next is likewise skillful in benefiting others;

the next two concern attaining the asceticism of the ṛṣis; the next two [verses] clarify how the body gains mastery over non-Buddhists to convert their heterodox followers—the first five distinguish these individually, while the last one summarizes them. Third, the final five verses clarify the great function of vocal action (*vākkarman*); therein:
The first [verse] provides a general explanation; the following three specifically clarify it. Within these, the first states, "or the border-dialect incantation.
In the Sanskrit original, this is *dālabhida-maṇḍala-pati-vi*. Regarding *dālabhida*, this is the name of a border kingdom in South India;
here it is translated as "melting away" (*xiāoróng*). *Maṇḍala* means "incantation" (*zhòu*). *Pativi* means "phrase" (*jù*).
It is said that the people of this country possess a pure and simple nature such that whatever words they utter all become divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*).
If a neighboring country commits aggression, they do not employ weapons or arms, but destroy the enemy with mere words; thus the opponent is immediately annihilated.
Therefore, it is called the "Country of Mantra-Syllables that Melt Away. Alternatively, it is said that only boys and girls can have their speech become mantra-syllables, while others cannot.

In the subsequent verse, it says, "skillfully refuting others. This means that by means of true refutation through the inference based on evidence (*upapatti-sādhana-anumāna*), one refutes those who advocate causeless theories and the like.
Regarding the phrase, "now, having faith in cause and effect, being unmoved by outsiders," this means establishing cause and effect through true proof (*sādhana*).
Because this inference cannot be moved by others, the final verse concludes the intended meaning: preaching the Dharma with a single mind is called the three [modes].
[The term] "obscuration" (*mèi*) likewise refers to the arising of function based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Within the eighty-first verse of the eighth section, "The Radiance of Body Hairs," there are three parts: first, verses one through eighty-one reveal the functional activity of the radiance;
second, the seven verses beginning with "According to their original conduct" explain away external doubts; third, the single verse beginning with "If there is" clarifies hearing.

The Benefit of Light. Within the initial analysis of the activity of light, there are eighty-one verses divided into two parts: first, eighty verses specifically clarify the function of the light from a single pore;

second, one verse categorically extends this to the function of the light from all pores. Within the former, there are two sections: first, seventy-nine verses clarify the functions of light through forty-five gates;
second, one verse concludes by summarizing the concise and reflecting upon the extensive, as well as the locus of the light.
Regarding the preceding forty-five sections, each contains four meanings: first, the designation of the light; second, the identification of the light’s function;

third, the cause of the light’s emergence; and fourth, the conclusion regarding the fruit of the light. Following these categories and their respective analogies, they are divided into thirteen segments:

the first concerns the salvation and deliverance through the initial light; the second concerns the manifestation of the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, practices, stupas, images, and so forth through the light. There is...

The first three lights represent the function of illumination; the causes arising from the second and third can both be understood. The fourth, the light of salvation, and the two lights below it represent the function of saving sentient beings.
Within the causes of these two lights, there are each two meanings: first, the cause of phenomena (*dharmas*), and second, the cause of the Dharma (*dharma*); these can be understood.
Regarding the fifth, the light of joy, the two lights below it represent the cultivation of life through affection for the Triple Gem. Within the initial cause:
First, creating images so that those who see them rejoice; second, praising the Buddha so that those who hear it rejoice. Within the subsequent section on the application of light:
first, causing one to take delight in the Three Jewels as the cause, which should lead to the practice of attaining the patience of non-arising regarding the Buddha as the fruit.

Regarding the four sections below the "Light of the Accumulation of Merit," they clarify the accomplishment of merit and wisdom: first, giving without merit; second, possessing the four [immeasurables], much understanding, wisdom, and preaching the Dharma correctly.
"Understanding the Dharma of Joy and Skillfully Expounding the Meaning of the Dharma Without Deficiency": The Sanskrit text says "variously proclaiming the meanings of the phrases of the Dharma.

"Non-acquisition wisdom that illuminates and perceives the principle with mastery" means that non-acquisition (*anupalambha*) itself is mastery. Fourth, "attaining dhāraṇī," which refers to revering and protecting that which upholds the Dharma.
Seventh, "the ability to relinquish light," where the seven lights below distinguish the six perfections, or [represent] the light.
The functions and causes within each [category] each have two meanings. First, maintaining pure precepts; second, generating the mind for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Within the light of wisdom, there are two: first, the wisdom of the Dharma, which causes one to awaken to the Dharma; second, the wisdom of the Buddha, which causes one to see the Buddha through its function. The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the eight lights of fearlessness, the latter two lights serve to comfort sentient beings: first, bestowing peace upon those who are terrified; second, causing those who are ill to recover. Ninth, seeing the Buddha.
The light descends as five rays, manifesting the Buddha’s joy in the Dharma, his wondrous voice preaching the Dharma, and the application of the sublime teachings of the Three Learnings.

First, it causes one to see the Buddha. If there are relatives—whether monastics or laypeople—or other sentient beings who are about to undergo this practice, they should immediately invite a sacred image and place it before them.
Taking any object, such as silk or thread, they should suspend it from the Buddha’s finger to effect the healing of the illness.
The practitioner holds one end with their hand, focusing the mind single-pointedly, performing it in accordance with the Buddha’s true arising and suchness-arising.
This will not only benefit the deceased, but the practitioner themselves shall also attain this vision of the Buddha’s light. Second, it causes one to delight in the True Dharma.

Third, to cause them to hear the Buddha’s voice; fourth, to bestow the nectar-like Dharma so that they may practice generosity and cultivate merit; fifth, to cause them to hear the most supreme Dharma of the Three Trainings.
Regarding the eight rays of light descending from the "Adornment of Ten Treasures": they are distinguished by their ability to provide jewel-treasuries for offerings to the Buddhas and other uses.
First, the inexhaustible treasure-treasury; second, the fragrance-adorned benefit for beings; third, the various names such as the jewel-banner and others; fourth, [the remaining category].
1. Causing the ground to be leveled and stupas and so forth to be adorned. 2. Producing five kinds of fragrant clouds and raining scented water to sprinkle upon the stupas and so forth.
3. Bestowing ornaments for adorning the body. 4. Bestowing precious delicacies. 5. Bestowing inexhaustible wealth upon the Three Jewels and the destitute. 6–11.

The six rays of light descending from the "Pure Light of the Eye" (cakṣuḥ-prabhā-viśuddha) manifest the function of purifying the six sense faculties; each may be understood through its respective verse. 12. The "Pure Light of Form" (rūpa-viśuddha-prabhā)... [and so forth].

Six lights. These distinguish the functions regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Within the "Pure Light of Dharmas," the first verse sets forth the names and functions, while the final verse serves as a concluding summary;
the rest may be understood accordingly. The preceding section has completed the detailed explanation of the functions of the forty-five lines of light.

From here on, one verse clarifies the summary of the concise and the revelation of the extensive, as well as the basis upon which these lights depend—namely, a small portion of what was previously explained in detail.
To speak in full detail, there are as many as immeasurable Ganges-sands; each of these individual karmic functions is distinct, yet all emerge from a single pore of the Bodhisattva.
The preceding section has clarified the function of light from one pore. From here on, the following verse categorically extends this to the functions of light from all pores;
that is to say, since the function of light from a single pore already equals the number of immeasurable Ganges-sands, the same applies to all others.
The function of the light from every single pore is likewise in each and every case. Thus concludes the second section, which generally clarifies the functional activity of the light.

Thirdly, regarding the resolution of external doubts: it refers to the concern that others, upon hearing the aforementioned description of the light’s functions—specifically that "this light awakens all sentient beings"—might give rise to doubt, saying:
"This Bodhisattva, out of compassion, emits this light at no particular time or place."
Regarding the limits [of this phenomenon], why is it that sentient beings of the present day are unable to see them? To sever this doubt, this text was composed.
Within the text, the seven verses are divided into two parts. First is the general explanation: the first line restates the preceding cause of following the light and attaining the fruit of light.

The next two lines provide the direct explanation for the doubt: that is to say, according to the past conditions, common practices, and so forth of various sentient beings, light is now emitted, and they each perceive it accordingly.
The final line concludes the application of the wisdom of emitting light. The subsequent six verses specifically manifest this;

among them, two verses provide the doctrinal explanation (*dharmadeśanā*), while the following four verses employ similes along with their synthesis. Within the former [two verses], seven types of sentient beings who obtain [the vision] are presented.
Upon encountering this light, there are seven [factors]: first, the initiation of karma; second, the longing for that practice; third, rejoicing in it;

fourth, seeing what has been performed [by others], where the preceding two or three may involve hearing from afar or being combined into one; fifth, personally practicing various acts of giving; sixth, practicing the act of making offerings to the Buddha;
and seventh, dedicating the merit toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). The subsequent analogies and their synthesis clarify these points; the first two verses explain the initial [two factors].

The analogy of the person born blind not seeing the sun is presented here. Among these, the first verse illustrates the analogy, while the subsequent verse applies the Dharma to correspond with the analogy.

The final two lines explain the doubt regarding "not seeing," referring to ordinary beings who have not yet practiced. The next two [lines] refer to those who, though they practice the Way, do so in a deviant or inferior manner—namely, non-Buddhists with false faith and the Two Vehicles with inferior understanding.
The final two verses clarify the analogies of anointing with fragrance, the precious palace, and the precious vehicle; this also begins with the first...
The verses on the Dharma shall be explained in detail later; this may be understood there. Regarding the fourth section, "The Benefits of Hearing the Light," there are three parts:

first, the generation of pure faith; second, the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); and third, the absence of doubt. Because one swiftly attains the fruit of Buddhahood through these causes, it is called the "Banner of Merit."

Within the ninth [section], the Samādhi of the Principal and its Retinue (*pramukha-parivāra-samādhi*), there are six verses divided into two parts. The first verse establishes the gateway and clarifies the intent;

the subsequent five clarify the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). Within the section on activity, there are two parts: the first four verses present the functional activity of one direction, and the final verse extends this by analogy to the remaining directions.
Regarding the former, within the single direction, the first verse clarifies the principal samādhi, and the following two verses clarify the characteristics of the retinue. Within those:
First, the heading; second, the explanation. Because the final verse presents both the primary and its associates together, the stars and moon are used as metaphors.
Within the tenth [section], the Samādhi of Quiescent Activity, thirty-four and a half verses are divided into three parts: first, one verse provides the heading and general analysis;
next, from "Alternatively, in the East" onwards, it correctly reveals the functional activity; finally, the subsequent verse beginning with "This is called" provides the summary. First...
The middle refers to how, in all directions, there is an interlacing of entry and exit like a net; therefore, it is called the "Net of Directions" (*dig-jāla*).
Within the section on activity, thirty-three and a half verses are divided into six parts.

The first two verses clarify the interlacing entry and exit throughout the ten directions, because one has attained mastery over the net of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). The second part consists of five verses, which clarify [mastery] throughout the ten directions.

The Buddha’s entry into and emergence from samādhi is unimpeded and sovereign. Within this, the first four [verses] specifically distinguish the two directions of east and west, while the final one summarizes all ten directions.
This explains the sovereignty over the world of sentient beings through the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.

However, there are two senses in which a bodhisattva exercises sovereignty over the three worlds: first, making their own body the three worlds; second, the bodhisattva [exercising mastery] over the three...
The mastery of manifesting within the world is present throughout the preceding and following contexts; it cannot be restricted to specific sections alone, as each passage shall be explained in turn.

For instance, in the section concerning the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is not necessarily limited to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), nor does it exclusively refer to Bodhisattvas entering or emerging from meditative absorption by manifesting their bodies within pores, atoms, or the tips of hairs. In this current passage, the preceding...

The two verses clarify that when entering from the east and exiting from the west, the states of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are attained simultaneously. The latter two verses clarify entering from the west and exiting from the east;

the meaning is established by reversing the logic of the former. It is not merely that when one enters directly from the east one exits directly from the west, and when one enters directly from the west one exits directly from the east;
rather, at the very moment of entering from the east, one also exits from the east, and at the moment of exiting from the west, one also enters from the west. Furthermore, one enters from the west...
The same applies to the eastern emergence. Why is this? Because the text of the summary states, "Because of mastery over samādhi.

For what reason does one attain such mastery over samādhi? It is because it is induced by such causes; that is to say, by observing that principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are neither identical nor separate.

Because they are not identical, principle conforms to phenomena without destroying their distinctness; each remains individually differentiated. Because they are not separate, phenomena conform to principle and are thereby integrated.

The one is identical to all, and all is identical to the one. Therefore, although the minds entering and emerging from meditative concentration differ, they are simultaneously identical and different.
Although all worlds, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and all bodies are distinct, they are simultaneously identical and distinct.
Subsequently, through unimpeded practice, one attains the fruit of non-obstruction; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*). This is to be understood according to the subsequent conclusion.

this is also the meaning of concealment and manifestation. Third, regarding the twelve verses beginning with "In the sense-faculties such as the eye," the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is clarified through the mutual correspondence of faculties and objects.
