To know that the ghost is a delusion of existence is called "knowing according to reality. To know that the ghost is fundamentally non-existent and that its entire substance is wood is called "knowing the true nature of the delusion's root.

Why is this so? Because one who perceives the ghost does not see the ghost; it is only by seeing the fundamental [reality] that one sees the ghost. Second, regarding the separation from the grasper (*grāhaka*):
since the previously mentioned grasped object (*grāhya*) has been exhausted, the grasper should likewise cease. The first half of the verse clarifies its persistence.
The capacity to perceive constitutes a defiled obstruction such that wisdom does not see the principle.

The second half [of the verse] clarifies that when one is free from the perceiving subject, wisdom sees the principle—just as when one perceives a ghost, one does not see the wood, but upon leaving the ghost behind, one sees the wood. The relationship between delusion and awakening is inverted; this is the natural order of things.

Next, the third section clarifies the contemplation of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in dependent origination: first, the elimination of the object of perception; second, the sublation of the perceiving subject; and third, the explanation of the contemplation itself.
Furthermore, in the beginning, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is clarified through two meanings: first, its illusory existence; second, its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Within this, the first half [of the verse] concerns the world of dependent origination, which is merely conventional discourse and illusory delusion. The second half concerns knowing that it is non-arising; only then can it be called "seeing the world.
Regarding the second point, the sublation of the perceiving subject: the first phrase reiterates the previous "seeing the world. If this seeing perceives the world...
To see is precisely the conceptualization of the world; to speak according to reality, seeing is no different from the world. Knowing it thus is called true seeing.
Regarding the benefits of the Middle Way among these three: the first phrase reiterates the aforementioned equal contemplation, while the following three phrases reveal the four benefits.

First, detachment from delusion; second, severing hindrances; third, realizing the untainted (*anāsrava*); fourth, mastery of function. The latter three clarify the contemplation of the naturelessness of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
First, restating that the former two natures are non-existent; second, correctly revealing the true nature; third, clarifying the benefit of the contemplation. Regarding the first [section]:
the upper three phrases clarify that the former two natures are both non-existent, while the lower phrase distinguishes that the nature of this non-existence is fundamentally pure.
Regarding the manifestation of true nature within the second [section]: the first half clarifies that the essence of true nature possesses characteristics yet lacks [conceptual] marks;

the second half clarifies that it transcends words and constitutes meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the three [points] clarifying the benefits of contemplation: first, one is free from false conceptualization regarding phenomena; second, one does not take pleasure in or cling to phenomena;

third, one realizes the principle without depending on cultivation; and fourth, one perceives the benefit of seeing the Buddha. The final [point] following these three, which dedicates the merit and manifests virtue, may be understood accordingly.

The sixth, "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī*), is so named because one perceives the principle through the accumulation of manifold virtues. The ten verses are divided into five sections: first, two verses set forth the Buddha’s actual virtues;

next, three clarify the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma; next, two eliminate the dualistic perception of subject and object; next, one verse concludes by knowing the benefits of the Buddha and the Dharma;
finally, two verses deduce the merits and provide a conclusion. Regarding the first section: first, the rarity of the Buddha’s virtues; second, the ability to perceive them.

This is difficult to obtain. Of the preceding [verses], the first two lines reveal that the virtue of benefiting others is twofold: first, manifesting what is rare to inspire aspiration; second, courageous vigor in benefiting sentient beings.
The subsequent line concludes these virtues by attributing them to the Buddha. The next line clarifies the virtue of self-benefit, which is also twofold:

first, being free from the stains of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); second, liberation from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The final line universally concludes both types of benefit. Hereafter...

The observer is free from attainment within the middle. The first half [of the verse] recounts what he himself perceives; the second half shows that only through the accumulation of wisdom does one behold suchness.
Second, regarding the three knowledges (*vidyā*) among the four characteristics of the Buddha’s teaching: the first verse clarifies that sentient beings are themselves the *dharmatā*.

The first three lines harmonize appearances with their underlying nature; the final line cites scriptural teaching to establish this proof. Within the former [three lines], the first two lines state that they quickly return [to the source].

Regarding "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and so forth: it means that the very characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are themselves exhaustion; they do not depend upon transition or destruction. This exhaustion is the virtue of inexhaustible exhaustion.
Being without self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Because the essence of dharma-nature is eternal, it is called "inexhaustible.

As the aforementioned passage states: "The inexhaustible, equal, and wondrous dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Instances of this text appearing above and below are indeed numerous. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:

The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible; it is of this same category. The second line distinguishes the essence through a metaphorical illustration, and the subsequent line cites scriptural authority to establish the proof;
both may be understood accordingly. Second, one verse clarifies that the speaker is identical to the subject matter. Within this, the first half harmonizes the characteristics.

The first phrase cites the preceding scriptural authority regarding the speaker; the second phrase states that because the spoken content itself lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is likewise no speaking.

The latter half provides the reason: it means that the intrinsic nature of the speaker is the inexhaustible *dharmatā*. Thus, one attains the convergence where characteristics are exhausted; that is, the nature itself is the exhaustion of characteristics.
Because this exhaustion is an "inexhaustible exhaustion," it is called "inconceivable. The three times and two phrases clarify that *dharmatā* is not...

Sentient beings—meaning that while the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is eternal, sentient beings are impermanent. In the previous assembly, the characteristics were shown to return to the nature, clarifying that nature and characteristics are not separate.
Now, it is revealed that they are not identical. The final two lines clarify that this reality is neither identical nor separate; thus, one sees the Buddha.
Third, when both subject and object are extinguished within the vision of the Middle Way, there is no subject or object acting as subject and object. That is to say:
Because the nature of sentient beings is empty, one takes that which is without sentient beings to be sentient beings; it is perceived in accordance with this.
Since the perception is also like that [which is perceived], it is thus a perception by means of non-perception. The second half [of the verse] provides the explanation:

because both perception and sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature, both subject and object are dispelled to manifest true nature. The first half dispels the perceiving subject and the perceived object, as well as that [nature].
Regarding "the seer": the second half [of the verse] refers to manifesting and fully knowing without destroying true nature (*tathatā*).
In the context of the fourfold summary, the first part summarizes the Buddha and the Dharma as known above, while the second part distinguishes the knowledge of the benefit.
This means that just as the light of Vairocana Buddha illuminates the world, this person shall likewise achieve these benefits.

Regarding the five concluding verses, the first two summarize the merit. In the first of these, the upper half shows the Buddha’s teaching of the single path (*ekayāna*), while the lower half explains that progress and wisdom constitute its multiplicity.
In the second, the upper half describes being free from the notions of existence and non-existence, while the lower half describes seeing the Buddha abiding in reality.

The seventh is the "Wisdom" [chapter]. It is so named because the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) reaches its ultimate limit, illuminating the realm of the Buddha. The ten verses are divided into four parts: the first reveals the meaning of its own name;
the next six show how ordinary fools, by contravening reason, do not see the Buddha; the following two verses show how one sees the Buddha by conforming to reason;

and the final one explains the etymological meaning of "Buddha" to reveal the ultimate truth. Regarding the first part, the first half-verse concerns the arising of wisdom through hearing the teachings.
Light. Light is the function of illumination. In the second half [of the verse], "universally illuminating and seeing the Buddha," there are two parts within the six sections.

First, one person clings to what contradicts reason. The first half clarifies that, in reality, there is no person; the second half describes the horizontal calculation of the creation of karma. The Sanskrit original says *skandha-āyatana*;
this refers to sentient beings among the sufferings of all sentient beings, for their self-nature does not exist even slightly therein. This...

This is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). The text should be rephrased as "the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and sentient beings. This is because within the self-substance of sentient beings there is not even the slightest thing;
it is merely a conventional designation. Regarding the two types of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) that deviate from reason:

the first half [of the verse] gives rise to attachment to phenomena, meaning that when one contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the body, the foolish and ignorant reckon internal phenomena and so forth to be real. The second half clarifies that the Buddha transcends those attachments; therefore, he is not like them.
[They] see [it]. With the wisdom-eye of the threefold non-dual emptiness, one does not see it. The first half [of the verse] concerns the loss of benefit;

that is, because the wisdom-eye is obscured by the veil of the two attachments, one does not perceive the True Principle, and thus does not see the Buddha. The second half concerns the presence of harm; that is, due to the two attachments, one wanders through the ocean of birth and death for many kalpas.
Fourth, the explanation of that birth and death: it refers to ordinary beings who possess afflictions, karma, and suffering, and who are in opposition [to the Truth].
Because it contradicts principle and gives rise to contention, it constitutes birth and death. For those of the Two Vehicles, they take perpetual cessation to be nirvana;

yet, since in reality [the Buddha] does not exist, it is said that both are unobtainable. Fifth, explaining the attachment of those of the Two Vehicles: regarding the paths of the two vehicles and the Great Vehicle, the first two are the paths of the Two Vehicles and the Great Vehicle.
Sixth, because of grasping at the Buddha, one cannot see him. Third, among the two types of seeing the Buddha in accordance with principle, the first is...
The first three lines of the verse reveal that the Dharma transcends words; the final line clarifies that the Buddha is likewise so.

The last line of the fourth section explains the meaning of the name "Buddha" to manifest its underlying principle. Within this, the upper three lines clarify the meaning, while the lower line concludes the naming.

That is to say, since the Buddha has eternally severed the root of conceptual discrimination—and this "root" is precisely the attachment to dharmas—it is clearly understood that one must depart from delusion before one can see the Buddha.
The eighth is "True Wisdom," so named because it perceives the true body of the Buddha’s dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This section consists of ten verses divided into five parts.

First, the initial five verses reveal that the Buddha’s name is capable of benefiting those who hear it. Within these, the first clarifies that because hearing the Buddha’s name brings such benefit, one should endure suffering in order to hear it;
the last [of these five] clarifies that in the past, one did not know this and was thus unable to endure suffering to seek out its hearing. The remaining...
Thus, one continues to transmigrate until now. Second, regarding the first [section], what is the meaning of the preceding name, and what benefit is gained by hearing it? The explanation states:

It is the non-erroneous direct realization of the objects of both the ultimate and the conventional truths. "Non-erroneous direct realization" means that one illuminates the appearance of conjunction as being, in fact, the appearance of non-conjunction.
When such awakening and illumination reach ultimate fulfillment, it is called "unsurpassed awakening. Third, the second [section].
To clarify what constitutes the basis for establishing these names mentioned previously: among them, the first [section] explains the meaning, while the last distinguishes the benefit.
Regarding the explanation, the name is established based on its essence; thus, the name is not different from the essence, and the name expresses its own essence.

Since the essence is not different from the name, and the name does not combine to form a meaning, the essence is likewise so. The benefit is as can be understood. Fourthly, two pairs further clarify the aforementioned names.

Within this, the first clarifies the wisdom of awakening that awakens according to the true and conventional objects: it means awakening to reality regarding the true object, and awakening to unreality regarding the conventional object;
it is the awakening that there is no conventional outside the true, and no true outside the conventional, such that the two objects are fused together.
Neither identical nor separate; this ultimate understanding is called "Buddha. The latter part clarifies the departure from both the subject and object of cognition.
That is to say, apart from the cognizing wisdom (*jñāna*), there is no distinct object of cognition; apart from the object of cognition, there is no distinct cognizing wisdom.

Because they are of one nature (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), it is through such realization of their oneness that they are termed "subject" and "object" of cognition. Since both are abandoned, the following line concludes [the argument].
It is said that not a single dharma can be apprehended. The five subsequent sections, consisting of three layers, further clarify the meaning of the non-combination of names and essences.
Among these, the first clarifies that all dharmas are without dependence, because they arise from the combination of many conditions and are thus devoid of the characteristics of combination.
Next, one [verse] clarifies that all phenomena lack agency and objectivity (*kartr-karma*), because they arise from the conditions of conceptual construction and karma.
Within these karmic conditions, each one, in relation to the others, functions as a single, manifold, or cooperative cause for the production of effects; thus, there is neither agent nor object.
The final [verse] clarifies that all phenomena lack abiding. The first three lines provide the explanation: because the conditions, karma, and fruits lack both agent and object.
The names and essences of all phenomena (*dharmas*) cannot ultimately be found when sought within any fixed location. The subsequent phrase provides the conclusion:

it means that the Buddhas abide in this state—without dependence, without fabrication, and without dwelling—and by being ultimately immovable, they realize the true essence; thus, they obtain the name "Awakened One."
Within the ninth [chapter], "Supreme Wisdom," the ten verses are divided into three parts: first, one verse explains the meaning of its own title;
second, eight verses manifest the Buddha’s supreme virtues; third, the final verse dedicates the merit and provides a conclusion. The first part is easily understood.

Within the second part consisting of eight verses, the first six clarify the Buddha’s virtue of internal realization, while the latter two clarify his virtue of external transformation. Among the former, the first two clarify...
The realization attained is profound. Next, two [verses] clarify the separation from that which realizes; the final two [verses] dissolve both the subject and object of realization.

Within the first two [of these], there are five general meanings. The first phrase of the initial verse indicates the object of realization; thus it says, "the place attained by the Buddha. Within this, there are four points:

first, it is not produced by conditions, nor is it realized through conditioned activity, because it is free from the characteristics of objective spheres (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*). Second, it is not accessible to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
It is also free from the characteristic of differentiation. Third, because it is not apprehended by the five consciousnesses, it is without coarseness.

Fourth, because it is not known by the mental consciousness, it is without subtlety. The first phrase of the subsequent verse also indicates that which is realized; therein, "one meaning" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because it does not fall within the realm of numerical reckoning. "Perfect Awakening transcends reckoning" here serves to manifest that which is indicated by the subject.

The following phrase concludes the object of realization. Regarding the next two [sections], the first four meanings are as follows: first, it indicates that both wisdom and its function are universal; second, it indicates the benefit of the function, namely, the extinguishing of the delusions of sentient beings.
Third, there is no function because it is free from the act of reflecting. Fourth, it functions without functioning because it is a non-reflecting reflection;
it extinguishes all delusions. The subsequent verse explains these six meanings. Among them, the first five meanings explain the aforementioned freedom from the act of reflecting.

That is to say: first, at the time of extinguishing the darkness of delusion, wisdom reflects back upon itself; since it does not grasp this as its own functional self-characteristic, it is unattached. Second, precisely by means of...
1. This non-arising possesses its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of activity; therefore, it is without recollection (*asmṛti*). 2. It does not rely on this activity as having functional efficacy;
therefore, it is without defilement (*asaṃkliṣṭa*). 3. In its activity toward objects, there is no duality of distinct entities in opposition; therefore, it is without abiding (*anāśrita*). 4.

When illuminating objects, it does not produce the characteristic of delimitation; therefore, it has no location (*adeśastha*). The final point explains that the preceding [state] is "without illumination" because it is itself illumination.

Therefore, it is said that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is indestructible. "Nature" (*xing*) refers to the essence (*ti*). This means that all functions of wisdom are *dharma*, for they all possess an essence.
In the latter two [verses], the subject and object of realization are dissolved. In the first half of the initial verse, the dissolution of this duality of subject and object is explicitly clarified:

since the two cannot be established, the one does not exist either; for the one is constituted by the two, and to speak of the one is still to speak of the two. The second half of the verse praises wisdom.
Skillfully demonstrating such a state, the subsequent verse eliminates even the traces of non-duality. Why is this so?

If one maintains a "non-existence" of duality, it still remains dualistic, because it is established by way of negating existence. Thus, non-duality is also dissolved. All things in the three realms are empty;

this is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) which is free from both existence and non-existence, for it is not an emptiness that stands in opposition to existence. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* verse states: "Grasping..."
To conceive of existence is called permanence; to calculate non-existence is called annihilation. If one is free from both existence and non-existence, this is called true emptiness.

To cling to existence is to grasp at substantial characteristics; to cling to non-existence is to be attached to the absence of substance. Not abiding in either existence or non-existence—this is therefore the true contemplation.

The benefit of the subsequent verse may be understood accordingly. The above concludes the explanation of the Buddha’s virtue of internal realization; the following two [verses] clarify the Buddha’s virtue of external transformation.

In the middle [section], the first verse teaches abiding in the True Dharma. The first half is a general instruction; the second half instructs one to abide in "non-abiding" and perceive the true reality of the body.
The subsequent verse explains and establishes this perception of the body's true reality. The first half explains the body, stating that it is "non-body as body."

Because dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature, it is said to be "non-arising"; this explains the phrase "not a body. Furthermore, because it arises precisely from this non-arising, it is said to be "manifestly arising";
this explains the phrase "and speaks of a body. The second half [of the verse] explains "seeing," meaning that since the body is not existent...
Seeing is also like the body. Since the contemplation of the body is thus, it is said that this is the Buddha’s unsurpassed body.

One may also see one's own true substance, which is precisely seeing the Buddha-body. In the latter part, the merit is attributed and the conclusion is reached; the first half attributes the merit to that which was explained.
The latter half concludes with the benefits of hearing [the teaching].
Regarding the tenth, "Firm Wisdom" (*Dṛḍhamati*): it is so named because his pure wisdom has increased and become firm through his realization of the Buddha’s realm.

The ten verses are divided into three parts: first, six verses reveal the virtue of the Buddha’s great compassion; second, three verses express the joy of having encountered and heard [the teaching]; and finally, one verse concludes by praising its inexhaustibility.

1. A general indication at the beginning and middle: the first half [of the verse] shows that [the Buddha] can save; the upper line indicates that the light of his wisdom is vast and great, while the lower line indicates that his compassionate vows are courageous and steadfast.
The second half [of the verse] concerns his appearing in the world for the sake of sentient beings. 2. Specifically revealing great compassion by observing the流转 (saṃsāra) of sentient beings.
3. Only the Buddha can save them. 4. Only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can bestow happiness. 5. Buddhas and their disciples are likewise [capable]. 6. The summary indication.
One gains benefit through seeing and hearing. Within the next three expressions of rejoicing in the encounter: first, rejoicing in the benefit gained from one’s own seeing and hearing;

second, rejoicing that the bodhisattvas in this assembly likewise possess the power of past causes and conditions for such seeing and hearing; third, rejoicing at the increase of pure faith and joy from seeing the Buddha again, whereby one is able to praise and expound the inexhaustibility of the Buddha’s wisdom.
In the final concluding praise, the first three lines conclude the many people capable of praising, while each [subsequent line]...
The preceding lines praise [the Buddha] across many kalpas; the following line concludes that the depth and breadth of the Buddha’s virtues are such that even this exposition cannot exhaust them.
Regarding the fifteenth chapter, "The Ten Abodes" (*Daśabhūmika*), there will be four sections for its explanation, identical to those previously mentioned.

First, regarding the explanation of the name: "Abiding" (*sthiti*) is so called because one has newly attained this stage and does not regress; furthermore, it is because the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas is able to dwell securely therein.
The lower fascicle of the *Mūla-karma-saṃgraha-sūtra* states: "Because one dwells in the stage of emptiness-nature, it is called a 'stage' (*bhūmi*). It continues:

"Because the mind gives rise to all merits, it is not called a 'ground' (*bhūmi*), but is simply called 'abiding'. There are many meanings of "abiding," but based on the principles, ten types are taught in summary.
"Ten Abodes" (*daśabhūmi*) is an explanatory compound based on number. According to the Sanskrit original, the full title is "The Chapter Explaining the Ten Abodes of Bodhisattvas.

Here, "bodhisattva" refers to the person who can attain the dharmas of the ten abodes; "ten abodes" refers to the dharma of the stages to be attained. Both of these constitute the signified meaning (*vācya*).
"Explaining" (*vyākhyāna*) means to reveal and manifest, and thus constitutes the signifier (*vācaka*). That is to say, in this chapter, the attainment of the bodhisattva is revealed and manifested.

Because it refers to the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). According to this interpretation, there are four types of analysis (*vigraha*): first, the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis, meaning "the ten stages of a bodhisattva";

second, the *dvigu* (numeral) analysis, because the name is manifested by means of the number ten; third, the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) analysis, because the ten stages are that which belong to the bodhisattva;
and fourth, the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis, because the person and the dharma are mutually identical.

Second, regarding the intent of the sequence: the preceding two chapters constitute the introduction to this assembly; the following three chapters constitute the main body (*śarīra*) of the teaching.
Therefore, they follow in succession.

Third, regarding the essential purport (*abhiprāya*): the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) constitute the essence, while the fulfillment of the subsequent ten practices constitutes the goal.

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: based on the three sections of the sūtra’s main body (*samyak-siddhānta*), there are three divisions: first, the explanation; second, the practice; and third, the qualities.
Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the prose (*gadya*); second, the verse (*śloka*). Within the former, there are seven divisions: 1. the section on samādhi; 2.
the section on empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) beginning with "by the power of that samādhi"; 3. the section on the emergence beginning with "the Bodhisattva Dharmamati"; 4. [and so forth].

1. The Section on Addressing the Fundamental Portion for All Inferior Beings; 2. The Section on the Five Buddha-Sons Explaining the Inferior Portion; 3. The Section on Auspicious Omens Appearing through the Buddha’s Supernatural Power at that Time;
4. The Section on the Formation of the Proof through the Buddha’s Supernatural Power once again.
Within the first section, there are four parts: First, the person who enters meditative concentration, namely the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
Why does this bodhisattva enter? Because he is the honored one of the assembly; it is to reveal that these ten stages (*bhūmi*) are understood through wisdom.

Second, "relying on the Buddha's power" is for the purpose of clarifying the principle of the teacher-disciple relationship, and to demonstrate that this bodhisattva is free from pride (*māna*). Third, the intention for entering meditative concentration...

There are five reasons: first, to show that the Dharma being taught is not within the realm of discursive thought; second, because this samādhi is the very essence of the Dharma; third, to show that it is not taught unless one has realized it through realization;
fourth, to observe the capacities of sentient beings and examine the Dharma; and fifth, to receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha. Regarding the name of the samādhi:
it designates the specific person and the distinct Dharma, as well as to distinguish it from samādhis that are not the fruit [of the path]. Thus, it is said that the Bodhisattva is able...

Because it gives rise to skillful wisdom, it is called "skillful wisdom of means" (*upāya-kauśalya*). Because it possesses many gateways, it is said to be "immeasurable. Regarding the term *samādhi*, when fully expressed it is called *samāpatti*;
this is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*). The details are as explained previously.

In the second section on the "Augmentation" (pratyaya), there are three parts: first, a general explanation of the augmenting Buddhas; second, for the purpose of increasing [the merit], a manifestation of what the augmentation is intended to achieve;
third, from "Good son, as below," a clear exposition of the characteristics of the augmentation. Within the first part, there are six sections.

First, to reveal the locations of the augmenting Buddhas, it is said they are "a thousand," because their conduct is inferior when compared [to the Buddha]. The number of subsequent Buddhas is the same as this. This explains the two meanings of the word "each" (prati).
First, regarding each of the ten directions; second, within each individual direction, the distance between the various lands is two thousand [yojanas] each.

Below, this clarifies the number of Buddhas who provide empowerment. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "For what reason do many Buddhas empower [the teaching], thereby manifesting the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher?
It is to increase the mind of reverence. Furthermore, it is to manifest that all Buddhas speak in concert. This applies to both those in the state of cause and those in the state of fruition.
Furthermore, the three [aspects] are all identical to what follows regarding the Buddha’s name being the same and his preaching the Dharma to the bodhisattvas. This is for four reasons:
first, to clarify that the Dharma attained is not different; second, because once these bodhisattvas hear that the Buddha’s name is the same as their own, their joy increases even further.

Third, it reveals that within the state of abiding, cause and effect are identical. Fourth, it reveals that the manifestation of all Buddhas through the gateway of abiding is itself named "Dharma-Wisdom" (Dharmamati), by virtue of the power of the Dharma and by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Fifth, "appearing universally before them" reveals that those Buddhas of the ten directions arrive without coming.

Fifth, from the words "Good son, you are able... onwards, it demonstrates the attainment of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the phrase "you are able": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)*
This is because it reveals that others are incapable [of entering it]. Why is this so? For one who enters this samādhi is rare and difficult to find;

unless it be through the power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, the past vows of Vairocana, the manifestation of his majestic spiritual power, and one's own roots of goodness, no one else is able to enter it.

Question: Why does the Buddha specifically cite the name of this samādhi and praise it in the midst of the assembly? Answer: It is because he wishes to cause each member of the assembly to know of it and to feel a longing for it.
Section Six, "The Six Sons of Good Family," explains the causes for attaining this samādhi from the perspective of the ten directions. This section has two parts: first, a detailed exposition;

second, a summary beginning with "Entering this... Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, explaining the primary causes for attaining the samādhi; second, [the section] beginning with "Furthermore, this... which transitions...

This clarifies the cause of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). That is to say, entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the cause for empowerment; empowerment, in turn, has aspirations (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth as its cause.

Although these causes differ, the empowerment and the meditative absorption are simultaneous; this shall be explained in detail later. Regarding the passage where the Buddhas therein describe how they themselves empower through their own power and so forth:
if the Buddhas did not speak, the assembly would not know [this], because Dharmamati was in meditative absorption and thus could not have spoken. For...
This is for the purpose of causing the great assembly to give rise to reverence and admiration. The empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by many Buddhas bearing the same name is as previously revealed.

Regarding the subsequent manifestation of the causes for this empowerment, there are three: first, the prior vow of Vairocana; second, the manifest power of Vairocana; and third, the power of one’s own roots of goodness. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"That Buddha previously made such a vow, and now he again empowers himself. As for why he had this vow beforehand, it is because the Buddha... [text continues]
In the past, I witnessed this very event; because I then made a vow, it is concluded here in two parts:

first, the conclusion regarding the cause for entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and second, the conclusion regarding the cause for preaching the Dharma. Question: Regarding the application of power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and meditative absorption, which comes first?

If absorption were prior and the application of power subsequent, then one should not say, "You are able to enter this samādhi," for this [samādhi] is that which is shared by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
[The Buddha] bestows [his power] upon you. Furthermore, it says from "Moreover, Vairocana... up to "...and by the power of your own roots of goodness, you enter this samādhi.

If the bestowal of power occurred first and the meditative concentration (samādhi) afterwards, then the section on the bestowal of power should not be explained only after the section on the samādhi. Moreover, the commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* explains the section on the bestowal of power as follows:
"For what reason is the bestowal of power given? It is for the sake of explaining this Dharma," and it does not say it is for the sake of entering samādhi.
Furthermore, regarding the intent of that commentary, it states within the section on "additions" (*ādhika*): "For what reason is only Vajragarbha added, while others are not?
It is because this bodhisattva has attained this samādhi, whereas others have not. Since both passages provide textual evidence, how are they to be reconciled?
Answer: According to these texts, it appears that the two occur sequentially; however, in reality, the two matters are accomplished simultaneously. Why is this?
If one were to enter meditative absorption before receiving empowerment, the resolve would not be capable of eliciting the power of the Buddhas' sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Conversely, if one were to receive empowerment before entering absorption, one's own power would be insufficient to enter such a profound concentration. Therefore, one enters absorption at the very moment of receiving empowerment.
This refers to receiving empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) at the very moment of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Regarding the eleven phrases concerning the purpose of this empowerment, the first ten distinguish the specific details, while the last one provides a summary.

Within the former, the first is for the sake of causing bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to hear the teaching on these stages, thereby increasing their teacherless, spontaneous wisdom (*anācāryaka-svayambhū-jñāna*). The second...

1. To cause the realization of the unimpeded dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); 2. To cause the mastery of all phenomena; 3. To cause the knowledge of the spiritual lineages (gotra) of those to be converted; 4.
To cause the absence of obstruction when proceeding to the places where those to be converted reside; 5. To cause one’s own practice to be free from hindrance; 6.

To cause the attainment of superior and wholesome qualities that increase the methods of conversion; 7. To cause the attainment of the Buddha’s realization of true gnosis (tattvajñāna); 8. To cause awakening.
The Buddha possesses the wisdom that thoroughly understands conventional reality. The ninth [purpose] is to enable the knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*) of those to be converted.

The tenth is to enable the attainment of *dhāraṇī* and eloquence (*pratibhāna*). The final one is a summary: it is for the purpose of inspiring those bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the ten stages (*bhūmi*) so that they may enter them.

Regarding the three types of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there are three [sections]. First is the empowerment of verbal action (*vākkarma*); next, at this time, the Buddhas immediately bestow the empowerment of mental action (*manaskarma*) as indicated below;

finally, at this time, each of the Buddhas extends the empowerment of physical action (*kāyakarma*) as indicated below. Within the first [section], why is the empowerment of verbal action bestowed first?
Because it follows upon the preceding speech. Why is there an empowerment of speech? To cause eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to increase. Regarding eloquence:

There are two kinds: first, accomplishment through the power of others; second, accomplishment through one's own power. As the Sūtra says: "Because of receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, one expounds the Dharma.

Furthermore, this exhortation to speak by relying on power constitutes the characteristic of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Second, regarding empowerment of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*), it is for the purpose of increasing wisdom.
This section has three parts: first, the empowerment; second, the inquiry "Why is this? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*); and third, the explanation beginning with "This samādhi... Regarding the first of these:
It is endowed with ten kinds of knowledge: first, the "unimpeded" refers to the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*pratisaṃvid*), because it is the basis for the teaching of the Dharma.
Second, the "unattached" refers to the wisdom of unattached eloquence (*pratibhāna*), because one is without attachment regarding that which is taught.

Third, the "uninterrupted" refers to the wisdom of spontaneous eloquence; it does not depend on a sequential order of speech, but rather the words flow without interruption, proceeding freely and at will in every instance.
1. Because it does not forget names and meanings; 2. It is free from delusion, because it clearly understands the words and their meanings without the darkness of ignorance;
3. It is without variation, because what is taught is identical to that of the Buddha and without distinction; 4. It is without error, because it is taught without seeking fame or profit; 5.
It is immeasurable, because it teaches all dharmas to all vessels as appropriate, without limit; 6. It is unsurpassed.
This cannot be penetrated by the wisdom of bodhisattvas; even the wisdom of other Buddhas cannot surpass it. Ninth, "unwearied," because there is no fatigue in preaching the Dharma.
Tenth, "irresistible," because nothing can outshine or eclipse it so as to cause it to become obscure;
based on this, its exposition cannot be suppressed or overcome to cause one to retreat or be disheartened. Next, the term "invokers" refers to all Tathāgatas.
Possessing power and compassion toward all bodhisattvas, he is able to bestow [these qualities] universally; why then would he bestow them upon Dharmamati alone?
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "The power of this samādhi is such by its very nature" means that Dharmamati attained this samādhi through the power of the Dharma-wisdom (dharmaprajñā).
By the power of samādhi, it is the natural law that the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas should be summoned. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because this bodhisattva has attained this dharma of samādhi, whereas others have not. Regarding the empowerment of the three bodies (*trikāya*), it serves to increase their majestic power and to cause the arising of samādhi.
In the text, the phrase "the various Buddhas" (four instances of "one") indicates the empowerment of many Buddhas; thus, it carries the sense of plurality.

As before, regarding the two hands each extending [to touch the crown]: this reveals that many Buddhas, each observing and touching the crown, do not obstruct one another, because these marks are themselves sovereign.
Furthermore, they do not leave their original positions, nor do their hands become elongated; this is the unimpeded nature of extension and contraction.
Furthermore, "departing" means that he dwells without obstruction. Third, "the right hand" signifies that the Buddha’s speech accords with the wisdom of the Dharma;

it also demonstrates that what is spoken by the wisdom of the Dharma accords with the Dharma-realm and its activities. Fourth, "touching the crown of the head" signifies that what is spoken by the wisdom of the Dharma is received from above through the power of the Honored One.
Regarding the third section, the "Arising from Samādhi," one emerges from meditative concentration briefly for four reasons: first, because the task of the samādhi has been completed;
second, because superior power has already been attained; third, because the time has come to preach the Dharma; and fourth, because meditative concentration itself is devoid of verbal expression.
This is explained in detail within the section on "Arising from the Dwelling of the Ten Stages."

In the fourth main section, there are two parts: first, clarifying the essence of the dwelling; second, distinguishing the characteristics of the dwelling, as in the passage "that bodhisattva dwells...

and so forth. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a comparative analysis of this stage against the preceding and succeeding stages; second, the formal explanation of the text. Regarding the first sub-section: why is this not explained within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)?

Because those levels have not yet established a fixed stage (*avasthā*), whereas this is the very essence of a stage. Why is this called a "dwelling" (*vihāra*)? [Because it is the place where one abides.]
This refers to the great bodhicitta of this Bodhisattva, which takes three types of mind as its essence: first, the straightforward mind; second, the profound mind;

and third, the mind of great compassion. Although these three minds constitute the essence throughout the stages of the three levels of worthies and the ten bhūmis, they are each designated as the essential nature by being associated with one specific stage in order to distinguish between the superior, middling, and inferior qualities of the worthies. Furthermore, these three minds... [ordinary beings...]

If one [of these] exists, the other two must necessarily be present; if they are lacking, it is not so. Now, this stage of abiding (*vihāra*) is due to the understanding derived from wisdom (*prajñā*), whereby the characteristics of the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*) become manifest.
Because wisdom is the basis upon which all practices depend, it is designated as the "place of abiding. In the older translations, this was rendered as "lineage" (*gotra*);

among the four types of lineage, it refers to the "cultivated lineage" (*śikṣita-gotra*), and within the five types of spiritual disposition (*pañca-gotra*), it refers to the "bodhisattva-disposition. This is the nature of the lineage.

The stage is also a dwelling place. The essence of the stage of the "Virtuous of the Middle" is called the "Practitioner" (*yogācāra*), because within the essence of this bodhicitta, there is a profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) that delights in cultivating all virtuous practices;

The essence of the stage of the "Virtuous of the Superior" is called the "Great Vow," because within the essence of this bodhicitta, there is a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that rescues and protects all beings.

Because of [compassion for] suffering sentient beings. That is to say, as the stages and characteristics of that Bodhisattva gradually ascend, their great compassion becomes increasingly profound.
