Continuation of the *Lüshù Kāndìngjì* on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Scroll Eight (Combining the Root and the Branches), [covering] up to the Tenth Dedication.
Within the sixth dedication, "The Dedication that Accords with and Fortifies All Roots of Goodness," there are two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.

The preceding section has two parts: first, the clarification of the stages and practices; second, from "When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this... onwards, the clarification of the fruits of the stages.
Within the first part, there are three sections: first, citing the name and raising a question; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, or for...
onwards, the extensive explanation based on that question; third, from "O Son of the Buddha, this is called... onwards, the conclusion of the name based on the explanation.
Regarding the beginning and middle: as for the "names," those listed within the preceding section on the fundamental divisions differ from these.

The former were named "entry into all equal roots of goodness" (*sarva-samānakuśalamūla-praveśa*), while here they are called "conformity with all firm roots of goodness" (*sarvakuśalamūla-dṛḍhānuloma*). The Jin translation reads "conformity with all firm roots of goodness.
According to this, "conformity" (*anuloma*) carries the meaning of the former "entry" (*praveśa*), and "firm" (*dṛḍha*) carries the meaning of the former "equal" (*sama*). That is to say:
The practice of cultivation consists in entering, in accordance with reality, the firm and equal *dharmatā*.

If one follows this interpretation, the names found in the original [Chinese] text and those in the Jin translation must both be reoriented and established here, because the term "all" (*sarva*) pertains to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
If one adopts the sense of the meaning, it should likewise state: "dedicating all roots of goodness so as to accord with the firm."
Regarding the explanation of the name, "conforming entry" means that which is able to conform and enter. The firm and equal roots of goodness are that which is entered by conformity.
That is to say, among all the practices and deeds cultivated, there is none that does not conform and enter the firm and equal *dharmatā*.
This refers to the conforming entry into the roots of goodness such as firmness; the dedication of these roots of goodness such as firmness all depend on the possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*).

This is an explanation. The *Mūlakarma-sūtra* explains it as follows: Because one practices the characteristics of conditioned goodness and unconditioned goodness non-dually, it is called "the dedication of all roots of goodness that accord with equality."

In the third section, the detailed explanation based on the inquiry, there are two parts: first, clarifying the body upon which the practice depends; second, from "endowed with" onwards, clarifying how practice arises based on that body.

Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, distinguishing the types [of bodies]; second, from "majestic power" onwards, praising their virtues. Regarding the first, the phrase "or as a sovereign king, etc.
means that the body through which a bodhisattva practices *dāna* (generosity) is not of only one kind, but varies according to what is appropriate for the capacities of sentient beings. Thus...
Setting aside the word "or. Question: If that is so, why not cite others? Answer: It is due to three reasons that the sovereign is cited first:
(1) because this body possesses things worthy of being given; (2) because citing the superior can encourage the inferior; and (3) because citing one category implies the rest.
Regarding the ten phrases in the subsequent praise of virtues: (1) his majestic reputation is vast and far-reaching; (2) he correctly transforms all those below him.
"Equally covering. Regarding the single canopy (*eka-āvaraṇa*), there are two meanings. First, the ten wholesome dharmas serve as the canopy;

it covers and shelters the multitude of beings. As stated in the "Canopy of Giving" section below: "In order to cause sentient beings to obtain the canopy of mastery, so that they may uphold all wholesome dharmas.
It further states: "In order to cause sentient beings to be able to cover each and every thing universally over all," and so forth. Second, by...
The canopy of loving-kindness: because it universally shelters and covers all sentient beings. As it is said in the vow within the *Parikara-dāna*:
"In order to cause sentient beings to attain a mind of equanimity that covers all beings; in order to cause all to universally cover all with various roots of goodness;
and in order to cause sentient beings to attain the great dedication that universally covers all sentient beings. Furthermore, as it is said:
In the sixty-sixth section below, the Great Foremost King says to Sudhana: "I know only this samādhi-door of 'Great Compassion as the Foremost' which accords with the world.
As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, because they universally shelter all sentient beings with their high-canopy compassionate hearts...
and so on, as extensively explained. Third, by means of "Free from Defilement" (*vimalā*), it indicates the foremost among the honorable.
4. Regarding "In the Dharma," the ten wholesome paths guide sentient beings. 5. "With the four" refers to gathering beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

6. The phrase "The Bodhisattva" below is a statement concluding the virtues; its text should properly be placed under "Free from karmic obstructions. 7. "Possessing greatness" refers to attracting an indestructible retinue. 8.
"Free from the multitudes" refers to the cultivation of the adornment of the body's marks and signs. 9. "Obtaining Nara" refers to the firmness of the body and physical strength.
Great. Tenth, attaining purity, whereby there are no obstacles of evil karma below; this may be understood as it is clearly revealed.
Second, regarding the practice arising from the basis of the body, there are three parts: first, the practice of dedication according to characteristics;

second, the practice of signless dedication, beginning with "When the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, dedicate their various roots of goodness in this manner, their bodies and speech... and so forth; third...
For what reason is it called "downward dedication"? To explain this term "dedication," there are two parts:
first, a brief presentation and listing of the causes and conditions for dedication; second, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, according to...
onwards, an extensive elucidation of the causes and conditions for dedication based on that brief presentation.

The preceding section has three parts: first, a listing of the donor and the objects given; second, the identification of the field of merit (*dakṣiṇīya*) through the categories of "middling" and "inferior";
third, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus... onwards, the skillful integration of the practice of giving to accomplish the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a general heading in one sentence; second, a detailed enumeration beginning with "or he gives... and so forth. Within this enumeration, the giving of one's own body and royal throne is excluded.
In addition to the aforementioned categories such as wives and children, there are seventy-five gates. If gardens and groves are distinguished separately, there are seventy-six kinds.

These are: drink, food, superior flavors, vehicles, clothing, flowers, garlands, mixed incense, unguents, couches and seats, houses, dwellings, lamps, medicinal decoctions, precious vessels, precious chariots, elephants, horses, thrones and canopies (twenty), umbrellas, and banners.
Banners; precious objects and ornaments; jeweled crowns; crest-jewels; royal sovereignty; one’s own body, wife, and children used to ransom prisoners held in confinement;
one’s own body taking the place of a prisoner facing death (30); skin, scalp hair, and head-hair; eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, head, crown of the head, hands, and feet (40);
blood, flesh, bones, marrow, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine (50), small intestine, thick skin, thin skin, and fingers.
The toes; the flesh-covered nails; seeking the Dharma by entering fire; suffering for the sake of protecting the Dharma; seeking the Dharma by relinquishing all that exists within the seas;
using the Dharma to guide and transform others (60); severing male organs; the Buddha’s arising to manifest them so they may be seen; giving away the great earth; and giving away servants.
Giving one’s own body as an offering and service to the Buddhas and sentient beings; giving cities, towns, villages, palaces, (70) gardens, wives, children, and all means of subsistence;
and establishing great assemblies of giving. (75) Second, within the discernment of the types of fields, there are three.

The first phrase indicates the general manifold categories; the subsequent "or" (vā) and following terms specifically manifest them; and the final "etcetera" (ādi) collectively summarizes their universal application.

The initial and concluding [phrases] are easily understood. Within the specific manifestations, there are seven phrases: the first five consist of five pairs making ten categories, while the latter two each comprise many categories, totaling seventy.
These are: first, differences in place of origin; second, differences in measure and conduct; third, differences in ritual and contemplation; fourth, differences between male and female.
1. The diversity of the five destinies; 2. The diversity of mental dispositions; 3. The diversity of seeking—these are all clearly manifest as they can be known.

Regarding the third [topic], the skillful inclusion of the practice of giving and its accomplishment as dedication for the practitioner: this is because, in order to demonstrate that the cultivation of practice accords with the dedication of firm roots of goodness, one first sets forth and enumerates the characteristics of dedicating all roots of goodness in accordance with firmness. Why is this so? Because of what was previously...
This passage brings forth the donor, the object, and the field to manifest the objective; it now follows the practice of the mind of firm dedication.
These ten phrases collectively summarize the wholesome gathering [of merit], as they manifest the ability to conform to a firm mind of dedication.

Thus, at the time of giving, one generates a wholesome, gathering mind and dedicates it all entirely. This means that because form is itself suchness, one gathers the form-objects belonging to the act of giving and dedicates them.
It should be understood that the same applies to the dedication toward the suchness of form, up to and including the dedication toward the suchness of consciousness. Why is this so?

Is it not the case that the roots of goodness to be dedicated have already conformed to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? Answer: It is precisely to clarify this point that roots of goodness which conform to the *dharmatā* are now being dedicated to the *dharmatā*;
only then are they called "roots of goodness dedicated in accordance with the firm [nature]. As stated in the subsequent explanation of the names, this is the sixth dedication.

This name is established based on this passage. One should know that within the subsequent detailed exposition, each individual practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is cultivated in reliance upon this.

The ten phrases in the text are divided into three parts: the first phrase provides a general heading; the section beginning with "That is to say" provides a specific explanation; and the final phrase, "Skillfully gathering wisdom and giving," provides a summary conclusion.

Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the restatement of the preceding practice of giving; second, the section beginning with "Generating goodness," which constitutes the actual exposition.
This can be understood. Next, the eight phrases specifically clarify the following: first, five phrases generally clarify the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the recipient;

therein, although there is a distinction between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), all are subsumed under the name "aggregate. Next, one phrase clarifies the five aggregates of the donor;

their inclusion and the manifestation of their stages are subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), because they follow the sequence of honor and status. Next, one phrase clarifies that which is given.

Sentient beings are comprised within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The next phrase clarifies that the external objects given as gifts are non-sentient and thus are comprised solely within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The final phrase is a summary; it summarizes how the preceding eight phrases do not include the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation of the causes and conditions for the practice of dedication, there are two parts: first, a preliminary analysis; second, the commentary on the text. Of these, the former is presented briefly.
This is analyzed through four sections: first, the distinction between the preceding and succeeding; second, the internal and external classification; third, the three types of giving;

and fourth, the three categories. Regarding the first: it means that what is extensively explained later is contrasted with what is briefly indicated earlier, such that they mutually possess or lack certain elements without distinction.

Specifically, the three acts of giving an umbrella, giving one’s head, and protecting the Dharma while undergoing suffering exist in the latter [section] but are absent from the former. Furthermore, among the acts of rescuing prisoners from jail mentioned earlier, the act of giving the Dharma is not present.

This necessarily reveals that [the kingdom] exists. In the previous section on bestowing cities and towns, there were no gates to prevent the collection of taxes; this subsequently reveals its existence.

In the previous section, relinquishing everything within the seas for the sake of seeking the Dharma constitutes a brief summary; this subsequently reveals the various categories such as the state, cities, and populace.

In the middle section, transforming and guiding through the Dharma corresponds to the subsequent revelation of prohibiting killing and establishing them in the precepts. All other matters are likewise extensive.

The same. Later, in the detailed exposition, there are sixty categories in total. If one counts the distinct types of color-form (*rūpa*), excluding repetitions from the intermediate sections, there are one hundred and seven kinds.
Yet, if discussed in terms of both the gross and the subtle, they are truly immeasurable; that is to say, within these eighty-seven [categories], there are further subdivisions.
Within these categories, there are further sub-varieties, such as the many kinds of powdered incense or the many kinds of lotus flowers.
Furthermore, it is because one gives all manner of things within a kingdom; because one provides every kind of requisite for sustaining life;

and because it is said that the objects given may be immeasurable and boundless. Moreover, it is said that the Bodhisattva provides for all the needs of sentient beings according to their requirements.
Because such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) items are bestowed as gifts, according to these various texts, the categories of objects are extremely vast.
For the sake of brevity, I shall describe them in their general characteristics; it is impossible to fix them definitively at one hundred and seven or any other number.

Formerly, Master Guangtong took the aforementioned introductory passages and synthesized them into one hundred and twenty gates of giving, with each and every practice being endowed with the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).

Each of these individually possesses the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) and the seven kinds of giving (*dāna*), which, when multiplied together, result in eighty-four thousand modes of practice.
Regarding the seven kinds of giving: there are three aspects of the mind, three aspects of time—namely, joy—and three aspects of the object, namely, the giver, the recipient, and the material gift.
There is one way of entering into principle: namely, illuminating the principle of the single quiescence of the emptiness of the three things.

Established according to this, although one wishes to broaden the gates of giving, one instead narrows its formal characteristics. Why is this? Because of the passages cited previously from five locations.
Second, regarding "internal and external," there are two types: first, taking one's own body as internal and the bodies of others as external; that is to say, the Bodhisattva...

Sacrificing one’s body to rescue prisoners, taking their place in death, seeking the Dharma, or protecting the Dharma; whether it be cutting one’s own flesh, acting as a servant, or providing labor and service—all these are called internal giving (*adhyātma-dāna*).
If one gives away one’s wife, children, kinsmen, servants, or even elephants and horses, all these are called external giving (*bāhya-dāna*).
Sentient beings are internal, while non-sentient things are external; thus, both the aforementioned internal and external are collectively termed internal. What is [the object] of this?
All other things are termed "external. Regarding the three types of giving: showing the way for a Buddha to appear is entirely the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).

Saving prisoners, substituting oneself for the death penalty, severing the intent to kill, and rescuing those whose male organs have been destroyed are all the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). All remaining acts are the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*);
these may involve giving food and clothing to free others from the terrors of hunger and cold, or providing the teaching of the Dharma to cause them to practice and thereby attain liberation.

The terrors of the evil realms and other such evils are all subsumed within the gift of fearlessness. Among the four categories of the three aggregates (*skandha*), there are three: first, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); second, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*);

and third, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Regarding the first, the five aggregates: this refers to giving one’s own body, wife, children, inner palace, retinue, servants, and even elephants, horses, and so forth;
these are all gifts of the five aggregates. All remaining objects of giving are not included in the category of sentient beings.

All of these are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Among the gifts of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), the expressive names, phrases, and syllables are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and are included within the aggregate of form as sound.
The meanings and principles expressed [by them] are not subsumed by any aggregate, because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Next, regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*):
since one gives away the six internal sense faculties belonging to the bodies of oneself and others, and among external objects, flowers, incense, music, food and drink, clothing, and the Dharma...

Within the act of giving, the means of expression (*abhidhāna*) and the objects expressed (*abhidheya*), and so forth, constitute the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*). Alternatively, within the gift of a single object, two, three, four, or more [bases] may be present;

for example, among food and clothing, there are the bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. All other cases should be understood by applying this principle accordingly. Regarding the subsequent eighteen elements (*dhātu*):
first, the twelve internal and external elements may be inferred from the [twelve] bases (*āyatana*). As for the intermediate six elements, they depend on the internal [bases].

Because it follows the faculties (*indriya*), one gives according to those faculties. Now, among these eighteen [types of giving], some constitute a temporary application of giving, while others constitute the permanent essence of giving;

this should be reflected upon according to reason. The subsequent explanation in the text has three parts: first, a general clarification of how various acts of giving accomplish the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

second, "That which is called... and below, a specific clarification of how various acts of giving accomplish the practice of dedication; third, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [and so forth].
The phrase "according to the various sentient beings" below serves as a general summary of the preceding practices of giving to establish the purpose of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

This section consists of two parts: first, a general enumeration of the objects given; second, the phrase "by means of those [objects]" below, which refers back to what precedes and introduces what follows. However, this passage should ideally be moved to appear after the section on "complete and perfect giving.
Alternatively, it may serve both general and specific functions: in relation to the general, it belongs to the preceding section; in relation to the specific, it belongs to the subsequent section.

Regarding the second section, the detailed explanation, there are sixty gates in total. Within the first [gate], the offering of food, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the practice of giving;

second, the explanation of the practice of dedication, beginning with "May all... and so forth; third, the simultaneous conclusion of these two practices, beginning with "This is for... and so forth. Within the first of these [three], there are four parts.
First, the excellence of the gift; second, giving to sentient beings clarifies the field of the gift; third, the humility of the mind clarifies the mind capable of giving.
Within this, the five phrases are divided into three parts: first, one phrase generally clarifies the purity of the mind; next, three phrases specifically manifest the characteristics of that purity:
(1) being associated with a thought free from greed; (2) the purity of the two wheels [of body and speech]; and (3) being associated with a thought free from stinginess. Finally, it is complete.

The next line concludes the practice of application (*prayoga*). Within the subsequent practice of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), there are two parts: first, the reference to the preceding [section] to introduce the following;
this text should have appeared previously, as already explained. Second, within the actual practice of dedication, there are ten vows: 1.

Because food can nourish the spirit, one vows to attain wisdom (*jñāna*). Since wisdom nourishes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is called "wisdom-food" (*jñānāhāra*). 2. Food nourishes the power of the mind; when employed, it is inexhaustible...

1. Obstruction: The eight consciousnesses are unobstructed, for they are the primary truth (*paramārtha*). 2. Sound, smell, taste, and touch must undergo transformation and decay to serve as sustenance;
their intrinsic nature does not exist. 3. Knowing that the nature of food is empty, craving does not arise. 4.
Within non-existence, one finds joy and delight, thereby attaining liberation. 5. Food can fill the void; may the wisdom of others be fulfilled. 6. Food does not endure for long.
May they instead attain firmness in the Dharma; may they have the eight kinds of nutriment to accomplish their capabilities. May they be able to gather what is wholesome;
may they have the nutriment of food for body and mind to travel and contemplate. May they attain two bodies that pervade the Dharma-realm;

may they attain transformation bodies to respond to the world and act as fields of merit for receiving offerings. The subsequent double conclusion of these two practices can be understood accordingly, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

On the fifteenth and the first day of the sixteenth [lunar day], it is also taught that one should offer food, drink, vehicles, clothing, flowers, incense, bedding, dwellings, lamps, and so forth, making a vow and dedicating the merit for each item.
There are various similarities and differences regarding these; one should cite both sets of teachings to clarify them.

In the second [section] on the giving of drink, there are three parts: first, a brief presentation of the practice of giving; second, from "By this" onwards, the clarification of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); and finally, from "This is for" onwards, the dual conclusion of these two practices.

The first and last [parts] are easily understood. Within the practice of dedication, there are two sections: first, the citation of the preceding [practice] to introduce the subsequent one (which is easily understood);

and second, the actual manifestation [of the dedication]. Within this manifestation, there are ten vows: first, because of the turbidity of craving regarding the understanding of the Dharma; second, that water may be ever-flowing...
1. It eliminates [suffering], because even small [causes] can produce great results. 2. The three waters are largely present and discerned, which causes thirst and craving to cease.
3. Because the five Buddha-wisdoms are free from worldly greed and craving for water. 4. Because the nature of the joy of Dharma is free from defiled craving. 5.

Because realizing the water of the Dharma-nature constitutes the attainment of the Dharmakāya. 6. Because the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) harmonizes the mind. 7. Because one realizes the ocean of perfect wisdom. 8. Ten.
Because the manifested clouds of the body of the dharma-realm respond to the rain of the Dharma.
Regarding the third [section], the bestowing of superior flavors, there are four parts: first, clarifying the practice of giving; second, from "By this...

onwards, clarifying the practice of dedication; third, "This is for... serves as the double conclusion of these two practices; fourth, from "In order to... onwards, clarifying the intent of dedication. Within the first [part], there are two sections; first, the general enumeration of giving.
The flavor can be understood. What follows—that is, the section below—reveals the substance bestowed. This consists of three parts: first, distinguishing the perfection of flavor;
second, "moistening" below to clarify the subtle texture of the essence; and third, "being able to" below to reveal its functional efficacy. These thirteen phrases can be understood accordingly.

Within the two types of dedication practice, there are two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the section beginning with "That which is called" below, which correctly elucidates them. Within this elucidation, there are ten vows.
The first is that whatever food the Buddha eats, he obtains the most excellent flavor. This is the mark of supreme taste among the thirty-two marks of a great man.

1. Because behind the Buddha’s great tooth there is a spring of nectar (*amṛta*). 2. Because of the wisdom that realizes the Dharma and benefits sentient beings. 3. Because one realizes the flavor of the jewels;

the place where the nature is realized and encountered is called the City of Dharma (*dharmapura*). 4. Because the clouds of the body pervade everywhere, preaching the Dharma to discipline and transform beings.

5. Because the joy of understanding the flavor of the Dharma through wisdom permeates both body and mind. 6. Because regarding worldly flavors one attains a thought associated with non-attachment, diligently practicing the flavor of the Buddha-Dharma.
Seventh, attaining the flavor of equality and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Eighth, the flavor of the Dharma nourishes wisdom so that one does not regress.

Ninth, realizing the Buddha’s equalizing dharma-wisdom, one transforms the faculties [of beings] such that the ultimate and conventional truths are unimpeded. Tenth, gradually deepening in the flavor of the Dharma, one presides over the ultimate state of non-obstruction.
These three summaries and four intentions are all easily understood.

In the fourth section on the giving of vehicles, there are three parts: first, a brief presentation of the act of giving; second, the practice of dedication as clarified by the passage beginning with "By all...

(*yena*); and third, the conclusion beginning with "This is for... (*idam*). The first and last parts are easily understood. Upon consulting the Sanskrit manuscript, the general term for "vehicle" is called *yāna*.
The syllable *ya* is pronounced as *yu-wo* (余我). If referring specifically to a "chariot," it is called *śakaṭa*; if referring to a "state carriage" (*lǜ*), it is called *ratha*.

Regarding *yun-a-la-ta* (yugānta), it is explained as follows in the sixteenth section on the "Giving of Chariots. Within the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, the citation of the preceding [text] to introduce the subsequent;
second, the actual manifestation of the content, beginning with "That which is called... and so forth. Among these, ten vows are revealed: the first is general, while the others are specific.

These specifics have no separate essence apart from the general; they are all identical to the general, differing only in that distinct meanings are established under specific names. First: "May it reach only up to Great Bodhi."

Second, it is not minor; third, it is not like the *ḍāka* and other [tantras] that were initially established and later discarded, for [this teaching] has been integrated into this [system]; fourth, it is uniquely supreme.
Fifth, it is not inferior; sixth, its wisdom is profound; seventh, its compassion is vast; eighth, it is equipped with an ocean of merit; ninth, it transcends all that is tainted (*sāsrava*);
tenth, it is universally operative, for it does not concern itself with only one direction or one sentient being.
In the fifth [section] on the gift of robes, the textual structure consists of three parts as before. Within the section on dedication (*pariṇāmana*), six internal points are explicitly revealed:
First, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are like outer garments that cover the body. Second, because one does not act without shame, one is free from the state of being naked.

Third, because robes serve as a protective covering and support, they cause the complexion to become lustrous. Fourth, because fine robes have a delicate touch, they cause the skin to become smooth and supple.
Fifth, because the exquisite garments have a subtle touch, they cause one to attain supreme bliss. Sixth, because of the gift of fresh and clean garments, one attains stainless wisdom.
Regarding the fourth section on the sixth gift of flowers, there are four parts: first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication at the time of giving.

The third [section] serves as the concluding summary for the preceding two; the fourth is intended to direct the merit toward the lower realms. Within the first [of these], there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the objects to be given;
second, from "in this manner" (*evam-ādi*) onwards, the clarification of the field to whom they are given. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the heading;

second, from "namely" (*tadyathā*) onwards, the clarification of the specific categories of the objects, which are tenfold and should be understood accordingly. Regarding the latter, the field to whom they are given, there are ten types; the first is one's own person as the field.
This has two meanings. First, because one's own person is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); for example, one seeks food to sustain the body in order to attain *bodhi*.

Second, because of the equality of self and others; that is to say, if the mind were not equal, one would necessarily regard others as the field and so forth, but this is not the case, as oneself is also the field. The rest of the text is easy to understand. Second, dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Within the practice, based on ten meanings of the flower, ten vows are generated: first, blooming, which means that by relying on the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), wisdom universally illumines the objective realm, thereby causing the true nature to bloom;
second, the meaning of seeing with joy without satiety; third, the meaning of seeing all things as harmonious and satisfying.

May they obtain this. Whatever they observe, may it all accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*), without grasping at illusory appearances. (4) It has the meaning of being free from defiled attachment;
(5) it has the meaning of causing those who see it to focus their minds with joy and not abandon it; (6) it has the meaning of causing all who see it to rejoice so that anger does not arise;

(7) it has the meaning of the flowers of the great vows bringing the fruits of practice to fulfillment; (8) it has the meaning of the great wisdom initiating practice like the sun opening the flowers.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle ten, states: "For example, when a lotus flower is shone upon by the sun, it does not fail to bloom. This refers to the red lotus (*padma*).
This means that the arising of the nine great compassionate practices is like the sun opening the flower. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty, states:
"For example, the sunlight can cause all *utpala* flowers to bloom and become bright and clear. This refers to the blue lotus (*utpala*). [The tenth is] the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Like flowers, seeing them necessarily brings about practice; one rejoices as if entering a treasure island. Both the covering and the joy are thus explained; the three fetters and four intentions may be understood accordingly.

In the seventh section on the offering of garlands, there are three parts: first, a brief restatement of the practice of giving; second, the passage beginning with "by means of all... which clarifies the practice of dedication.

This constitutes the lower pair of concluding verses for the two practices; the beginning and end may be understood accordingly. Within the practice of dedication, there are two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent;

second, as indicated by "namely" (*yad uta*) below, the actual manifestation. In this manifestation, using garlands as adornment serves a function through ten meanings, whereby ten vows are generated.
These vows are that sentient beings may attain the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—bodies that people delight to see, revere, desire to approach, regard with kindness, and cherish.

Through yearning and longing, one’s sorrow is removed and joy arises. "Those who leave evil behind" do so because they have abandoned a mind of aversion. "Those who draw near to the Buddha" act as attendants to the Buddha, like floral garlands used for adornment.
"Pure" refers to the fact that the substance of the garland—the pearls and flowers—is pure. "Delighting in the sight" means that love and joy are aroused.

Because there is a distinction between seeing what has not yet been seen, one abandons sorrow and gives rise to joy; because there is a distinction between having sorrow and being without sorrow, one leaves behind evil and arouses purity;
because there is a distinction between evil and the absence of evil.

In the eighth [section], "Offering Fragrance," there are four parts. The first three are the same as before. The fourth is intended to clarify the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) for those below;

the other sections may be understood accordingly. In the second part, "The Practice of Dedication," there are two sections: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, the section beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*), which correctly elucidates the content. Within this elucidation, there are twelve vows:
the first eleven vows constitute the accomplishment of causal practice, while the final vow concludes the result achieved through those causes. Regarding the former...
In this section, the first [phrase] is general, while the subsequent ten are specific. That which is called "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) refers precisely to the attainment of these ten.

Regarding the term "fragrance" (*gandha*): it is because there is no foul odor of defilements; because there is the scent of pure *brahmacarya*; because it purifies the faculty of the nose for those who smell it;

because people delight in smelling it; and because they do not loathe it. Within the specific section, the single character "attain" (*prāp-*) in the first [phrase] runs through the following nine sentences. It does not...

Those who have deficiencies maintain the three clusters [of precepts]. This is because they are like those protecting a life-preserving float. Second, it is because they distance themselves from the delusions of non-Buddhists.

Third, it is because they distance themselves from defiled minds. Fourth, it is because they distance themselves from the delusions of the two vehicles. Fifth, it is because they distance themselves from falling away midway;

that is to say, even if they should mistakenly give rise [to such thoughts], they harbor deep shame and remorse—how much more so for those who intentionally commit offenses or commit them repeatedly without shame or remorse, being deeply attached to their transgressions.

Is this seeing [the result] as merit or as transgression? Sixth, because it is free from delusion, karma, and suffering; seventh, because it is maintained constantly as at the beginning; eighth, because it is free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism; ninth, because it is maintained free from the mark of self;

tenth, because it is the cause for accomplishing the other shore (*pāramitā*). Regarding the conclusion of the causes and the accomplishment of the fruit, it is called the "fivefold dharma-body" (*pañca-dharma-kāya*).
On this point, there are two explanations. One says that this should be understood solely as the precept-body (*śīla-kāya*) of one who has attained Buddhahood through aspiration.

Now, it is said that while the general meaning is the same, the specific intent differs. One interpretation holds that the nature of the Bodhisattva precepts differs from those of the Two Vehicles because they possess the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Because the aggregate of the dharma-nature precepts attains the five divisions of the dharma-nature and is fused in unimpeded harmony, the subsequent section on the intention of dedication states:
"To cause all sentient beings to fully attain the unimpeded aggregate of precepts. Question: Are the aggregates not a burden?

[Question: Regarding the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*), it carries the sense of a "collection. Since the form that is the nature of the Buddha-dharma is neither a collection nor characterized by fusion and non-obstruction, how can it be called an "aggregate"?
[Answer: In truth, it is not an aggregate; it is merely designated as such by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

In the ninth [section], the offering of scented unguents, there are three parts: first, the restatement of the practice of giving; second, the clarification of the practice of dedication through the passage beginning with "By all... (*yena...*);

and third, the simultaneous conclusion of these two practices through the passage beginning with "This is for... (*idam...*). The first and last [parts] are easily understood. Within the practice of dedication, there are two sections: first, the restatement of the preceding to introduce the subsequent;

and second, the actual manifestation of the dedication through the passage beginning with "That is to say... (*yad uta...*). Within this manifestation, there are ten vows, which are the practices of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). The first six lines [correspond to the first six perfections].
This may be understood. Regarding the latter four [factors]: first, the dharma of skillful means; second, the merit of great vows; third, the power of the bodhicitta;
and fourth, the dharma of pure, white wisdom—meaning untainted (anāsrava) wisdom—because it is able to sever afflictions (*kleśa*).

Each of the ten practices possesses the significance of perfuming (*vāsana*), stimulating, nurturing, and clearing away; for they remove obscurations and because they perfume, stimulate, and nurture the bodhicitta.

The tenth [section], the giving of beds and seats, consists of four parts: first, a brief summary initiating the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication through the various [verses] beginning with "For all... In the Sanskrit original, it says *śayyā*. The sound of *śayyā* is pronounced as *yu-he-chu-fan*. This translates as "bedding" (*woju*).

Although the character for "bed" (*chuang*) would not be contradictory, the character for "seat" (*zuo*) would cause a discrepancy, as the seat one sits upon is not bedding. The Jin translation uses "bed and bedding" (*chuangfu*), which is deeply appropriate.

Within the section on the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, the actual exposition of what follows. [The following is] the exposition.

The ten vows of the middle [section]: First, to attain birth together with all Buddhas upon the bed of liberation, which is called the "bed of the devas," because in the second chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha is named the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*).
Second, the bed of the bodhicitta, because it is the common reliance of the worthy and the holy.
1. The bed of the three great fruits of enlightenment (*bodhi*). This corresponds to the bed of ordinary beings, for it brings rest from the suffering of fatigue and attains bliss.
2. The bed of the sovereign bliss of the four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This reverses the bed of ordinary beings' sleep, for it takes the sovereignty of body and mind as bliss.
3. The bed of teaching the Dharma with equanimity. It serves as the basis for the cultivation of sentient beings through perfuming. 4. The supramundane purity...
1. The bed of karma, because it is the basis for the most excellent fruits. 2. The bed of nirvāṇa, because it is the bed of ultimate peace and security. 3.

The bed of suchness (*tathatā*), because it is the basis for the Buddha’s wisdom. 4. The bed of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), because it is the basis for faith, understanding, practice, and so forth.

The ten Buddhas are lions among men; they always lie on their right side to manifest that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rely upon and accord with the fundamental non-arising of the unconditioned (*anutpāda*).

Now, I vow to obtain a Buddha-bed, intending thereby to bring about the attainment of Buddhahood. The three fetters and four intentions are all easily understood. Regarding the eleventh [vow], the giving of dwellings:
the text has four parts as before—the first, the last two, and the middle one—which may all be known. This is the dedication.
Regarding the two sections within the practice, they are the same as before. In the section on the actual manifestation, there are ten vows:

first, adorning through giving; second, adorning through diligent effort; third, gathering the distracted by abiding in the center; fourth, relinquishing attachment at the time of giving; fifth, purifying the three spheres of giving;
sixth, the giver abandoning birth-and-death while the recipient abides in Bodhi; seventh, constant spontaneity in taming and transforming others.

For the sake of sentient beings, they constantly and correctly abide in the noble, celestial, and Brahma abodes. "Noble" refers to the signless and so forth; this refers to the four dhyānas. "Brahma" refers to the four immeasurables.
The eighth is the cause for abiding in enlightenment. The ninth is the roots of goodness associated with the dharmatā. The tenth has two meanings:
first, it is because the preceding seventh expresses exclusion to indicate difference; second, it is because one abides in the dharma-realm, the chamber of great tranquility.
In the first vow, the five characters “vowing for all sentient beings” (願一切眾生) run through all subsequent vows; one should know that the rest is as explained previously.
Regarding the twelfth [section], the dwelling in giving (*dāna-vihāra*), there are four parts, the same as before. First, the citation of the practice of giving can be understood.

Second, within the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts, also the same as before. Finally, in the actual manifestation, there are eleven vows: the first is general, and the remaining ten are specific.

Regarding one of the slips [of text] from another source that relies on a heterodox teacher, the seventh fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To rely on the Dharma means to rely on the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvāṇa.
All Buddha-dharmas are the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). This dharma-nature is the Tathāgata; therefore, it is eternally abiding and unchanging.
It continues by stating that those who do not know the dharma-nature should not take it as their refuge. Its aspiration is for all sentient beings...
The five characters "arising" (*sheng*) permeate all subsequent vows. Second, it excludes reliance on deluded consciousness. Third, it excludes reliance on evil friends.
Fourth, it excludes reliance on sutras of incomplete meaning; one should instead rely on the Mahāyāna teachings of definitive meaning. The sixth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"This Mahāyāna sūtra is called the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), and this Buddha-vehicle is the most supreme and most excellent. Fifth, it excludes unwholesome and indeterminate actions.

Therefore: [the sixth] and [the seventh] together exclude heterodox deliverance; the eighth excludes contaminated (*sāsrava*) activity; the ninth excludes the mind of birth-and-death, because one constantly abides in a profound and upright mind of compassion;

the tenth excludes the path of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The three concluding phrases are easily understood. Within the fourth section, which clarifies the intention of dedication, the ten phrases are easy to comprehend.

Regarding the two types of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), first, the preceding is restated to introduce the subsequent; second, from the words "that is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, it is explicitly revealed.
Within this, there are ten vows: first, the wisdom that illuminates the teachings of the Dharma; second, the knowledge that perceives the physical form of the Buddha appearing in the world.

1. The wisdom of the body; 2. The wisdom that realizes the emptiness of sentient beings; 3. The wisdom that illuminates objects with the light of the body; 4. The wisdom that illuminates the signified meaning; 5.

The non-apprehension of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); 6. The non-apprehension of unity and multiplicity; 7. The non-apprehension throughout all time; 8. The wisdom that subdues Māras and non-Buddhists;

9. The wisdom corresponding to supernormal powers. Regarding the three types of wisdom for bestowing intentions, there are two [sections]. First, the two gates of benefit and peace are briefly indicated. The meaning is as follows...

The preceding has been explained. Hereafter, these ten phrases below extensively manifest its characteristics, as can be understood. The four pairs of conclusions and the five dedications are both easy to comprehend.

The fourteenth [section], on the giving of medicinal decoctions, has three parts: first, a brief restatement of the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication as clarified by the passage beginning with "With all... (*sarvair...*);

third, the dual clarification of the purpose of these two practices as found in the passage beginning with "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva... (*bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ...*); the first section is easily understood.

Within the second section on the practice of dedication, there are two parts: first, a restatement of the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the actual manifestation of the ten vows, beginning with the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*). First [of the ten vows]:
Because medicine dispels illness. Regarding the "envelopments" (*nīvaraṇa*): the "envelopes" (*nīvaraṇa*) refer to the five envelopments (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

They are so named because they cover the true meaning and prevent wholesome qualities from becoming manifest. The five are: sensual desire, ill will, doubt, lethargy-and-drowsiness, and restlessness-and-remorse.
The first three take the three factors among the root afflictions as their essence; the next one takes that which is defiled in nature among the four indeterminate states as its essence;

and the last one takes the secondary afflictions as its nature. The first two obstruct the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*); the next one obstructs the aggregates of liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision [of liberation] (*jñāna-darśana*);

the next one obstructs the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*); and the last one obstructs the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). These details are fully explained as in the treatise. [This concludes the section on] the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments).
These refer to the ten types of *paryavasthāna* (entanglements). They are so called because they entwine the active mind and so forth, rendering it lack of mastery. Namely:

lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), sleep (*middha*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*). Among these, the six—lack of shame, lack of dread, stinginess, envy, anger, and concealment—have the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The remaining four are as previously explained under the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances). The detailed classification according to various categories is as fully set forth [in the treatises].
A Separate Chapter: 1. Because it causes the body to be free from illness and become robust; 2. Because those whose fatigue has been healed are able to further save others;
3. Because the practice of giving does not cease; 4. Because medicine can sustain their physical life, they attain the Buddha-body; the body itself is the medicine; 5.

Because they teach the sick to take the medicine, they attain the four proximate knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidāḥ*) and the three types of wisdom (*tisro vidyāḥ*); 6. Because they bestow the most supreme medicine.

1. Because it removes the source of illness once the period of mourning has ended; 2. Because the eightfold mind of giving completely cures all illnesses; 3. Because it employs wholesome contemplation to observe the symptoms of the illness and its medicine;
4. Because it seeks out methods for the sake of rescuing sentient beings. These three pairs conclude the two practices within the third section of the mind.
This refers to the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are ten phrases; the first six are easy to understand.
Regarding the seventh, which mentions "attaining the vajra-like [qualities]," it is as explained below in the *Buddhācintyadharmaparivarta* (Chapter on the Inconceivable Qualities of the Buddha).
Among the ten kinds of vast powers, the great Nārāyaṇa-banner, and the courageous dharmas, the first states: "All Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras..."
The garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, piśācas, rākṣasas, and others, exerting all their strength, rained down great golden vajras as large as Mount Sumeru;
they fell all at once throughout the trichiliocosm. Yet the Buddha was without alarm or fear. It is even said:

"Even if [the rain] were not restrained, though it should pour down, it would ultimately cause no harm. If that which is sustained by the Buddha and that which is the Buddha’s own domain, nothing can injure."
How much more so for the body of the Tathāgata? The commentary states that, according to this, one prays to attain the Buddha-body.
Regarding "attaining firm power and so forth," this is because it is one of the ten powers among the aforementioned dharmas. That text says:

Therefore, the tenth [point] is also as stated in the first of the ten kinds of vast and powerful Nārāyaṇa-dharmas.
It says: "The bodies of all Buddhas are indestructible; their lives cannot be severed; they cannot be affected by worldly poisons;
and the calamities of water, fire, and wind in all worlds cannot harm the Buddha-body."
The fifteenth [section], the "Vessel for Giving," contains four parts: first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) starting from "mahā-";

second, "That is to say" and below, the actual exposition. Within the exposition, there are ten vows: first, because the vessel and its contents are not lost or scattered; second, the purity of the gift.

Regarding the three preceding sections, the author has omitted details for brevity; in reality, each contains many varieties. Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 49, it says:
"If there are sentient beings who come seeking various objects of giving that lead to frivolous pleasure or lead to what is meaningless, one should not..."
One should give; how much more so when it concerns giving beautiful women as concubines? Would this not lead to unwholesome conduct driven by craving and attachment?
Nor can it be said that a bodhisattva practices only the act of giving while remaining ignorant of other matters.
Why is this? Because it contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* cited previously. That treatise further states: "When giving away one's wife and children, one should not give them to an enemy."
Regarding those of evil family, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or those engaged in cruel and violent deeds, when it comes to bestowing the position of a king:
if one knows that the petitioner, once having obtained the throne, will harm sentient beings, one should not grant it. Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Although a bodhisattva has attained mastery over wealth and status, there are five causes and conditions for which they do not give to sentient beings who are destitute of such things.
First, they see that the beings have heavy karmic obstructions regarding wealth and status.

Second, they see that if they were to bestow wealth and status upon those beings, it would obstruct the arising of wholesome dharmas. Third, they see that if those beings were to lack wealth and status...
Because revulsion has manifested before him; fourth, because he sees that if he were to provide those sentient beings with wealth and status, they would accumulate unwholesome causes;
fifth, because he sees that if he were to provide those sentient beings with wealth and status, it would become a cause for the harm and affliction of countless other sentient beings.
For this reason, the bodhisattva does not give to them. Regarding this, there is a verse which says: "Seeing that karmic obstructions have manifested..."
Because it accumulates harm and affliction. [Question: It is observed that there are sentient beings who do not receive the gifts of a bodhisattva. [Answer: There are two types of givers.
First, if one knows that the beggar has obtained the gift intended to harm sentient beings, then the bodhisattva does not give;
in this case, there is no transgression. If one does not know for certain, the bodhisattva acts solely with a mind of benefit and peace; even if he gives, there is no fault.

How much more so in the case of these palace ladies, who are all fellow-practitioners and companions of the Bodhisattva; one can know for certain that giving them [to others] will be beneficial and cause no harm.
Or rather, they may first comply and later be transformed through the power of his vows. Question: Does the Bodhisattva maintain the precepts by not causing affliction to sentient beings?
How is it that one practices *dāna* for oneself by giving away one's own children and others? Answer: These children and others given as gifts fall into two general categories.
First, there are those who previously formed a vow together with the Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood, acting as mutual leaders and companions.

Now, being able to give them away fulfills their original aspiration; they rejoice at the completion of the practice—how could they feel any further distress? Even if they were to speak of sorrow and suffering, it would all be...

Thus it is demonstrated. Second, regarding the extension and arousal of vows: since one’s power of resolve is still slight, even when about to give away land, one should inquire three times as before.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (49) states: "When giving away one's wife or children, one should first instruct and persuade them until they are joyful, and only then give them away;
one must never coerce them so as to cause them distress or sorrow. Furthermore, one should not give [them] to enemies, wicked people, or yakṣas."
Regarding the "rākṣasa-like practitioners of violent karma," the commentary states: this teaching is established for those of the initial faculties.
Subsequently, based on the five types of fields (*kṣetra*), the practices such as giving (*dāna*) are specifically elucidated and divided into five categories.

First, the dedication of offerings made to the Buddha and his shrines. This section has four parts: first, a restatement of what precedes; second, the actual manifestation of the dedication starting from "By this... and so forth; third, the summary starting from "This is for... and so forth;

fourth, the clarification of the purpose of the dedication starting from "In order to... and so forth. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, a restatement of the objects of offering;

second, the field [of merit]; third, the causes of the roots of goodness. [The text] distinguishes the persons who should erect stupas and the positions represented by the stupas. Next, the length... [text continues].
The Āgamas state that four types of persons should have stūpas erected for them: first, a Buddha; second, a pratyekabuddha; third, an arhat;
and fourth, a cakravartin king. According to the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, citing the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, eight types of persons should have stūpas erected for them.

Because there are sacred teachings stating that followers of the Two Vehicles are the same as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The second chapter of the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "The Vātsīputrīyas and others perceive a self within the body;
they do not believe in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nor do they believe in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as suchness (*tathatā*). Thus spoke the Buddha.

Such a person is no different from a non-Buddhist outsider (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in seven fascicles states: "Mahāmati, what constitutes the evil views of outsiders?

It refers to not knowing that objects appear through one's own conceptual discrimination; regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of intrinsic nature, they engage in verbal expression by perceiving existence or non-existence.

The commentary explains: Since those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) grasp at external phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature, [they are likewise categorized with outsiders].
Not to believe in "mind-only" is the position of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, the second [section] states:
