Master Zhaolun’s *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* states that the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*) are the foundation, as each single wholesome action is adorned by the other nine. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains...

The practitioner of the hundred blessings refers to the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). To be partially free from killing, up to being partially free from wrong views—this is called the first stage of the ten practices.
To be largely free from killing, up to being largely free from wrong views—this is called the second stage of the ten practices.
To be entirely free from killing, up to being entirely free from wrong views—this is called the third stage of the ten practices. If for a short time...
Abstaining from killing for even a short time, up to abstaining from wrong views for even a short time, is called the fortieth practice.

Abstaining from killing for a long time, up to abstaining from wrong views for a long time, is called the fiftieth practice. Abstaining from killing for as long as one lives, up to abstaining from wrong views for as long as one lives, is called the sixtieth practice.
Abstaining from killing oneself, up to abstaining from wrong views oneself, is called the [seventieth] practice.
Seventy practices: if one exhorts others not to kill, up to exhorting others not to hold wrong views, this is called the eightieth practice.
If one extols and praises not killing, up to extolling and praising not holding wrong views, this is called the ninetieth practice.

If one sees [beings] abstaining from killing and feels joy and great delight, up to seeing them abstaining from wrong views and feeling joy and great delight, this is called the tenth of the ten practices.
By means of these hundred practices, the hundred marks of merit are accomplished. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-four, states:
When a bodhisattva cultivates non-killing, there are five kinds of mental states: namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and supreme-superior.

This applies likewise even up to right view. These fifty mental states are called the initial resolve; when they are fully perfected and determined, the completion of these fifty mental states is called "fulfillment.
Thus, one hundred such mental states are termed the "one hundred merits"; being fully endowed with these one hundred merits, one achieves...
"One mark," up to "fully endowed with the thirty-two marks. The commentary states: If one relies on the eleventh [chapter], the causes for each of the thirty-two marks are distinct.
Furthermore, this is explained here in terms of the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

If one relies on the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgara-parivarta*) and other sections of this sutra, the Buddha possesses as many marks as there are atoms in the oceans of *kusumagarbha* world-systems; each individual mark consists of as many [sub-marks] as there are atoms in a single world-system.

The accumulation of merit is accomplished; it is not merely that one hundred merits constitute a single mark (*lakṣaṇa*). There are thirty-two marks, as this is explained in reference to the marks of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
As stated in the previous chapter, the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornment" (*Vyūha-parivarta*), in the verse by the Water-Ruling Spirit Cloud-Banner-Universal-Arising:

"The gates of pure compassion, as numerous as the atoms of a world-system, together produce a single wondrous mark of the Tathāgata. Not a single one of these various marks is not [thus produced]. Therefore...

1. Those who see it are never satiated. 2. The fourfold mind of giving is in accordance with principle and is undisturbed; it is because one gives what is appropriate to the recipient’s needs, and because all gifts are fresh and exquisite. 3.
One gives with gentle words to comfort those who have been humiliated, those who come to take [what they need], and those who offer apologies for their shame. 4.

When giving, one praises the recipient, not begrudging one's own labor, thinking, "This completes my practice of *dāna*. 5. When giving, one expounds the True Dharma (*saddharma*) as is appropriate for them.
Therefore: (8) at the time of giving, one illuminates the purity of the three spheres so that the mind is not distracted; (9) at the time of giving, the mind encompasses all *pāramitās*;
(10) at the time of giving, one clearly illuminates the *dharmadhātu*. The three conclusions and four intentions can be understood as before.

Regarding the twenty-third [section] on the bestowing of the jeweled crown and the hair-knot jewel, there are four [points]: first, the practice of giving; second, returning [the merit] from below that...
"Directed toward practice. The third [point] serves as the concluding summary for the lower [category]. The fourth is intended to cause those at the lower level to turn their minds [toward it].

Regarding the first two [of these], the initial [part] can be understood. Within the second, "the practice of dedication," there are two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent, which can be understood; second, the section beginning with "that which is called," which correctly elucidates the matter.
In the ten vows revealed in the *Madhyamāgama*, all refer to "wisdom" because the crest-jewel possesses the meaning of illuminating vision.
Regarding the second vow, which mentions "possessing a topknot," the Sanskrit original states: "Attaining the Buddha’s conch-like topknot, one accomplishes the foremost wisdom."

The remainder is the same as in the eighth [section]. Regarding "the ocean of jewels" (*ratnasāgara*) and so forth: the Buddha’s wisdom is noble and precious, thus termed a "jewel," and it is profound and vast like an ocean.
As for the phrase in the ninth section, "reaching the summit of the great earth": this refers to the ultimate limit of the Bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi*).

The remaining text, concerning the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and the "crown" (*makuṭa*), and their accomplishment of the most supreme, can be understood through reflection. The three summaries and the four intentions are likewise clear.
The twenty-fourth [section], "Giving One's Wife, Children, Wealth, and Body to Rescue Prisoners," consists of four parts:

first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha"; third, the conclusion, beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the clarification of the intention, beginning with "In order to...".

Within the first [part], there are three: first, the gift of fearlessness; second, the gift of material wealth, beginning with "Having rescued..."; and third, the gift of Dharma, beginning with "Thereafter... First, the gift of fearlessness:

This section has two parts. First, it clarifies that those to be saved are undergoing suffering, which can be understood [by the text]. Second, from "After the Bodhisattva saw this" onwards, it clarifies the saving from suffering.
Within the section on saving, there are three parts: first, giving up what is difficult to give; second, from "In the prison... onwards, saving those whose suffering is difficult to save;

third, from "Just as with Great Compassion... onwards, citing examples to establish the proof. Regarding the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, wealth and treasures; second, wife and children; third, one's own person. Within the citations from antiquity...

Although the practices of these bodhisattvas are many, for the sake of brevity, one mundane and one supramundane practice are cited as primary. This also demonstrates that bodhisattvas master both the mundane and the supramundane in their transformative activity;

all subsequent passages should be understood according to this principle. The remainder of the text is self-evident. Within the second section on the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts:

first, the restatement of the preceding to introduce the following; second, the actual exposition beginning with "That is to say. Within this exposition, there are ten vows, the first of which is "Liberation from Suffering."
1. Because they are bound by their bodies; 2. Because they rescue those facing death so that they may be born, vowing to realize the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing;

3. Because they rescue and liberate them from the suffering of mental anguish and distress within the dark dungeon; 4. Because they rescue and liberate them from imprisonment and confinement; 5. Because they rescue and liberate them from the bondage of anxiety and distress, which deprives them of autonomy; 6.
Because they rescue and liberate them from the myriad schemes of fear and alarm that arise during periods of detention; 7. Because they rescue and fulfill [their needs].
1. Because they delight in restraining and binding the mind; 2. Because they rescue and fulfill the desire for release from prison through the gift of Dharma;

3. Because they rescue and fulfill the aversion toward confinement and the lack of autonomy; 4. Because they enter the prison to give the gift of Dharma and to liberate others from suffering. These are the three fetters.
The four intentions can be understood.

Regarding the twenty-fifth [section], "Sacrificing One's Body to Substitute for a Prisoner Sentenced to Death," there are four parts: first, the practice; second, the practice of dedication, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha";

third, the dual conclusion, beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the manifestation of the intention, beginning with "In order to...". Within the first [part], there are four sections. The first clarifies that which is...
1. The savior undergoes suffering. 2. When the Bodhisattva sees this, he forms the thought of sacrificing his own body to take their place. 3. Regarding "How could it be otherwise?

(*katham anyathā*), this cites examples to establish the point as previously explained. 4. "At that time, the Bodhisattva... and so forth, correctly clarifies the sacrifice of the body to save them from suffering.

This section contains four parts: first, stating the intention to save; second, revealing the fault of not saving; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation—all of which clarify the characteristics [of the practice]. 2. [End of section].

Within the section on the practice of dedication, there are two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the section beginning with "That which is called" (*yad uta*), which correctly reveals the ten vows.
1. To rescue and liberate from the calamities of life-ending untimely deaths and accidents. 2. To rely upon the power of the Bodhisattvas so as to be included among those who do not die.
3. To rescue and liberate from the fear of death. 4. To rescue and liberate so as not to let life end prematurely, thereby enabling the realization of [immortality].

The realm of the knowledge of deathlessness: (1) because the five bodhisattvas protect and shield [beings] from the perils of death; (2) because they rescue and liberate those who have committed evil deeds from death by the sword;
(3) because they rescue and liberate [beings] from the causes of fear of death and cause them to subdue the four māras;

(4) because when practicing the gift of fearlessness, they also practice the gift of Dharma; and (5) because through these causes, they cause [beings] to attain pure faith, become free from the fear of the great assembly, and resolutely preach the Dharma.
Ninth, to rescue and liberate from the suffering of being bound and confined, whereby body and mind lack autonomy. Tenth, to rescue and liberate from the fear and suffering of death.
[The following] three points and four intentions are as can be understood.
In the twenty-sixth [section], "The Gift of the Topknot with its Skin," there are four parts: first, clarifying the practice of giving; second, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
"Next, 'Sā' [refers to] the practice of dedication. Third, 'This is for... is the summary. Fourth, 'In order to... clarifies the underlying intent.

Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts: first, the restatement of the topical outline; second, from 'Just as Ratnaśikhin... onwards, the actual exposition. Within the exposition, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that Bodhisattvas such as Ratnaśikhin collectively cultivate this practice; second, from 'Therefore, I should... onwards, clarifying that this [practice] is identical to theirs."
All bodhisattvas act in accordance with their practice. This section has two parts. First, the practitioner is identified; this also has two sub-sections:

first, the individual names are briefly presented, and second, the phrase "and so forth" serves as a general conclusion for the numerous categories. Regarding the two characters "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), in the Sanskrit original they merely indicate the various forms to show their multiplicity.
Following this, the passage beginning with "At that time, the bodhisattva... clarifies the characteristics of the practice being performed. Within the text:

Second: First, clarifying the preliminary preparations for practice; subsequently, taking up the following section to clarify the actual characteristics of the practice. Within the former, there are four parts:
first, the donor’s joy, because the recipient has enabled him to accomplish the practice of giving (*dāna*); second, the phrase "and he speaks," which clarifies that his joyful mind is unshakable.
1) No stinginess, because of the fear of suffering and so forth. 2) Third, not dwelling on the inferior, which clarifies fearless rescue;

that is, not hoping for present fame and profit as rewards, nor craving future pleasure, nor seeking the fruits of the two vehicles. 3) Fourth, clarifying what is correctly sought, which has two parts.

First, Nirvāṇa is clarified. Later, following the explanation of "diligence," the seeking of Bodhi is clarified. Following that, within the correct clarification of the aspects of practice, ten kinds of giving are presented:
1. Enduring suffering; 2. Reverence; 3. Looking up to and recollecting the virtues of the Honored One, for this is also a form of practice;
4. Joy; 5. Superior aspiration and delight; 6. Mental clarity and understanding; 7. Non-attachment of the mind toward painful sensations; 8. Knowledge of the five... [text ends].
9. Knowing that the five feelings have no intrinsic nature and that, from the very beginning, these feelings do not arise. 10.

Knowing that the five feelings arise from causes and conditions, and that they all undergo transformation and are shifted by formative forces (*saṃskāra*); subsequently, one’s own self should likewise be the same.

Among the two aspects of this practice cultivated by all Bodhisattvas, first is the general [aspect], which means practicing this giving together with the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. Second is the specific [aspect], which has five parts; the first is the arousal of profound...
1. Faith. 2. Attachment to defiled pleasures. 3. Seeking omniscience. 4. Diligence. 5. Awakening to the principle that is without a teacher.

Regarding the two aspects of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), first, the preceding is cited to introduce the subsequent; second, from "that which is called" onwards, it is explicitly revealed. Within this explicit revelation, there are ten vows.
First, "attaining right view," etc., means causing [beings] to attain the superior characteristics within the two stages of the supramundane cause and fruit: namely, the stage of the Buddha-fruit.
The mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*). The two marks of the hair-tuft like a stupa (*uṣṇīṣa-śiraskatā*) have two meanings:

first, the hair-tuft of the Bodhisattva is coiled in tiers like the shape of a stupa; second, his hair is worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans, as it yields the merit of offering to a stupa.
According to the Sanskrit original, it should be said: "One obtains the Bodhisattva’s hair-tuft as a stupa for the world, such that no one can see [its top]."

The crown of the head. Among these two [features], the color is deep blue; its virtue is firmness and its substance is fine and soft. "Firmness" means that it does not undergo transformation and is indestructible.
These three matters are merely indicated here, which is to say: he vows to become a Buddha. As for what is vowed in the eight subsequent vows:
All of these are the Buddha’s hair; this should be understood. Regarding the three [features], according to the Sanskrit original, it should be said:
"May all sentient beings obtain lustrous hair, reaching to the topknot and forehead, with a head and face that are perfectly rounded like a *pūrṇaghaṭa*. This term means "full jar";
since the belly of the jar is round, we now take only the circular aspect of the belly and do not take the top or bottom of the jar. Regarding the fourth, it may be...

Explanation: Regarding the five [types of hair], according to the Sanskrit original, they are made to possess two characteristics of hair: namely, the *śrīvatsa* characteristic hair and the *svastika* characteristic hair;
these are explained according to the meanings of their respective sounds. Regarding the sixth, "attaining the Buddha-characteristic hair," the Sanskrit original says:
"attaining the *nandyāvarta* characteristic hair. The remaining text is the same. The seventh and eighth vows can be understood accordingly. Ninth...
The Central Indian manuscript reads: "Obtaining that which is fit to be a shrine (caitya), fit to be an object of offerings (pūjā), and [fit for] the hair of the crown.

The remainder of the text is the same. The commentary explains: "Fit to be established as a shrine" and "fit to be an object of offerings" refers to the Buddha’s hair; for it is called a *caitya* when the Buddha’s relics, such as hair and nail-clippings, are enshrined therein.
This can be understood from the ten points. Regarding the third pair, the conclusion: within the intention of dedication, there are three benefits: first, stability; second, ... [text ends].

Upholding. Regarding the wisdom of the ten powers of the three Buddhas, there are four sections in the twenty-seventh [chapter], "Bestowing the Eye": first, the practice of bestowal; second, the practice of dedication, beginning with "By this..."; third, the conclusion, beginning with "This is for...";
and fourth, the clarification of the intent, beginning with "In order to...". Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the opening of the topical outline; second, as in the *Huan*...

Regarding the section on "Joy," this correctly elucidates the second [topic] within the middle [division]. First, examples are cited to establish the proof; subsequently, from "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, the actual characteristics of the practice are clarified.
Within this, there are three parts: first, generating the remedy for the practice and purifying the mind; second, from "toward those who beg" onwards, clarifying the purpose of the practice;
third, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva" onwards, generating the thought that the beggar benefits oneself. Regarding the first of these, there are two parts; first, the heading.
Next, the text provides an exhortation regarding the application of the mind. There are seven ways to apply the mind: first, purifying the three spheres; second, not grasping at signs;
third, generating the light of understanding according to the teachings, thereby destroying the darkness of non-understanding;

fourth, the word "Middle Way"—according to the Sanskrit original, *bodhi* refers to the manifestation of awakening before one's eyes through contemplation; fifth, dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-wisdom; sixth, [sharing] with all...
Because Bodhisattvas practice giving equally; seventh, because their faith in the Buddha’s unimpeded eye is difficult to destroy.

Regarding the three points concerning the purpose of the practice: first is the general heading; second, "for the sake of ultimate [enlightenment]" and so forth, which specifically clarifies the purpose; third, "as for the following," which provides a summary.
Regarding the five phrases within the separate section, they are all easily understood. Third, concerning the ten phrases on the thought of benefiting oneself when encountering a petitioner:
the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. Within the specific section: first, one establishes a gathering for the sake of benefiting oneself through affection;

second, because affection is the Dharma, one increases the practice of the Dharma; third, because affection is objectless, one abandons worldly affection and views; fourth, because one does not give rise to worldly...

1. Lovingly abandoning negligence. 2. Using the love of the Dharma to eliminate the bonds of desire. 3. Lovingly practicing for the sake of accomplishing conduct, which is itself the cultivation of bodhi.
4. Bringing peace to oneself by fulfilling the minds of others. 5. Causing the mind to be fully satisfied. The preceding phrase refers to whatever object [is involved].

This phrase follows [the previous section] by excluding several items. There are nine types of non-differentiated giving (*anāviśeṣadāna*). Within the two types of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), there are two:

first, the restatement of the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the actual manifestation, which is what is shown below. Among these, fifty vows are revealed, wherein all that is obtained as eyes is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).

This is similar to the ten eyes explained below in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), differing only in one or two particulars, while the remainder are largely identical. Text.
It is evident that this can be understood. The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four intentions are also easy to comprehend.
Regarding the second [section], within the twenty-eighth [chapter] on the giving of ears and noses, there are three parts: first, a general exposition of the practice of giving;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, a specific clarification of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); third, from "This is for... onwards, a general conclusion of these two practices. Within the first [of these three], there are three sub-sections: first, the restatement of the two chapters. Second...

As for "Just as in superior practice," the following provides examples to establish the proof. Regarding "The three bodhisattvas thus... and so forth, this correctly reveals the characteristics of the practice.

Of these two [sections], the first can be understood by itself. The second, concerning the citation of examples, has two parts: first, listing the names and numbers; second, from "At the time of giving" onwards, clarifying their characteristics.

Within the first [part], there are two: first, the listing; second, which can be understood generally. Within the latter, the section on characteristics, there are fifteen phrases; the first one is general.
The rest are all distinct. Among them, those who possess the Buddha-lineage (*gotra*) are those from the stage of "Ten Understandings" (*daśa-avabodha*) upward.

Those who are born into the family of the Tathāgata are those from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward. As for the two characters "pure" (*viśuddha*), they correspond to the various faculties (*indriya*), merits (*guṇa*), and wisdom (*jñāna*).

The remaining text is easily understood. Within the third section, which correctly reveals the practice, there are eleven phrases; the first phrase summarizes what precedes and introduces what follows.
The final ten phrases specifically clarify this: "Entering the ocean of great giving" refers to the eighty-seven gates explained within this dedication.
Alternatively, it refers to all animate and inanimate things belonging to the human world under the jurisdiction of a Cakravartin King;
or it is said to be immeasurable and boundless; or it is said to be whatever forms, such as *asaṃkhyeya* and so forth, that sentient beings require.
These are things of a similar category. The remaining text is easy to understand. Second, the specific explanation of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) has two parts:

first, the dedication of the ear; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... onwards, the dedication of the nose. Within the former [the dedication of the ear], there are four sections. First, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent.

The second [section] is the actual exposition; the third is the conclusion; and the fourth is for the purpose of clarifying the underlying intent. Regarding the first [section], it may be understood as it stands.
Within the second section, the actual exposition, there are ten vows; the first two and the seventh are all termed "without attainment" (*anupalambha*), according to the Sanskrit original.
The first is named "Non-attachment" (Aśaṅga); the second is named "Non-grasping" (Anupādāna); the seventh is named "Non-abiding" (Apratiṣṭhita). Regarding the fourth [point], it says:

"One does not give rise to a discriminating mind based on the ear-sphere. This means that one does not, because of the ear's ability to hear sounds, grasp at the ear as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

To grasp at something as having an intrinsic nature is a discriminating mind; this is because it pertains to the ear-sphere (*śrotra-āyatana*) among the twelve spheres. This is due to being free from discrimination.
It is distinct; it is called "pure. Regarding the fifth [of the five faculties], that the dull consciousness never arises again is because the clear and sharp ear-organ constantly manifests.
The eighth [verse] says, "the indestructible ear. In the Sanskrit original, this is named "the uninterrupted ear.
It skillfully understands all treatises, and there is none who can interrupt it. The ninth and tenth [verses] say, "vast and pure, the sovereign of all ears. This means, regarding all...

Regarding the ear that can hear from afar and the ear free from conceptual discrimination: because it is the most supreme among those that have attained mastery, the tenth [vow] in the Sanskrit original states:
"May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the divine ear (divya-śrotra) and attain the ear of a Buddha. The remaining vows and the concluding summary may be understood accordingly.
In the subsequent section on the dedication of the gift of the nose, there are four parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, "That which is called... and so forth.

The third [section] is the concluding summary; the fourth is for the purpose of clarifying the intent of what follows. The first [point] is easily understood. Regarding the second, the explicit exposition contains twenty vows:
the first ten are the primary vows, and the latter ten are the secondary, consequential vows. Why is it that within the vow concerning the gift of the nose, the face is mentioned?
It is because the nose is the central pivot of the face, as beauty or ugliness arises from it. This refers to the vow made upon giving the nose.

He attains the face. Among the ten previous vows, the second states that he "attains the nose of the secondary marks" (*anuvyañjana*), because among the eighty secondary marks it says that the two nostrils do not protrude.
The third states that he has "excellent features," meaning he possesses the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). As stated in the *Lakṣaṇasāgara* (Ocean of Marks):
"The Tathāgata’s nose possesses the mark of a great man, named 'Cloud of Wisdom for All Divine Paths,' which is pure."
It is adorned with exquisite jewels, and the radiant colors of various gems completely cover its surface.

Within it appear immeasurable transformation Buddhas, seated upon jewel lotuses, who travel to all worlds to expound the inconceivable ocean of the Buddha-dharma for all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings.
(The sixth cloud says: "They manifest in accordance with what is appropriate, as they are not fixed to a single form. (The eighth cloud says: ...

"Subduing the enemy" means that Māra sees his wife subdued. "Ninth, Good Vision" (Sudarśana) means that seeing it necessarily gives rise to a wholesome mind. The remaining vows may be understood accordingly.
Within the latter ten [vows], two mention "the face of all phenomena. "Face" has the meaning of "directly facing"; it refers to the mind being directly oriented toward the nature of all phenomena.
"Good Vision" follows in accordance with the previous explanation regarding the nose. The remaining vows and the conclusion may be understood accordingly. Four.

The manifestation of the mental faculty (*manas*) consists of ten gates: namely, because it is that into which odors enter; because it apprehends odors; because it cognizes odors and abides in the maintenance of the scent;
because it perceives the scent just as the eye sees forms; because it knows through conjunction just as touch is realized;

because it discriminates odors, which is to say it achieves accomplishment therein; because the sense organ (*indriya*), the illumination, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are clearly discerned; and because the odor serves as an offering and adornment.

Because they are equally pure, and because all five components of the Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya) are termed "fragrance," the three [preceding] cases can be understood through their connection to this.
Regarding the twenty-ninth [case], the gift of teeth: these two objects of merit are combined in the explanation because their karmic fruits are similar.
The text consists of four parts: first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva...";

third, the double conclusion, beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the clarification of the intent, beginning with "In order to...". Within the first part, there are three sections. The first is the presentation of the topical outline.

Regarding the phrase "abiding securely within the stage of mastery," the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle 14, states: "Just as the tusks of an elephant king [are indestructible], such is the Dharmakāya."

Because he is a bodhisattva. Second, as further illustrated by the following example, it is established as proof. Regarding the statement "the six-tusked elephant king Bodhisattva," the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, chapter four, says:
"In the distant past, there was a kingdom called Kāśa. Its king was named Brahmadatta. He commanded a caṇḍāla..."
There was a great elephant king named Blue Lotus Eye (*Utpalākṣa*), who possessed six tusks and dwelt on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*).
"You should go there and extract his tusks and bring them back. If you do not succeed, you five shall certainly have no hope of survival," he said. ... [and so on] ...
At that time, the great elephant king immediately extracted his own tusks and gave them to the *caṇḍāla*. The details are as extensively described therein. Three Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...

The section beginning with "Sā" (薩) explicitly reveals the practice of giving (*dāna*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the section beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*), which clarifies the arising of the mind that perceives [giving] as marvelous and difficult to attain.
There are twelve kinds: first, having no limit; second, being ultimately unimpeded; third, being forever without regret.

Fourth, the non-arising of greed, hatred, and delusion. Fifth, the absence of any remaining stinginess. Sixth, for the sake of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). Seventh, for the benefit of sentient beings.
Eighth, there are two kinds: first, the superior great; second, the unsurpassed great. The superior great is also called "unequaled," meaning that among all forms of giving.

There is nothing else equal to it; thus, the unsurpassed is also called "the unequally equal" (*asamasama*). This is because, among all gifts that have no equal, these are mutually identical and equal.
Ninth, they are the most excellent among all gifts. Tenth, they are also called "sublime," because giving with sovereign wisdom is supreme.
Eleventh, they are also called "most sublime," meaning that giving with sovereignty, being free from all afflictions, is the most preeminent.

Therefore, [the first] twelve [vows] benefit others while being deficient for oneself, because the joy of benefiting others exceeds that of benefiting oneself. Second, within the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts:

first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, the actual manifestation. Within this manifestation, there are ten vows; the first vow is to obtain the Buddha’s teeth.
First, because he was worthy of erecting a stūpa and receiving offerings; second, he vowed to obtain the mark of even teeth among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha;

third, he raised his mind to grasp wisdom—where the words are general but the meaning is specific, whether as a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) or a *sāmīpya* (proximate compound)—such that wisdom can bring about pliancy and gentleness.

Alternatively, when softened, it is the practice for crossing over to the other shore; its sprout can then be tamed as food. Once the food is cooked, it is fit to serve the purpose of sustaining the body’s strength.
This is the "white and pure" mark among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha, specifically the teeth.

As explained in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks," the right auxiliary teeth of both the upper and lower jaws, along with the general characteristics of the teeth, are all adorned with various jewels, fragrant flowers, and radiance.
The majestic presence and the Buddha’s supernatural power in preaching the Dharma and so forth are all matters worthy of recollection.
Sixth is the mark of forty teeth among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha. Seventh, according to the Sanskrit original, it is the vow that all sentient beings may obtain such teeth.
The patterns of the veins are like excellent lotuses; the *sambastika* (crossed) and *nandika-paṭṭa* (pleated) marks are all fully accomplished.
The eighth and tenth [marks] are for the most part the same as those described in the previously cited "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks. The ninth is easy to understand.
There are three pairs of fetters. The four [points] for the fourth [section], "Manifesting What Is Knowable," are clear.

Regarding the third [section], "The Tenfold Giving of the Tongue," there are four parts: first, the practice of giving by the Bodhisattva; second, at that time, the practice of dedicating all [merits] to the lower [stages];

"May all sentient beings obtain the marks of a great lotus, like those of Nandika-mudrā, and the marks of the physical excellence resulting from the karma of the ten powers."

[The term] *yán* (rigorous/ornamented). The commentary states: Regarding the karmic retribution of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the activities of the hands and body all derive from the strength of the ten fingers.
Taking the giving of the fingers as the cause, one attains the ten great powers and the heroic dharma of the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner.

As for being "adorned with the marks and signs" (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*), "signs" refers to the mark of copper-colored fingernails, which are finely raised between the fingers. The remaining text, as well as the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) and the four intentions (*caturmanasikāra*), may be understood accordingly.

The fortieth [section] consists of four parts concerning the practice of giving the Dharma for the sake of seeking it: first, the act of giving; second, the dedication of merit at that time, which is the practice of dedication;
third, the conclusion, beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the manifestation of the underlying intention, beginning with "In order to...". Within the first of these, there are three parts.

First, the aspects of practice are revealed. Next, as in the section "seeking below," examples are cited to establish the proof. Finally, as in the section "for the sake of seeking below," the purpose of giving is clarified.

Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts: first, the conditions for giving; second, the actual manifestation of the practice of giving, beginning with "If there is... The subsequent citation of examples and the final section on the purpose are clear and may be understood from the text.
Second, regarding the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the structure of the text is the same as above. Finally, as in the section "That which is called... it correctly...
The ten vows revealed in the *Madhyamaka-āloka* are all [descriptions of] the Buddha’s fingernails. Regarding the first vow, it says "the appearance of red copper (*tāmra-varṇa*).

Here, "appearance" refers to a minor mark (*anuvyañjana*), because red copper is considered excellent. Regarding the second vow, it says "the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*)," which refers to the luster and smoothness of the red copper.

Regarding the fifth vow, it says "unstained by the world. There are two senses here: first, that the red color of the Buddha’s fingernails is not produced by artificial dye; second, it refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because the claws do not grasp at objects within their spheres. Eighth, "entering into all that is equal" refers likewise to the claws of wisdom.

Ninth, regarding the phrase "attaining the claws of well-born," the term "well-born" (Sanskrit: *sujāta*) is a designation for the proper etiquette and formal conduct of the Western Regions; it signifies the correctness of one's speech and demeanor.
The remaining text and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are as can be understood from the four intentions.
In the forty-first section, "Seeking the Dharma by Entering a Pit of Fire," there are four parts: first, the practice of entering the fire-pit to seek the Dharma;

second, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva... and so forth; third, the conclusion beginning with "This is for the sake of..."; and fourth, the intention of dedication beginning with "In order to cause... and so forth.

The first two sections consist of: first, a brief presentation of the headings; second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics of practice, beginning with "There is one who... and so forth. Within this section on characteristics, there are two parts:

first, a question-and-answer format to clarify the practice of regarding the body lightly and the Dharma as paramount; second, citing examples to demonstrate parallel cultivation, beginning with "Just as when seeking... and so forth. Both passages are clear and can be understood from the text itself.

Regarding the second part, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the textual structure is the same as above. Following this, the section beginning with "That is to say" correctly elucidates the ten vows.
The first and ninth [aspirations] take the vow for seeking the Dharma as their object; the remaining eight all take the vow for entering the fire as their object.

Therefore, it is said that one leaves behind afflictions, suffering, perilous difficulties, and terrors to attain happiness and so forth. The intermediate text and the three summaries, along with the four intentions, are clearly manifest and thus easily understood.

The forty-second [section] consists of four parts within the practice of seeking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings while undergoing various sufferings: first, the practice of undergoing suffering while seeking the Dharma;
second, the practice of dedication from this point downward; third, the conclusion from "This is for... downward; and fourth, the intention of dedication from "Desiring to... downward.

The first and second [sections] consist of two parts: first, the presentation of the practitioner who is capable of cultivation; second, for the sake of seeking [the goal], the clarification of that which is to be cultivated.

Within the section on cultivation, there are three parts: first, the eleven phrases clarifying the purpose of the cultivation. The first phrase is general; the next nine phrases are specific; and the final phrase concludes by identifying it as the cause of suffering.
In the general [section], the character "for" (wèi) runs through the nine specific phrases, with the text clearly elucidating each other. Second, "as in seeking... [and so forth].

The following citation provides an example to establish the proof. Regarding the three [points] that clarify the aspects of practice (*ākāra*) below: first, it indicates the cause for undergoing suffering;
second, "even unto" and so forth refers to taking the place of evil persons to undergo suffering. The phrase "even unto" is used because by citing a heavy case, the light cases are thereby revealed.
Third, the reason for seeking the lower realms and undergoing suffering can be understood from both [the preceding and following sections].

Second, regarding the section on the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the two-part structure is the same as above. The latter, namely the "lower" section, correctly reveals the ten vows of the middle [section].

Third, regarding the phrase "attaining a body that manifests like a reflection," the Sanskrit text reads *pratibimba-upamām ātmabhāvām*. This is translated here as "attaining a body like a reflected image. It says:
"Constantly experiencing peace and bliss" means that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one attains a body like a reflected image that manifests according to the capacities of beings;

it is "bliss" because it benefits sentient beings. "The fourth, transcending the prison of suffering" means exiting the triple world (*tridhātu*). "Accomplishing the practice of wisdom" means that the causes for Buddhahood are fulfilled.
The remaining text, the conclusion, and their underlying intent may be understood accordingly.
The forty-third section: The King Residing in the Quest for the True Dharma. He is able to relinquish all that exists within the ocean-like world, specifically four things:

first, the practice of seeking the Dharma; second, the bodhisattva’s subsequent practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); third, the conclusion of the preceding section; and fourth, the intention for the subsequent dedication.
Regarding the first [of these four], there are three parts: first, clarifying the practice of seeking the Dharma; second, "is able to fully... and so forth, which clarifies...

The practice [is as follows]. Third, as in the section on "Great Power" (*mahānubhāva*), examples are cited to establish the proof. Regarding the first [of the three], there are three points: first, ascending to the royal throne has three meanings:

(1) it is high, so as to encourage those below; (2) it possesses objects for giving; and (3) it manifests the dignity of the Dharma. Second, from the section on "Seeking the Dharma" onwards, it is shown that this is not for any other purpose.
The phrase "up to and including... (*yāvat*) is used to illustrate the many by means of the few. Third, the difficulty of birth.
A single phrase clarifies the extreme gravity of the Dharma. According to the various sūtras, there are many such bodhisattvas who practice this;

now I shall briefly manifest a few examples. First, as stated in the *Bodhisattva-mūla-pratipatti-sūtra*: while serving as King Janaka, he carved his own body into a thousand lamps in order to seek a single verse.
Second, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita went to Dharmodgata...

1. At the place of the Bodhisattva Kṣema, he sought the Dharma by cutting and selling his own flesh; these three cases are as explained in the "Devadatta" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. 2.
There was a king who sought the Dharma from the seer Asita, offering his own body as a slave and a seat. 3. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 22, states:
"In the past, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, for the sake of hearing from a Buddha that the Tathāgata realizes nirvāṇa..."

Verse: Selling his body and cutting his flesh, he took three *liang* daily for a full month. Although his wounds were agonizing, through the Buddha’s supernatural power they were restored to their former state.
(3) Thirty-third: It is said that the Bodhisattva, seeking the True Dharma, had a thousand nails driven into his body.
(5) Like Prince Sārdūlakarṇa, who gave up his life for half a verse. (6) Like King Maitrībala, regarding the five...

He sought the Dharma from yakṣas, even allowing them to consume his own warm flesh and blood. In the seventh fascicle, within the "Entrance into the Dharma Realm" chapter, Samantabhadra says to Sudhana:

"Within my ocean of Dharma, there is not a single word or phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the position of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and even all that one possesses. Such passages are as extensive as [described] therein.
Separate Record. Fearing prolixity, I have not included it in full. Third, "The Capabilities" (the three capacities) fully explains the actual practice of giving; this may be understood.
Within the second section, "The Purpose of the Practice of Giving," it says "the path to omniscience. The character for "path" (*mārga*) in the Sanskrit original is *bodhi* (enlightenment).

Third, within the section on "Citing Teachings to Establish the Proof," there are two parts: first, citing the person; second, from "diligently seeking" onwards, revealing the practice. Within the practice, there are eleven phrases; the first...

One is general; the remaining nineteen are specific. Regarding the phrase "free from worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*"): there are two kinds of conceptual proliferation. First, the fourth of the four types of false views (*caturvidha-apavāda*).
Second, any phenomenon that merely follows verbal designations is itself conceptual proliferation. All other [points] clarify these characteristics.

Within the two types of dedicatory practice (*pariṇāmanā-caryā*), there are two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "That which is called" (*yad uta*) onwards, the actual exposition.

Within this exposition, there are ten vows. The first two are exclusively vows of the practice of giving (*dāna-caryā*). The third, sixth, and seventh are both vows of seeking the Dharma and vows of practice.

The remaining [vows] are all exclusively vows of seeking the Dharma and vows of practice. Regarding the ninth vow, which speaks of "the light of bodhi": this refers to the practice being accomplished through the illumination of the intrinsic nature by the light of untaught wisdom (*asāmketikajñāna*). The others...
The text and the three fetters [are explained]; the four intentions can all be understood.

In the forty-fourth section, "Discriminating for the King’s Cessation of Butchery," there are four parts: first, the practice; second, from "By this" onwards, clarifying the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);
third, from "This is for" onwards, the double conclusion; fourth, from "In order to" onwards, the intention of dedication. Within the first [part], there are two.

First the general, then the specific. Within the general section there are three parts: first, the body as the basis for practice, meaning that by bestowing the Dharma upon the king’s person, one brings about mastery;
second, the universal practice which clarifies the gift of fearlessness; third, the single phrase "universal bestowal" which concludes the latter. Within the specific section there are nine phrases.
1. Not relying on one's own power to deceive, oppress, or take life; 2. Extensively cultivating great practices; 3. Governing all things with compassion; 4.
Not relying on one's influence to cause harm or distress; 5. Causing sentient beings to dwell in peace, like a wish-fulfilling jewel; 6. Resolving to attain bodhi; 7.

Abiding oneself in the threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*); 8. Enabling others to abide in the threefold aggregate of precepts; 9. Causing those who are unable to uphold the threefold aggregate of precepts [to do so].

This causes them to abide in the five precepts; guarding against the first [transgression] is most urgent. Second, regarding the two [aspects] within the practice of dedication: first, the preceding is restated to introduce the subsequent;
second, from "That which is called" onwards, the actual manifestation is revealed. Within this manifestation of the ten vows, each contains a vow of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-praṇidhāna*).

Although they vow for long life, the distinction lies in the fact that, through the giving of fearlessness, one is freed from panic, terror, and the loss of mindfulness. This applies to the first and the tenth [vows].

In the middle [vows], one aspires to attain wisdom. This is because, by bestowing fearlessness, one causes others to rejoice. In the second and eighth [vows], one aspires to attain offerings and veneration for the Buddha.

This is because, by bestowing fearlessness, one ensures that others do not experience terror, do not have their lives cut short, do not suffer changes in their physical appearance, and do not undergo suffering until the end of their natural lifespan. In the third, fourth, and tenth [vows], one aspires to cultivate and attain [the respective qualities].
Regarding "no aging, illness, or death": by bestowing fearlessness, one causes others not to be terrified.

Regarding the third [vow], it is the wish to be free from calamities and poisons, because one’s life is regained according to their wishes. Regarding the fourth, it is the wish to attain mastery over lifespan, so that one may abide according to one's will;
and regarding the seventh, it is the wish to fulfill great vows, because one is able to remain by relying on the king’s commands.
Because of joy. In the ninth [chapter], he vows to learn the learning of the Buddha and attain the joy of the Dharma.
Because of the King’s instruction, he attains fearlessness regarding the dread of death. In the tenth [chapter], he vows to attain courageous diligence.

Regarding what is called the "gate of longevity" in the sixth [chapter], it refers precisely to this gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), as it serves as the means for longevity. It is from this very gift that one increases the Buddha[-nature].
Roots of goodness. The remaining text and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as the four intentions, may be understood by analogy.

In the forty-fifth section, "Rescuing Those Who Have Lost Their Masculinity," there are four parts: first, explaining the practice; second, the dedication beginning with "At that time the Bodhisattva...

and so forth; third, the conclusion beginning with "...is for the sake of..."; and fourth, the intention of the dedication beginning with "...in order to cause... and so forth. Within the first [part], there are three sections. First, only the absence of...
The gift of material wealth constitutes the gift of fearlessness. Second, the gift of Dharma following "you" constitutes the gift of fearlessness.

Third, the gift of material wealth following the words "thus speaking" constitutes the gift of fearlessness; the texts for these are all easily understood. Regarding the third point—that only the gift of Dharma constitutes the gift of fearlessness—there are two parts:

first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "namely. The former refers to teaching the Dharma so that it may bring joy and so forth, because it rescues [beings] in conjunction with compassion. This is the latter explanation.

The middle section has two parts. First, the explanation of "preaching the sublime Dharma. Second, from the phrase "that person" onwards, the explanation of "causing them to rejoice. Within the first part, there are three sections: 1.

Showing the causes and effects of suffering, causing one to fear suffering and abandon its accumulation (*saṃudaya*), thereby enabling the cessation of the cycle of rebirth; this is called the "Dharma of tranquility" (*śānta-dharma*). 2.

The single phrase "cultivating pure karma" shows the result and encourages the cultivation of the path; this is called "pure karma" (*śuddha-karma*). 3. From the phrase "mutually arising" onwards, it exhorts the reforming of the previous state of mind.

He transforms enmity into intimacy. Later, within the context of "releasing and causing joy," since the Dharma is called "joy" because one practices according to what has been taught, one abandons evil deeds.

This is the skillful means of the Bodhisattva to save sentient beings through impartial compassion. Otherwise, he would merely save those whose current suffering is being inflicted upon them, but not save those who will suffer for having harmed others.
When a Bodhisattva acts toward sentient beings, how could his love not increase? Now, he causes them to rejoice.

"Delight" means that upon hearing the Dharma, one understands and resolves enmity; it is not through the suppression of royal power. Furthermore, one abandons evil karma and its bitter fruits, so that this person and that person become harmonious.

The Bodhisattva establishes this through his own practice, and as they mutually cause one another [to progress], they together become companions on the Path. This is explained for those who intend to practice the Bodhisattva path.
Within the two types of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "What is meant by... onwards, the actual exposition.
The ten vows within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* each contain a vow that is a concordant result (*niṣyanda*) of the preceding practice; this is clear from the text and easily understood.
However, the distinction is as follows: in the first vow, because it causes one to attain Buddhahood, it says "one attains the mark of the horse’s sheathed organ.
In the second, because those whose faculties are incomplete have weak minds and thus fail to accomplish the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it says "one arouses courage."

Regarding "the courageous" and so forth: since the practice of rescue causes one to be exempt from fear and the like, the dedication [of merit] likewise causes one to obtain that which is similar to what was thus exempted.

Among these three, one who possesses the wisdom of a man may act as a leader; the rest is the same as before. Among the four, the abandonment of desire is the same as the previous "holy life" (*brahmacarya*).
Among the five, the qualities of a son of good family are the same as the previous cultivation of the holy life; possessing wisdom is also as previously explained. Regarding the six:
Those with deficient faculties generally lack firmness in physical strength, mental power, and resolve; therefore, it is said that they "possess great human power" and so forth.
Among the seven [qualities], this contrasts with those who lack willpower and cannot practice firmly. Furthermore, these are not objects of the mundane world, for they are wisdom.

Among these eight, the first is as previously explained regarding the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The ninth refers to the Buddha’s wisdom, which is able to subdue beings and cause them to have faith in the [Buddha’s] doctrine.
The tenth, in relation to the ninth, refers to the "great man" (*puruṣa*) in the stage of a cause. The three concluding points are to be understood accordingly.

Within the fourfold intention of dedication, the eleven phrases are divided into three parts: the first is general, the next nine are specific, and the last one is a concluding summary of the intention.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses the form of a man," there are two meanings: first, possessing the male organ; second, possessing the organ of a *puruṣa* (a true man).
What is the distinction between these two organs? It means that while a "man" (*nara*) merely differs from a woman, a "*puruṣa*" additionally manifests the Path.
Regarding "virtue" (*guṇa*): here, the intention is to take the latter sense, thus it says "great man" (*puruṣa*), not "male. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 18, states:
"All men and women, if they possess four dharmas, are called 'great men': first, approaching virtuous friends;
second, being able to hear the true Dharma; third, contemplating its meaning; and fourth, practicing according to the teaching. Furthermore, fascicle 23 states: "If there is a person who can..."
He makes offerings to his parents; he shows reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; he cultivates wholesome dharmas;

his speech is truthful and free from deception; he is able to endure all evils; and he bestows gifts upon the poor and destitute—he is called a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Regarding the phrase "guarding" and so forth:
because he protects sentient beings and does not allow them to lose their male organs, he dedicates [the merit] so that they may be able to guard themselves. He practices the *vyāma*...

Now, as for "practice" (*caryā*): it causes one not to fall back and to be born into the family of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and so forth. Within the subsequent specific [explanation], there are three parts:

first, causing oneself to cultivate and accomplish the conduct of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-caryā*); second, cultivating the superior conduct of a great man, which refers precisely to the practice of rescuing from suffering and bestowing fearlessness within this chapter;
third, "possessing the qualities of a great man," which refers to the manifestation of the seven paths of the great man through these very functions. The word "path" (*mārga*)—

According to the Sanskrit manuscript, *kṛti* (the character for *kṛti* is pronounced with the initial *d* and the final *i* as in *ding-yí*). This means "karma" (*karman*). Regarding the "seven types of persons" (*sapta-puruṣa*), there have been three traditional explanations since antiquity.
The first states that these are the seven noble beings (*saptāryapudgala*). 1. The follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*): This person resides on the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*).

Because they attain broad understanding through others and follow them, they are designated by this name during the period of skillful means (*upāya*). 2. The follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*): This person resides on... [text continues]

Regarding the causal stage: they are so named based on their original practice of acting in accordance with the Dharma and following the Dharma. Third, those liberated through faith, because they attain deliverance by means of the faculty of faith.
Fourth, those who have attained vision, because they attain deliverance by means of the faculty of wisdom. Fifth, those who have realized through the body.
The concentration of cessation is mindless, because it is realized through the body as the eighth liberation.
Sixth are those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), who attain liberation through wisdom by being freed from the various afflictive obstructions such as ignorance.

Seventh are those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), who attain liberation of wisdom and the concentration of cessation by being freed from both the afflictive and the meditative obstructions. Among these seven types of persons, the first two belong to the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The Path. [The first] three, four, and five [stages] are in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); the sixth and seventh are in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

These seven persons are called *puruṣa* in the Sanskrit original, which is translated here as "great man" (*zhàngfū*). The old translation was "human being. Question: Why is it that this dedication is for the sake of causing sentient beings to achieve the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle?
Answer: This is merely a wish to cause them to accomplish the tasks of these seven persons. By means of these tasks, they are [great men].

As for "practicing," it does not mean that one wishes to attain those minor fruits. One interpretation states that these are distinguished according to the seven stages (*bhūmi*) as the "seven types of persons":

first, the stage of the nature of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*); third, the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*); fourth, the stage of practicing correct conduct (*caryāpratipattibhūmi*);

fifth, the stage of certainty (*niyatabhūmi*); sixth, the stage of certain conduct (*niyatācaryābhūmi*); and seventh, the stage of reaching the ultimate (*nisthāgamanabhūmi*). Among these, the first two—

The first [stage] is prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*). The next one is the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). The next one extends from the second ground to the seventh ground. The next one is the eighth ground. The next one is the ninth ground.

The final one comprises the tenth ground and the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). One interpretation states that this is based on the *Mūlapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, which divides the stages of the grounds according to cause and fruit.

There are also seven classes of persons (*puruṣa*): first, the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*); second, the ten abidings (*vihāra*); third, the ten practices (*caryā*); fourth, the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

fifth, the ten grounds (*bhūmi*); sixth, equal enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi*); and seventh, wondrous enlightenment (*sūkṣmābhisambodhi*). Regarding the three aforementioned explanations, if one follows the sequence of the names, the first interpretation is superior;

however, if one considers what is appropriate according to principle, the latter two are superior. As for the "fourfold perfection" and so forth, these are seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the Sanskrit original.
This refers to the character "form" (rūpa). First, because it is like the body of a lion king; second, because it is adorned with the five types of majestic command;

third, because it does not spare its own life or body during the three periods [of past, present, and future]; fourth, because it undergoes the sufferings of the Avīci Hell on behalf of sentient beings for limitless kalpas without ever retreating even for a moment;

fifth, because it possesses excellent discernment and resolution; sixth, because it thoroughly purifies the obstacles of afflictions. The final point summarizes the overall meaning. It may be understood thus.

[The commentary on] the forty-sixth [section], "Praising the Appearance of the Buddha in the World," consists of four parts: first, the practice of giving the Dharma; second, the practice of dedication by the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and below;
third, the dual conclusion of these two practices, beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the manifestation of the intent of dedication, beginning with "In order to..."
The first section has three parts: (1) seeing the Buddha arise and preach the Dharma; (2) using a great voice to bestow the gift of Dharma and benefit living beings;

and (3) using "innumerable" [verses] to conclude the actions performed. The first part can be understood as it stands. Regarding the second part, the bestowing of the gift of Dharma to benefit living beings, there are six sections:

(1) causing them to hear the Buddha’s name and thereby benefit them by removing pride; (2) further encouraging them to quickly see [the Buddha] and accomplish the six kinds of practices to benefit them.
Third, for those below, he preaches that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, thereby enabling them to attain the four benefits beginning with pure faith.

Fourth, for those below, he enables them to attain the four benefits beginning with hearing the names of the Buddhas. Fifth, at that time, for those below, they attain the two benefits beginning with purity.

Sixth, for those various beings below, they attain the benefit of feeling shame for their ingratitude. Third, the summary of the actions performed, along with the preceding text, clearly reveals what is possible.

[He] knows. Within the two types of dedicatory practice, there are two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the section beginning with "That is to say," which correctly elucidates [the practice]. Within this elucidation, there are ten vows: 1.

By means of exhorting others to go [to the Buddha], one causes them to attain the state of going without needing exhortation. 2. By means of exhorting others to see the Buddha, one causes oneself to always joyfully behold him.
3. By means of hearing the Dharma, one causes the attainment of wisdom for upholding it and so forth. 4. [One] causes [others] to hear the Dharma...
1. Dedication through the practice of cultivation. 2. Dedication that causes one to recollect the Buddha and observe the Buddha.

3. Dedication that causes one to see the Buddha swiftly. 4. [The seventh] is the same as the previous observation; however, the distinction is that the Buddha pervades the realm of space, being neither localized nor non-localized.
5. Dedication that causes the arising of corresponding realization. 6. Dedication that causes one to encounter the Buddha and hear the Dharma. 7. By means of... [the tenth].
The dedication following the praise of the Buddha’s appearance [in the world] consists of four parts;

three are the formal conclusions and the fourth is the intended meaning, which may be understood as follows. Regarding the forty-seventh section on the gift of the great earth, there are four parts: first, the act of giving; second, the practice of dedication by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and others;

third, the conclusion beginning with "This is for..."; and fourth, the clarification of the intention beginning with "In order to...". Within the first of these, there are three sub-sections, the first of which is a general exposition.
The field of giving may be twofold; alternatively, when distinguishing the recipients of giving in detail, there are fourteen categories based on the field (*kṣetra*):

namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the Saṃgha, parents, individuals, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, the poor and the orphaned, the fourfold assembly, and reliquaries and temples.
These may also be seventeen types, because the fourfold assembly is counted as four separate categories. "Individuals" refers to those who are personally...

Regarding material wealth, as stated in the *Acintyaviṣaya-sūtra*, because a bodhisattva’s [generosity] applies to all, whereas a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is restricted to those who specifically benefit oneself.
According to this text, including the categories of giving canopies, vehicles, servants, and so forth—excluding the heavy items from the middle field of merit—there are twenty-five types in total.
Specifically, there are seventeen here, and among the gifts of canopies, there is the category of "fame" for Dharma masters.
Regarding all Buddha-dharmas, the various teachers, monks, and venerable elders, those who have first resolved upon bodhicitta,
the giving of servants, the suffering of illness, the True Dharma, and so forth— the term "all Buddha-dharmas" here comprehensively encompasses the practitioner of the ten dharmas.
The various languages of sentient beings include those of spirits, devas, ghosts, and so forth;

since animals are also included among those who receive food, drink, and other offerings, it is summarized at the conclusion of all acts of giving that beings from all realms of existence gather together.

If one considers the field of merit to which the roots of goodness from such giving are dedicated, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing all classes of beings—saints and ordinary people alike—in numbers beyond measure. Question:
Furthermore, regarding the various fields mentioned above, how are they subsumed within the three types of fields? The answer is that there are two approaches: first, the primary classification;

second, the inclusive classification. If one were to consider only the primary classification, then the Buddha-dharma, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, stūpas and temples, the Saṃgha, the four assemblies, those renowned as Dharma-preachers, all the Buddhadharma, venerable masters, monastics, those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, and so forth, would all [be included].

The field of respect (*guru-kṣetra*), the field of parental kindness (*mātā-pitṛ-kṣetra*), and the poor, the orphaned, the sick, and animals constitute the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*). If categorized by their mutual inclusion, there are eight permutations:
first, those who are objects of respect but not of kindness or compassion, namely the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and one portion of the fourfold assembly of monks;

second, those who are objects of kindness but not of respect or compassion, namely parents and worldly virtuous friends; third, those who are objects of compassion but not of kindness or respect, namely the poor, the orphaned, and the sick; fourth...

1. This is compassion (*karuṇā*) and respect (*gaurava*), but not gratitude (*upakāra*); this refers to those who were previously mentioned in the first category and are now afflicted by illness. 2. This is gratitude and respect, but not compassion;

this refers to parents, those who have entered the Path, and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who have gone forth. 3. This is gratitude and compassion, but not respect; this refers to those who were previously mentioned in the second category and are now afflicted by illness.
4. This is respect, as well as gratitude and compassion; this refers to impoverished and sick bodhisattvas who have gone forth. 5. This is neither respect, nor gratitude, nor compassion.

Compassion (*karuṇā*). This refers to when an individual possesses their own wealth, or perhaps due to [the influence of] non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Question: Regarding the various fields (*kṣetra*) in comparison to one another, what is their relative superiority or inferiority?
Answer: These matters are so vast and extensive that they cannot be recorded in full; they are as explained in the *Pṛthag-vyākhyā* (Separate Record). Third, regarding those who are thus inferior...

This clarifies that he gives excellent locations as well as the necessary implements and requisites for those locations. According to this internal arrangement of the text, it differs slightly from the Sanskrit original.

those places shall all be peaceful and free from fear, devoid of any terrors such as enemies, bandits, or the bristling of hair. Thus, the Bodhisattva...

Below, this follows the Han edition. Within the second section on the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, the section beginning with "That which is called...

which correctly elucidates [the subject]. Within this elucidation are ten vows. Regarding the term *bhūmi* (ground), it possesses multiple meanings, namely: generating, producing, abiding, maintaining, being unable to differentiate, and so forth.

Second and third are the meanings of maintenance. Fourth is the meaning of non-conceptualization within the middle. Fifth is the meaning of maintaining and accomplishing within the middle.
Sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth are the meanings of abiding and maintaining. Tenth is the meaning of generation. Third is the conclusion; the four intentions can be understood [thereby].
The forty-eighth [section], on the giving of servants, has four parts: first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva...

Its cause is pure karma; that is to say, it is obtained through the dedication of all roots of goodness by means of the power of vows while practicing the bodhisattva path together with others.

It is not produced by the karmic retribution of the offense of theft. Second: First, the preceding section introduces the subsequent one; the latter, "What is meant by... and below, correctly reveals the ten vows.

Within this revelation, the ten vows concern the nature of the servants bestowed, such as being well-disciplined, compliant with the master’s instructions, and performing good deeds in accordance with what is appropriate. Among these, the first vow concerns benefiting through a disciplined nature;

4. Regarding diligent compliance with activities; 5. Regarding diligent activity itself; 6. Regarding receiving instructions without forgetting them and without opposition or refusal;
