10. Skillfully governing one’s own sphere (*ātma-āyatana*). 11. Being in accord with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). 12. Not giving rise to calculations concerning body or life. (The Sanskrit manuscript states:
"Possessing a mind of various jewel-like natures" [*nānāratnadhātucitta*]. This means that by possessing this, one attains the state of being established within [the lineage]. Regarding "various":
the minds of the various Bodhisattvas, through their diverse understandings, are precious like jewels; because this precious mind constitutes the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it is so called.)
13. It is the nature of the mind (*citta*). 14. Giving without expecting a reward, or not seeing that there is a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the future fruit. 15.

To clarify the teaching (*dharma-deśanā*), as explained throughout the preceding and following sections of this chapter. 16. To avoid contradicting what is expressed by the teaching. 17. To cause one to attain the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). 18.
To employ the teaching to illuminate the capacities of sentient beings. 19. To cause one to attain the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Wisdom. Second, within the explanation of the practice of dedication, there are two parts. First, the dedication according to characteristics is explained; later, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this way, he does not cling to...
and so forth, the dedication free from characteristics is explained. Within the former [section], there are two parts. First, the explanation of...
One dedicates one’s own roots of goodness to sentient beings. Subsequently, by further exhorting the assembly to do so, one instructs others to dedicate their roots of goodness to sentient beings.
Within this [section], there are two parts: first, the actual explanation of dedication; second, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner."

The section beginning with "At that time, generating joy" clarifies the dedication of merit for its intended purpose. This consists of two parts: first, restating the preceding [sections] to introduce the subsequent;

this can be understood as follows. Second, the section beginning with "That which is called" correctly reveals [the dedication]. Within this revelation, there are ten phrases, all of which concern the dedication of the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the internal and external objects previously given.
The first concerns the previous giving of wealth and treasures; the second concerns the previous giving... [and so forth].
The fruits of retribution—both the primary and secondary environments—induced by these roots of goodness are all bestowed upon sentient beings;

furthermore, through the dedication of these roots of goodness, one practices the six kinds of infinite giving. This is an inexhaustible treasury of merit. Third, regarding the previous giving of beds and seats:

according to the Sanskrit original, this includes the full enumeration of bedding and furniture. Fourth, regarding the previous practice of giving for the sake of all sentient beings: this accords with the Bodhisattva path.
1. Karma. 2. Regarding the aforementioned objects of giving, all of which are sublime and free from signs. 3. Regarding the aforementioned gift of elephants, horses, and jewels. 4.
Regarding the aforementioned gift of elephants and horses, because they travel swiftly throughout the four continents. 5.

Regarding the aforementioned gift of female and male musicians, as it reverses and reveals defiled passions and affectionate attachment. 6. Regarding the aforementioned gift of a mind that is impartial and without discrimination.

Therefore, the tenth [verse] concerns the aforementioned difficult circumstances involving the giving of one’s body, head, eyes, blood, flesh, marrow, bones, slaves, servants, and laborers—situations characterized by suffering and lack of autonomy.

By enduring the pain of giving flesh from the body, and [observing that] slaves and others lack autonomy, he vows that sentient beings may be born in places free from suffering, where they possess autonomy and are unhindered.
In the subsequent section clarifying the purpose of the dedication, there are two parts; first, the actual manifestation [of the vow].

Regarding "what is done": later, the Buddha-son Bodhisattva thus expresses compassion for those below, concluding what was previously done. Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, restating the previous to introduce the subsequent;
that is, restating that because sentient beings will certainly obtain the roots of goodness dedicated at the time of the previous dedication, joy is generated.
Second, "in order to... and so forth, which correctly reveals the following. Within this revelation, there are one hundred and ten phrases, based on the original text.

Commentary: The text is divided into six sections. First, from the beginning, there are twenty-three phrases intended to cause one to cultivate wholesome conduct and attain the stage of a worthy and noble person.
Among these, the eleventh phrase says "without regret," because one rejoices after having given. "Without affliction" means that one personally delights in giving.
The thirteenth phrase says "abiding in a mind of compliant giving," meaning that one accords with whatever the petitioner requires.
Because it fulfills their wishes. The fourteenth [verse] says: "Abiding in the mind of giving that gathers [beings]," because one gathers sentient beings through giving.
The nineteenth says: "Abiding in the mind of giving with power as great as a vajra," because the mind of giving is firm and indestructible.
The twentieth says: "Abiding in the mind of giving like the light of the sun," because the light of wisdom destroys the obscuration of stinginess.
Therefore: (21) because the wisdom of the three wheels being purified becomes the wisdom of Buddhahood;
(22) there are two meanings: first, because it takes a multitude of roots of goodness as its retinue; second, because it takes those who possess many roots of goodness as its retinue;
(23) because the wisdom that skillfully causes roots of goodness to grow manifests in continuous succession. The remaining text is easy to understand.

Second, from "attaining the perfection of the indestructible pure mind" downwards, there are eight phrases that cause one to accomplish the practice within the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The first phrase concerns causing the attainment of the culmination of faith. Third, from "accomplishing the immeasurable pure supernormal powers of a bodhisattva" downwards, there are ten phrases that cause one to accomplish the practice within the stage of conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). Regarding the tenth phrase, "immeasurable mind":
These are the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). "Vast mind" means it is without limit. "Supreme mind" means it is unsurpassed.
"Completely pure" means it is in accord with selflessness (*anātman*). The remainder of the text is understandable.

Following the phrase "from accomplishing the mind of pure giving," there are eight lines that cause one to accomplish the practice of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) within the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).
The seventh phrase causes one to attain the accomplishment of a pure, untainted, and boundless essence and activity.
This is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in which principle and phenomenon, and phenomenon and principle, are non-dual. The remaining text may be understood accordingly.

From the fifth [phrase], "From abiding in impartial conduct, the accumulation of wholesome dharmas is entirely perfected," there are ten phrases that cause one to practice at the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The ninth phrase causes one to realize skillfulness.
The wisdom that gives rise to merit. The tenth phrase brings about the roots of goodness born of the great compassion of the same essence (*sāmbhogika-kāya*).
Riding upon *sarvajñā* (omniscience), one comes to transform sentient beings; this is the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajña-yāna*). The remaining text is easy to understand.
From "From the thorough purification and perfection of all Buddha-fields" downward, there are fifty-one phrases that bring about the practices for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. The first...
The four lines state: "May they attain sixty kinds of vocal tones; their speech shall be truthful and worthy of faith and acceptance;
adorned with hundreds of thousands of dharmas; and may the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits and wondrous voice be fully perfected.
Regarding this, the "Inconceivable Qualities of the Buddha" chapter below states: "All Buddhas are fully endowed with sixty kinds of vocal tones. (1)
Each single sound has five hundred divisions, and each division possesses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pure sounds that serve as its adornment.
Thus it is said. The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, fascicle six, states: "The Tathāgata possesses sixty kinds of inconceivable vocal qualities.
As explained in the *Buddhaguhyaka-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these sixty [qualities]."
Various kinds of vocal sounds, namely: those that are moistening, soft, articulate, pleasant, pure, and so forth; thus it is explained in detail.
Among these, "moistening" means that the roots of goodness of sentient beings can be sustained. ... up to the sixtieth name, "Proclaiming All Auspicious Sounds. The commentary states:
"The *Guhyaka-sūtra* refers to the *Guhyakapada-baladeva-sūtra*. The treatise contains only five [chapters]."

There are eighteen types; their enumeration is complete in the sutras and is fully elucidated as in the chapter. The sixth phrase clarifies that the Buddha’s inexhaustible eloquence adapts to the capacities of beings when teaching the Dharma.
The eighth phrase indicates that once sentient beings hear the teaching, they do not fall into the vehicles of the two *śrāvakas*.

The tenth phrase means that the Buddha, at the appropriate time, utilizes things to cultivate practices for the benefit of others. In the eleventh phrase, the word "all" (*sarva*) signifies "equally."
The twelfth phrase, "in one adornment, there are immeasurable adornments," means that within each of the two fruits—the primary and the secondary—there is such adornment.
The thirteenth phrase, "equally entering the equal," means causing all to enter the realm of the Buddhas of the three periods of time without exception.
The seventeenth phrase, "performing immovable karma and attaining the fruit of non-attainment," refers to its cause.

There are four [aspects]: first, the gift of Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings; second, the vow of non-obstruction; third, transcending self through compassion and taking birth for the sake of others;

and fourth, practicing the cultivation of the melting fusion of the *dharmatā*, whereby the three karmas become effortless (*anābhoga*), responding universally and simultaneously throughout the realm of sentient beings without any hindrance.
Regarding the eighteenth phrase, "the faculties" refers to the eye and other sense organs. The nineteenth...
The phrase "one mark" refers to the absence of marks (*animitta*), because one knows that all phenomena are without marks.
Regarding the twenty-fifth phrase, "the field of great power," it is as explained in the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta*: planting even a small root of goodness with respect to the Tathāgata.
Because it can destroy all conditioned afflictions, up to and including the ultimate wisdom of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
Regarding the twenty-sixth phrase, "supreme firmness" and so forth: it means that because his compassionate vows are definitive, they are indestructible.
The thirty-second phrase states that by means of a single practice-vow, one universally fulfills all practice-vows.
The thirty-eighth [phrase] states that by means of a single mind, one knows all minds. The forty-third [phrase] states that by arising in a single place, one arises in all places.
44. It is said that one assembly is adorned and purified; all assemblies are thus adorned and purified. 45.
It is said that within a single buddha-field, one universally perceives all buddha-fields as equal;
this is because the one is all, and all is one. 49. Regarding the phrase "attaining non-identity and so forth," there are two meanings. The first concerns the cultivation of causes, namely:
Because one contemplates that the conditioned and the unconditioned are neither identical nor different, one cultivates all roots of goodness. Second is the attainment of the fruit:

namely, by means of the aforementioned causes, one attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) corresponding to the *dharmatā*, whereby one exercises mastery and unimpededness such that all entities of the defiled and pure realms are mutually identical and mutually functional—neither identical nor different.
This is explained according to the gate of karmic function. Thus far, this has been discussed provisionally based on a single characteristic.

[The division into] these six sections is, in fact, not correct. Why is this so? Because it is only within the thirty-first, thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth, and thirty-sixth verses of the sixth section—within the stage of the fruition of Buddhahood—that it is stated that one causes [beings] to attain the cultivation of bodhisattva practices and to encounter spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore, we know that each verse individually dedicates [merit] toward its respective purpose; it is not necessarily based on [the aforementioned division].

Because these are explained according to their sequential order, one cannot assign specific topical sections (ko-dan) to individual positions. In the subsequent conclusion of the preceding "that which is performed," there are twenty phrases:
the first phrase generally restates the preceding "agent" as the mind; the subsequent section beginning with "all cause... correctly concludes the preceding "that which is performed."
These nineteen phrases belong to the preceding one hundred and ten phrases; their general categories can be understood. Fearing prolixity, they are not described here.

Following this, the third section clarifies the instruction for others to dedicate roots of goodness to sentient beings, which has three parts. First, a brief explanation of the goodness of dedication.
I. The Root. II. "In order to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely," and so forth, clarifies the purpose for which the dedication is made. III.

"Furthermore, by means of all [roots of goodness]," and so forth, correctly reveals the dedication itself. Question: Why is it clarified here that the Bodhisattva himself dedicates his own roots of goodness?

Thus, in the previous [section], dedication was explained first and the purpose second; now, in this section on causing others to dedicate roots of goodness, the purpose is explained first and the dedication second.
The answer is that, in reality, there is no distinction between them. However, this statement is made to differentiate between oneself and others.
Regarding the lack of distinction: it is as when one says, "I dedicate for the sake of this matter," or "I dedicate for this."
This is merely a difference in phrasing; the meaning is not distinct. Regarding the first section, which briefly clarifies the three types of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*):

first, the eight characters beginning with "Furthermore, he exhorts" (*yòuquàn*) distinguish the preceding teaching as being for the sake of others rather than oneself. Next, the passage beginning with "Universally for" (*pǔwéi*) clarifies the cultivation of the roots of goodness.

Finally, the eight characters beginning with "Expedient means" (*fāngbiàn*) reveal that the cultivated goodness is intended for dedication (*pariṇāmana*). The initial and final points are thus understandable. [The text continues with] the cultivation...
Within the roots of goodness, there are two aspects. First, the eight characters [from "大慈悲" onwards] represent the practice of great compassion that eradicates suffering;

second, from "以" (yi) onwards represents the practice of great wisdom that observes reality—this should be understood. Second, regarding the purpose for which [the practice is undertaken], there are six phrases.

The first phrase is to cause [beings] to abide in the ocean of virtues of the resultant stage of Buddhahood, as these are all sublime and purely untainted (*anāsrava*). The second [phrase] concerns the essence, nature, and functional utility of the middle [state].

This is the functional capacity. The remaining text is easy to understand. Third, regarding the actual manifestation of the dedication, there are two parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows;

second, from "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, the actual manifestation. Within this manifestation, there are ten vows. The first is called "peaceful stability" (*kṣema*), because it is not subject to transition.
The third is called "bliss" (*sukha*), because it is characterized by satisfaction. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

In the subsequent section on the dedication that is free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, the actual explanation of the dedication; second, from "When a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dedicates in this way...
onwards, the explanation of further dedicating these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) through the dedication itself.

Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the restatement of the preceding [dedication] with signs (*sanimitta*); second, from "not being attached... onwards, the actual explanation of the dedication free from signs. Regarding the first of these, why is there a restatement?

Regarding the former: because at the time of the correct following of characteristics, there is this departure from characteristics. Regarding the latter, within the ten phrases of the correct departure from characteristics:
first, departure from the cause of giving; second, departure from the fruit of giving; third, departure from internal giving; fourth, departure from external giving;

fifth, departure regarding the place where practice arises; sixth, departure regarding the location where practice arises; seventh, departure from permanence regarding the one who is satisfied; eighth, departure from annihilation regarding the beggar.

Ninth, one is free from the view of existence regarding the objects of giving and the act of giving itself. Tenth, one is free from the view of non-existence regarding the objects mentioned in the preceding phrase.

The latter part clarifies that the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla), being free from such characteristics, are further dedicated; this dedication consists of two parts. First, it clarifies the citation of the aforementioned roots of goodness as they are about to be given. Second, beginning with "May all...
and so forth, it clarifies the dedication of the roots of goodness from the act of giving toward sentient beings. Within this, there are six [sections], the first of which is...

1. The perfection of the fruit-wisdom; 2. the exhaustion of the two types of afflictive and cognitive hindrances; 3. the clarity of wisdom; 4. the concentration of the mind; 5. liberation from the bonds of objective conditions; 6. becoming the seed of Buddhahood.

Regarding the third section, clarifying the accomplishment of benefit through practice, there are two parts. First, the actual manifestation of the benefit: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."

The Bodhisattva thus cultivates the comparison of the lower [stage] to manifest its superiority. This consists of two parts: first, restating what preceded; second, transcending the lower to correctly manifest [the superiority].
Within this manifestation, there are eleven types: (1) transcending the world; (2) universal cultivation; (3) cultivation of the lower; (4) universal practice of the lower cultivation.
3. Being able to descend and see many lands without obstruction; herein there are two parts: first, going there, and second, seeing. 4.
Furthermore, being able to descend and see the practices of Bodhisattvas in many lands. 5. Skillfully explaining the profound Dharma through excellence; herein there are two parts:
first, discernment of meaning, and second, attaining unceasing discernment through *dhāraṇī*. 6. In every thought-moment, making offerings to Buddhas in many lands. 7. Mindfulness...
1. Contemplating the adornment of many lands below. This has two parts: first, the adornment of the fruit; second, the adornment of the causes, beginning with "at which time" below. 2. Eight:
contemplating the purification and accomplishment of many lands and sentient beings below. 3. Nine:

within those many lands below, diligently practicing the various perfections (*pāramitās*), gathering in sentient beings, and accomplishing pure karma. 4. Ten: attaining unimpeded ears below, hearing the Buddhas of many lands turning the wheel of Dharma.
The wheel. One does not give rise to a mind of weariness. Eleventh, abiding in the non-apprehension of the lower stage, the bodhisattva possesses non-apprehending supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Within this, there are two parts: first, the differentiation of names; second, the manifestation of function in the section below.

Regarding the statement "to have a view identical to that of all bodhisattvas," it is because they share the same view of non-apprehension, non-reliance, and non-attachment through action. In the subsequent section on comparative evaluation to manifest superiority, there are two parts.

First, the comparative measurement is clearly revealed; subsequently, from "all Buddha-fields" onwards, it is explained again by following the objections. Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, the presentation of the inferior;

second, from "how much more so" onwards, the manifestation of the superior can be understood. Regarding the subsequent explanation by following the objections, this refers to that which was presented among the inferior.
It is said that one is even able to accomplish the words of "immeasurable and ineffable pure merit.
Fearing that others might not yet understand, this is further elucidated separately. The text is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of attaining the dharma-gate;

second, from "When dedicating in this way, sentient beings do not oppose [the vow]" onwards, the explanation of accomplishing practice; third, "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this way..."
At this time, one attains the lower grade of karma. This clarifies the benefits of contemplation. Regarding the first two [sections], there is first a detailed explanation, followed by a summary:
"When a son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dedicates in this way, he attains all... Within the preceding section, there are ten phrases;

each is described as "pure and equal" because, when compared with one another, they share the same nature and are without distinction based on their respective categories of phenomena. The remainder of the text and the conclusion follow accordingly.
This can be understood. Within the second section, "Establishing Contemplative Practice," there are fifteen pairs, divided into three parts.

First, the initial six pairs clarify that heterogeneous phenomena, when viewed in relation to one another, are non-apprehendable. Next, the two pairs following "Dharmatā" clarify that homogeneous phenomena—both principle and phenomena—when viewed in relation to one another, are non-apprehendable.

The subsequent section on the equality of realms consists of seven pairs. This clarifies that there is no attainment regarding the fourfold propositions of dissimilar phenomena and principles. Regarding the first pair: (1) the environment and its inhabitants;

(2) the two types of karmic results, explained in terms of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); (3) the locus of kingship; (4) the two aspects of subject and object; (5) the results of completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*);
and (6) the path of action, which is the cause upon which karma depends—namely, the volition (*cetanā*) associated with projecting and completing karma within the five or six consciousnesses.
One creates karma through volition (*cetanā*), because karma depends upon volition. The Jin translation states: "Karma does not deviate from its track; the track is now the path.
The original commentary (*Ben shu*) says: "Definitive volition is the place traversed by bodily and vocal karma; it is called the 'track of karma' (*karmapatha*).

Furthermore, the volition of the first moment serves as the path, which induces the volition of the second moment to constitute the substance of the karma; thus, the path is the track. Moreover, [the same applies].
The essence of volition (*cetanā*) constitutes karma; it perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to form seeds, which serve as the "traces of karma" (*karmapada*).

Furthermore, volition is karma, and the capacity of that karma to evoke the retributive fruits of the various realms of existence is the "path of karma" (*karmapatha*). The path is itself the trace. Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty stated:
"The mind of understanding or delusion, upon which the arising of karma depends, is called the 'trace of karma'. Master Bian stated: "The preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of creation is termed..."

Karma. The fundamental paths of action are termed "traces. Next, within the two pairs concerning the non-attainment of principle and phenomenon, in the former pair, the single nature is mutually fused;
in the latter, arising and non-arising are mutually fused. Regarding the subsequent seven pairs where the four alternatives of phenomenon and principle are mutually fused:
as in the first pair, taking one land and sentient beings as two phenomena that are relative to one another, each of these two phenomena possesses its own equality.
The first is the equality of phenomena relative to phenomena; the third is the equality of lands relative to lands, which is the equality of principle and phenomena relative to one another;

the fourth is the equality of sentient beings relative to sentient beings, which is likewise the equality of principle and phenomena relative to one another. Although these four phrases distinguish their respective characteristics, within the contemplation of their mutual fusion, they are unified.

Each and every phrase contains all other phrases without any obstruction. The phrase "the limit of detachment from desire" is also subsumed within the single principle of non-attainment (*anupalambha*);
the rest of the text may be understood by analogy. Third, regarding the benefit of contemplating the realms (*kṣetra*), the twenty phrases are easy to understand.
The third [section], based on the commentary, allows one to understand the conclusion of the title.
In the subsequent explanation of the stages, there are two parts: first, the restatement of the prior accomplishment of the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which can be understood;

second, the actual manifestation of the capacity [to overcome]. Within this manifestation, there are nineteen phrases. The first is to destroy the four māras by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*). The first [of these] is to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*).
1. Through the increase of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one subdues the celestial Māras. 2. By realizing the true nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), they cannot obstruct the path.

3. Deeply understanding that non-arising cannot be bound by death. 4. Greed and desire act as thorns; they wound the feet of ethical discipline on the path to untainted enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhi*).
5. Because it serves as the cause for attaining the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). 6. Because one abides in the true nature of the Middle Way. 7. Out of reverence...

1. Because merit gradually increases; 2. Because the mind of compassion is profound and deep; 3. Because mastery over the gathering of merit is attained; 4. Because mastery over the manifestation of supernormal powers is attained;
5. Because traveling through buddha-fields is unimpeded; 6. Because one enters into reality through resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) regarding both phenomena and principle;
7. Because one practices with every body; 8. Because whatever is cultivated according to one's vows is all accomplished; 9. Because one thoroughly understands the teachings.

14. To serve the Buddhas and reach all Buddha-fields. Although the Sanskrit manuscript simply states that one is "able to pervade all Buddha-lands," the meaning of "reaching" (*wang zhi*) following the word "pervading" (*bian*) can be understood from items fifteen and sixteen.
17. All objects of focus give rise to roots of goodness. 18. The mind is always equanimous. 19. Attaining the first [stage].
The nature-body (*dharmatā-kāya*). This is identical in essence to the fourth [verse], though the skillful means (*upāya*) and practices differ;

this can be understood from the summary. Within the second verse-verse section, there are two parts: first, the introductory ritual (*nidāna*) of the Sūtra master which sets forth the topic; second, the section beginning with "What the Bodhisattvas do," which correctly elucidates the subject.
Within this elucidation, the twenty-one verses are divided into three parts. The first verse generally elucidates that all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are entirely...

Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The final verse generally concludes the meaning of the preceding dedications. The intermediate nineteen verses correspond to the preceding text. This section is divided into three parts:
first, the initial three verses correspond to the preceding practice of giving (*dāna*); second, the four verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva, in order to deliver...
correspond to the preceding practice of dedication; third, the twelve verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva dedicates [merit] so as to reach that... correspond to the preceding...
The practice accomplishes benefit.

Within the eighth dedication, the Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), there are two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. Within the prose, there are two sections:

first, clarifying the practice of the stage; second, clarifying the fruit of the stage, beginning with "When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this... Within the first section, there are three parts; the first is the introductory inquiry.

[The title] "Names. Second, from "O Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva... below, it provides a detailed explanation based on the inquiry. Third, from "O Sons of the Buddha, this is the... below, it concludes the name based on the explanation.

Regarding the first part, as for what is called "the dedication of the aspect of True Suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), it means that by means of the roots of goodness to be dedicated, one vows that they be identical to the essence of True Suchness.

Regarding the "dedication of the characteristics of activity" (*lakṣaṇakarmaprayoga-pariṇāmanā*): because it predominantly explains characteristics, it is specifically termed as such. This refers to the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness).

It is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the dedication of the characteristic of *tathatā*. Upon examining the Sanskrit original, it is named "the dedication of the mastery over the characteristics of *tathatā*" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-vaśitā-svabhāva-pariṇāmanā*).

Here, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the attributes (*guṇalakṣaṇa*), while "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the essential substance (*dharmatā*). However, since nature and characteristic are neither identical nor separate, both are mentioned together.

The *Benye jing shi* (Commentary on the Sutra of Original Karma) states: "Because it constantly illuminates both the two truths of existence and non-existence, and because all phenomena are of a single unified character (*ekasamagraha-lakṣaṇa*), it is called the 'dedication according to the aspect of suchness' (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*).

In the second section, the detailed explanation following the inquiry, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the dedication according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anupraviṣṭa-pariṇāmanā*); second, [the passage beginning with] "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva... [and so forth].

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of these roots of goodness, [proceeds] to the section on dedication characterized by the departure from signs (*nimitta-vigata-pariṇāmanā*). This section consists of two parts:

first, the observation and dedication of previously cultivated roots of goodness; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees what is delightful" onwards, the observation of present objects and the dedication of roots of goodness through the arousal of vows.

Regarding the first of the three [sections] in the preceding part, there are two sub-sections: first, the explanation of the characteristics of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, the explanation of the observation of those roots of goodness. Within the first of these: 1. Clarifying the accomplishment of the roots of goodness, both in their origin and their culmination.

2. From "With all roots of goodness... onwards, the formal explanation of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). 3. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly... onwards, clarifying the purpose for which the dedication is made. Within the first of these [three], there are two parts:

In this context, first dedicating to one's own person and subsequently dedicating to all sentient beings is likewise not contradictory. Why is this?

Because dedicating to oneself is also a dedication for the sake of sentient beings; it is also for the sake of sentient beings. Since both are for the sake of sentient beings, what priority or distinction can there be?

Regarding the second section, which clearly elucidates the dedication (*pariṇāmana*), there are one hundred gates.

Since ancient times, various masters—including those such as Master Yuyi and Master Jue—have all divided this text into ten sections and assigned them to the stages (*bhūmi*) and grounds (*bhūmi*). However, their respective systems differ. Master Yuan judges it into two parts:

the first ten gates correspond to the stage prior to the grounds, while the remainder belong to the grounds themselves. The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "Now, regarding these various gates..."

Each of these is a distinct teaching, collectively encompassing the entirety of the essence, attributes, and functions of *tathatā* (suchness). They cannot be conflated or categorized into discrete segments.
Regarding those who currently categorize these various expositions into segments, there is no such scriptural authority; their textual basis is not explicit and thus cannot be adopted in detail.
We shall simply follow the original commentary without establishing a fixed categorization. Why is this? Because this section briefly reveals the immeasurable virtues of *tathatā*.

Among these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the first one hundred gates may be applied to the stages (*bhūmi*). If that were so, where would the remaining virtues and characteristics beyond those one hundred be assigned?

It is clear that you do not know this. However, in the present [text], most of the gates distinguish characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) while discussing little of essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*).

Characteristics are virtuous characteristics. As the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* says: "The greatness of the characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇamahattva*) is that it is fully endowed with..."

This is because it possesses the qualities of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Herein, for the time being, one hundred [similes] are revealed. Furthermore, within each of these individual similes, there are three phrases:
first, the statement of the "suchness" (*tathatā*) with which [the subject] is identical; as the Sūtra says: "For example, just as true suchness pervades all places and is without limit.
Second, the citation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) dedicated in accordance with that [suchness]; as the Sūtra says: "The dedication of the roots of goodness is likewise."
Therefore, the three are combined as they share the same characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness). As the Sūtra says: "Because it pervades all places and is without limit.
Alternatively, one may form two phrases in total, by binding the latter two phrases into one; all subsequent sections should be understood according to this principle.
Regarding the first phrase, "for example" (*tadyathā*), when consulting the Sanskrit original, it should simply be "like" (*tathā*), not "for example" (*tadyathā*). This is why...
Why is this? In the Sanskrit original, it simply says *yathā*; it does not say *utpāda*. *Yathā* is a term that refers back to what precedes and anticipates what follows;
beneath *yathā*, there must necessarily follow the word *tathā*. This case is likewise so. If it were not followed by *yathā*, it would simply mean "as such.

If True Suchness shares its same essential nature with all phenomena, being inseparable from them and omnipresent, how much more so within its characteristics? How could there not be essence and function therein? Therefore, there is none.
[It is] attained. Seventy: "The existence and non-existence of the nature of non-existence are identical, as if within existence and non-existence.

97. Regarding "the past is not the beginning," etc.: the Jin translation states, "The past is not the same [as the future], the future is not the cause, and the present is not different.
On this point, the ancients exhausted their subtle thoughts, delving deeply into its study and analysis.
Jiexian Fashi said: "This refutes the attachment to the three periods of time held by the Hinayana.
They maintain that the past exists; if it were to exist, it would be identical to the present. Since it has now ceased and no longer exists, it is said not to be identical [to the present].

As for the statement that the future is not [identical], the Hinayana also maintains that dharmas from the future flow into the present. If that were so, they ought to be 'identical' [to the present]."

Regarding "Dharma": since it has not yet come in the present and its conditions have not yet arrived, it is ultimately non-existent; therefore, it is said to be "not the same" (non-existent). Regarding "the present is not different":
those [opponents] maintain that the present is definitively existent. Now it is clarified that [the present] is a provisional conjunction dependent on conditions;

when analyzed, it is non-existent, and thus it is not different from the non-existence of the past and future; therefore, it is said to be "not different. Master Yu stated: "The past is not the same."
That which arises through accumulation is without accumulation; that which is not old in the future is transformation without being transformed;
that which is not different in the present is differentiation without being differentiated. That which initiates anew and anew is called the past.
That which eliminates birth and death is identical to the future. That which gives rise to purity is like what is not different. Master Yuan said: "The past..."

Dharmas are impermanent; they all return to extinction and, in principle, are fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is said they are "not the same. Future dharmas are newly produced and do not possess an inherent nature from the beginning;
therefore, it is said they are "not old. Present dharmas are all empty; therefore, it is said they are "not different. These three "non-s" are designated as suchness (*tathatā*). Master Jù stated:
"The past is not the same" clarifies that the essence of suchness is detached [from temporal states], even though it exists in the past...

It departs, yet it does not transmigrate or perish; thus it is not the same as non-existence. "The future is not old" means that although it arises through accumulation, it lacks the characteristic of arising;

this clarifies that the locus where [a dharma] has already arisen is not old. "The present is not different" means that although it exists in the present, it has no form or location, and is therefore not different from the past and future.
Master Mo said: "Past dharmas that have ceased are similar to *tathatā* (suchness), and are thus named..."
"Same" refers to [the conventional]. Now it is clarified that arising new vows and practices based on Suchness is not like that [conventional state], and is therefore called "not the same.

"Old" refers to karma from past lives which one must receive as retribution; this is termed "old. Now it is clarified that by realizing Suchness, one abandons those old karmas, and is thus called "not old.
"Different" refers to present karmic fetters, which differ from those of the past and future; these are termed "different. Now, observing these karmic fetters, they are fundamentally non-existent.
It is produced; it is ultimately pure. Therefore, it is said to be "not different. "Arising anew" and so forth explain the past. "Eliminating and ceasing" and so forth explain the future.
"Pure" and so forth explain the present. The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "In general discussion of the dharmas of the three periods of time, there are two gates:

first, the gate of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); second, the gate of the establishment of existence. As for the gate of the emptiness of nature, it refers to the past which has already..."

It is empty because it has ceased; it is empty because the future has not yet arisen; it is empty because the present does not abide. Now, within this passage, the perspective is that of the gate of establishing existence (*yōmon*).
This means that while the dharma of the preceding moment is past and has ceased, it is capable of inducing the arising of the dharma of the succeeding moment.
Therefore, the past is not merely a state of total extinction or annihilation. The succeeding moment is the future of the preceding moment; although—

Because the cessation of the preceding thought-moment causes this succeeding thought-moment to arise, yet no dharma of the preceding moment can be transmitted to the succeeding moment, it is said that the future is not the same [as the past].

Therefore, the old dharmas within the preceding moment do not exist now. A present dharma is the same as the future when viewed in relation to the preceding moment, and the same as the past when viewed in relation to the succeeding moment; hence, it is said that they are not different. Thus, regarding the preceding moment...

It is extinguished. Although it is not an identical exhaustion, no dharma reaches the subsequent moment. Although the subsequent thought continues from the preceding one, the dharma is new and not old.
Therefore, in the dedication, one who arouses ever-new bodhicitta causes the subsequent thought to arise in succession because the preceding thought is not identical;
thus, bodhicitta is made unbroken. Because the subsequent thought is not old, [the continuity is maintained].
"By mindfulness of the new. Mindfulness of the new means that the bodhicitta is not constant. It eliminates death and purifies birth, thereby manifesting the activity of the mind.

Furthermore, "attaining perfect enlightenment in every present moment" means realizing that the present is also equal [to the past and future]. To perceive this principle is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
In the Jin translation, there was an error in the sequence where the latter section was translated into this section; thus, there are ninety-nine [instances], whereas here...

Thus, it is established that there are one hundred [verses] in total. Ancient masters were unaware of this error, and because the phrase "because they are the same" was difficult to understand, despite each exhausting their ingenuity, they failed to accord with the original intent.
Now that this new translation has been made explicit, the deficiencies of the old versions can be clearly understood without further hesitation.
As for the statement that "the past is not a beginning," it refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The nature of this [reality] possesses no characteristics of the three periods of time—beginning, middle, or end; yet it does not obstruct the characteristics of the beginning, middle, and end within the three periods.
Therefore, the past is not the beginning, yet it does not obstruct the past being the beginning; even so, the present is not something other [than the past], and the same applies to all.
Because this "present" is established by looking back at what precedes it and forward at what follows it within the continuum of beginning and end, it is called "distinct" (*anya*).

Regarding the dedication formula, "for the sake of all [beings]," etc.: this refers to the essence of bodhi, which does not belong to the past, future, or present; yet, it is not obstructed from arising as the practice of bodhi within every moment of thought.
Therefore, it is called "ever-new. The ninety-eight dedications likewise begin with the equality of the three periods of time. Nine.

Nineteenth, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the realization of *tathatā* (suchness) as their essence. One hundredth, *tathatā* does not coexist with afflictions (*kleśa*). The remaining text may be understood by applying this principle accordingly.

Fourth, the subsequent verses beginning with "If one can" (*caturthaṃ yadi śaknoti*) praise the benefit of dedication (*pariṇāmana-anuśaṃsā*).

Regarding the twenty-ninth verse, which states "The Bodhisattva contemplates the mind," etc., the Sanskrit original says: "The Bodhisattva contemplates that the mind does not abide within; nor is it to be found without."
[It is] attained. One realizes that the essence of the mind is non-existent; it exists through conceptualization and is absent when one is free from it.

Within the ninth dedication, "Unattached, Unbound, and Liberated," there are two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the practice of the stage;
second, the explanation of the fruit of the stage, beginning with "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this... Within the first of these, there are three parts.

First, the names are cited to raise a general inquiry. Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, these are the bodhisattvas... onwards, the inquiry is addressed by providing specific explanations. Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, for this reason...
onwards, the specific explanations are used to conclude the names.
The opening statement, "Dedicating that which is unattached, unbound, and liberated," serves as a general inquiry into the ten kinds of non-attachment, non-binding, and liberation;
it is not an inquiry into each one individually. As for the reason why the mind and so forth are not explicitly cited in the explanation of the names:

it is because this Bodhisattva, regarding the ten dharmas beginning with the mind, performs the dedication of the roots of goodness produced by the practice of contemplation—viewing them as unattached, unbound, and liberated—in order to fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra.
There are dharmas such as the three types of karma; that is to say, when observing them, one does not follow after the bonds of signs or become attached to views.
Because the absence of attachment and bondage is itself liberation, the ten vows are inexhaustible; it is not merely ten dharmas.

Thus, the absence of attachment and bondage—that is, liberation—is the subject of observation, while the ten dharmas are the objects of observation. If one explains this according to the comprehensive meaning of the name, the absence of attachment and bondage is liberation. There is no...

The terms "attachment," "bondage," and "liberation" are all *karmadhāraya* (descriptive) compounds. If explained according to their distinct designations (*nāmavyākhyāna*), the subject and object of observation are stated together;
thus, it should be said that "the mind free from attachment and bondage is dedicated," and so on up to "wisdom is dedicated.

These [latter terms] function as both *karmadhāraya* and *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds. The *Benye jing* (Fundamental Action Sutra) states: "Because all phenomena are non-dual, through the non-arising Prajñā and the Two Truths..."
Because the three periods of time are equal and unified as a single mark, it is called the dedication of non-binding liberation.

Within the second section, the extensive explanation, there are three parts: first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, from "With these roots of goodness... onwards, correctly clarifying the dedication itself;
third, from "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this way... onwards, clarifying the accomplishment of benefit through practice.

Benefit. This consists of two parts: first, clarifying the respect for all roots of goodness; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, regarding those [roots] below," clarifying the benefit of respecting the roots of goodness.
Within the former, there are three sections: first, a general indication of respect for all roots of goodness; second, namely...
The first part specifically reveals the various virtues that are honored; the latter part concludes with such [honoring].

Within the first section, as to why all are honored, it is because they are all causes of enlightenment (*bodhi*); if even one were lacking, the ocean of the Buddha’s qualities would not be fulfilled.
The nine phrases within the specific revelation are explicit in their wording, and both the conclusion and the summary are likewise clear. This concludes the latter section.

Regarding the two points on the benefits of respect: first, the preceding section is restated; second, from "ultimate" onwards, the actual explanation is presented. Within this explanation, there are two:
first, taking delight in all roots of virtue with joy and affection, never ceasing; second, possessing an indestructible resolve regarding all roots of virtue.

Third, being able to practice it oneself; fourth, causing others to practice it as well; fifth, practicing while remaining free from signs (*animitta*); sixth, accumulating [merit] until it reaches purity; seventh, having a distinguished intention (*āśaya*);
eighth, the mind abiding in the realm where the ultimate and conventional truths are fused; ninth, when the power of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) increases;

and tenth, fully understanding the various causes and conditions of the roots of goodness. According to the Sanskrit original, the first phrase is general, while the remaining nine phrases are specific.
What is meant by "conforming to and accepting" at that time? It is when one ultimately delights in relying upon and cultivating those roots of goodness;
when one makes those roots of goodness firm; when one directs oneself toward those roots of goodness; when one establishes a mind of great majesty within those roots of goodness;
when the mind remains unattached to those roots of goodness; and when one is able to accumulate and perfect the giving within those roots of goodness.
At that time, when those roots of goodness have achieved a superior aspiration and delight that is indestructible; when those roots of goodness are made to abide within the realm of the Tathāgata;
and when one universally perceives that those roots of goodness have attained the increase of power—one dedicates those roots of goodness in this manner.
(The same applies to the following.)
In the second section, which clearly explains the dedication, there are ten gates of the unattached, unbound, and liberated dedication:
first, mind; second, body; third, speech; fourth, action; fifth, faculties; sixth, the world; seventh, buddha-fields; eighth, sentient beings; ninth, phenomena; and tenth, wisdom.
Among these, the first gate is extensively detailed, and the remaining nine gates follow the same pattern. Within the first gate, there are two parts; first, the restatement [of the subject].

The latter can be understood from the former. The latter, namely "the lower," explicitly reveals this. Within this explicit revelation, there are two parts: first, it clarifies dedication according to characteristics;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, dedicates without discrimination" onwards, it clarifies dedication free from characteristics.
The preceding section contains sixty-one vows, which, according to their textual characteristics, are divided into ten segments. First, there are three vows:

dedicating all previous roots of goodness to aspire for the accomplishment of the body, speech, and mind of Samantabhadra. Second, there is one vow: aspiring to be able to initiate the diligent practice of Samantabhadra.
Third, there are four vows: aspiring to attain the dhāraṇīs of Samantabhadra. Fourth, there are twelve vows.
May I accomplish the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra. (5) There are eighteen vows: may I accomplish the practices of Samantabhadra. (6) There is one vow:
may I accomplish the Dharma-gates of Samantabhadra. (7) There are three vows: may I accomplish the skillful means of Samantabhadra. (8) There are three vows:
may I cultivate and accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra. (9) There are three Buddhas: may I cultivate and accomplish the wisdom of Samantabhadra. (10) There are...
First, there is one vow: to abide in the bodhisattva practices. Eleventh, there is one vow: to cultivate the wisdom of the Worthy and Worthy Ones. Twelfth, there are eleven vows:
to likewise cultivate and accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra.
The first three [vows] correspond respectively to the fact that the actions of body, speech, and mind are immediately the dharmadhātu as both cause and fruit.
Among the [next] two, one vow manifests effortless and uninterrupted diligence.
Among the three [categories], there are four vows. The first, "vowing to attain dhāraṇī," is self-evident. The second is that all Buddhas are constantly manifest before one.
The third is to understand the speech of others as being identical to one's own speech. The fourth is to practice universally throughout all times and places.
Among the twelve vows within the four [categories], one vows to attain the power of mastery (*vaśitā*). First, to practice throughout a single eon and within the bodies of sentient beings;
second, to universally manifest in the assemblies of Buddhas; third, to accomplish the inexhaustible power and function of cause and effect within the ten bodies (*daśakāya*);

fourth, to appear according to a single gate—that is, to manifest within a single skillful means of transformation—this is the "pure gate. Fourth is the "miscellaneous gate," which refers to other skillful means.
The same as before. Fifth, causing sentient beings to abide in the ten powers (*daśabala*) by means of the empowerment of sovereign power (*vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*).

Sixth, manifesting the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha within the bodies of sentient beings, and causing them to abide and practice therein. Seventh, causing every word to produce all words.
May all be established in the stage of Buddhahood. Eighth: may each single body contain all bodies, and one considers oneself to be the Buddha. The remaining four vows can be understood [by analogy].
Within the fifth group, there are eighteen vows that constitute the practice of Samantabhadra. Regarding the fifth [vow], the phrase "not being in contradiction with... consists of six clauses.

This reveals that the one who expounds the Dharma does not contradict the expressive words [of the teaching], such as the unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "entering into one, etc. in the sixth [section]:
because one is all and all is one, wisdom accords with one at a single moment, and thus accords with all. As for the expression "emitting light," it means that wisdom illuminates the teachings.
The seventh [section] has five phrases. Regarding "reaching [the state of equality], etc.": this refers to the time of preaching the Dharma, when [all things] are by means of...
The fourth is the analytical knowledge of non-attainment (*aprāpti-pratisaṃvid*), which observes and expounds [the teachings]; this is called the adornment of reaching the further shore.

Regarding "the ninth, obtaining the light of the Dharma," etc., it means obtaining the dharma-knowledge of all bodhisattva practices. Regarding the tenth, "obtaining wisdom within all skillful means," there are two parts:

first, the general heading can be understood; second, the ten phrases below provide the specific explanation. Of these, the first two concern knowing quantity and number; the next two concern knowing the fruit and the cause.

Next is one who knows the faculties; next, one who knows the teachings; next, one who speaks at the appropriate time; next, one who is skillful in exposition; next, one who expounds extensively without fear of exhaustion;

and finally, one whose explanations are all of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). These eleven [qualities] consist of five phrases, because their physical actions manifest in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
The twelfth [section] has three phrases; the text is clear. The thirteenth has eight phrases. Regarding "vast sentient beings" and so forth:
it means that their faculties and capacities are vast, and thus they are capable of receiving the teaching of the vast doctrine. Regarding "vast adornments, perfect," and so forth:

it refers to the Sūtra-piṭaka of the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), which reveals the principle without deficiency. The fourteenth has ten phrases. Regarding "the objective realm" and so forth: wisdom is...

This refers to the mental consciousness associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Consciousness itself is the faculty (*indriya*), as explained previously in the sixth dedication.
The explanations of the *dhātu* and the vajra are both as stated before. This phrase refers exclusively to the illumination of reality.

One among the six vows accomplishes the dharma-gate of purity; this is precisely the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation. It is explained according to its functional activity, and the meaning of the text is clear and can be understood.

Within the seventh [stage], one accomplishes the skillful means of Samantabhadra. Internally, there are three vows: first, within each moment of thought, one manifests the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout many kalpas;
second, with a body that pervades the entire dharma-realm, one individually receives the bodies of all sentient beings;

third, one abandons the three inversions and constantly perceives the marks and signs of all Buddha-bodies, while adorning the mouth with the preaching of the Dharma so that sentient beings may receive, uphold, and fully awaken to it.
Within the eight [sections], there are three vows for the cultivation of Samantabhadra’s conduct. The first has both general and specific aspects; within the specific, there are two:

first, clarifying the entry into the characteristics of the lands; second, clarifying that the fundamental characteristics remain as they were. Within the former, ten types of entry into the lands are clarified within a single thought-moment.
The first six [verses] distinguish how one world-system enters into many world-systems; the latter four reveal how many world-systems enter into one world-system.

Of these ten, the first two are easily understood. Verses three and four together clarify the world-systems within a single layer that are arranged in three successive tiers, winding around one another like a net.
Verse five refers to the various world-systems within the twenty layers above a single world-system seed (*kṣetraprakṛti*), because this world-system seed rests upon a lotus flower.
Because within the ocean of Buddha-lands of the [ten] directions, they are arranged in successive order like the net of Indra;

therefore, from this perspective of the encompassing locus of dependence, it is said that "the skillful means are distinguished by the Indra-net," meaning that the analogy of the arrayed net of Indra is used as a skillful means for manifestation.
Sixth, because they exhaustively encompass all lands within the ocean of Buddha-lands, it is said that "all dharma-realms are universally distinguished. Seventh.
Various diverse lands enter into a single land; many enter into one. Ninth, all lands throughout the Dharma-realm enter into a single land.
Tenth, all lands throughout the realm of empty space enter into a single land. These ten correspondences are manifested for those to be guided; therefore, it is said that "he causes them all to see.

Among the nine [aspects], the accomplishment of Samantabhadra’s wisdom consists of three vows: first, to know many locations within each and every location;

Within the Dharma, one knows a single dharma.
Within the tenth [stage], there is one vow for abiding in the bodhisattva practice: among all sounds and voices, to know each of the many sounds and voices.
Within the eleventh [stage], there is one vow for cultivating the wisdom of Samantabhadra. This section has three parts: first, accomplishing practice through causal wisdom; second, by means of...

The stage of practice and abiding. Third, preaching the Dharma according to stages. Within this preaching of the Dharma, there are seven aspects: first, within each individual teaching, many teachings are explained;
second, within those many teachings, each possesses numerous distinctions; third, each individual teaching gathers and transforms many corresponding capacities;

fourth, they gather and transform over many periods of time; fifth, there are four types of correspondence: first, inclination; second, understanding; third, faculties; and fourth, the appropriateness of the timing.
Sixth, by means of desire and so forth, they cause many assemblies to rejoice. Seventh, they cause all the assemblies of every Buddha to fill the entire dharma-realm and attain benefit.

In this text, for the sake of brevity, only one Buddha is explicitly mentioned while the others are omitted. There are seven ways in which benefit is attained: first, establishing superior resolve; second, generating expansive wisdom;

third, comprehending all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); fourth, abiding in the stage of Samantabhadra; fifth, realizing what has been taught; sixth, increasing [virtue] in each moment; [and seventh, attaining mastery].
Possessing great wisdom, they continue until the end of the future. They bring to full completion their cultivation throughout all seven realms of existence.
Within the twelve [aspects], they cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra. There are eleven vows; in the first and the last, there are general and specific [sections].

Within the specific sections, there are three: first, knowing many faculties through a single faculty; second, comprehending many inclinations and desires; third, generating many practices, which has two parts. First, the attainment is clarified.

The wisdom regarding subtle objects. Subsequently, the mind’s capacity to know the characteristics [of these objects] is revealed; this too is the benefit of such realization. Within the preceding section, there are three parts: first, a general statement;

second, a detailed exposition beginning with "attaining form," which reveals the wisdom regarding the ten subtle objects; and third, a conclusion beginning with "such as these," which summarizes the swiftness of that knowing capacity.
Regarding the term "subtle" in the detailed exposition, according to the commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asvabhāva, it refers to the subtle [nature].
The name is given because it is difficult to know. Regarding the phrase "later one is able to know within the characteristics of practice" and "not being terrified":
although the objects are subtle, one is not afraid because they are difficult to know. The remaining text is to be explained accordingly. There are three parts: first, the general heading;

second, from "one is able to know" onwards, the specific listing of the ten subtle objects; third, from "such as these" onwards, the conclusion. From "one is able to know" onwards, the objects and wisdom are specifically revealed. [End of section] "Such as these."

First, unchanging suchness (*avikāra-tathatā*); second, suchness according to conditions (*anupravṛtti-tathatā*); third, the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-niḥsvabhāvatā*); fourth, the separation from causal marks (*nimitta-vigama*); fifth...

1. Because the phenomena of the nine periods of time are manifested in a single thought-moment; 2. Because the six emptinesses are free from affliction; 3. Because they are quiescent from the very beginning;
4. Because they do not abide in any location; 5. Because they are eternally firm; 6. Because they are equal.
The seventh dedication, "Vowing that sentient beings become Dharma-teachers," consists of two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent;

second, the section beginning with "That is to say," which correctly reveals the content. Within this revelation, there are twenty vows: 1. Because speech issued from the bodhicitta is necessarily protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
2. To cause sentient beings to attain the wisdom of the Buddhas. 4. To cause them to attain the wisdom of the principle and the wisdom of the teachings. 5. From the state of non-... [text continues]
7. Eloquence that brings about direct realization: because it issues from the wisdom of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*) and produces skillful exposition.

This is like visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), which perceives its object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) without depending on the induction of the five [sensory] consciousnesses as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does.

According to the Sanskrit manuscript, it says "for the sake of the Dharma-preacher who is the eye," rather than "like" (*yathā*). This means it serves as the eye for sentient beings, enabling them to see the right path. 8. Eloquence that attains mindfulness and retention.

1. Power (*bala*), because it does not contradict the meaning of the phrases spoken by the Buddha. 9. The characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) is the sublime characteristic (*sūkṣma-lakṣaṇa*). 11.

This is because [the Buddha] intends to transmit the Dharma and gather in sentient beings; and because the twenty bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma all vow to dedicate [their merit] toward bringing peace to the world.
As for the remaining points not explained here, they should all be understood by analogy.
In the eighth dedication, the vow is to attain freedom from all grasping while practicing the conduct of dedication. This section has two parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows;

second, the passage beginning with "That is to say," which correctly reveals the ten phrases within the middle [section]. It should be understood that in each case—such as regarding karma—one does not employ grasping as the means for dedication.
The ninth dedication vows to attain the accomplishment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and not for the sake of the world;

the text of this dedication has two parts, as before. Within the actual exposition, there are twenty-eight phrases divided into two sections: the first seventeen phrases are an exalted manifestation, while the subsequent section, beginning with "merely for the purpose of teaching and transforming," is an explanatory interpretation.

Non-attachment. Eighth, not seeking pleasure. Eleventh, not seeking the conditions for pleasure to come together in harmony. The rest of the text can be understood. In the subsequent sequential explanation:
seventh, because it realizes the ultimate of non-arising; eighth, because the ocean of all practices adorns the lineage and manifests the fruition.

In the tenth dedication, within the passage concerning the mind of equality with the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), there are two sections as before.

In the main exposition, the thirty phrases are divided into two parts: the first ten phrases clarify the mind capable of dedicating; the latter twenty phrases, beginning with "Furthermore," clarify the dedication itself.

Regarding the purpose [of the preceding section]: first, one realizes that all phenomena arise through conditions and are thus without distinction; second, one realizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
fourth, one is without contention because there is neither "this" nor "that"; fifth, one realizes that all phenomena are unarisen;

sixth, one realizes the wisdom-mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) which does not lose the sequential states of cause and effect. The remainder of the text is self-evident. Regarding the purpose of the subsequent section: seventh, it says "entering."

Regarding the "Wheel of the Ten Powers": it refers to realizing the wisdom of the Buddha’s ten powers to crush Māra, just as the wheel of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*) crushes his enemies.

Regarding the "Vow of the Eight Pure Practices" and the "Fourteen Fearlessnesses of Bodhicitta": this mind is courageous; it does not fear the constraints of birth and death, nor is it shaken by favorable or adverse conditions.
It does not fear that enlightenment is difficult to achieve, that sentient beings are difficult to deliver, or that ascetic practices are difficult to perform.
Because it is a practice. The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
In the eleventh dedication, which begins with "May one obtain the dedication of pure right mindfulness," there are four parts: first, a restatement of the roots of goodness previously dedicated;
second, from "right mindfulness" onwards, an explanation of the purpose for which the dedication is made; third, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... [and so forth].
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates [merit] in this manner, they should not fall into inferiority. One should understand that dedication should not be performed [with such faults].
When the four sons of the Buddha—the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—dedicate in this way, they attain pure dedication and benefit. Within the first [section], there are twenty-two types;
the first three should all have the word "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), but they are not mentioned here due to brevity. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "One is free from the two attachments."

This refers to the two attachments to persons and phenomena, or the clinging to a self and what belongs to a self. Because one contemplates dependent origination as the eleventh [point], there is existence because of dependent origination, yet non-existence;
thus existence and non-existence are unimpeded, being neither identical nor separate. To observe in this way and to expound in this way is the twelfth.
As for "valiant," it means entering the ocean of birth and death to ferry across sentient beings, undaunted by any hardships, like Śakra.

The "Victory Banner that Subdues Enemies" (Dhvaja-śatru-nigraha-vīra) refers to the thirteenth banner, namely the Imperial Banner (Cakravarti-dhvaja), which enemies cannot overcome. It is established as the wisdom-banner of the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi-jñāna-dhvaja), such that none can surpass it.
"Treasury" (kośa) carries the sense of firmness; the remainder of the text is self-evident. Regarding the third [section], it should not be treated as the middle three.

1. The heading: This refers to the instruction that one should not perform dedication while being attached to existence (*bhava*) and so forth. 2. The interrogation: "For what reason? The intent of this interrogation is as follows:
Since a Bodhisattva’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and vow require them to constantly dwell within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), why would they not perform dedication?

3. The explanation: From the words "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards is the explanation. The intent of this explanation is as follows: If one performs dedication while being greedily attached to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), it is not great compassion. Therefore, one should [perform it] with non-...
Dedicating [merit] while [remaining free from] greed and so forth. The nine phrases in the text may be understood accordingly.
Fourth, regarding the ten phrases on the benefit of dedication: first, attaining pure faith; second, joyfully enduring and accepting the bodhisattva practices;
third, cultivating the path to pure great enlightenment (the text says "the path of the great bodhisattvas," which is likely a scribal error); fourth, possessing the Buddha-seed; fifth, the Buddha...
1. Attaining wisdom; 2. Abandoning evil; 3. Departing from the works of Māra; 4. Associating with virtuous friends; 5. Having already fulfilled great vows; 6.
Requesting to establish assemblies for the sake of sentient beings.
The twelfth dedication, the section on "Sounds," has two parts: first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows; second, from "That is to say" onwards, the actual exposition.

It is the vow that sentient beings may attain forty-four kinds of sounds. Regarding the fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth [vows], the character *jñāna* (wisdom) is added because they produce sound based upon wisdom;
thus they are called "wisdom-sounds. The underlying intent, however, still lies in the sounds themselves. Twenty-seven.

The "Vajra Phrase-Sound of Total Retention" (dhāraṇī) means that within this phrase-sound, many dharma-gates are gathered and retained, and it is capable of destroying calamities and perils because it cannot be suppressed or controlled by the sounds of devas, humans, māras, or Brahmās.
Because many words and phrases are produced from within its sound, it is called the "Treasury of Wisdom. The remaining text is easily understood.

The thirteenth dedication consists of ten dharmas, beginning with "may sentient beings obtain a body free from faults," and so forth. The text is divided into two parts: first, the summary of the preceding section that introduces the subsequent one;
second, the actual exposition, beginning with "that is to say. Within this exposition, seven vows are intended to cause the attainment of skillful wisdom such as right faith (*śraddhā*).

The eighth, "faith and understanding" (*adhimukti*), refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), because deep patience (*kṣānti*) within faith constitutes resolute conviction. The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
[He] knows.
In the fourteenth dedication, regarding the vow to personally attain ten kinds of bodies, there are two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent;

second, "That which is called" and below, the actual manifestation. Within the manifestation, there are three sections: first, listing the vows to be attained, namely the body of vows; second, "In all... and below...

This clarifies how the three types of karmic manifestations appear based on the body. The section beginning with "The three bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" below summarizes the benefits of manifesting these bodies.
Within the first part, there are ten aspects of the body: (1) the entire body is light; (2) it is not obscure or dim; (3) it is not defiled by water; (4) its nature is inherently pure;
(5) it is the ultimate among purities; (6) it is not covered by dust or grime; (7) even the most minute particles do not adhere to it.
Eighth, it is eternally free from defilement. Ninth, it is endowed with marks that are lovely. Tenth, it responds to sentient beings without limit, regardless of distance.

Regarding the second [point], the manifestation of the three types of karmic transformation based on the body, there are two parts. First, a general demonstration; second, a specific analysis beginning with "all sentient beings' great bodhi.

Within the first of these, there are two further sections: first, manifesting according to location; second, clarifying the spontaneous nature of what is manifested, beginning with "how does it clarify... and so forth. Of the former...
The middle three [manifestations] are: first, manifesting bodily action (*kāyakarman*) within the lands; second, manifesting vocal action (*vākkarman*) within the world;

and third, manifesting mental action (*manaskarman*) within the palaces through skillful establishment of all matters. Subsequently, within the spontaneous manifestations, each occurs according to what is appropriate, without depending on deliberate attention (*manasikāra*).
This is because they manifest accordingly. Later, when the transformations of the three types of karma are distinguished individually, there are ten kinds divided into three groups:

the first six are vocal karma, the next three are bodily karma, and the last one is mental karma. Thirdly, in the summary of the benefits of manifesting the body, it is stated that all beings are caused to attain the Buddha-body.
The fifteenth dedication consists of two parts within the section on "attaining the non-empty body and so forth": first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent;

second, clarifying the realization of all dharmas through speech, beginning with "entering among all sentient beings. Within the former, there are ten types: first, the non-empty bodily karma; second, tirelessness...
1. Cultivation; 2. The three great compassions are vast; 3. Constantly accords with the teachings; 4. Constantly brings forth mindfulness; 5.

Mindfulness of the Buddha is ever-present; 6. Cultivates goodness with a sincere heart; 7. Places things upon the path; 8. Attains the wisdom and function of the teachings; 9. Attains extensive reception, upholding, and cultivation; 10.
Subsequently realizes the two [truths] within all phenomena. First, it clarifies that which is realized; subsequently, the following line concludes [the section].
One practices by relying on the ten entries. Among these, there are ten phrases: first, awakening to the true nature of things;

seventh, awakening to the bodhisattva’s wisdom that can generate the roots of goodness in sentient beings; eighth, awakening to the bodhisattva’s wisdom that contemplates the dharma-nature. The remaining phrases may be understood accordingly.

The sixteenth dedication regarding the Pure Land has two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the actual manifestation of the vow beginning with "May all Buddha-fields...
