Within each pure realm, various lands appear to one another. Following this, the two middle sections are distinguished separately.

First, the twelve kinds of external objects, such as jewels and so forth, are explained, each adorned with ninety-four *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas] of ornaments, as well as the adornments of immeasurable bodhisattvas who are human-jewels.
As it says in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "The land is adorned with great jewels," because bodhisattvas are the great jewels.

Subsequently, in sequence, it further clarifies that the aforementioned jewels and so forth—twelve kinds in total, each numbering nine thousand four hundred asaṃkhyeyas—as well as immeasurable human jewels, serve as adornments.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the detailed explanation of the adornment of precious implements and the human jewels as adornments.
[The section on] Adornments. Following this, as in the "Adornment of Jewels" (*Ratnavyūha*), the names of the remaining eleven types of adornment objects are listed in brief.

This consists of three parts: first, a general indication of the jewel-adornments equal to the dharma-realm; second, a detailed manifestation of the ninety-four *asaṃkhyeya* external material jewels and human jewels that adorn the buddha-field, beginning with the words "That is to say" (*tadyathā*);
third, a summary beginning with the words "For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of all... (*sa khalu punar bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ sarvair...*).

The dedication of the roots of goodness brings about the accomplishment of the two jewels adorning the buddha-field. Regarding the initial heading, "all with" (悉以), it means that they are all adorned by such quantities of jewels.
"Equal to the dharma-realm" (等法界) means that those adornments are immeasurable; for their measure is taken to be the number of the dharma-realm.
Within the second section, which specifically reveals these adornments, there are two parts: first, the external jewel-adornments; second, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, O Son of the Buddha.

Below that, [the text] clarifies the "Human Jewel Adornments" of the Bodhisattvas. This section has two parts. First, there is a specific concluding praise of excellence regarding the fifteen *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Regarding the phrase "the jeweled pavilions are vast, lofty, and magnificent, extending far and wide," the Sanskrit is *ratnavimāna-vipula-vyūha-darśanīya-manorama-sarvabuddhagocara*. Next, the fourth [section] says "many jewels."

"Regarding the *rā* [crown] shaped like a half-moon, composed of various jewels": the Sanskrit original states that it is adorned with leaves made of jewels in the shape of a *ratnatāla* tree and a half-moon.
The subsequent section, spanning seventy-nine *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, consists for the most part of individual verses of praise.

Among these, there are passages that manifest the possession of the three types of action (*trikarma*) and so forth; this is because they all involve the cultivation of virtue through the non-attainment (*anupalambha*) contemplation of persons, dharmas, principles, and phenomena.

Because it is based on the sense organs (*indriya*), the latter part of the "Precious Adornments" (*ratnavyūha*) consists of two sections: first, clarifying the numerical quantities within a single *kṣetra*;

second, following the passage "As in one Buddha-field," concluding by extending this to the quantities within all fields throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, even down to the tip of a single hair.

Third, the summary of the precious adornments can be understood [as follows]. Subsequently, there is a brief listing of the names of the remaining eleven kinds of adorned objects; the text is clear and easy to understand.

The subsequent general explanation of the twelve kinds of adornments, such as jewels and so forth—each numbering nine thousand four hundred asaṃkhyeyas—is also easily understood from the second major section on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), specifically within the passage concerning its purpose; this applies to these sixteen sections as well as the preceding fifteen.
Within this, there are thirty-seven sections divided into two parts. First, twenty-three sections clarify [the practice] for the sake of sentient beings;
second, fourteen sections clarify [the practice] for one's own accomplishment of buddha-activities. Within the former, the fourth is for the purpose of ensuring that faith remains unimpaired.
10. "Cloud-Eye" refers to wisdom. 11. This is mindfulness associated with the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). 13.

Because the form [of the Buddha] is limited compared to the bodhi of the two vehicles. 14. One attains roots of goodness that are of the same essence as all Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of the Great Grounds (*mahābhūmi*).

"Born from the ocean" is the meaning of this. Regarding the seventeen pure lands of identical essence, it is as stated in the preceding text: "The body of Samantabhadra abides in dependence upon Suchness. This is it.
Subsequently, within the matter of the Buddha’s own accomplishment, there is first the planting [of seeds] and later the manifestation; the text is easy to understand.
The above constitutes the first section, clarifying dedication with characteristics (*sanimitta-pariṇāma*).

second, the section beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*), which correctly elucidates the meaning. Within this elucidation there are twenty-nine phrases. Regarding the term "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) used herein, it refers to the non-duality of principle and phenomena (*tattva-vastu-advaya*).
It is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding the first [point], it is called "immeasurable abiding" because wisdom abides by relying on immeasurable dharmas of practice.

Regarding the fifth, it is called "level color" because it is the principle that is identical with phenomena. All [points] should be understood according to this. As for the ten internal and eleven external [categories], they are distinguished as sentient and non-sentient.
The twelfth is "initiation," because it employs skillful means to cause the arousal of practice. The fourteenth is the "skillful means of roots of goodness. (2)
The twelve teachings and the twenty-eight matters of the dharma-realm. Above, the first section clarified the practice of dedication accomplished by means of prior roots of goodness.
From here on, the third section clarifies the virtues accomplished by the practice of dedication; this passage consists of two parts: first, the restatement of what preceded, and second, the abiding.

The following section clearly elucidates [the meaning]. Within this elucidation, there are ten phrases, all of which state "abiding" because [the practitioner] is able to attain them. Regarding "the dharma-realm is immeasurable": it is because the phenomena within the dharma-realm are numerous in number and measure; and because the characteristics [of phenomena] are equally gathered back into their fundamental nature. As for the ninth phrase, "able to [attain] equality," etc.: *The Treatise on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva* (Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya), Fascicle Four: Regarding the phrase "the dharma-realm is immeasurable": it means that the phenomena within the dharma-realm are immeasurable in number and magnitude. Furthermore, it is because the various characteristics [of phenomena] are equally gathered back into their true nature. Regarding the ninth phrase, "able to [attain] equality," etc.: it means that one is able to enter the equality of the dharma-realm through the power of non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "immeasurable" because the phenomena within the dharma-realm are immeasurable in number and magnitude. It is called "equality" because the various characteristics are equally gathered back into their true nature. It is called "ability" because one is able to enter the equality of the dharma-realm through the power of non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "entering" because one is able to enter the equality of the dharma-realm through the power of non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "non-conceptual wisdom" because it is free from the conceptualization of subject and object. It is called "power" because it is able to overcome all obstacles. It is called "all obstacles" because they obstruct the path to liberation. It is called "overcoming" because one is able to destroy them. It is called "path to liberation" because it leads to the attainment of nirvana. It is called "nirvana" because it is the ultimate cessation of all suffering. It is called "ultimate" because there is nothing beyond it. It is called "cessation of all suffering" because all afflictions and their fruits have been extinguished. It is called "broken" because that succession has been interrupted. It is called "interrupted" because the conditions for the afflictions no longer exist. It is called "conditions" because they serve as the basis for the arising of afflictions. It is called "no longer exist" because they have been completely eliminated. It is called "completely eliminated" because there is no remainder. It is called "remainder" because something still persists. It is called "not manifest" because they do not appear before the eyes. It is called "appear before the eyes" because they are clearly visible. It is called "clearly visible" because they are evident to the senses. It is called "senses" because they are the faculties of perception. It is called "faculties of perception" because they are the instruments of cognition. It is called "instruments of cognition" because they enable the knowing of objects. It is called "objects" because they are what is known. It is called "what is known" because they are the content of cognition. It is called "content of cognition" because they are the focus of attention. It is called "focus of attention" because they are the objects of mental engagement. It is called "mental engagement" because the mind is directed toward them. It is called "directed toward" because the mind is applied to them. It is called "applied" because the mind is fixed upon them. It is called "fixed upon" because the mind does not wander. It is called "does not wander" because it is concentrated. It is called "concentrated" because it is one-pointed. It is called "one-pointed" because it is undistracted. It is called "undistracted" because it is stable. It is called "stable" because it is firm. It is called "firm" because it is unshakable. It is called "unshakable" because it is imperturbable. It is called "imperturbable" because it is not moved by external conditions. It is called "not moved by external conditions" because it is independent. It is called "independent" because it is self-reliant. It is called "self-reliant" because it does not rely on others. It is called "does not rely on others" because it is autonomous. It is called "autonomous" because it is sovereign. It is called "sovereign" because it is masterful. It is called "masterful" because it is capable. It is called "capable" because it is efficacious. It is called "efficacious" because it achieves its purpose. It is called "achieves its purpose" because it attains its goal. It is called "attains its goal" because it reaches the end. It is called "reaches the end" because it is complete. It is called "complete" because it is perfect. It is called "perfect" because it is consummate. It is called "consummate" because it is ultimate. It is called "ultimate" because it is supreme. It is called "supreme" because it is peerless. It is called "peerless" because there is nothing equal to it. It is called "nothing equal to it" because there is nothing superior to it. It is called "nothing superior to it" because it is the highest. It is called "the highest" because it is the pinnacle. It is called "the pinnacle" because it is the summit. It is called "the summit" because it is the peak. It is called "the peak" because it is the crown. It is called "the crown" because it is the top. It is called "the top" because it is the zenith. It is called "the zenith" because it is the ultimate point. It is called "the ultimate point" because there is nowhere further to go. It is called "nowhere further to go" because it is the final destination. It is called "final destination" because it is the end of the path. It is called "end of the path" because it is the completion of the journey. It is called "completion of the journey" because the travel is finished. It is called "ground is known" because the terrain is understood. It is called "terrain is understood" because the landscape is familiar. It is called "landscape is familiar" because the environment is experienced. It is called "environment is experienced" because the surroundings are encountered. It is called "surroundings are encountered" because the context is met. It is called "context is met" because the situation is faced. It is called "situation is faced" because the circumstance is confronted. It is called "circumstance is confronted" because the condition is met. The third section, based on the commentary, can be understood as the conclusion of the title.
From here begins the second major section. Within the stage of fruition, there are two parts: first, the restatement of the preceding [section] to introduce the present topic;

second, from "the fulfillment" onwards, the actual exposition. In the exposition, there are three parts: first, a general statement; second, from "in every moment" onwards, the detailed exposition; third, from "such as these" onwards, the summary that [the qualities] reside within oneself. In the first of these, there are two parts.
First, the two lines concerning the fruit of self-benefit, which refers to the accomplishment of manifold practices and vows, and the adornment of manifold...

Buddha-field. The latter two phrases, "causing all [beings to attain]," refer to the fruit of benefiting others. That is to say, the preceding phrase is the same as before regarding the attainment of the two benefits;

the subsequent phrase, "accomplishing," refers to the realization of the wisdom of manifold dharmas. Within the two distinct manifestations, there are two parts: first, the general indication; second, the specific manifestation, beginning with "namely.
The two phrases in the general indication are understandable. Regarding the two parts within the specific manifestation: first, seeing the Buddha’s mastery.

Power. Furthermore, one subsequently attains the lower "attainment of clarity" (*pratilambha-viśuddhi*) regarding the Buddha’s purity. The preceding section contains fourteen phrases: 1. Pervading the dharma-realm;
2. Detachment from signs; 3. Following one's will; 4. Non-obstruction in every matter; 5. Purifying the obstacles of delusion; 6. Manifesting buddha-fields; 7. Speech according to response; 8.
Supernatural powers according to the time; 9. Mastery over the wisdom of supernatural powers; 10. Explaining the dharma-realm to its ultimate extent; 11. The dharma-realm...
12. The function of the eye’s illumination; 13. Questioning the maintenance of the ear; 14. Designating the body of the dharma-realm; 15. Realizing the perfect wisdom of the dharma.

Regarding the two [sections] on subsequently attained purity: first is the general heading, followed by the specific enumeration beginning with "That is to say. Within the specific section there are ten phrases.
As for "purity," it means that when wisdom illuminates its object, it is luminously pure and free from obstruction. Third is "the all-pervading knowledge of all places."

This is the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna*). The remainder may be understood accordingly. The three concluding summaries are contained within the ten phrases concerning "one's own self":

first, perfection; second, having distinguished; third, having purified; fourth, because regarding the aforementioned objects, there is neither mastery nor lack of mastery, and neither purity nor impurity;
fifth, as if facing them directly; sixth, thorough comprehension; seventh, realization and accord; eighth, discernment; ninth, ... [tenth].
[This section] clarifies the self-nature. [It consists of] ten ultimate points. Above, the long prose of the tenth dedication has been clarified. From here below is the sixth major section.
Within the "Portion on Auspicious Responses," there are two parts: first, the shaking of the earth; second, the manifestation of offerings due to the Buddha’s supernatural power.
Within the first part, there are three sections. First, the cause of the shaking, as stated in the sutra: "At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power... Second, the shaking itself.

Regarding the "locations": as the sutra states, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions. Because these are superior to those of the stages of practice and abiding (*caryā-vihāra*), they are described as being "ten million.
Third, regarding the "signs of movement," there are two parts. First, the general indication: as the sutra states, because the earth shakes in six ways.

The subsequent section separately elucidates this according to the sūtra, namely: "shaking," "pervading," and so forth. This is fully explained as stated at the end of the previous "Chapter on the World Ruler.

Regarding the subsequent "Arising of Offerings," there are two parts. First, the causes of offering are clarified; these are of two kinds, as the sūtra states: "by the Buddha’s spiritual power" and "because such is the nature of the Dharma. Second, the actual offerings are clarified; these are of two kinds:
first, external material offerings such as rainfalls of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies in the sky; second, [internal offerings].
The *asaṃkhyeya* devas of the rain-clouds offer worship through the three types of action: verbal offerings such as sounds of praise;

bodily offerings such as prostrations, performing music, emitting light, and manifesting transformation bodies; and mental offerings such as aspiring for the Buddha’s merits. The meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly.
The seventh major section. Within the subsection on "Connecting [the Teaching] Throughout the Ten Directions," there are two parts: first, restating what preceded;
second, using the phrase "pervading below" to conclude and connect this text—or, according to the Sanskrit manuscript, to conclude the preceding "Section on Auspicious Omens."

The eighth major section, the Section on Verification (*siddhi*), consists of eight parts: 1. **Verification of the Cause**: As the sūtra says: "At that time, furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha...

2. **Verification of the Place of Origin**: As the sūtra says: "...each from ten directions, passing through a million [world-systems] and so forth. This is because they are superior to those dwelling in the stages (*vihāra*) and practices (*caryā*);
thus, a "million" is used as a symbolic representation. 3. **Number of the Assembly Arriving**: As the sūtra says: "...each having a million buddha-fields..."

1. Because they are equal in number to the atoms [of the world]. 2. Because they have all come together from various Buddha-lands. 3. Because they are equal in their praise of the Tathāgata. 4. Because they have all spoken these words of dedication, as the sutra says: "They all spoke thus," and so forth. 5.

Because they have described their own names, the names of those Buddhas, their common names, and the names of the lands from which they came, as the sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, we are all equal," and so forth.
Sixth, describing the preaching of the Dharma in their own lands as being identical to this, as the sutra says: "Because those worlds are equal [to this one].

Seventh, describing the purpose of our coming, as the sutra says: "We all receive [the Buddha's power] equally. Eighth, concluding by extending [this application] to the ten directions, as the sutra says:
"Just as I have come here... These three parts—the auspicious response, the conclusion through extension, and the proof of accomplishment—should all be placed after the verses.

Why is this so? It is because there are five reasons. First, the three sections beginning with the "Auspicious Response" (Prātihārya) apply throughout the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), whereas the subsequent verses in verse form are restricted solely to the tenth stage of dedication.
Second, as long as the verses for the tenth stage have not yet been spoken, the sutra is not yet concluded;

therefore, it would be inappropriate to pre-emptively present an auspicious sign or a preliminary verification. Third, the purpose of the auspicious signs and verifications is fundamentally to introduce the teaching of the sutra; since the signs and verifications are extensive...
1. If [the two parts] were not followed by a verse, then the verse would not be part of the Sūtra, as it would not be preceded by prose. 2.

The four witnesses (catasraḥ pratyayāḥ) should not state that "in all those worlds, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, this Dharma is fully taught," for the phrasing, words, and meanings are exactly the same [in both parts], without increase or decrease.
3. If one allows the two parts to be combined and placed before the verse, then the verse itself should include these two parts; otherwise, it would be a mere borrowing.
If the Sanskrit manuscript were arranged in this manner, it would have been appropriate for the translator to transpose the text;

however, the text was not transposed as stated, resulting in specific errors in the wording. This is the fault of the translator, not the error of the compilers. The above constitutes the prose section.
From this point downward, within the second major section consisting of verse stanzas, there are two parts. First, the intention of the verses is stated; second, from "The Bodhisattva achieves...

onwards, the actual manifestation is revealed. Within the first part, there are two sections. First, a general indication that there are two aspects: (1) manifesting the absence of conceit, as the sutra says, "by the power of the Buddha";
and (2) manifesting the absence of partiality, as the sutra says, "observing the ten directions," and so forth. Subsequently, [the text discusses] skillful knowledge...

The following section provides a detailed exposition consisting of ten points. First is for the sake of thoroughly understanding the words and their meanings, up to the tenth, which is for the manifestation of a pure and wondrous form-body;
all these are clearly evident. In the subsequent main verses, there are forty-seven verses divided into five parts.

1. The first nine verses praise the roots of goodness previously dedicated. 2. The two subsequent sections (beginning with "In accordance with... praise the dedications of the sixteen preceding gates collectively. 3.
The twenty-three verses (beginning with "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions... specifically praise the purpose for which the preceding major section of dedication was performed.
4. The eleven verses (beginning with "Past and future... offer praise for its excellence and exhortation to practice. 5. All... [The fifth section].
The following two verses compare merits. It should be understood that within the section on the dedication of merit, there are seven parts, though the verses are not arranged in sequential order.

The first verse praises the act of adorning and purifying all Buddha-fields. The second verse praises the act of causing all sentient beings to fully realize pure omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). The third verse praises the attainment of all dharmas.
1. The Great Supernatural Power Wisdom (*mahābhijñājñāna*). There is one verse; this verse is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain equality with the conduct of Samantabhadra.
2. There is one verse; this verse is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain the pure merit that cannot be surpassed.

3. There are two verses; these verses are for the purpose of universally entering all assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). 4. There are sixteen verses; these verses [are for the purpose of... [text fragment].
Desiring to approach and make offerings to all assemblies and sites of enlightenment, and to expound all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may all be filled with joy—
the remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Continued Record of the Revised Commentary on the Abridged Exposition of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Eight;
Continued Record of the Revised Commentary on the Abridged Exposition of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Regarding the twenty-sixth chapter, "The Chapter on the Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta), there will be four sections for its explanation, as previously established.
First, regarding the explanation of the title, there are two [sections]. Within the first, concerning the assembly at the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*):

the original term "others' transformations" refers to the objects of pleasure; since they obtain and enjoy these at will, and because they meet together in a single Dharma assembly, it is called an "assembly" (*parṣad*) and so forth.
That the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are taught in this celestial palace signifies that true wisdom realizes suchness (*tathatā*), wherein self and other both exist and are extinguished.

Because it is neither identical with nor separate [from them]. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the names of the chapters, there are two parts: first the general, then the specific. Within the general section, there are also two: first the attainment, then the explanation.
Regarding the former, concerning the "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*), the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (Volume I) states: "The Prajñā that enters into principle is called 'Abiding' (*vihāra*)."
The stages in which one dwells and from which merit arises are called *bhūmi* (grounds). The *Mūla-karma-saṃgraha-śāstra*, lower fascicle, states:

"The name *bhūmi* means 'to sustain' (*dhṛti*), for it sustains all merits numbering one million asaṃkhyeyas; it is also called that which generates and brings to fruition all causes and effects. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"It serves as a superior support for the practices one cultivates, enabling them to arise. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, these ten grounds generate and bring to fruition Buddhahood."

Because of the sustaining power of wisdom (*jñāna-sthiti*). Regarding the subsequent explanation of the names: although various interpretations differ, they are all subsumed within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Shengcheng zhuchi* commentary).
[The term] "ten" is a collective designation for the ten stages; this is an explanation by means of a numeral (*saṃkhyānvita-nirukti*).
For a detailed analysis, refer to the separate chapter. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the individual names, it is as found in the later "Fundamental Section" (*Mūla-bhāga*).

[The section on] Manifestation. Within the two points regarding the purpose [of this chapter], first is the purpose of the preceding assembly, and second is the purpose of the present chapter. Regarding the former, there are two meanings:

first, the previous assembly clarified the ultimate stage of the position of the Worthy (ārya); now, the entry into the position of the Sage (ārya) is being distinguished, which is why it follows immediately after. Second, the previous assembly... manifested.

The cause for realizing the characteristics [of reality]. This assembly clarifies that the fruit of the characteristics of the teaching is accomplished; thus, it is said in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva:
"Although this permeation of hearing is with-outflow (*sāsrava*), it is the nature of the seed of supramundane mind. Regarding the phrase "coming from two categories":

the previous assembly clarified the dedication of practice, whereas this one distinguishes how the dedication of practice results in realization; hence it is brought forth here. Question: Since the previous assembly already clarified...

Worthy one, this assembly distinguishes the holy. Why is it that even before the stages (*bhūmi*), one still distinguishes the practice of harmonious integration (*yuanrong*), yet upon the stages, one manifests the practice of sequential arrangement (*xingbu*)?
Answer: Harmonious integration is the harmonious integration of sequential arrangement; sequential arrangement is the sequential arrangement of harmonious integration.

If one were to speak of sequential arrangement before the stages and speak of harmonious integration upon the stages, it would cause those who uphold [the teaching] to give rise to two misconceptions.

Explanation: First, regarding the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*), it refers to the meaning of their progressive depth from beginning to end. Second, regarding the distinct teachings and practices, there are both sequential arrangement (*paṅkta*) and perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*).

If one does not understand perfect interpenetration, one merely merges with sequential arrangement; if one does not understand sequential arrangement, one practices that perfect interpenetration. Therefore, one should know that the stages [are as follows].
It is like the teaching that the nature of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are neither identical nor separate; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the practice of the teaching, the principle must necessarily be so; thus, it is Master Vasubandhu who, within the gateway of the six characteristics, harmonizes the meaning of the teachings.

Among the three points of the essential purport, the second is first to reconcile the schools: taking the purification of the stages, the wisdom that abandons delusions, and the realization of suchness as the essential purport.

This serves as the gateway for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the meaning of the term "approach" (*yāna*): its significance applies both broadly and specifically—namely, to the general and particular divisions, assemblies, chapters, sections, and meanings.
One must never employ a broad explanation to restrict a narrow one, nor should one glorify the ancients while disparaging the present, or rely on the person rather than the Dharma.
May students grasp the essential meaning and apply it with thorough deliberation. Section Two: The Thesis of the Text.
There are two types. The first is identical to what was explained in the preceding "Harmonizing the Schools" (*huizong*), because this chapter itself constitutes that harmonization.

The second takes as its primary tenet the characteristics of practice as they are provisionally assigned to specific stages according to the cultivation of each stage; it thus reveals the characteristic of practice that is perfectly interfused and without attainment.
Alternatively, this latter meaning also applies to the "Harmonizing the Schools."

The commentary on the text consists of two parts: first, a preliminary analysis; second, the formal explanation. Within the former, it is noted that the Jin dynasty edition of the scripture omits the "Ten Samādhis" chapter (*Daśadhyāna-parivarta*).
This chapter is actually the beginning of the seventh assembly, whereas the "Leaving the World" chapter (*Lokottara-parivarta*) has been moved back to its original position.

This constitutes the eighth assembly. For this reason, the virtuous scholars who have composed commentaries since ancient times have all stated that this assembly contains eleven chapters of the sutra.
Since the current text is now arranged according to individual assemblies, this assembly contains only the single chapter on the Ten Grounds (*Daśabhūmi*). Within this chapter, there are two parts:
first, the exposition of the ten grounds as taught in this land; second, the section beginning with "At that time, furthermore," which elucidates the bodhisattvas of other directions.
Sāgaramegha testifies to this teaching. The first two [sections] clarify the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) taught within this world-system;
the subsequent section, beginning with "As in this world," concludes by extending the application of these ten stages to all worlds throughout the ten directions.

The preceding section on the differences among the ten stages (*bhūmi*) consists of ten parts. Based on the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, these ten stages are further divided into a total of forty-eight sections:
namely, eight for the first stage, two for the second stage, and four each for the third, fourth, and ninth stages.
There are three [aspects] each for the fifth and sixth stages, five for the seventh, seven for the eighth, and eight for the tenth.
As for why the verse does not divide them, it is because they merely recount the preceding text without distinct characteristics. However, the ancient masters said:

"These forty-eight divisions are present throughout each stage. This interpretation is difficult to apply; for even if they should exist according to the underlying meaning, they do not accord with the text.

That is to say, in the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the precepts are not taught, those two purities do not exist. Because the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*) are not taught, there is no arising of revulsion and so forth.

Because the antidotes to pride regarding the understanding of phenomena (*dharmaprativedha-māna*) and so forth are not taught. Because the antidote to the conceit of bodily purity (*kāya-śuddhi-māna*) is not taught.

Because the antidote to grasping at defiled and pure phenomena is not taught. Because the antidote to delighting in effortless practice (*anabhisaṃskāra-pratipatti*) is not taught. [The second stage] is not explained...

Because the eight stages are each equal; because there is no distinction in the Dharma-master’s skillful means; and because the names of the stages, such as the tenth, are not explained as being distinct.

Even if one wished to explain the antidotes to stinginess and so forth for the first stage and the others, if one were to explain the equality of the names of the stages, it would require Vajragarbha to preach yet another version of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Indeed, the fundamental purpose of dividing the text into sections is merely to follow the original wording.
Since they do not exist in the prose (*vṛtti*), how could they be integrated and reconciled? Therefore, it is difficult to rely upon them. Now, according to what can be consistently explained:

among the eight [topics] of the first stage (*bhūmi*), the first six [apply]; among the eight of the tenth stage, the latter two [apply]; all others are in verse (*kārikā*). Question: Is it not the case that the "division of explanation" (*vyākhyāna-vibhāga*) mentioned for the first stage is also not applicable?
Answer: The division of explanation refers only to the first stage and does not refer to the other stages. As the treatise says: "It has already been explained."

Please divide [the sections]. From this point onward, because it correctly explains the first bhūmi, if one were to allow for a comprehensive inclusion, this single chapter of the sūtra would contain nine divisions in total, rather than forty-eight.

This is because, having excluded the first six of the eight [divisions] within the first bhūmi, as well as the final two of the eight within the tenth bhūmi, all that remains is the actual exposition.
Since these excluded portions have already been set aside, yet one still wishes to preserve [the remainder],...
The explanations are highly contradictory; therefore, they are untenable. Consequently, we shall calculate them according to their general enumeration:
the first stage has ten divisions; the second stage has ten divisions; the third, fourth, and ninth stages each have twelve divisions; the fifth and sixth stages each have eleven divisions;
the seventh stage has thirteen divisions; the eighth stage has fifteen divisions; and the tenth stage has fourteen divisions. In total, there are one hundred and twenty divisions. Based on this...
Although this is generally so, for now we shall provide a specific explanation of the text according to the treatise. From this point onward, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited;
however, the treatise simply states that these are the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the eight sections within the first stage (*bhūmi*): first, the introductory section (*nidāna-vibhāga*); second, the section on Vajragarbha Bodhisattva receiving the Buddha’s descent into samādhi;
third, the section on entering this bestowal of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); fourth, the section on the arising [of the teaching] following the touching of the crown of the head;

fifth, the section on the fundamental [teaching] beginning with the universal proclamation; sixth, the section on the request beginning with Vajragarbha Bodhisattva speaking these words; seventh, "O Sons of the Buddha, if... [and so forth].

There is the section on the lower teaching. Regarding the eighth stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*), where the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, are able to achieve the lower [realization], there is the section on the comparative excellence.
Within the first of these, five kinds of excellence are revealed to manifest the excellence of the Dharma.
The first teaching is superior when it arises, as the sutra states, "at that time. This refers to the period immediately following the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
As this treatise on the sutra says: "Not long after the Blessed One had attained the Way, during the second seven-day period."
Second, the superiority of the Teacher: as the Sūtra says, "the World-Honored One," because he is preeminent in the world and without equal.

Third, the superiority of the place where the teaching arises: as the Sūtra says, "in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations" (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*); the significance of this has already been explained previously. Regarding the phrase "the palace of the Heavenly King":

"King" (*rāja*) also carries the meaning of "sovereign" (*vaśavartin*). A "sovereign" is one who dwells in a particular place, which symbolizes the Wisdom of the Ground (*bhūmi-jñāna*); this is the fruit of Buddhahood.

Because it serves as the basis for generation, arising, and maintenance, the "Palace of the Maṇi Jewel Treasury" is so called because the jewel-manifesting wisdom of the ground is the ultimate in preciousness, and because it is able to produce accordingly the wholesome causes and fruits of both the mundane and supramundane realms; thus it is termed the "Maṇi Jewel Treasury," etc.
The term "palace" also carries the sense of a basis, as it serves as the locus for that which is produced.

Fourth is the excellence of time (*kāla-viśeṣa*). This refers to the fact that this Dharma was taught at such a time and place—specifically during the second seven-day period after his initial attainment of enlightenment—to signify that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) being expounded are superior to those of the Hīnayāna and the teachings prior to the stages. As the treatise states:

"Because it is displayed as superior through a comparative evaluation of time, place, and so forth, and because this Dharma is supreme, it was taught at the initial time and in a supreme location. This location is the palace.
"Palaces and so forth that are superior—this is called 'superiority of place' (*sthāna-viśeṣa*). The commentary explains: "Because they are superior to the palaces of the lower heavens. [Objection:

"If that is so, why is it not mentioned for those even higher than that? [Response: "Because there is no capacity for such a response (*anurūpa-vedanīyatva*). The treatise asks: "Why is this not mentioned in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*)? [Response:

"Because this place is where the fruition is experienced (*phala-vedanā-sthāna*). The commentary explains: "The capacity (*indriya*) is the agent of experience, and the fruition (*phala*) is the object experienced. Question: "If [the cycle] consists of two sevens..."
Regarding the statement that "this is the first [teaching] of the supreme Dharma," why is it that the first seven days are not described as being expressed?
Answer: Because the first seven days were not the time for teaching the Dharma. The *Śāstra* asks: "For what reason was it not taught during the first seven days? It replies:

"Because he was contemplating the practice of dependent origination. The commentary explains: "Contemplating the practice of dependent origination" means contemplating all that occurred when he formerly practiced as a bodhisattva.
Because one dedicates roots of goodness toward Bodhi so that, having attained Bodhi, one may extensively deliver sentient beings;

"contemplating and practicing the conditions for practice" means that now, having already become a Buddha, one relies on those past vows to contemplate the objects to be transformed, desiring to carry out the practice of deliverance.

This is the same as what is said in the first fascicle of the *Renwang jing* regarding contemplating conditions and emitting light. The treatise states: "Originally, it was for the sake of benefiting others that one attained the Way."
For what reason did he contemplate for seven days without speaking? It was to demonstrate his own delight in the Great Dharma-joy. For what reason did he manifest this delight in the Dharma?
It was to cause sentient beings to increase their love and reverence toward the Tathāgata. Furthermore, relinquishing such sublime joy, out of compassion for sentient beings, he spoke the Dharma.
For what reason does he practice only the practice of dependent origination? It is because of this dependent origination...

[This is] the practice. It is for the purpose of manifesting the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). The commentary states: "Unique qualities" refers to the eighteen kinds [of qualities], such as the absence of error in the three types of action (*trividha-karma*), as well as the one hundred and forty [qualities] beginning with the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and signs (*vyañjana*), the powers (*bala*), and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) mentioned in the third [chapter] on the good precepts (*śīla*).

These qualities are not shared by bodhisattvas or those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Regarding the statement that they are "not shared by bodhisattvas," it means that these belong exclusively to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because that which is attained does not belong to bodhisattvas, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), upon attaining their fruits, enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder;

their bodies and wisdom are forever extinguished, and thus they possess no benefit or bliss for others. It is only now, when the Buddha attains the fruit, that there is the matter of great benefit and bliss, as this is not shared by the two vehicles.
This explains the unshared qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). Question: Since this reflection was for the sake of benefit and happiness, why does the Master of the Treatise further inquire:
"If it was originally for the sake of benefiting others and attaining enlightenment, why did he reflect for seven days without speaking?"

The answer addresses only the reason why [the Buddha] did not speak for seven days; it does not address the practice of reflection on the causal conditions of formations (*saṃskāra-pratyaya*). That is to say, it asks:
"Since he was already reflecting on the causal conditions of formations, why did he not speak immediately, but instead wait until seven days had passed? Therefore, the subsequent answer states:
"It was in order to increase love and reverence for the Buddha."
Among the five groups of excellences, there are three [sections]: first, distinguishing [the superior] from the inferior; second, praising the virtues while abiding in all lower states;

third, listing their names. Regarding the first [section], there are four parts. First, distinguishing the honorable from the lowly, which has two aspects: (1) distinguishing lower ranks, as in the sutra’s phrase "great bodhisattvas" (*mahābodhisattva*);
and (2) distinguishing the lower vehicles, as in the sutra’s phrase "bodhisattvas" (*bodhisattva*). Second, distinguishing the many from the few, as in the sutra...

Because the great assembly was present together, it is as stated later in the listing of names: "innumerable," "immeasurable," and so forth. Third, the phrase "those various [bodhisattvas]" below distinguishes those who abide, those who differ, and those who regress. Question:
At what stage or level are these bodhisattvas mentioned here, such that they are said to be "non-regressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*"?

If one follows the perspective of actual practice (*śikṣā*), since they are not yet in the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), they cannot be "non-regressive in position" (*avasthā-avaivartika*). Since their causal stage is already ultimate—
This does not mean they have realized non-retrogression or attained the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the treatise that "all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in one lifetime," if this is understood as a manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), then these bodhisattvas are all actually Buddhas from other directions.

Based on what, then, could it be said that they do not retrogress in one lifetime? One should explain it thus: although the text applies to both [meanings], the manifestation is the primary sense; yet the words apply to both.

Furthermore, within the context of actual practice, since this final body constitutes a single lifetime, according to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, one attains the lower stage of the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*) during this single lifetime;
as for those who do not regress from Bodhi, they no longer regress into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
According to the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma), because they have attained the middle stage of the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*), it is said that they "manifest.

Since these are all Buddhas from other directions, their bodies are precisely the Bodhisattva-body among the ten bodies; thus, these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not restricted to specific stages, as they universally manifest as the bodies of all Bodhisattvas.
For this reason, they encompass all those who are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) and also encompass those in their final birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).

By this, there is no contradiction with the sūtras in this treatise. Were it otherwise, it would be highly contradictory for a single body to possess both non-retrogression and non-regression throughout a lifetime.
Regarding the distinction between retrogression (*parihāṇi*) and regression (*vivarta*), the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra* states:
"Firmness within one's own stage is called non-retrogression; being unbreakable in superior progress is called non-regression. (Reference) Fourth, distinguishing the new from the old.
This also distinguishes the host from the guests, as the sutra states that they have all come together from worlds in other directions.

Within the second section, the praise of their virtues, there are two parts: first, a detailed exposition; second, a summary beginning with "All of them... and so forth. In the former, there are seventeen phrases. First, the universal cause-stage:
this refers to the fact that this assembly consists entirely of bodhisattvas among the ten bodies of Buddhas and bodhisattvas; therefore, it says:
One dwells in the sphere of the practice of the wisdom of all bodhisattvas. There are two kinds of spheres: first, principle (*li*), which refers to the true nature that is contemplated;

second, phenomena (*shi*), which refers to the sentient beings to be transformed. Regarding these two, there are two meanings of "entering": first, penetrating through with wisdom; second, practicing within those spheres. The two spheres are the same as before.
The phrase "exerting oneself without ceasing" intends to manifest entry without hearing [instruction], rather than to manifest effort.

1. Constant application. 2. Skillfulness in performing miraculous feats (*ṛddhi*) that transform according to what is appropriate. 3. Timely adjustment and transformation of beings. 4. Unobstructed attainment of vows, cultivated universally across time and space.
5. Perfection of merit, bringing forth benefit without deficiency. 6. The ultimate limit of skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). 7. The simultaneous practice of both the provisional and the real.
8. The middle two [categories]: first, the enumeration of virtues; subsequently, from "all that which" onwards, the analysis of activities. Regarding the former:

As the fifth chapter of the treatise explains: "Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "vimokṣa" refers to the four formless attainments (ārūpyas); "samādhi" refers to the four immeasurables (apramāṇas);
and "samāpatti" refers to the five supernormal powers (abhijñās). The commentary states: regarding the statement that "vimokṣa" refers to the four formless attainments...
This refers to the last five among the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), as they all rely upon the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this so?

It is because these four liberations—the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—are designated as "liberations" by virtue of being free from the constraints of the mind that takes space and so forth as its object.
The fifth liberation, however, is designated by way of the observing mind itself, which is weary of the faults of mental exertion and conceptualization.
...and so forth, even to the point of causing the seeds of the subtle mind of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) that preceded it not to manifest.

Because the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*) is defined by the prevention of the arising of the mind, this is fully explained as in the chapter. Since the Master of the Treatise here speaks from the perspective of the majority, he states that "liberation" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
As for "the samādhis being the four immeasurables," this is because the mental applications (*manasikāra*) of loving-kindness and the others [are involved].

Regarding the phrase "Based on meditative concentration (samādhi), the *samāpatti* is for those with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)," *samāpatti* is here translated as "equilibrium" (*tingdengzhi*).

This is the very foundation of meditative concentration. Because one suppresses dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) through the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one reaches this foundation of concentration;

thus, the arising of the five supernormal powers all depends upon the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the four dhyānas. In the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant while concentration is scarce. In the four [fundamental dhyānas], however, both are present in equal measure.

In the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), wisdom is slight while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is abundant. Because they lack the assistance of the [meditative] factors (*aṅga*), these supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) do not arise.

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also state this. If one follows the commentary on the third dhyāna in those treatises, it is said that even in the formless realms there is the assistance of the four factors;

however, the current explanation concerns only the fact that because concentration is abundant and wisdom is slight, the five supernormal powers do not arise, and does not concern the absence of assisting factors. If one relies on the *Saṃyuktāgama*...

Regarding "Accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*): although it pertains to all four dhyānas, it primarily relies on the fourth, because the wise hold that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) severs delusions and illuminates reality.

Furthermore, "clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to the three clarities (*tisro vidyāḥ*) or the ten clarities; "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the three wisdoms (*trīṇi jñānāni*). Regarding the subsequent explanation of "function" (*karman*):

this refers to performing deeds to benefit sentient beings based on the aforementioned dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth, accomplishing them according to one's will; thus, it is said they are "all sovereign. (10)

1. By effortless supernormal power, they swiftly arrive at the assemblies of all Buddhas; 2. Eleven: the foremost leaders request the Dharma; 3. Twelve: they extensively protect and uphold the teachings;
4. Thirteen: they make offerings and serve all Buddhas; 5. Fourteen: they diligently cultivate sublime practices; 6. Fifteen: their physical actions manifest universally throughout the world;
7. Sixteen: their preaching of the Dharma pervades the entire Dharma-realm; 8. Seventeen: their minds illumine the three periods of time. The final summary consists of two [sections].
First, the completion of the practice is established; subsequently, regarding the "unfathomable," the establishment of the vastness of their virtues and measures can be understood.

Third, among the listing of names, there are three parts: first, the listing of the names; second, from "such as these" onwards, the establishment of the number; third, from "Vajra" onwards, the manifestation of the leaders of the assembly.
Regarding the first [the listing of names], there are thirty-nine bodhisattvas in total. Among them, the first thirty-eight share the same name, "Treasury" (Gaṇḍa).
The preface intends to explain that each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses the meaning of solidity, for the *garbha* (womb/essence) is itself solid, just like the core of a tree.

The one named Liberation Moon (*Vimukticandra*) at the end refers to the foremost petitioner of the Dharma, who dispels the darkness of doubt among the assembly; he is like the night moon, which alone dispels the gloom.
This is a designation used to represent a dharma: the moon possesses the capacity to dispel darkness, and thus it is named "Liberation" (vimukti).
Among the enumeration of the fetters (saṃyojana), nine items are listed in brief;

that is, from the one hundred-fifth item to the one hundred-twenty-first item among the total of one hundred twenty-three items, with a single interval between each successive entry, as detailed below.
Regarding the third point, which reveals the leader of the assembly: the reason he is named Vajragarbha (Vajra-treasury) is to signify the Dharma he is about to expound.

The treatise states that while all afflictions are difficult to destroy, this Dharma is able to shatter them; because his roots of goodness are firm and solid like a vajra, he is designated by this name without distinction.
Furthermore, "store" (*garbha*) means "firmness. It is like the core of a tree; it is as if a person were in the womb within that store.
Therefore, this firmness is like a vajra. Like the Vajragarbha, these roots of goodness possess the most supreme power among all other roots of goodness, just like a vajra.
Moreover, they can generate the practices leading to the realms of humans and devas, for they cannot be destroyed by any other roots of goodness.

It is named "Vajragarbha. The commentary explains: the phrase "afflictions are difficult to destroy" is intended to show that they can only be severed by relying upon non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

"The roots of goodness are firm and solid" means that untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) culminate in the fruit of Buddhahood. "Not different" refers to the fact that there is no difference between the name and what is expressed.
"All other roots of goodness" refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), as well as those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), and so forth.

Because of the roots of goodness. Within the second section on the divisions of samādhi, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the text; second, an analysis of its meaning. Within the former, there are two sub-sections:

first, clarifying the basis for entering meditative concentration; second, from "The Bodhisattva" onwards, revealing the names of the concentrations entered. Regarding the first of these, the phrase "relying upon the power of the Buddha" reveals—

One is able to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) because it is not by one's own power alone. "Entering" means that the mind and principle are unified in a state of single-objectivity (*ekālambanatā*).

The term "Bodhisattva" is used to distinguish this from the concentrations of the resultant stage; it refers to the causal practice. The definition and meaning of "Bodhisattva" are fully explained as stated above.

Regarding "great wisdom" and so forth, this refers to the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*), which distinguishes it from that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as from the wisdom of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it is said:
It is "Great" (*mahā*). Furthermore, because its power is able to sever delusions, realize principle, and give birth to the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "Great.

This very decisive discernment that accomplishes severance and realization is therefore termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*). The meanings of the terms "luminosity" (*āloka*) and "samādhi" are fully explained as stated above.
The subsequent explanation of the intent is briefly twofold: first, for the purpose of receiving empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

As the Sūtra says: "Because one who has attained this samādhi-dharma is thus. The commentary states: If one does not enter meditative absorption, the distracted mind is incapable of sustaining the Buddha’s empowerment.

Second, for the purpose of revealing that the Dharma is free from attachment. The Treatise says: "To demonstrate that this Dharma is not the sphere of discursive thought (*tarka*)," as it arises from meditative concentration.
Pure awakening is precisely what is called non-distracted vitarka and vicāra, as it serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Within the third section on the "Application of Power" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there are three parts: first, a general explanation of the causes for applying the power; second, the desire to cause you [to understand], which distinguishes the purpose of the application;
and third, "Good son, you should now," which correctly reveals the characteristics of the application.

The first part has three sections: 1. Clarifying the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); 2. Revealing the cause of the empowerment through the passage beginning with "Vairocana"; and 3. Question and answer according to the treatise.
The first of these [three] has two parts: first, a single line that restates what preceded; second, the section beginning with "At that moment," which correctly reveals [the empowerment].

Within this revelation, there are two parts: first, manifesting a body of the same name; second, the section beginning with "He spoke thus," which praises and reveals the empowerment. Regarding the first of these [two], there are six points. The first is "At that moment."
1. "Clearly [the Buddhas] are in meditative absorption" indicates that they are currently in samādhi. 2. "The twenty directions" indicates that the teaching pervades all quarters. 3.
"Each exceeding [the previous] by tenfold" clarifies the quantity of their places of origin. 4. "Each having [a specific number]" reveals the number of Buddhas;

compared to the preceding assembly, this is increased tenfold, taking one million as a "koṭi" (億) in accordance with the second numerical category. 5. "Having the same names" is for the purpose of enabling Gañjadhara...
Because it increases courage and joy. Sixth, as for "manifesting the body": it is to cause sentient beings to perceive the Dharma and give rise to profound reverence.
This consists of three parts, identical to those in the subsequent section on praise: first, praising the attainment of the difficult-to-attain samādhi, hence saying "is thus able to";

second, revealing the number of Buddhas who provide empowerment; third, correctly clarifying the act of empowerment. Second, within the section revealing the causes of the empowerment, there are three parts: first, the past vows of Vairocana; second, the present...
Regarding the majestic spiritual power (*anubhāva*): the three [instances] also refer to the following phrase, which concerns Vajragarbha’s own power.
As for the three question-and-answer sections: why do many Buddhas bestow their empowerment? It is to manifest an increase in reverence for both the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher.
Why do those who empower him share the same name, "Vajragarbha"? It is due to the power of his original vow. Why did the Tathāgatas make such a vow? To demonstrate the manifold...
Because the Buddha, when he was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, was named Vajragarbha in all those instances and taught this same Dharma;

now that he has attained perfect enlightenment, he is named Vajragarbha, and thus it is not a different name but an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, because this bodhisattva, having heard that the various Tathāgatas share his own name, increases his courage and joy.
Why does it not say "beyond immeasurable worlds"? It is a skillful means (*upāya*) to manifest that there are many Buddhas.
The commentary states: Regarding the question, "Why is this vow made to manifest many Buddhas?

it means that those many Buddhas, during their causal stage, collectively relied upon the practices and vows of these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Thus, it is said that the skillful means (*upāya*) manifests many Buddhas.
Within this, there are two kinds of skillful means: first, not counting by numbers such as one, two, three, four, up to hundreds or thousands, but rather counting by *kṣetra* (buddha-fields).
Regarding "measured by dust": this is skillful means for manifesting multiplicity. Second, it does not manifest multiplicity through a high number;
rather, by mentioning ten, it manifests multiplicity—this is skillful means for manifesting multiplicity. Why is it specifically stated that there are "ten billion Buddha-fields"?
It is because this sutra frequently employs the number ten to explain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and because these Buddhas share the same name due to their original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*).

This means that although the Buddhas of the ten directions and this Buddha all possess original vows and their empowerments occur simultaneously, because the relationship between the principal and the attendant is not lost, it is also permissible to say that this Buddha empowers first and the other Buddhas empower later. The treatise states:
"It is through the power of Vairocana Buddha’s original vow that he bestows empowerment."
The second section, explaining the purpose of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), has two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a specific analysis beginning with the words "That is to say.

Within the former, the phrase "desiring to cause... and so forth generally clarifies the intent behind the purpose of the empowerment. The statement "for all bodhisattvas" identifies the intended audience (*vineya*). The *Śāstra* states:

"This refers to bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*)," which encompasses two types: first, the bodhisattvas of the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*).
The Bodhisattva himself has personally realized suchness (*tathatā*); this is because he gives rise to faith and practices based solely on the teachings.
Second, although the Bodhisattvas of the Great Stages (*mahābhūmi*) hear these teachings, they give rise to faith and practice based on their own personal realization and vision of suchness.

Regarding the "inconceivable Buddha-dharmas of verbal expression," this refers to the analytical discernment of the supramundane factors conducive to enlightenment (*lokottara-mārga-pakṣya*). "Supramundane" (*lokottara*) has the meaning of being untainted (*anāsrava*), and "path" (*mārga*) is...

Wisdom (*jñāna*). This category consists of its outflow (*niṣyanda*); that is, the untainted (*anāsrava*) teachings that flow forth from the Buddha’s untainted wisdom are called the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).
When bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) hear them, they subsequently give rise to the untainted wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
When bodhisattvas on the stages hear these teachings, their wisdom becomes even more luminous. This wisdom is of the same category as the Buddha’s untainted wisdom.

Because they are the outflow [of the path], they are called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*). Regarding the term "light," the *Śāstra* states: "Because of seeing, knowing, attaining, and realizing. Master Yuan says:

"Seeing, knowing, attaining, and realizing are identical in meaning though different in name; it is like the distinction between 'eyes' and 'sight. Thus, seeing and knowing constitute the understanding of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while attaining and realizing constitute the practice (*caryā*).
Understanding has a beginning and an end: seeing is the beginning and knowing is the end. Seeking and investigating is called 'seeing'; decisive resolution is called..."

Wisdom (*jñāna*) has a beginning and an end; one attains the beginning and realizes the end. When the Dharma manifests within the mind, it is called "attaining the mind. This is a profound union that accords with the name of its realization.

Now, in explaining this passage, it is appropriate to speak in terms of its general characteristics; if one were to dissect the individual characters for a literal explanation, one would lose the original intent.

That is to say, light possesses two meanings: the dispelling of darkness and the merging with space. This is because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) likewise possesses two meanings: the severing of delusions and the realization of principle.

Because the metaphor is explained by means of the Dharma, what is called "light" refers to wisdom-vision (*jñāna-darśana*) and realization (*adhigama*). Wisdom-vision is the severing of obscurations, while realization is the conformity with suchness (*tathatā*).

According to the third chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, wisdom serves as the general objective condition (*sāmānya-ālambana*), whereas vision serves as the specific objective condition (*viśeṣa-ālambana*).
The intent of this treatise is to clarify the benefits for two types of spiritual capacities upon hearing the teaching.

If a bodhisattva prior to the stages (bhūmi), having heard this teaching, is able to give rise to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), thereby severing delusions and realizing the principle, they are said to "enter. This refers to attaining realization through faith and aspiration.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asvabhāva states: "Although this perfuming (*vāsanā*) from hearing is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is nonetheless a supramundane mind (*lokottara-citta*)."
Regarding the nature of the seeds: if a bodhisattva on the stages hears this Dharma, their realization of the stages becomes further clarified because they sever delusions and realize the principle.

Thus it is said that "those with clarity see through wisdom and attain realization. Now, for this reason, I shall explain this Dharma of attaining realization through the wisdom of vision belonging to those on the stages.
This refers to the "inconceivable" and so forth.
Subsequently, there are twenty-two distinct phrases. The first ten clarify self-benefit; the latter twelve, beginning with "furthermore, one causes," clarify benefit for others.
Although this is the general classification, if one distinguishes them in detail, both categories encompass both types of benefit. Thus, the treatise says:
When a bodhisattva teaches other sentient beings, they are simultaneously fulfilling their own buddha-dharma. Therefore, benefiting others is also called benefiting oneself.

Regarding the first ten phrases among these, according to the treatise and the sūtra, they are identical to the preceding general phrase and constitute a single sentence. The treatise extracts the latter nine from the first phrase.
The first states, "causing them to enter the stage of wisdom" (*jñānabhūmi*); "the stage of wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and "causing them to enter" means...
"Entering" (*praveśa*) means "attaining. It also carries the sense of "proceeding into. This refers to enabling all bodhisattvas to attain entry into the four stages (*bhūmi*).

These are subsequently indicated by assigning them to the following nine phrases: first, the initial four phrases enable bodhisattvas at the stage of faith and aspiration (*adhimukti*) prior to the stages to enter the [first] stage;

second, the next single phrase enables them to attain the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); third, the final three phrases enable them to attain the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*). Within this, the first...
The first phrase refers to the period from after the sixteen moments of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage.

The next phrase refers to the eighth and ninth stages. The subsequent phrase refers to the tenth stage. The final phrase of the four [sections] brings about the attainment of the ultimate state (*niṣṭhāpada*). If the nine phrases are explained individually:

First, "encompassing all" means that within the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), all roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are subsumed. Second, "discrimination" refers to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

1. Because of skill in wisdom regarding all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). 2. Because of attaining immeasurable kinds of meaning through wisdom regarding all phenomena that are contemplated. 3.
Because of skillfully explaining, in accordance with the meanings contemplated, by means of complete names and terminology. 4.

Because, at the time of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) realizes all phenomena as being of one suchness (*tathatā*); the treatise calls this "equality," for wisdom is free from discrimination.

Therefore, the Sūtra says it is "pure. As for the statement in the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-śāstra* that "during the stage of cultivating the path, one is free from all afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*)," this is said because, although in reality one is also free from the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) during the stage of cultivation, the explanation follows the literal wording of the text.

That is to say, being unstained by worldly phenomena means one is free from the afflictive hindrances. Seventh, the supramundane factors of enlightenment (*lokottara-bodhipakṣadharma*) consist of the three wholesome roots, beginning with non-greed.

Because the faculties (*indriya*) are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called "pure" (*śuddha*). Eighth, at the time of superior progress in the tenth stage, within the state of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one attains the secret of the Buddha’s wisdom.
However, this secret is not accessible to the speech or thought of those in lower stages; therefore, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
This secret wisdom is itself the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), or rather, it is the objective sphere known by secret wisdom. This reaches the ultimate limit of the Bodhisattva stages.
As explained below in the section on the "Great Perfection" (Mahāpariniṣṭhāna), this refers to the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage entering the ten secret wisdoms of the Tathāgata.
Ninth is the attainment of the ultimate wisdom of the Buddha-stage; here too, wisdom is itself the object, and the object of wisdom is both [wisdom and its object], as before.
However, it differs from the preceding because the cause and fruit are distinct. Thus far, the nine specific phrases differ from the initial general phrase.

It is neither identical nor separate. Now, this distinct explanation is made solely to reveal that the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*) possesses a sequential progression toward increasing excellence.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise employs the latter six characteristics to demonstrate that the preceding general and specific [aspects] are neither identical nor separate.

As for the statement "excluding the entities of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)," this refers exclusively to the pure dependent origination (*paratantra*) of the outflowing (*nisyanda*) untainted (*anāsrava*) teachings. It is also...

True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions to manifest as supramundane dharmas; it does not rely upon the three categories of existence (triskandha) which are characterized by outflows (sāsrava). Therefore, it is said that these are "excluded. The Treatise states:
"The 'total' refers to the fundamental entry (mūla-praveśa); the 'particular' refers to the remaining nine entries. The particular relies upon the fundamental, for it fulfills that fundamental.

That is to say, the total and the particular serve as one another's support; without the total and the particular, they cannot be established. It is through the particular that the total is formed: if there were no particular, what would constitute the total?"

The "identical characteristic" (*sādharmya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to entry; that is to say, because all particulars are identical to the fundamental [nature], there is the sense of entry. The "different characteristic" (*vaidharmya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristic of increase;

that is to say, because all those [particulars] are collectively entered under the name of "difference," it is called the different characteristic. The "established characteristic" (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*) refers to brevity; that is to say, because the various phrases are combined into one, it is established as a summary.
The "dissolved characteristic" (*bhinna-lakṣaṇa*) refers to elaboration; that is to say, when those various phrases are joined together at once, they become one.

First, when subjected to logical scrutiny, nothing can be established; each remains fixed in its own position. Thus, through extensive investigation, [the opponent's position] fails to be established and is thereby refuted.
In this manner, these ten phrases of the scriptural text are harmonized and integrated to reveal the characteristic of being neither attained nor characterized by identity or difference.
All other dharmas should be explained accordingly through appropriate skillful means. The six characteristics are extensively elucidated as in the separate chapter.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the twelve phrases on benefiting others: the treatise combines the sixth and seventh phrases of the sūtra into one phrase;

the remaining phrases follow the same order. The first phrase is general, while the remaining phrases are specific. The treatise states that this phrase constitutes the fundamental beginning and end, because within each of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there is both a beginning and an end.
Thus, it says "causing [them] to attain the beginning and end of the bodhisattva’s ten stages. Here, "beginning" refers to the initial arousal of the resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
One has faith and delight in the Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), draws near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and listens to and receives what they teach.

"To the end" means that, relying on the instructions of virtuous friends, one maintains them in memory without forgetting. Within this specific classification, eleven phrases are assigned to three stages: the first three pertain to the stage prior to the [first] ground, consisting of the cultivation of reflection (*cintā-bhāvanā*) for the benefit of others;

the next one pertains to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); and the remaining seven pertain to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). These eleven, from beginning to end, are narrower than the preceding eighteen.
The preceding section explained the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); the subsequent section encompasses the Buddha [wisdom] entirely. As for this difference:

since both the wisdom derived from hearing and the Buddha-wisdom are not [the stages of] the fundamental ground (*maulabhūmi*), and as these have already been clarified prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), they are not analyzed again here. In reality, they all apply as previously stated.

Regarding self-benefit, there is the wisdom derived from hearing because one personally accomplishes the wisdom derived from hearing, and only after having heard it can one explain it to others. Now, regarding this benefit...

Among them, there are those who possess the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Because they reflect and then explain it to others, and because their own wisdom increases through such reflection, the first point—“explaining according to reality” and so forth—means that the wisdom of the wisdom of reflection retains and explains the specific meanings of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as they were heard, in accordance with the capacities [of the listeners] and according to principle;
therefore, it is called “explaining according to reality. Second, it causes [beings] to focus their mindfulness and realize entry into all Buddha-dharmas.

Third, when practicing the cultivation of wisdom through observation, because one gives rise to conceptual verbalization regarding the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) on the stages (*bhūmi*) and understands them while still bearing signs (*sanimitta*), it is so called.
Fourth, at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-jñāna*) skillfully discerns that the "self" of phenomena is unobtainable;
this is named "the Radiance of Thorough Discernment. It is designated as "Great" because it is adorned by the perfection of this wisdom, surpassing the small [vehicle]. Fifth, the cultivation...

Within the stages of the Path (*mārga-avasthā*), the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is skillfully able to enter [the truth], because the means of the signifier and the signified are definitively established without doubt.
As the *Śāstra* says: "By the power of supramundane wisdom, one attains entry into the Dharma and its meaning. Thus far, we have relied upon the stages from the second to the seventh bhūmi.
From here below, the six phrases of the *Śāstra* explain the remedies for the obstacles that bodhisattvas face regarding enlightenment (*bodhi*). This is based on...
From the eighth stage up to the Buddha stage, these are explained as obstacles. These obstacles exist from the seventh stage through the tenth stage:
