The obstacle to practice is precisely the distancing from the wholesome, as it causes one to depart from the state conducive to outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Unwholesome conduct is the commission of evil karma.
The third [point] clarifies the fault of experiencing suffering up to its greatest limit; this refers to the fault of receiving the retribution of suffering.

The commentary explains: "To receive" means to take in the fruit of these karmic causes; "to reach" means to arrive at the fruit. The sufferings experienced therein are largely characterized by opposition (*pratigha*).
Because it obstructs, it is called "confrontation" (*pratigha*). When confrontation reaches its limit, it is called "great. Furthermore, there are two kinds of great confrontation:

first, receiving a body that experiences suffering; second, arriving at a place of suffering. The fourth section, "Wandering in the Wilderness," clarifies the fault of frequently committing sinful causes;

this refers to the increase of the fault of false views. The *Śāstra* commentary states: "Due to frequently committing sinful causes, at the time of death, one sees the signs of evil retribution, and the mind gives rise to..."

[The stage of] Remorse (*kaukṛtya*): Although one perceives the characteristics of one's faults, one is unable to assemble the antidote of right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). Subsequently, there are three stages of transformation:
first, transforming [the practitioner] so that they obtain the unimpeded pure eye; second, by obtaining the pure eye, seeing phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*);
third, because of seeing phenomena as they truly are, not following the teachings of others, for one sees that all phenomena are nothing but one’s own mind.
The five sciences transform those sentient beings who pursue future retributions by practicing virtuous deeds.

This refers to those who, due to delusion regarding the true meaning, create non-agitated merit in order to seek the retribution of humans and devas in the future. Regarding the nine phrases within the initial clarification of those to be transformed, they are divided into three parts.
First, "being in [the realms]" and so forth refers to the nature of the perilous path; that is, because their roots of virtue are meager, they [seek] the retribution of humans and devas.

"Dangerous" means it is easily subject to overturning and falling; it is called a perilous path (*khata-patha*). Next, "about to fall," and so forth, refers to the obstacles within that perilous path.

Among these, there are seven points: first, although one seeks liberation, one follows worldly ways and falls into the three evil destinies, just as one on a worldly perilous path stands on the brink of a precipice.
Second, "entering into evil," and so forth, means entering the net of the fruits of suffering while falsely conceiving the notion of pleasure.
Just as a perilous path in the world is difficult to traverse because it is crisscrossed with climbing vines and thorns, so too are the objects of the five desires;
for one falsely deems them real and is thus detained, making escape difficult. Third, regarding "being obscured by ignorance," one is shrouded by a dense forest of darkness.
Because one is covered by the latent tendencies of that ignorance, one fails to realize the cause of suffering when it is explained, just as there are dense forests on a perilous path in the world.
It obstructs the path. Because one is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one does not perceive the cause of suffering. Regarding the "four kinds of pursuit":
because one pursues the path of false conceptualization and acts with perversion, it is like a worldly dangerous road where there are many wild beasts;
though one intends to advance, one instead turns back. Within birth and death, the world is filled with false dharmas; thus, when one intends to advance, one instead turns back. Fifth, for example:
"Those who are such" refers to those who are blind and obscured, being blinded by attachment and craving for the fruits of existence.

Just as people on a perilous path who lack eyes may walk astray yet claim it is the right way, so too ordinary beings lack the eye of wisdom; they cling to the pleasures of the human and celestial realms because their minds are shrouded by delusion and craving.

Regarding the phrase "the six are not transcendence, etc.": this refers to desiring *nirvāṇa* yet proceeding toward other realms—namely, taking the Brahmā heavens and the Brahma-worlds as the correct view of transcendence.
It is like a person in a perilous place who, having lost their way, mistakenly enters another path;

likewise, while seeking *nirvāṇa* within this cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one mistakenly seeks the Brahmā heavens and, by erroneously seeking them, takes the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of the Brahmā heavens and their secondary environment (*upabhoga*) as the goal. The word "etc. [indicates further such cases].
The three higher dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and so forth—these are all considered by them to be *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the "seven entries into Māra" and so on:
when an enemy or bandit travels through the realm of Māra and becomes attached to various desires, his merits are plundered and exhausted, preventing him from accumulating [wholesome roots].

It is like a person in a place of peril who fears being harassed by bandits and finds it difficult to escape; it is the same within *saṃsāra*. The evil Māra of the five sensual desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) interferes...
Disturbance. The five objects of sensual pleasure are the realm of Māra; greed and the like are the mind of Māra. To be attached to and follow them is called "evil bandits.

They plunder existing virtues until they are exhausted and prevent unaccumulated virtues from being gathered. Regarding the first, seventh, and eighth lines of the preceding section, ancient masters have attempted to correlate them with the Four Noble Truths;
while there is some slight logic in this, it is not mentioned in the treatise itself. I shall not trouble myself to establish such a correlation by force.
The final phrase, "those who distance themselves from the Buddha’s intent," clarifies the loss on the perilous path.

While the *Śāstra* contains three phrases, here there is only one, which clarifies the ground of performing wholesome wisdom and discernment; that is to say, it clarifies the loss of supramundane wholesome dharmas.

To give rise to a mind that accords with the Buddha is called "the Buddha’s intent"; to oppose it is called "distancing. The preceding three sections and nine phrases collectively clarify those to be transformed.

The latter two [stages] of the transformative power involve: first, "extracting [them]" and so forth, which remedies the very nature of the previous perilous paths; and second, "causing them to abide" and so forth, which remedies the previous obstacles and losses.
This concludes the explanation of the distinctions in the creation of karma within the two preceding sections. The five preceding segments collectively conclude the second major section:
the transformation of sentient beings who seek sense-desires.

In the third major section, which elucidates the transformation of sentient beings who seek existence, there are two parts: first, the differentiation of paths, referring to the faults of wandering through the five destinies;
second, the differentiation of realms, referring to the faults of being fettered by the three realms.
The preceding section has two parts: first, the clarification of those to be converted; second, the clarification of the converter, which I shall explain below.
Within the first part, the initial phrase provides a general indication, while the subsequent section beginning with "entering desire" provides a specific analysis.

Regarding the general indication, "sinking in the great river" refers to the fault of being submerged and drifting in the five destinies by the torrential flood of afflictions, which is like the waters of a great river. "Seeking existence within it" constitutes that fault. Within the specific analysis, there are thirteen phrases. [End of] Treatise.

These are subsumed into three categories: first, the afflictions constitute the substance of the river of the five destinies; second, the abundance of harm in those places is termed "arising difficulties";

and third, being separated from the supramundane path is termed "loss. Furthermore, the first is called the substance of delusion; the second clarifies the obstruction of the path; and the third is the loss of virtuous friends. Regarding the first, there are five parts.
First, as for "entering the flow of desire" and so forth, this reveals that greed is both deep and manifold, for it is by means of this great river that the four flows are possessed.
Therefore: (2) "The cycle of birth and death" refers to the continuous flow of wandering and returning without interruption, as afflictions constantly operate.
(3) "The river of craving" refers to being submerged by the waters of craving; because craving possesses a more powerful force for transmigration than other delusions, it alone is given this name.
(4) "Rushing full [of waves]" refers to the violent drifting; just as when crossing a flowing stream, one may easily exit if the water is slow, but if it is rapid—

It is difficult to cross. When the afflictions (*kleśa*) are lax, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) can arise; however, if afflictions arise without interval, it is difficult for the Noble Path to manifest, as there is no opportunity for contemplation due to the absence of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
The phrase "five [types of] thoughts of desire and so forth" indicates its vastness. It is like crossing a river: if a river is narrow, one may still cross it even if the current is swift;
but since this [state] involves the frequent arising of many evil thoughts, it is difficult to cross. Furthermore, it is like a river that is free from venomous insects.
Then it is easy to cross. Because there are harmful insects of evil perceptions here, it is difficult to emerge. Next, regarding "the view of a self-body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth:
from this point downward, the second difficulty of arising is clarified; it has four types, and this is the first. That is to say, it is the attachment to the cave-dwelling of "self" and "mine."

1. Because they cannot be moved away from it. 2. Regarding "bringing them back": because after having previously abandoned desire, one turns back again to enter into thoughts of desire. 3. Regarding "in what [is experienced]":
because at the time of enjoyment, one seeks after and becomes attached to the pleasures of desire and so forth. The first two are craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
the first refers to returning because the seeds have not been extinguished, and the second refers to being mired in the defilement of active manifestation (*samudācāra*). 4. Abiding.
"When we perform our tasks, we are the most excellent"—these three types of conceit involve self-exaltation and the disparagement of others;

the last type is simply pride (*māna*). It is like a person in a river who faces four difficulties in getting out: first, being held back; second, being swept by the current; third, sinking into the mud;
and fourth, being stranded on a dry island without reaching the opposite shore. This is the metaphor for how craving causes the mind to sink.

The river is deep, yet its current does not reach the mountain of *nirvāṇa*. Arrogance causes the mind to be uplifted; it is likened to parched land on dry ground where the water of the Dharma cannot moisten it.

In the treatise, the phrase "ourselves and others" (*asmad-ādi*) is used; "others" includes three types, as found in the [discussion of] the first three grounds: first, the pride of self-elevation over those who are inferior; second, the pride of self-aggrandizement toward equals;

and third, the pride of superiority over those who are superior. The first refers to being haughty toward those below oneself; the second, to being conceited toward those who are one's equal; and the third, to [being arrogant] toward those above.
"Respectfully. Regarding the subsequent mention of 'establishing the six bases' and so forth: from here below is the third section, which clarifies the losses. This section has three parts:
first, the loss of the intention to depart; second, the loss of rescue; and third, the loss of departing for another place. This [passage] refers to the first.

That is to say, because within the good realms there is no mind of renunciation. Second, regarding 'the lack of virtuous rescue' and so forth: it means that while dwelling in the evil realms, there is no one to provide deliverance."

Regarding "those who are unable to equal [the Buddha]," this refers to those born in places of hardship who do not encounter the era of a Buddha. Later, within the explanation of the capacity for transformation (*nirmāṇa*), there are two parts.
First, regarding "among those," this clarifies the arising of the transformative mind. Second, regarding "by means of all [beings]," this clarifies the accomplishment of transformative practice.

Within these practices, there are four aspects: first, "causing them to be without equal" is because they have abandoned the fruit of suffering; second, "freedom from defiled attachment" is because they have abandoned the cause of suffering; third, "tranquility" is...
It is for the sake of enabling them to attain *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "the four abide in equanimity," it is for the sake of enabling them to attain *bodhi*.

In the subsequent explanation of the distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*), there are first three types of those to be converted within [the realms]. First is the general description: that is, dwelling within the three realms is like being in a prison, difficult to escape from.

Next, within the specific description, five kinds of faults follow along: first, the matter of suffering; second, the exhaustion of wealth; third, separation from what is loved; fourth, bondage; and fifth...

Obstacles. This demonstrates five difficulties: first, "many [afflictions]" and so forth refers to the difficulty of being free from illness, because one is plagued by the delusions and distress of manifold sicknesses and sufferings;
second, "constantly harboring" and so forth refers to the difficulty of sustaining life, because one is bound by hatred and attachment toward objects that are either agreeable or disagreeable;
third, "arising for oneself" and so forth refers to the difficulty of kinship, because when loved ones perish, sorrow and grief increase; fourth, "craving" and so forth... [text truncated]

"Et cetera" refers to the obstacle of morality (*śīla-vipakṣa*). Although one may be born among the Form or Formless Realms and temporarily abstains from violating morality, one does not escape being contrary to moral conduct because one is bound by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving and desire.

"The five [obstacles], beginning with ignorance" refers to the obstacle of views (*dṛṣṭi-vipakṣa*). Even if one attains worldly knowledge, it is contrary to that [liberation] because one is shrouded by the latent tendencies of ignorance.
Regarding the phrase "later, within the capacity for transformation, causing them to be permanently free," there are two types: first, the antidote (*pratipakṣa*);...

The preceding difficulties have been addressed. Second, the previous fetters and confinements are remedied. The two preceding sections clarify that the transformation of sentient beings who seek existence is complete.
Within the fourth major section, which clarifies the transformation of sentient beings who seek the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there are two parts:

first, transforming those who seek false holy lives so that they abandon the false and return to the correct; second, transforming those who seek the correct holy life so that they abandon the Small Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle.

Within the preceding section, there are two parts. First, the objects to be converted are clarified. This consists of seven phrases divided into three sections: the first phrase is general; the next five phrases are specific;
and the final phrase is a conclusion. The initial general statement, "those who cling to a self," refers to the fault of grasping at the marks of a self.

This is cited specifically because it is the root of other views; it encompasses both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) [ignorance]. Next, regarding the five phrases in the specific section: first, "regarding all... and so forth.
Those sentient beings who wish to proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa cannot set out from the house of the five aggregates because they possess the notion of a self (*ātman*).
Second, "relying on the six sense bases... and so forth. Relying upon and maintaining the conception of a self, they desire to give rise to Nirvāṇa.
1. The false view of self dwells within the village of the six sense bases; though one wishes to travel the right path, because of these inversions, one instead travels that deviant path.
2. The four great elements and so forth undergo the three and eight kinds of suffering;

though one loathes them and desires to be free from them, they cannot be escaped and constantly follow the body. 3. The five aggregates and so forth are like vengeful enemies who pursue one relentlessly, never granting release.
The final section is a summary, which states that "those who undergo immeasurable suffering" are constantly pursued by various kinds of sufferings; this is also external suffering.

Regarding the latter part on "the power of transformation," there are two sections. First, "causing them to abide [in the truth]" refers to causing them to abide in the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), thereby counteracting the aforementioned attachment to the mark of a self (*ātman*).

Second, "causing them to realize" refers to causing them to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), thereby counteracting the five faults and the concluding summary mentioned in the previous section on specific [faults].
The fault within the phrase.

This is followed by two parts clarifying the faults of seeking the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) that is concordant with the correct holy life (*brahmacarya*) through transformation. First, there are three internal aspects of those to be transformed.

Regarding the first, "their minds," etc.: this is the fault of not delighting in the causes for the Great [Vehicle]. That is to say, although one ought to bring benefit to many sentient beings, [one does not do so].
This refers to being indolent and thus unable to deliver beings extensively. Second, "not practicing equality" refers to the fault of the aspiration based on the Hīnayāna mind;
because one aspires to the Hīnayāna, these first two are faults of the seeking mind. Third, "although desiring... and so forth refers to the fault of practice.
This means that although sentient beings of the indeterminate group truly possess the Mahāyāna method for transcendence, they instead delight in practicing the methods of the Hīnayāna.

This refers to their faults. Later, in the section clarifying the "transformer," there are two parts. First, regarding the phrase "causing them to abide," etc., this remedies the fault of the Hinayana practitioner's aspiration;
it means causing them to abide in the vast mind of the subtle and unsurpassed Buddha-dharma. Second, regarding the phrase "vast," etc., this remedies the previous practice;
it means that by relying on the practice of the precepts, one attains the power of these precepts and is thus able to perform wholesome dharmas. Wholesome...

Because they skillfully initiate various virtuous practices. Regarding "relying on the practice of ethical discipline" (*śīla-carita*), this refers to relying on the previously mentioned ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and the ethical discipline of gathering virtue (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) to give rise to the power of the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*). The treatise calls this "relying on the practice of ethical discipline.

Having attained this power of ethical discipline, one is therefore able to perform virtuous dharmas, because one skillfully initiates the virtuous practice of benefiting sentient beings. Thus, it is said that one extensively generates great compassion. [End of] *Brahma*...

The *Běnshì* (Original Text) states: "In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the power of ethical discipline (*śīla-bala*) and is well able to increase the mind of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-citta*).

The two preceding sections clarify the completion of transforming sentient beings who seek the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). The ten preceding sections are subsumed into four groups, collectively clarifying the completion of the accumulation of fruits.
Thus far, the accumulation of wisdom, vows, and practices, as well as the accumulation of fruits, collectively clarify the third [section]: the gathering of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*).
The section on the precepts is concluded. The above constitutes the second part, which specifically clarifies the three types of precepts.

From here on, the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, O Bodhisattva" serves as the summary, which may be understood accordingly. Thus far, the three precepts have clarified the essential nature of the stages (*bhūmi*).

From here below is the second section, which clarifies the three aspects within the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*). The names of the fruits are the same as those of the preceding stages. Within the first, the fruit of flexibility (*mṛdu-karmaṇyatā*), there are three parts:

first, the characteristics of flexibility; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva... onwards, the clarification of the specific characteristics of the stage's practice; and third, from "O Son of the Buddha, this is called... onwards, the conclusion of the name.

The first three sections consist of the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis. Within the Dharma section, there are three parts: first, seeing the Buddhas as the condition for refining one's practice;

second, from "Regarding all Buddhas" onwards, clarifying that which can refine the practice; third, from "These Bodhisattvas" onwards, clarifying the purity that is refined. Within the section on that which can refine the practice, there are two parts:

first, making offerings to the Buddhas; second, from "Regarding all Buddhas" onwards, receiving the Dharma. One receives the ten wholesome dharmas upon the ground of the precepts. As the Treatise says:

Regarding "those that exist" and "those that are identical": the three qualities of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth are identical to those in the preceding stage. Regarding "those that do not exist" and "should be known":

it should be understood that there is no fruit of departure (*abhinirhāra-phala*). Regarding "the superior matters herein": among the types of pliancy, these are superior to those in the preceding stage.

Among the three kinds of purification through training, this refers to purifying the perfection of generosity and ethical discipline by being free from the stains of stinginess, envy, and immoral conduct throughout many eons.

Because of such superior matters as these, both types of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in this stage are established as pure by nature; whereas in the preceding stage, ethical discipline was not yet pure by nature, and thus giving (*dāna*) was also not yet pure.

If that is so, why was the preceding stage called "the predominance of giving"? Because it was superior relative to what came before, whereas now, having reached this stage, it has become even more excellent.
Furthermore, the practices of the stages have four meanings: first, they are distinguished according to their specific differences. In the first stage, there is only giving (*dāna*). And so forth.

Upon reaching the tenth stage, it is characterized solely by the predominance of wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding the distinction between superiority and inferiority: the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) is superior in the first stage;

the bodhisattva is superior in the second stage; the three perfections are superior in the third stage; and so on, up to the ten perfections being superior in the tenth stage. This is because each subsequent stage encompasses all preceding ones.
The latter is superior to the former, because the former does not encompass the latter; thus, the former is inferior to the latter.

Third, regarding the practice of actual cultivation, each and every stage (*bhūmi*) fully possesses the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). Fourth, regarding the practice of realizing the principle, it is solely equal and equal—neither one nor many.

The subsequent stages should be understood by analogy; both the metaphors and their applications can be discerned accordingly. Within the specific characteristics of the stages, because one is free from the four verbal transgressions, it also includes pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).

Regarding the inclusion of the *cakravartin* (Golden Wheel-turning King) among the fruits of retribution, this surpasses the previous stage; where the former had a hundredfold, this has a thousandfold. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"One should know that its majestic power exceeds the former tenfold. The remainder is as can be known from the preceding stages and the treatise.

Within the third major section, the *Gāthā-varga* (Section of Verses), there are fifteen verses divided into six parts: first, one verse summarizes the ten kinds of straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*) mentioned previously;
second, two verses summarize the *saṃvara-śīla* (morality of restraint); third, two and a half verses summarize the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (morality of gathering virtuous dharmas);

fourth, four and a half verses summarize the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (morality of benefiting sentient beings); fifth, four verses summarize the ripening of the fruits of suffering through the cultivation of gentleness and flexibility.
The sixth [section] consists of one verse, which concludes by praising what has been taught. This completes the Second Ground.
Regarding the Third Ground, there are two parts: first, a brief summary; second, the formal explanation of the text.
Regarding the first two of the three gates: first, the explanation of the name; second, the purpose of its inclusion. Concerning the first, the *Ninth Chapter of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because one achieves supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇī of the Dharma, and is able to radiate the light of boundless sublime wisdom, it is called the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

The commentary explains: "Supreme meditative concentration refers to *samāpatti* (attainment) and *samādhi* (concentration). The 'Great Dharma' refers to the teachings, and 'dhāraṇī' refers to hearing and retaining them. [This stage is characterized by] mindfulness and wisdom."

The essence is the light of sublime wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*), which consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. That is to say, by means of *dhāraṇī*, one remedies the obstacle of forgetfulness and is able to give rise to the two types of wisdom—of hearing and reflection—that take phenomena as their object, as well as the wisdom of cultivation that relies on meditative concentration and takes phenomena as its object. This stage is able to give rise to such a sublime light.
This is named according to its fruit. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"Because the samādhi of immeasurable wisdom-light and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining serve as its basis, it is called the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

Because it is the basis for non-retrogressive meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), and because it is the basis for the great light of the Dharma, it is called the "Radiant Ground" (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because in this ground [one possesses] samādhis and samāpattis..."
They are never separated, because there is no regression. Because it can rely upon the light of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it is named the Ground of Emitting Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Dhyāna is called *samādhi* (equipoise); the formless [attainments] are called *samāpatti* (meditative absorption). Alternatively, *samādhi* refers to one-pointedness of mind;
*samāpatti* refers to the manifestation of correct reception (*samyak-prativedha*). Regarding that which is the basis for the light of the Great Dharma, within the Mahāyāna...

Dharma. Because this stage is the causal basis for attaining the light of wisdom, it is named the Stage of Radiant Light (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*). The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* share the same intent as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* states that it is the locus where one realizes the aggregate of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi, and the great light of wisdom.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Successively learning extensively, one preaches the Dharma for the multitude; one is able to..."

It is called the "Luminous Stage" (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*) because it acts as an illumination; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it the "Radiant Stage," while the *Renwang jing* names it the "Stage of Luminous Wisdom.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains it as previously stated. Regarding the second point, the purpose for its inclusion, there are three reasons: first, because it follows the sequence where the preceding stage is ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the subsequent one is meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

second, because although the preceding stage was able to maintain subtle precepts, it had not yet perfected mundane meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and concentrations (*samādhi*); [and third, ...].

Having arrived [at this stage], and in order to attain the *dhāraṇī* of hearing the Dharma in its entirety before it is perfected, this ground is described so as to encourage its cultivation and study.

As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, "three" refers to the first three grounds, which are designated as the mundane stages of giving (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Since giving and ethical discipline have already been analyzed previously, they are presented here to clarify cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The detailed analysis of these various categories is found in other chapters.

The second part, the actual explanation of the text, consists of three sections: first, the section on praise and request; second, the section on the formal exposition beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha...";
and third, the section on the restatement in verse beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha, wishing to repeat..."

The first six verses of the beginning are divided into two parts: first, three verses celebrating the hearing of the preceding stage; second, three verses requesting the explanation of the subsequent stage.

Within the former, there are three sections: first, half a verse generally indicating what was previously heard; second, one and a half verses on the worship of the three karmas; third, one verse clarifying the intention for speaking.
Within the latter, the request to hear the subsequent stage, there are two parts: first, two verses by the various bodhisattvas making the request; second, one [verse]...

The verse requests liberation. In the preceding section, the first [line] generally requests the practice of the three stages, while the last [line] specifically requests the practice of the ten perfections.
Within the subsequent request for liberation, the praise of Vajragarbha’s exposition of the meaning of the stages is like a lion’s roar, because he has attained fearlessness.
As for the phrase "gentle and so forth" in the following line, it means that the bodhisattvas of this stage have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

Within the second section, the "Correct Exposition," there are two parts. First, according to the Master of the Treatise’s topical outline (*śāstrakāra-vibhāga*), the preceding four sections are analyzed.

Second, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Radiant Stage" onwards, the fruit of the stages is clarified. Regarding the first part, there are four sub-sections: 1) the section on generating the practice of world-weariness;

2) the section on generating the practice of world-weariness, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the third [stage]"; 3) this Bodhisattva attains hearing... [text continues].

The section below on "Dharma" clarifies the stage of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*). Fourth, the passage beginning with "O sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva’s mind follows... clarifies the stage of the fruit of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-phala*).

In this stage, one cultivates dhyāna and suppresses the afflictions; thus, it is called the "stage of aversion" (*vidūṣaṇā-bhūmi*). The initial mind that enters the stage and cultivates that aversion is called the "practice of aversion" (*vidūṣaṇā-caryā*).

The preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entering the stage that gives rise to that practice of aversion is called the "stage of initiating the practice of aversion" (*vidūṣaṇā-caryā-prasthāna-bhāga*). This refers to the beginning of the stage where [the aversion] has been initiated.

The stage of the practice of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-bhāgīya*) is so named because one cultivates the eight dhyānas and so forth while correctly abiding on the ground. Because the ground is fully perfected, it is called the stage of the fruit of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-phala-bhāgīya*).

Furthermore, these four stages correspond, in order, to the four paths: the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Within the first section, there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, from "What are... onwards, the formal elucidation of the ten mental states; third, from "The bodhisattva, by means of these...
onwards, the conclusion on entering the stages through practice. Regarding the ten mental states: first, "purity" arises based on the previously mentioned pure precepts;
this inclination toward meditative purity serves as the heading for the nine subsequent phrases. Second, "abiding securely" refers to firmly remaining within one’s own Mahāyāna.

Because they are not abandoned. Third, regarding "disgust and relinquishment": because one aspires to seek the supreme Dharma and gives rise to skillful means, one is able to feel disgust for future desires.

Once the second stage (*bhūmi*) is fulfilled, one proceeds toward the third stage; this is called "seeking the supreme Dharma. Fourth, regarding "detachment from craving": because one does not crave present desires.
The former two cases rely on future craving that has not yet arisen and can only be felt as disgusting; when present craving is actively relinquished, it is termed "detachment."
Greed obstructs dhyāna; therefore, one develops weary detachment. Fifth, "non-retrogression" refers to proceeding by not abandoning one's own vehicle.

Sixth, "firmness" refers to being indestructible by the afflictions of one's own stage. As for "one's own stage," this refers to the third bhūmi. Master Yuan stated that it refers to the preceding two bhūmis.
Master Bian stated that it refers to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Both [views] are correct.
It is difficult to rely upon. Seventh, "abounding in clear knowledge" (*vidyā-udbhūta*): because one relies on mastery over meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

This means that the fundamental concentration (*dhyāna-mūla*) is the basis for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and "abounding in clear knowledge" is simply another name for such mastery. Eighth, "valiant" (*vīra*): because one relies on the power of mastery over meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Although one may be born in a lower realm, one does not fall away from it; that is to say, although one has cultivated and attained higher concentrations, one is not reborn according to the level of those concentrations.

Although born in a distracted state, one does not retreat from the concentrated mind. This clarifies that because the cultivation of concentration has reached maturity, possesses power, and is sovereign, it is called "valiant.
Ninth, "extensive" means that even when relying on the births of the desire realm, afflictions cannot defile one;

that is to say, since the power of wisdom is already extensive, one even employs afflictions for the sake of the Buddha-work. Tenth, "great" means that by relying on the benefit of sentient beings, one does not interrupt the various [practices].
Because of existence. That is to say, because great compassion does not abandon the benefit of sentient beings, one constantly dwells within existence.

The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) may be understood accordingly. In the second section on the practice of aversion, there are three parts: first, clarifying the aversion toward and renunciation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which is called the practice of guarding against afflictions; second, from "Seeing thus...

onwards, abandoning the narrow and inferior mind, which is called the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); third, from "The Bodhisattva, having thus become averse and renounced... onwards...

This clarifies the practice of cultivating skillful means (*upāya*). In the beginning, there are twenty phrases that clarify the contemplation that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and without refuge.

Of these, the first ten phrases contemplate impermanence to know the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena; the latter ten phrases contemplate the lack of refuge, manifesting the faults through the perspective of persons.

Within the former [section on impermanence], there are two parts: first, a general statement indicating the object of contemplation; second, the specific explanation beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*). Regarding the former: as it says...
"True reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as being impermanent according to their own nature.

When the treatise states, "because the formations of life do not abide," it means that the continuity of form and mind, throughout its various stages during a single lifetime, undergoes momentary arising and ceasing.

This is the contemplation of impermanence in terms of general characteristics. In the subsequent detailed explanation, eight phrases are divided into two parts; first, six phrases clarify the impermanence of the conditioned.
The intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). The latter two lines clarify the meaning of impermanence regarding those phenomena.

Within the former [section], the first four lines concern the primary retribution (*sambhogika-niṣyanda*), while the latter two lines concern the secondary retribution (*āśraya-niṣyanda*). Regarding the first [of these], "the impermanent" refers to premature death caused by the power of not guarding against various evils;
"and so forth" means that one’s life is brought to ruin through the force of failing to avoid treading upon dangerous ground or consuming poison. This line...

The various phrases following "crown" refer to suffering, impermanence, impurity, impermanence, and so forth. Regarding the two types of suffering, they arise through the power of the body’s transformation, giving rise to three kinds of suffering.
That is to say, when the life-force of the body is about to transform, its retributive essence undergoes moment-to-moment arising and ceasing.

Although one dwells in pleasure, it is not autonomous; therefore, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) arises. At this time, because of separation from beloved internal and external things, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) arises.
When the retribution is actually unfolding, because the physical form is dissolved by the winds of sensation, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) arises. Regarding the three impurities:
by the power of the excellence or deficiency of food and drink, the complexion and form increase or diminish; furthermore, food and drink transform into impurity.
Therefore, "the four states of non-quiescence" refers to the fact that within the six realms of saṃsāra there is no temporary cessation;

that is to say, not ceasing is non-quiescence, and non-quiescence is precisely impermanence. "Destruction" refers to the destruction caused by the power of the formation and dissolution of the previous world-system.

This means that because destruction occurs based on the power of formation. Regarding the sixth point, "not abiding for long," it refers to the fact that due to the lack of stabilizing power from material resources, one cannot remain in a single position as a sovereign.
In the subsequent explanation of the meaning of impermanence, there are two phrases. The first phrase, "arising and ceasing moment by moment," refers to impermanence over a brief duration;
that is, both arising and ceasing occur within a short time, rather than remaining constant. The latter phrase states:

Regarding the phrase "not from [the past]," etc.: because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not established as real and is impermanent. This means that the causes and effects of the three periods of time are impermanent;
they all lack intrinsic nature, are not established as real, and are impermanent. For example, when a past cause produces a present effect, one analyzes and finds no producer or produced.
When a present cause produces a future effect, one analyzes and finds no movement toward the future. At the very moment the present phenomenon is manifesting, it is directly present before one.
At that time, because one investigates that which is non-abiding, the dharmas of the three periods of time flow and circulate; yet this circulation is itself non-circulation.

This takes the absence of impermanence as the very essence of impermanence. As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "The non-arising and non-ceasing of all dharmas is the meaning of impermanence. Thus it is.
Second, the explanation of being without rescue is divided into two parts: first, the general; second, the specific, beginning with "being without rescue.

Within the former, it says, "Furthermore, one contemplates this dharma," which refers back to the previously contemplated practice of impermanence; because this is now a renewed contemplation, it says "furthermore, one contemplates.

Within the latter, the specific section, there are four divisions: first, the initial four lines explain being without rescue in terms of arising; next, the following two lines explain it in terms of seeking external objects of sensation.
It is said that there is no rescue. The next three phrases describe the lack of rescue in terms of old age, youth, and illness.

The final phrase generally reveals that all nine [conditions] previously mentioned are devoid of reality and cannot be rescued. Regarding the first four: first, "having no refuge" means that when one is in the prime of youth and vigor, death has not yet arrived;
yet one looks toward the future arrival of death, finding no one to whom one can appeal or falsely rely for mutual rescue to avoid it. Second, "sharing in sorrow" means having no...
When death has arrived, there is no one who can save them. Because they mostly lack sorrow and suffering, it is said that the apprehension and fear of death is called "sorrow" (*śoka*).

Sorrow is a mental factor (*caitasika*) that is associated with the mind; thus it is termed "associated with sorrow and suffering. Its continuity is termed "abundant. Third, regarding "those who share in grief" (*sārdhamśokaiḥ*):

because they share in the same grief during the intermediate state, the meaning of "sharing" is as explained previously. That is to say, when the aggregates arise and undergo transformation and decay, and the signs of death manifest before one, this is called the "intermediate state. Sorrow...
The increase [of this] is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*), because compassion is identical with the mind. Regarding the phrase "dwelling together with the four types of suffering and affliction":

it means that within the circumstances of shared suffering and affliction, sorrow and lamentation follow along; their power is weak, and they further increase the heat of distress. This refers to the intensification of the heat of distress within the circumstances of shared suffering at the very moment of death.
The next two phrases clarify the lack of rescue regarding external objects of sensory experience. The first phrase says "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the increase of what is bound: when seeking the necessities of life, one desires agreeable things and does not desire disagreeable things. Thus, through such false conceptualization, craving increases and one constantly guards them.
As for the subsequent phrase, "sorrow and distress increase further," this is because during the time of enjoyment, pleasure is slight while suffering is great;
that is to say, once they have been obtained, there is much guarding against their being harmed, even to the point of risking one's life and undergoing much affliction.
Regarding the suffering at the time of poverty, the latter three phrases concern old age and so forth, clarifying that there is no refuge. First, it says that "death has accumulated":

when the body grows old, compared to its youth, its flourishing complexion can never be gathered again; thus, one calls this the impermanence of old age, for which there is no rescue to provide exemption.
Second, it says "greed, anger, and so forth": during the time of youth and vigor, one possesses the three types of sensation, and greed and the rest constantly burn [the mind].
Therefore, it is said: from the sensation of pleasure arises greed; from the two sensations of pain and grief arises hatred; and from all three sensations together arises delusion.

Because one constantly experiences these three sensations, the fires of the three poisons constantly arise, incessantly burning one’s own roots of goodness. This is the meaning of "constant. Third, regarding "the multitude of afflictions" and so forth:
at the time when the years have declined, immeasurable suffering from illness increases. Although illness is common to old age, [it is specifically mentioned here].
[It is] small; however, it increases as one grows old. Therefore, it is explained in terms of old age. When this suffering of illness arrives, there is no means of rescue or escape.
Regarding the final phrase of the four [lines], "like an illusion, unreal," this universally reveals that the preceding nine [points] all lack substantial reality and cannot be rescued.

That is to say, although an illusory person may manifest the appearances of youth, old age, and sickness, as well as the seeking of external objects and so forth, none of these possess true [reality].
Indeed, because there is nothing that can be saved.
Second, regarding the clarification of protecting the practices of the Hīnayāna, there are thirty phrases. The first ten phrases clarify the protection of the small mind;

the latter twenty phrases, beginning with "The Bodhisattva perceives thus," clarify the protection of the narrow mind. Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, the general [overview]; second, "perceiving the Buddha."
The distinction between the general and the specific. Regarding the phrase "seeing such as this" in the general section: this cites what precedes to introduce what follows.

That is to say, having already generated weariness and detachment toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one proceeds toward the wisdom of the Buddha; because the mind of weariness now surpasses its former state, it is said to be "increased manifold.

Within the specific section, the ten phrases are divided into two parts: the first five phrases clarify the greatness of the merit gathered by relying on the Buddha’s wisdom; the latter five phrases rely on the Buddha’s... [text truncated]

The greatness of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-mahattva*). Regarding the first of these, "seeing the Buddha and so forth," it is the greatness of the merit comprised by spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).
Second, "unequaled" (*asama*) refers to the greatness of the merit comprised by being peerless, as there is no adversary.

Third, "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) refers to the greatness of the merit comprised by the great purpose, because it is capable of extensively benefiting immeasurable sentient beings. Fourth, "difficult to obtain" (*durlabha*) refers to the merit comprised by being beyond reproach.

The greatness of merit is due to its rarity and difficulty to attain. Regarding the five types of non-confusion: they are not the same as the "greatness of merit through inclusion," because they are unmixed with the various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
Among the latter five purities, first, "being without affliction" means that one is free from the suffering of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions and attains *nirvāṇa*.

"Being free from the underlying tendencies of the afflictions" means being free from the habitual traces (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions, as one is unmixed with ignorance. Second, "being without sorrow."
Regarding this, the *Śāstra* on the Sūtra states: "There is no suffering" means that the root of suffering has been exhausted, and thus sorrow and lamentation are also exhausted accordingly.

While suffering resides in the body and sorrow in the mind, their meaning as "oppression" is the same; when one is exhausted, the other is likewise exhausted accordingly. All these [explanations] are consistent and without contradiction.
Third, "reaching the city of fearlessness" means attaining the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Fourth, "no longer returning" refers to the Bodhisattva reaching *nirvāṇa*.

City. No longer retreating. Fifth, being able to rescue sentient beings from immeasurable suffering and hardship means that because one reaches that city without retreating, one is able to benefit sentient beings, attaining the superior matters of worldly and world-transcending nirvana, and obtaining the wholesome transformation of humans and devas;

this is called attaining the "worldly. Attaining the superior matter of world-transcending nirvana through the teachings of the Three Vehicles is called attaining the "world-transcending. Furthermore, merit...
Virtue is called "worldly," while wisdom is called "transcendent. Both of these are supreme matters pertaining to nirvāṇa;
it is because they perceive this benefit that bodhisattvas seek them.

Subsequently, within the "Narrower Mind" (*saṃkṣipta-citta*), the first ten lines initiate compassion (*karuṇā*), while the latter ten lines effect deliverance (*paritrāṇa*). Alternatively, the first ten may represent the mind of compassion and the latter ten the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, the restatement of the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the presentation of the number as a general heading.

This means that because one perceives the superior benefits of the Buddha’s wisdom and sees the manifold faults of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one feels pity for sentient beings. Below the phrase "What are they? (*katame*) and so forth, the meaning is explicitly revealed.

Among these, the first phrase is the general [statement] within the specific; the remainder are the specifics within the specific. Regarding the term "solitary and without support," the treatise says they are "without rescue.
Rescue is precisely support; the eyes function in a similar manner. In the world, one without a father is called "solitary" (*gu*), and one without a son is called "alone" (*du*).
Now, all sentient beings are the children of the Buddha; those who are distant from the Buddha, their compassionate father, are called "solitary."
The "Son of No-Virtue" is called "alone. He is to be pitied because he suffers from this solitude and lacks refuge or protection; this phrase applies universally beneath all subsequent clauses.
Among the nine distinct clauses, the first two concern sentient beings who seek sensory desires (*kāma*). The next three concern sentient beings who seek existence (*bhava*).
The final four concern sentient beings who seek a false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya*). Within the first two, one refers to those who are impoverished and so forth.
This refers to one who seeks wealth without satiety and constantly harbors a sense of insufficiency; this is called "poverty and destitution. Second, regarding the phrase "the three poisons, etc.":
seeking others' resources without cessation is called "burning with the fire of the three poisons. That is to say: the initial seeking of life gives rise to greed (*rāga*);

Because it contravenes the production of wholesome factors, or because it is generally defined as the relinquishing of all unwholesome states associated with the desire realm.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter eight, states: "It can sever desire, ill-will, and harmfulness of the desire realm. Regarding the two types—*savitarka* and *savīcāra*—these are the antidotes through cultivation (*bhāvanā-pratipakṣa*).
The *Śāstra* states: "It is like ringing a bell; the coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka* (applied thought), and the subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained thought).

In the newly translated sūtras and śāstras, these are termed *vitarka* and *vicāra*. Both have unwholesome wisdom (*daurprajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, yet they differ in their coarseness and subtlety.

Because they seek out and examine the faults of the desire realm, they are able to eliminate them. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states: "One treats desire with the meditation on impurity, hatred with loving-kindness, and [ill-will] with compassion."
Because they remedy harm, one cultivates the three modes of conduct to remedy the three afflictions and enters the first dhyāna. Regarding "joy and bliss born of seclusion":

this refers to benefit. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 8, states: "By means of the factors of vitarka and vicāra, once that which is to be remedied has been remedied, there arises joy and bliss born of seclusion."
This means that because joy and bliss arise from being free from their opposites, mental gladness is called *prīti* (joy), and physical gladness is called *sukha* (bliss).
One who dwells in the four [dhyānas] relies upon the first dhyāna; this refers to the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) as the basis for both the antidote and the benefit.
Why is it not said that it is the basis for what is abandoned? Because that which is abandoned is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) [of the dhyāna]. (*Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*)

The first is called one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). This is the factor of essential nature (*svabhāvāṅga*) upon which those two depend, because vitarka and the other factors proceed by relying on the power of concentration.
Since the mind and its object are united as if they were a single entity, it is termed "one-pointedness of mind."

Regarding the first point in the Second Dhyāna, "the cessation of vitarka and vicāra," this refers to the obstacles that are abandoned. That is to say, vitarka is coarse and mobile, giving rise to the three consciousnesses and causing disturbance;
in the Second Dhyāna, it is like ripples on still water, whereby nothing is seen [due to such movement]. As for the second point, "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) and so forth:

This serves as the antidote. The *Śāsanodbhāvana* (19) states: "Internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) has the three factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) as its nature;
these are precisely the factors among those [factors] of the third dhyāna. The *Yogācārabhūmi* (63) also speaks in this same way.

Regarding "a single mind free from vitarka and vicāra," the *Śāriputrābhidharma* states: "In the stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), mental activity occurs in six locations; [these are] the six consciousnesses."

Because the body perceives the six sense objects, mental activity in the stage of the first dhyāna occurs in four locations, as the four bodies of consciousness perceive their respective four objects;

this is because from the first dhyāna upward, there are no olfactory or gustatory consciousnesses. From the second dhyāna upward, mental activity occurs in a single location, as only the body of mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the mental object (dharmadhātu) as its condition.
Furthermore, because it continues without interruption, it is also called "the mind being one" (*cittaikāgrya*). This is the joy born of the third concentration.
"Joy" (*prīti*) is the factor of benefit for practice. In the first *dhyāna* mentioned previously, one has newly turned away from desire and evil;
thus, there is the joy born of separation. In this second *dhyāna*, joy arises from within the Dharma, giving rise to bliss (*sukha*). Joy and bliss are the same as before.
The four abidings in the two *dhyānas* are the concentrations that serve as the basis for these two.

Regarding the abandonment of joy within the third dhyāna, this refers to the removal of obstacles—namely, the joy of the second dhyāna. Because it arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*), it is subject to many faults due to its instability;
the third dhyāna is therefore more tranquil and must eliminate it. It is like a poor person who feels joy upon finding treasure, yet falls into deep sorrow if it is lost;

only when both sorrow and joy are severed does one truly experience bliss. In the second [dhyāna], one abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*) with mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*).
This refers to the factors that serve as antidotes. "Equanimity" refers to equanimity of formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), which abandons the fault of that joy.

"Mindfulness" means remembering the faults of the previous joy and maintaining the mind on a single object. "Clear comprehension" means discerning the faults of joy and clearly seeing its disadvantages.

Furthermore, these three are profound, subtle, and tranquil; whereas the joy of the lower stages is exultant and restless, and because movement and stillness are mutually contradictory, [the lower states] are what are to be remedied.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Abiding in equanimity" means that because one cannot tolerate the joy already arisen, one dwells in a state of equality, uprightness, and immovability.
"Mindfulness" means that while joy does not function, one maintains clear and unforgetting recollection.

"Clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*) means that at times when mindfulness might fail and joy functions, one dwells with clear comprehension within the three bodies. "Experiencing bliss" is the limb of benefit; this refers to joy.

Pleasure belongs to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), whereas joy belongs to the five sensory consciousnesses; therefore, it is called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*). Furthermore, there are two types of pleasant feeling: first, that which is of inferior grade and consists of satisfaction residing in the mind;

and second, that which is of superior grade and consists of satisfaction pervading both body and mind. Because it is named according to its locus of pervasion and from the perspective of its ultimate extent, it is designated as such.
Regarding the phrase "experiencing with the body," the statement that "the noble ones speak of being able to relinquish" reveals the profound excellence of this bliss;

it is only the noble ones who can declare it a fault and are capable of relinquishing it, whereas such is not possible for ordinary beings. As for the fourth [dhyāna], "dwelling in the experience of bliss with mindfulness," this refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which serves as the basis for those two [preceding states];
that is, one constantly maintains mindfulness of the benefits of the blissful experience of one's own stage while dwelling in this dhyāna.

In the fourth dhyāna, the initial abandonment of pleasure (*sukha*), the prior removal of pain (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*), and the cessation of joy (*prīti*) constitute the obstacles to be abandoned.

This means that although the superior pleasure of the third dhyāna is beneficial as a form of happiness, it is utterly incompatible with the fourth dhyāna, much like a person suffering from a grave illness.
The observation of subtle music constitutes an obstacle to the fourth dhyāna; therefore, it must be eliminated. If that is so, one should eliminate both [pleasure and pain] together;

why then is it necessary to specifically state first that "pain is eliminated"? The commentary explains: In reality, the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been abandoned from the second dhyāna onward.

The reason for restating this here is to demonstrate that at this stage, among the five types of feeling (*vedanā*), there exists only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is immovable. (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter 11)

It is said: "The first dhyāna eliminates the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*); the second dhyāna eliminates the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); the third dhyāna eliminates the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
and the fourth dhyāna eliminates the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Furthermore, it asks: "For what reason is it said that the faculty of suffering is not yet abandoned within the first dhyāna?
It answers: "Because the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category have not yet been abandoned. It further asks: "By what cause does [the faculty of suffering] arise?"
Regarding suffering: although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has not been abandoned by one in the first dhyāna, it does not manifest.
The answer is that this is because, in relation to its associated factors, those sufferings comprised within the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) have already been abandoned.
If the faculty of suffering were already abandoned in the first dhyāna, then there would be no distinction in the stages of experience when a practitioner enters the first dhyāna versus the second.

"Because both possess joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*). The commentary explains: Since the first and second dhyānas both possess joy and bliss, if they were equal in terms of being free from suffering, then these two feelings would not differ.
However, in the first [dhyāna], the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of suffering has not yet been abandoned; it is simply that it does not manifest (*samudācāra*).
There is the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*). Furthermore, according to this minor school (*kṣudraka-nikāya*), this [pleasure] is merely pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and not feeling (*vedanā*).

Moreover, because the joy (*prīti*) of the first dhyāna is inferior and is still accompanied by the coarse and heavy nature of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*), it is not called the "extinction of suffering. In the second dhyāna, the joy is superior;

because it extinguishes the coarse heaviness of suffering, it is called the "extinction of the faculty of suffering. As for the "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" [feeling], it is a factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsā-aṅga*). In all subsequent dhyānas, this is explained first.

[This section concerns] the treatment [of the subject]. Here, the benefit is explained first because, by contrast with my previous elimination of suffering and pleasure, it clarifies that which is neither suffering nor pleasure;
this serves to manifest the meaning of "benefit" (ānuśaṃsa) more conveniently, though in principle it should actually come later. Question: This [state] merely eliminates pleasure.

Why does it not simply say "without pleasure," but rather say "without suffering and without pleasure"? Answer: It is in order to clarify that the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is distinct from both suffering and pleasure.

Question: Regarding the previous discussion on the abandonment of hindrances, it was stated that "joy and sorrow cease. Why is it not also said that there is "neither sorrow nor joy"? Answer: There are two reasons.
First, these [neutral states] are not the primary cessation of those [feelings], nor do they correspond to suffering and pleasure; thus, they are not analogous to suffering.

Second, if the five types of sensation (*vedanā*) are subsumed into three, then sorrow and joy are included within suffering and pleasure respectively. This is because suffering and pleasure are broader categories. Therefore, [the state is called] equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Feeling toward that object is designated simply as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Regarding "the purity of equanimity and mindfulness": this refers to the factor of counteraction.

In the first three dhyānas, because they are obscured by pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity and mindfulness are not pure; now, because this [fourth dhyāna] is free from the pleasant feeling of those lower stages, it is called "pure.
Since equanimity and mindfulness are incompatible with pleasant feeling, they constitute the factor of counteraction. Fourth, one abides in the fourth [dhyāna].
"Dhyāna" refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as the basis for those two [liberations].

Regarding the latter, within the explanation of the four emptinesses, there are two parts: first, a preliminary analysis by way of meaning; second, the formal explanation of the text. Within the former, there is a brief differentiation by means of two gates:
first, the explanation of the names; second, the determination of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
In the *Śāstranāmavyākhyā*, there are two parts: first the general, and later the specific. Regarding the general, the *Kṣudravastuka-vibhāṣā* (Xiao-zong pōshā), fascicle 141, states:
Question: For what reason are these four called "formless" (*ārūpya*)? Answer: Because within these four stages, all dharmas possessing form (*rūpa*) have been transcended;
because they are contrary to and destructive of all dharmas possessing form; and because there is no possibility for dharmas possessing form to arise therein. Therefore, they are called [formless].

It is formless (*ārūpya*). This has no other designation; as for the term "distinct," it is because there are four successive explanations in the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 80.
It says: "The first concentration of emptiness is called the 'concentration of the sphere of infinite space' (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*) solely by virtue of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
That is to say, a beginner first does not contemplate the characteristics of space above walls, trees, riverbanks, mountain peaks, houses, or other such heights; rather, they grasp this [space]."
Having thus characterized it, one forms a conceptual resolution and observes and clearly realizes the sign of infinite space.

Because one practices the preparatory application by first contemplating the sign of infinite space, thereby successively inducing the first formless absorption, this is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Furthermore, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), the initial stage of detachment from the realm of form is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. Furthermore, by the very nature of things, the initial...

Because one is liberated from form, this stage is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Upon emerging from this meditative absorption, a corresponding perception of space necessarily arises before one.
It is heard that once a bhikṣu had emerged from this absorption, he raised both hands and felt about the empty sky.
Someone saw him and asked, "What are you searching for? The bhikṣu replied, "I am searching for my own body. The other said, "Your body is right here!"
On the bed. How could one seek for one’s own body elsewhere? Therefore, emerging from this, one gives rise to the perception of infinite space (*ākāśa*).

This perception is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of meditative concentration; thus it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). The full explanation is as stated there. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* agrees with the first interpretation.
The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmasamudgaya* agree with the first three [interpretations] of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Furthermore, regarding the second [point], consciousness is non-existent.

Regarding the "sphere of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*): the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that it is designated as the "concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*) solely by virtue of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
That is to say, a beginner should first contemplate the characteristics of the six types of consciousness, such as the pure visual consciousness.

Having grasped these characteristics, they should cultivate imaginative conviction (*adhimukti*) and clearly discern the characteristic of infinite consciousness. Thus, one cultivates the preparatory application by means of having previously contemplated the characteristic of infinite consciousness.
By proceeding in this manner, it successively induces the second formless attainment; therefore, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Furthermore, it is named the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness because of its nature as a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*);

that is to say, when a practitioner emerges from this meditative absorption, a corresponding perception of consciousness necessarily arises before them, and they abide in a state of joyful delight toward that perception of consciousness. For this reason, it is called "consciousness."

The Sphere of Infinite Space is explained at length as in that [text]. Its intent is the same as the first interpretation in the *Abhidharmakośa*. The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* agree with the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Regarding the third, the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Question: Why is this called the Sphere of Nothingness?"
Answer: Because within this [state], there is neither self nor what belongs to a self (*ātman* or *ātmīya*). Question:
Since there is no self or what belongs to a self in all stages (*bhūmi*), why is this one alone named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)? Answer:

There is no other stage that can cause the grasping at a self and the grasping at what belongs to a self to become so weakened, attenuated, and diminished in power as this stage does; therefore, it alone is named the Sphere of Nothingness. Furthermore...
Furthermore, because this stage is devoid of any truly real, permanent, or unchanging phenomena, it excels all other stages by subduing the view of eternalism;
for this reason alone, it is named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Moreover, because this stage possesses no destination, refuge, house, or dwelling that can provide protection, it excels all other stages by crushing pride, indolence, and negligence.

This alone is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "If, through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one abandons all that exists, that which is accomplished through preparatory application (*prayoga*) is called the Sphere of Nothingness;
this means that the coarse effort of infinite mental aspects is employed in order to bring about wearying detachment."

One initiates this preparatory application (*prayoga*). Therefore, this stage is called "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*), because within it one no longer delights in performing infinite mental images (*ākāra*), and the mind remains in tranquil abiding, relinquishing all that remains. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* agrees with this.
Regarding the fourth [dhyāna], the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: Question:

Why is this called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception? Answer: Because within this stage there is no manifest characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*), nor is there a characteristic of non-perception;

therefore, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. That there is no manifest characteristic of perception means that it is not like the "perceptual absorption" (*saṃjñāsamāpatti*) found in the seven stages.

Nor is there a characteristic of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), because it is not like the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Because this stage is uniquely tranquil yet weak, indistinct, and indeterminate, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

The intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, the *Abhidharmanyāyānusāra*, and other such works is identical to this. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Regarding these four formless spheres, they are all termed 'spheres' (*āyatana')..."

Because these are the places where existence (*bhava*) grows and develops. That is to say, these four places serve as the locus for the growth and development of various karmas and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, it is to clarify that they are falsely conceived as *nirvāṇa* that the Buddha spoke of them as "places where existence grows.
According to the Mahāyāna school, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 33, states: "Furthermore, because one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding space, all..."

Because the manifest colors associated with blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth do not appear, and because of the cultivation of wearying detachment from desire, one is able to transcend and eliminate all such perceptions of form and various conceptualizations. Having done so, one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of infinite space.
By having already transcended the preparatory application of the threshold stage (*sāmantaka*), one enters the superior fundamental state through ultimate mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the meditative concentration on the mental application of the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage, it should be understood that herein, as long as one has not yet entered the higher fundamental absorption, one takes only space as the object;
once one has entered the higher fundamental absorption, one likewise takes space as the object.

It also takes as its object all the aggregates belonging to its own level. Furthermore, within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), it also takes as its object all the aggregates belonging to the lower levels.
If one wishes to enter the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one first relinquishes the signs of the Sphere of Infinite Space.

One then gives rise to a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding that very consciousness as having the aspect of being infinite. At that time, one transcends both the preparatory and fundamental stages of the Sphere of Infinite Space.

The sphere of consciousness. By means of that, having transcended all the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness, up to the mental application of the culmination of the practice (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*), one enters the meditative absorption of the fundamental state, the mental application of the fruit of the culmination of the practice (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*). Furthermore, from the sphere of nothingness...
When seeking to advance further, because one gives rise to coarse perceptions regarding the signless state of nothingness, one is able to abandon the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
This occurs when first entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, wherein all perceptions of having something are transcended.
Now, having further transcended the perception of nothingness, it is therefore said that there is "neither-perception.

Consciousness may possess either the perception of something or the perception of nothingness, yet it is not non-perception—meaning it is neither the state of non-perception nor the attainment of cessation.
All perceptions have completely ceased, and there remains only a subtle perception that functions by taking the signless object as its condition; it arises right within this state.

At the time of resolute conviction, one transcends all access and fundamental stages of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as well as the access stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), up to the attention that culminates the application (*prayoganiṣṭhamanaskāra*).
One then enters the meditative absorption of the attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphalamanaskāra*) of those fundamental stages.
A detailed explanation is as found in the third chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra*).

Second, regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*): according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (following the *Nyāyānusāra*), fascicle 77, it states that the general characteristic of the essential nature of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) is also comprised within the wholesome;
they take "one-pointedness of mind" (*citta-ekāgratā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, among their associated factors (*sahāya*), these exclude the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because in the formless realm there is no accompanying form (*anuvartaka-rūpa*). Therefore, they have the [remaining] four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.

According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 84, there are two kinds: namely, meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and birth (*upapatti*). Meditative absorption refers to the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Regarding birth, some say it refers to birth in the formless realm; if one is born in that place, it consists of non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This statement refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) as having maturation (*vipāka*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141, conveys essentially the same meaning.
According to the Mahāyāna school, the definition of the characteristic of exhaustion (*kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*) and the determination of its substance are the same as in the Sarvāstivāda;
