however, the point of distinction is that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) includes the form that is the result of meditative objects (*dhyāna-viṣaya-phala-rūpa*), which extends even into the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Thus far, these two sections have briefly clarified the names and substances [of the aggregates]. If...
The detailed analysis is fully contained in a separate chapter.

Second, regarding the four emptinesses and five meanings within the commentary on the text: although this sutra briefly omits the practice of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa-caryā*), the Master [Vasubandhu] has established them here based on their underlying meaning.
Within the first, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the initial statement "transcending all... various perceptions" refers to that which is...
"Free from obstructions. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "To distance oneself from the perceptions of odor, flavor, and tangibility;
to extinguish that which is resistant" means to extinguish the perceptions of form, odor, flavor, and tangibility, because these are characterized by mutual resistance.

"Not to attend to perceptions of distinctness" means to extinguish the perception conditioned by sound, because sound arises through the striking together of various conditions and is therefore termed "distinct. This [explanation] follows the Mahāyāna and differs from the previous teaching.
Although form (*rūpa*) is of many kinds, it is subsumed into six: namely, the five sense objects and the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). When further condensed, there are only three:

first, that which is visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*), because it is the domain of visual consciousness; second, that which is invisible and resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha*), because it is the domain of the other four consciousnesses;

third, that which is invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*), because it is the domain of mental consciousness, such as non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and so forth. Within these, one is excluded.

"Every" [refers to] being free from the perception of visible forms that are the objects of eye-consciousness. Why does it not simply say "transcending form," but rather "transcending perception"? The explanation says:
because this meditative absorption is cultivated while still in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one has not yet abandoned the shape of form.

Why does it speak only of the cessation of perception and not of the other mental factors? The explanation says: in reality, it applies to the others as well; however, perception grasps signs (*nimitta*).

Because it is powerful. Second, "the cessation of the perception of resistance" means being free from the four types of resistant form that are invisible and serve as the objects of the other four consciousnesses.

Third, "not attending to perceptions of diversity" means being free from the perception of form within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) that serves as the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The treatise states: Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates all phenomena, it pervades all dharmas; however, in this context, we specifically select the mental consciousness that takes the periphery of form as its object.
As for the mental consciousness that takes other objects when perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased, it is not excluded here. Question:

Since the perception of odor and taste has already been abandoned in the first dhyāna, and the perceptions of form, sound, and touch have already been eliminated in the second dhyāna, why is it said here that they cease in the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)? Answer: [Because] they are far removed.

The Dharma Master said: There are four kinds of remedies (*pratipakṣa*). First, the remedy of destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) contemplating the impermanence and other [defilements] of the lower tainted states (*sāsrava*).

Second, the remedy of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) correctly severing the faults of the lower [realms]. Third, the remedy of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*).
This refers to liberation as the primary factor, along with all subsequent uninterrupted liberations.

At that time, that unconditioned state prevents the four types of distant counteragents from being lost or destroyed—namely, liberation as the primary factor, along with all subsequent unimpeded liberations—which cause the prior obstacles to never arise again in the future.
Since this present concentration on emptiness relies upon the fourth counteragent, it is described here as "separation. (From the *Mūla*)

The Commentary states: "Now, we shall further explain that although within the Second Dhyāna there are no perceptions of form, sound, touch, or thought, one can still rely upon the three consciousnesses of the First Dhyāna to see, hear, feel, and touch; therefore, these perceptions persist even up to the Fourth Dhyāna.

It is because one has now attained the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) that they are said to be extinguished. If this is so, why are the two perceptions of odor and taste also mentioned? There are two explanations for this."
Regarding the meaning: first, there is also the reason for borrowing [the term]; second, because it is invisible and resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha*), just as sound and tangibility are.

This is explained similarly to how the fourth dhyāna is said to "extinguish sorrow and suffering" (*daurmanasya-duḥkha-prahāṇa*). Second, this specifically identifies the essential nature of the obstacles from which one is liberated.
This clarifies the subject and object of practice. Regarding the statement, "the three phrases refer to transcending the conceptualization of objects such as form":

in the meditative absorption of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one is detached from those conceptualizations of objects such as form; therefore, it is called "transcending. How does one transcend? By means of non-discrimination (*avikalpa*). How is there non-discrimination?

Because one perceives non-self, this clarifies the actual antidote (*bhūta-pratipakṣa*). Question: Since there is already the cultivation of an antidote herein, does it possess the [five] factors (*aṅga*)?

Answer: According to the *Mūla-karmasiddhi-sūtra*, each of the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) possesses five factors, namely: perception (*saṃjñā*), protection (*rakṣā*), tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).

However, according to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* and other texts, because all formless absorptions have the single flavor of the characteristic of tranquility (*śamatha*), [they do not possess these factors].
There is no establishment of constituent parts. Fourth, "entering the sphere of infinite space" refers to the benefit of cultivation;

that is, the three perceptions of form are extinguished, resulting in a vast and boundless state. Fifth, "abiding in the sphere of infinite space" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is the basis for those two [preceding states].
Of these two, the first—transcending all of the sphere of infinite space—is the obstacle to be abandoned; the second is the vision.

The coarse conceptualization of external objects is a fault; its remedy is cultivation. This means that because one perceives the fault of coarse conceptualization regarding the mind’s focus on external conditions as being empty, one sees this deficiency and eliminates that perception.

Third, "entering the sphere of infinite consciousness" refers to the benefit of practice, meaning that by abandoning the external, one abides within. Fifth, "abiding in the station of infinite consciousness" refers to the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

In the middle [section], first, "transcending consciousness and so forth" refers to the abandonment of hindrances. Second, "perceiving the faults of conceptualization regarding coarse objects" refers to the cultivation of the antidote;
that is, because one still perceives abiding in consciousness as a coarse affliction. Third, "entering into the state of having nothing whatsoever" refers to the cultivation of benefit;

that is, while previously one abandoned the external and dwelt in the internal, it was still considered a coarse notion—this [state] is the simultaneous relinquishing of both internal and external, wherein there is absolutely nothing.

All methods are for the sake of benefit. It should be understood that the essence of this concentration (*samādhi*) consists of the four abidings (*vihāra*), which are peerless. Among these four, the first transcends all equals;

it is the abandonment of hindrances. The second, because one perceives that abiding as having the fault of coarse thought regarding the perception of non-existence (*akiṃcanya-saṃjñā*), is able to counteract that perception.

This is the antidote. According to the Jin edition, the passage "knowing that neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful" refers to the benefit of cultivation; this [current] edition has omitted it.
This means that because coarse perception has ceased, it is called "not having perception," and because subtle perception has not yet ceased, it is called "not being without perception.

It is said to be "non-existent" from the perspective of noble wisdom; that is, worldly concentration perceives this as non-existent, whereas the essence of the fourth dhyāna can be known. This is the third illumination.
Regarding the phrase "entering the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) within the mental states of equanimity" and so forth:

it means that entering these eight attainments is not something done out of one's own personal preference, but rather is entirely for the sake of conforming to those beings who are to be converted. Thus far, the practice of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa*) has been briefly explained.
The fourth major section, on the stage of "Aversion to the Fruits," consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that the four immeasurables are the fruit of the practice of skillful means;
second, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva, O Son of the Buddha, attains the five supernormal powers, which are the fruit of the functional application of this practice;
third, it concludes by summarizing the mastery of this Bodhisattva regarding all [phenomena].
This section consists of two parts: first, a brief exposition of the meaning; second, the formal explanation of the text. Within the former, there are four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Briefly, two gates are presented. First is the explanation of the names: because they take immeasurable objects as their focus and give rise to immeasurable practices, they are called "immeasurable.

The number "four" is a numerical designation. Second is their essential nature (*svabhāva*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter fourteen, states: "None of these four are not... [The text continues with the definition of their nature].

Its essence consists of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness; its nature is non-aversion (*avyāpāda*). Compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering; its nature is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) rejoices in the happiness of others; its nature is non-envy (*anīrṣyā*). Causing others to abandon delusions has the nature of skillful relinquishment (*tyāga*).

These various classifications are explained extensively in other chapters. Regarding the two explanations within the text, there are two parts: first, manifesting the practice of immeasurable compassion; second, abiding...

The section on "Compassion" (karuṇā) below briefly indicates the remaining three [immeasurables]. Within the preceding [section], there are thirteen phrases divided into three parts: the first phrase is the general statement;

the next eleven phrases constitute the main body; and the final phrase is the conclusion. Regarding the initial statement, "This bodhisattva," etc., it means that loving-kindness arises in accordance with sentient beings.
Next, within the specific analysis, there are three divisions. The first eight clarify compassion directed toward sentient beings. In the treatise, moment by moment...

This refers to "conditioned mindfulness. Next, one verse clarifies compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*); the final two verses clarify objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).

Regarding the first section on compassion directed toward sentient beings, it is divided into four parts across eight lines: the first four grant happiness; the next two remedy obstacles; the next one brings about purification; and the last one encompasses the fruit.
Within the first four lines that grant happiness, the first describes "extensiveness," because it grants all the pleasures of the human and celestial realms within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is called "vast" because it accords with the pleasure of spaciousness. Regarding the two "greats": "great" has the meaning of being lofty and expansive;

this is because it shares in the joy and pleasure of the first and second dhyānas. Here, "pleasure" is said to be "shared" because it arises simultaneously with joy. Regarding the three "immeasurables":
It differs from the joy and bliss of the third dhyāna and above; here, it is called "distinct" because it is free from both suffering and [ordinary] joy.
It is called "immeasurable" because its bliss is supreme. Regarding the four types of non-duality: because the first three kinds of bliss are shared equally with sentient beings, they are non-dual.
Within the next two [types] that remedy obstacles: first, "being without enmity" remedies the obstacle of aversion, meaning one does not inflict harm upon enemies.
Because it is non-harming. Second, regarding "non-opposing" (*apratigha*): it counteracts the obstacles to love (*maitrī*), meaning that one bestows happiness upon those who are dear.

If there were partiality of mind, there would be resentment and opposition. Next, regarding "unobstructed": this refers to being free from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and possessing the purity of the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).

That is to say, loving-kindness arises based on dhyāna; within the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), it receives the direct fruit of its practice, and through the residual force of that loving-kindness practice, there is no affliction within the subsequent gathering of its fruits.
Such a person, within the desire realm, experiences the fruit of their practice: freedom from suffering and affliction, and abiding in peace, security, and joy, as described in the *Maitrī-sūtra*.

Furthermore, as a sutra states: "One who cultivates the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) sleeps in peace and awakens in peace; they are protected by devas and loved by humans; they are not harmed by poison or weapons, nor do water or fire cause them loss;
they have no bad dreams while sleeping, and upon death, they are reborn in the Brahma-heaven. Whatever benefit is obtained therein is conditioned by sentient beings.
The section on Compassion is concluded. Next is one phrase: "Pervading all places" refers to compassion with the Dharma as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Taking the dharmas that benefit sentient beings as the object is called 'Dharma-object'. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Taking both sentient beings and dharmas as objects—namely, the causal conditions of the five aggregates—is called 'Dharma-object'.
Now, this *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* possesses both meanings: first, knowing the dharmas of ordinary and noble beings; and...
Knowing the conceptual constructions arising in the minds of sentient beings, one employs them for their transformation.

The latter two phrases, "throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space," clarify non-referential compassion (*apratigha-maitrī*). This has two aspects: first, the preceding phrase refers to the essence itself being non-referential;

by contemplating the selflessness of phenomena, one attains the supreme state within the world, hence it is called "entire. This clarifies that the essence is non-referential. Second, the subsequent phrase refers to its pervasiveness.

This leads to the contemplation of the inexhaustible. This clarifies that there is no limit to its scope. The final phrase, "abiding throughout all worlds," employs the term *zhu* (abide) in two senses.
One belongs to the concluding clause of the preceding immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*), and the other belongs to the subsequent three practices.

Regarding the sense belonging to the preceding clause, *zhu* carries the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*); that is, it means practicing throughout all worlds, thereby establishing the significance of "immeasurability."

The second [section] clarifies the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) as the fruit of the application of practice, which consists of two parts: first, a preliminary analysis; second, the explanation of the text. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the names;

second, the discernment of their essence. Within the first, there are two further divisions: general and specific. Regarding the general: that which is wondrous and its application difficult to fathom is called "spiritual" (*shen*);

that which is sovereign and unimpeded is termed "supernormal" (*tong*). "Five" is a number; this is thus an explanatory compound based on a number (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the specific names: the first is "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*).

The "penetration of the object and wisdom" (*viṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*) means that the application of which is unfathomable is called "divine" (*śiva*). Taking the internal body and external forms as the basis for penetration, the object of focus is termed the "object" (*viṣaya*), and the definitive investigation is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

"Divine object" (*śiva-viṣaya*) is synonymous with "resolve" (*praṇidhāna*); thus, "penetration" refers to the resolve regarding the divine object. This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).

Alternatively, if the essence of wisdom itself is the penetration, it is designated by a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Or, it may be called the "supernormal power of the bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhi-pāda-abhijñā*), because of [the role of] desire (*chanda*).

Diligence, mind, and wisdom serve as the feet of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This is because the powers depend on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and concentration depends on desire and so forth.

Alternatively, "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) is taken as the foot, because one can go and return; since the power itself is the foot, and the power-foot is the power itself, these are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.

Regarding the second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): "divine" (*divya*) refers to light, and "eye" (*cakṣus*) refers to seeing forms. Because this power relies upon the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to illuminate and perceive without obstruction, it is called "divine."

The "clairvoyance of the eye" (*cakṣur-abhijñā*) is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound). Regarding the "clairaudience of the gods" (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), the meaning of "god" (*deva*) is the same as before; that which hears sound is called "ear.

Since wisdom (*prajñā*) relies upon the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*) and is able to function without obstruction, it is called "clairaudience"; this is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa*. Fourth, regarding the "clairvoyance of others' minds" (*para-citta-jñāna-abhijñā*):

the "minds of others" are the object (*ālambana*), and "clairvoyance" is the subject (*ālambaka*). This is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa*. Fifth, regarding the "clairvoyance of recollecting past abodes" (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*): [the term] "passed away" (*kṣīṇa*)...

Past events are termed "the past" (*atīta*). Events belonging to the category of having passed away are termed "abiding" (*sthita*). These past and abiding events are the object-condition (*ālambana*); consciousness is the subject-condition (*ālambaka*).

This is also explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Second, regarding the determination of its essential nature (*svabhāva*): according to the *Śata-dharmā*, it has discernment (*prajñā*) as its specific mental factor (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) for its nature.

According to the three categories (*triskandha*), it consists of a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). According to the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Both have post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their nature, because they take conventional objects as their domain. Why is there no untainted (*anāsrava*) supernormal power?

It is because the first two and the third grounds are provisionally presented as being identical to the mundane. This has been briefly explained; for a detailed analysis, refer to the *Prakaraṇa* (Chapter on Separate Explanations).
In the second explanation of the text, the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) constitute five sections.

Within the first, the supernormal power of the psychic bases (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*), there are eleven phrases divided into three parts, which demonstrate the attainment of three kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*).
Specifically, the initial general phrase—“this bodhisattva, even unto the great earth and so forth”—refers to mastery over the world, being able to move the world and the great earth.

Therefore, in the subsequent section on specific [powers], the first two phrases refer to mastery over the body. The upper phrase, "a single body," etc., refers to mastery over aggregation and dispersion.
The lower phrase, "or objects," etc., refers to mastery over concealment and manifestation. The final eight phrases refer to mastery over the bodily performance of actions:
(1) "through stone walls" and so forth refers to unimpeded movement across horizontal surfaces; (2) "in empty space" and so forth refers to mastery over upward movement.
1. "Entering others, etc. refers to superior movement. According to the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, it says: "Entering and emerging from the earth" refers to upward and downward movement.

2. "Treading upon water below" means crossing over water without sinking. 3. "The body emerges below" refers to blazing radiance. 4. "Again, the two lower parts of the body can remain in the water. 5.
"The sun and moon are below" means the ability to touch them with one's hand. 6. "His body below" clarifies mastery (*vaśitā*).
Up to the realm of Brahmā, one possesses mastery over the transformation of the receptacle world at will.

Within the second [supernormal power], the divine ear, there are three parts: first, the heading that identifies the one who has attained the power; second, from "the divine ear" onwards, the manifestation of the essence of the power;

and third, from "hearing all" onwards, the discernment of the function of the power. The first heading is clear. Regarding the term "pure" (*viśuddha*) within the section on the essence, it signifies being distinct and lucid.

Therefore, regarding "surpassing human hearing": it is because one can hear sounds that humans cannot hear. Among the subsequent karmic results, one is able to hear all sounds—whether from the heavens or the human realm, distant or near, small or large.

Regarding the third [supernormal power], the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three parts: first, a general statement on the person and the activity of the supernormal power; second, a detailed explanation of the activity of the supernormal power, beginning with "That is to say...";

and third, a summary, beginning with "In this way, the bodhisattva... The general statement, "by means of the mind that transforms," refers to the two kinds of minds—the actual object (*vastu*) and its reflected image (*pratibimba*).
Which of these minds does one know? Why is this so? If one knows the actual object, it is merely consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Regarding the principle: if one knows [the object] as a reflection, how can it be called a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*)? For these two reasons, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"How is the knowledge of others' minds [possible]? It knows the object as it is not; like the mind that knows itself, it does not know [the object] as it is, such as the realm of a Buddha.
Based on this meaning, Dharmapāla and Sthiramati established different tenets and held differing interpretations. That is to say, Dharmapāla stated: "The Buddha..."

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): it knows the minds of others as being extremely similar to their actual substance (*bhāva*). For a Bodhisattva, however, they are not so extremely similar;

therefore, it is said that "he does not know them as they are in the Buddha's sphere. Sthiramati states: "The Buddha's wisdom knows their actual substance, whereas the Bodhisattva takes their reflection (*pratibimba*) as an object; therefore, it is said that he does not know them as they are in the Buddha's sphere.
Next, the twenty-six minds within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are specifically revealed. An ancient master said: "There are thirteen minds," because...
Since each mind possesses a pair consisting of existence and non-existence, these combined constitute thirteen. Now, although these are relative pairs, they are nonetheless opposites.
Because the three pairs of mental modes (*ākāra*) seek their objects in heaven, they are differentiated into twenty-six. The treatise subsumes them into eight;
that is to say, the first six minds—beginning with greed—are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because they arise in accordance with conditions. Regarding the present...

The arising of the mind—because that which is intermittent is called "detachment" (*vairāgya*), detachment is also termed an affliction (*kleśa*). All subsequent instances are to be understood according to this principle. Master Yuan said:

"Detachment is mentioned here because it stands in contrast to the afflictions. Furthermore, regarding what are called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): although greed and so forth are specifically designated [as primary], they are also included here.

This is because it refers to those secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that arise following greed and so forth. Second, the two [types of] minds are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies), because they constitute the nature of affliction and are termed *anuśaya* in relation to the person.
Now, these are precisely the ten great afflictive *anuśayas*. Third and fourth, they are called "birth" (*jāti*), as they are named according to the characteristics of the place of birth.
Among humans, the mind is small; therefore, it is called the "small mind. [This refers to] the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu-deva*).

Because it is more extensive than that of humans, it is called "Extensive" (vibhūta). Because the mind of the gods of the Form Realm is greater than that of the gods of the Desire Realm, it is called "Great" (mahā).

Within the Formless Realm, because the minds of the first two meditative absorptions of emptiness take as their objects the boundless realm of space and the boundless realm of consciousness, the perceiving minds themselves are also of boundless measure;
thus, they are called "Immeasurable" (apramāṇa). These two types of mind are the two liberations among the eight liberations.

It is the mind. Furthermore, there are two types of liberated meditative minds (*vimokṣa-samādhi-citta*). By relinquishing the previous mental objects of the "infinite" (*anantya*), one contemplates only non-existence (*akiñcanya*) and subtle perception (*sūkṣma-saṃjñā*).
Taking the signless object (*animitta-viṣaya*) as its focus, it does not take the boundaries or limits of an infinite realm as its object;

therefore, it is not called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). Fourth, the names of the four types of minds in samādhi: first, when one has newly practiced and the concentration is not yet deep, it is called "brief" (*saṃkṣipta*); second, after a long time...
1. When practice becomes proficient and gradually clear, it is called "not brief. 2. When one does not dwell single-mindedly while practicing concentration, it is called a "distracted mind.

3. When one dwells single-mindedly while practicing concentration, it is called "non-distracted. 4. Next, these two types of mind are called "attaining samādhi," because one has attained one-pointedness of mind;
thus it is called a "concentrated mind. Because one has not yet attained one-pointedness of mind, it is called a "non-concentrated mind. 5. Next, these two types of mind...

One is called a "liberated one" based on whether there is bondage or lack of bondage; that is, the mind of one who has already been freed from the two obstacles, and the mind of one who has not yet been freed from the two obstacles.
These seven pairs of minds are termed "erroneous conduct" and "right conduct," and they are termed the arising of hope within the midst of fame and reputation.
This is because of conformity and non-conformity. That is to say, conforming to the desire for fame is deluded practice; not conforming to such desire is correct practice.
As stated in the treatise on the sutra: "seeking the mind" and "not seeking the mind. In this present sutra, these two types of mind are omitted.
Alternatively, this refers to what is called "the afflicted mind" and "the non-afflicted mind.

Eighth, those called "ordinary persons with overweening pride who have not attained the four minds" are so designated because they practice coarse and subtle habitual tendencies, such as [the notions of] "having a superior," "being unsurpassed," "extensive," and "not extensive," and so forth.

Although this is separated from the defiled mind, its sequential arrangement should be thus. Regarding "coarse and subtle habitual tendencies": the pride of external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) is coarse, while the pride of internal ordinary beings (antarapṛthagjana) is subtle.
This subtle pride is the residue of that [coarse] state; thus it is called "coarse-subtle. While the subtle is distinguished in contrast to the coarse, it does not include the coarse itself.
Because this subtle [pride] is the lingering vapor of that coarse state, it is termed "habitual practice" (*vāsanā*). As stated above, it is "knowing in accordance with reality."
Because the objects are not erroneous.

Regarding the fourth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), there are three parts: first, a general enumeration; second, a specific explanation beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*);

and third, a summary beginning with "In this way, the past... The general section reveals the wisdom that is capable of recollecting and knowing; the specific section explains the objects that are known. Within the objects...
Second: First, clarify the recollection and knowledge of the number of one’s own previous births; subsequently, during the kalpa of formation, one recollects and knows one’s own past events.

Within these past events, there are eleven types: the first is the number of kalpas of formation and destruction, up to the eleventh, which concerns the knowledge of speech and sounds—all of which are easy to understand.

Within the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), there are two parts: first, the general overview; second, the specific manifestation of seeing various lower realms. Regarding the general overview, it says "the divine eye" to indicate that this is a supernormal power of wisdom capable of seeing;

"purified" to indicate clear and precise vision; and "surpassing the human eye" to indicate the ability to see at a great distance. Within the subsequent specific section, there are four points: first, seeing the time of birth and death;

second, seeing the distinct physical characteristics of retribution, such as beautiful colors and so forth; third, [seeing] the happy destinies (*sugati*); [and fourth, seeing the suffering of the miserable destinies].

The general retribution is [determined by] equal views. Fourth, following the karma, the subsequent sections extensively clarify the creation of wholesome and unwholesome karma and the fruits thereof, as explained in the Second Bhūmi; this may be understood accordingly.
Third, this Bodhisattva summarizes mastery over all lower [realms]. This section has two parts: first, clarifying mastery over compassion;

that is, although their cultivation of meditative concentration is fully matured such that they enter and emerge from it with ease, they do not undergo rebirth in those dhyāna realms as a result of that cause.

Second, clarifying mastery over wisdom and vows regarding the lower [realms]; that is, although they do not undergo rebirth in those dhyāna realms as a result of the cause of concentration, yet for the sake of...

Because they fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), they are also born therein through the power of their vows. Regarding the phrase "the various dhyānas and so forth" mentioned previously, the treatise states:
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). This term is omitted here for brevity.
Because the four formless attainments are included within the enumeration of the eight liberations, they are called "liberations. "Samādhi" refers to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Three...

*Samāpatti* refers to the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). That is to say, *samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium" (*ting-zhi*). Equilibrium is the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in which body and mind are peaceful and balanced.
By the power of having previously suppressed dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) through preparatory practice, one causes body and mind to reach this state of equilibrium.
From this state of concentration, one gives rise to the five supernormal powers; thus, the name of the fruit is used for the cause. This means: equi...
This concludes the section on the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Next, the second part clarifies the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi-phala*). Within this, there are three fruits, which constitute three sections: first, the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-phala*);

second, the fruit of the maturation of rewards (*vipāka-phala*) for Bodhisattvas dwelling herein; and third, the fruit of the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna-phala*) for Bodhisattvas who... First, the fruit of pliancy.

Within the section on the "Fruit of Softness" (*mṛdu-phala*), there are four parts: first, the essence of the practice of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-caryā-svabhāva*); second, the stage of the practice of patience (*kṣānti-caryā-avasthā*) as clarified by this bodhisattva’s endurance;

third, the specific characteristics of the stages of practice (*bhūmi-caryā-lakṣaṇa*) as distinguished by this bodhisattva regarding the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*); and fourth, the concluding summary of these characteristics as stated by the name "O Son of the Buddha.

Regarding the first [of these four], there are three sections: first, the teaching (*dharma*); second, the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*); and third, the application (*upanaya*). Within the teaching, it says: "This bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*)."
Regarding "neither arising nor ceasing, existing by way of causes and conditions," the *Śāstra* states: "Within purity, one does not see the increase of afflictions;

within delusion, one does not see the cessation of afflictions. As for the word "because" (*gù*) in the phrase "because they arise through the gathering of causes and conditions," it has two meanings:

first, because they arise from the gathering of conditions, there is neither increase nor decrease, and thus they are said to be "without arising or ceasing"; second, because they arise from the gathering of conditions, there is increase.
Because they diminish, it is said that there is arising and ceasing. This single cause of dependent origination constitutes two meanings.
Therefore, by constantly giving rise to the antidote of dependent origination and practicing in detachment from defilement, one never perceives the marks of arising and ceasing.
Regarding the statement "the bonds of perception first cease" and so forth, up to "all become transformed and attenuated," these four bonds refer to all afflictions of the desire realm.
Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called the "bond of desire" (*kāmayoga*).

Excluding ignorance and views, all afflictions of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) are called the "bond of existence" (*bhavayoga*). Ignorance throughout the three realms is called the "bond of ignorance" (*avidyāyoga*). All views throughout the three realms are called the "bond of views" (*dṛṣṭiyoga*).
Because these four types bind sentient beings, they are termed "bonds. Furthermore, because they cause sentient beings to drift, they are also termed "flows" (*ogha*). Moreover...
Because it causes sentient beings to be oppressed by suffering, it is also called "oppression" (*upadrava*).

Since the delusions of discrimination within the three realms are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is said that the "bonds of seeing" (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*) are first extinguished.

Because all afflictions belonging to the Desire, Form, and Formless Realms—which are abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)—along with their causes, namely the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance and karma, are all gradually attenuated and distanced, it is said that "all bonds become subtle."
"Thin": This refers to the fact that the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*) of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), such as greed and so forth, have been attenuated.

As for "and the cause of hatred": because these are extinguished at this stage along with the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of that same level. As for "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and karma of ignorance are all thin":

because they have not yet been completely exhausted, it is merely said to be "thin. Regarding "no longer accumulating or severing the three poisons": this is because the subtle [poisons] have been severed, while the coarse ones have not.

Therefore, within the virtues of the practice of the two types of patience (*kṣānti*), there are thirteen mental states: 1. **Patience** (*kṣānti*): Because one willingly accepts the infliction of evil by others.

2. **Gentleness** (*sauratya*): Because one is able to protect the minds of others so that they do not give rise to anger. 3. **Suspecting those who have committed evil**: This refers to a person who has previously harmed or troubled a bodhisattva;
because of this, they suspect that the bodhisattva harbors resentment. However, the bodhisattva protects them [by remaining free of such suspicion].
Because he employs affectionate speech (*priyavāda*) to welcome and engage those with whom he works, it is said that he "manifests as a companion" and so forth.

This explains his harmonious compliance, his joyful mind, and his beautiful mind. When physical harm is inflicted upon him, not naming [the offender] is called "non-anger. When verbal insults are directed at him, not naming [the offender] is called "immovability.

Not being distressed when practicing patience is called "non-turbidity. Regarding "being without high or low": having long cultivated non-arrogance toward those who are inferior, he approaches them with virtuous speech concerning himself.

It is because one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others. Regarding the mind that does not expect recompense: it is because one does not hope for respect from others. Regarding the mind of gratitude:
it is because one constantly desires to repay those who have shown kindness to oneself. Regarding the non-deceitful mind:

it is because one performs acts of benefit with sincerity rather than through insincerity, partiality, or similar means. Regarding the non-delusive mind and the absence of a crooked or biased mind: [it is because... subtle...
Because the subtle, hidden, and defiled minds have all been completely distanced, the characteristics of the distinct stages and the fetters can be known.
The results of the maturation of retribution and the results of the vow-knowledge are as explained for the first stage.

From here below, within the third major section, the Section on Verses (Gāthā-vibhāga), there are eighteen verses divided into five parts: first, one verse praises the section on the practice of renunciation;

second, twelve verses praise the section on the practice of renunciation, among which the first two verses praise the practice of guarding against afflictions (*kleśa*), the next three verses praise the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), and the final seven verses praise the practice of gathering through skillful means (*upāya*). Third...
There is one verse that praises the stage of disillusionment (*vidūṣaṇā-bhāgīya*) and the fruit of practice; four verses praise the fruits of the stages (*avasthā-phala*);
and the final verse at the end praises the concluding statement. Thus ends the Third Ground.
Regarding the fourth bhūmi, there are two parts: first, a preliminary analysis; second, an explanation of the text.
Within the former, there are two sections: first, defining the name; second, the purpose of its inclusion. Regarding the first, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, chapter nine, states:

"Because one dwells securely in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and because the flames of wisdom that burn the fuel of the afflictions increase, it is called the 'Blazing Wisdom' (*Arciṣmatī*) bhūmi. This concludes the citation.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) incinerate all obstructions. Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:
"Because there is 'blazing wisdom' (*jvalanaprajñā*) within this stage, it is called the 'Blazing Stage' (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). Sthiramati’s commentary states:

"It is able to burn all root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) until they are reduced to ashes; thus it is named the 'Stage of Blazing Wisdom' (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "By means of bodhi..."
Discriminating wisdom (*prajñā*) is the intrinsic nature of the flame; the two obstructions of afflictions and cognizable objects (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are the intrinsic nature of the fuel.

Because the Bodhisattvas of this stage can burn these two obstructions as fuel with their flaming wisdom, it is called the Stage of Flaming Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"It is able to burn away afflictions through the great increase of the light of wisdom, and because it is the locus for cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), it is named 'Flame'. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

Because the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) attained therein burn away all afflictions (kleśa), and wisdom is like a flame, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (78th fascicle) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (fascicle □) explain this in much the same way.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the majesty and power of generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning blaze intensely, it is called the 'Flame Stage' (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Second, regarding the purpose [of this stage], there are three meanings. First, according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the preceding...

First, regarding the "Luminous" (*Prabhākari*) stage: it is so named because from this stage downward, the wisdom arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous; thus, it is brought forth here.

Second, according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the first three stages are categorized as being analogous to the mundane, whereas this stage is categorized as supramundane; thus, it is brought forth here.

Third, following the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, although the preceding stages attained mundane meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs, one was not yet able to attain [the supramundane]. Thus, it is brought forth here.

The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) come about through the relinquishing of attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma. A brief exposition is thus provided; the detailed analysis according to various categories is as found in other chapters.

The subsequent commentary on the text consists of three parts: first, the section of praise and request in verse; second, the section correctly elucidating the characteristics of the stage (bhūmi); third, [the section] in verse.
The Section of Verses (Geya).
The first part consists of six verses divided into five sections: first, one verse clarifies the Bodhisattva’s joyful reception of the Dharma and his making of offerings;

second, two and a half verses clarify the resonance of the teaching; third, three and a half verses clarify the heavenly maidens’ joyful praise; fourth, three verses clarify the [heavenly maidens']...
Regarding the sequence of the request [for the teaching]: first is the request prior to the exposition, and the fifth is the final verse following the request by Candraprabha.

Second, within the section correctly clarifying the characteristics of the stage (*bhūmi*), there are two parts. First, based on the treatise, it is shown that by relying on the pure concentration (*samādhi*) and dhāraṇī of the preceding stage, the wisdom of this stage is made pure according to reality;
therefore, it is called the "Blazing Stage" (*Arciṣmatī*). Subsequently, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Blazing Wisdom Stage..."
This section clarifies the excellence of the fruits at this stage. Within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, this stage is divided into four parts:
First, the part on the causes for the increase of cultivation through pure remedies. This refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) for entering the stages (*bhūmi*), and is thus called the "cause.

Second, the part on the clarification of purity when a Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva, dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This refers to the initial emergence from entering the stage.

It is purified because it removes obstacles to practice. Third, O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas dwell in this fourth stage, the Radiant (*Arciṣmatī*), it is the section on the increase of the cultivation of remedies.
This means that by correctly abiding in the practices of the factors conducive to the stages (*bhūmi-pakṣa-dharma*) and so forth, they are able to eliminate [defilements];
because they progress toward higher and higher remedies, it is called the "increase of cultivation. Fourth, O Sons of the Buddha, regarding all the bodies [of those] dwelling in this Radiant Stage...

The following explains the section on the increase of the fruit through the cultivation of remedies. This refers to the fruit of the increase of the cultivation of remedies for purification upon the completion of that stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the first [of these] is the cause of the stage; the last is the fruit of the stage; and the middle two are the characteristics of the stage.
Moreover, the first is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); the next is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*); the next two are the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); and the last...
First is the path of superior progress. Why is liberation called "antidote"? Because it manifests the stages by severing hindrances. Within the first section, there are three parts:
first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one; second, from "What are... onwards, the formal exposition of the ten gates;

third, from "By this, the Bodhisattva... onwards, the conclusion regarding the efficacy of the Dharma. Regarding the first, the "Gate of the Illumination of Dharma" (*dharmāloka-mukha*): "Dharma" refers to the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and so forth.

There are ten kinds. "Clarification" (*vidyā*) refers to the realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) within the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). "Gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*). The treatise calls this "entry" (*praveśa*);
that is, these ten dharmas, such as the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), serve as the skillful means for entering the stage by way of realized wisdom.
This is because one enters the fourth stage through the contemplation of these ten dharmas. Question: If that is so, why did the ancients explain these ten dharmas as being the "gates"? It is...

It is that which is entered, not that which enters, because it is entered by the illumination of wisdom. The answer is: if these ten dharmas were merely the gate of entry, the Sūtra should not have stated, "Desiring to enter the fourth bhūmi, one still cultivates the ten gates of the illumination of dharmas," and so on, up to "by means of these ten dharmas, one attains entry into the fourth bhūmi.
Among these ten, they are divided into two parts: the first five phrases [expound] the basis upon which one relies, and so forth, up to the object...

Regarding the bases (*āśraya*): first, one contemplates the provisional designation of the primary retribution; second, one contemplates the defiled phenomena upon which that primary retribution depends; third, one contemplates the environmental retribution;

fourth, one contemplates the inexhaustible realm of emptiness upon which the world depends; and fifth, one comprehensively contemplates the consciousness upon which both the environment and the primary retribution depend.

This means that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the basis for both defiled and pure phenomena. Furthermore, five phrases clarify the causes for transcending and extinguishing defilement.

Specifically, the first three phrases clarify that by contemplating the defilement of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of afflictions, one establishes the three realms. The latter two phrases clarify that by contemplating the vastness of faith and resolve, one establishes the cause for the three realms;
because of this vast mind of faith and resolve, the afflictions do not defile, and thus the afflictions do not defile.
Because of the great resolve and resolute belief (*adhimukti*), one does not abandon sentient beings. These two are called "vast" because they both transcend the sphere of the Two Vehicles.

As for "resolute belief," it refers to deep patience and aspiration regarding the Truths and the Jewels. "Patience" (*kṣānti*) means superior discernment, certainty, and the holding fast with conviction.

Within the second section on the "Purified Portion," there are three parts: first, a general exposition; second, a specific illustration beginning with "What are..."; and third, a summary concluding with "These are the ten. Within the first part, there are four sub-sections:
first, the designation of having attained the stage (*bhūmi*); second, because one dwells in this stage, one is able to mature sentient beings through the ten knowledges (*jñāna*);
third, because of this maturation, one attains the internal Dharma; fourth, because one attains the internal Dharma, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata. Internal...
There are two aspects to the Dharma: first, revealing the Dharma by way of the person, because it is the Dharma inherent within the Tathāgata’s own being;

second, establishing the person by means of the Dharma, because the Buddha is revealed through the Dharma. The *Śāstra* states: "All the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata’s own body—by means of these dharmas, the Tathāgata is manifested.
This refers to the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge that bring about teaching, transformation, and maturation, thereby giving birth to the Tathāgata.

Regarding "the family" (*kula*): because this stage is the foremost position for entering the supramundane, it is said that one is "born into the Buddha-family," just as it was with the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Within the second section, which provides specific examples, there is first an inquiry and subsequently a clarification. This clarification consists of ten phrases, which are subsumed into four groups.

First, regarding "the non-retrogression of the profound mind": this refers to the ultimate wisdom within one's own abiding place; this is the Mahāyāna Dharma, which is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva. Abiding in the Mahāyāna, [one attains this].

The non-retrogression of the mind is called ultimate wisdom (*atyanta-jñāna*). Second, regarding "the [faith] in the Three Jewels and so forth": this refers to the ultimate wisdom of equal reverence for the Three Jewels;

that is, because one attains indestructible faith in the Three Jewels, it is called "ultimate. Third, the two lines beginning with "all conditioned phenomena" (*sarva-saṃskāra*) clarify the correct wisdom that realizes suchness (*tathatā*).

Of these, the preceding line, "contemplating all conditioned phenomena and so forth," refers to the contemplation of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*), wherein the conventional person (*pudgala*) is merely the aggregates (*skandha*).

The aggregates (*skandha*) originally have no person; they are established by grasping the aggregates and follow their shifting and flowing, and are therefore called "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding the latter phrase, "contemplating all phenomena as equal," this is the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This means that since phenomena arise from conditions, they themselves lack intrinsic arising; the conditions are likewise so.
As for the term "non-arising," in reality, the former contemplation also involves non-arising, and the latter contemplation also involves shifting and flowing. This is for the sake of... [text ends].
This reveals the distinction between the two. The text is also abbreviated by way of mutual implication; thus, they are mentioned alternately.

The four lines beginning with "observing the world as the accomplished object" and the following six lines constitute the wisdom of subsequent attainment (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) that discerns what has been explained. Alternatively, these may be subsumed into two categories: the defiled and the pure.
Alternatively, there are three: namely, first, the defiled; second, the defiled-pure; and third, the pure. Alternatively, there are four:

namely, the first two phrases refer to the two retributions—the primary and the secondary—which constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), because they arise following from the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Within the next phrase, the first half refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

the treatise calls this the "world" (*loka*), which is precisely the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) because it arises following from the secondary afflictions. The latter half of that phrase refers to Nirvana, which is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

Because it is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it is said: "that which is purified. Because the latter three phrases constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it is said: "according to that which is purified.

Furthermore, in the first two [phrases], because the world of objects (*bhājana-loka*) is concordant with afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, and the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) arises from causes such as karma, they are said to have a "common cause.
Next, the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa refers to the two truths of Origination (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*); these are also [the aspects of] defilement.
"Purifying the dual observation": although the whole is non-dual, because the two dharmas are not intermingled, it is called "discriminating.
The following three phrases refer to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); because they also manifest the pure dharmas of *nirvāṇa* accordingly, it is called "according to what is purified.

First, regarding the differentiation of one's own karma in teaching and transforming sentient beings within the Buddha-worlds so that they become Bodhisattvas, it is called "observing according to what is purified. Thus, it is called "observing."
The karma that produces the buddha-field refers to the karma of purified differentiation performed toward sentient beings.

Second, because the prior limit consists of the defiled phenomena of saṃsāra and the subsequent limit consists of the pure phenomena of nirvāṇa, they are called "defilement by afflictions" and "purity.

Third, within the defilement of the prior limit, one does not perceive a single dharma that can be diminished, because it is precisely empty; likewise, within the purity of the subsequent limit, one does not perceive [any dharma].

One dharma can be increased because its nature is inherently full. Furthermore, it is explained that one contemplates the realms of form and mind at the prior and posterior limits—those already ceased and those not yet reached—and sees that these are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is equal to the nature of the present dependently arisen lack of intrinsic nature.

Subsequently, one contemplates the nature of non-arising in present conditions, which is no different from the natures of those two limits—the already ceased and the not yet reached. Thus, they are not distinct; this excludes what is not so.
Because it is the exhaustion of that which has been extinguished, it is called the "exhaustion of non-existence.
In the third major section, which clarifies the stage of the increase of the cultivation of antidotes, there are two parts. The first clarifies the protection against afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is practice distinct from that of ordinary persons; it is also practice for one's own benefit. Hereafter, the Bodhisattva practices in this manner; the following clarifies the protection against the practices of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
This is practice distinct from that of the Two Vehicles; it is also practice for the benefit of others.

In the preceding section, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) were clarified. First, their names and essential natures were briefly presented; subsequently, the text itself was formally explained. Within the former [section], there is first a general exposition and then a specific one.

Generally, they are called the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment. *Bodhi* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "awakening" (*jue*), referring to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the three vehicles, which illuminates and fully comprehends all objects. "Factors" (*pakṣa*) has the sense of "cause. These thirty-seven...

Because they can serve as the causes for awakening, they are also called the "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*). "Path" (*mārga*) refers to the wisdom of the fruit, while "factor" (*aṅga*) has the sense of a category.

Since these [practices] are the categories that lead to the fruit, they are collectively termed the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). This is an analysis based on a numerical designation (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*).

Subsequently, there are seven distinct names among them, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Regarding the first, these are body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*). These four factors—body and so forth—are the objects of observation; wisdom (*prajñā*) is the observing faculty.

Because it is associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*), it is termed "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) due to its proximity [to mindfulness]. These are the objects of observation, which are to be contemplated.

Because it is the locus where wisdom dwells, it is also called a "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The "body" (*kāya*) is so named because it is an accumulation of the five faculties, the great elements, and so forth.

"Feeling" (*vedanā*) is so named because it experiences what is favorable or unfavorable. "Mind" (*citta*) is so named because it arises through aggregation. "Phenomena" (*dharma*) are so designated because they uphold their own characteristics and serve as a guide.

The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are also called the "right abandonments. They are merely one form of diligence established as four according to its specific functions. That is to say, regarding evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen and those that have not yet arisen...
They cause [unwholesome states] to cease and not arise; they cause already arisen and yet-to-be-arisen wholesome states to grow and be produced.

Among these four functions, they are called the "four right abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*) because they eliminate the obstacle of laziness specific to each [function]. They are all the power of diligence (*vīrya*); they are called "right efforts" (*samyagvyāyāma*) because they abandon that laziness.

Since "effort" (*vyāyāma*) is itself abandonment (*prahāṇa*), this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. As for the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), their wondrous function is difficult [to fathom].

"Measuring" (*pramāṇa*) is called "divine" (*ṛddhi*). The four meditative concentrations, such as desire and so forth, are called "bases" (*pāda*) because they can serve as the support for that [divinity]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 29, states: Question:

For what reason and by what causal conditions is it called "basis of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*)? Answer: Just as one who possesses feet is able to go, return, leap, and spring; is vigorous and courageous;
and is able to attain and realize all the extraordinary dharmas found in the world—those extraordinary worldly dharmas are what is called "divine" (*ṛddhi*).

"Divine" (*ṛddhi*). These four are called "bases of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*) because one is able to reach [the goal] by means of them. What are these four? They are: desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).

The longing for an object is called desire. The cessation of evil and the advancement toward good is called effort. That which gathers and arises is called mind; furthermore, it is called mind because it encompasses and integrates the mental states.
The discernment of objects is called investigation. Since these four are all causes for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are termed "divine."

Because they serve as the feet for that [supernormal power], it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Alternatively, they are called "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*) because their activities follow the mind, and thus they are called "as one wishes.
Regarding the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), they are called "faculties" in the sense of being predominant. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 29, states:
"In what does faith predominate? Answer: It acts as the leader in the arising of supramundane dharmas, and in the ability to initiate diligence..."
Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom serve as its predominants. As for its five factors of training, they are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Regarding faith: it is the acceptance of the objects of the Truths and the Jewels; diligence is defined as purity, vigor, and the undertaking of practice; and mindfulness is...

Regarding the objects of focus: "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to one-pointed attention toward the object; "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the discernment of what is beneficial and what is detrimental. Faith is the faculty (*indriya*);
thus, from faith up to wisdom, all are explained according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. As for the five powers (*bala*), their five names are as previously stated.
They are called "powers" because they cannot be overcome or suppressed. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 29, states: "Question: What cannot be overcome? Answer: This pure faith. If...
Whether gods, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or anyone else in the world, there is none who can lead it away or seize it; nor can the entanglements of the afflictions (kleśa) cause it to be bent.
Therefore, this is the foremost and the precursor. The other factors, such as diligence (vīrya) and so forth, are also called "powers" (bala), all of which are *karmadhāraya* compounds.
As for the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), they are: the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya), diligence (vīrya), and so on.
Mindfulness, joy, lightness, stability, and concentration: that is to say, observing gain and loss; cultivating the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome;

clearly maintaining awareness of the object; experiencing mental pliancy; remaining free from lethargy and agitation; attaining equanimity and tranquility; harmonizing body and mind; and dwelling single-mindedly upon the focal object while discerning phenomena.

Up to and including concentration, these factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are all explained by way of the *karmadhāraya* compound. Regarding the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*): that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) within the mind is called "noble" (*ārya*).
That which opens the way to Nirvāṇa is called the "path" (*mārga*). It is also called the "Eightfold Right Path," because it is free from the eight wrong paths. These are:

right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāk*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). [One] deliberates...

The investigation of principles is called right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Speech free from the four types of wrong is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*). Bodily action free from the three faults is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

Untainted bodily and vocal actions free from the five types of wrong livelihood are called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). Diligence (*vīrya*) is the courageous capability for cultivating the good and abandoning the evil.

Clearly remembering the object of focus, gathering the mind so it is not distracted, and investigating the truth of the principles are, respectively, right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This refers to right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) up to right view (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*), which constitute the branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*). All are *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.

Regarding their essential nature, they are briefly categorized by two approaches: first, according to the three aggregates (*skandha*); second, based on the five groups (*pañca-puñja*). Within the former, the three aggregates have the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) as their nature.

These three aggregates—namely, right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*)—are unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) consisting of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

They are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*). The essence of the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); the remaining thirty-seven are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
These thirty-seven factors collectively have the three aggregates of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) as their nature.

They are subsumed under a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), because they include a portion of the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) subsumed under the sphere and element of phenomena. Regarding the second [classification], the five groups: first, the mental concomitants (*caitasika*). Three...

The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) consist of five aggregates: the four [material] forms, the five [mental] dissociated phenomena, and the unconditioned. Within these five groups, they have only two natures:

namely, mental concomitants (*caitasika*) and matter (*rūpa*). Specifically, among the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold path, mindfulness, concentration, diligence, view, and intention—these thirty-four have mental concomitants as their substance. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three are matter.

The nature of the non-informative (avijñapti) within the aggregates is the same for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools. A detailed analysis of its various categories is found in the *Pṛthag-caryā-paṭala*. Regarding the two explanations in the main text:
first, it is clear that the practitioner who cultivates the meditation is generally indicated; second, from the section on "the internal body" onwards, the meditation that is cultivated is clarified.

This text consists of seven sections, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Within each of these, [the following is explained].
All [of these] possess a name, essence, auxiliaries, objects of focus, cultivation, and fruits; however, it need not be understood that all of these are present in every case.
One should know that they are briefly indicated according to necessity, appearing as two, three, or four [factors].

Within the first foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are two parts. First, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is explained in detail; subsequently, the phrase "knowing this to be inferior" briefly indicates the remaining three foundations.

Within the former contemplation, there are further three types of contemplation: first, contemplating the body internally; second, contemplating the body externally; third, contemplating the body both internally and externally.

Regarding the first, "internal body," this refers to the five sense faculties within one's own person, as they are comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and belong to the category of sentient beings.
Therefore, for one who practices the contemplation of the body, because the body of the discerned image resembles the actual body,
they follow the observation of the thirty-six impure and loathsome substances of the body, such as hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, by means of carefully observing the image and its substance.
This emphasizes the body. Regarding "diligent, courageous, mindful, and aware": this is because the mind that cultivates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is single-minded and exerted.

Regarding "removing worldly greed and sorrow": this clarifies the benefits of contemplation. The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "At this time, because the practitioner is prone to generating much greed and sorrow, they specifically eliminate them.
That is to say, when one first abandons the five desires and thinks of what was formerly loved, this gives rise to greed; yet, one has not yet attained the dharmas of the Path."
Therefore, sorrow arises; it is for this reason that it is eliminated. Furthermore, greed is frequently aroused by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

it clings to objects and is difficult to relinquish. It is the root of rebirth and the primary of the three poisons. Thus, among the afflictions (*kleśa*), greed is specifically mentioned as that which eliminates the sorrowful mind.

For those who are exclusively devoted to sensual desire, the arising of obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is most severe; because they must first abandon it within dhyāna, it is specifically mentioned as that which eliminates sorrow among the five feelings (*vedanā*). This is so.
Therefore, if one speaks of removing greed, the remaining fetters are accordingly dispelled; if one speaks of removing sorrow, all feelings are accordingly extinguished.

It is like splitting bamboo: when the first node is broken, the others follow. Second, regarding the observation of the external body: this refers to the five external sense objects and the five external bases, which are categorized as non-sentient and are therefore called "external.
The rest of the text is as before. Third, regarding the internal-external body: this refers to the five sense faculties within one's own body.

The sense bases that support the faculties and their objects are called "internal" because they belong to the category of sentient beings; they are called "external" because they are subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).

Furthermore, regarding all internal bases of form within the bodies of others: from the perspective of the bases (*āyatana*), they are established as "internal," but from the perspective of the body, they are established as "external.

The same applies to the remaining cases. Regarding the two applications of mindfulness on feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*): "internal feeling" refers to feelings produced by the internal body, which take the eye and other bases as their conditions.
Regarding "for the sake of objects": external feeling (*bāhya-vedanā*) arises conditioned by the external body and takes form and other sense bases as its objects;

this is explained in reference to the bodies of others. Internal-external feeling (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-vedanā*) arises taking internal sense bases within one's own body as its objects, and it arises taking internal sense bases within the bodies of others as its objects. Mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are likewise. Regarding feeling and mind...

Regarding the Dharma, the cultivation of meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) should each be understood according to what is appropriate. A detailed explanation of this meaning is found in the tenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*.
Why must there necessarily be these three types of contemplation, such as the internal and external? It is because there are three categories of persons who cultivate these contemplations.
First, regarding a single person, the arising of greed at different times is not fixed; for now, we shall rely on attachment to the internal.

First, it is said that one calculates one's own body to be pure and thus gives rise to greedy attachment. Second, one calculates another's body to be pure and gives rise to attachment. Third, one calculates both oneself and others to be pure and gives rise to greedy attachment.
Second, regarding a single person practicing meditation in successive stages: first the internal, then the external, and finally the combined observation. Third...
The cultivation of the contemplation differs according to three general types of persons: first, those who for the most part are attached to their own bodies as pure;
second, those who for the most part are attached to the bodies of others as pure; and third, those who are attached to both as pure.

Consequently, the terms "internal" and "external" in the latter three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) should all be explained in accordance with this. Within the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are both general and specific aspects.

That is to say, if one contemplates conditioned existence as suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), it pervades all five types of sensation (*vedanā*), for all are accompanied by the factor of change (*vipariṇāma*).

If one contemplates suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), it exists only within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). If one contemplates suffering through change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), it exists only in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is relatively heavy there and is thus termed "suffering.

Within the three applications of mindfulness regarding mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*), it pervades all eight consciousnesses, for they are all impermanent (*anitya*). In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), there are six consciousnesses and four [applications of] dharmas.
Within the foundations of mindfulness, the five aggregates are empty of intrinsic nature; because they are empty, there is no self. This is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
According to the Lesser Vehicle, since there is no agent that arises as a provisional person upon the aggregates, the absence of a self within phenomena is termed the selflessness of phenomena.

Within the second [set] of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), there are two parts. First, the practitioner who is capable of cultivation is designated; subsequently, the "not yet arisen" [effort] specifically reveals the characteristics of the practice (*ākāra*).

Within these characteristics, there are four. The first two efforts for abandonment are the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*); the latter two efforts for cultivation are the practice of application (*vyāyāma*).

Regarding the former practice of tranquility, the first internal section has two parts. Since it first designates the unwholesome dharmas to be abandoned, it says: "all unwholesome [dharmas] not yet arisen..."

Regarding unwholesome dharmas, for the purpose of their non-arising, the subsequent desire to give rise to the "correct application of effort" (*samyak-prahāṇa*) clearly manifests the aspect of diligent abandonment.

That is to say, "desire" (*chanda*) means aspiration; "arising" (*utpāda*) means production. Because one aspires to correctly abandon those unwholesome dharmas, one initiates the practice of vigor (*vīrya*).

The latter [application] regarding the abandonment of already arisen unwholesome dharmas may be understood by analogy with the former. Regarding the latter two [applications] concerning diligent cultivation, there is only the correct practice itself.

It is appropriate to treat this as equivalent to the right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*); the remaining text may be inferred accordingly. Where it is said that there are "four right efforts," it is because one diligently cultivates two types of goodness in order to sever laziness.

Within the third [section] on the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), first the practitioner who is capable of cultivation is presented, followed by the actual cultivation; below, the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the practice are clearly revealed.
