Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*), there are two parts: first, the individual analysis of the initial one; second, the general clarification of the remaining three through the cultivation of diligence (*vīrya*).

Within the former, it says "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*): desire is the auxiliary companion (*sahāya*) to concentration in this context, capable of giving rise to the fruit of this concentration.

It is designated by its objective condition (*ālambana*), and because it is the very essence (*svabhāva*) of the practice, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter ten, states: "The auxiliaries to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are desire and diligence."
These include mental observation (*cittāvalokana*) and its associated mental states (*caitta-dharma*), among others. Regarding "concentration through desire" (*chanda-samādhi*):

it is attained only when there is intense aspiration (*tīvrābhilāṣa*) and intense reverence (*gaurava*). Regarding "concentration through diligence" (*vīrya-samādhi*): it is realized only through constant exertion (*nitya-vīrya*) without even momentary interruption. Regarding "concentration through the mind" (*citta-samādhi*):
it refers to the growth of the functional capacity of the seeds (*bīja-śakti*) by means of having repeatedly cultivated the power of concentration in previous lives.

"Spontaneous transformation of the mind toward concentration" means that by causing the mind to naturally conform to and transform within meditative absorption, one is able to swiftly realize concentration.

"Contemplating concentration" refers to realizing concentration through internal discernment based on hearing the teachings of others. "The practice of abandonment" clarifies the functional activity of the practice;

it means that through the practice of concentration, one is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* is termed "abandonment," and since this practice is the practice of abandonment, it is [so called]. This constitutes accomplishment.

Regarding the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*): following the aforementioned concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), it clarifies that what is cultivated depends upon disenchantment (*nirveda*) and so forth. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states:

"In accordance with their sequence, the objects of the Four Noble Truths are revealed as one cultivates the bases of supernormal power. Why is this? If one takes the substance of suffering (*duḥkha*) as an object..."
When one contemplates suffering as suffering, because one necessarily seeks weariness toward the object of suffering, it is called "relying on weariness" (*nibbidā-nissita*).
When one contemplates the origin of suffering as the origin of suffering, because one necessarily seeks detachment from this object, it is called "relying on detachment" (*virāga-nissita*).

When one contemplates the cessation of suffering as the cessation of suffering, because one necessarily seeks its realization within this object at the time of cessation, it is called "relying on [realization]. (*nirodha-nissita*)
"Quiescence and dedication toward equanimity" means that by the power of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, one abandons suffering;
therefore, when taking this as an object, because one must necessarily seek its cultivation within that very object, it is called "dedication toward equanimity.
Some sources state that regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), all their sublime functions proceed from the mind, just like the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*).
Since this is so, the same applies to the remaining three.

Within the fourth and fifth faculties, there are two parts: first, the designation of the practitioner who is able to cultivate; second, from "cultivating" onwards, the actual manifestation of the modes of practice.

Within the aspects [of practice], there are two parts. First, the single aspect of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is distinguished separately; subsequently, the remaining four faculties, beginning with diligence (*vīrya*), are collectively elucidated.
Regarding the former, the meanings of "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "faculty" (*indriya*) are explained; regarding the latter collective elucidation, the basis (*niśraya*) and so forth are discussed.

The meaning of the fourfold arrangement (*catuṣkoṭi*) is as previously stated. Within the subsequent collective elucidation, concerning the cultivation of these five: "faith" refers to the capacity for receptivity (*kṣānti*) toward the principles of the Truths (*satya*). "Diligence" refers to...
Regarding the truths: for the sake of awakening after having attained receptivity (*kṣānti*), one initiates the practice of diligence;

the practitioner of mindfulness, having applied effort toward the truths, initiates the practice of non-forgetfulness; the practitioner of concentration, having fixed the mind upon the truths, initiates the practice of one-pointedness;

and the practitioner of wisdom, having attained mental stability regarding the truths, initiates the practice of discernment. As for the fruit, by means of these, one is able to swiftly bring it forth.
It is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) because it is the actualization of the truths. By its predominant power, one will soon be able to give rise to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, it can cultivate and refine the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), induce Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), and thereby enter the stage of the Aids to Penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within this very body.
The fourfold classification based on aversion (*nirveda*) and so forth is the same as previously described.
Regarding the fifth [section], the five powers (*pañca-balāni*): the textual analysis and the explanation of their meaning are the same as those for the faculties (*indriya*).

However, the distinction is that these are able to suppress and destroy obstacles such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and thus they are superior to the former. Although they share a similar objective range with the five faculties, their meaning is distinct;
that is, they are "unyielding" (*anabhibhūta*). The reliance upon disenchantment (*nirveda*) and so forth is also explained as before.

Regarding the sixth [section], the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*): first, the practitioner who is capable of cultivating insight is presented; subsequently, the cultivation of the practice below clearly reveals the characteristics of that practice.

Within these characteristics, there are two parts: first, the individual analysis of the single factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-bodhyaṅga*); second, the general explanation of the remaining six factors, beginning with the cultivation of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
Within the former, "mindfulness" is treated identically to the other six during the subsequent stage of cultivation, relying on revulsion (*nirveda*) and so forth, as established by precedent.

The preceding [factors] are easily understood. Cultivation of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the factor of support, for by means of binding the mind with mindfulness, all wholesome dharmas are not forgotten.
The investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is the factor of its own essence, because it realizes their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Diligence (*vīrya*) is the factor of departure, because by its power one is able to reach the destination to be reached. Joy (*prīti*) is the factor of benefit, because by this...

Power (*bala*): because the body is well-adjusted. Regarding serenity (*praśrabdhi*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*): these are factors that are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

Because they are non-defiled, because they rely upon the non-defiled, and because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is non-defiled—specifically, because the non-defiled pliancy can eliminate the fault of heaviness (*dausthulya*) and because one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) by relying on meditative concentration—equanimity is the essence of the non-defiled. It is forever...

It excludes greed and sorrow, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in a state that is undefiled. The cultivation of the fourfold sets, such as disenchantment (*nirveda*), follows the previous pattern.

The fruit refers to the permanent abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) constitute the very essence of the path of seeing.
Regarding the two [factors] among the eight branches of the noble path: first, the practitioner who is capable of cultivation is designated;

subsequently, from "cultivating right view" onwards, the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the practice are clearly revealed. Within these characteristics, there are two parts: first, the individual clarification of the single factor of right view;

second, from "cultivating right intention" onwards, the remaining seven factors are collectively clarified. Within the former, right view is explained in the same manner as the other seven. It is based on disenchantment (*nirveda*).
The cultivation of the equal illuminations is as previously explained; the subsequent [explanation] is the same as in the commentary.
Right view is the factor of discernment, because it discriminates the reality as it was previously realized. Right intention is the factor of instructing others, according to what has been realized.
They are established through skillful means because they give rise to speech. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the factors that cause others to have faith;
in their respective order, they cause others to have certain conviction in those who have realized the truth, because of the purity of their views, conduct, and right livelihood.
Why is this so? It is because, by means of right speech, one is well able to engage in questioning, answering, discussion, and definitive analysis according to what one has personally realized;
through this, one understands that one’s views are pure. Furthermore, by means of right action, one’s physical conduct—whether moving or staying—is fully endowed with correct practice.

From this, one understands that there is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*) by virtue of right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), for one seeks and begs for robes, bowls, and requisites in accordance with the Dharma as permitted by the Buddha.

From this, one understands that there is purity of livelihood (*ājīva-viśuddhi*). Right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is a limb for the obstruction of the afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), because it brings about the permanent abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is a limb for the obstruction of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa-āvaraṇa*) conducive to purification. By...

Because this non-forgetfulness of the characteristics of correct tranquility (*śamatha*) and exertion (*pragraha*), etc., never admits secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as laxity (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).

Correct concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is the factor that purifies the obstacles to the most excellent qualities, because it brings forth immeasurable superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Its attendants and its cultivation are as explained previously in the section on the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). As for the fruit, it is discernment (*pravicaya*).
The instruction is intended to purify the obstacles to the superior qualities of faith, the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

The objective referent (*ālambana*) herein is the true nature (*tattva*) of the Four Noble Truths, which is clarified subsequently; for it is the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) perceived after the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
This is because its essence consists of the true nature of the various truths previously perceived. Thus far, the practice of guarding against afflictions has been explained.

Second, regarding the explanation of the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) within ten phrases: the first phrase is the general [statement], while the remaining phrases are the specific [details].

Among these, it means that when a bodhisattva cultivates these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they do so solely for the sake of not abandoning the benefit of sentient beings, unlike the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Acting for one’s own benefit. Within the intermediate section, there are nine phrases which the treatise subsumes into four categories: first, the beginning; second, the benefit; third, the aspiration; and fourth, the practice.
The first three protect the mind, while the last one protects the practice. Within the first [category], the initial phrase concerns the beginning, as it serves as the basis for initiating practice;
thus, one takes the original vow as the beginning. Next, the two phrases concern the benefit, wherein one benefits beings through compassion and a heart of pity.
Therefore, there is one phrase for each of the three [sections]. "Rarely" means for the sake of sentient beings; it means seeking the fruit of Buddhahood.

Thus it says, "contemplating the knowledge of all-knowledge. Within the subsequent practice, there are five phrases: first, "accomplishing adornment," etc., because of practicing the cultivation of the pure land;
second, "accomplishing the Tathāgata," etc., because of practicing the cultivation that gives rise to the Buddha-dharmas; third, "seeking the higher and higher..."
"Et cetera" refers to practicing the means of that stage without weariness or satiety. "The four conformities, et cetera" refers to practicing the entry into the stage of non-retrogression.
"Contemplation, et cetera" refers to practicing the activity of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
In the fourth major section, concerning the stage of increasing the fruit through the cultivation of antidotes, the treatise determines that there are six kinds of fruits:

1. The fruit of distancing oneself from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*). 2. This Bodhisattva, if he sees... [the text here indicates] the fruit of distancing oneself from the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), as clarified below.
3. "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, according to what follows... [the text here indicates] the arising of superior excellence within supreme qualities.
1. The fruit of the desire-mind. 2. From "This bodhisattva knows gratitude" onwards, it clarifies the fruit of the mind of repaying kindness within the section on teaching the Dharma and so forth.
3. From "This bodhisattva, in this way" onwards, it clarifies the fruit of exerting diligent vigor within the section on skillful means (*upāya*). 4.

From "That bodhisattva’s mental realm" onwards, it clarifies the fruit of the fulfillment of the fundamental mental realm, which is the basis for that superior desire (*adhimukti*). Of these six [sections], the first two are...
Of the four fruits following the fruit of separation from hindrances, the latter four are the fruits of accomplishment.

Regarding the former two, the first clarifies the fruit of separation from the hindrance of afflictions. This section has three parts; first, it identifies those who have attained separation from hindrances.

Next, the section beginning with "All those views of a self" (satkāyadṛṣṭi) explicitly reveals the mode of activity (*ākāra*). The subsequent section, beginning with "In this way," concludes what is to be abandoned.
However, within the explicit revelation, the treatise divides [the content] into five parts: first, from "views of a self" to "arising and passing away," there are eight factors;

three phrases clarify the root; one phrase on "contemplation" clarifies the arousal; one phrase on "observation" clarifies the activity; and the three phrases beginning with "remedy" [clarify the antidote].

Clarifying the Protection. The first line clarifies the fault regarding the five points of attachment. Within the initial text, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is the root from which pride arises, and it is also the root of the sixty-two views.
To think, "I am the knower" and "this great knowledge is the object to be known"—this is the pride of understanding the Dharma within the third stage.
To think, "I am the practitioner" and "this is what I practice," and furthermore to reckon that meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is the self—[this is the pride of practice].

This refers to the pride of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-māna*) in the third stage. Within this, the notions of "self," "person," and so forth constitute the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*), while the notions of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth constitute the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
"Emergence" (*niṣkramaṇa*) refers to the calculation that one has arisen from samādhi; "submergence" (*nimajjana*) refers to the calculation that one has entered samādhi as it ceases.
Furthermore, "emergence" refers to the cultivation and arising of the various dhyānas, while "submergence" refers to the falling away and loss of those dhyāna-concentrations. Master Yuǎn stated:

"Emerging" refers to the cultivation and arising of various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). "Subsiding" refers to what is eliminated by those concentrations. Regarding the "two types of reflection," this clarifies the second arising;

that is, the arising of improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) with the desire to give rise to pride regarding concentration. "Observing" clarifies the third practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

The mind operates within its objects; regarding the eight dhyānas and other dharmas attained by oneself, one seeks superior characteristics in order to make others know them and for the sake of cultivation—this is the fourth protection. "Cultivation" refers to repeated observation.
"Self" refers to the arising of the notion of self. "Wealth" refers to the enjoyment and preservation [of possessions]. "The locus of attachment" clarifies the fifth.

This is an error. It refers to being stubbornly attached to the meditative absorption one has attained, because the mind rests complacently amidst various objects; thus it is called "the place of attachment. This is craving for that absorption.
The subsequent summary regarding its elimination and severance can be understood accordingly. Question: Why is it said here that delusions are severed? Answer:

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, these are the innate view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions within the sixth consciousness, along with the faults they give rise to. One attains the [first]...
This is explained here because the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*) is able to eliminate [defilements] through the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*). Furthermore, another interpretation states:

if categorized by their provisional stations, the preceding stages are provisional worldly [stations], whereas this one corresponds to the supramundane. This is said in order to distinguish between the mundane and the supramundane; thus, it is taught that [defilements] are severed.
This interpretation is also acceptable, as this [stage] arises from discernment (*vikalpa*), and the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) designates the fourth stage as *srotāpanna*.
Because it is the stage of the *Huan* (Avīci).
Second, regarding the two types of results produced by the defilement of karma that arise from distancing oneself: first, it clarifies the abandonment of actions that ought not to be performed;

second, if one perceives that karma is conducive to the lower [realms], it clarifies the cultivation of actions that ought to be performed. Within the former, the treatise states: "All that ought not to be performed..."
Regarding karma, there are two matters that should not be performed: first, because one does not praise the Tathāgata Buddha;
and second, because one fears ill repute and gives rise to afflictions. Regarding the matters that may be performed during subsequent cultivation, there are likewise two matters:
first, seeing that there is no ill repute or gain, and thus conforming to the bodhisattva practice; and second, reverencing the Tathāgata Buddha and praising him.
Because of this praise.
Third, regarding the result of generating a mind of superior aspiration toward supreme qualities: from here below, the latter four kinds of results of accomplishment are clarified.
This consists of two parts within the first section: first, restating the preceding to introduce what follows; second, "practicing in such a manner."
The following section provides a formal exposition. Within the preceding middle portion, the passage concerning the protection against the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is restated.

This is because [the practitioner] possesses wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), and thus practices these factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth. Herein, first the arousal of aspiration is indicated; this should be understood.

Next, the phrase "according to what has arisen" and so forth restates the previously practiced objective. The Treatise says: "In whatever way, according to whatever skillful means and wisdom have arisen, the practitioner... [The text continues: "not..."

Because one practices for the sake of abandoning all sentient beings, as previously explained. The repetition of the phrase "according to what" (*yathā-yathā*) is because the practices to be undertaken are not singular.

Regarding "cultivating and accumulating the Path": the Path is its essential body (*mūla-bhāva*). "Together with the factors conducive to the Path" refers to all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), as they are the branches of the Path.
Later, in the actual manifestation, the ten mental states are divided into two; the first is the general [category], and the remainder...
The ninth is the distinction. Regarding the general [explanation], it relies on the three types of mind previously arisen to clarify the mind of aspiration (*chanda*).

Because of the power of cultivation through the previous application of diligence, one perceives the actual benefit in the superior qualities; therefore, a particularly sublime intention (*adhyāśaya*) arises.
It causes the mind to become supple and gentle, seeking that supreme Dharma (the character "turn" [轉] appears in the 672nd verse).

The *Śāstra* states that it "accomplishes a moistening and beneficial mind," because seeing superior virtues can moisten and benefit [the mind], and because it gives rise to a mind of profound aspiration. Thus it says "profound desire, love, and respect.

What is here called "moistening and lubricating" (潤澤) is intended as no different from that. As for the nine distinct minds mentioned later, they are extracted from the general category. The *Śāstra* states:
That moistening and benefiting mind has three characteristics. First, "gentleness" (*mṛdu*) refers to the mind being gladdened by the realization of the Dharma;
this is called the excellence of joyful practice (*sukha-pratipad*). Second, "docility" (*praśrabdhi*): "docile" means harmonized, and "pliant" means compliant.

This refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its associated mental factors being mutually compliant and without contradiction; this is called mastery over samādhi. Taking these two superior practices as the essence of the path, third—
"Benefit and happiness" refers to the excellence of the remedy that abandons faults; this is its functional application (*kriyā*).

From this mind, the six subsequent minds emerge, collectively clarifying that they are capable of abandoning faults and being fit for purposeful activity. Below, the abandonment of the six faults is specifically revealed: 1.
"Being free from defilement" remedies the fault of craving for food, or the fault of a jealous mind regarding the teaching of the Dharma. 2. "Seeking the ever-higher, supreme Dharma..."

1. This remedies the fault of having few desires (*alpecchatā*) regarding the virtues of ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and the like, for one does not delight in practicing generosity (*dāna*) and so forth.
2. Seeking superior wisdom remedies the fault of knowing [only] little; for one does not take pleasure in seeking supreme knowledge. 3.

Rescuing all the world remedies the fault of indolence (*kausīdya*), for one does not diligently act for the sake of sentient beings. 4. Reverencing those of noble virtue and not contradicting their instructions [remedies the fault of disrespect].
"Life-span" (*jīvita*) refers to the remedy for the fault of self-grasping (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because [otherwise] the mind would not accord with the sublime Teaching.

"Six" refers to the thorough cultivation of all teachings as they have been heard; this remedies the fault of being dominated by equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one does not practice according to what has been taught.
To act in accordance with what has been taught is superior to making hearing and reflection primary; since equanimity is made primary here, it is a fault.
The fourth [section], clarifying the fruit of generating a mind of gratitude toward the Honored One who expounds the Dharma:

This refers to the fact that because one heard the Dharma from a teacher in the preceding stage, that teacher is designated as the "Honored One who expounds the Dharma. Consequently, proceeding from that preceding stage, one practices according to the Dharma and brings it to completion;
this is called "gratitude" because it accords with that [teacher's] intention. The text has two parts: first, the designation of the practitioner; second, the knowledge...

The section on "Gratitude" (*kṛtajñatā*) is now clearly elucidated. Within this elucidation, there are two parts: first, a general statement consisting of one line; second, a detailed explanation consisting of nine lines.

Regarding the general statement, "knowing gratitude" refers to the mind that recognizes and seeks to repay kindness. Within the detailed explanation: 1. "First, knowing how to repay kindness" means that toward those who have shown kindness, one universally practices acts of repayment. 2.
"Second, the mind is exceedingly harmonious and good, dwelling together in peace and happiness" means that based upon those who share the same Dharma, one gives rise to... (the following).
1. Guarding the mind: This means acting in accordance with the intentions of the one who preaches the Dharma, so as not to contradict them. 2. Being upright, straightforward, and gentle:
This means practicing in accordance with the Dharma, following and receiving the teachings, and being able to endure contrary circumstances.

3. Having no conduct that is like a dense forest and being free from deceit and crookedness: This refers to the manner of consuming food; toward the donor, one does not conceal one's own faults nor boast of one's own virtues. 4. Being without... [The text ends here.]

"Free from pride" means that one does not give rise to arrogance based on one's own superior merits. Sixth, "well-receiving instruction" means that one correctly receives the words according to the teaching.
Seventh, "grasping the intention of the speaker" means that one receives [the teaching] without error according to the instruction.
Regarding the third line above, it is divided into two lines according to the treatise and the sūtra. According to the treatise, the fourth line below is missing one phrase, which says:
There is no guile or crookedness. Therefore, including the previous seven phrases, there are nine distinct phrases in total.

Within the fifth [section], the fruit of exerting diligent effort, there are two parts: first, citing what preceded to introduce what follows; second, "attaining the non-substantiality" and below, which correctly reveals the latter.

Within the former [of these two], there are two: first, concluding the preceding; second, "mental attention" and below, which introduces what follows. Within the former [of these two], there are three distinct explanations.
Practice. The subsequent summary consists of three types of accomplishment. First, the accomplishment of patience:

this refers to the fulfillment of the practice of repaying kindness toward that Honored One, meaning one is able to endure difficult tasks as the fruit of repaying kindness. Second, the accomplishment of pliancy:
this is the increase of the preceding remedial practices, meaning those remedies are perfected within this state. Third, the accomplishment of the mind of quiescence.
"Attainment" refers to the power of increasing through the cultivation of antidotes; this is the fruit of the two aforementioned types of seclusion.
"For the sake of a mind of tranquility" refers to the power of the antidote that guards against afflictions. The subsequent summary of these three points is clear from the text.

Regarding the ten phrases in the section on the actual manifestation [of the practice], they are divided into two parts: first, the single phrase "attaining non-interruption" is the general statement; the remaining nine phrases are specific details. This is the general [summary].
It is because one does not cease in the midst [of practice] and cannot be turned back. Specifically, within this, there is one [aspect] that is free from the faults of increase and decrease:

namely, diligence that is neither indolent nor characterized by attachment. Second, it is because of abiding firmly in one’s own vehicle. Third, it is because of extensive mindfulness for the benefit of others.
Fourth, it is because of making vows to bring benefit to infinite sentient beings. Fifth, as for "blazing," the treatise and the sūtra call it "fierce and sharp" (*tīvra*), which means:
1. Because it is courageous and difficult to restrain; 2. Because it surpasses the inferior and equals the superior; 3.
Because it cannot be destroyed by any activity of Māra or afflictions; 4. Because it brings about maturation through its grasping [of beings]; 5. Because it possesses meaning:
first, it can sever the doubts of others, and second, it subdues the speech of others through correct cultivation.

Regarding the sixth, the fruit of the fulfillment of the fundamental mind-realm (*cittadhātu*), "fulfillment" here refers to what is called "purity. This section consists of two parts: first, the designation of the practitioner;
second, the actual exposition beginning with "the mind-realm," which itself has two sub-sections: first, one sentence as a general summary; second, nine sentences as a detailed analysis.

First, regarding the purity of the central realm of the mind: it is because the mind is fulfilled by the aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). Second, regarding the non-loss of the profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) within one specific subsequent category:
it is the mind that seeks the factors of enlightenment; because this is increased through prior diligent cultivation, it is called "not losing the profound resolve.

Third, regarding the clarity and sharpness of realization: it is because a definitive certainty arises with respect to the superior realization. Third, [the increase of] the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
1. Increasing: because the causes for higher realization increase through the cultivation of remedial practices against faults.
2. Free from worldly defilement: because all obstacles are eliminated. 3. Severing all doubts: because the secret matters of this stage are no longer subject to uncertainty.
4. Endowed with clear discernment: because, having removed doubt, one attains certainty regarding other points. 5. Filled with joy and bliss.

8. The power of beings who have no support: this refers to the ability to transform sentient beings through the empowerment of the Buddha’s power. 9. Being personally protected and remembered by the Buddhas:
this is because they correspond with the internal realization of superior practice. 10. Having fully accomplished immeasurable aspirations and inclinations:
this is because, by manifesting immeasurable samādhis, their minds attain the purification of cognitive obstructions.
From here below, the second section clarifies the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi-phala*), which consists of three parts: first, the clarification of the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-phala*);

second, the clarification of the fruit of karmic retribution (*vipāka-phala*)—wherein it is shown that when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they mostly manifest as [a universal monarch]; and third, the clarification of the fruit of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna-phala*)—beginning with "If by means of the Bodhisattva’s excellence...

The first of these [three] has four sub-sections: first, the practice of pliancy; second, the purification of the knowledge of instruction, beginning with "Like Ma..."; third, regarding this Bodhisattva, at the four...; [and fourth, the purification of the knowledge of maturation].

The Practice of Other Stages. The four "sons of the Buddha" constitute the concluding summary of the names. Regarding the first [section], there is first the teaching (*dharma*), second the analogy (*upamā*), and third the application (*anusandhi*).
Within the teaching, first, seeing the Buddha serves as the condition for refining the practice; second, "both being respectful and equal" and so forth constitutes the practice that is refined;
third, "furthermore" and so forth clarifies the purity that is refined. Within the section on the practitioner, there are five points, the first of which is proximity to the Buddha. Second...

1. Listening to the Dharma; 2. Receiving and upholding it; 3. Practicing it; 4. Leaving the household life. Because this stage is based upon the supramundane, the inclusion of the fruit of retribution for leaving the household life is not explicitly stated as it would be incongruous.
In the first two stages, because they are based upon the retribution of a human king, there is the possibility of leaving the household life.

In the third stage, because one is a celestial king, leaving the household life is incongruous and thus is not mentioned. Regarding the "gentle flexibility," the fifth stage is like a golden ornament.
The treatise states: "The analogy of the *āgama* (scriptural transmission) is for the purpose of manifesting the adornment of realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) so that realization may be attained.

Second, the analogy of the *maṇi* (jewel) refers to the purity of the wisdom of the teaching. Regarding the absence [of these] in the preceding stages of the Dharma-ground (*dharmabhūmi*), it is because they are provisionally entrusted to the worldly realm.

Within the specific characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are two parts: first, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and second, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). Both of these belong to the fourth stage, as they are assigned according to the respective grounds. The rest is as explained in the treatise.
Within the third section, the Section of Verses (Gāthā-varga), there are seventeen verses divided into six parts: first, one verse praises the preceding section on the causes for increase;
second, two verses praise the preceding section on purification; third, four verses praise the preceding section on the increase of the cultivation of antidotes.
Among these, the first two verses praise the practice of guarding against afflictions, and the latter two verses praise the guarding against minor [faults].
The practice of the vehicle (*yāna-caryā*). The four sets of four verses praise the preceding stage of increasing the fruit through the practice of remedies (*pratipakṣa-caryā-vardhana-phala-bhāga*).
Within this, the six kinds of fruits can be understood by their respective distribution. In the final verse, it says, "becoming even more diligent and non-retrogressive.

The two characters for "even more" (*zhuan geng*) should, according to the Sanskrit original, be read as "further increasing" (*mi yi*). The five sets of five verses praise the preceding three stages, such as flexibility (*mṛdu-tva*), and so forth.

[The section on] the Result. The final verse of the sixth [chapter] clarifies the conclusion of the exposition. Within it, the phrase "conjoined with the meaning of merit and wisdom" (guṇārthajñānasahagata) appears;
in the Sanskrit original, it reads: *guṇārthajñānasaṃyogād uktavān asmi buddhasya putrāṇām*. This means:
"Because they are conjoined with the meaning of merit and wisdom, I have spoken for those sons of the Buddha. According to the Chinese version, however, the "merit" (guṇa) is not understood.
To which category does the term "knowledge of meaning" (arthajñāna) belong? This concludes the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).
Within the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjaya*), there are two parts: first, a preliminary analysis; second, the explanation of the text.

In the former, two gates are briefly presented: first, the explanation of the name; second, the sequential order. Regarding the first, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun):
The ninth [stage] says: Because the modes of activity of the two types of knowledge—ultimate and conventional—are mutually contradictory, yet they are brought into correspondence;
because this is extremely difficult to master, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) stage. Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states:

"In this stage, the knowledge of ultimate truth is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), whereas worldly knowledge of crafts and so forth is conceptual. These two are contradictory and should be cultivated until they are unified. It is able to...

It is called the "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) because it brings together what is difficult to combine into correspondence. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and Asvabhāva’s commentary both explain it in this same way.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In this stage, it is revealed that the bodhisattva’s definitive and sublime wisdom regarding the noble truths is extremely difficult to overcome;
therefore, it is named the 'Difficult to Conquer' Stage. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "This is the excellence of the skillful means of cultivation."
Because mastery of wisdom is difficult to attain, and because the afflictions of views and mental disturbances cannot be subdued, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (Durjayā) stage.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Because the skillful cultivation of those very factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is extremely difficult, it is named the 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer' (Sudurjayā) stage.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* says: "In the fifth stage, there are two kinds of difficulties: first, the difficulty of encouraging [others] to act without causing distress; second,..."

Because birth does not follow one’s own will, there are no afflictions or difficulties; since a Bodhisattva on this stage is able to overcome these two difficulties and achieves victory over them, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya).
The *Xianyang lun* states: "The attainment of the subtle wisdom that realizes the extremely pure objects of knowledge—the truths—becomes exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
because it abides neither in saṃsāra nor in the quiescent noble path, it is named 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer'. The *Shizhu lun* states: "The third..."
In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), the power of merit is perfected; because no māras can destroy it, it is named the "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) Stage. A question is raised:
the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states that in the first stage, the Bodhisattva and the Four Heavenly Kings both illuminate the path of the equality of the two truths.

Why, then, do other sources all state this occurs in the fifth stage? An ancient master said: "According to the actual reality, the two wisdoms are both illuminated in the first stage; [the statement regarding the fifth stage] is made from the perspective of their spontaneous attainment."
Because they reside therein, five stages are taught. Now, the explanation here is not so; since the first stage is where one initially attains perfection, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the sequence of the second [stage], there are three meanings. First, with respect to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, these are collectively associated with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

In their respective order, regarding the first fruit (srotāpanna) and the fourth fruit (arhat), as well as the pratyekabuddha, only the first and last are mentioned, while the two intermediate fruits are not included.
This is according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other such texts. Question: If that is so, why does the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra* state that one attains arhatship at the seventh bhūmi?

Answer: The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* correlates the stages with the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) of the two vehicles based on the characteristics of the practices being observed; thus, the Four Noble Truths are applied universally.

Because the second vehicle practices [the first three stages]; because the sixth stage of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) universally encompasses the practice of the *pratyekabuddha*; and because the seventh stage of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) is exclusively the practice of the bodhisattva.

In the lower fascicle of the *Renwang jing* and the upper fascicle of the *Sengluo jing*, the stages are assigned according to the practitioners: the first three stages are identical to those of ordinary worldlings;

furthermore, the subsequent four stages are assigned to the four fruits of the śrāvaka to manifest their four distinctions, while the seventh stage has not yet transcended the stage of partial realization.

First, because it is a stage [of the Bodhisattva], it is categorized together with the lower levels. Second, regarding the practices of the Two Vehicles, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) come first, while the Four Noble Truths come later;

therefore, this ground is explained after the four preceding grounds. Third, regarding the previous grounds, although one has attained transcendence, one has not yet been able to accord with the world;
the fifth point clarifies the gathering and transforming [of beings]. Now, within this ground, one cultivates and realizes those dharmas, which is why it is presented thus. Above was...
A brief presentation of the classification of the dharma-gates is provided here; the detailed exposition is as found in a separate chapter.
In the subsequent section on the formal commentary, there are three parts, the same as before.

Within the first part, the section on praise and request, there are nine and a half verses, divided into four sections. The first verse clarifies the three types of action (*trikarma*) of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The offering consists of two parts, with one verse for each. The first describes the Heavenly King and his clouds of light making offerings to the Buddha.

The second consists of six and a half verses, describing celestial music and verbal praises of the Buddha; within this, there are three sections: the first verse provides a general heading, the next four and a half verses provide specific elaborations, and the final verse provides a general conclusion.
The general praise is thus understood. Within the specific elaborations, there are five parts; the first verse indicates the two benefits [of self and others].

The fruit. The first half [of this section] concerns self-benefit, and the second half concerns benefiting others. The following single verse specifically clarifies the function of the fruit of benefiting others.

Regarding the phrase "the great ocean now begins to stir": the Buddha-fruit manifests in accordance with the capacity of sentient beings; it appears as suddenly as the ocean, and its manifestation is described as "stirring.

The subsequent one and a half verses specifically clarify the fruit of self-benefit. The first half [verse] indicates that because merit is complete and wisdom is perfected, darkness and the like are extinguished. The latter...
The first verse praises the purification of both obstacles and the transcendence of the two vehicles; the final verse praises the Buddha as the supreme field of merit for the world;
and the fourth verse contains the formal request by the leaders of the assembly.
Within the second section, the Section on the Correct Exposition (*samyag-deśanā-vibhāga*), there are two parts: first, the classification of the treatise according to its topical outline;

second, the clarification of the fruit of this stage, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Within the former, the treatise is divided into three sections: first, the elucidation of the antidote to pride regarding superiority;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, as it truly is... onwards, the excellence of the practice of the path of non-abiding; third, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... [and so forth].
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this [state]; the following clarifies the excellence of its fruit. This consists of three parts:

first, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) of this stage together with the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the initial stage of abiding are combined as the first part; second, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the stage of correct abiding constitutes the second part;
third, the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) of the perfection of the stage constitutes the third part.

Regarding the first section, as for the antidote to the pride of superiority (*abhimāna*), the *Vyākhyā* explains at length: "There are two kinds of pride. First is the pride of other stages (*parabhūmi-māna*):

this refers to attaining supramundane knowledge within the first four stages and grasping their superior characteristics; this is called the pride of superiority. Below, ten types of equanimous mind are used to overturn it, which are termed its antidotes.
Second is the arrogance of one's own stage (*svabhūmi-mada*): this refers to seeking superior characteristics within these ten [equanimous] minds."

Furthermore, this is considered conceit. It is countered by practicing in accordance with the Way (*yathā-mārga-caryā*). The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "The present explanation [addresses] the obstacle of conceit regarding the understanding of phenomena (*dharma-avabodha-māna*) within the preceding stage;
it counters the obstacle of the pride of self-purity of the body (*kāya-śuddhi-māna*) which is to be remedied in this stage. This [remedy] belongs to the preceding stage."
One attains supramundane purity and grasps it as a basis for pride. On this stage, the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) contemplates the ten equalities (*samatā*) to directly subdue those obstacles.

At the moment of first entering the stage, within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one directly abandons their seeds. Therefore, both of these are called antidotes to the pride of superiority.

Because the antidote to the obstacles was explained at the beginning of the preceding stage, once one has reached the stage of formal abiding (*niṣṭhita-bhūmi*), one merely cultivates the practice of conditions regarding the mundane world.
Because they dwell in the supramundane, untainted state without attachment, they are able to conform to the world in order to gather in sentient beings.

This first section is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the stage; second, the explanation of the first dwelling-place, wherein it is stated that "the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, dwell in this fifth [stage].
Within the former of these, there are three sections: first, concluding the previous topic and introducing the subsequent one; second, [the question]: "What is..."

The section beginning with "Next, the manifestation" clearly elucidates the subject. The section following "the bodhisattva below" concludes the ability to enter the stages; the beginning and end of these are easily understood.
Within the clear elucidation, the explanation of the equality of the ten minds means that because the mind attains purity within the state of equality, it is called the "equal mind."
These ten equalities differ from the equalities within the subsequent six stages because, in the preceding stage, one takes pure phenomena as a basis for pride;
thus, this [stage] specifically contemplates the equality of pure phenomena, whereas the subsequent stages universally contemplate the equality of both defiled and pure phenomena.

These are all dharmas that are abandoned by turning one's back on the stages. Regarding the ten minds, the treatise divides them into two parts; the first three are called the "Dharmas of All Buddhas," namely:

These are the resultant dharmas (*phala-dharma*). This means that the ten powers (*daśabala*) throughout the three periods of time are entirely equal. Furthermore, another interpretation states that by citing the "powers" and so forth, one includes other meritorious qualities.

The latter seven are called the "dharmas following the Buddha" (*buddhānugata-dharma*), which are the causal dharmas (*hetu-dharma*). If the phrase regarding the "doubt of views" is expanded, there are eight [categories].

Among these, the first six pertain to self-benefit (*svārtha*), and the last one pertains to the benefit of others (*parārtha*). Regarding the first six, in terms of practice, they are established as the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). First...

First is purity of precepts (*śīla-viśuddhi*), followed by purity of concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*). The remaining four are practices of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*). Separated, they constitute the seven purities: first, purity of precepts; second, purity of concentration; third, purity of view (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*);

fourth, purity through overcoming doubt (*kāṅkṣā-ativartana-viśuddhi*)—the preceding two [precepts and concentration] are combined into a single category; fifth, purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*mārga-amārga-viśuddhi*).

These first five types have identical names in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The names of the final two differ in the Hīnayāna: sixth is called purity of practice (*caryā-viśuddhi*), and seventh is called purity through the abandonment of practice (*caryā-prahāṇa-viśuddhi*). This is because...

In that school, because one proceeds toward the exhaustion of cessation, there are six names in the Mahāyāna: the seventh is called "the purification of the progressively higher factors of enlightenment through reflection.
This is because in this school, based on the abandonment of practice, one gives rise to the superior aspiration. If these are distinguished according to their stages within the Hīnayāna school:

the first two are prior to the path of seeing; the next three are in the path of seeing; "purification of practice" is in the path of cultivation; and "abandonment of practice" [is in the path of no-more-learning].

In the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the Mahāyāna practice consists of the factors of enlightenment that abandon conceptualization; both are included in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). All else is the same as before.

Why are the first two [the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts] prior to the path? It is because one must rely upon ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in order to be able to give rise to that untainted noble wisdom (*anāsravāryaprajñā*).

Why do the next three [purifications] occur within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)? Because in the Path of Seeing, one abandons the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one attains the purification of seeing (*dṛṣṭiviśuddhi*).

Because one abandons doubt (*vicikitsā*), one attains the purification of transcending doubt (*kāṅkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhi*). Because one abandons the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one attains the purification of the path and non-path (*mārgāmārgajñānaviśuddhi*).

At the moment of entering the Path of Seeing, all ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned simultaneously. Why, then, are only three mentioned? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that these three are weighty; that is to say, among the ten latent tendencies, five...

Views and doubt specifically obstruct the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the remaining four [afflictions] obstruct both the paths of seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Among these six, three are primary and three are secondary:

namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is primary, while the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is secondary; the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is primary, while the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is secondary; and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is primary, while false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is secondary.

Therefore, because the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three secondary tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned, these three fetters establish the three purities (*viśuddhi*). Furthermore, regarding the two that remain in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
because one abandons obstacles and accomplishes virtues within the path of cultivation, there are those two. The rest is as explained in the treatise.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the treatise names it "Like the Practice of the Path" (*yathā-mārga-caryā*). This section consists of two parts: first, a general exposition; second, a detailed analysis following the verses.

Within the general exposition, the two phrases beginning with "by means of well-cultivated" (*su-paribhāvita*) refer back to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) cultivated in the preceding four stages, which serve as the basis for giving rise to the ten profound and pure minds of this stage.
As for the third and fourth phrases, beginning with "further seeking" (*punar-anveṣaṇa*), they [refer to the specific qualities].
Furthermore, based on this profound and pure mind, one further seeks this stage; this is the superior practice of the path of non-abiding that destroys pride.

This means that in the previous four stages, there arises pride from grasping at the path, for which purity serves as the antidote. Moreover, the aspiration for this superior path with a pure mind is itself a form of pride;

therefore, "conformity to suchness" (*yathābhūta-anuvartana*) serves as the antidote, because by practicing in accordance with suchness, one does not grasp or cling within the dharma of suchness. Furthermore...
This is called the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path. Regarding the subsequent detailed analysis: from the preceding section on "conformity to suchness," eight points are derived.
First, "by the power of aspiration" and so forth, refers to the cultivation of the bodhicitta. Second, "regarding all [beings]" and so forth, refers to being free from weariness.
Third, "accumulating" and so forth, refers to attaining the power of roots of goodness. Fourth, "diligence" and so forth, refers to not abandoning sentient beings.
5. Regarding "arising" and so forth: it is because of correct cultivation; incorrect cultivation is not a root of goodness. 6. Regarding "observation" and so forth: it is because of insatiability;
that is to say, there is no sense of satiety regarding oneself or others, as one observes with ever-increasing upward progression.

7. Regarding "receiving from the Tathāgata" and so forth: it is because of attaining the superior power of the stages (*bhūmi*) and because one's practice becomes increasingly superior, thereby attaining other Buddhas.

Regarding "the empowerment of power" and "the wisdom of the eight recollections," etc.: it means that virtue is perfected within oneself because one has personally attained supreme power, because one has accomplished the mind of non-retrogression, and because one practices the cultivation of wisdom free from obstacles.

The second section clarifies the excellence of the practice of the path of non-abiding, which has two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the interpretation of the text. Within the first part, there are two types:
(1) the excellence of the purity of wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge, which is for one’s own benefit and consists of guarding against afflictive conduct while not abiding in the world;
(2) from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains such treatises... onwards, it clarifies the benefiting of others.
The excellence of generating diligent skillful means is for the benefit of others; it involves protecting those who practice the Lesser Vehicle and not abiding in nirvāṇa.

Regarding these two statements, although they occur sequentially in time, their practice is necessarily simultaneous and does not correspond to temporal succession. They are said to be "simultaneous" because they are taught as being concurrent; therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
If this were not the case, one would first abide in nirvāṇa and subsequently become attached to the world. Thus, we know that both occur together.
Regarding the aforementioned wisdom that is entirely pure and supreme: first, the real dharmas of the Four Truths are clarified through their differentiation;

subsequently, the distinctions in the transformation of beings according to the Ten Truths are clarified within the context of skillfully knowing the conventional truth. This is because one performs these ten kinds of observation upon the aforementioned Four Truths.

This constitutes the ten aspects of the Truths (*daśa-satya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Abiding" (*Vihāra-paṭala*), states: "Because this stage understands the Four Noble Truths as they truly are through ten modes of activity.

Regarding this, it is briefly analyzed here by way of two gates: first, the explanation of the names; second, the discernment of their essence. Within the first [the explanation of names], there are two parts; first, the general [explanation].
The subsequent section is distinct. Regarding the general [classification], "noble" (*ārya*) refers to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) abiding in the mind.
"Truths" (*satya*) refers to not deviating from the characteristics as they have been described. By means of this observation, one reaches ultimate purity and attains definitive reality.
This means that the two types of cause and effect—mundane and supramundane—are necessarily free from falsehood and cannot be subject to error. Such is the correspondence with definitive reality.

Because it purifies both phenomena and principle and is the exclusive domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), it is called a "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*). This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, meaning "the truth of the noble ones.

When stated collectively as the "Four Noble Truths," it is a *saṃkhyā-pūrva* (numeral-determinative) compound. Within the individual [truths], that which oppresses is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*), and that which causes growth is called "origination" (*samudaya*).

Quiescence (*śānti*) is called cessation (*nirodha*); renunciation (*naiṣkramya*) is called the path (*mārga*). Second, regarding the discernment of their essential nature: all name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) constitutes the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);

karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*); the exhaustion of afflictions constitutes the truth of cessation; and tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) constitute the truth of the path.

The detailed analysis according to various categories is as found in other chapters. In the treatise, these are termed "real dharmas" (*bhūtadharma*): the two truths of suffering and origination exist whether a Buddha appears or not.

The Buddha [taught that] the nature of the world consists of the causes and effects of defilement, whereas the two truths of cessation and the path are by nature the causes and effects of supramundane purity.
Later, in the explanation of the ten truths, Master Yuan distinguished them according to four propositions from the *Śāstra*: first, their establishment; second, their opening and closing.

Third, distinguishing the general and specific aspects in relation to the actual dharmas; fourth, explaining the text. Regarding the first: within the gateway of the Four Truths, the meaning encompasses the entire *dharmadhātu*.

Within this, the Bodhisattva’s illumination and penetration are exhaustive and leave nothing remaining. For the time being, these ten truths are taught according to the numerical sequence of a single cycle [of teaching], though a detailed analysis would be difficult to exhaust.
These are all objects of knowledge known by the Bodhisattvas themselves; they are manifested through the medium of those to be converted to reveal their distinctiveness. Therefore:
The title of this treatise is "Purity of Wisdom Regarding the Dharmas to be Known. Second, regarding the opening and closing [of the categories]:

they may be consolidated into one, namely, because they are distinguished according to the transformation of sentient beings. Alternatively, they are divided into two according to the magnitude of those to be transformed: the first nine transform those of small capacity, while the final one transforms those of great capacity.
Or, they are divided into three according to the functions they initiate: the first five transform sentient beings by causing them to produce understanding; next...

The first four transformations cause [beings] to initiate practice; the final one causes them to enter realization. Alternatively, based on differences among individuals, they are divided into seven categories:
first, the transformation for those whose faculties are not yet mature; second, for those whose faculties are already mature; third, for those who harbor doubts regarding profound teachings;

fourth, for those who have misconstrued the teachings; fifth, for those who have strayed from right mindfulness; sixth, seventh, and eighth, for those with right view. Ninth, [the transformation for those who]... [are established in right view].
These ten transform sentient beings who are capable of being transformed through the Mahāyāna; alternatively, they are divided into ten according to the differences in the teachings.
Regarding the distinction between the general and the specific in relation to the three pairs of real dharmas: these ten gates are each universally applicable to the four preceding truths.

1. The first conventional truth is to universally contemplate the distinct characteristics of the four truths as phenomena. 2. The second is to universally contemplate the emptiness of the essence of the four truths. 3.

The third is to universally contemplate that the four truths are neither existent nor non-existent. 4. The fourth is to universally contemplate that existence and non-existence regarding the four truths are each distinct.

5. The fifth is to universally contemplate that the four truths are integrated through dependent origination. 6. The sixth is to universally contemplate that the four truths result in the reality of suffering due to delusion. 7. Due to delusion...

1. The arising and formation of the Four Truths; 2. The thorough penetration of the Four Truths and the attainment of the cessation of the truths; 3. The comprehensive understanding of the Four Truths and the attainment of the knowledge of the Path;
4. Because of the ultimate realization of the true nature of dependent origination within the Four Truths as the pure Dharma-realm, one accomplishes the causes and fruits of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.

The commentary on the text has two parts: first, the listing of the ten names; second, their sequential explanation. Among these, although two or three names differ slightly between the new and old translations, they do not contradict the meaning;
this can be understood through a comparative analysis. The treatise states, "sentient beings of the Hīnayāna who are to be converted.
This does not mean converting sentient beings to enter the Hīnayāna; rather, it means converting those who are already of the Hīnayāna disposition so that they may enter the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, for those whose single faculties are not yet matured and who are incapable of entering the Great [Vehicle], he teaches the Four Truths, the twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra*), and so forth;

this is called "knowing the conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is the conventional truth within the third layer of the fourfold two-truth system. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It is based on the awakening of others.
The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "This sutra and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* apply universally to all capacities, whereas the present treatise focuses specifically on..."

Regarding those whose faculties (*indriya*) are not yet matured: for two reasons, because those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) whose faculties have matured are capable of entering the Great Vehicle, the ultimate truth of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*) is taught for them.

As a sutra states: "The One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) causes those of the Lesser Vehicle to enter the Great; there is no other vehicle beyond it. Furthermore, this is because, in principle, there is no duality.

It is also called "the single characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Yoga relies upon one's own internal wisdom. There are three types of persons who do not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and claim it to be absolute annihilation;

these are called sentient beings who harbor doubts regarding the profound Dharma. Those who know the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*) are those who know that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent because they possess a single, true characteristic.
Furthermore, another explanation is that having heard the true truth, they mistakenly believe it to be the annihilation of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

Therefore, it is called "doubt regarding profound dharmas. To cause the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of dharmas to be clearly distinguished, it is called "the truth of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇasatya*).

This is stated based on the name of the "common locus" (*ubhayāśraya*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The commentary explains that this refers to the aforementioned "common locus" of the two truths, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

Regarding the phrase "four are erroneous understandings," etc.: upon hearing of the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyam*), to claim it is definitively one is called "erroneous understanding," and so forth; now, one knows there are two.
The distinctions among the truths are not one. In the former case, there was doubt regarding their unity; here, there is delusion regarding their diversity.
Having heard that the five [aggregates] possess distinct natures, they fall into contradiction with the Right Path and are thus called those who have strayed from right mindfulness.

"Knowing that the truths are established through teaching" means knowing that the various phenomena of the four previously distinguished truths are merely accumulated through the causes and conditions of verbal expression, and thus lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the explanation of "establishment": the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it is named according to its reliance upon the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās.

Regarding the sixth point, "correctly guiding sentient beings": this refers to causing them to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

based on the intrinsic nature of present sufferings, based on the generative nature of future causes of suffering, and based on the exhaustion of those causes and the consequent exhaustion of suffering.
The nature of non-arising. This refers to the nature of practicing the means for its abandonment. As the Sūtra says:
"Reaching the dharma of non-duality" refers to the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), because it is able to reach the principle of non-dual cessation (*nirodha*).

Tenth, those who are to be converted by the Mahāyāna refers to bodhisattvas who proceed directly and do not come from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); they know the causes and effects of a bodhisattva, and as for knowing them at the stage of fruition, it is simply...
This is the wisdom of contemplative observation that is the image of the power of faith and understanding; it is not known by the inexhaustible wisdom of the fruit of Buddhahood.

This distinguishes between the superior and the inferior. A similar distinction is made in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*); that text refers to practice (*caryā*), whereas this refers to understanding (*adhimukti*).
Regarding the subsequent clarification of the excellence of diligent skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, there are two parts. First is the general manifestation;

second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains such power of wisdom" onwards, is the detailed analysis. Within the first part, there are also two sections: first, contemplating the faults of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, clarifying the arousal of compassion. Within the first of these, "falsehood" refers to contemplating the internal five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Because false conceptualizations (vikalpa) such as permanence and so forth lack any correspondence with reality, they are empty. This clarifies that the grasped object (grāhya) is not real, being neither permanent nor the self (ātman), and because it is not an object for pride (māna).
For this reason, it is revealed that the grasper (grāhaka) is not true; it is false and deceptive.

That is to say, regarding the aforementioned empty characteristics, one falsely grasps them as "self" and so forth, acting with fraud and delusion. Thus, one contemplates the six external sense objects (viṣaya), realizing that worldly phenomena are entirely subject to destruction.
"Deception. This clarifies that the grasped object is unreal; it is merely a deceptive worldly phenomenon (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) that appears to continue and appear as such.

If something has utility yet truly perishes rapidly and cannot be found, to say it "exists" is nothing but deception. Worldly phenomena are a fraud because they entice foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
This reveals that the grasper is deluded regarding reality; that is to say, through false grasping, it causes those worldly phenomena to conceal their own emptiness.

"Deception and reality cause the world to greedily grasp; they delude and confuse the foolish. This summarizes the unreality of both the internal and external, pointing out the faults regarding persons.
That is to say, a false object inducing the mind is termed "delusion" (*vañcana*); the mind being bewildered by the preceding object is called "confusion" (*moha*).

Within the internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that precede it, the objects are the "deceptions" and the mind is the "confusion. This can be understood from the commentary’s citation and explanation. As for "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*):
Relying upon that, one correctly grasps the body of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"); in other translations, this is rendered as "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).

Below, it clarifies the actual arising of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Among these, "compassion" refers to feeling pity for those sentient beings; "great" refers to being superior to the compassion prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*);
"further superior" refers to the excellence of not abiding in the path of practice. "Loving-kindness" refers to manifesting supreme benefit; "light" refers to rescuing the multitude.

Because the skillful means for generating [insight] are accomplished through knowledge, there are two subsequent sections for detailed analysis: first, restating the preceding to introduce the following; second, from "constantly seeking the Buddha’s wisdom" onwards, the actual exposition.

In the preceding section, the phrase "attaining such power of wisdom" restates the prior knowledge of the faults of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). The phrase "not abandoning [sentient beings]" and so forth restates the prior intensification of compassion.
In the subsequent section that explicitly reveals the meaning, the phrase "constantly seeking the Buddha’s wisdom" carries the sense of rescuing all sentient beings.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the elucidation of the contemplation of great compassion; second, "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva... [and so on].
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further forms this thought: "These various sentient beings are inferior.

This clarifies the contemplation of great compassion (*maitrī*). Within the preceding [section], there are two aspects of compassion (*karuṇā*): first, contemplating the accumulation of the causes and conditions of suffering; second, O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further forms this thought:
"These various ordinary people are inferior. This clarifies the contemplation of profound and heavy suffering. Within the preceding [section], it says: "contemplating one..."

Regarding "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in terms of their prior and subsequent limits": this refers to observing the causes of the prior limit and the results of the subsequent limit in general.

"Knowing from below" refers to specific observation. Within the specific [observation], one first observes the prior limit; subsequently, as with the prior limit, the subsequent limit is revealed by analogy. Within the prior [limit], there are two parts: first, the observation of the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*);
second, from "non-self" (*anātman*) onwards, the absence of self and what belongs to self (*anātma-ātmīya*) is revealed. Within the first part, it is simply stated that there is no...

The mention of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) reveals the cause of saṃsāra. This pertains to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not to noble ones (*ārya*). Although in reality there are also other conditions such as karma and so forth, why are they not mentioned?

It is because ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving are the fundamental causes that initiate and moisten rebirth; therefore, these two alone are specifically cited. Regarding "birth" (*jāti*), there are three kinds of birth for sentient beings:
namely, the pursuit of sensual desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), the pursuit of false asceticism (*mithyā-brahmacarya-tṛṣṇā*), and the pursuit of existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*). This clarifies...
The "prior limit" refers to the fruit [of past actions]. Those who "wander through birth and death" are sentient beings who seek sensual pleasures (*kāma*).

Those who [dwell] in the "house of the aggregates" and so forth are sentient beings who falsely seek the holy life (*brahmacarya*); these are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), not followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), and for this reason they are called "false."

Regarding the phrase "unable to move out," the Sanskrit original states: "Those who lack the intention to seek liberation and instead increase the mass of suffering are *saṃsārin* (beings subject to cyclic existence).

Within this, two types of [beings] are subsequently revealed through the teaching of non-self (*anātman*). First, the four lines clarify non-self; second, one line clarifies the absence of what belongs to the self (*anātmīya*).
Within the former, the first line establishes the name based on its general meaning, while the remaining lines apply it according to specific meanings. Generally, it is called...
"Selfless" means that when one searches for a provisional person (*pudgala*) among the aggregates (*skandha*), it cannot be found.
"Among the distinct [aggregates], there is no life-principle (*jīva*)" means that when one searches for a living being (*sattva*) existing as a composite, it cannot be found.

"There is no nourisher (*poṣa*)" means that when one searches for a self or person (*ātman/pudgala*) that is permitted to exist and grow by depending upon food and clothing, it cannot be found. "There is no further... [text fragment].
"Those who repeatedly take up bodies in future destinies" means that one cannot find anyone who seeks out various destinies again and again without weariness.
The final phrase clarifies "the absence of what belongs to a self" (*anātmiya*): since even a "self" (*ātman*) cannot be found, how much less can there be "what belongs to a self"?
The subsequent category reveals the middle of the future limit; that is, just as in the previous limit, by what cause is that delusion and craving restated?

Because all sentient beings are subsumed under the aforementioned fruit; because all ascetic practices are subsumed under the aforementioned non-self—meaning that there are only the fruits of suffering and the practices that cause suffering, while fundamentally there is no self or what belongs to a self; thus it is said that the future limit is also like this.

"All are non-existent and false" means that the fruit of suffering has craving as its cause of origination (*samudaya*), its total exhaustion is the fruit of cessation (*nirodha*), and renunciation is the cause of the path (*mārga*).
"Whether existent or non-existent, one knows them all according to reality" means that because cessation and the path are real, they are "existent";
because suffering and origination are false, they are "non-existent. Regarding these objects of existence and non-existence, one knows them in accordance with their nature, free from inversion.

Indeed. Regarding the subsequent clarification of "profoundly grave suffering" and "great compassion": this means that throughout immeasurable lifetimes one has followed after such profound suffering, and these various forms of suffering are grave.
First, one contemplates sentient beings as objects of pity; subsequently, by the phrase "thus exhausting and extinguishing," the preceding censure is restated.

Next, various forms of suffering are clarified. This consists of two parts: first, the clarification of those who are pitiable; second, from "there are countless" onwards, the revelation of the reasons for their being pitiable.
Regarding the term "pitiable," there are two meanings: first, they undergo suffering without knowing weariness or seeking liberation;

second, they give rise to craving and attachment toward that which is non-existent. Thus, they are called "foolish and ignorant. The subsequent section clarifies the reasons for their being pitiable, namely, on account of ignorance (*avidyā*).
