nor are they those who will not receive it, for their [defilements] have not yet been severed. Furthermore, it is not the case that these occur at the same time.

This clarifies that what was previously done or not done, and what has been attained or not attained, [is determined by this]. If one personally performs the lower protection (*ārakṣā*), there is the fault of the second [point], which is the failure to receive retribution:
namely, that one who acts must receive [the result] themselves. Why would another receive it? Because another did not perform the act.

Third, there is the fault of losing the third [point], which is the protection: namely, that by abandoning those three things, one fails to attain [the result]. Therefore, there are no karmas that do not yield their fruit.

Therefore, there is no fault of failing to provide for one’s livelihood. The conclusion at the end may be understood accordingly. Third, regarding the classification by means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

when a bodhisattva sees those among the non-Buddhists who, practicing heterodox paths in their quest for liberation, falsely calculate that there is no cause and so forth, he gives rise to a mind of great compassion.

He contemplates this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to rescue them from their attachment to false views. As the treatise states, "the causes of the prior and middle limits": the two members of the past are the "prior."
The middle limit acts as the cause for the present consciousness and so forth. Regarding the statement "the causes of the middle and subsequent limits":

the craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) of the middle limit act as the causes for the future, the subsequent limit. Regarding the statement "because of the two limits, prior and posterior, within the middle limit":

within the middle limit itself, the five results beginning with consciousness are categorized as belonging to the prior result, while the three causes beginning with craving are categorized as belonging to the subsequent limit. Since this is so...

How can one say that this cause does not exist? Therefore, the conclusion states: "If such commonality [of karma] were absent, then the various fruits and effects for sentient beings would also not exist.
Fourth, regarding the analysis according to great wisdom, it is called the reliance on the contemplation of power and lack of power for entering into faith.
The two past links have power in relation to the present, but lack power in relation to the future; the three links beginning with craving (tṛṣṇā) lack power in relation to the future.

The former [two] lack power; looking back from the latter, they lack power. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the two past [stages] possess power, while the five present [stages] lack power;
the three present [stages] possess power, while the two subsequent [stages] lack power. This is because that which can produce is "possessing power," while that which is produced is "lacking power.

Because the Bodhisattva raises these transformed persons to cause them to depart [from error] and enter the correct path, it is called "entrance through faith and reliance. Because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom illuminates them, it is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). It is said:

Regarding "the conditions for conversion in the past, present, and future," this is a further explanation for establishment. "Past, present, and future" refers to power and lack of power; "conditions for conversion" refers to entering through faith.
This means illuminating the three periods of time to convert sentient beings for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The seventh [section], "The Threefold Aggregation," also consists of four gates. The first, based on the Sūtra, clarifies that these links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are all aggregates of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*).

In order to explain the causes of the three types of suffering, it analyzes the discrimination associated with feeling (*vedanā-sahagata-vikalpa*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* asks: "How many fruits are concomitant with feeling?

It states: "Excluding two, the remainder. That is to say, excluding feeling itself and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the remaining ten possess pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), because feeling does not coexist with feeling.
Because they coexist. In the stage of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), because there is generally no pleasure, how many are associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*)?

It is those same [factors] and one from among those excluded; that is to say, excluding only the constituent of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the remaining eleven are associated with painful feeling. How many are associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣāvedanā*)?

As explained regarding pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), because at the stage of old age and death there is generally no possibility of relinquishing it, how many [factors] do not coexist with feeling?
It refers to one among those excluded, namely the limb of feeling (*vedanā-aṅga*), because feeling does not coexist with feeling itself. This is also stated similarly in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Next, regarding the analysis of the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*), there are two approaches: first, the approach of actual universal pervasion, as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) comprises ten members in their entirety, as well as a portion of the member of sensation (*vedanā*). That is to say, it includes pleasant sensations—excluding the suffering within the member of sensation—and the suffering of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
The suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) comprises eleven members in their entirety, as well as a portion of the member of sensation. That is to say, it includes painful sensations.

All instances of suffering are included within the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Alternatively, there may be ten types of suffering that are not subsumed under these two members; namely, [the suffering of] non-existence...

Suffering that is not pleasant feeling; therefore, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) comprehensively encompasses all twelve [links]. The eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* agrees with this.

Second is the gate of manifesting according to the increase of characteristics, as stated in this sutra: namely, because the characteristic of flux is manifest in the first five branches, they are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

Because the two types—contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*)—confront and give rise to suffering, they are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). As for the remaining [branches] being the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), it is simply because of change...
Pleasure is called "suffering through change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Since there is no pleasure to be changed within the factors of old age and death, why are they called "change"?

The commentary explains: There are two kinds of change. First, the destruction of pleasure becomes suffering; this is stated in reference to that which is destroyed. Second, change itself is suffering; therefore, it is called "suffering through change.
Because these factors of old age and death can destroy birth, they belong to "suffering through change. The rest of the text is clear. (2)

Regarding the contemplation of revulsion toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the Master [Vasubandhu] states that within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) view, this is the fifth among the various types;

it is called the "contemplation of non-revulsion regarding revulsion. This means that while ordinary beings do not feel revulsion, Bodhisattvas do; thus it is termed "non-revulsion regarding revulsion. This refers to the coarse aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, while the followers of the two vehicles do not find weariness [in suffering], Bodhisattvas are able to find it. This is because it refers to subtle suffering;

thus it is called "various subtle sufferings," since one discriminates that all these are suffering. As for the weariness toward various coarse sufferings, this is what the followers of the two vehicles find weariness in, and Bodhisattvas likewise find weariness in it.

Moreover, it is understood that the former subtle [suffering] is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), while this coarse [suffering] consists of the other two types of suffering. (3)
Regarding the analysis according to the conformity of great compassion: it is out of pity for those non-Buddhists who do not comprehend the ultimate truth and seek a divergent liberation.
There are four aspects of true liberation; by presenting the correct, the erroneous is revealed. First, "being free from all marks of suffering" refers to the quality of bliss in *nirvāṇa*.

Second, the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the quality of permanence (*nitya*). Third, the characteristic of being free from flux (*anāsrava*) is the quality of purity (*śubha*).
Fourth, the supramundane (*lokottara*) characteristic is the quality of self (*ātman*). As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Mastery and detachment regarding worldly phenomena is called 'self'.

Regarding the statement that those conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are suffering, this distinguishes the false from the correct. In the four subsequent sections of the scripture, each is assigned one of these meanings; now, in this [passage]:
Initially, it was stated that suffering follows one even unto the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

By citing these three types of suffering, [the text] reveals that for those non-Buddhists who seek the state of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth as *nirvāṇa*, the Bodhisattva observes that these are all phenomena of the twelve links of dependent origination characterized by the three types of suffering.
How, then, could there be any meaning of the quality of bliss in *nirvāṇa*? Therefore, he gives rise to compassion accordingly. (4) This is the fourth point concerning the one.
Regarding the discernment of the wisdom of all characteristics, this constitutes the seventh [category].

As for those who enter contemplation through faith—whether they possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or do not—the Śrāvakas who fail to perceive the subtle are said to have overweening pride because they claim for themselves that there is no suffering; yet they do perceive gross suffering.
This is called "not being overweening. By citing this, it refers to the subtle suffering of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) through which those of the two vehicles enter the Mahāyāna.
Because the Bodhisattva illuminates this, it is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). "Not knowing it as it truly is" explains below the characteristics of pride (*māna*).

This single section previously relied on great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to convert non-Buddhists; now it relies on great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) to gather in those of the two vehicles. Thus, according to the text:
This is because [the text] emphasizes the correct grasping of the meaning.

Regarding the eighth [link], the dependent origination of formations (*saṃskāra*), there are likewise four sections. The first concerns the scriptural text; in reality, however, ignorance (*avidyā*) is considered in relation to formations.
Regarding the meaning of "absence of causes and conditions" while stating that "conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions," there are two interpretations.

First, taking one's own seeds as the cause and ignorance as the condition, they are spoken of collectively as "causes and conditions. However, because the direct seeds are concealed and this predominant condition is highlighted, it is called "ignorance as the cause and condition.
Second, those [seeds] serve as the predominant condition; yet, in relation to their own predominant fruit, they remain the direct cause. Therefore...

It is taught that ignorance is the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*); the same applies to the others. This is intended to clarify that effects do not arise of themselves but must proceed from causes, and that these causal conditions, being mutually dependent, are each devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, to say they are "produced by causes and conditions" is precisely to reveal their non-arising (*anutpāda*).

This can be understood through the simultaneous cessation of both forward and reverse contemplation, wherein neither arising nor non-arising exists. Second, regarding the section on wearying detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*):

Within the six gates of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is the sixth, called "Profound Contemplation" (*gambhīra-vipaśyanā*). Within this profound contemplation, the final three gates are subsumed to form four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, not self-arising; second, not arising from another; third, not arising from both; and fourth, not arising without cause.

Regarding the explanation of these four propositions, various treatises differ; briefly, there are three interpretations. The first concerns the refutation of non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), namely:

Because all phenomena do not arise from their own intrinsic nature, they are said to be "not self-arisen. Second, because they do not arise from Brahmā, Maheśvara, or other such [deities], they are said to be "not from another.
Third, because they also do not arise from the aggregation of atoms at the beginning of a kalpa, they are said to be "not co-arisen.
Fourth, because they do not arise without a cause—since there is no resultant phenomenon apart from causes and conditions—they are said to be "not causelessly arisen. Second, with respect to...
"Causes and conditions exclude [independent] form. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Because it exists from its own seeds, it does not arise from another;
because it depends on various conditions, it is not self-made; because it lacks [independent] activity, it is not co-arisen; because it possesses functional capacity, it is not causeless.

Generally, regarding all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is already profoundly deep when one discards the two extremes of suffering alone; how much more so when one discards all four positions [of the tetralemma]. Therefore, dependent origination is the most profound of all. Third, in terms of...

This is the gate of unimpeded dependent origination. Although fruits arise from causes and conditions, when causes and conditions are viewed in relation to one another, each possesses two meanings: first, being entirely efficacious;
second, being entirely non-efficacious. That is to say, when a cause is viewed in relation to its fruit, it may be entirely non-productive, whereas a condition necessarily produces entirely.

1. Because that which arises from conditions does not arise without a cause. 2. Regarding the relationship between the two conditions and the fruit: since the conditions do not produce the fruit entirely, while the cause must produce it entirely, how can one say that the conditions do not produce it?
It is because they arise from their own respective causes. 3. Because these two powers do not coexist, they do not produce [the fruit] together. 4.

Because these two lack power and likewise do not coexist, there is no arising without a cause. As for the statement, "With ignorance as a causal condition, volitional formations arise," the treatise and the sūtra state:
"Ignorance conditions the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This demonstrates that the cause gives rise to the effect, clarifying that [the effect] is not produced by another.

To say that "conditions can produce volitional formations" clarifies that the effect arises from its cause, showing it is not self-produced. Furthermore, because ignorance is the specific cause of volitional formations, they are not produced by another;
nor are they self-produced, because prior to their existence, the substance of the formations does not exist within ignorance, yet they subsequently arise from it. The same applies to the others.
It is also thus; reflect upon this accordingly. Within this section, the Master of the Treatise opens it into two phrases: "not by oneself" and "not by another.

Third, regarding the analysis based on great compassion: it clarifies that among the various non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation, what they seek—such as the Heaven of Non-perception—is revealed to be nothing other than the phenomena of dependent origination consisting of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); it is not [true liberation].

Unconditioned nirvāṇa is the nature of permanence; therefore, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion accordingly. Fourth, regarding the analysis according to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*):
within the nine gates, the eighth and ninth gates are combined into one, the "contemplation of beginninglessness.

Master Yuan says: "This is the contemplation of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because one sees that the collection of conditions for phenomena has no inherent nature, it is called [the contemplation of beginninglessness]."

"Beginningless. The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "The dharmas arising through causes and conditions have no original source; they arise based upon this [sourcelessness], and thus are called 'beginningless.

This is the same as what is taught in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where all dharmas are established based on the 'root of non-abiding' (*anālaya-mūla*). Regarding the phrase 'because it arises in the middle, it arises in the end':
this cites a dharma to provide an explanation. That is to say, this dependent origination is itself non-arising; therefore, it is called beginningless. This is the meaning.
This refers to the dharmas known by great wisdom.

Regarding the ninth [topic], the bondage of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-bandhana*), there are likewise four gates. First, concerning the sūtra’s statement that "ignorance conditions formative forces" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) as the bondage of arising and ceasing:
this means that these ten [links] look toward one another such that, in forward order, they give rise to one another, while in reverse order, they cease one another. However, as for their arising...

It ceases together with [the arising]. One does not escape the bondage of existence and non-existence. If one contemplates that the arising of marks is non-arising, then cessation is likewise non-cessation;

only then is one liberated from bondage. This is the intended meaning of the sutra. In the text, the contemplation in accordance with the flow (*anuloma*) is first clarified, and following the phrase "without cessation," the contemplation against the flow (*pratiloma*) is clarified.
This can be understood. Second, regarding the profound contemplation of the four gates based on wearying detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is the third unique [point of] non-action.

As for the statement that "it is not produced by both self and other," it may mean that the cause is taken as self and the conditions as other, or that the effect is taken as self and the causes and conditions as other;
since these two—self and other—both do not produce it, if neither self nor other produces it, how could it come to be?

Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): in order to resolve this doubt, it is said that [things] merely "accord with arising. This means that while arising is spoken of according to worldly convention, in ultimate reality there is no arising.
As for the statement that there is "no cognition," this is precisely because causes and conditions depend upon one another;

each lacks its own independent capacity to act, yet they can function in conjunction. How could there not be the accomplishment of an effect? At the very moment of accomplishment, there is no accomplishment; therefore, it is called "the time of acting."

Third, regarding the classification according to Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): This refers to those non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation, taking the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" state and so forth to be *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhisattva observes that these are merely links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) and do not involve freedom from the bonds of defilement;
because they have lost the true, pure three virtues of *nirvāṇa*, Great Compassion arises. Therefore, it is said: "In this way, further defilement gives rise to bondage. Fourth, concerning the one...

In the gate of the analytical wisdom of all characteristics (*sarva-lakṣaṇa-jñāna-vibhaṅga-mukha*) within the beginningless contemplation, it is called "conforming to bondage" (*anuloma-bandhana*). This means that arising and ceasing are merely bondage because they conform to what is without foundation.

In the tenth, the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence (*niḥsvabhāva-kṣaya-darśana*), there are likewise four gates. The first, based on the sūtra, clarifies that these links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) are empty appearances.

Having exhausted all conformity with the object of non-existence, one reaches the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This reveals that while not destroying the conventional, one remains eternally in the true.
Thus it is said: "With ignorance as a condition, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise. This is conformity with non-existence. Question:
Since the arising of formative forces from ignorance conforms to existence, why is it said to conform to non-existence? Answer: By following the sequence of the formative forces, one arrives at...
This demonstrates that when ignorance is about to produce the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), one immediately accords with non-arising and enters into principle.
Question: Since the forward contemplation is thus, what is the reverse? Answer: Since arising is by nature exhausted, one is detached from both existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is said to "accord with non-existence. Exhaustively contemplate this. Second, regarding the detachment from the conditioned, this is called the fourth [stage].

It is not that it is produced without cause, for it accords with existence (*bhava*). Why, then, is it called "accordance with existence" (*anuloma-bhava*) in the treatise when the sutra speaks of "accordance with non-existence" (*anuloma-abhava*)?

The intention of the sutra is explained by returning to the principle through conditions; the intention of the treatise is explained by following the characteristics from their nature. Each clarifies a distinct meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, the sense of "accordance with existence" within the treatise reveals non-arising (*anutpāda*); therefore, its intention is no different from that of the sutra. Below follows the specific [explanation].

Regarding the refutation of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), there are three parts: first, the refutation by concession (*abhyupagama-bhaṅga*), meaning that [the effect] would have to arise constantly; second, the refutation by denial (*apavāda-bhaṅga*), meaning that it never arises at all;
third, the refutation by censure (*ākṣepa-bhaṅga*) from "this is not the Dharma" onwards, meaning that asserting causelessness is the greatest of false views.

From "if that were so" onwards, the non-existence of causelessness is concluded. The phrase "thus it is named" concludes the explanation. Regarding the term "characteristic of truth" (*lakṣaṇasatya*): "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of the answers established previously.
Truth (*satya*) is the differentiation of the former two truths. Third, regarding the classification according to that which accords with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

this refers to those non-Buddhists who seek a distinct liberation, taking it to be the self (*ātman*) or the qualities of a self (*guṇa*) as *nirvāṇa*. The Bodhisattva, out of pity for them, gives rise to great compassion.

Fourth, regarding the classification according to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): this is the ninth, called "various observations," which refers to the totality of the three realms of existence.
"Various" (*nānāvidha*) refers to the many distinct types of forms. The subsequent section provides an exegesis to clarify their characteristics;

these are the mundane objects of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Because great wisdom illuminates these, they serve as the "gateways. The preceding section concludes the individual explanations of the ten gateways.

Second, the phrase "In this way, [regarding] the inverse and direct order" below summarizes the ten chapters. Since it speaks of "ten kinds of inverse and direct," it is clear that the preceding ten gateways are being referred to.
Within [these] there are both reverse and direct [contemplations]. That the preceding text did not include the reverse contemplation was because it was abbreviated.

[The nine aspects are: first, distinct practices; second, subsuming [them] into the one mind; third, the mutual generation of functional powers; fourth, the mutual connection of preceding and succeeding;

fifth, the revolving cycle of the three paths; sixth, cause and effect across the three periods of time; seventh, the faults of the three types of suffering; eighth, the lack of intrinsic nature in causes; ninth, appearing as if existent.

If they do not exist, the ten [perfections] are extinguished and identical in equality; this can be seen by correlating them with the preceding ten passages. The explanation of the practice of the non-abiding path is complete.

In the third major section, regarding the excellence of that fruit, there are two parts: first, clarifying the excellence of that fruit; second, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva dwells... [and so forth].

From this "Stage of Presence" (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*) downward, the fruits of the stages are clarified. Within the preceding *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, these are divided into five parts: 1. Attaining the practice of remedies and the removal of hindrances;

this is the fruit of the remedy for the aforementioned pride of superiority. 2. From the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s great compassion increases further," one attains the excellence of practice;
this is the fruit of the non-abiding path of practice mentioned previously. 3. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva abides... [text continues].

In this Abhimukhī-bhūmi (the Ground of Presence), one attains entry into the lower [stages] and acquires superior samādhis. These are described as the fruit in comparison to the superior remedies of the preceding stage;
that is to say, while the three doors of liberation were cultivated previously as the remedies, those remedies now increase further.

Furthermore, when the four classes of Buddha-sons dwell in this Abhimukhī-bhūmi, they again attain the superiority of an indestructible mind. This is described as the fruit in comparison to the removal of obstacles in the preceding stage, due to the cessation of those obstacles.
Therefore, the mind of samādhi is indestructible. The five Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas, by means of this mind, descend in accordance with the Buddha’s bodhi;
this clarifies that they have attained the superior power of mastery (*vaśitā*). That is to say, compared to the preceding mind of cultivation, it is called the "basis for the fruit-dharma.
The unimpeded advancement beyond the preceding cultivation is termed the "power of mastery. The explanation of these five fruits is divided into five sections.
In the first section of the text, there are two parts: the first clarifies the excellence of the remedy, and the second, beginning with "The bodhisattva thus," reveals the abandonment of hindrances.

Within the former, there are three sections concerning the meaning of the gates of liberation, analyzed through five categories: (1) defining the essence, (2) explaining the names, (3) the remedies for hindrances, (4) the inclusion of practices, and (5) the distinctions.

Regarding the first, the essence: it takes as its nature the previously mentioned meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and teachings that destroy [afflictions]. Regarding the second, the explanation of the names, there are two parts.
First, the names are established; second, the names are explained. Within the first [section], the former is general while the latter is specific. Regarding the former general [explanation]:

"liberation" (*vimokṣa*) is the general name, which refers to *nirvāṇa* as the state of transcendence. "Gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of "expedient means. This means that this meditative gate is the preliminary expedient for *nirvāṇa*;

thus, it is designated as a "gate of liberation" by forming a possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*). If one speaks generally of the "three gates of liberation," it is explained by attaching the numeral (*dvigu* or *bahuvrīhi*).

Regarding the subsequent distinctions: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and non-self (*anātman*) within the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) are termed the "emptiness gate" (*śūnyatā-mukha*).
The four aspects within the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are termed the "signless gate" (*animitta-mukha*). The remaining ten aspects are termed the "wishless" (*apraṇihita*).

According to the Mahāyāna, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) arising from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is termed "emptiness. The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that takes this as its object is termed the "emptiness liberation" (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*).
The "gate of liberation through signlessness" (animitta-vimokṣa-mukha): "Signs" refers to the ten signs, namely form, sound, odor, taste, touch, male, female, birth, old age, and death.
Because nirvāṇa is devoid of these phenomenal characteristics, it is called "signless. The samādhi that takes this as its object is named the "gate of liberation through signlessness.

"Vow" (praṇidhāna) refers to seeking or aspiring. By contemplating the suffering of the three realms, one has nothing left to seek or aspire for; thus, it is called "wishless" (apraṇihita). The samādhi that takes this as its object—

It is called the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). This is explained in detail as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To know that the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of all stages is ultimately empty is called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

Having known this emptiness, not to contemplate whether phenomena are empty or not empty, existent or non-existent, and so forth, is called the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). This is because one knows that all things are devoid of marks."

Not accepting and not clinging to any phenomena is called the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*). Furthermore, the eighteen kinds of emptiness are called the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Not seeking after the various modes of existence with the mind is called the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Regarding the characteristics of all phenomena...

Knowing destruction and not recollecting it is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*). Regarding the explanation of its name: the first [of the three gates] is named according to the practice of liberation and its dissolution;
the latter two are both designated based on the absence of other perceptions. The analysis according to other categories is as found in the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Chapter on Separate Practice).

Within this section, there are two parts. First, it generally demonstrates that all ten preceding sections on the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) possess these three gates of emptiness contemplation.

Second, from "knowing there is no self" (*anātman*) onwards, it specifically demonstrates them. Within this demonstration, the gate of emptiness is clarified first. This treatise is divided into three parts.

The first three phrases clarify that the substance of arising is empty. Regarding the phrase "knowing there is no self": because the subject is non-existent, there is no person. "Person" (*pudgala*) takes the sense of abiding in the present as its meaning.
Because that which currently abides cannot be apprehended, there is no life-span (*jīvitendriya*). "Life-span" has the meaning of encompassing what follows;
thus, when one examines the encompassing of this present life-span by a subsequent life-span, it cannot be apprehended.

The first two lines [of the verse] regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) reveal the emptiness of the essence of phenomena (*dharma-bhāva*). The latter two lines regarding the absence of an agent and an experiencer reveal the prior birth.

Regarding the application of emptiness within the Dharma, it is attained accordingly; the names of the meditative seals (*mudrā*) may be understood from this. Second, regarding the phrase "extinguishing these phenomena," this clarifies the gate of signlessness (*animitta*), which also possesses three meanings.

First, as for "extinguishing obstacles": because one contemplates that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is extinguished, it is said that "these phenomena are extinguished.

Question: What is the difference between this and the previous [gate of] selflessness (*anātman*)? Answer: The former clarifies selflessness by way of all phenomena (*dharma*); here, however, one wishes to...
It differs [from the previous state] because it dispels the mind that grasps at signs. Second, regarding the attainment of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*):

the treatise quotes the Sūtra as saying, "Constant liberation is manifest," and the Sūtra says, "Abiding in ultimate liberation. Third, regarding the non-occurrence of the characteristics of recollection and mindfulness (*smṛti-vyāpāra*):

because one sees the locus of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), not even the slightest characteristic of a dharma can arise; thus it is said, "The others do not continue. Yuan (Yuǎn) says: "Among these three, the first is cessation."

Regarding "obstructions": first, the grasping at intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) ceases; second, taking the principle as the antidote; third, the mind that grasps at characteristics (*nimitta*) is extinguished because not even the slightest dharma is seen to arise.
Thus, one is free from the discriminating mind that grasps at characteristics. The former cessation of grasping at intrinsic nature distinguishes this from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

the present freedom from grasping at characteristics distinguishes this from those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Third, from "knowing this" onwards, the Gate of Wishlessness (*apraṇihita-mukha*) is clarified, which also has three parts. The first two are as follows: [End of excerpt]

1. Because it is the basis for wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), it is called the "support" (*āśraya*). 2. Because it reveals wishlessness by showing a lack of delight in existence (*bhava*), it is called the "essential nature" (*svabhāva*). 3.

Because it is superior to the two vehicles (*yāna*) by taking great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth as its object, it is called "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*). Second, regarding the clarification of being free from obstacles, there are two parts.

First, "being free from that self and so forth" refers to what is abandoned by the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Second, "being free from the mark of existence" refers to what is abandoned by the signless (*animitta*).

Furthermore, regarding the third [aspect], "separation from the markless" (*animitta*): because it is that which is separated from the wishless (*apraṇihita*), it is said to be "separated from the marks of existence.
Since one does not grasp at the markless, it is called "wishless"; because the mind is markless, there is nothing to be wished for or sought. The *Śāstra* states: "In this sequential order..."
Below the first five stages, the inferior is raised to manifest the superior. First, the five stages are raised to manifest the superiority of this gate of emptiness in being free from self.
This text is inverted; it should correctly state: "By means of the ten profound and pure minds of equality, one remains far removed.
That is to say, one remains far removed from the pride of bodily purity in the fourth stage, because one employs profound emptiness to extinguish those two types of self. This is the superiority.
Second, the four stages (*bhūmi*) are cited to demonstrate the departure from hindrances; in this text, the superiority of being free from agent and recipient is emphasized.

Third, these six stages and others cite the ten equalities at the beginning of this stage to refute existence, non-existence, and so forth, thereby manifesting the fulfillment of the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*) in the present stage.
It dispels existence and non-existence because all aggregates are exhausted; it is called "supreme" because it is preeminent.

Regarding the second [section], which clarifies the excellence of practice, there are two parts: first, the actual practice; second, the subsequent passage beginning with "immediately attains," which clarifies the excellence of practice.
The preceding section has two parts. First, it clarifies courageous practice; second, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva, observing in this manner, is a "great man" (*puruṣa*) who practices.
Regarding "courageous practice," it means that one’s initial cultivation is uninterrupted. Regarding "the great man who practices," it means that the fruit is decisively cultivated to completion.

Within the first of these two parts, there are two further sections: first, the mind of practice, which refers to observing those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) through the three types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and [second], compassion.
Because sentient beings dwell [in saṃsāra] without awakening to it, compassion increases further.

This increase of compassion is the mind that benefits others; that which has not yet fulfilled bodhi and so forth is the mind that benefits oneself. In the following section clarifying the excellence of practice, there are two parts:

first, cultivating wisdom without attachment to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, from "other sentient beings" onwards, cultivating compassion without dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within the former, there are also two parts; first:

[One] knows. Subsequently, one becomes weary. Within this knowledge, there is the presence or absence of the combination and separation of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth; there is increase and decrease.
Once one realizes that these phenomena possess such faults and disadvantages, one immediately gives rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*), thinking, "I must not allow them to combine.

Thus it is said, "I know conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth. The treatise states: "Knowing that conditioned phenomena have many faults, one distances oneself from birth, karma, afflictions, and so on. Below, [one] practices cultivation.
The transformation through compassion can be understood [from this]. Regarding the subsequent passage, it refers to the sequence within the practice of cultivation: first wisdom, then compassion.

Within wisdom, what the treatise calls "contemplation of the counterpart" (*pratipakṣa*)—wherein "the conditioned" is termed the "counterpart"—is a further explanation establishing the contemplation of the many faults [of the conditioned]. As for "extinguishing the counterpart":

Because it clarifies that the nature of the conditioned is extinguished, [the text] speaks of "the absence of nature" and so forth. In the subsequent clarification of the excellence of practice, there are two parts.
First, the manifestation of the excellent characteristics. The treatise states: "Wisdom and great compassion are the excellences that accord with [the path].

This refers back to the two practices mentioned previously, each of which possesses both compassion and wisdom, and is thus able to ascend in accordance [with the goal]. Regarding the phrase "the unimpeded *prajñā* manifests based on the non-abiding path," this clarifies that one relies on the aforementioned compassion.

The path of non-abiding wisdom causes the light of unimpeded gnosis (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) of the Buddha-bhūmi to manifest before one. One realizes the equality of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and nirvāṇa.
Regarding the understanding that wisdom and compassion do not abide [in extremes]: the reason they do not dwell together is to understand the meaning of non-abiding;

that is, because wisdom does not coexist with conditioned phenomena. Thus it is said, "yet it also does not abide," and so forth. Furthermore, compassion does not coexist with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it says, "nor does he dwell therein," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because those practices that assist the path are not yet fulfilled," this explains the purpose for not dwelling:

in order to fulfill the aids to wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*), he does not dwell in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); and in order to fulfill the aids to merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), he does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus it says, "desiring to be fully endowed with," and so forth.

Third, regarding the explanation of the excellence of samādhi, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the concentration on emptiness; second, the manifestation of the other two. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, citing the ten types of emptiness as the primary examples; second, concluding with many categories. Herein, the "ten thousand" mentioned in the treatise refers to what the sūtra calls "hundreds of thousands of millions.

Among the aforementioned ten types of emptiness, the treatise subsumes them into four: first, contemplation, which is the analytical understanding; second, non-negligence, which arises based upon that understanding.

Practice (*caryā*). It is so named because it is free from faults. Third, "attaining supremacy" (*adhipatya-lābha*): through the cultivation of virtues, one attains superior qualities. Fourth, "due to activity" (*vastu-hetuka*): based on these qualities, function arises;
since samādhi is the root of great function, it is therefore called "due to activity. Excluding the fourth samādhi at the beginning, the remaining five are termed "contemplations" (*vipaśyanā*):

first, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); second, the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); third, the combined taking of both.
"Emptiness" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the four reliances, one contemplates them based on the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
because this is the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" among the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbhas, it is called "Great Emptiness. Fifth, one contemplates the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*):

since they do not exist apart from the Tathāgatagarbha, arising only through conjunction and lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called "conjoined emptiness. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The seven consciousnesses are likewise; they arise together through conjunction."
It is further stated that there are eight unimpaired characteristics (*akṣaya-lakṣa� signlessness is itself signless; this is the first. Second, regarding "non-negligence" (*apramāda*):
"discriminating in accordance with cultivation" refers to one's own level (*svabhūmi*), while "cultivating without weariness" refers to superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

Because these two cultivations are fulfilled, they are called "ultimate. Third, regarding "attaining superior merit": because superior virtues arise and manifest based upon emptiness, it is so called.

The emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*). Regarding the four causal factors that distinguish this from the other three samādhis: first, by relying on this concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one purifies the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);

for this reason, it is called "truly departing from delusion" (*yathābhūta-mithyā-viveka*). Second, by relying on emptiness, one gives rise to compassion (*karuṇā*) and does not abandon sentient beings; therefore, the treatise and the sūtra call this "not abandoning emptiness.
Third, by relying on the samādhi of emptiness, one vows to remain within the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) while remaining free from defiled attachment; this is called "detachment."
[This involves] conceptual differentiation; however, in accordance with [the state of] detachment, there is non-differentiation. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Within the section on the four types of attainment of the excellence of the indestructible mind (*akṣobhya-citta*), the ten phrases are divided into two parts: the first one is general, while the remaining nine are specific.

Regarding "the profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*): it is profound, subtle, and difficult to move. In the treatise and the sūtra, "indestructible mind" refers to being firm and non-retrogressive. The first [of the nine] concerns the principle (*tattva*).
1. Faithful contemplation; 2. being capable of receiving training through the two practices; 3. having no fear or terror in one's mind regarding profound and secret teachings;

4. not losing one’s own portion [of practice]; 5. proceeding toward excellence without rest; 6. not envying the virtues of others and not breaking one’s own precepts, because the two practices are universally pure—this is called "vast mind";
7. generating universal benefit through compassion; 8. seeking the wisdom of the higher stages; 9. skillfully transforming sentient beings.

Regarding the third [section] within the fifth power of mastery (*vaśitā-bala*), there are three parts: first, the heading that indicates the arousal of the mind of further exertion once the practice of faith is perfected;

second, the main body which correctly elucidates this through the section beginning with "fulfilling"; and third, the conclusion by the son of the Buddha, beginning with "by means of this," which summarizes it.

Within the heading, the phrase "furthermore" and so forth refers to practicing without weariness. Within the main body, the ten mental states are divided into two: the first is general, and the remaining nine are specific.

Because these are derived from the general [category], they are: first, the power of subduing; second, the power of understanding; third, the power of relinquishing the small; fourth, the power of deep faith; fifth, the power of crushing Māra;
sixth, the power of treating afflictions; seventh, the power of universal treatment; eighth, the power of skillful means for others; ninth, the power of treating obstacles.
This is as revealed in the treatise (*śāstra*); the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) may be understood accordingly.

Below this, the second section clarifies the fruits of the stages (*avasthā-phala*). Among these, the first three fruits are the same as before. Within the first [fruit], "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*), there are three aspects:

within the practice of pliancy, one listens to and receives the true Dharma and practices according to what has been taught. Regarding the phrase in the treatise and the sūtra, "attaining the light of samādhi and wisdom," the commentary explains this by the meaning of "attainment."
"Holding" means being able to practice according to what has been taught. "Based on that" means based on that meaning, one holds to the practice;

therefore, it is said that by relying on this supreme samādhi, one attains *śamatha*. This is the samādhi of reality (*yathābhūta*), which is *vipaśyanā*. It is the supreme practice of the light of wisdom mentioned previously.
Regarding "having practiced and holding [it]," it means being able to maintain that practice. Among those who have trained and purified [themselves], such a person is [described].

"Up to 'luminous and pure'" means that one is liberated from those obscurations; it explains the purification through training because one realizes that meaning. It explains "knowing the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the supremacy of supramundane wisdom within the analogy," this reveals the excellence of the luminous purity of the essence of realized wisdom (*jñāna*), as well as the excellence of its function, thereby manifesting its essence.
Through the excellence of the light of the wisdom of the teaching, it manifests realized wisdom; furthermore, it is supreme.
The passage beginning with "By means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) and so forth" explains the text on the combined metaphors. Unimpeded *prajñā* is the light of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding the two explanations within the purification of the knowledge of the teachings (*śāsana-jñāna-viśuddhi*): because the previous stage took the metaphor of the lunar disk (*candramaṇḍala*), it was small;
this stage takes the metaphor of moonlight (*candraprabhā*), which is superior to the former because it is vast and great. Following the four currents (*catuḥ-srotas*) is the work of Māra.

Because it is cited, it is called the "path of Māra. This is named the Evil Māra; this is that path of Māra. Third, the concluding summary of the names, their mutual inclusion, and the vows and knowledge of retribution are to be understood according to the preceding [sections].
This is the third major section from here on. Within the section consisting of thirty-four verses of the *Saṃgīti* (Repetitive Verses), there are five parts.

First, the initial two verses correspond to the ten superior antidotes to pride regarding the equality of dharmas mentioned previously. Second, there are eleven verses that correspond to the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path (*apratisthita-mārga*).
Among these, first, there is one verse that corresponds to the general contemplation of dependent origination by the mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*). Second, there are two verses.

The first section, on causes and conditions, consists of one verse that sequentially contemplates the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). The second section, on being encompassed by a single mind, consists of one verse. The third section, on the differentiation of one's own karma, consists of one verse.
The fourth section, on not being separated from one another, consists of half a verse. The fifth section, on the non-interruption of the three paths, consists of half a verse.
The sixth section, on the differentiation of the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*), consists of one verse. The seventh section, on the three time periods (*trai-kālya*), consists of one verse.

Section on Differentiation: nine and a half verses praise the contemplation of arising, ceasing, and transformation; ten and a half verses return to praising the eighth contemplation of dependent origination;
eleven verses praise the contemplation of conforming to the exhaustion of non-existence; twelve verses [praise] one verse.

The verses conclude the names of the ten gates. The three sets of four verses praise the excellence of those fruits. Among them, the first two verses praise the excellence of the antidotes mentioned previously;
the next verse praises the excellence of practice; the next half-verse praises the excellence of the indestructible mind;
and the final half-verse praises the excellence of sovereign power. The four sets of four verses concern the fruits of the stages. Among these, the first two verses praise pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

The fruit. The final two verses summarize the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*); the fruit arising from aspiration (*praṇidhānaphala*) is omitted from this summary. The final verse of the fifth [chapter] concludes with a praise of its excellence.
This completes the sixth stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), there are two types of explanation:

first, a detailed analysis; second, an explanation of the text. Within the former, it is briefly distinguished by two gates: first, the explanation of the name; second, the purpose of its inclusion. Regarding the initial explanation of the name, there are briefly three types.
The first is named according to the exhaustion of effortful application (*prayoga*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It reaches the culmination of effortful practice..."
Regarding the phrase "because it is the final stage," Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "In this stage, one attains the ultimate limit of effortful practice (*prayoga*).

Although there is no longer any movement whatsoever, it is still termed 'possessing practice' (*sa-abhisamskāra*) with respect to the signless (*animitta*). Second, regarding the two meanings, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"One is able to enter far into the signless mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is flawless, uninterrupted, and adjacent to the pure stages (*viśuddha-bhūmi*)."

Because it connects [to the next stage], it is called "Far-Reaching" (dūraṃgama). The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "It is without deficiency or interruption; it is far from the preceding six stages, adjacent to the Pure Grounds (*śuddhābhūmi*), and proximate to the subsequent eighth.

Regarding these three points, there are three meanings. The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) says: "It reaches the final limit of effort within the Stage of Signlessness (*animittabhūmi*)."

Because it transcends the two paths of the self within the world, it is called the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūraṃgamā bhūmi*). This is consistent with the explanation in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Because one practices far from the meditative concentrations of liberation—characterized by non-appropriation, continuity, and signless mental application—this stage is pure, unobstructed, and unhindered;
thus it is named the Far-Reaching Stage. The *Vyūha-śāstra* states: "Within the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva, [one is] near..."
The path of the One Vehicle is called "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*). Question: Who goes far? Answer: One who has reached the culmination of effort and skillful means;

because this one can go far, it is named the Stage of Far-Going. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it is distant from the three realms and near to the station of the Dharma King, hence it is the "Body Stage.
The *Renwang jing* names it the "Stage of Far-reaching Attainment," because one has already attained what was far. (2)

Regarding the intent of this [section], there are now three meanings: first, whereas previously it was entrusted to the Two Vehicles, it is now revealed for Bodhisattvas, following a gradual sequence;
second, prior to this stage of signless contemplation (*animitta-darśana*), the preceding ground was not yet pure, whereas here one enters into signlessness through this contemplation;

third, the effort of the preceding ground was not yet fulfilled, whereas here it is fulfilled. Furthermore, there are other methods of analysis as explained in the *Bie xing zhang* (Chapter on Separate Practice).
The subsequent commentary on the text consists of three parts: first, the section of praise and request; second, the section of the formal exposition beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha...";
and third, the section of the summary verses.
Regarding the first part, the praise and request, it consists of twelve verses divided into four sections. The first three verses clarify the offerings and praises; within these, the first two—

The celestial hosts offer precious gifts and praise the Lord of Dharma who expounds the teaching. Subsequently, one celestial king, Fragrant Light (Gandhaprabha), makes offerings to the Buddha; this section consists of two verses.

The third section, consisting of six verses, describes the celestial hosts rejoicing and praising their attainment of hearing the Dharma of the stages (*bhūmi*). It clarifies how the Buddha’s power causes the goddesses to praise the Buddha amidst their music.
Of these, the first verse describes the basis for the praise, while the subsequent five verses properly manifest the words of praise. Within those words, the first verse is as follows:
The first clarifies the three types of action (*trikarma*) of non-abiding practice; the next one clarifies the three types of action of non-grasping practice;

the next one concerns the three types of action for making offerings—the Sanskrit original states that because one has attained mastery over wisdom, the notions of "land," "Buddha," and "self" are all extinguished;

the next two concern the three types of action regarding the two lands; and the final one concerns the three types of action free from faults. The four [sections] contain two verses clarifying the request for the Dharma, within which:

The first [section] concludes the preceding summary and gives rise to the desire for what follows; the latter one praises the assembly and requests the teaching, whereby the mind attains the aspiration to speak with both conceptualization and desire.

Within the second part, the "Section on the Actual Exposition," there are two divisions. First is the clarification of the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*). This treatise is divided into five parts: first, the practice of joy and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

1. The Section on Antidotes; 2. The Section on the Antidotes to Those Obstructions, wherein it is said, "O Sons of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has dwelt in this seventh stage, he enters into the immeasurable...
3. The Section on the Initiation of Practice, wherein it is said, "O Sons of the Buddha, by means of profound wisdom...
4. The Section on the Distinctions of Superiority in the Higher Stages, wherein at that time Vimukticandra asked... 5. For what reason, O Bodhisattva...
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) downwards, this is the section on the differentiation of its fruits. Regarding the first point, "joy and so forth":

within the preceding six stages, attachment to the three emptinesses was termed "joy" and "effortless action" (*anābhoga*). In this stage, one does not cling to emptiness according to its presence; therefore, it is called the "antidote.

This is the cultivation of the dharma of equanimity (*upekṣā*) throughout these stages. Regarding the second point, "its obstacles and so forth": although the joy of the preceding stage was treated during the preparatory practice (*prayoga*), [it remains an obstacle here].
The mind of emptiness, because it possesses measure and effort, is itself an obstacle.
Therefore, at the time of the first stage (bhūmi), one cultivates immeasurable and effortless practice as an antidote; this serves as its name. Third, regarding the three types of practitioners:
Since the stains and hindrances have been removed, the higher contemplations function simultaneously. Regarding "the four [aspects] such as the preceding superior":

the effort (*prayoga*) of this stage surpasses that of the previous six stages and excels that of the subsequent three stages. Regarding "its fruit": because the stage is fulfilled, it is called its fruit, as the preliminary practice has reached its culmination.
Below this, there is a detailed explanation.

Within the first section above, there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding section and raising the subsequent one to encourage entry into practice; second, from "What is it? onwards, the actual manifestation of the characteristics of practice;
third, from "The bodhisattva, by means of such... onwards, the conclusion regarding the efficacy of the practice.

The first two sections [of this chapter] are as follows: First, a general summary of the obstacles to the effortless (*anābhoga*) joy of the preceding stage; second, the cultivation of the lower remedial skillful means.
This involves not abandoning sentient beings, the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) as the antidote, and the undertaking of superior practices (*viśeṣacaryā*).

These serve as the remedy for the arising of a mind that seeks pleasure within effortless practice. Regarding the cultivation of the ten kinds [of equality], this practice cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without being obstructed by emptiness, while practicing existence (*bhava*).
It does not cling to existence. Because it can counteract the practice of dwelling exclusively in the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it is called "skillful means wisdom" (*upāya-prajñā*).

Since it can accomplish the knowledge of this stage, it is said to be the cause of the "excellent path. Furthermore, this practice is the most supreme among all practices that emerged in previous lives, for they are all inferior to this;
thus it is said to be "superior. These correspond respectively to the first, second, and third stages, which are categorized as mundane, while the fourth and fifth [stages] are supramundane.

Because the sixth stage is associated with the supramundane, within the "Correct Manifestation" [section], there is first an interrogation and subsequently an explanation. Within the explanation, there are ten practices (*caryā*), each of which consists of the wisdom of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) as the practice of both the provisional and the real.
The treatise clarifies four kinds of merit that subsume these ten practices into four gates; namely, the first three...

Each individual virtue is distinct, while the latter seven are combined into a single virtue. Within this context, the first phrase, "although one has well cultivated emptiness and so forth," is largely the same as the treatise’s scripture;
however, there is a slight difference regarding the "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) and the "aids to the path" (*bodhipakṣa*).

This initial merit refers to the accumulation of the merit that serves as the superior cause for both wealth and the body, whereby one obtains whatever is required, according to one's wishes, from the causes of wealth and the body.
Therefore, regarding the statement "the matters of the superior causes for wealth and body," this refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).

That is to say, the Bodhisattva’s fruit of inexhaustible wealth and the unimpeded faculty of the body are accomplished through meritorious practices that do not stagnate in quiescence; thus, skillful means is said to be their superior cause.

"Whatever is required is wealth; take this body according to your will," meaning that one may take birth at will. Second, regarding the phrase "even though they have attained the state of all Buddhas," the *Śāstra* (Treatise) states:

"They enter into the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-span, and the absence of a sentient being, yet they do not abandon [compassion], because they give rise to the four immeasurables.
According to the *Śāstra*, the latter explanation differs from this sūtra. That is to say, the intent of this passage is to manifest the realization [of the truth].
One attains the equality of the three wisdoms of the Buddha within one’s own person; yet, this does not obstruct the joy of constantly making offerings to the Buddhas.

The treatise on the sūtra clarifies the matter of guarding against the causes of evil conduct. Attaining supreme and immeasurable cultivation, one does not give rise to deluded actions among sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "guarding against the causes of evil conduct," it refers to the wisdom of skillful means; that is, compassion that does not afflict sentient beings is called "guarding against evil."
Skillful means serve as the cause for this; thus it is so named. Because one gives rise to compassion from within emptiness itself, it is called "non-deluded practice.

This constitutes the second merit. Regarding the third point, "entering the contemplation of emptiness," etc.: herein, [the treatise] first presents the wisdom of emptiness and subsequently the accumulation of merit.

The Sūtra, however, first initiates the accumulation of merit and subsequently contemplates that there is nothing to be grasped. Although the wording differs slightly, the general meaning is the same.

This is the third merit: namely, the matter of protecting the roots of goodness. Because one attains that superior cause as a dominant influence, there is the practice of the higher stages of meritorious dharmas through the practice of the pāramitās;
that is to say, one protects and upholds the roots of goodness by means of skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

It causes [the roots of virtue] to grow; therefore, it serves as the cause. The following clarifies the initiation of superior practice. The phrase "attaining that superior cause as the dominant condition" cites what precedes to introduce what follows.
The phrase "the increase of merit and so forth" correctly reveals the superior characteristics. Thus, it says "extensively gathering" and so on.

According to the Master’s judgment, the first three lines concern practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*), while the latter seven lines concern practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha*). Therefore, they are the same.
This is called the matter of gathering sentient beings through causes. In all cases, skillful means-wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) serves as the cause for gathering beings.

Among the seven [points], the first—here translated as "although he remains far removed," etc.—refers to taking birth in accordance with the needs of beings. The next two refer to causing others to leave behind obstacles; the final four refer to gathering them and establishing them in goodness.

Regarding the first of these, because he takes birth through the power of his vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*) to act as their leader, it is said that he "adorns the three realms" (*traidhātuka-alaṃkāra*). This is from the *Śāstra* version of the Sūtra.
It is said: "Because it adorns the practices of the three realms. Why is he alone made the head? Because he leads sentient beings along, following them to receive transformation.

Second, he ultimately causes them to leave the hindrance of afflictions by teaching the remedies. As for the wisdom that cuts off delusions, one necessarily does not perceive any delusion that could be cut off;
therefore, he ultimately extinguishes the flames of all afflictions. This is precisely what is meant here.
Regarding the first, it is because the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) are precisely the aspect of what is to be severed; for there is no mutual obstruction between what is severed and what is not.
Regarding the second, although it is said that one knows all phenomena to be like illusions and so forth, this is to cause one to depart from the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the third, although one knows all lands and so forth, this clarifies that for the sake of sentient beings, one gathers and arises within the Dharma assemblies to adorn the lands. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Although one knows all Buddha-lands and..."
While sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land and teaches and transforms all sentient beings; this is explained in the same way.

Regarding the fifth point, "knowing that the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is equal," [it means that] for the sake of beings, the primary retribution (vipākaphala) manifests as the three karmas. First, one distinguishes one's own karma. If the Dharma is free from marks, why does it manifest form?
It is for five conditions through which one brings about the merit of transformative birth (*nirmāṇa*) for sentient beings: first, seeing; second, hearing; third, intimacy...

[The Buddha] is proximate. [This is because he possesses] (1) the four offerings; (2) the practice of receiving the Dharma; and (3) the knowledge of all Buddhas and so forth, whereby his verbal activity functions to turn the wheel of Dharma;

(4) the conformity to all Buddhas and so forth, whereby his mental activity realizes distinctions such that even over a long period of time it does not depart from a single thought-moment, yet it does not obstruct various distinct explanations according to the capacities of beings. The third point is a summary of these superior capabilities, which may be understood. Thus far.

This explains "excellence. Below, it explains "skillful means wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*). The treatise states: "These ten initiations of superior practice are collectively opposed" clarifies that they are collectively opposed by skillful means wisdom;
that is, while not clinging to names within emptiness, this is the skillful means wisdom, and the existence of names within emptiness itself is the superior practice.
Now, explaining that skillful means wisdom "appropriates and counteracts" clarifies that one arises in existence without obstructing emptiness.

Because it involves practice, this state of having practice is able to counteract the mind that delights in emptiness. It is said to be "comprehended" because it is subsumed under the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
Below, the sūtra is cited in brief; the first two phrases are presented as a contrast, while the remainder are all equal to them.
In the second section, which clarifies the remedies for those obstacles, there are two aspects: first, the cultivation of immeasurable varieties;
and second, the clarification that this non-action is mindfulness, which explains the cultivation of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).

Regarding "the various kinds of immeasurables practiced in the first stage": because the limited nature of the remedies for attachment acts as an obstacle, the immeasurables are cultivated as the antidote.

Regarding "the practice of effortless cultivation in the subsequent stage": because the effortful application of mental attention (*manasikāra*) in cultivating the remedies for attachment acts as an obstacle, effortless cultivation is practiced as the antidote.
This first clarifies how twenty phrases are subsumed within the cultivation of the immeasurables.
There are ten pairs. Within each pair, the object to be followed is first clarified, followed by the capacity for following.

According to the treatise, these ten pairs of practice are subsumed within six phrases; the term "entry" (入) in all cases signifies "following" (隨), meaning the activity of one who is capable of following through transformation.
Because they are taught according to those who are to be converted, all are said to "enter. Regarding the first pair, it says:
"The realm of sentient beings and the teachings of all Buddhas," and so forth; this refers to what is performed according to circumstances. As for which sentient beings are benefited:
it means that within the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, they are taught by means of immeasurable karmic activities. This is also a general statement. The second pair states: "The world..."

Regarding the phrase "encompassing the pure lands of all Buddhas," this refers to the passage through which sentient beings pass; that is, it causes them to rely upon the practice of pure lands within immeasurable worlds.
There are three pairs of two [meanings]. By what kind of wisdom? First, it is said to be the wisdom of the Buddhas' manifest awakening to the various differentiated phenomena.
Second, it is said to be the wisdom of the Buddhas' realization of the three periods of time throughout the enumeration of kalpas.

"Et cetera" means that because one awakens through the wisdom of the immeasurable and manifold *dharmadhātu*, one penetrates the three periods of time throughout immeasurable eons, and likewise enters into the awakening of wisdom.
Regarding the four pairs and eight classes [of noble ones], by what kind of mind is this meant? It refers to:

first, the mind that perceives how sentient beings, with their various differences in faith and understanding, delight in the manifestation of the Buddhas' various names, forms, and bodies; and second, the mind that perceives the desires and inclinations of sentient beings.
Regarding the various faculties and the various languages of the Buddhas: it means that there are sentient beings who believe in various deities;

because [the Buddha] acts in accordance with their conduct and speaks in accordance with their beliefs, he knows the past mental habits and whether their faculties are dull, medium, or sharp, and thus teaches the Dharma as is appropriate for them.
The fifth consists of one pair. By what practice? It refers to the various mental activities of sentient beings;
the Buddhas, through their vast wisdom and virtue, fully understand these and teach the appropriate remedies according to the minds of sentient beings.

This one may belong to the internal benefit within the first three categories of mind. The sixth consists of three pairs. What vehicle is established here? It refers to faith within the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

First, the penetration of the Buddhas' wisdom, which causes beings to have faith and understanding. Second, faith and understanding among Pratyekabuddhas, because the Buddhas cause them to enter by teaching the gate of profound wisdom.
Third, the skillful practice of Bodhisattvas, because the Buddhas cause Bodhisattvas to enter by teaching the matters of the Mahāyāna compendium;
that is to say, within the three vehicles, they respectively transport and establish beings according to their needs.
In the subsequent section on effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), there are two parts: first, the clarification of the skillful means of contemplative understanding;

second, the formal manifestation of cultivation, beginning with the passage "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... The former also has two parts: first, citing that among the immeasurable practices, the immeasurable spheres of all Buddhas are to be known;
second, from the passage "I am deluded" onwards, the arousal of the mind that seeks [enlightenment]. Within this, regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), the treatise states:

The Sūtra says, "Spontaneous; not by means of discrimination, etc. The Commentary explains: "Spontaneous" means that because the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is free from discrimination regarding conditions.
This refers to the state of effortless application (*anābhoga-citta*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, which is called "spontaneous" and so forth.

Because it is able to give rise to virtuous conduct through its pure reliance on nature, it is called "self-nature. One practices by relying on that power capable of giving rise to the realm of the Buddha. Therefore, one cultivates [it].

Discriminating mind cannot eliminate conditions and so forth; thus, it fails to illuminate the *dharmadhātu*. It must rely on non-discrimination and non-apprehension of signs, which is precisely what is meant by "effortlessness" (*anābhoga*).
Later, within the section on "Correct Practice," regarding the cultivation of "skillful wisdom" (*upāya-prajñā*), this refers to the ten types of skillful knowledge mentioned previously.
Why was it considered an obstacle before, yet now serves as its remedy? It is said that there are two ways in which obstacles are remedied.

There are two types [of obstacles]: first, defilement is the obstacle and purity is the remedy; second, the arising of practice is the obstacle and the maturation of practice is the remedy. Here, the latter explanation is adopted.
The former refers to the initial stage of cultivation, where one exerts effort to give rise to functional application; therefore, it constitutes an obstacle.

In this present section, because the cultivation has reached a state of pure maturity, it constitutes the remedy. This is because it is a cultivation that is free from effort (*anābhoga*), and thus it differs from the eighth stage. It abides peacefully...
"Moving" means that one's practice is firm and non-retrogressive; it is not the same as the "immovability of effort" found in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

Within the third section, "The Division on the Undertaking of Practice," there are four parts: first, the uninterrupted undertaking of practice; second, the superiority of faith, indicated by the phrase "constantly not abandoning";
third, the ability to accomplish great benefit for sentient beings, indicated by the phrase "this bodhisattva, in every thought-moment"; and fourth, the ten *pāramitās* of the Buddha-sons.

The following clarifies the distinctions among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). The Master of the Treatise concludes this great meaning with a summary verse, which seems misplaced within the section on the factors of enlightenment.

Why is this? If these ten perfections (*pāramitā*) were subsumed under the factors of enlightenment, then the "great meaning" should also be called a factor of enlightenment, as both consist of the ten perfections.
Nevertheless, for the time being, we shall follow the Master’s arrangement; among these four sections, the first concerns the "self-nature" (*svabhāva*).

The latter three are the stages of superior progress. The first refers to the internal realization where the practice has matured and both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* manifest together; this is called the "arising of the two practices. The external cultivation being constant and continuous is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).

Within the former [the uninterrupted], there are three parts. The first clarifies that the manifestation of the two practices occurs without obstruction within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). As the treatise says: "Within a single thought-moment..."
Because the two practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā are present before one, in the stage of these two practices, it is clearly understood that the two practices arise continuously and constantly.
The treatise states: "In all practices, when practicing them, they proceed without interval, without interruption, and without cessation.
"Without interruption" means they do not completely stop; "without cessation" means they do not temporarily rest or abandon them. Third, up to...
In dreams and so forth, it is clarified that one leaves evil and dwells in goodness.
Second, regarding "superior faith": the initial arising of faith is termed "superior" because it is decisive toward what is above. The treatise states:

"Because within that immeasurable wisdom, the marks of the distinct meanings of adornment appear before one, and one maintains exclusive mindfulness. This refers to [the mind] following whatever the Buddha manifests in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Object: Because of focused attention, it is said that one "never abandons such recollection.

Third, regarding "being able to accomplish great benefit": based on faith, one initiates practice; this practice possesses purposeful benefit, and because this superior benefit is called "great cultivation" (mahābhāvanā), it is termed "accomplishment.
Within this, there are two parts: first, a general statement; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "Why is this so? In the detailed explanation, first—
