"Because its intrinsic nature is undefiled. The characteristic of being produced by illusion is the "causal characteristic," because it arises through the power of the vows of the bodhisattvas.
Do you not know that these two are the minds of bodhisattvas who have realized and attained faith on the stages (*bhūmi*)? Now, I shall provide an auxiliary explanation: namely, this very mind...
Regarding all such dharmas: their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while their nature (*svabhāva*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because one has not yet reached ultimate realization that [the unconditioned] is neither identical to nor different from the conditioned, this lack of correct faith is called "practice" (*caryā*). If one reverses this, there is complete realization.
This is to be free from improper faith; it is not called "practice.
Within the second section, the detailed explanation according to chapters, there are eleven parts.

Regarding the first, "knowing the dense forest of the mind," there are three sections: first, a general heading in a single sentence; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "That is to say"; third, [the illustrative example] beginning with "Just as..."

This is the concluding summary. Regarding the term "various" mentioned in the heading: if briefly indicated, there are ten types; if extensively analyzed, there are hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions.
Within this, the fact that each one is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the meaning of "aspect" (*ākāra*).

Among the specific [categories], while the treatise and the sūtra have nine, they are subsumed into eight to result in ten phrases; these can further be subsumed into nine, namely: the first eight each constitute one, and the latter...
The second is made into one. Yuan [Hui] said: "Among the eight, the first four are the deluded mind (*vibhrama-citta*), and the latter four are the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
This judgment is not definitive. Why is this so? It is because among the three [stages], the stage of non-destruction is not merely deluded;

the fourth is the perception of formlessness, for the *Śāstra* states it is "the characteristic of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*) and also states it is "by virtue of the intrinsically pure mind" (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*). Furthermore, the sixth and seventh [stages] are not defiled...

"Because of defilement" and "because of the refinement of the mind"—these two phrases manifest the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*). The eighth phrase, "because it follows the Path," manifests the arising of defilement. The commentary states:

"When examined in detail, the distinction between the real and the false is clarified. Regarding the nine [phrases], the first is called "arising in a mixed manner" because its characteristics are mixed;
that is to say, the eight consciousnesses have distinct objects of perception, which is termed "mixed. "Mixed" implies differentiation, and they arise simultaneously.

Because they arise as names, the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are distinguished into six types; that is, by way of the mind, the intellect, and the six consciousnesses.

The differences and similarities among the mind, intellect, and consciousness are to be understood as explained elsewhere. Second, regarding "swift transition" as the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):

this refers to the flux of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). These conditioned phenomena arise and perish in each moment (*kṣaṇa*). Since their transition is already swift upon the cessation of a single [moment], how much more so for a single *kṣaṇa*, which furthermore possesses nine [sub-moments].

"One hundred births and deaths" refers to the ultimate limit of this rapid transformation. Regarding "the three [aspects of] disintegration and non-disintegration": the preceding phrase reveals that the active mind (saṃskāra-citta) is called "disintegrating" because it rapidly transforms;

this phrase reveals that when the active mind is actually undergoing transformation through the characteristics of arising and so forth, both the transformer and the transformed are unobtainable, and thus it is called "non-disintegrating.
This phrase was originally omitted from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (the *Lun jing*), as it is present in both the complete edition and the Jin translation.
The ten phrases previously cited are subsumed into nine by this treatise; it is in this way that it differs from ancient expositions.
"The four formless [qualities] are the characteristic of the ultimate truth" means that when one contemplates that mind as being apart from the mind, neither mind nor body can be apprehended.
"The five boundlessnesses are the specific characteristic" means that they accord with the grasping of immeasurable objects; that is to say, the mind follows after objects without limit.
Taking [this up], it is possible only through the mind; therefore, it is called "self. Sixth, "purity is the non-defilement of self-nature" means that its fundamental nature is pure.
Seventh, "stain and stainlessness are the same, yet afflictions and the absence of afflictions are different" means that although it is within the bonds of entanglement, it is not defiled.
Eighth, "bondage and non-bondage are the same, yet latent tendencies and the absence of latent tendencies are different" means that the mind and greed...

They are associated and share the same object of craving; because the object binds the mind, they are called "identical latent tendencies" (*samāna-anuśaya*). That which is contrary to this is called "non-identical latent tendencies.
Other latent tendencies and other bonds should be understood accordingly. The final two phrases are combined to form the ninth phrase.

Regarding the statement that "that which is produced by illusion, arising in accordance with the various realms of existence, shares the same causal characteristic": this refers to the Bodhisattva’s taking birth through the power of compassion and vows, as opposed to others.
Sentient beings are born according to their physical karma; these two types of mind that take birth are both causes for inducing future retribution.
However, the Bodhisattva does not seek a place of birth for his own sake, but only wishes to be born wherever there is benefit and happiness for sentient beings.
Since such birth is not fixed, the location manifests in accordance with conditions; therefore, it is said to be "created by illusion," unlike the case of other sentient beings.
All births follow one’s own karma; because karma is not separated from its bonds, one is said to be born according to the various realms of existence (*gati*).

Second is the knowledge of the dense forest of the activities of the afflictions (*kleśa*). The structure of the text is the same as before, consisting of three parts. Within the detailed explanation, there are nine phrases which the treatise subsumes into three groups:
the first two each constitute one group, and the latter seven constitute the third group. Regarding the first of these, "that which has followed for a long time": this refers to—

Because it penetrates far as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). According to the Hīnayāna school, it is said that the final limit of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is the stage of the Peak of Existence.

However, according to the Mahāyāna school, up until the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), one speaks only of the realms (*dhātu*); it is not the case that the afflictions of the faculties or stages constitute the final limit.

This applies generally to both the Great and Small [Vehicles], and there is no contradiction in principle. Regarding the "arising of the two boundlessnesses": when cultivating various roots of goodness, it is difficult to discern because afflictions accompany them.
This means that due to the cultivation of goodness, these afflictions arise; being subtle, they are difficult to perceive. From this point downward, the seven phrases are divided into three parts:
first, three clarify the depth of the afflictions; second, two clarify the afflictions by way of birth; third, two [clarify them] by way of... [text ends].

The karma-exposition clarifies that afflictions are the root of delusion. Regarding the first three [categories], the first is "that which is innate and not abandoned. This is because it conforms to what binds;
that is to say, the mind does not attain mastery due to the bondage of the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*), as greed and the other [afflictions] are mutually inseparable.

The second is "the single meaning of dormancy and arising. This refers to the question: by what is one bound? It means that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their manifest activity are distinct in terms of seed and manifestation, yet they share the same nature of delusion.
Because they are one and the same. Herein, the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*). Because these underlying tendencies exist, liberation is not attained.

Regarding the statement that "affliction (*kleśa*)" and "underlying tendency" have the same meaning, this is raised to harmonize with and explain the Sūtra. That is to say, when distinguishing afflictions, why is it called an "underlying tendency"? It is because they share this same meaning.

If they have the same meaning, why does the subsequent section further clarify the "active manifestation of underlying tendencies" (*anuśaya-samudācāra*)? An underlying tendency has only the sense of being a bond (*bandhana*).
And the sense of "following after. This is based on the former meaning; the following [passage] relies on the latter meaning, and thus they are not contradictory.

Regarding the third point, "associated with or dissociated from the mind": this refers to the objects that are bound. That is to say, if the mind is dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*), liberation is possible;
otherwise, it is bound. The next two phrases clarify the afflictions in terms of birth: first, abiding while undergoing birth according to one's destiny.
Regarding the distinction between the two and three realms, the *Śāstra* explains in combination as follows: "The body is the cause for the arising of the path and the realm;

thus, the upper phrase refers to the arising of the path, while the lower phrase refers to the arising of the realm. The latter two phrases clarify the afflictions and the root of delusion in terms of karma.
As for 'craving, views, ignorance, and pride entering deeply like arrows'—among these three factors, karma acts as the cause that obstructs liberation. This refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Sensual desire is the pursuit of existence; delusion is the pursuit of existence; and views are the pursuit of false holy life. All of these obstruct liberation.

Their fault is like an arrow buried deep in wood, difficult to extract; so too it is for those who enter the evil realms. This is because the causal conditions of their two or three types of karma remain unsevered.
Because they conform to the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the world, they constitute an uninterrupted cause for arising.

That is to say, pride and delusion lead to the commission of grave karmic offenses; since these afflictions are the causes for committing offenses through these three types of action, they are called an uninterrupted cause for arising.

In the concluding summary that follows, regarding the mention of "eighty-four thousand," according to the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra*, the total number of perfections (*pāramitā*) bestowed by the World-Honored One throughout his entire career of teaching was three hundred and fifty.

From the initial "Perfection of Radiance" (*Prabhāsa-pāramitā*) to the final "Perfection of Distributing Relics" (*Śarīra-vibhāga-pāramitā*), each of these was practiced with the six perfections as its application, resulting in two thousand one hundred. When this is paired with...
To remedy the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the six sense-decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the ten kinds of afflictions, there are thus twenty-one thousand [remedies].

The four great elements are the internal retribution; the six sense-decays are the external objects. Because they cause the decline of wholesome dharmas, these twenty-one thousand [remedies] each transform four types of sentient beings:

first, those with much greed; second, those with much hatred; third, those with much delusion; and fourth, those with equal proportions [of the three poisons]. Altogether, this constitutes eighty-four thousand [remedies].

The various dharma-gates of the perfections (pāramitās) have as their obstructing delusions the eighty-four thousand afflictions (kleśas). The same applies to the lower karmas and other such categories;
one should understand them all accordingly.
Third is the knowledge regarding the dense forest of karma. The three textual sections are the same as before. Within the detailed exposition, there are ten phrases.

Regarding the first, "wholesome and so forth," this refers to the differentiation of the causes of the path; that is, it is said to be "differentiated" because the three natures are generally taught to be the causes for the six destinies.

Projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, whereas completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) pertains to all three natures. Among the habitual tendencies of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*), those that express meaning are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*). This clarifies...

Because their objects possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 17), indeterminate karma is explained by distinguishing its presence or absence through the correlation of the three natures as causes with the five kinds of results.
That verse states: "Regarding the wholesome and so forth, for the wholesome and so forth; in the first [case] there are four, two, and three; in the middle [case] there are two, three, and four;
in the last [case] there are two, three, and three results. The five results are: maturation (*vipāka*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and dominance (*adhipati*).

[This refers to] dissociation (*visamyoga*). The Commentary states: "The final statement 'all as follows' (*yathākrama*) indicates that, as appropriate, the meaning [of the preceding categories] applies universally to the preceding gates.

For instance, taking each of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [states] as a cause, one should distinguish the number of fruits in relation to the three types of phenomena—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—in their respective order.
The subsequent examples should be understood accordingly. This continues until the explanation of the fourth phrase, which says: "There is none after."
Karma that is recorded as wholesome has two fruits: all *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort) and *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruits).

Karma that is unwholesome has three fruits, excluding *vipāka-phala* (ripened fruit), *visamyoga-phala* (fruit of dissociation), and *niṣyanda-phala* (outflowing fruit). Why? Because karma belonging to the categories of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (view of extremes) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Since all unwholesome states are the outflow of these [indeterminate views], indeterminate karma has three fruits, excluding *vipāka-phala* and [the others].
Regarding "separation from bondage" and "the two that have representation," etc.: this is due to the distinction between intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and differentiation (*viśeṣa*).

This [action] is of two kinds: first, the time of deliberation; second, the time of performing the act. Deliberation occurs on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) and consists of two types of volition (*cetanā*): that of investigation (*vicāraṇā*) and that of determination (*niścaya*).

Performing the act occurs on the levels of body and speech, each consisting solely of the volition of initiation (*samutthāna-cetanā*). Herein, it is intended to clarify that the essence (*tattva*) of all three types of action is volition by nature.

It is said that they differ by nature. Furthermore, if one speaks generally of the three vehicles, they consist only of body and speech; if speaking specifically of the Bodhisattvas alone, they also extend to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

Such is the case for informative action (*vijñapti-karman*). Moreover, according to the Hīnayāna school, the two types of informative action—bodily and vocal—are respectively the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).

[The Vaibhāṣikas] consider these to be its nature: bodily form and vocal sound are the substance of the two [physical] karmas, while volition associated with the mind is the substance of mental karma.

In the Mahāyāna, it is not so; the two bases of form and sound are the manifestations of body and speech, but they are not themselves the two karmas, because the two karmas of body and speech have volition as their nature.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The volition that moves the body is called bodily karma; the [volition] that initiates speech..."

Volition (*cetanā*) is called verbal action (*vāk-karman*). This is because bodily and verbal form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one were to analyze this in detail, it would be as in other chapters.

Regarding the phrase "three [factors] arise simultaneously with the mind" and so forth: this refers to the distinction of skillful means (*upāya-viśeṣa*). That is to say, because [volition] arises together with the mind and perfumes the mind, it does not produce a separate fruit.
This clarifies that this volitional karma arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), and having arisen, it follows its own nature of being wholesome or unwholesome.

It immediately perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), forming various [seeds] that resemble the perfuming agents; thus, it is said that no separate fruit is produced. This explains the meaning of "not being apart.

Regarding the fourth reason—that although the self-nature perishes moment by moment, the accumulation of the fruit is not lost—it is because the distinctions of the accumulated fruits are fully gathered.
That is to say, while karma from beginningless time naturally perishes and disintegrates moment by moment, the accumulation of its fruit is not lost.
Regarding "conditioned karma": this explains spontaneous destruction, meaning that conditioned phenomena are necessarily impermanent.

Regarding "the accumulation of causes": this reveals that the functional capacity is not yet exhausted; it explains the sequence of the accumulation of results, meaning that these momentary causes are fully capable of drawing forth their effects.
Regarding "having retribution and so forth": this is due to the distinction between those results already experienced and those not yet experienced; that is to say, past retribution.

Karma that is currently being experienced is called "having retribution" (*savipāka*). Karma from the past whose later fruit has not yet been experienced in the present is called "without retribution" (*avipāka*);

this does not mean it is entirely non-existent, for these terms are spoken in reference to what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred. Regarding the six types of black-black and so forth, which yield various fruits of retribution:
Regarding their differentiation: namely, black karma in relation to white karma; white karma in relation to black karma; non-black-and-non-white karma in relation to both types of karma;
and both types of karma in relation to non-black-and-non-white karma. In this context, the terms "black" and "white" are repeated because each has two aspects—cause and effect.
The phrase "in relation to both types of karma" refers to the preceding single instances of black and white karma. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, chapter eight, states: "There is..."

There are four distinctions of karma: 1. Black karma with black maturation (*kṛṣṇa-kṛṣṇa-vipāka-karma*). This refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*) and similar actions, because they are defiled and their maturation is undesirable.
2. White karma with white maturation (*śukla-śukla-vipāka-karma*). This refers to wholesome (*kuśala*) karma of the three realms, because it is undefiled and its maturation is desirable.
3. Black-and-white karma with black-and-white maturation (*kṛṣṇa-śukla-kṛṣṇa-śukla-vipāka-karma*). This refers to mixed karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Because it is mixed with both wholesome and unwholesome [elements], how can a single action (*karman*) be both wholesome and unwholesome?

This is because it is categorized as a single action based on its intention (*āśaya*) and its preparatory effort (*prayoga*); it does not mean that a single momentary action is simultaneously wholesome and unwholesome.

That is to say, there may be an action where the intention is black but the preparatory effort is white; for example, there might be someone who, in order to deceive another, first manifests a certain appearance to cause that person to believe them.

[It is] thus. Regarding the practice of the gift of wisdom (*prajñādāna*): "The means (*upāya*) is black while the intention (*āśaya*) is white" refers to a case where someone, wishing to establish their disciples and others in a place free from danger, manifests various forms of coarse and harsh physical and verbal conduct out of compassion;
at that time, defilement (*saṃkleśa*) arises. "Neither black nor white karma without ripening (*avipāka*)" refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter sixteen, states: "All unwholesome karma is exclusively called 'black' because its nature is defiled;
its maturation is also black because it is disagreeable. Wholesome karma of the form realm is exclusively white because it is not mixed with evil;
its maturation is also white because it is agreeable. It is stated in the Sūtras, and in some places it is also said that wholesome karma of the desire realm is [called white].
It is black-and-white because it is interspersed with evil; its maturation (*vipāka*) is also black-and-white because it is interspersed with desirable and undesirable fruits.

This designation "black-and-white" is established based on the continuity (*saṃtati*) [of the agent], not according to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is because there is no single karma or single maturation that is both black and white, as these are mutually contradictory.
Regarding the phrase "seven are like fields, being immeasurable," this is due to the differentiation of causes and conditions; that is to say, according to the majority...

Regarding causes and conditions: they are all capable of initiating karma. Eighth, the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones: it is the distinction between those who have not yet accumulated [karma] and those who have already accumulated it;

that is to say, supramundane karma has not yet been accumulated, while mundane karma has already been accumulated. Ninth, [the distinction between] karma to be experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives.

This is due to the distinction between determinate and indeterminate retribution. That is to say, karma performed in the present and experienced in the present is called "karma with present retribution" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

Karma performed in the present and experienced in the immediately following birth is called "karma with retribution in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*). Karma performed in the present and experienced from the second birth onwards is called "karma with subsequent retribution" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*).

This is because they are determinate or indeterminate with respect to these three periods of time. Furthermore, it is due to the determinacy or indeterminacy of the ten vehicles and non-vehicles. As for the vehicles, there are three types of vehicles.

Because of being determinate or indeterminate. Regarding those who do not belong to a vehicle (*ayānika*), they are determinate or indeterminate within the world; that is to say, because there is falling back or no falling back.

Among those who do not belong to a vehicle, within the world, they are easy or difficult to deliver because of being determinate or indeterminate. The treatise discusses the determinate and indeterminate delights regarding both vehicles and non-vehicles.
The conclusion at the end concerning the eighty thousand [dharmas] and so forth may be understood accordingly.
The fourth [section], "Knowing the Forest of Faculties," consists of two parts: first, the detailed explanation, and second, the summary. This concludes the preceding section.

Within that, there are ten phrases which the Master of the Treatise condenses into nine, because he combines the fifth and sixth phrases into one. First, "the inferior, the middling, and the superior" refers to the distinction of the vessels [for the Dharma];
that is, the vessels to whom the Dharma is bestowed at the time of preaching. "Inferior" (mṛdu) means low, and "superior" (viśiṣṭa) means high.

Nor is it the middle between the two. It is also called "dull-middle" and "sharp. Receiving [the result] quickly is called sharp; receiving it slowly is called dull; that which is neither is called the middle.

Regarding the equality of the two limits of before and after: this refers to the differentiation of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*). The phrase "faculties of the before and after" explains the limits of before and after.
The phrase "because the preceding faculty increases, diminishes, or remains level" explains the distinction and non-distinction; that is to say, the preceding is...

That which can produce is the cause; that which is produced is the result. If the result increases, the preceding faculty (indriya) decreases; if the result decreases, the preceding faculty increases; when the faculty is thus balanced, they are equal.
Regarding the three—superior, middling, and inferior—these are the distinctions of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), namely, the natures of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The superior is the Bodhisattvayāna; the middling is the Pratyekabuddhayāna; and the inferior is the Śrāvakayāna. Regarding the four afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth... [text fragment ends]

Because of the distinction between affliction (*kleśa*) and secondary affliction (*upakleśa*). That is to say, because they are defiled by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the secondary afflictions associated with the five faculties of feeling, such as joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*).
Furthermore, because they are co-nascent and inseparable. As the third chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Among the defilements (*saṃkleśa*), the five feelings, beginning with pleasure, possess predominant influence. Why is this? Because the Sūtra says: 'Craving increases in accordance with pleasant feeling; [craving] in unpleasant feeling..."*

Hatred increases [therein]. Because ignorance increases in feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant. The commentary states: "The meaning of 'faculty' (*indriya*) is that of predominant function.

Regarding "the five vehicles and non-vehicles": this refers to the characteristics of being determined or undetermined. Regarding "the characteristic of being thoroughly tamed and supple": this is because of the distinction between the determined and the undetermined.
Regarding "among the three vehicles" and "among the worldly": these explain the vehicles and non-vehicles. [This concerns] the ripening of the determined and the undetermined.

"Because they are not matured" is the general explanation. This means that within the Mahāyāna, those who are matured are fixed, while those who are not matured are not fixed, because they may turn toward the Mahāyāna from within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Within the three vehicles, those who are fixed in each are so because they attain liberation within their respective vehicles;
thus it says "each individual vehicle," and so forth. Regarding "fixed by retribution," "those who have abandoned" refers to those within the world.

Because it is impossible to transform them so that they enter the Path, "abandonment" (śeṣa) refers to temporary abandonment; this is said because, according to the three vehicles, each remains within its own vehicle before the time of further advancement.
Regarding the sixth point, "following the net of faculties with light transformation and harboring," there are three kinds of conforming practice (*anuloma-pratipatti*):

first, conforming practice based on the body, which involves mutual transformation through the successive interaction of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This explains "transformation according to the faculties."

Furthermore: (2) because birth and cessation proceed in accordance with [conditioning] and are easily destroyed; this explains "easily destroyed. (3) Because one grasps at marks through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);

this explains the mark of deeply grasping at marks. Regarding "the seven superiorities" and so forth: it means that because the superior obstacles to the distinct practices of the Śrāvakas' purity are extinguished, they can achieve [their goal];
in comparison to ordinary beings, these are superior practices. This explains the first phrase, followed by the accomplishment of the practice that severs obstacles.

Regarding the explanation of the distinction between the eight types of non-retrogression—those who retrogress and those who do not—the differentiation of the bodhisattva’s purity occurs as follows: it involves "turning back" prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), but does not involve turning back once on the stages.
Furthermore, the first seven stages are termed "turning," while from the eighth stage upward they are termed "non-turning. As for the phrase "far-reaching following" and so forth:

This is because it demonstrates the distinctions in the inclusion of all faculties (*indriya*). That is to say, it refers to the distinctions among the faculties of those at the stage of initial practice, those employing skillful means, and those whose retribution has matured.

Thus, both the faculties and the practices are termed "co-arising. Since practices have a beginning and an end, the faculties likewise follow suit. The conclusion at the end [of the section] will be clear.
Fifth is the dense forest of understanding (*adhimukti*). "Understanding" refers to resolute confidence (*adhimukti*), because it causes one to maintain the focal object.
Sixth is the dense forest of nature (*prakṛti*). "Nature" refers to that which has become an inherent disposition through repeated habituation.

The seventh is the knowledge of the thicket of desire and inclination (*chanda-gahana*). Because one gives rise to longing for the objects of one's desire, there are three sections herein, each briefly illustrating one phrase—soft, medium, and superior—which are then concluded with the words "briefly explained" and so forth. The treatise states:

"Because such natures enter [into one another]. This commentary does not explain the reason for this at length because the four factors, beginning with the faculties (*indriya*), are mutually compatible in their nature and characteristics and thus enter into one another. Only...
The faculties (*indriya*) are explained in detail, while the others are all treated briefly because they are similar and have no distinct meaning.

Regarding the eighth [topic], "the dense forest of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of knowledge," there are two parts: first, a general heading; second, the specific exposition beginning with "namely" (*yad uta*).

In the former, both the Jin translation and the *Śāstra-sūtra* refer to them as *paryavasthāna* (outbursts/defilements); that is based on their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), whereas this [text] refers to them by way of their seeds (*bīja*). However, according to...
Regarding the meaning of the text, it is best understood in its comprehensive sense. "Latent proclivities" (*anuśaya*) are so named by way of analogy with a messenger:

just as a messenger pursuing a thief seizes an opportunity to bind him, so too do the afflictions pursue sentient beings and seize an opportunity to bind them. As for "dormant tendencies" (*anusaya*), this refers to the seeds of the two obstructions;

they are called "dormant" because they follow along with the practitioner, lying hidden and not yet arisen. Since wholesome seeds such as faith are not termed "dormant tendencies," [the term applies specifically to the seeds of the obstructions]. Yoga...

The second [section] of the *Gāthā* says: "If seeds are subsumed under categories such as faith and skillfulness (*kauśalya*), they are not termed 'heavy dysfunction' (*dausthulya*), nor are they 'latent tendencies' (*anuśaya*).
Why is this? Because when these dharmas arise, the basis—the personal entity (*ātmabhāva*)—is capable and not incapable.
Later, among the twelve phrases specifically revealed, the treatise subsumes them into two; that is, the first six phrases are called "where" (*yatra*).

[The phrase] "pursued" [is explained]. Regarding the six subsequent phrases, they are called "that which is pursued by what. Among the preceding [six], the first two phrases are combined into one in the treatise and the sūtra.

As for the expression "together with the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) and so forth," this is because [the former] is a mind of maturation (*vipāka*) while [the latter] is not. This clarifies the locus of what is pursued in terms of the mind:
that is to say, a mind born of maturation is called "profound" because it has existed for a long time; a mind of cultivation (*bhāvanā-citta*), being newly arisen, is not called profound. Now...
It is said that this messenger constantly cultivates practice because it arises in opposition to the mind; therefore, it is said that the mind does not depart from manifest phenomena.

Regarding the two types of correspondence (*saṃprayoga*), there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior within the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). That is to say, in terms of the realms, one clarifies the locus where [the mind] follows:

the realm of desire is inferior, the realm of form is middling, and the realm of formlessness is superior. As for the phrase "not departing from characteristics," it refers exclusively to [the mind] being associated with a different realm.
Because they are associated with the mind. As for "non-associated," it means they are not associated with minds of a different realm.

Furthermore, that which arises within its own realm is called "associated," while that which is viewed in relation to a different realm is called "non-associated. The *anuśayas* (latent tendencies), however, are not like this, because they are associated with everything;

thus, they are said to be "inseparable from their characteristics. Third, as for "following along for a long duration," it means they follow [the being] all the way up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This...

Regarding the clarification of the stages and the locations they accompany: this refers to the extent up until the exhaustion of afflictions in the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Fourth, "those which are beginningless and cannot be uprooted": in boundless worlds, there is only wisdom that views [existence] with fear as if it were an enemy or a bandit; yet, one has never previously possessed the wisdom of hearing, reflection, or cultivation. Therefore, these do not cease.
This means that these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as obstacles to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*); knowing them, one is constantly fearful and they always follow along.
Because they bind and afflict sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "contrary to all dhyānas and so forth":

because worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and the like cannot extinguish the mental tendencies that follow [the outflows], this explains the spheres of what is followed by way of their activity.

That is to say, due to these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), dhyānas, liberations, and so forth are unable to transcend the world. The definitions and meanings of "dhyāna" and the others are as explained in the Fifth Stage (*Pañcamabhūmi*).

The subsequent explanation of what follows along within the six statements begins with "first, the three realms," etc. There is a continuous following along because existence (bhava) follows along through the production of similar latent tendencies (anuśaya).
That is to say, because of the latent tendency of existence, it is able to cause the three existences (trai-dhātuka) to continue in a similar succession;
therefore, it is called "bound to the three realms. This explains the following along in terms of the preceding locus. Second, it causes the mind to become boundless...

“Etc. means that it follows [the mind] over a long duration. That is to say, although the mind has been boundless since beginningless time, its moments have continued in succession without ever being interrupted.
Because this [habitual tendency] pursues [the mind], whatever is performed accumulates; once the continuity has arisen, there is no interval [between its occurrence and its result].
Regarding "opening the gates of the various bases": the various bases refer to the six internal bases; this is the same as what is called "entrances" (*āyatana*) in the Sūtra and the Śāstra.
Regarding "arising and following along with the body": this means that the faculties, consciousnesses, and objects pervade the entire body.

Regarding "the six kinds of arising and gathering of consciousness at the gates of the eyes and other entrances, arising and following along together with the proclivities (*anuśaya*)": this means that based on the faculties, consciousness arises, and that which is gathered therein arises together with the proclivities.

Regarding "and because it follows due to the perfuming of the *ālayavijñāna*": when consciousness conditions objects and perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to form seeds, it likewise persists and follows along.
Regarding "fourth, it is firm, solid, and difficult to refute": this refers to the fact that the unreal persistence serves as the counteragent to the meaning of reality;
that is, one takes the failure to attain reality as its counteragent. Regarding "fifth, the accomplishment of the locus and so forth": it refers to subtle persistence. At [the stage of]...

Within the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), because the body of afflictions (*kleśakāya*) follows along with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is said that throughout all places within the three realms and nine stages, these [afflictions] follow along and are difficult to eliminate.

They are not established in the Sphere of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of these proclivities (*anuśaya*) is so subtle as to be difficult to discern.
Six [of these] are removed solely by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*); they depart from the pursuit of suffering and proceed toward supramundane practice (*lokottaracaryā*). The remainder...

Because it cannot be abandoned by the [six] modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-ākāra*). That is to say, this latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is extremely subtle; only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises as its antidote and brings about liberation, not the six modes of practice and so forth.
The ninth [section], "Knowing Birth within the Dense Forest of Sensations," consists of two parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words "That is to say.
Within the general heading, the term "various" is used because sensations involve various different types of physical forms.

The eight phrases in the detailed exposition are derived from the preceding general heading, and they likewise clarify the causes for the aforementioned "various births. The first is "conforming to karma," which arises through karma.

1. Because there are various kinds of bodies, which are manifold. 2. Regarding "the six destinies" and so forth: this refers to the dwelling places, namely the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*). 3. Regarding "those with form" and so forth:

this refers to the various distinctions of the higher and lower [realms] regarding the perception of form; that is, in terms of the upper and lower levels of the realms, there are those with form (*rūpin*) and those without form (*arūpin*).
Regarding "the four [factors] such as perception": this is because they differ in terms of having perception, lacking perception, or being intermediate.

Regarding "karma as the field, up to the body of future existence": this is because the external causes of material form are likewise diverse; that is to say, just as grasses and trees arise depending on the earth and other factors, karma is said to be the cause.
Regarding "name-and-form": this is because their specific characteristics are diverse; that is to say, name-and-form arises together with matter.
Because this is the essence of retribution, it is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. Regarding the seven [factors] such as delusion and craving:

because they are various types of causes that accord with origination—meaning they are causes that accord with primary birth—and since they arise from delusion and craving while still acceding to them, they are termed "delusion and craving. Regarding the eight [factors] such as sensual craving:
these two subsequent phrases constitute a single meaning, as they comprise the various aspects of the Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering (*duḥkhasamudayasatya*). That is to say, in the present...

This accumulates future suffering. Third, regarding the various terms for the different ways sentient beings accumulate suffering through seeking, it is because they desire, delight in, crave, and grasp at feeling (*vedanā*), and because they seek through grasping (*upādāna*).
This is the "seeking of desire" (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) because sentient beings, driven by craving and grasping, pursue and seize objects everywhere.
As for "desiring birth," it refers to the love that sentient beings have for their own and others' bodies and minds in a future existence (*punarbhava*), and their attachment to signs (*nimitta*).
Because of grasping at and attachment to the upper and lower realms as one comes and goes, this is the craving of sentient beings who seek existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).
"One's own and others' bodies" refers to one's own realm and the realms of others; it is by means of mental attachment to signs that one comes and goes between the upper and lower realms.

This refers to those sentient beings who seek false holy life (*brahmacarya*) due to beginningless attachment to signs and so forth—namely, the four great immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). This collectively reveals the craving for the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

In this regard, there is truly no liberation; yet they falsely claim that there is liberation. As for those who claim that the absence of the signs of perception constitutes escape from the wheel of existence (*bhava-cakra*), they take what is rootless to be nirvana and call it the revolving wheel of the three realms of existence; however, in truth and in reality, it is nothing other than the continuous, revolving cycle of suffering.

The tenth [point] is the knowledge of the dense forest of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The text has two parts, as before. Herein, "habitual tendency" does not mean a seed, nor does it mean lack of functional capacity;

it is so named simply because it is a matter of repeated practice. Among the ten phrases that specifically clarify this, the first is the distinction between that which acts and that which does not act.
This refers to the distinction between yielding results in the present versus not in the present. That is to say, it concerns past habitual practice, such as that of a constant stream.

The daughter of the river had the habit of harsh speech; Śāriputra had the habit of [handling] snakes. Because they heard the Buddha’s reproach regarding eating unequally, they vomited up what they had eaten.
Mahākāśyapa heard of the Gandharva king’s habit of dancing while playing the lapis lazuli lute, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "practiced or not practiced" used here: it means that although there are past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), some manifest in the present while others do not. (2)

Regarding the permeation according to the destinies (*gati*): this refers to the distinctions in the permeation of the path. That is to say, within the six destinies, when one is about to undergo birth in a subsequent destiny, there is the reception of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from a previous destiny.
For example, a person who has previously been born in hell and experienced suffering may see others undergoing similar punishments;

although they do not consciously remember it, upon seeing them, they feel displeasure or experience fear. Conversely, if they see those who have previously enjoyed happiness among humans or devas, [they feel joy].

One should understand that this is explained at length, including the practice of delighting in seeing and loving [others], the practice of purity and impurity, and the practice of lying down, reclining, or facing upward.

Third, regarding those who follow the ways of sentient beings: because they are deeply attached to sentient beings, it is like a person who becomes good by associating with the virtuous and evil by associating with the wicked;
only those of superior intelligence or the lowest stupidity do not change their nature, while those of the middle way [are influenced]. To keep livestock... [is likewise].

There are indeed such cases. For example, it is said that if a war elephant is stationed near a monastery, it no longer desires to fight; yet if it is stationed near a slaughterhouse, it fights as before.

Regarding the four types of afflictions that follow karma, because the karma and afflictions are heavy, this refers to internal negligence, or perhaps due to wealth and status, one fears for oneself and habitually indulges in sexual desire, drinking alcohol, and so forth—thus achieving a state of habitual practice. As it is said:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Just as a person who loves sleep will find their slumber increasing, so it is with those who crave lust and indulge in wine.
Regarding the five wholesome and unwholesome [factors]: because the karma of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) is heavy, whatever undertakings one engages in do not fall outside these three natures.

Undertakings of wholesome karma include both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*); unwholesome karma and neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma are exclusively out-flowing. These three...
1. Those whose nature is their karma: even in dreams, they continue to practice that karma. 2. Those who follow into subsequent existence: because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is weighty;

that is to say, during the time of the intermediate state, there is the habituation of the preceding prior existence (*pūrvabhava*), just as a person who delights in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) remains free from sensual defilement even when entering the intermediate state.
3. Those whose sequence is weighty: because the sequence of the results is weighty; that is to say, according to...
First, regarding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): because within the various realms of existence (*gati*), one receives bodies in succession, all of which possess those respective habits.

Regarding the eighth point, "the non-abandonment of afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth: this distinguishes the weightiness of the causes for mundane dhyāna. It refers to entering deeply into the heavy state of not abandoning the afflictions, which are like a palm held in the hand.

The subsequent section explains the preceding phrase by distinguishing it: that is to say, it is because within dhyāna one does not abandon the afflictions, which remain as if held in the palm of the hand.
Because those born in the higher realms still possess the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of that state, it is said they "enter from afar. Regarding the phrase "the nine are real or unreal, etc.":

this refers to the difference in their dharmas. As for "non-Buddhists whose practice and realization are heavy," this means they are called "different" because their various non-Buddhist paths do not accord with the Buddha-dharma.
They take the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as liberation; thus, because both the false and the correct each have their own respective habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is so stated.

There is the real and the unreal. The real refers to the Hīnayāna; the unreal refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Regarding the "ten [types of] seeing, hearing, and so forth," this is because of the distinctions between the vehicles' weightiness.
That is to say, they are contrasted as Great and Small; for when people of the three vehicles see, hear, or draw near to any phenomenon, there is always a heavy habituation [of that karma].

The eleventh [section], the "Thicket of the Three Multitudes" (*trikaṇḍaka-gahana*), has two textual divisions as before. Within the specific [explanation], there are five parts. The first concerns the division of the three multitudes according to spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
those who lack the nature for nirvāṇa are of the "wrongly fixed" (*mithyātva-niyata*) category; those who possess the nature for nirvāṇa are of the "rightly fixed" (*samyaktva-niyata*) category.
Within right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are each distinct and exclusively fixed for themselves.

Apart from these two types, there is the indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*). This treatise speaks in terms of stages; those who do not grasp the intended meaning when it says "it is not fixed as five natures" are merely creating false confusion.

Second, the three groups (*tri-rāśi*) are distinguished according to delusion and awakening: namely, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the cause of wholesome conduct. Among the three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*), right view alone is fixed.
The arising of wholesome karma is called "right determination" (*samyaktva-niyata*). Non-greed and non-hatred that do not necessarily give rise to wholesome states are called "undetermined.

False view is the cause of unwholesome conduct; specifically, among the afflictions, the single factor of false view invariably gives rise to unwholesome karma and is thus called "wrong determination" (*mithyātva-niyata*).

The others are called "undetermined. These three categories are distinguished according to their karmic activity, namely, each of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) within the category of unwholesome action.

Sin inevitably brings about rebirth in the evil realms; this is termed "wrongly fixed" (*mithyātva-niyata*). In the Sanskrit original, these are called the five *ānantarya* [sins]. As for the characteristics of being wrongly fixed:

this refers merely to cause and effect, and thus the name and its meaning do not conflict. The five faculties, such as faith, which definitely bring about a happy destination, are termed "rightly fixed" (*samyaktva-niyata*).
That which is contrary to the above is termed "undetermined" (*aniyata*). These four categories are divided into three groups based on the two positions of wrong and right. Namely:

Reversing the Eightfold Noble Path results in what is called the Eightfold Wrong Path; based on this, the heterodox positions of external paths are established and termed "wrong determination" (*mithyā-niyata*).

The state of being born into the right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is termed the "right position"; based on this, the right position of the Śrāvakas is established and termed "right determination" (*samyak-niyata*).

The five "straight" [paths] concern the gains and losses of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, by which they are divided into the three groups (*tri-koṭi*). Regarding those who are "defiled and attached to wrong dharmas" and are of "wrong determination":

The treatise explains the characteristics of envy, stinginess, non-reformation of evil conduct, and false concentration according to the sūtras. "Envy" refers to the failure to relinquish those who are capable of being transformed.
"Stinginess regarding wealth" is termed the impairment of the *pāramitās*. As for their opposites, it is because these six obscurations obstruct the practice of the six perfections.
The names are contradictory. That is to say, envy obstructs the latter three [perfections]—wisdom, meditative concentration, and diligence; stinginess obstructs the practice of giving;

and misconduct obstructs the two practices of ethical discipline and patience. Because of these obstructions, the correct practices of Bodhisattvas are not accomplished, and they are described as being of "wrong determination" (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*).
By analogy, those of "right determination" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and "undetermined" (*aniyata*) can be understood.
The third [section] summarizes the three aforementioned types of accomplishment; it should be understood as concluding the stage of "well-established abiding.

The fourth [section] clarifies two aspects within the explanation of accomplishment: first, a general indication; second, a specific exposition beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva is well able...

and so forth. Within the former, the phrase "knowing the various practices of sentient beings" restates what was previously mentioned, while "entering into knowledge" refers to enabling them to become vessels for the Dharma.

The "Liberated One" (Vimukta) is so called because he teaches the Dharma according to the faculties [of his listeners]. Hereafter, the middle four [stages] are specifically revealed: 1. Accomplishment of Wisdom (*jñāna-saṃpad*). 2.
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, whether good or evil... and so forth; this is both the accomplishment of wisdom and the accomplishment of vocal action (*vāk-karma*).
3. "By means of the immeasurable... and so forth; this is exclusively the accomplishment of vocal action. 4. "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the ninth stage... [and so forth].
The section on the accomplishment of the Dharma-preacher consists of two parts: the first and the second. First, it clarifies that which is known, namely the Dharma to be taught;

subsequently, from "in all spheres of conduct" onwards, it clarifies that which is relied upon, namely the vessel to be reached. Within the former, the phrase "skillfully able to expound the Śrāvaka-yāna and so forth" refers to the teaching.

Because the vessels for liberation have reached maturity; that is to say, it is taught that by preaching the transformative Dharma, one brings the vessels of sentient beings to maturity for liberation.

Because the essence of liberation is the true crossing over; this is the differentiation of liberation, as one causes them to attain the liberation of the fruit of Buddhahood through the three vehicles of the Dharma.

Regarding the subsequent three points concerning what is relied upon: first, a general explanation of preaching the Dharma according to the vessel; second, the specific manifestation of the capacity to conform [to the vessel] below.
Regarding what has been explained: the third section, "causing the arising of faith and understanding," serves as a summary of the benefits for those being transformed.

In the first part, it says, "one who acts in all places" (*sarvatragacārin*), because one acts in accordance with the mental dispositions and the spheres of activity of the recipients (*bhājana*). (The phrase "the forest of taming the mind" from the *Caryāpraveśasiddhi* is omitted here.

Regarding the phrase "because wisdom follows the practice" (*jñānānuvṛttitvāt*), this means that, according to the speaker’s wisdom, one acts in accordance with the mental dispositions and spheres of activity of those recipients. As the treatise asks: "How?"

The phrase "according to what is relied upon" means that the teaching is expounded in accordance with the capacity of the recipient; thus it is called "expounding according to the faculties," and so forth.

As for the statement "bestowing the remedial dharma in accordance with what is appropriate," this explains the sūtra’s reference to "following the latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), meaning that the remedy is applied in accordance with those latent tendencies.

The first two phrases constitute the *dharmaparyāya* (the method of transformation); [this refers to the general heading within this section]. The statement "the vessel for the taught dharma is perfected" clarifies the "vessel of the dharma" (*dharmabhājana*) and explains "according to the faculties."
...and so forth. Because the teaching is delivered according to the capacity [of the vessel], one preaches the Dharma in accordance with their faculties and their inclinations.

Regarding these two phrases, "this is the speaker," this constitutes the concluding summary at the end. Within the detailed exposition, the four characters "able to follow sentient beings" (*neng sui zhongsheng*) and the subsequent four characters "preaching the Dharma for them" (*er wei shuo fa*) are applied universally to the ten intermediate phrases.
This text is similar to the preceding passage on entering the dense forest of practice (*xing choulin*).

The same. [This text] is abbreviated and lacks the mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*). There are differences in the number of items compared to the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, and there are distinctions in their nomenclature.

This *sūtra* has ten designations, whereas the *śāstra* sūtra has thirteen kinds. 1. **Mind** (*citta*): The *śāstra* sūtra contains this; it is present in the preceding text of this [sūtra], but it is not found in the current passage.
2. **Latent Dispositions** (*anuśaya*): Here, these are called "sleeping bonds" (*middha-bandhana*). 3. **Roots** (*mūla*): These are present in both this and that [text]. 4. **Faith** (*śraddhā*).
This is translated as "understanding," which has already been explained previously. Regarding the "various habitual tendencies of the distinctions among objects":
this refers to desire, meaning that one gives rise to longing for agreeable things. "Distinctions" means it differs from objects that are not sought after.
"Various activities" means that the objects are not singular. Sixth, "conformity with all objective knowledge" refers to this...

This is the supernormal power of knowledge born of retribution (*vipākaja-jñānābhijñā*). It possesses three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), but it is not derived from hearing, reflection, or cultivation (*na śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya*).

It possesses seven natures, eight births, nine afflictions, ten karmas, eleven habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and twelve categories such as the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*)—these six are common to both [this and other powers]. Regarding the thirteenth, the vehicles (*yāna*): this [power] does not possess them.

The treatise generally classifies these into six kinds of vessels (*bhājana*): first, the initial five are called the "metaphorical vessels" (*aupamya-bhājana*); thereafter, it immediately cites the...
There are five phrases. The first four establish the proof. If there is no inclination (*chanda*), the vessel is not formed. Why is this so?

Within the body of the teaching, which is a collection of accumulated [elements], it is stated only that [the teaching] follows the inclination of the listener’s consciousness; it does not say it follows other mental factors (*caitta*).
To speak of the "vessel as a metaphor" means that just as one transforms raw materials to create the nature of a vessel, such as in the cultivation of crops.

When the Dharma possesses five causes and conditions, the seeds it plants will achieve maturity and become functional. First, there is the presence of a mind capable of producing [the fruit], which is a metaphor for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Second, the removal of obstructive conditions to production is a metaphor for the subduing of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Third, there is the presence of faculties that augment the power to produce life.
The first four are analogies for the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*), which are definitive and ultimately productive; they serve as analogies for resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

The fifth, from the faculties onward, refers to that which can rapidly progress through successive stages; because it serves as an analogy for aspiration (*chanda*), it is called the "vessel of analogy.

Second, the single [faculty] that accords with all objects of knowledge is called the "vessel of various diverse activities"; this is wisdom born of maturation (*vipākaja-jñāna*) and is associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because of the three natures, such as the wholesome (*kuśala*), there are three [stages]. The first is called the "dense forest of conduct" (*caritavipina*) that accords with the nature;

it continues until one attains the "vessel of accomplishment" (*siddhibhājana*). This is the fruit of the vessel-family by way of analogy; that [forest] is its cause, because through repeated cultivation from the cause, the nature is ultimately perfected.

Thus it is said, "until accomplishment. The fourth is called "discrimination according to words" (*yathāruta-prativijñapti*), which accords with the arising of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and karma.

"Vessel" (*bhājana*) refers to that which gives rise to afflictions and karma; it acts as the basis for the three obstructions, accomplishes the weight of transformative activity through shared practice, and brings about the transformation of habitual tendencies.
Thus, the fifth [category] is called the "vessel of the roots of transformation, definite or indefinite," according to the distinctions among the various accumulations.

This means that according to what is appropriate for each, they are led to further advancement. The sixth [category], the "one who follows the vehicle" (*yānānuvartin*), is so named because of faith in the vehicle;

as those who are "vessels capable of being carried forth" each rely on their own respective vehicle to achieve liberation, this passage serves as the general conclusion for this section of the sutra, summarizing how these various vessels obtain benefit according to their own vehicles. Third, the summary of the preceding vessels: by following...
They follow with faith and understanding, increase their wisdom, and each attains liberation according to their own vehicle (*yāna*).

Regarding the phrase "both the accomplishment of wisdom and the accomplishment of vocal action": in the treatise, the vocal action is first briefly questioned, and it concludes by stating that wisdom is accomplished.

This is because, from the preceding perspective, it is wisdom; for through wisdom, one knows the proper etiquette of preaching. From the subsequent perspective, it is the accomplishment of vocal action, as the Dharma-preacher possesses twenty kinds [of qualities].

Because of virtue. That which is spoken of in the treatise refers to verbal action (*vākkarman*). "Entering" refers to the profound meaning. "Upholding" refers to the accomplishment of wisdom, manifesting the protection of the Dharma.
The twenty kinds of Dharma-preachers are fully detailed as explained in the treatise.
The three [types of eloquence] consist solely of vocal karma, while the middle two are established first by clarifying that non-acquisition wisdom (*aprāpti-jñāna*) can give rise to speech;

subsequently, from the passage "What kind... onwards, the four types of non-acquisition are explicitly revealed. Within the former section, there are four parts: first, clarifying the conduct of the Dharma Master, which refers to the protection of the Dharma;

second, the phrase "by means of the immeasurable," etc., refers to what was previously explained as "skillful wisdom" (*kauśalya-jñāna*), because it is able to give rise to these four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*). Thus one knows the Bodhi...
The fourth [of the four analytical knowledges] does not rely on vitarka and vicāra, but arises from pure awakening. Regarding "the three functions are equal to those of a bodhisattva":
this is because his speech is gentle and supple. Regarding "always following [others]" and so forth: this is because at all times, what he speaks never departs from unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*).

In the subsequent detailed analysis, the four analytical knowledges are briefly distinguished by way of four gates: first, the explanation of their names; second, the discernment of their essence; third...

The basis consists of the four outflows (*āsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Regarding the first [section], the explanation of the names, there are two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific.

As for the term "unimpeded" (*pratisaṃvid*), it refers to the accomplishment of mastery in teaching the Dharma according to the faculties [of listeners]; this is collectively termed the "four unimpeded knowledges," explained by attaching the number [to the noun].

Regarding the specific [explanation]: *dharma*, *artha*, *nirukti*, and *pratibhāna*—where *pratibhāna* also implies eloquence (*pratibhāna*). That which gives rise to understanding in beings and maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called *dharma*. That which is elucidated and manifested through the teachings is *artha*. *Nirukti* refers to language. *Pratibhāna* refers to the capacity for spontaneous exposition. These are the specific names.

"Meaning" refers to the name. "Analysis" refers to the clear exposition [of that meaning]. It is also said that "eloquence" (pratibhāna) means to accord with the faculties of sentient beings and cause them to give rise to joy.
These four are the objects of cognition; "understanding" (pratisaṃvid) is the wisdom that takes these as its objects—specifically, the wisdom that takes the teachings as its object.

Regarding the object of focus—a single name, phrase, and so forth—it is called the "unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) because it can manifest all expressive phrases within that single unit;

this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. The other three [analytical knowledges] should be understood by analogy. Further detailed classifications according to other gateways are fully explained in a separate chapter.

Following this, in the section that correctly elucidates the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), there is first a brief explanation and subsequently a detailed exposition. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation beginning with "That is to say.
In the explanation, first the four names are listed, and then, from "This bodhisattva... onwards, the actual elucidation occurs.

The essence of these four unimpeded knowledges is simply the single wisdom of subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); it is divided into four kinds according to their respective objects of focus (*ālambana*). First, regarding the essence of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*): it clarifies...
1. The essence of the dharma itself (*dharmasvabhāva*). 2. The essence based on the object (*ālambanavastu*): this refers to the aspect of differentiation within the essence of the dharma.

3. Bestowing upon sentient beings according to what one has personally attained: this means speaking of bestowing [the dharma] upon sentient beings based on what one has realized for oneself. 4. Seeking to bestow through immeasurable gateways.

In accordance with the various distinctions of what sentient beings correctly seek, [the Buddha] provides immeasurable gateways. In the subsequent detailed explanation, the first part explains the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

Regarding the phrase "internally comprised by that which arises while remaining far removed from the two extremes": it is called "far removed from the two extremes" because it excludes all other phenomena; it is called "comprised by the arising of phenomena" because it manifests its own essence.
This is illustrated by the example of the obstructive characteristic of form (*rūpa*), which serves to indicate that this applies equally to all other things. This is the second explanation.

"Meaning is non-existent within [the object]" refers to the aforementioned phenomena such as detachment (*viveka*). From "knowledge in accordance with reality" (*yathābhūtajñāna*) downward, the objects are distinguished according to the phenomena.

"The Bodhisattva abides therein" distinguishes the objects according to the person. From "such as form" (*rūpa*) downward, analogies are cited to reveal false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), thereby correctly clarifying the meaning of their specific distinctions.
While the Hīnayāna explains that form possesses meanings such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*), here it is treated according to the Mahāyāna.
This teaching of "form" (rūpa-dharma) is merely a product of deluded conceptualization; in ultimate reality, the term "form" does not exist at all.

Regarding the three explanations of etymology, the phrase "one who possesses correct knowledge speaks according to what others prefer" means that one understands the words favored by others and thus explains them with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

The explanations of "according to others" (*anuparivartana*) and so forth are provided as follows. Regarding the fourfold explanation of "joyful speech" (*pratibhāna*): first, the preceding term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) is cited;

subsequently, the immeasurable varieties of meaning within joyful speech are analyzed. "Speech" (*vāk*) refers to the distinctions within words and phrases; this explains the "immeasurable gateways. The phrase "according to knowledge" (*yathājñānam*) and below provides the explanation and application.
It is also called the "analytical knowledge of joyful speech" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), which means to dissect and clarify [the meaning] so that others may delight in speaking it.
Therefore, in the detailed explanation that follows, these four principles actually encompass all phenomena according to their conventional designations.
Now, by enumerating them through a single complete cycle, ten categories are set forth to manifest their inexhaustibility: first, specific characteristics; second, common characteristics; third...
1. The aspect of practice; 2. The aspect of the four explanations; 3. The aspect of wisdom; 4. The aspect of being free from conceit; 5. The aspect of the Small Vehicle and Great Vehicle;
6. The aspect of the bodhisattva stages; 7. The aspect of the tathāgata stage; 8. The aspect of performing and maintaining [the teachings].

Among these, the first five provide a general understanding of principle and teaching, while the latter five understand the pure virtues of the three vehicles. Within the former group, the first four specifically address the objects of knowledge to clarify non-attainment (*anupalambha*).

The latter one is based on the knowing wisdom (*jñāna*). Among the former three, the first three know the meaning (*artha*), while the last one knows the teaching (*deśanā*). Within the former group, the first is based on knowing phenomena as entities (*vastu-dharma*);

because these entities have distinct objects of cognition that abide separately without intermingling, they are called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Second is the knowledge of phenomena as principles (*tattva-dharma*);

because these principles are pervasive and universal, they are called "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). These two clarify phenomena according to their respective natures. Third, phenomena are distinguished according to time; that is to say, the three...

They are called the aspect of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*) because they involve the transition and flow of the world. The fourth is called the aspect of teaching (*deśanālakṣaṇa*) because it refers to the proclamation of the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.

The fifth is called the aspect of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) because it concerns the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) based on the wisdom that knows; it is not merely knowing about wisdom itself.

Among the latter five [aspects], the first is the total knowledge of the three vehicles as being free from marks and pure realization, which is called the absence of pride (*nirmāna*). Of the latter four, the first among them is the comprehensive knowledge of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

"Great. The remaining three [chapters] separately explain the causes for the stage of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva; the latter two explain the results. It should be understood that these consist of two aspects:
first, the essence (*tattva*), and second, the function (*vṛtti*). Next, in the sequential explanation, these ten chapters are explained as ten sections.

Regarding the first [of the four] specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): "phenomenon" (*dharma*) and "meaning" (*artha*) constitute the pair of the general and the particular. Within dependently arisen phenomena, one knows their general specific characteristic and knows their particular distinctions.
"Expression" (*nirukti*) and "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) constitute the pair of the concise and the extensive. A few names that manifest a phenomenon are called "expression.

Numerous diverse names that stabilize that meaning and cause others to find delight in it are called "eloquence. As for the phrase "the stability of conceptualization," it refers to conceptualization...

This is the basis for the arising of speech. Therefore, in other treatises, it is sometimes called "perception" (*saṃjñā*), sometimes "sound" (*śabda*), sometimes "name" (*nāman*), sometimes "syllable" (*vyañjana*), and sometimes "designation" (*prajñapti*);
these are all alternative designations for "name. Because names express meanings and cause those meanings to become firm, they are called "firmness of perception" (*saṃjñā-sthiti*).
There are many types of this firmness of perception, which constitute the distinctions among names and perceptions. In the repeated explanation, the term is restated without alteration.

"According to what is realized and understood by oneself" means this is called teaching without error. "In accordance with their manifestations" means teaching in response to the capacities of those beings.
"Successive and uninterrupted" is termed "unceasing," which refers to constant teaching.

"Immeasurable and manifold" and so forth mean that for each and every dharma, one explains extensively using immeasurable different names. "To stabilize that meaning" means to do so by means of these various names.
This extensively explains the "mind" (manas) in order to establish the fundamental meaning and to make it firm.

Second, the following clarifies the common characteristics (sādharmya). Within this, the first two [sections] distinguish the meaning of phenomena (dharma) according to the two truths; the latter two distinguish them according to their breadth and brevity.
First, all phenomena are identical in four ways: (1) they are equally devoid of intrinsic nature; (2) conditioned phenomena are equally characterized by impermanence;

(3) regarding the identity of conventional designations, phenomena are equally non-existent and are both spoken of through provisional designations; (4) regarding the identity of designations within designations, they are further elucidated by means of yet another provisional designation.
Below, the detailed analysis of entering into selflessness through impermanence explains the meaning in accordance with the Dharma, namely, the contemplation of impermanence.
"Permanence" means the immediate understanding of non-self (*anātman*). Therefore, the second gate enters the cognitive sphere of the first gate. This is as it says in the sixth stage:
"By conforming to the observation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one enters the second, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Next, regarding the phrasing of the text:

because one further employs other provisional designations (*prajñapti*) upon the previously mentioned provisional dharmas, teaching them according to the faculties [of beings], it is said to be "uninterrupted. Next, "indestructible."
"Boundless" refers to the term "eloquence. It means that while not destroying the previous provisional designation, one is able to speak using other, different provisional designations;
that is, although different names are used in the explanation, they do not contradict the preceding words, and thus it is called "not destroying."
Third, the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). To clearly know the present functioning of dependent origination in a single moment is called "phenomenon" (*dharma*);

to know the functioning of dependent origination in the past and future is called "meaning" (*artha*). Regarding these two aforementioned phenomena, one provisionally establishes names and words; by means of these very names, one proclaims those things.

This is called "eloquent exposition. Regarding the detailed explanation in the section below, the phrase "because each world is present" refers generally to the past and future, as each possesses its own present.
Thus, it is said that they are "subsumed within their respective worlds. Within each individual world, there are many different approaches and diverse explanations.
Regarding the statement, "having seen the faults, one does not know the present": this explains the meaning in accordance with the Dharma. Thus, the subsequent conclusion establishes the preceding;
that is, by means of the subsequent meaning, the unimpeded objects of the preceding Dharma are established. The following section explains eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

Regarding the statement, "the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharma*) and their activities do not transcend the three times": this explains the phenomena previously mentioned. In the Sūtra, each and every world-period does not transcend the three times. As for the statement:

"Boundless illumination of the Dharma" (*ananta-dharmāloka*) refers to an illumination distinct from [ordinary] illumination. Since this distinct illumination is the illumination of phenomena through the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*), it is explained within the context of the characteristics of the fourth illumination.
