Regarding "entry": this refers to the extensive explanation of the mutual entry of the temporal divisions of kalpas and the temporal divisions of non-arrival kalpas.
The ancient commentaries on their conformity and contradiction, as well as the explanations of the remaining text, are all as stated above in the "Chapter on the Merits of Generating the Mind."
Seventh, the elucidation of the wisdom of entering the path. This is because one skillfully recognizes the methods by which sentient beings enter or do not enter the path.

The three sections of the text are the same as before. Within the specific section, there are fourteen phrases: first, the wisdom of entering the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Relying on the ground of ordinary beings, there is a subtle mind of faith;

when moved by the conditions for the path, one explains for them the dharmas such as the three types of mundane wisdom—listening, reflecting, and meditating. Second, the wisdom of entering the... [text fragment].
Regarding "the one with dust-like wisdom" (*rajas-jña*): this is for the sake of sentient beings who possess the conceit of self (*asmimāna*). There are two interpretations of this.

First, it is said that for those sentient beings who give rise to arrogance by relying on heterodox arts, the Buddha leads them into the midst of dust; since they do not know where they are going, he shows it to them so they may know, thereby subduing them.

Second, it is said that for those with the conceit of self, it is to cause them to contemplate that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is merely a collection of dust, thereby shattering their pride.

Third, regarding the knowledge of the body that enters the buddha-fields: for those who rely on faith to be born in heaven, this knowledge manifests a pure land so that they may see it, thereby transforming their aspiration for heaven into a superior resolve.
Fourth, fifth, and sixth, regarding the three types of knowledge that enter the bodies, minds, and activities of sentient beings:
Regarding "observing sentient beings by means of vitarka and vicāra": this refers to the general designation of *vitarka* and *vicāra* as the afflictions that disturb the mind.

This is stated in accordance with their respective antidotes. Regarding "the seven entrances that accord [with them]": this is because the ten thousand varieties of sentient beings differ from one another;

yet, speaking generally, it is because they exist in all places. Regarding "the eight entrances that manifest the knowledge of universal engagement": sentient beings have many thoughts and perceptions, and the Buddha reaches them all everywhere.
Regarding "the mind reaches": first it is the same as [the world], and later it is said that it is severed. Regarding "nine types of conforming conduct" and so forth:

when sentient beings perform conduct that conforms to the world, it is also first the same [as the world] and later severed. Regarding "ten types of counteracting conduct" and so forth: untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*) can oppose birth and death;
because the Buddha has long cultivated and perfected it, he now demonstrates its cultivation. Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, and so forth—all [are likewise].

This is taught as being "identical" for the sake of sentient beings. Its affairs are identical to those of the world, and thus it is "conceivable. Because its actions are difficult to fathom, it is called "inconceivable.
The rest should be understood by analogy with this explanation.

From here below is the second section, which clarifies the Great Liberation. This has three parts: first, the heading; second, a brief exposition; and third, the conclusion of the detailed exposition with the words "These ten," etc.

Within the brief exposition, there are ten phrases. First, "inconceivable liberation" means that based on the spiritual transformation of external phenomena, its wondrous function is difficult to fathom.
Second, "unimpeded" means that by the power of the wisdom of vows, one can swiftly reach the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
The realms are unimpeded. Regarding the three types of pure observation: they are objects known by pure wisdom. There are three kinds of pure conduct:
first, knowing the mundane and supramundane, distinguished according to stages; second, knowing those in training and those beyond training, distinguished according to cause and fruit;
third, knowing the śrāvakas and others, distinguished according to individuals. This constitutes mastery over the objects of knowledge. The former two are common [to all], while the latter one is...

4. Wisdom (*jñāna*). This wisdom knows whether the faculties and natures of the three vehicles possess obstructions or are free from them; it knows the superior [Buddha-vehicle] above and the two lower vehicles below.
Because their wisdoms differ in excellence and because they are all objects of purity, it is called the "differentiation of pure wisdom. 5. Universal Illumination (*samantaprabhāsa*).

This refers to the activity of transformation according to one's will, meaning that in accordance with sentient beings, one manifests various bodies of sovereign mastery through the gateway of all forms and images. 5.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the dharma-dhāraṇī, because it refers to the true nature of all that is known (*jñeya*) which possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Sixth, "conformity" and so forth means that one can refute the arguments of others without retreating. Seventh, "thorough penetration" and so forth means that throughout the kalpas of the three periods of time, one can turn [the wheel of Dharma] according to one's will.
Eighth, "the liberation of the liberation of the dharma-dhātu-garbha": in the Sanskrit original, there is only one [term].
This is the "Cylindrical Liberation. There is no redundancy here; it refers to the wisdom that understands the causal conditions of all phenomena in all their aspects.
Regarding "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) herein: because the myriad existents of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are not merely singular, they are called "all phenomena.

Sentient beings are mostly deluded regarding conventional truth, giving rise to attachments and failing to realize ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). One must therefore skillfully master the causal conditions of conventional truth, knowing them according to their actual reality.

He is named "Skillful Transformation. This is to be understood as above in the section on knowledge. Ninth, the "Wheel of Radiance" refers to light that does not depart from the body yet shines everywhere.
Tenth, "The Realm Without Remainder" refers to knowing the minds of sentient beings in immeasurable worlds at all times.
The concluding summary may be understood accordingly.
The third is the greatness of samādhi; the fourth is the greatness of dhāraṇī; and the fifth is the greatness of supernatural powers (abhijñā).

These should be understood according to the previous [explanation of] the section on the greatness of liberation, including the brief introduction, detailed exposition, and concluding summary. The section on the Great Perfection is completed.

From here begins the fifth major section. Within the "Explanation of Names" sub-section, there are three parts: First, it is called the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Cloud of Dharma Stage) because [the Bodhisattva] is able to receive the clouds and rains of the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma.

Second, "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, by the power of his own vows..."—this explains that he is able to pour down the rain of Dharma to extinguish the dust and flames of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings; thus it is named the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*. Third, "O Son of the Buddha, on this stage, the Bodhisattva... [and so forth].
First, it clarifies that because this stage can pour down the rain of Dharma to produce the roots of goodness in sentient beings, it is named the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Cloud of Dharma Stage).
Regarding the first point: if named according to what is received, it should be called the "Rain of Dharma"; if named according to that which receives, it should be called the "Ocean of Dharma.
Now, it is simply designated as the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi* based on the locus where that Dharma is received. Therefore, the treatise explains: "The single cloud and the Dharma are similar."
"Because it covers everywhere. Regarding the phrase "in this stage, hearing the Dharma is similar [to a cloud]": the Dharma heard therein is vast and all-pervasive;

for this reason, it is called a "cloud," as it is similar to the Dharma. It says, "like space, because the body covers everywhere," clarifying that the body capable of hearing the Dharma is the *dharmakāya*.
This means that one receives [the Dharma] from its source, which is exclusively space; therefore, the *dharmakāya* capable of receiving the Dharma is said to be like space. If one follows...
Regarding the Buddha: the Buddha’s body is like a cloud, and his preaching of the Dharma is like rain. If that which is received is like rain, then that which can receive it is like the ocean.
If, with respect to the Dharma being preached, it is like a cloud that universally covers, then that which is received is like a cloud, and that which can receive it is like space.

[The remaining points]—second, the extinction of dust; third, the deliverance of sentient beings—are clear from the treatise. Regarding the first [of these three], it first provides a general clarification of the accomplishment of the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).

This explains, in brief, the meaning of receiving and upholding [the Dharma]. Second, under the section "In a single thought-moment," it clarifies the capacity to receive the Dharma. This section has three parts: first, hearing and receiving many teachings from the Buddha;
second, from "O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean" onwards, hearing and receiving the True Dharma from many Buddhas;
third, from "The moon of liberation" onwards, questions and answers that reveal the limits of the preceding two parts. Regarding the first part, there is the Dharma...

The analogy and its application consist of two parts in the commentary’s explanation. First is the general explanation: it refers to the fact that the Buddhas of the ten directions preach simultaneously, which is why it is called "many teachings.
Second is the specific explanation, which has three parts: first, explaining the "immeasurable light of Dharma" within the initial teaching by way of Dharma;

second, entering the subtle and secret realm of the Tathāgata to explain the "subtle and secret rain of Dharma" in the application; and third, explaining "swiftness" as the ability to receive [the teaching] in a single thought-moment.
Because one hears the superior [teachings] within this stage, one is able to receive many dharmas. Although what is received is much, it would not be difficult if it were coarse and shallow;

therefore, it is further described as "profound" (*guhya*). Even if the dharmas are numerous and profound, they would still not be difficult to master if they were received gradually over a long period of time.

Furthermore, it is superior because it can now receive [the teaching] with the swiftness of a single thought-moment. The treatise states: "Within this, the immeasurable [qualities] are explained individually below according to the preceding three [categories].
The first two are the teachings heard; the last one reveals the virtue of the one who hears. First, the teachings heard are explained:

that is to say, they are distinguished into two aspects based on their nature and their production, namely, what is known by the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). This is called the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the Dharma. It is taught...

Bestowing [the Dharma] upon sentient beings is called "acting" (*kṛti*). In the detailed explanation of their nature: the "great illumination of the Dharma" (*mahā-dharmāvabhāsa*) is subsumed under the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*);

the "great radiance of the Dharma" (*mahā-dharma-prabhāsa*) is subsumed under the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī prajñā*). How does one act as the great rain of the Dharma? It is like a great cloud bestowing the rain of the Dharma upon others.
The following explains the capacity for hearing: giving rise to faith is called "receiving" (*pratigraha*); comprehending the teaching is called "settling" (*sthiti*). This is the text.
Holding and grasping the meaning and name is what constitutes "retention" (*dhāraṇī*). To gather and receive the meaning of the preceding text without loss is called "retention.

In the treatise, the term "established" (*sthāpana*) in the sutra is rendered as "capable," and "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) is rendered as "contemplation" (*cintā*). Regarding the second explanation, within the dharmas received from many Buddhas, the metaphor of the great ocean has four meanings;
their characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood. Third, regarding the analysis of the boundaries through question and answer, there are two [sections]; first—
Question: [The text] answers later. Within the answer there are also two parts. First, by bestowing the measure, it demonstrates the vastness of what was heard, clarifying the first section.

Second, from "As at the place of one Buddha" onwards, it classifies this according to many Buddhas, clarifying the second section. Regarding the phrase "the dharma-treasury of the three periods" in the former part:
the treatise explains that within the *dharmadhātu* there are three kinds of treasuries of phenomena (*vastu-kośa*), namely, illumination, clarity, and rain, which constitute the three types.
Contained within the *dharmadhātu*, it is called a "store" (*garbha*).
In the second [section], the explanation of the name, there are two parts: first, by means of the clouds, lightning, and so forth, the Bodhisattva’s virtue of being able to transform is revealed;

second, from the passage beginning with "in a single thought-moment," it is shown that the duration of transformation is brief, while in the preceding sections, the scope of transformation is shown to be vast. The remainder concerns the benefits of the transformation.
It is superior. Furthermore, regarding the clouds, thunder, lightning, and so forth, one should understand them as explained in the treatise (*śāstra*).
In the third section, "Explaining the Names," the eight characteristics manifesting, the gradual increase, and the excellence of things are easy to understand from the text.
The sixth major section, which clarifies the portion concerning the supreme and non-supreme powers of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), is divided by the treatise into six parts.
First, regarding that which relies on the internal: these powers rely upon internal virtues and are of four kinds, namely: (1) inconceivable liberation; (2) meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

(3) the arising of wisdom and dhāraṇī; and (4) supernatural faculties. These are also the five kinds of greatness found within the previous section on the Great Perfection (*mahāpariniṣṭhāna*), as they are based on wisdom.
It is combined with the *dhāraṇī* and explained as fourfold because they are all the virtuous functions of this stage; thus, these texts are stated concisely.
Second, "according to the thoughts of the mind" and below: this relies on the external karmic function of great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arising from external objects.
Third, "the mutual exertion of power within the preceding section" is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That is to say, the function of transformation is supernormal power.
[The] Characteristics. These latter two sections have the same scriptural text, but their meaning is divided into two interpretations; therefore, they constitute two sections. 4.

"Or, manifesting within a single thought-moment according to the mental inclinations [of beings]" and below refers to the characteristic of sustaining [the teaching], which is constantly employed without interruption. 5.

"At that time, within the assembly" and below refers to the characteristic of causing joy, which severs the doubts and afflictions of the multitude. 6. "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva..."
"Having already been able to dwell securely below" refers to this great, supreme mark that transcends the preceding stage.

Within the second reliance on the external application of activity, external objects such as the earth and so forth are what are moved, because they are the *niśraya-vipāka* (retribution of the environment).

Furthermore, there are external objects such as one's own and others' bodies; these are the subsequently manifested bodies and so forth, which are the *samyag-vipāka* (correct retribution). Why is this?

The body and so forth are said to be external objects of attachment; this is explained by contrast with the aforementioned liberation, greatness, and so on, because those are internal attainments, whereas this body and so forth are spoken of as external phenomena.
The three types of self-characteristics are also of two kinds: first, those that transform external objects and so forth, which together with the bodies of others are termed "external" and so on;
second, those that manifest as one's own transformed body and so forth. This passage also subsumes these two. Regarding the first, the transformation of external objects, there are three [types].

First, the transformation from the brief to the extensive within the same category; second, the transformation of different matters regarding defilement and purity; third, the transformation of mastery over objective realms, such as the world-receptacle and its contents.
The third [type] can be understood through its own characteristics.
The fourth section, "Performing and Maintaining," consists of three parts: first, a general statement; second, a detailed exposition beginning with "Manifesting the Ineffable";

and third, a concluding summary by the Buddha’s son. Within the detailed exposition, there are ten points: first, offerings and praise through body and speech; second, the eightfold correspondence with the capacities of sentient beings;

third, the manifestation of events of the three periods of time through the body; fourth, the inclusion of lands within the body; fifth, the emission of wind from the pores; sixth, the appearance of Buddhas from oceanic flowers; seventh... [and so forth].

The bodily light shines everywhere; eight, the earth shakes as he exhales from his eight mouths; nine, he manifests the arising of the three calamities; ten, his body and the lands manifest signs. The conclusion at the end may be understood accordingly.
Fifth, in order to sever the doubts of those who have been inspired with joy, there are two kinds [of methods]: first, by manifesting the supernatural power of his own essence...

This section resolves the doubts of the assembly. Second, "O Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva abides in such wisdom," and so forth, clarifies the teaching of the Dharma in order to resolve the doubts of the assembly.
Within the preceding portion, there are two question-and-answer sequences; the first question-and-answer sequence reveals the unsurpassed supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) to cause the assembly to rejoice.
Later, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra spoke: "O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva [descends]... This clarifies the subsequent dialogue.

This supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is supreme and causes the assembly to rejoice. Within the preceding section, there are also two parts: first, the doubt of the great assembly—meaning that they raise doubts regarding the bodhisattvas, not doubting the Buddha;
second, Vimukticandra takes up these doubts and requests an explanation. Within Kūṭāgāra’s response, there are four parts: first, the person...

1. The definitive resolution of doubts; 2. At that time, the section beginning with "Liberation" reveals the names of the concentrations; 3. The section beginning with "Furthermore, he asks" clarifies the scope of their functional activity; 4.

The section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas dwell in the Cloud of Dharma" illustrates their vast abundance through analogy. Within the first of these four sections, there are also four parts.

First, the Dharma Lord enters meditative absorption; second, the assembly manifests within his body; third, they see the Buddha within his body; fourth, he withdraws his transformative functions and returns to his original state.
Within the section on "Manifesting Names," there is first a question and then an answer. Since his name was already revealed at the time of his initial entry into absorption, why is it asked again?
The commentary states: At that time, the Lord of Dharma entered meditative absorption in silence. Later, the compilers of the canon took this [passage] and placed it there.
Since it was not made manifest at the time [of the Buddha’s passing], this question is raised. In the response, the phrase "the essential nature of the Buddha-land" refers to entering this samādhi.
Because it can manifest Buddha-lands. Within the section on the scope of the functions of the three karmas, there are two parts: first the question, and then the answer.
In the answer, it is shown that not only does it manifest all lands as previously described, but its body can also manifest Buddha-lands exceeding the number of atoms in sands of the Ganges.

Regarding the threefold manifestation of its vastness through four aspects, the first is the vastness and multiplicity of what is attained; this refers to the fact that what is attained in this stage is neither one nor two. Therefore, it says:
One attains such immeasurable qualities as these. Second, from here below, the inconceivability of their karmic functions is elucidated.
Within this, twelve types are divided into two parts: first, an individual exposition; second, a concise summary. The first three concern the inconceivability of the actions of karma;

the second concerns the greatness of the aforementioned supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the third concerns the threefold knowledge of the past, present, and future (*traividya*); and the fourth concerns the aforementioned samādhis.
"Great. The first five powers of knowledge constitute the greatness of prior wisdom. The sixth, the playful engagement with the gates of liberation, constitutes the greatness of liberation.
The seventh, transformations and so forth, refers to external matters such as emanations; the concluding summary at the end may likewise be understood.

The second [section], the explanation of the questions and answers regarding that which has a superior, consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer by Vajragarbha and others. Within the former, the doubt of the bodhisattvas is raised as being equal to that of the Buddha.
The wording of the question is the same as above, and the intended meaning of the doubt can be understood by referring to the answer.

Within the latter, the actual answer, there are two parts: first, a general rebuke of the incorrectness of the question; second, from "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, a specific demonstration of the incorrectness of the question. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the analogy.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent section on the analogy: the "single clod of earth" is described in the treatise and the sūtra as being "two or three *māṣa*-sized lumps of soil.

The rest may be understood accordingly. In the subsequent section revealing [the meaning], there are two parts: first, a general clarification that the Buddha cannot be compared to the virtues of the Cloud of Dharma;

second, a provisional explanation of the characteristics of this incomparability, beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha, I now... Within the former, there is first the analogy and then the application to the dharma. Regarding the analogy, it says: "Just as the four continents..."
"Taking a small amount of earth from below" is a metaphor for the virtues of the previously mentioned Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) stage.

"The remainder is immeasurable" is a metaphor for that which was previously mentioned as being external and largely unstated. In the subsequent teaching, the phrase "this Cloud of Dharma and so forth" is precisely the synthesis of those remaining points not yet stated.
How much more so, then, regarding the Tathāgata; when the virtues of the Bodhisattva stages are fully explained, they will surely be inexhaustible.
[Even] for a *kalpa* of eons, how much more so now that we have only begun to speak briefly? To immediately desire to compare [this] to the Tathāgata is improper.
Within this, there are three levels: first, soil the size of a bean; second, the soil of the four continents (*cāturmahādvīpaka*); and third, the soil of the ground of infinite worlds.
It would be impossible even to compare the soil of the four continents to the soil of infinite worlds, let alone to compare the soil the size of a bean. By means of the Dharma-cloud...

One who possesses such virtues cannot even be compared to a Buddha, much less can a small portion of them be likened to the Tathāgata. Regarding the subsequent section that clarifies how they are not comparable, there are two parts:

first, a general statement; second, the actual clarification beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, even if... This clarification also has two parts: first, the means of comparison; second, the object of comparison beginning with "This one Tathāgata...
Within the former, there are three points: first, the multiplicity of the basis; [second,] each of the ten directions is individually... [no comparison].

1. The number of peripheral lands is greater than that of the central land. 2. The status of those who rely upon them [the Buddhas] is higher; that is, the Bodhisattvas who have attained this stage. 3. Those of high status are numerous;
that is, within the aforementioned many lands, they dwell packed shoulder-to-shoulder in succession, like rice or hemp stalks. 4.
Each of those many Bodhisattvas has accumulated practice for a long duration, namely for hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* kalpas. Among those compared hereafter...
Second. First, it clarifies comparing the many to the few; that is, the practices of many high-ranking positions over many kalpas are compared to a single Tathāgata.

Subsequently, from the "one hundredth part" [verse] downward, it clarifies that even this is not a fit comparison; that is, it is not merely that the aforementioned many, when viewed against the one, fail to compare.
Furthermore, even if one were to compare it to a hundredth part of a single Buddha’s merit, taking even a single portion down to the smallest fraction, it would still not approach it.
The subsequent section on "Expounding the Dharma to Sever Doubts" has two parts: first, the explanation of the practice of gentleness and flexibility;

second, from "The wisdom of the Bodhisattva on this stage" onwards, the teaching on the purity of knowledge. Both of these preceding passages contain the elements of the doctrine, the metaphor, and the application; they may be understood accordingly.

The sixth [chapter] on Great Victoriousness has two parts, each with two sub-sections. First, it clarifies mastery in teaching; second, "O Son of the Buddha" and so forth concludes the characteristics of this stage.

Within the first part, there are two: first, it clarifies the excellence of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); second, from "if one were to practice" onwards, it clarifies the excellence of calculation within the maturation of rewards (*vipākaphala*).

Because these two types of emptiness surpass all the preceding stages, they are called "Greatly Surpassing" (*mahāviśeṣa*). Within the preceding section, there are two parts: first, the restatement of what preceded;

second, from "All Buddhas... onwards, the actual exposition. This exposition consists of six phrases: the first five are specific, and the last one is a general conclusion. Among the five specific phrases, the treatise condenses them into three:
the first two are each one unit, and the latter three constitute one unit. First, regarding "the wisdom of the three periods of time": this is for the purpose of severing doubt.
Practice. Because it penetrates the three periods of time, it is called the supramundane path; thus, it bears the meaning of "path.
Second, the wisdom of the dharma-realm is the practice of swift supernatural power, for it consists in hearing the exposition of the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma.

Third, the final three phrases are called the auxiliary practices of equal action, meaning that one brings about equal transformation and benefit for all sentient beings. Within this, first, "purity" refers to the purification of the Buddha-land.

Because the Buddha transforms sentient beings with impartiality: second, "equal illumination" refers to the transformation through the wisdom of teaching, which is the equality of the light of the Dharma;

third, "equal compassionate mindfulness" refers to the transformation through the wisdom of realization, which is the equality of attaining perfect enlightenment. The final phrase is a summary, as can be understood.
The seventh major section: Within the "Section on the Reflections of the Ground," there are four metaphors that illustrate the four virtues of the ground.
The first three are based on scripture (*āgama*), while the last one is based on realization (*adhigama*). Regarding the former, the first metaphor of the pond illustrates the merit of cultivation;

this refers to the practice initiated within the various grounds. The second metaphor of the mountain illustrates the virtue of superior excellence; this refers to the virtues perfected based on the preceding cultivation, wherein the stage of virtue rises high above others. The third is the ocean.

This illustrates the merit of being difficult to cross and yet capable of crossing over to the great fruit. That is to say, the virtues accomplished through prior cultivation are able to reach the great fruit;

"crossing" (*tāra*) carries the sense of reaching. The analogy of the four jewels illustrates the merit of transformation, exhaustion, and firmness. This means that because one advances from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), it is called "transformation.
Because the stages have reached their limit and obstacles are exhausted, it is called "exhaustion. Because the realization of principle has reached its ultimate, it is called "firmness."

Within the initial cultivation of virtue, there are the elements of the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis. In the explanation of the Dharma, the stages beginning from the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā*) and ending with the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) are called the "gradual practices.

That these causes result in the great fruit is called "proceeding toward omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). In the analogy, the Anavatapta Lake—also known as the Lake Free from Heat and Torment—is named after its dragon king;
this represents the virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*), for they are free from the afflictions of hindrances. From it, four [rivers] emerge...
Regarding the rivers: the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* mentions eight rivers, while the *Āgama* states there are twenty.

In the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), it simply says that two thousand five hundred rivers emerge from Jambudvīpa and flow into the great ocean, without specifying their source.
As for the emergence of the four great rivers, this is based on the fundamental teaching. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter eleven, states: "From the center of this Jambudvīpa, toward..."
To the north, each of the three regions has its own triple range of Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇa-parvata*). To the north of these Black Mountains lies the Great Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*);

to the north of the Great Snowy Mountain lies Fragrant Intoxication Mountain (*Gandhamādana*). North of the Snowy Mountains and south of Fragrant Intoxication Mountain is a great body of water called the Untroubled (*Anavatapta*), from which four great rivers flow.
The rest is abbreviated as explained below in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, but since the Ten Samādhis are most comprehensive, they may be understood by seeking them there. Second.
Regarding the "ten rivers," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: The four rivers depart from the lake, each at a distance of forty *li*.

Each further divides into four branches that encircle the lake once and flow toward the great ocean from their respective original directions. Thus, including the four primary rivers, they total twenty.

(Examination) In the correspondence of the Dharma, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for benefiting others correspond to the four rivers; they fulfill [the needs of beings] inexhaustibly until all [beings are reached].
When wisdom increases, one accomplishes self-benefit and attains great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), merging into the great ocean. The *Śāstra* states:
"The practitioner relies on the power of their original vow. This explains that the water of roots of goodness and great vows flows forth from the bodhicitta.

"Benefiting others through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)" explains how those four means fulfill the wholesome qualities of sentient beings and oneself; thus, self-benefit can be understood.

Regarding the second section, the analogy of the mountains concerning superior merits, there are three parts: first, a general presentation of the dharmas; second, an illustration through the analogy beginning with "Just as...";
and third, a summary beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, these ten... In the first part, regarding the fact that the ten stages have distinctions because they are caused by the Buddha-wisdom:
This means that by taking the Buddha’s wisdom as the causal basis, one transcends these ten stages (*bhūmi*).

This Buddha-wisdom is of a single flavor and equality, serving as the basis for the distinctions of the ten stages, just as the great earth, being level, serves as the basis for high and low mountains.
The treatise states: "Because it relies on the superior practices of omniscience. Of the two metaphors used to illustrate this, the first lists the names of the ten mountains, followed by...
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the foot of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*). Each [section] is combined separately.

Regarding the preceding middle section, the Sanskrit names for the various mountains such as *Vidhara* and so forth are all clarified as they appear in the first volume of the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings). In the subsequent separate combinations, first, "medicinal herbs" (*oṣadhi*) are a metaphor for the noble wisdom of the first stage (*bhūmi*), because it is skilled in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Second, "various fragrances" are a metaphor for the second stage, because it is "fragrant. These two do not rely upon... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Because "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the primary factor for its name, the first stage is compared to an earthen mountain. Since the remaining eight stages are established based on wisdom, they are all compared to jewel mountains.

As for the three stages being "concentration" (*samādhi*), it is because their essence consists of the three types of wisdom and they are subsumed under wisdom. Regarding the "various jewel metaphors," these metaphorically represent the eight stages.
Furthermore, as for "the excellence and purity of the stages beyond aversion," this refers to the eight stages from the third stage upward.
"Jewel" (*ratna*). This is a further clarification. Regarding "all kinds of jewels": through pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they become weary of and detached from afflictions (*kleśa*);

since both this concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*) are worthy of esteem, it is so described. Regarding "the seers with the four supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi-vidhijña*): this is a metaphor for the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) transcending the mundane world.
Because the divine sages (ṛṣis) transcend the human realm, they represent the [first] five stages. The five yakṣa deities are a metaphor for the [next] five stages;

because they possess skill in the ultimate and conventional truths, they are able to harmonize what is difficult to harmonize and have attained mastery over the supernormal powers (abhijñā). The six fruits represent the contemplation of the gathering of causes and conditions, as they are provisionally associated with the fruits of the śrāvakas.

The seven nāga deities are a metaphor for the wisdom of the skillful means of emptiness in the seventh stage, as they are provisionally associated with the fruits of the pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, regarding those above this...

In the second stage, [the teaching] is based upon the Śrāvakas; the Bodhisattva transcends them, yet speaks of their realization of the fruit, for the questions and answers therein are inexhaustible—this is illustrated by the metaphor of the mountain producing fruits without end. Subsequently, [the teaching] is based upon the Pratyekabuddhas;

the Bodhisattva transcends them, yet speaks of their realization of the fruit, for the questions and answers therein are inexhaustible—this is illustrated by the metaphor of the mountain producing great powerful nāgas and spirits without end.

8. The various *īśvaras* (sovereigns) symbolize the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, who, without exerting effort, respond universally like water or a mirror image because they have attained the ten masteries (*vaśitā*).
9. The *asuras* symbolize the characteristic of the great power of the Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage, who skillfully gather and sustain sentient beings.
10. The various *devas* symbolize the sense of being preeminent; for the tenth stage is the most excellent among all other stages.

The treatise says: Furthermore, below the various mountains, it explains all things found within those mountains. These include sentient beings, such as ṛṣis and devas, and non-sentient entities, such as medicinal herbs and jewels.
Among these, the medicinal herbs and the like, which can support the internal retribution [of the body], are called "objects of enjoyment" (*paribhoga-vastu*).

Specifically, their removal of illness is called "remedial treatment for increase and decrease. Fragrant fruits that nourish the body are called "objects of growth" (*puṣṭi-vastu*). As for the substance of the jewels...
These are not for the sake of sustaining the body, but are merely stored away to eliminate poverty; this is what is meant by "guarding" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the Snowy Mountains and so forth," this specifies the location, namely the first three and the sixth [perfections], which are non-sentient. The subsequent explanation clarifies that they rely upon sentient beings.
Within this, six kinds of hardships are remedied: first, by making offerings to the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) possessing the five supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), one attains wealth.

1. Overcoming the hardship of poverty: This is analogous to the Bodhisattva of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), who practices the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). By transforming and curing the poverty of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), he benefits sentient beings;

this is like the two yakṣas who exercise sovereign control over their retinues so as not to allow them to harm sentient beings. 2. Overcoming the hardship of death: This is analogous to the Bodhisattva of the fifth stage, who practices the non-abiding path (*apratisthita-mārga*).

Although both [the fourth and fifth stages] are without abiding, [the fifth-stage Bodhisattva] remains constantly within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to rescue those in suffering; this is like the dragon’s descent.

"Rain" treats the difficulty of parsimony. This is a metaphor for the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), because its ultimate practice of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) benefits others by treating the parsimony of effortful application.
"Obtaining mastery over the assembly" treats the difficulty of those who are undisciplined. This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage for two reasons:
first, because they obtain the Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi to manifest his form and protect those beings of fierce nature, so that upon seeing him, they are transformed.
Second, the attainment of the ten masteries for the purpose of taming sentient beings. Fifth, the asuras who recite mantras to remedy the difficulties of evil karma;
this is analogous to the bodhisattvas of the ninth stage, who attain the forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence and skillfully preach the Dharma, let alone their ability to remedy afflictions and karma.

Sixth, the devas of great majesty and power. The treatise states that the four Great Kings exercise mastery over the difficulty of hostile enemies; however, the sūtras and śāstras present different explanations.

Regarding the name: the Sūtra says "Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahātejas*), which reveals that Śakra and the other thirty-three heavenly kings are able to subdue the enemies and adversaries, the Asuras.
The Treatise says "those who govern the enemies of the Four Heavenly Kings," because they are adjacent to Śakra.

It is a metaphor for when one attains the rank of a Buddha at the tenth stage, gaining the powers and fearlessnesses to subjugate Māra, his enemies, and the non-Buddhists. The Treatise says: "All these..."
That which is gathered within the mountain is that which, according to its function, can produce all things; this refers to all things existing within the mountains.
That which is said to be gathered therein and is inexhaustible is so because it proceeds in accordance with its nature without interruption or rest.
"Proceeding in accordance" (*anupravṛtti*) means successive continuity; "without interruption" (*anucchinna*) means not being permanently severed, rather than merely being temporary.

Because there is no [other cause], it is called "uninterrupted. To explain below the names derived from the mutual dependence of mountains and seas: it means that because the mountain depends on the sea, it receives the name of being "high and eminent";
because the sea depends on the mountain, it receives the name of being "deep and vast. Previously, the reliance upon the earth was explained; now, the reliance upon the sea is explained.
Because those ten mountains rely upon these two locations, they are mentioned in relation to one another. This explains the analogy of the shared characteristics of the Dharma:

that is to say, the Buddha’s wisdom is like the ocean, and it gives rise to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) based upon it; because their qualities of height and depth are mutually manifest, it is said that cause and effect are mutually manifest.

Thus, beneath each and every mountain there is a great ocean, and within each and every stage there is the Buddha-stage. One should know that the essence of the Buddha is omnipresent throughout all [stages].

The Grounds. If that is so, the Buddha-body is likewise omnipresent within the bodies of all bodhisattvas on the ten grounds; this is explained according to the principle that their nature and characteristics are neither identical nor different.
Third, the ten aspects of the great ocean illustrate the merit of the great fruit—the difficulty of being crossed and the ability to cross it. This section has two parts; first, the analogy.
This clarifies the subsequent correspondence between the bodhisattva practices and the lower dharmas, each having both general and specific aspects.

Regarding the statement in the preceding section that they are "incapable of being shifted or taken away," this means that these ten characteristics, like a single great ocean, cannot be altered or deprived of their single flavor.

The dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise identical to the Buddha-wisdom; though conceptually divided into ten, they cannot be shifted or made different. The *Śāstra* states: "Difficult to cross, yet capable of being crossed..."

Regarding "the one who possesses great merit for crossing over": because cause and effect accord with one another, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are like a great ocean capable of crossing over that which is difficult to cross, for they result in the attainment of the fruit of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
