[He] knows. The fourth dhyāna is concluded.

Regarding the fifth, the Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of Knowing Transcended Dharmas, there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. The initial inquiry may be understood [by the reader].

In the second part, the explanation, there are five sections. First: knowing the characteristics of the sequence of deeds performed by past Buddhas when they appeared in the world. There are ten [points].
[The preceding] phrases may be understood. Second, "O Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains" and below clarifies the increase and expansion of wisdom.

Regarding the previously mentioned benefits of the lands (*kṣetra*), within the ten phrases therein, the fifth states: "knowing the Dharma. This has two meanings: first, knowing the teachings (*śāsana*);
second, knowing mundane and supramundane phenomena (*dharma*). The rest may be understood accordingly. Third, "O Sons of the Buddha, this samādhi is named" and below clarifies...
A single thought-moment enters into kalpas; from the few to the many, there are thirteen stages, which may be known. [The passage] "O Sons of the Buddha, those Bodhisattvas...
below clarifies that although they enter the concentration of the past, they do not extinguish present phenomena.

Furthermore, because they do not exert effort to take the past as an object, it is said that they "do not take the past as an object. Why do they not extinguish the present? If they were to extinguish the present, [it would follow that...]
Thus, there is no past that can be taken as an object. Why is this? For even the nine periods of time are but a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is itself the nine periods of time;
how much more so, then, could the past and the present not coexist? Among the five clarifications regarding the benefits obtained upon emerging from meditative absorption, three are presented here:

first, a general explanation enumerating the categories, which states that reaching the culmination of the stages and attaining fruition is called "receiving the inconceivable dharma of consecration. Second, [the benefit] belongs to oneself.

1. Attainment (*prāpti*). 2. Purification through the attainment of cleansing (*viśuddhi*). 3. Fulfillment (*niṣṭhā*), termed accomplishment (*siddhi*). 4. Convergence (*anupraveśa*), termed entry (*praveśa*).
5. Realization (*adhigama*). 6. Perfection (*paripūri*). 7. Sustenance (*dhṛti*). 8. Universal equality (*samatā-sarvajñatā*). Regarding the "purity of the three wheels" (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*):

it refers to the three types of action (*trikarma*) being free from obstructions. Within the second section, "What are they? and so forth, there are ten internal points. Of these, the first four are the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). It may be...

This is known. There is no error in speaking of two minds. The next two serve as a basis for those who have not yet experienced suffering so that they may avoid it, and for those who have already experienced it, so that they may be rescued and liberated.

The final two are excellent due to their causes and sublime in their resultant state. The three summaries are attained at the time of realization; this can be understood through the combination of the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
The names of the summaries are easy to understand. The fifth [chapter on] concentration is concluded.

Regarding the sixth, the Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom, there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. The initial inquiry is self-evident.

In the subsequent explanation, there are ten sections: the first six correctly clarify the functional activity (*karmayoga*) of this samādhi, while the latter four clarify the benefits gained from abiding in this samādhi.
Regarding the first section, the first [of the three] generally knows all future Buddhas; the second, "namely, below," specifically knows their names and titles, consisting of nine phrases;
the third, "constantly appearing, below," clarifies the Buddha’s activities, which consist of twelve phrases: the first two concern appearing to benefit sentient beings;
the next two concern acting as Dharma-kings, succeeding previous Buddhas, subduing Māras, overcoming outsiders, and so forth; the next two concern preaching...
Regarding worldly and world-transcending merit: the next two [verses] explain the progression toward good and the treatment of evil as the correct divisions.

Within these two divisions of good and evil, "good" is one's own portion; therefore, the next two clarify the cultivation of signs and the signless. The final two positions represent the fulfillment of the fruit. Fourth, from "Those Tathāgatas... onwards, the wisdom is elucidated;
the ten phrases concerning those Buddhas' perfection of causes and fulfillment of fruits can be understood accordingly. Fifth, "Those Tathāgatas... [continues].
When [the names] of their coming, lineage, and clan appear, one also knows the names, lineages, and deeds of those Buddhas, as well as their entry into *nirvāṇa* and so forth.

Sixth, regarding "this bodhisattva" and below: "being able to enter such inexhaustible eons in a single thought-moment" explains the number of eons in which future Buddhas will appear, which was previously mentioned; thus it says "entering eons as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm."
One enters into kalpas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field. This passage must be verified against the Sanskrit original;

according to the eighth dhyāna, it proceeds from the trichiliocosm to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great trichiliocosms. Thus concludes the formal elucidation of the matter of samādhi.

The subsequent four sections clarify the benefits gained by abiding in this concentration: first, the benefit of attaining the gate of sustaining entry; second, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, O Son of the Buddha...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling herein obtain the benefit of excellent merit below; the [first] two above are for their own benefit.

Third, O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thus obtain the benefit of non-emptiness below. Fourth, O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling herein obtain the benefit of reverent support below;
the [first] two above are for the benefit of others. Within the first [section], there are ten kinds: first, mindfully recollecting and upholding the Buddhas, they are protected by the Buddhas.

1. Because of mindfulness; 2. because the mind abides in and sustains the Dharma, attaining *dhāraṇī* and eloquence; 3. because sustaining practice fulfills one's vows; 4. because one’s spiritual power cannot be overcome; 5.
because the power of wisdom sustains the practiced Dharma without obstruction; 6. because one sustains the Dharma through compassion to preach it for the sake of sentient beings; 7.
because one skillfully sustains phrases and syllables so that the Dharma becomes clear and pure; 8. because one does not fear the cycle of birth and death—this is what is received.
Taking birth in the three realms is called the "Dharma-holding of the Lion’s Birth.

This means that with such courage in the mind and a resolve for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), one does not avoid the mud, but rather emerges from it. Ninth is the power of wisdom, which sustains practice without rest.
Tenth is the power of spiritual friends, which supports and purifies many capacities. Eleventh is the power of non-abiding, which sustains the ability to enter into many [realms].
Kalpa. Twelfth, through skillful wisdom, one knows that the nature of all phenomena is pure; this is the sustaining power of not entering into phenomena.

Within the second section, "The Benefit of Skillfulness in the Dharma," there are three parts: first, the explanation of the dharma; second, the illustration by means of a simile beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising of the sun";
and third, the application of the dharma beginning with "This great samādhi. Within the first part, there are twelve kinds; the first two are skillful...

Regarding the periods and locations of abiding: next, three [knowledges] skillfully know the categories of the faculties of sentient beings; next, three skillfully know the faculties, conduct, and intentions of sentient beings;

next, two skillfully know the teaching of the Dharma and the appearance of Buddhas; and the final two skillfully know the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Regarding the analogies used to illustrate these:

the analogy of the light of the sun being without thought is presented first, and the subsequent application of the Dharma (*dharma-saṃyoga*) may be understood accordingly. Within the third section on attaining non-empty benefits, there are ten types.
This means that if there are sentient beings who see, hear, or dwell together with this bodhisattva regarding the activities of his three karmas, they all obtain superior benefit;
none pass by in vain. Therefore, it is called "not empty. The text is easy to understand.

Fourth, because sentient beings receive this non-empty benefit, the ten kings, including the devas, subsequently offer congratulations, gratitude, and offerings; these points are likewise easy to comprehend. First.
The six concentrations are concluded.

Regarding the seventh concentration, "The Concentration of Thoroughly Knowing the Buddha-Adornments of All Worlds," there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.

Within the initial inquiry, there are two layers: the first inquires into the meaning, and the second inquires into the name. In the subsequent explanation of the meaning, the name is explained first.
The following provides an explanation of the meaning: Because one abides in this meditative concentration, one is able to enter the worlds of the ten directions in succession;
this is the thorough knowledge of all worlds. To see all Buddhas appearing in the world and manifesting their spiritual powers and so forth is the adornment of the Buddhas.

Within this, there are two parts. First, the essential nature of this samādhi is clarified; second, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi and achieves...

onwards, the benefits of attaining this samādhi are clarified. Within the first part, there are eight sections. The first clarifies that by dwelling in this samādhi, one can enter the worlds of the ten directions;
these are the present worlds, as they are distinguished from the preceding two samādhis which clarify the past and future. Second, all...
The following section clarifies ten matters concerning the extensive observation of the activities of the appearance of various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
However, these ten matters do not belong to a single Buddha alone; rather, they apply universally to the many Buddhas throughout the ten directions, all of whom possess them equally.
To manifest inexhaustibility, the ten [categories] are clarified. All subsequent sections should be understood according to this principle.

Third, "also seeing the assemblies of all Buddhas" and so forth clarifies the seeing of the various retinues and followers of all Buddhas, as well as the capacities of those they transform; the distinctions among these ten types may be known accordingly.
Fourth, one also sees that the assemblies are small in scale; one sees that the number of those in the assembly varies, differing in quantity.
One may understand that the twenty gates are missing one. Fifth, one also sees the various Buddhas therein;

one sees those Buddhas each manifesting different signs within their own respective assemblies for the sake of transforming sentient beings; thus they are called "various signs. This is because the duration of their stay varies.
Regarding the phrase "various times" and so forth, the ten types [of visions] may be understood by analogy.

Sixth, the passage beginning with "the bodhisattva-mahāsattva also sees himself going there" clarifies that the bodhisattva goes among the various assemblies, whether to preach the Dharma or uphold it, up to the point where he sees himself entering the various dharmas;
this constitutes nineteen gates. Seventh, the passage beginning with "when seeing thus" clarifies that although one sees while in meditative concentration, the mind does not...
Movement is likewise without conceptual differentiation. This consists of the union of the dharma and the metaphor. Within the dharma, the eight phrases may be understood as follows:

it clarifies that the various dharmas which are the referents (the signified) cannot conceptually differentiate their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet they do not abandon that intrinsic nature. The same applies to the sounds and names which are the designators (the signifiers);

they do not conceptually differentiate themselves, nor do they extinguish the names. Regarding the synthesis, following the sequence from the end, the synthesis does not abandon the practice of practice.

This means that when a bodhisattva practices the relinquishing of what accords with the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) without abandoning it, and acts in accordance with worldly conventions without extinguishing names and designations—
yet remains unattached to these two— it accords with the non-differentiation of each of the preceding two stages. From the passage, "O sons of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the immeasurable light and color of the Buddha," below, it clarifies that the physical dimensions of the Buddhas they perceive differ.

Among these five, first is the clear vision [of the Buddha]. Second, "or seeing the Buddha’s body with various lights," and so forth, clarifies that ten types of visions of the Buddha’s body differ in color.
Third, "or seeing the Buddha complete in measure," and so forth, clarifies that the proportions of the Buddha’s body parts differ.
4. "O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas see thus below. This refers to the color, form, and activity of the Buddha-body as it is perceived.
5. "O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas see the Buddha-body thus below. This clarifies that although there are differences in what is seen, the Buddha has neither increase nor decrease.

Within this, there are three metaphors: first, the metaphor of emptiness having neither increase nor decrease. It is like when worldly people take a mustard seed and [compare] the empty space within a cypress tree...

In many worlds, the space within them varies in width and breadth; yet true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not like this, for it conforms to the magnitude of phenomena while its principle remains infinitely vast and devoid of dual characteristics.
Thus, it neither increases nor decreases. This may be understood through analogy. The analogy of two moons neither increasing nor decreasing can likewise be applied to the Dharma.
Third is the analogy of the mind manifesting according to birth: that is, through wholesome karma one perceives purity. This may likewise be understood through application to the Dharma.
The Sanskrit text says: For example, when sentient beings, after the end of their lives and just before they are about to take rebirth, recollect [their past] with a pure and unobstructed mind;

so too it is for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Abiding in this samādhi, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, he knows the various adornments of all worlds with a pure and unobstructed mind. "O Son of the Buddha" and below, as in the previous section.

The essence and function of samādhi are concluded. Second, regarding the elucidation of the benefits of attaining meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), there are seven types. First, the benefit of swiftly accomplishing practice and vows consists of ten phrases, which may be understood through the standard commentary.
Second, from the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva... up to the attainment of the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*) equal to that of a Buddha, there are ten kinds of benefits.
Among these, the first two indicate equality in merit and wisdom; the next two indicate equality in the objects of the Two Truths; and the following two indicate equality in essence and function.
The same. Next, the two [verses] on non-abiding are identical. The first line indicates not abiding in saṃsāra; the second line indicates not abiding in nirvāṇa.

Finally, the two [verses] on skillful means and equanimity are identical. From "O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish this" onwards, it clarifies how the person is perfected through these virtues and benefits others.
Within this section, there are two parts: first, the general designation of the name to manifest the perfection of cultivation; second, from "This is the Great Teacher" onwards...

This clearly explains its benefits. Within this section, each instance first identifies the person and subsequently explains their virtuous functions. The first two form a pair: first, possessing self-virtue that does not depend on others;
second, possessing great resolve capable of awakening others. The next two form another pair: first, internally realizing the purity of nature;
second, externally saving the world. The final two form yet another pair: first, comforting those who are terrified; second, causing them to abide [in the Dharma].
Regarding the spiritual lineage (*gotra*): the next two form one pair: first, the reality of wisdom; second, the reality of speech. The final two form another pair:

first, being fully replete within the treasury of the Dharma; second, sprinkling the rain of the Dharma externally. As for the four similes of the Buddha below, they demonstrate the benefit of attaining the treasury of vast knowledge.

Within this, there are two parts: first the simile, and then the application to the Dharma. In the simile, the analogy of the crest-jewel of the Heavenly Emperor Śakra is presented, which may be understood through its ten superior characteristics.

Within the ten [knowledges] among the dharmas, the first two are the knowledge that illuminates the lands and knows the arising of beings; the next two are the knowledge of transformation and entering the body of a Buddha;

the next two are the knowledge of the pure dharma of the Buddha-dharmas; the next two are the knowledge of causing entry into the Dharma-body and seeing the Dharma; and the final two are the knowledge of reaching the shore without remainder.
Below this, when the five sons of the Buddha—the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—abide [in these], they obtain the benefit of a tranquil, pure, and majestic body.
This refers to the names derived from emitting light from the body and manifesting transformations with mastery. Among these ten, they are: first, illuminating lands; second, purifying them;

third, harmonizing sentient beings; fourth, drawing near to the Buddha; fifth, serving the Buddha; sixth, making offerings to the Buddha while harmonizing sentient beings; and seventh, bringing sentient beings to maturity.
8. Inviting the Dharma from afar; 9. Ensuring that seeing and hearing are not in vain; 10. Revealing the secret Dharma. From "The Buddha’s son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having attained this...
onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the perfect benefit of benefiting others. Within this, there are two parts: first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent;
second, from "What are the ten? onwards, it clearly reveals the ten benefits. Among these ten benefits, the first two cause one to see the Buddha.
They have faith in the Buddha. The next two [powers] cause them to hear the Dharma and know the buddha-fields. The next two cause them to see the power of the Buddha and the power of his karma.
The next two cause their meditative concentration to become perfected as they enter the pure realm of the Buddha. The final two cause them to give rise to the wisdom-mind and achieve perfection.

The Sanskrit original states that these enable sentient beings to attain the perfection of ten kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Following this, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the seven sons of the Buddha, cause sentient beings to descend [into the stages].

This clarifies the benefit of turning [the faculties] toward benefiting others so that they may perform the deeds of a Buddha. This section has two parts: first, restating the preceding to introduce the subsequent;
second, from "What are the ten? onwards, the actual exposition. Within the exposition, the first two [faculties] awaken sentient beings through sound and form.

The next two [faculties] internally employ recollection and externally move the world-system. The next two [faculties] manifest signs within dreams as skillful means for awakening. The next two [faculties]...

The illumination of practice; the next two [refer to] attaining Buddhahood and turning the wheel of Dharma; the final two [refer to] the Buddha-activities of remaining in the world for a long life and entering parinirvāṇa.
These comprise twelve types, which is an increased enumeration. The concluding names at the end may be understood accordingly. The seventh concentration is finished.

The eighth [section], "The Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of All Sentient Beings," contains three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this...
and so forth; and third, the conclusion beginning with "This is called...". The initial inquiry is clear. Within the explanation, there are three sections.

First, the ten dharmas of non-attachment through the virtue of dwelling in this samādhi can be understood by reference to the previous explanation. Second, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [and so on].

Below this, [the text] clarifies the characteristics of entering and emerging from samādhi. Within this section, there is first a question and subsequently an explanation. In the explanation, there are both the principle (*dharma*) and its analogies (*upamā*).

Regarding the principle, there is a brief general classification into ten categories: either entering and emerging among the forms of sentient beings within the six destinies of the primary retribution (*sambhoga*);
or entering and emerging within the objects and things of the secondary environment (*niśraya*); or entering and emerging based on the correspondence between the primary and secondary [retributions].

They emerge. This may refer to entering and emerging according to the number of things, whether many or few; or entering and emerging within the numerical range of sentient beings, whether many or few;
or the mutual entry and emergence of defiled and pure sentient beings; or entering and emerging regarding the various sense faculties, such as the eye;

or entering and emerging within the quantity of atoms; or entering and emerging into different holy bodies; or entering and emerging through the recollection of eons; or entering and emerging within both principle and phenomena.

Next, the "Son of the Buddha" provides four similes, beginning with "Suppose there were a person," to briefly correlate them with the preceding teachings. First is the simile of a ghost’s power sustaining a person; the application to the Dharma can be understood.
Second is the simile of raising a corpse through incantation; the application to the Dharma is likewise intelligible. Third is the simile of an Arhat manifesting supernatural powers;
the application to the Dharma can be known and is easy to comprehend. Fourth is the simile of one field and many sprouts; the application to the Dharma follows the analogy.
Third, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling below these [stages]. This clarifies the characteristics of the benefits obtained while dwelling in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Within this section, there are five parts. First, the benefit of receiving praise equal to that of the Buddha-fruit; the ten types [of praise] should be understood. The Sanskrit original states:

"Dwelling in this samādhi, one receives the praise due to one through ten kinds of methods of praise. Second, the benefit of obtaining radiant illumination; the ten praises should likewise be understood.
Third, the attainment of the benefit of non-action. This also has ten aspects, all of which clarify that the functional activity is without action;

this should be understood. Fourth, "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, dwelling in this... and below clarifies the sphere of the great function of mastery in entering and emerging from this samādhi, in two parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, "For example, like a magician" and below, uses six metaphors to illustrate that great function. The former...

The explanation according to the Dharma can be understood [as previously stated]. Within the metaphors: first, the metaphor of a magical illusion manifesting six objects; second, the metaphor of an asura secretly entering a lotus fiber.

In both cases above, the application to the Dharma can be understood. Third, the metaphor of a farmer sowing seeds, which illustrates the Bodhisattva’s virtue of mastery over both the one and the many.

The fourth is the analogy of conception and growth, which illustrates the bodhisattva’s virtue of accomplishing tasks through samādhi. The fifth is the analogy of the dragon sending clouds down from above;

the sixth is the analogy of the universal manifestation in the Brahma palace. Both analogies and their corresponding dharmas can be understood accordingly. From "O sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva...

onwards, it clarifies reaching the shore of the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which is easy to understand. The conclusion of the name follows, making it easy to comprehend. The eighth concentration is finished.

Regarding the ninth [concentration], the "Mastery over the Dharma Realm," there are three parts: first, the interrogation; second, the explanation beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... and so forth; and third, the conclusion beginning with "This is called...
The first part, the interrogation, is easily understood. In the second part, the explanation, there are three sections: first, the direct revelation of the essence and function of the concentration;

second, the clarification of the benefits achieved by attaining the concentration, beginning with "The bodhisattva thus well-knowing... and so forth; and third, the analogy, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Lake Anavatapta... and so forth.

Below, the analogies clarify the preceding two [sections]. The first [section] has four parts: (1) entering meditative absorption through the pores of one’s own body and understanding the phenomena of the three periods of time;
(2) "The Bodhisattva therein... and below, clarifying the cultivation of practice over many kalpas; (3) "Furthermore, therein...

and below, clarifying the entry into and emergence from samādhi over those many kalpas, as well as the performance of what is to be done and its formal explanation; and (4) because of attaining [realization] within the *dharmadhātu*.

Because of mastery. Fourth, "skillful discernment" and below clarifies that because one has mastery over the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one is able to skillfully discern the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth to their ultimate limit;
this may be understood. Second, within the section clarifying the benefits achieved through attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are ten types.
In one lifetime, they achieve ten thousand koṭis of merit; this may be understood through twenty-one phrases.
Second, "O Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess... and so on; they further attain inexhaustible functional power, which consists of twenty phrases.

Among these, the first ten clarify the capacities possessed, while the latter ten clarify the characteristics of those possessed capacities. Third, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... [and so forth].
The Mahāsattva dwells herein below. It is clarified that he is sustained by the Buddhas of the ten directions. This section has three parts: first, being sustained by the Buddhas;
second, the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma; third, causing those dwelling below to cultivate practice, obtain benefit, and enter the Dharma.

Fourth, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling herein below," which concludes the formation of benefits through the protection and mindfulness of those Buddhas. Fifth, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... [text continues].

Below this, it should be understood that the Bodhisattva dwelling here attains the benefit of the ten masteries of the ocean (*daśa-sāgara-vaśitā*). Sixth, one further attains the ten abilities (*daśa-śakti*), which are easy to understand.

Seventh, one further attains the benefit of the ten powers (*daśabala*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the ten powers are explained individually; second, the general capacity for manifold powers is explained.
8. "The Bodhisattva, Son of the Buddha" concludes [the section]. It should be understood that it possesses the ten phrases of the aforementioned superior capacities. 9.
"The Capabilities of This Bodhisattva" below clarifies that no one is able to describe the limits of this bodhisattva’s capabilities. 10.

"The Attainments of This Bodhisattva" below clarifies that his capabilities are so vast and numerous that they cannot be fully described. The above concludes the explanation of the benefits. Third, the analogies.

Of the two preceding sections, there are three parts: first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, the actual simile; and third, the application of the Dharma to the analogy. Within the first [section], there are two parts:

first, the thorough knowledge of the samādhis ranging from "unspeakable-unspeakable" onwards; second, the thorough knowledge of the objects of cognition and the tasks to be performed within each and every one of those samādhis—both of which can be understood.
In the second [section], the actual simile, three points are briefly explained: first, the lake from which four rivers flow; second, the space between the rivers.
Regarding the flowers and grasses, the manifestations of the three Dharma-jewels have many broad meanings, as will be analyzed below in the section on the conjunctions.

Third, regarding the "Son of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra) and the "Heatless" (Anavatapta) below, there is a conjunction of dharmas consisting of twelve sections. First, the four types of eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) are conjoined with the four rivers; first, the general conjunction.

Later, they are combined separately. Among these, "inexhaustible discernment" (*akṣaya-pratibhāna*) refers to the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna-bala*). The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the passage "like the four great rivers" and below:
this combines the three karmas of the Bodhisattva, which flow in the four directions and enter the ocean of fruition, with the analogy of the four rivers encircling a lake and entering the four seas.
As for the "four directions of the Bodhisattva": first, seeing the Buddha; second, hearing the Dharma; third, the perfection of wisdom; fourth, [the attainment of liberation].

The fulfillment of compassion is like the flowers between the four great rivers; it arises from the bodhicitta through the teaching of the Dharma and the training of beings, causing them to perceive the adornment of the buddha-fields—this may be understood by combining these points. Fourth, as described below regarding Lake Anavatapta:

because the bodhicitta is boundless, it may be understood that it is filled with the purity and goodness of those [fields], being vast in length and breadth, unturbid, and free from defilement. Regarding the six [aspects] within the bodhicitta:
[The character] *zi*. In the Sanskrit text it says: Within the realm of those to be converted, five points are like the Anavatapta Lake;
below this, the adornment of the shore with the jewel of bodhi-wisdom and the scattering of various fragrant incenses can be understood through their correspondence. Six:

Like the subtle wisdom and so forth at the bottom of the Anavatapta Lake, the golden sand corresponds to the various jewels of the Dharma, and the various *maṇi* gems correspond [to the various teachings]. Seven: Below "Anā" is the Bodhisattva.

"Manifesting birth without defilement, harmonizing with the Dragon King, and being free from affliction. Regarding the passage "The eight and four rivers moisten [all beings]," etc., it means that by means of the four wisdoms of the Bodhisattva, they moisten humans and devas, causing them to enter the ocean of the Buddha.
These four are: first, the wisdom of vows; second, the wisdom of practice; third, the wisdom of the Jewels; and fourth, the wisdom of compassion.
The correspondences can be understood as follows: 9. As with the four great oceans below, it clarifies that the bodhisattva practice culminates in entry into the ocean of the Buddha-fruit.
10. As with the four rivers below, it clarifies that the wisdom of practice enters the ocean of the Buddhas without anything able to create an obstruction.

11. As with the four rivers below, it clarifies that the practice enters the ocean of the Buddhas without weariness or fatigue. 12. "O Son of the Buddha, like the light of the sun" below, it clarifies the Bodhisattva...
Within each and every pore, one sees Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable lands; these merge with the golden sands and other elements, mutually reflecting one another.
Second, regarding the phrase "For what reason," and so forth, there are ten gates through which the manner of this interpenetration may be understood.
Second, [the passage] beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... shows that the Bodhisattva exercises mastery over both the provisional and the ultimate.
The twenty phrases of the section may be understood as follows. Regarding the third phrase, "although he skillfully enters the momentary [samādhi]," the Sanskrit original states:
"although he skillfully enters the meditative concentration on the limit of the moment (kṣaṇakoṭi-samādhi), he benefits sentient beings"—the subsequent parts are identical.
Next, regarding the passage "just as space," the Sanskrit original states: "just as space, although it can contain all things..."
Free from the notions of existence and non-existence, the names are subsequently concluded. This concludes the explanation of the ninth concentration (*samādhi*).

Within the tenth, the Unobstructed Wheel Concentration (*anāvaraṇa-cakra-samādhi*), there are three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters this...

and so forth; third, the conclusion of the name beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this is... The first, the inquiry, is easily understood. In the second, the explanation, there are two parts; first, the clarification... [text ends]... is explained.
The functional activity of samādhi at the time of entering meditative absorption also reveals the name of this concentration.

Following the passage "Afterward, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, abide in this... and below, the functional activity of samādhi at the time of emerging from absorption is clarified.

Within the preceding twenty phrases, the first eleven distinguish the function by way of causal practice, while the latter nine distinguish the function by way of the fruit. Second, [the section on] emerging from absorption.

Within the section on functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), there are six parts: 1. The function of contemplating the Buddha’s wisdom; 2. From "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses a lotus flower...

onwards, clarifying the function of manifesting the accomplishment of deeds; 3. From "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva enters such [a state]... onwards, clarifying the function of realizing and entering all phenomena (*dharmas*);
4. From "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in Samantabhadra... onwards, clarifying the abiding in Samantabhadra.

"The ten bodies" (*daśakāya*). Regarding the "ocean of the characteristics of the ten bodies," this is correctly explained both as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) and as a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound).

Second, as for the purpose of its inclusion, there are two aspects: first, it is a remote response to the question concerning the virtues of the Buddha-fruit at the beginning and end of the second assembly;

second, it is a proximate response to the preceding chapter, which generally elucidated the dharmas of the fruit, whereas this chapter specifically reveals the virtue of its characteristics. Therefore, it is included here.

Regarding the three essential points (*piṇḍārtha*): the thesis (*piṇḍa*) is to discern the ocean-like, boundless marks of the Buddha-fruit; the purpose (*artha*) is to reveal that distinct causes produce distinct fruits.

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text, there are three parts: first, the admonition to listen and the permission to speak; second, from "The Tathāgata’s crown" downwards, a brief explanation of the ninety [marks].

Seven aspects. Below the passage on the three sons of the Buddha, Vairocana, there is an extensive description of the marks numbering as many as the atoms within the ten Flower Treasury Worlds (*kusumagarbha*).
Within the second section, the "Brief Explanation," there are forty-six instances where the supporting locations of the marks are revealed.

If discussed in detail, the number of supporting locations for the marks is equal to the number of the marks themselves, because there are no overlaps. Within the text concerning each individual mark, there are sometimes five...
The four [categories] are the number three, two, and so forth. The five [aspects] refer to: first, the locus upon which the marks depend; second, the names of the marks; third, their adornment;
fourth, their functional activity; and fifth, the benefits they accomplish. Whether these are complete or incomplete is made clear by the respective texts.

Herein, the mark of the uṣṇīṣa is explained first and the mark of the feet is analyzed last, according to the *Buddhadhyānasamādhisāgara-sūtra*. There are both reverse and direct modes of contemplating the Buddha; here, it is the direct mode.
Contemplation. If one begins the contemplation from the feet, this is "contemplation in reverse order. Question: This clarifies the [thirty-two] major marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

As for the merit of these marks compared to the merit of the [eighty] secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) explained in the subsequent chapter, which is more substantial? Answer: Because the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* (or *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra*) itself contains a comparative analysis, the later text states:
"All the merit possessed by all the world does not equal the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata. A single [hair-pore of the Tathāgata...]"
The merit of all the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) does not equal that of a single primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

The merit of the collection of all eighty secondary marks does not equal that of a single primary mark. The merit of all the primary marks does not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) mark.
Furthermore, the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* does not equal the merit of the *uṣṇīṣa* (invisible crown protuberance) mark.

Regarding the first characteristic, there are three parts: first, a general indication of the locus of the characteristics and their common adornment; second, a specific exposition beginning with "Among them... and so forth;

Within the second, third, fourth, and fifth [characteristics], all follow the same three-part structure as the initial text. Regarding the two types of adornments within the sixth [characteristic]:

first, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva wears a crown made of jewel-flame *maṇi*; second, it clarifies that he possesses a garland made of jewels such as the Buddha-powers. [This concludes the section on] karma.
The middle [of the seven] can be understood. Of the seven, three can be understood. Within the eighth, there is the adornment of the interior.

As for the distinction between the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) and the *maṇi-ratna* (jewel-treasure), it is because the term *maṇi* alone signifies the "mind" (*citta*). Within the ninth, the three are the same as before with an addition. Within the tenth, there are three that benefit sentient beings. Within the eleventh, the three are the same as before. Within the twelfth, the karma benefits the world.
One attains the pure land and severs deluded thoughts. Regarding the thirteenth [chapter], three points are the same as above.

19. Regarding "endowed with a thousand wheels," the Sanskrit original says "endowed with a thousand-spoked wheels.

Twenty can be understood [as previously explained]. 21. Within the section on functional activity, it says: "manifesting the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

Regarding "Wondrous Treasury" (Sugatakośa): it refers to the sound emerging from the light, which explains the Buddha’s and Bodhisattvas’ wisdom and skillful means in preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
[Verses] twenty-two, twenty-three, and twenty-four can be understood from the text. Regarding verse twenty-five, concerning "karma," it says:
"extending a great net of flames," up to "manifesting to all sentient beings the entire ocean of karma. This refers to the sound emerging from the light that explains [this].
Wholesome and unwholesome karma is certain not to perish. Alternatively, it is said that this is because the ocean of karma for each and every sentient being is vast and expansive;
thus, [the points] twenty-six and twenty-seven may be understood accordingly. Regarding the twenty-eighth [point], light manifests within the three worlds;

thus, [the point] twenty-nine may be understood as lacking the description of adornment. Within the [thirtieth] karma, there is clarity regarding benefit; thus, it may be understood. Within the thirtieth, there is likewise no [description of] adornment.
Adornment (*vyūha*). Among the [thirty-one] marks, it brings about the benefit of seeing that which is not seen. Among the thirty-two [marks], there is likewise no adornment;

among the [thirty-three], as above, there is the name "adorned karma" (*vyūhakarma*). The preceding section has separately clarified the mark of the crown of the head. The passage beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata... is the conclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the fact that the term "cloud" (*megha*) is used throughout these various marks to express their names, the commentary on the old translation states:

This [term] has the meaning of pervasiveness, the meaning of moistening and benefiting, the meaning of having no substantial body, the meaning of non-obstruction, the meaning of manifesting signs, and the meaning of raining down.

It is said that throughout the preceding and following passages, when various offerings, Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, or the transformative Buddha-activities and so forth are described, this term is frequently used;
they all share one and the same meaning: namely, that when there is a response to a stimulus, a form appears, and that form necessarily brings about benefit, yet it comes without...

From wherever it arises, once its function is fulfilled, it departs; its departure leaves no lingering trace. Possessing these five virtues, it is like a cloud in the world; therefore, it is called a "cloud.
Third, from here below, there is one mark between the eyebrows (the *ūrṇā-kośa*). This has four aspects: its basis, its name, its adornment, and its function.

Seventh, regarding the statement "The tongue of the Tathāgata is further... and so forth: according to the Sanskrit original, the character "further" (復) is the character "characteristic" (相).
There are five points in the text: first, the basis; second, the name; third, the nature and form of the basis; fourth, the adornment; and fifth, the activity. Regarding the activity, it says:
"Its light universally illumines all buddha-fields that are composed of atoms. In the Sanskrit original, this reads: "the intrinsic nature of all buddha-fields is free from [atoms]."
Regarding the marks of dust: by the power of this light, it causes the marks of form and the lands to lack the mark of combination, thereby manifesting the mark of dispersed dust.

Those who are to be delivered according to their capacity see this and obtain benefit. This light is precisely the teaching of the Dharma of causes and conditions given during his time as a bodhisattva.
That there is no combination is due to the fact that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thirty-eighth: on the tip of the tongue, there are two marks.
In the preceding section [39], there are five parts: first, the locus; second, the name; third, the adornment; fourth, the activity; and fifth, the benefit.
In the subsequent section [40] regarding the thirty-nine marks, the five parts are the same as before. Regarding the fortieth mark: on the upper palate there is one mark;

Regarding the statement in the section on "karmic function" that he "dispenses the milk of the Dharma," "Dharma" refers to the teachings for bodhisattvas, for they are able to nourish their spiritual embryo.

It is called "milk" because it causes the accomplishment of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). It is called a "lamp" because it causes one to act in reliance upon that resolute conviction; because this is precious, it is called a "jewel.
These three are identical within the stage of the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), or they may be individually assigned to the three stages of the *śaikṣa*.

The basis, the name, and the function—these constitute the forty-seventh mark of the neck, with four textual sections. Regarding the accomplishment of the deep blue lotus among the ornaments, it is as explained in the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms).

The three characteristics. The first characteristic consists of four textual sections: namely, the locus (*āśraya*), the name (*nāman*), the adornment (*vyūha*), and the activity (*karma*). The second characteristic consists of fifty-one textual sections:

The original text reads *Śrī-vatsa*. [The characteristics consist of: 1) name, 2) adornment, 3) function, and 4) benefit.

[The mark of] increase. The fourth [set] consists of excluding the single [mark of] benefit. The fifty-ninth auspicious mark on the left side consists of five marks:
namely, the fifty-ninth, the sixty-sixth, the sixty-first, the sixty-second, and the sixty-third. In each of these textual passages, there are four [descriptions], as previously explained.

Regarding the "lower marks": here, the left and right sides are briefly omitted without being indicated; this was an omission by the translators. Upon re-examining the Sanskrit original, there are four items in each section:

From here begins the third major section: because a detailed explanation would be exhaustive, this follows with a summary of their inexhaustibility. It says:
"The Tathāgata Vairocana possesses such great beings as these, numbering as many as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury world-oceans."
They are equal. Regarding the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies," a brief outline of its textual structure shall be understood as follows.
In the thirty-fifth chapter, "The Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance," the explanation of the text for this chapter follows the same fourfold method as before.

First, regarding the explanation of the names: "Tathāgata" means one who has mounted the path of reality as it is. "Anuvyañjana" (secondary marks) means that they follow the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and further enhance the physical beauty.
"Prabhā" (light) means that which shines forth and dispels darkness. "Guṇa" (virtue) means that which is accomplished through practice and brings about benefit and assistance.

This indicates the person by means of their characteristics; from the characteristics, light is emitted; and through the light, benefit is obtained. Collectively, this is termed "the merit of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks (anuvyañjana) and radiance.
It is both "the light of the secondary marks" and "the secondary marks of the Tathāgata"; in all cases, the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound is applied.
If the secondary marks and so forth belong to the Tathāgata, they are called "the Tathāgata’s secondary marks," etc., which is precisely [the application of the dependent determinative].
These are all *vyadhikaraṇa* (possessive) compounds.

Second, regarding the intent [of this section]: the preceding chapter elucidated the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*); now, this chapter distinguishes the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Since the secondary signs possess superior benefits, they are manifested by means of the primary marks.
Regarding the three categories of tenets (*siddhānta*), there are two meanings: first, taking the discernment of excellence as the tenet and the manifestation of characteristics as the goal;
second, taking the exposition of excellence as the tenet and the revelation of benefit as the goal.
The commentary on the text has two parts. First, it clarifies the marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*) as the fruit; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, for my sake...

onwards, it distinguishes the marks of excellence as the cause. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, addressing the leading Bodhisattva; second, from "The Tathāgata... onwards, the actual exposition of the marks of excellence.

Regarding the first section, addressing "Ratnapāṇi" (Jewel-in-Hand): "Jewel" refers to merit; "hand" refers to faith. This is because he is about to explain the merit of the excellent light, and not [because his hand] is deep.

"One who plants the faculty of faith is not [defiled] by them; this is the indication. In the subsequent formal exposition, the Buddha himself states that "this is a subtle mark" because its function is vast;
had he not stated it himself, one might fear it would be difficult to accept with faith. Thus, the ancient masters said:
"The *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* is the point where the causes of differentiation are fulfilled; this chapter is the point where the fruits of differentiation are fulfilled. Each is exhaustive."
Because it is definitive. Regarding the statement that "the Buddha himself spoke [this]," this may not necessarily be the case. Why is this?

Because the *Daśadharma-samādhi-parivarta* (Chapter on the Ten Samādhis) is not the same as that [other text], and within it, there is also that which was spoken by the Buddha himself. There are three parts to the text: first, the excellent name;

the name "Ocean King" (*Pūrṇasāgara-rāja*) is given so that those who see or hear it may generate the merit of ultimate sovereignty. Second, following this, the name revealed by the light; it is named "Blazing" (*Jvalita*).

Because of the excellence of his virtues, the section on the light and its retinue is distinguished in three parts and seven hundred lines. Following this, within the explanation of the excellent marks of the cause, there are six sections:

first, the mark of the Bodhisattva emitting light from Tuṣita; second, the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, beneath the Bodhisattva’s feet," which clarifies the benefit of the light emitted from the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) beneath the feet;
third, the passage beginning with "O sons of the gods, you should all resolve," which exhorts the generation of the Great Mind (mahācitta); fourth... [and so forth].
1. "Purifying their minds" and below: exhorting them to repent and eliminate obstacles. 2. "When this Dharma was preached" and below: the assembly hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit. 3.
"At that time, the various devaputras [offered] superior flowers" and below: mutual benefit through successive transmission.

(3) the name of the light; (4) the places illuminated by the light; and (5) the benefits bestowed by the light upon that world below. Within the benefits, there are four: (1) liberation from the suffering of hell;

(2) the attainment of the ten faculties, such as the eyes and ears; (3) rebirth in the heavens; and (4) hearing the celestial drum explain the causes and conditions for rebirth in the heavens. Within this last point, there are four further sub-divisions.
First, because of non-negligence; second, because of planting merit; third, because of having previously associated with virtuous friends; fourth, because of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.

Excellent Name. Third, constantly setting aside [self-importance] to clarify excellent karmic function. Within karmic function, there are two parts: first, the indication of the total number; second, from "Among these...

second, the actual manifestation of what was said by me, beginning with "As I have said. Within the first part, there are three sections: 1. The exhortation of the celestial drum; 2. From "At that time, the sons of the gods...
onwards, they marvel at the sound of the drum and seek its cause; 3. From "At that time, the celestial drum... onwards, the drum explains the cause for its speaking. Regarding the cause:

This refers to the roots of goodness of the various devaputras. Hereafter, the six points are explicitly revealed: First, the drum proclaims "no-self" (anātman) while [the world] speaks of "self" (ātman). This is a metaphor for the Buddha realizing "no-self" while [the world] speaks of "self.
The analogy between the metaphor and the dharma in the text can be understood. Second, from the passage "Just as my voice...

onwards, it shows that the conditions for the drum's sound have no point of origin. This is a metaphor for the fact that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) has no place of arrival. The analogy between the metaphor and the dharma in the text can be understood.
Third, "For example, as with you all" and below. Hell and the body have no place from which they come; this is illustrated by light and sound having no place from which they arise.

This section contains two parts: first, the illustration; second, the application. Question: In the illustration, it says, "It is only because of your own perversions, etc., that the body of hell arises.
This implies there is an actual place from which it comes. Why, then, do you say that this has no fundamental basis? Answer: It arises from conditions.

All phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is precisely their lack of a fundamental basis. Other passages identical to this should be understood accordingly. 4. "For example, beneath Mount Sumeru...

This is a metaphor for the sourcelessness of objects of enjoyment; it is like a drum having no origin. Within the text, both the metaphor and its application are provided. 5. "For example, with a billion *nayuta*s...
This is a metaphor for how a single voice preaching the Dharma corresponds to many [beings]; it is like the light from a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) of a Bodhisattva manifesting as many.
The power of mastery consists of two parts: first, the actual application; second, the manifestation of superiority, beginning with "all śrāvakas... and so forth.
Within the first part, it says "great joy" because [the Buddha] accords with the faculties and inclinations of each individual. Thus, although he teaches for a long time, no weariness arises;

although he teaches for many assemblies, no discouragement arises; although he receives much reverence, no arrogance arises; and although he experiences much peace and happiness, no negligence arises.
[The section on] "Leaving. Sixth, [the passage beginning with] "O sons of gods, you should go down" and "exhorting them to offer worship while free from desire" contains two parts:

The five desires. Second, [the section on] being able to repay kindness and virtue. Within the subsequent distinct [sections], there are three parts. First, explaining the faults of the five desires in order to cause [beings] to abandon the obstacles of lacking wholesome roots;

this passage consists of three parts—the teaching, the metaphor, and the application—which can be understood accordingly. Second, from "You all should now... onwards, clarifying the loss and benefit of repaying kindness;

Now, you should resolve the dual bonds of harm and benefit. That is to say, if one abandons non-retribution and cultivates the practice of retribution, one turns from harm toward benefit;
therefore, it is said, "You should quickly turn [the mind] toward [enlightenment]," and so forth. Fourth, "As I am the celestial drum," and below, he preaches the Dharma for their sake.

Within this, there are two parts. First, the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness is explained; second, from "If you all can... onwards, it concludes by showing the benefits of accomplishing the contemplation.

Within the first part, there are two sections. The first clarifies emptiness regarding arising; first is the analogy, followed by the application of the principle (*dharma*). this reveals the departure from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. The subsequent section, beginning with "Just as I [and] the celestial drum," clarifies emptiness regarding phenomena (*dharma*); it is also...
First the analogy, then the teaching. Within the teaching, "the five aggregates do not arise" means they are not permanent; "they do not cease" means they are not annihilated.
Finally, the conclusion on the accomplishment of the benefit of contemplation: "Thus one enters the Seal of Non-reliance. "Seal" (mudrā) has the meaning of certainty;

it signifies that this concentration has no point of attachment and does not rely upon the sense faculties, objects, consciousness, or any other phenomena. All dharmas are sealed with this Seal of Non-reliance. One.
Because all phenomena are entirely without dependence. Regarding the subsequent section on the exhortation to practice offerings, there are seven points:

1. Abiding in the womb; 2. The assembly of the various devaputras below: each devaputra leads his retinue of bodhisattvas to attend upon him; 3. At that time, from within the celestial drum below:
the drum reveals the provisional and real aspects of the bodhisattva’s various births. Within this [section], there are two parts: first, the illustration by analogy;
second, the explanation according to the Dharma. In the explanation, it says "free from conceptual construction," meaning that the bodhisattva manifests the taking of birth, yet it is not real.
Because of birth and death; by removing arrogance, one prevents oneself from claiming that the celestial palaces are superior, thereby remaining free from defiled attachment;
and by causing one to renounce the five desires and seek bodhi.

Regarding the third section, "Exhorting to Generate the Great Mind," as for the term "Great Mind" (mahācitta) whose Sanskrit name is *anuttara* and so forth, this is translated here as "the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and universal enlightenment.
There are three aspects to the essence of this mind, as explained above.

In the fourth section, "Exhorting Repentance to Remove Obstructions," there are three parts. First, it clarifies the exhortation to repent for karmic obstructions. Second, from "Upon hearing these words" onwards, it asks about the method of repentance.
Third, from "At that time, the celestial drum" onwards, it explains the method of repentance. Within the first part, there are four sections.

First, it briefly indicates that the two karmas of body and mind serve as the conditions for repentance. Regarding the phrase "purifying the mind": it means to cause one to abandon defilements and purify conceptual discrimination.
Regarding "abiding in virtuous deportment": this means causing one to cultivate the characteristics and protocols of wholesome conduct without abiding in signs (*nimitta*).

Second, regarding the confession and removal of the obstacles to be confessed below, there are four kinds of obstacles: 1. **Karmic Obstacles**: In the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the five heinous acts (*ānantarya-karma*) obstruct the Noble Path;

here, seven heinous acts are listed, as the preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*) have been added. 2. **Afflictive Obstacles**: In the Lesser Vehicle, these consist of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), these constitute the hindrances.

Here, they refer to the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions—including the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and others—along with their derivative outflows, which are grasped as a real self through both conceptual and innate [ignorance].

Because they obstruct the two paths of seeing and cultivation, as well as the means for those paths, they are collectively termed "hindrances. Third, regarding the hindrance of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*): according to the Lesser Vehicle, it refers to the three evil destinies and the northern continent (*uttarakuru*).

The retributions of the Uttarakuru and the Unconscious Heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*) are obstructions because they can obstruct the Noble Path. Now, these are further augmented by the four fruits and four candidates for the [Śrāvaka] path;
these all constitute extreme obstructions to the two paths of seeing and meditation regarding Great Bodhi. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"It is not that going to the evil destinies is an extreme obstruction to Great Bodhi in the same way that abiding in the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha is."

Furthermore, various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras extensively elucidate this principle, as fully explained in the separately circulated chapter. Regarding the fourth, the obstacle of views (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*):
this refers exclusively to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), differing from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) which speaks only of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Were it not so, there would be the fault of redundant speech, as the five views are already included within the aforementioned afflictions. As for its mode of activity (*ākāra*), it consists in differentiating between the ultimate and conventional, and between principle and phenomena.

This clinging arises from being deluded regarding the meaning of the two aspects—true suchness following conditions yet remaining unchanging—and even clinging to the Buddha’s four wisdoms of enlightenment as being conditioned and untainted.
The second [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It may be said that the Tathāgata is the same as the conditioned for those with the false views of non-Buddhists;
however, a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts should not think so. If one says that the Tathāgata is conditioned, that is..."
"Lying. One should know that such a person, upon death, enters hell. ... up to the passage: "One should know that the Tathāgata is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Third, from "exhausting the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) downwards, there is a further elucidation of the vast repentance of the three karmas. This section is divided into four phrases, which are further categorized into three parts.

The first two phrases expand upon the previous practice of abiding firmly in dignified deportment and performing the five-fold wheel-prostration (*pañcamaṇḍala-praṇāma*). Of these, the first phrase concerns the body (*kāya*), which reveals—
The two elbows and two knees are the four wheels. The phrase "the crown of the head" at the end clarifies the wheel of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa-cakra*), which includes the preceding five.

Next, the single phrase "the tongue" extensively clarifies the activity of speech (*vāg-karman*); it explains that the nature of karmic obstructions is without dependence. Following this, with the passage beginning "exhausting the entire dharma-realm...

and even virtuous bodily activities," etc., the three activities (*tri-karman*) are summarized as all being equal in number to the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm. This is because...
Since beginningless time, hindrances have arisen and were never remedied; thus, one has engaged in攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging) toward objects without limit.
Because these hindering conditions pervade the realm of sentient beings, and because one now wishes to repent and eliminate them, the number [of recitations] must equal that [realm].

In the second section, the method for repentance (*kṣamaṇa*), there are two parts: first, hearing and rejoicing in the subject and object of repentance; second, from "Then he asked... onwards, the actual exposition.

In the third section, the explanation of the method for repentance, there are two parts: first, revealing the cause for the explanation; second, from "The various devaputras... onwards, the actual explanation.

Within the actual explanation, there are two parts: first, a general statement; second, from "The various devaputras, as I... onwards, the specific manifestation. In the former [the general statement], there are three parts. First, the citation...

One must be able to recognize the nature of karmic obstacles; for if one does not recognize them, they cannot be eliminated. Why, then, is the Bodhisattva specifically singled out? It is because the various devaputras deeply revere and place great faith in the grace of the Bodhisattva. Next, following the descent from the east, the text clearly elucidates the characteristics of repentance. Question: In this section, four obstacles are addressed regarding repentance; why is it that only karma is discussed? Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, [the other obstacles] are subsumed within karma. Second, karma is the most fundamental among the obstacles. Furthermore, since the obstacles of afflictions and the like arise from karma, by repenting of karma, one simultaneously repents of the others. Therefore, although there are four types of obstacles, the text speaks only of karma. Finally, because the Bodhisattva’s compassion is vast and his power is supreme, he is uniquely capable of eliminating these obstacles. Thus, the text mentions only karma. As for the phrase "descending from the east," this refers to the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s physical form. Regarding the question of why the Bodhisattva is mentioned first: it is because the Bodhisattva is the primary object of worship for the devas, and thus he is cited at the outset. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is the one who can eliminate these obstacles. For these reasons, the text mentions him first. As for the phrase "not descending from the east," this indicates that the Bodhisattva has already descended previously and is now manifesting his form in the space before the assembly. This is the meaning of "not descending. The term "space" (ākāśa) here refers to the void of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because the Dharma-realm is inherently pure and free from all obstructions, it is called "space. Because the Bodhisattva’s body is born from the Dharma-realm, it is said to "descend from space. This is the meaning of "not descending from the east. As for the phrase "manifesting his form": this means that the Bodhisattva manifests his physical body in order to preach the Dharma and save sentient beings. This is the meaning of "manifesting his form. First, because the four obstacles are mutually dependent and inseparable: the obstacle of views is the basis for afflictions;

based on afflictions, karma arises; and based on karma, retribution is experienced. Second, because they are equally observed through the contemplation of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in dependence upon conditions:
since a single contemplation universally remedies all four obstacles, if one relies on this understanding, the obstacles will not fail to cease, as there is no need to eliminate them separately.

[The previous section] is concluded. Regarding the three bodhisattvas, because they have formed wholesome consciousnesses that obstruct the essence of suffering, the latter part separately elucidates two points.

First, it specifically clarifies the method for repenting and removing obstructions through six gates, each with its respective metaphor and teaching. Second, from the passage "If one knows thus... onwards, it summarizes the true characteristics of the method of repentance.
Within the first of these [six], there are six [points]: first, the drum sound explains that karma is non-expressive yet expressible; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s non-expressiveness.
Furthermore, it is said: (1) The sound of the two celestial drums is without arising or ceasing, yet it can accord with awakening; this is a metaphor for how karma can accord with its retribution.

(2) The three drums constantly produce sound, free from the extremes of annihilation or permanence; this is a metaphor for how the Buddhas constantly teach, free from the extremes of annihilation or permanence.

(3) The drums allow all to hear joyfully according to their mental inclinations; the Buddhas are likewise, causing all to see [the truth] according to their minds. (4) A crystal mirror manifests the reflections of both the environment and sentient beings; this is a metaphor for... [the Buddha-body].
Karma and its manifest fruit have no coming or going. Just as a magician’s illusions deceive the eyes of others, so too karma and its manifest fruit are ultimately without reality.

In the final summary, it says: "If one knows thus," this restates the previously explained general and specific points—that the four obstacles are like illusions, arising through conditions and lacking intrinsic substance.
This is true repentance; it is directed against those of the Lesser Vehicle who, out of provisional Mahāyāna attachments, cling to the existence of subject and object.

Regarding the essence of the remedy: because that [remedy] is not ultimate reality, the claim that "all evils are completely purified" refers to the view that causes both the object to be remedied and the remedy itself to cease;
this is not ultimate purity, for it merely removes an obscuration by means of another obscuration.
Regarding the fourth section on the benefits gained by the assembly hearing the Dharma during the fifth period, there are four parts:

first, the sons of the Tuṣita devas from other realms attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); second, the sons of the devas of the six heavens of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-devaputra*) resolved their minds upon unexcelled bodhi;

third, all the goddesses (*devī*) of the six heavens of desire relinquished their female bodies and likewise resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle; fourth, at that time, the sons of the Tuṣita devas in this very place gained benefit. Regarding these...
The middle section has six parts: first, the benefit of attaining the stage of realization; second, the benefit of attaining samādhi; third, the benefit of greatly purifying the three karmas;
fourth, the confession and removal of the four obstacles; fifth, seeing many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and sixth, the fact that these benefits have not yet reached their full manifestation.
This means that although one has attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because it is not yet ultimate, one does not manifest even a small portion of one's power.
Regarding the sixth [section], the fourfold progressive increase: first, the benefit of the universal rain of fragrant flowers offered to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

second, the benefit for sentient beings who see the parasol beneath which they are situated; third, the benefit for those who, having briefly descended, see the previous wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) emitting [light]; [and fourth, the benefit of...]

The *Maṇiprabhā-vibhūti*. These four accomplishments are thus further elucidated by means of the analogy of the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Furthermore, there is the benefit of hearing the exposition of this analogy.

Within the first [of these], there are the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis. Within the Dharma, there are three parts. First, regarding "the superior multitude of flowers": the character "superior" (*shang*) is from the Sanskrit original.

The characters for "middle" (*zhōng*) and "before" (*qián*) refer to the various devaputras. When they were about to go before Vairocana Bodhisattva to make offerings, they manifested flowers, incense, music, banners, canopies, hymns, and so forth;
these are the flowers from among those manifestations. Second, many flowers further emanated from the pores of their bodies to collectively offer to the Buddha.
As for the scattering of flowers upon the bodies of billions of Buddhas, this symbolizes that one who scatters flowers will inevitably realize the fruit of their practice.

The third [point] concerns how, prior to this, the rain of fragrance benefits all lands; within that metaphor, it is further illustrated that those who are touched by the fragrance have their karmic obstructions eliminated and attain the bliss of liberation.

This is not because they experience actual pleasure through a transformation in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna, for that stage is characterized by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), not pleasure.
Thus, the metaphor is stated by taking a partial similarity. In the application (*yojana*), it says: "If there are any who hear it..."
This refers to none other than those who previously received the fragrance. This passage consists of four parts: first, "the fragrance" [refers to] citing those who previously received the fragrance;

second, "those various... and so forth, reveals the number of afflictions extinguished; third, "thoroughly knowing... and so forth, clarifies the distinction between subduing and destroying [afflictions];

fourth, "accomplishing... and so forth, distinguishes the benefit of attaining wholesome roots. Question: Since all six types provide benefit, why is it specifically said that they "hear"? Answer: Because...
Because incense brings benefit, among the categories of delusions, these eighty-four thousand afflictions possess only general names rather than specific details.
Consequently, various masters of the past have established diverse classifications. First, it is said that there are ten root afflictions of sentient beings;
yet each of these afflictions has ten further aspects, totaling one hundred. This should be divided as follows:

There are nine grades; however, because the superior grade is heavy, it is divided into three grades, while the middle and inferior grades, being light, each constitute one grade, totaling five grades, which equals five hundred.
Furthermore, these arise with respect to external and internal objects; that is, taking one's own five sense-objects as "internal."

Taking the five external sense-objects as external, there are five hundred for each, totaling five thousand. These represent distinct delusions regarding the Four Noble Truths, which constitute twenty thousand;
when added to the original one thousand, they total twenty-one thousand. Based on the many [afflictions] of the three poisons and the equal portion (*sama-bhāga*), they become eighty-four thousand.
Another explanation states that the ten unwholesome actions are the basis, which develop and mutually reinforce one another, with each [action] having five hundred...

Ten [factors] multiplied result in one hundred. Being deluded regarding one's own five sense objects results in five hundred; being deluded regarding those of others is likewise. Combined, there are one thousand.

This refers precisely to being deluded regarding the tenfold Dharma-gate of the Truths—namely, the Four Truths, Three Truths, Two Truths, and One Truth—or alternatively, the ten truths such as the "Truth of Sincerity" (cheng-di) and so forth, which differ according to the perspective of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
These further divide into twenty thousand. Or, it may also be categorized according to the ten wholesome paths of action and the two truths. It is also thus.

Twenty thousand, together with the original one thousand, total twenty-one thousand. Based on the predominance of the three poisons and their equal distribution, they constitute the eighty-four thousand afflictions.
Thirdly, according to the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra*, there are another eighty-four thousand.

This has been explained in the commentary on the Ninth Ground above. Although there are three interpretations, I shall now rely on the first two, as these two accord with the internal and external aspects of the scriptural text of this sūtra.
Regarding the passage in the section on "subduing and destroying" which states, "to fully realize that all such things are entirely false and illusory":

This merely involves realizing that the objects of the six sense faculties and so forth are illusory, thereby suppressing the afflictions so they do not arise; it is not their destruction or severance.

Alternatively, one may destroy and sever them such that all phenomena are realized as illusory, the marks [of phenomena] are exhausted, and the principle is realized—this is precisely the severing of delusions and the realization of Suchness (tathatā); there is no contradiction here. The fourth [stage], the attainment of the roots of goodness, may be understood accordingly.

Within the second section on the benefits of the two hindrances (*dṛṣṭi-nīvaraṇa*), there are three parts: the Dharma, the analogy, and the application. Regarding the first of these, there are two sub-sections.

First, it clarifies the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) numbering as many as the sands of one *gaṅgā-nadī*. According to the Sanskrit original, it is not merely the roots of goodness of one king and one *gaṅgā*; rather, it refers to the roots of goodness of wheel-turning kings equal in number to the sands of one *gaṅgā*.
Thus, the Sanskrit text states that they are "equal to the sands of the *Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-sama*). Subsequently, it describes the Bodhisattvas who dwell as sons of the Buddha.

The following clarifies the benefits for those to be converted by one who has attained this royal station. Regarding the phrase "among hundreds of thousands," etc., it precisely clarifies the scope of the realm.
According to the first fascicle of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Banyejing*), a Bodhisattva of the First Ground acts as a Caturmahārājika king;

he has ten thousand sons and, through a hundred dharma-bodies, transforms the sons of the gods throughout the ten directions within a hundred Buddha-lands. A Bodhisattva of the Second Ground acts as [a Śakradevendra]...
The Deva King Śūra has twenty thousand sons; from this point onward, the number of sons in each successive stage is the same. For brevity, the scope of their transformative realms is not detailed.

Since the first stage already encompasses a hundred Buddha-lands, one should know that the number increases progressively in each subsequent stage, until the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage becomes a Deva King of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
