According to his transformative realm, he [governs] as many pure golden [worlds] as there are grains of sand in one *gaṅgā-nadī*.
This is equal to the Universal Monarch of the Net (*jālapaticakravartin*), because this Bodhisattva has reached the ultimate limit of the stage of maturation (*vipākāvasthā*).

Next, in the analogy and its application, it is clarified that by merely hearing the name of that Buddha, one will necessarily be born in that Buddha-land; this reveals that upon seeing even a single tenth-stage Bodhisattva, one immediately attains the stage of the tenth bhūmi.

Third, within the section on the increasing radiance of the body of the previous wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*), there is a presentation consisting of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis (*yoga*).
Regarding the principle, it says: "If one encounters this light even for a moment," which refers to the preceding wheel-turning king emitting the radiance of the *maṇi* jewel.

Although such a person has not yet transcended the stage of fragmented existence (*bheda-bhava*), they will certainly attain the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). The phrase "by means of previously cultivated roots of goodness" clarifies this superior benefit; it does not arise without cause.

This is due to conditions; it is not by way of minor causes and conditions, but must necessarily arise from the planting of roots of goodness for this Great Teaching in past lives through seeing, hearing, believing, and rejoicing in it.
Thus, the analogy states: "Although one has not yet reached the end of life, one sees the abode of Brahmā," and further says: "One attains the various dhyānas," and so forth.
This is analogous to the three preceding dhyānas. It combines the middle two [stages]. First, it clarifies the emission of light;
subsequently, if there are sentient beings, it further clarifies the attainment of benefits. Within this, there are five points: first, attaining the stage of the tenth bhūmi;

second, accomplishing immeasurable wisdom-light; third, attaining ten kinds of purity for each of the six sense faculties; fourth, attaining the possession of immeasurable profound samādhis; fifth, even if...

The following uses analogies to further clarify this. Within the section on the benefits of hearing the explanation of the analogies, there are two parts: first, the clarification through the analogies;

second, from "If there is a son of good family" onwards, the clarification of the benefits of hearing the explanation of the analogies. Regarding the first part, it further clarifies that the "obscurations" and "light" seen above were all seen with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
What the fleshly eye perceives as obscurations and light is merely color-form (*rūpa*) within the obstructed space. How could they [otherwise] exist? How could one attain them?

Is it truly so beneficial? Although the text states that this is due to the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas and the merit of the Golden Net Wheel-Turning King Samādhi, in the end, it remains difficult to believe.

The second part, the detailed explanation through analogy, has two sections. First, a hypothetical analogy is presented to demonstrate the vast number of world-systems seen by the physical eye of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), as numerous as the atoms in those worlds.
Second, the passage beginning with "He also sees ten billion... clarifies the vastness of his vision of Buddhas. Within the first section, there are five parts.

The first is seeing world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in ten million *nayutas* of worlds; then, these worlds are further reduced to dust, which is distributed throughout the ten directions in numbers equal to the aforementioned atoms.
[He] then drops a single mote of dust from one world-system; he does the same for each of the ten directions until all the motes of dust from those world-systems have been dropped.

Furthermore, he takes the total number of world-systems represented by both the motes already dropped and those not yet dropped, and consolidates them all into a single world-system. [The Buddha] then uses his two jewel-hands to ask you questions and provide answers below this [consolidated world-system] to manifest its vastness.
Third, if there are sentient beings of inferior capacity, they gain benefit by hearing the explanation through parables, because it reveals that the buddha-fields are inconceivable.
Fourth, from "Even if one with a jewel-hand" onwards, the preceding numbers are accumulated again to reveal the vastness of the fields;

that is, taking those previously described vast fields and accumulating them until they equal the number of atoms in a thousand billion fields, and then pulverizing them into dust, one takes all the resulting dust particles—just as in the previous parable—and gathers them together to form a single land.

Furthermore, these are ground down into dust. This process is repeated eighty times. Fifth, all of this below clarifies that through the retribution of karma, the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) perceives, within a single thought-moment, the minute particles of all the vast world-systems before it. Subsequently, it perceives the vast multitude of Buddhas;
herein, the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis are presented, the text being clear and thus easily understood. This concludes the explanation of the Chapter on the Minor Marks (*anuvyañjana*).
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra (according to the Sanskrit manuscript, it is titled "The Exposition of the Conduct of Samantabhadra").
To explain the text of this chapter, it is analyzed through four sections.

In the initial explanation of the title, there are two parts: first, how the name is obtained; second, the explanation of the name. Regarding the former: this chapter designates its title based on the person.

The term "Universal" (*samantabhadra*) signifies pervasiveness, virtue, the Path, and the cause. This means that the body of this Bodhisattva pervades the entire Dharma-realm—whether the environment or the beings therein—even down to lands as small as atoms or the tip of a hair.
Furthermore, it is because he is fully endowed with the ocean of all virtuous qualities. Although...
Having attained perfect enlightenment, they do not abandon their causal practices; they exhaustively reach the furthest limits of the future, constantly cultivating benefit and happiness without end.
Therefore, the "Samādhi of Samantabhadra" chapter states: "Samantabhadra dwells pervasively in all lands, sitting upon a precious lotus flower, beheld by all."
It further says: "Samantabhadra constantly manifests various bodies, circulating throughout the entire dharma-realm and filling it completely. It also says:
"He manifests his form in all the lands belonging to all Buddha-bodies and proceeds to them. And it says:
"The vast ocean of Samantabhadra’s merit and virtue goes everywhere throughout the ten directions to attend upon the Buddhas; he is able to proceed to every land within all atoms."
It is clearly manifested. Furthermore, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, you are able, with your universal body, to go to all lands throughout the ten directions;

you deliver all beings within the great ocean of sentient beings, and there is not a single atom of the dharma-realm that you do not enter. It further says: "Entering into every atom of the dharma-realm, your body is inexhaustible and without distinction, pervading everywhere just like space.

Also, from the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities): [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific verses from the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* as requested.*
It says: "Because the self-body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is all-pervasive. The commentary explains: Here, "Samanta" (Universal) and "Bhadra" (Worthy/Excellent) each have distinct meanings;
this is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. If stated collectively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, because it refers to the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Second, regarding the intent of this section: from the preceding "Chapter on Names and Titles" up to the "Chapter on Minor Marks," the differentiated causes and effects were elucidated.

From this chapter onward, the manifestation of causes and effects is elucidated. Within this, the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" distinguishes the cause, while the "Chapter on Manifestation" clarifies the effect;
thus, it follows in sequence.

Regarding the three points of essential purpose (*abhiprāya*): these two subsequent chapters both concern the accomplishment of the fruit of mastery. Their essential purpose is the manifestation for the sake of sentient beings through cause and effect;
their ultimate aim is the provision of benefit and happiness throughout the limits of the future.
The commentary on the text has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. Within the prose, there are also two parts: first, the actual exposition;

second, from "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards, the manifestation of auspicious signs. Within the first part (the actual exposition), there are also two parts: first, the statement of the cause for the teaching; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... onwards, the actual revelation.
The preceding section has three parts: 1. The first points back to what was previously stated, namely that this is a brief explanation according to the capacity [of the audience].

This refers to the aforementioned distinctions between cause and effect. 2. The second part consists of the interrogation: "Why is this so? The intent of this interrogation is to ask why those aforementioned distinctions of cause and effect are presented here in such a concise manner.

3. The third part, beginning with "All Buddhas," provides the explanation. The intent of this explanation is as follows: Since both the distinct causes and the common causes are causes of causes, their practice has not yet... [text ends]
Universally, the fruits of differentiation are merely cause and effect. To briefly manifest the marks and signs would not yet permit a full exposition.
As for the manifestation of cause and effect: the cause consists of each and every practice that exhausts the entire Dharma-realm; the fruit is the realm of the fruit-of-fruits, which is like space.
The causes and effects are both exhausted; yet, because the benefit and happiness for future beings are inexhaustible, it was previously said that [the teaching] is brief and slight.

If this is so, why not simply speak of the manifestation of the causes and effects? Therefore, this commentary explains: "Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of sentient beings who are evil."
Regarding the explanation of the manifestation [of the Buddha], it is first explained by way of its distinctions.

It is said that he appears for the sake of all sentient beings who are ignorant and who follow the distant path of the current. Within this explanation of the reasons for the distinctions, ten types are briefly shown.

First, "ignorance and lack of wisdom" (*avidyā*) includes both the independent (*mūla-avidyā*) and the associated (*saṃprayukta*) types. Second, "the various entanglements of committing evil" (*paryavasthāna*)... [this exists].
There are eight kinds and ten kinds. The eight are as follows: torpor and drowsiness—these two obstruct *śamatha*;

restlessness and remorse—these two obstruct *vipaśyanā*; envy and avarice obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*); lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) obstruct ethical discipline (*śīla*).

The ten are as follows: to the aforementioned eight, anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are added. These all manifest and entangle the mind, causing it to lack autonomy. This is explained in detail in the treatise.

Explanation: Regarding the three types of "self and what belongs to self" (*ātman-ātmīya*), these pertain generally to both the views of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as detailed in a separate chapter.

Fourth, regarding the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*): among the five views, it refers exclusively to the view of a self-entity. Fifth, regarding the three, four, seven, and eight inversions (*viparyāsa*): "three" refers to the inversions of thought, perception, and view;

"four" refers to the inversion of taking the impermanent to be permanent, and so on, up to the inversion of taking the impure to be pure; "seven" refers to the aforementioned first three and the [first] four.
The eighth refers to the four [misconceptions] previously mentioned, namely the four such as regarding the impermanent as permanent. The sixth, doubt (*vicikitsā*), refers to mental hesitation.

The seventh, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), refers to a view among the five views that deviates from correct principle. The eighth, the fetters (*saṃyojana*), are of three, five, and nine kinds. The three are:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt. The five are: craving, aversion, pride, envy, and avarice. The nine are: craving and pride.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), grasping (*parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*). Regarding the nine fetters (*bandhana*), there are two types: fourfold and twofold.
The twofold consists of *nimitta* (sign) and *dausthulya* (dysfunction). As for *nimitta*, there are two explanations. One says that *nimitta* refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*);

because it is acquired through outflows (*sāsrava*), it causes the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) to lack autonomy, and this is termed the "fetter of signs" (*nimittabandhana*). This sign itself is the fetter, hence it is called the "fetter of signs. Another says:

The seventh manas-consciousness serves as the essence of the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*). Because of the seventh consciousness, the other consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, do not attain mastery over their respective objects of perception.
If one speaks of the bondage of signs based on this, it is called the bondage of signs. Regarding the bondage of heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*), there are also two kinds.
One says that the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*) within contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is called the bondage of heavy dysfunction; it is associated with the contaminated.

The dharmas are neither identical nor different. Because they lack a separate substantial essence, they are not real; because there is a distinction between those that are severed and those that are not, they are not one.

Second, it is said that the seeds of the two obstacles are collectively termed *dausthulya* (heaviness). Although there are these two explanations, taking the seeds as the primary meaning is superior.

Alternatively, some say that all outflowing (*āsrava*) objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) are called the "bondage of signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*), because they cause the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) to lack sovereignty. That is to say...

That which binds the various afflictions (*kleśa*) upon the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is called the "bond of heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulyabandhana*), because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse. To state it generally:

the objective aspect that serves as the object of perception is called the "bond of signs" (*nimittabandhana*); the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) that perceives it, along with the various afflictions such as greed, is called the "bond of heaviness.

Fourth, greed, hatred, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)—these ten should be understood as the "far-reaching paths" (*anuśaya*). The final phrase is a conclusion; it concludes [the section].
The intent is this: the World-Honored One appeared for the sake of sentient beings who are hindered by manifold delusions;
therefore, he first had to explain the causes and effects of differentiation, and only afterwards did he explain the causes and effects of manifestation.
Next, the actual exposition clarifies two types. First, it distinguishes the objects to be remedied, which are extensive and numerous, consisting of one million hindrances.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... onwards, it clarifies the remedies, which are vast and consist of sixty types of practices. Within the first of these [two], there are three parts: first, a general enumeration;

second, a detailed explanation starting with "What are they..."; and third, a conclusion starting with "O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva... Within the first of these [three], there is first the heading.

First the inquiry, then the explanation. Regarding the first: according to the Sanskrit original, it says, "O Son of the Buddha, among all the faults of bodhisattvas, I do not see a single dharma that surpasses a bodhisattva giving rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva. The commentary states:
Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are equally capable of obstructing all noble paths (*āryamārga*), anger alone is singled out for mention because it possesses two specific characteristics.
First, the obstacle of attachment prevents a bodhisattva from gathering in and benefiting sentient beings.
Second, among all obstacles on the bodhisattva path, this is the most grievous. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "A bodhisattva would rather give rise to hundreds of thousands of greedy thoughts..."
To give rise to even a single instance of anger violates and harms great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to no greater extent than this. The *Śīlasūtra* (Good Precepts Sūtra) explains it in the same way.

Within the second section, "Detailed Manifestation," there is first a formal inquiry (*praśna*), followed by the manifestation [of the answer]. Within the manifestation, there are one hundred gates (*dvāra*), which are divided into five stages based on their respective positions:

first, the obstacles to the practice of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); second, from "not delighting in the Buddha-dharma" onwards, the explanation of the obstacles to the ten levels of dwelling (*daśa-vihāra*); third, not attaining the various [qualities] of a bodhisattva...

The first [hindrance] is the obstruction of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) by the root [of ignorance]. The fourth is the obstruction of the great vow-practices of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) by not delighting in the speech of those who slander all-knowledge (*sarvajña*).
The fifth is the obstruction of the practice of true realization of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) by not delighting in dwelling together with bodhisattvas.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, not even hearing the unimpeded Dharma with one's ears," the Sanskrit original states: "the obstruction of receiving a body in a place where the Dharma is not heard with the ears. The commentary explains:

This means that because one is born in a place where no Buddha resides, and because the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva do not exceed these [five], the arising of even a single thought of anger at any stage of the five positions immediately obstructs everything.

Furthermore, since the *dharmadhātu* which is obstructed is like an imperial net (*indrajāla*) of infinite layers, the obstructor is made to correspond to the obstructed, such that both are likewise inexhaustible.
A single instance of anger constitutes ten billion obstructions; in principle, they are truly inexhaustible. [End of] the section on the fetters.

Three parts: first, the formal conclusion; second, the inquiry "Why is this? which serves as the interrogative intent; third, the explanation beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... which establishes the proof.

This also constitutes the subsequent clarification of the vastness of the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*). Within the clarification of the vastness of the counteractive measures, there are three sections:

first, a general manifestation based on what preceded; second, a specific elucidation beginning with "Therefore, all bodhisattvas..."; and third, the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears..."

The following section concludes with an exhortation. The initial part may be understood as before. Next, the six stages of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are specifically revealed; in each case, the subsequent stage arises based upon the preceding one.
Within the first stage, there are three parts: first, the restatement of the exhortation to practice purification; second, the inquiry based on that exhortation;

third, the formal revelation beginning with "That is to say," which contains ten phrases subsumed into five pairs. Of these, the first two concern persons: the former is not abandoning those below, and the latter is not being arrogant toward those above. Next...

The second [section] concerns the Dharma: first, not slandering the teaching; second, not being deluded regarding phenomena. The next two concern mental conduct: first, delighting in practice; second, firmness of mind.

The next two concern subduing and overcoming the afflictions (*kleśa*): the former is subduing, the latter is overcoming. The final two concern compassion and wisdom: the former is compassion, the latter is wisdom.

Within the second [stage of] purification, the three sections are the same as before: the first refers to attaining freedom from defilement by relying on the aforementioned practice of the true Dharma.
Because it is supreme, the ten phrases of purity are also subsumed into five pairs: the first three concern purity regarding the teaching—first, faith; second, seeking; and third, protection.

The next two concern purity regarding the principle of the Dharma—first, vastness; and second, extreme greatness. The next two concern purity regarding the transformation of beings—first, discerning the vessel;
and second, the merit of the Saṃgha. The final two concern purity regarding time and kalpas—first, non-attachment; and second, exhortation and examination.

The last one constitutes the nature [of wisdom]. Third, because the vast wisdom of the Knower is made expansive by being free from the obscuration of defilement (*kleśāvaraṇa*), these ten phrases also form five pairs:

the first two are the wisdom that understands those to be converted; the next two are the wisdom that knows the methods for conversion—the first being the expressive signifier (*vyañjana*) and the second the expressed meaning (*artha*);
the next two are the wisdom that knows retention and eloquence; the next possesses the wisdom of the functional activity of body and speech; and the final two...

This accords with right knowledge. Regarding the fourth [section], the "Ten Universal Entrances": because one attains expansive wisdom that can universally accord with all objects of knowledge, causing them to enter into one another.
Within these ten statements, each pair contrasts a greater number with a lesser. The first two contrast great physical form with small space as they mutually enter;
the next two contrast many bodies with a single body as they mutually enter; and the next two contrast many eons with a single moment as they mutually enter.
Next, two [cases] involve the mutual inclusion of multiple dharmas and a single dharma; next, two involve the mutual inclusion of multiple locations and a single location;

next, two involve the mutual inclusion of multiple faculties and a single faculty; next, two involve the mutual inclusion of multiple faculties and their objects; and finally, two involve the mutual inclusion of multiple thoughts and a single thought.
Next, the second [stage] involves the mutual entry of many vocal sounds and a single vocal sound; the third involves the mutual entry of the three time periods and a single time period.

Regarding the fifth stage, "abiding in the ten excellent and wondrous minds": because one transforms them without obstruction to benefit others according to their capacities, the mind attains excellence and wonder.

To clarify this directly: first, abiding in that which is beyond words; second, abiding in that which is beyond thought; third, abiding in the cause and fruit of impermanence; fourth, abiding in the permanent.
The fruit and cause: the fifth stage is profound in its secrets; the sixth stage is profound in its equality; the seventh stage eliminates doubt;
the eighth stage is equal toward all worlds; the ninth stage is equal toward the Buddhas of the three times; and the tenth stage consists of the Buddha’s ten powers and four immeasurables.
At the sixth stage, one attains the skillful wisdom of the eleven types of Buddha-dharmas. Relying upon the previously mentioned sublime mind, one gives rise to this skillful wisdom. Correctly...
Manifesting the Middle Way: 1. The dharma of realizing the principle; 2. The dharma of generating practice; 3. The dharma of proclaiming the teaching;
4. The dharma of realizing the fruit; 5. Clearly understanding the three vehicles (*triyāna*); 6. Awakening to and comprehending the one vehicle (*ekayāna*);

7. Teaching with skillful terminology; 8. Teaching through the pure gate; 9. Teaching through the diverse gates; 10. Knowing the distinction between the dual and non-dual, and the non-duality of the two non-duals.

Eleventh, regarding the ultimate realization through the gate of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) in the first noble truth, there are three sections within the conclusion and exhortation (*parīndanā*).

First, the actual manifestation of the exhortation; second, the inquiry "Why is this so? which serves as the intent of the interrogation; third, the explanation of the intent of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, because by hearing this Dharma one attains the fruit of Buddhahood, because the ocean of merit is fulfilled, and because of benefiting sentient beings and so forth.

The second section, the discernment of the auspicious omens, has two parts: first, the manifestation of the omens; second, from "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" onwards, the clarification of their confirmation.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, this world-system; second, from "Just as in this world" onwards, the summary that extends to the ten directions. Within the first of these, there are two sections: first, the revelation of the causes of the omens;

regarding these causes, there are two, namely the power of the Buddha and the natural law (*dharmatā*). Second, the elucidation of the characteristics of the omens; within these characteristics, there are two [sections], the first of which is...

The earth trembles. Subsequently, clouds of various colors rain down; these can all be understood. Furthermore, within the section on "Establishing the Proof," there are also two parts: first, this land;
second, from the passage "In this place of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) onwards, it concludes by extending the application to the ten directions. Question:

Since this manifestation of auspicious omens occurs within the assembly at the Great Palace of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsaprāsāda*), why does the concluding extension state, "under the Bodhi tree, at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), in the palaces of the bodhisattvas"?
Is it in the middle? The answer is that the Bodhi tree is the fundamental basis; thus, throughout the various assemblies before and after, they are neither identical nor different.
Within the second verse, there are two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the actual verse. Within the former, there are two parts. First, the indication of the characteristics:
this means that the two powers of self and others are the causes. "Contemplating the ten directions" refers to mindfulness of those to be transformed. "Contemplating the dharma-realm" refers to...
Because of the intention to explain what has been taught, the following intent is set forth below. That is to say, in order to explain these ten kinds of intent, this verse is spoken:
first, clarifying causal practice; second, manifesting resultant virtue; third, proclaiming the great vows; fourth, the time and place of the arising of practice.
1. The ripening of the five faculties; 2. the Buddhas’ aspiration; 3. the bestowing of the Dharma according to the faculties; 4. the benefit of what is taught; 5.

clarifying the attainment of the fruit through causes; 6. the pure body of the fruit; 7. the manifestation through vocal action—these ten meanings are fully and clearly revealed in the subsequent verses of praise.
Within the main verses of praise, there are one hundred and twenty-one verses divided into two parts: the first twenty-two verses clarify the teaching.

[This is] the demarcation. The remaining ninety-nine verses correctly elucidate the characteristics of Samantabhadra’s conduct. This is not a mere repetition of the preceding text; rather, it interweaves with it to further reveal the application of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
That is to say, the former provides a brief explanation while this offers a detailed exposition; the former concerns the essence and the latter concerns the function.

Within the former section, the first two verses admonish the audience to listen and grant permission for the teaching. The second [section], beginning with "Furthermore, throughout all kalpas," consists of eight [verses].

Verse. This clarifies that this Bodhisattva studies the vast vows and practices of the Buddhas of the past. Third, from "In this single Bhadrakalpa" onwards, eleven verses clarify the characteristics of study:
studying the practice of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) as cultivated in the present and future. Within this, the first seven [verses] cite the Buddhas of the present and future.
The final four [verses] establish the pure practice of the three wheels. The fourth section concludes the "Section on the Conclusion" with one verse.

Within the second part, which correctly reveals the characteristics of Samantabhadra’s conduct, there are two sections: first, sixty-nine verses that clarify the conduct of great wisdom regarding one's own virtues;

second, thirty verses beginning with "Those who have not yet attained peace, I shall cause to attain peace," which clarify the conduct of great compassion regarding external transformation. The former has been explained.

Within the ten types of Samantabhadra’s practices of great wisdom, there are three sections: first, the seven initial verses clarify the practice of skillfully entering the great wisdom of the Indra’s net;
second, the seventeen verses beginning with "Deeply entering the subtle" clarify the practice of wisdom regarding the subtleties of time and place;

third, the five verses beginning with "Worlds and Tathāgatas" clarify the practice of understanding the secret essentials of the minds of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—namely, the names of the worlds.
And the names of the Buddhas—these are the coarsest [objects], yet even over many eons they could not be fully described;

how much less so the spheres of knowledge known within the Buddha’s mind, such as the truly wondrous Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)? Nevertheless, this Bodhisattva is also able to understand the accomplishment of the great wisdom-practices of Samantabhadra.
(4) Thus, the following four verses concerning the future world describe the activities of his work of conversion and guidance in the future. (5)
The first four verses, beginning with "Now encompassed by the present," explain the practice of penetrating the realm of the Buddhas of the present.

The next five verses, beginning with "Six births of the non-obtaining eye," clarify the practice of the transformative functions of the six sense organs. The ten verses, beginning with "The profound wisdom of all Buddhas," clarify the practice of mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The final six verses, beginning with "Thoroughly knowing all worlds," clarify the practice of the perfectly awakened wisdom.

[The section on] "Mastery in the Intervening Conduct. The nine verses from "The Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya-garbha" below clarify the conduct of manifesting the Dharmakāya despite not being a [physical] body.

The six verses from "Just as a skilled illusionist" below clarify the conduct of the pure mind that is neither measurable nor immeasurable. This has been understood through the self-arisen wisdom and virtue.

Within the second [section], the "External Conduct of Great Compassion," there are likewise ten types of conduct. The first six verses cause sentient beings to be transformed and to resolve upon Bodhicitta.

1. Contemplating the practice of the mind. 2. "The bodies of sentient beings are immeasurable," etc., the two following verses: praising the practice of manifesting as Buddhas to gather in sentient beings.
3. "All Buddhas are able to manifest their bodies," etc., one verse: clarifying the practice of distributing the relics of the past. 4. "In this way, in the future," etc., one verse:
clarifying the ability to give rise to the virtues of future Buddhas. 5. "In this way, throughout the three periods of time," etc., the four following verses.
1. Illuminating the profound practice of the Wheel of Dharma: six verses on the immeasurable and boundless [realms]. 2.

Understanding the defiled and pure practices of the mind-vessel of beings: three verses beginning with "All sentient beings are deluded. 3. Understanding the practice of the dependent origination of the karma and retribution of objects:

five verses beginning with "The eyes, ears, nose, and tongue. 4. Understanding the practice of non-attainment regarding the faculties and their objects: one verse beginning with "The Buddha said... 5. Understanding the three [vehicles].

The wheel of the practice of teaching the Dharma throughout the three periods of time is explained. The final two verses of the tenth chapter clarify the characteristics and practices of the three periods of time, as fully elucidated in the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the thirty-seventh chapter, "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," the text of this chapter is analyzed through four sections.

In the initial explanation of the name, there are two parts: first, how the name is acquired; second, the explanation of the name. Regarding the first part, "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) has, briefly, two meanings.
First, one comes from the causal practice of the vehicle of wisdom to achieve fruition. This wisdom is itself the "Thus" (tathā); therefore, although there is a coming, there has never been a coming.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.

When the wisdom of the second fruit accords with reality as one suchness, it is unimpeded in its constant response to those to be converted; thus, he "comes. The "Chapter on Teaching and Transforming" in the *Renwang jing* states:

"Transcending both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), [he attains] the awakening of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) of the eleventh stage, which is neither existent nor non-existent."

Profoundly serene and pure, eternally abiding and unchanging, identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he possesses great compassion without conditions to teach and transform all sentient beings.
Because he comes to transform the three realms by means of the vehicle of Prajñā, this present appearance is "the latter" and not "the former.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the name: it may be understood as "coming like suchness," or "suchness itself coming," or "the appearance of suchness-coming."
Alternatively, "the Tathāgata appears" [is explained as follows]. Regarding the first two characters, "tathā" (thus) and "āgata" (come): they are neither identical nor different.

Therefore, although the *tathatā* (suchness) does not destroy the coming, this coming is the coming of suchness; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Although it comes, it does not lose its state of being suchness;
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. As for the latter two phrases: first, at the very moment of the actual coming, it is suchness... [it does not...]
"Obstructing the vehicle" refers to the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-yāna*). When one comes to transform the three realms, this is the manifestation of the Tathāgata;

this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Second, when one correctly rides the vehicle of omniscience to come and transform [the world], this is the Tathāgata's further manifestation;

this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compound). Question: The Jin translation names this "Arising of Nature" (*xingqi*), whereas here it is called "Manifestation" (*chuxian*). Why is this so?

Answer: In the old translation of the four characters "Tathāgata-xingqi" (如來性起), the two characters "Tathāgata" (如來) correspond exactly to the Sanskrit original. The character "xìng" (性, nature) is entirely absent.

As for the character "qǐ" (起, arising), it may be considered applicable; this is because the term *utpatti* is correctly translated as "shēng" (生, birth), yet it also carries the sense of "arising" (*udaya*) in the context of manifestation.

Second, regarding the intent of its presentation: The preceding chapter elucidated the manifestation of the cause of the fruit; this chapter distinguishes the manifestation of the fruit of the fruit. It follows in sequence according to the logical progression of the meaning.

Third, regarding the central thesis: This chapter takes the manifestation of the fruit of the fruit as its thesis, in order to bring about benefit and happiness for all beings until the very end of time.
Sentient beings have no end to their destinies.

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: this chapter is divided into seven sections. First, the Section on the Bestowal of Power; second, from "At that time, the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising" downward, the Fundamental Section;
third, from "At that time, Nature-Arising Wondrous Virtue" downward, the Section on the Request; fourth, at that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
1. The section on the Mahāsattva’s instruction; 2. The section on the five sons of the Buddha [stating] that this Dharma is called the "Secret of the Tathāgata";

3. The section on the explicit names for receiving and upholding [the teaching]; 4. The section on the manifestation of auspicious signs through the Buddha’s spiritual power at that time; 5. The section on the certification of the signs; 6.
The section on the verses by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva at that time, which summarizes the entire work.

The first and second [sections] of the beginning: first, the light from the *ūrṇā* (tuft of hair between the eyebrows) empowers the Dharma-preacher; subsequently, at that time, the Tathāgata descends into his mouth, and the light from his mouth empowers the Dharma-preacher.
Within the former [of these two], there are two: first, the prose; second, the verse praise. Within the former [of these two], there are two: first, the empowerment by light;

second, the benefit to the assembly as clarified from "at that time, in this *maṇḍala*" onwards. Within the first [of these], there are ten [points]; the first is the place where the light emerges: the *ūrṇā*.

First, "the interval" signifies that the path of realization is free from the two extremes. Second, "the white tuft" signifies that the Middle Way Dharma-realm serves as the foundation for all teachings.
Third, the manifestation of the light named "The Appearance of the Tathāgata" intends to signify that the Buddhas possess unobstructed attainment, manifesting the appearance of the fruit of fruits.
Fourth, "immeasurable," and so forth, refers to the activity of the cause of the light; "that light" refers to the activity of its extension.
1. Circumambulating to the right and so forth are acts of reverence. 2. Awakening and so forth are acts of realization. 3. Eliminating and so forth are acts of correctness.
4. Overwhelming and so forth are acts of subjugation. 5. Manifesting and so forth are acts of demonstration. 6.

From "Having performed these deeds" onwards clarifies the act of integration. Regarding "entering the crown of Mañjuśrī," this precisely clarifies the signs of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). For what reason is there empowerment?

This Bodhisattva, wishing to inquire about the dharmas that constitute the fruit, acts to manifest the meaning of the Vajra lineage. Subsequently, within the section clarifying the benefits for the assembly, there are two parts:
first, obtaining the benefit of joyful exultation; second, from "Furthermore, he acts in this way" onwards, it is known that light is the preliminary sign of the teaching of the Dharma.

Within the subsequent verse of praise, there are also two parts: first, identifying the person who utters the verses; second, from "The Perfectly Awakened One" onwards, the actual manifestation of the praise.

The ten verses of the "Manifesting the Middle" (*Madhyamakāvatāra*) are divided into six sections: first, one verse praising the Buddha and proffering salutation; second, five verses praising the Buddha’s emission of light;
third, one verse praising the benefits of the aforementioned light; and fourth, one verse praising the assembly for possessing the virtue of being worthy to hear [the teaching].
The five verses consist of one stanza praising the Buddha’s compassionate wisdom for benefiting the world, and thus [the Buddha] first emits light before preaching the Dharma.

The sixth consists of the final stanza, requesting the Buddha to reveal his intention for preaching the Dharma. Why does he not directly request the Buddha to preach the Dharma, but instead requests him to instruct others?
There are two reasons for this: first, when the light entered their bodies, they were already made aware that the Buddha would not speak on his own initiative.
The second point is as in the previous many instances where the Buddha does not speak of himself. Regarding the intention behind the teaching through the empowerment of light from his mouth later on:
since he was previously requested to reveal it, he now reveals it. This section has two parts: first, the empowerment; second, the benefit bestowed by the descent of that light.

Within the first part, there are ten points. First, the source from which the light issues: "emitting from the mouth" signifies that the path of teaching has attained penetration. Second, the name of the light: "Unobtainable" (Anupalabdha).

"Those" indicates that their eloquence is unhindered. "Fearless" means they do not dread what is profound or difficult to explain; it manifests that they have already transcended all worldly majesty and power.
The remainder is as explained previously. "Entering the mouth of Samantabhadra" means causing them to speak just as the Buddha speaks.
Because it was transmitted orally. Why is Samantabhadra added? It indicates that what is being taught here is the Dharma of Samantabhadra.

As for not entering the *uṣṇīṣa*, it is because this is a combined teaching. Regarding the subsequent addition of benefits, the phrase "exceeding ten billion times the original" reveals the power of the empowerment;
"and exceeding others" distinguishes it from the rest; and "excluding only the Buddha" clarifies the distinction between the superior and the inferior. The section on the empowerment is concluded.
In the second part, the "Section on the Main Body," there are two sections: first, the question; second, the answer beginning with the words "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra said.

Within the answer, there are two parts: first, citing the past to illustrate the present; second, manifesting auspicious signs following the words "Having spoken these words," which consist of two types of signs.

First, "the shaking of the earth" signifies that Samantabhadra draws forth the resonance of the past. Second, "the emergence of the light of the Dharma-question" indicates the presence of a bodhisattva who asks the question, representing the subject of the inquiry;

that is to say, it refers to the teaching of the dharma-gate of the manifestation of the Buddha-fruit, which causes the one who asks to give rise to the sublime virtues of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Thus, it is called "the Tathāgata-nature-arising Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue."

In the third section on the request for the division [of the teaching], there are two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. Within the former, there are two sub-sections: first, the request by citing the Dharma in its general characteristics;

second, the request by listing ten gates, beginning with "Excellent, O Son of the Buddha. Within the first of these, there are three parts: first, the request by citing the Dharma; second, the request by praising the assembly, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, regarding all these...";
and third, the request by praising the speaker, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, you have already... The first [of these] is the request which may be accepted.

[This section] is understood. Of the two [parts], there are three [subdivisions]: first, praising the greatness of the assembly; second, from "All have long... onwards, praising the loftiness of their virtues; third, from "Endowed with such as these...

onwards, concluding the gathering of the assembly. The first is easily understood. Within the praise of virtues, there are ten types: first, the long duration of pure precepts; second, the perfection of mindfulness and wisdom.
4. The culmination of the four vows; 5. Possessing the Buddha’s deportment; 6. Recollecting the Buddha; 7. The contemplation of great compassion; 8. Thoroughly penetrating the objects of cognition;

9. Attaining the empowerment of the Buddha; 10. Receiving the Buddha’s teachings. The three concluding sections are as follows: within these three, two are first explained individually, followed by a summary.

Within the former [the individual explanations], there are ten types: 1. Frequenting the Buddhas; 2. Accomplishing sublime conduct; 3. Mastery over meditative concentration; 4. Realizing the secret...
1. Esoteric; 2. Five ways of knowing the Dharma-teachings; 3. Dispelling the doubts of the assembly; 4. Empowered by the Buddha’s power; 5. Knowing the faculties of beings; 6.

Teaching according to their inclinations; 7. Accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom. The conclusion at the end may be understood accordingly. Following this, the ten gates of the specific request are listed, of which three are presented first:

initially, praising his virtues and generally stating the request; next, from "the marks of the body" onwards, the individual gates are listed. Regarding the phrase "turning the Dharma," the Sanskrit original says *dharmacakra-pravartana* (turning the wheel of the Dharma).

The wheel. Following this is the concluding summary. In the subsequent verses of the *gāthā*, ten verses are divided into three parts: first, one verse that introduces and praises the speaker and the listener; second, from "How does a bodhisattva...
onwards, which is the main body of the verses, specifically listing the questions and requests; third, from "This teaching... onwards, which praises the virtues and provides an exhortation.
Within the separate listing of the actual verses, the four verses are divided into seven parts. The first half-verse praises the appearance of the Tathāgata.
The next line praises the sphere of body, speech, and mind—where "speech" refers to sound. The next line praises the Buddha’s conduct. The next line praises the attainment of *bodhi*.
The next line praises the turning of the wheel of Dharma. The next line praises *parinirvāṇa*. The next...

In the two verses, one verse describes the roots of goodness arising from seeing, hearing, and attending upon [the teaching]. In the section praising virtues and exhorting to teach, there are five verses divided into six parts:
first, half a verse praises the assembly’s reverence for the Dharma and their esteem for the person; next, half a verse extols the virtues of Samantabhadra and requests him to speak.
This is because it is the sphere for listeners to give rise to an ocean of merit; furthermore, it is that which can thoroughly purify the afflictive obscurations of sentient beings.
Next, one verse raises six points as a request: namely, by means of causes, analogies, proofs, and reasonings, they are brought into correspondence with the truth.
Having heard this, his resolve was awakened, his doubts were dispelled, and his wisdom purified. Next, with one verse, he requested instruction on four matters;

that is, by means of causes and skillful analogies, he showed that the Buddha’s body is no different from the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions. The first half of the verse presents the example, while the second half poses the question.

The next verse praises the rarity of the assembly and makes a request; that is to say, within immeasurable eons in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, it is difficult to encounter an assembly such as that now gathered.
The following verse praises the assembly’s aspiration for the Dharma and their reverence for the person, requesting that the pure mind be fully manifested and the Dharma explained.
This concludes the section on the requests.

In the fourth section, the "Section on Exposition," the ten preceding questions are answered in ten segments. Each segment consists of two parts: first, a prose exposition (*gadya*), followed by a verse summary (*śloka*).
Among these ten, the first answers the question regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance; this Dharma constitutes the causal conditions upon which the appearance relies.

The subsequent nine segments answer the questions concerning the body and the other nine aspects, correctly manifesting the characteristics of the appearance as that which relies [upon those causes]. This is analogous to a cause...
The fruit is not the cause, because both are phenomena manifested within the fruit. Regarding the initial prose section, there are three parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, the manifestation through analogy, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is like...";
and third, the general conclusion based on the Dharma, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows the Tathāgata... Each of these three sections contains ten gates. However—
Regarding the initial ten: each one penetrates the intermediate ten gates. These causal conditions comprise four layers in total.
First, it is called "tenfold" based on the initial brief enumeration. Second, it is called "hundredfold" because the initial ten enter into the intermediate ten;
thus, each one possesses ten, resulting in one hundred gates. Third, it is called "thousandfold" because the subsequent conclusion of eleven [gates] each summarizes the preceding hundred.

There are one thousand gates. Regarding the four immeasurables and the asaṃkhyeyas: within those one thousand gates, each subsequently contains many causes and conditions, such as the four wisdom-wind wheels, the ten radiances, and so forth.
Furthermore, they also comprehensively encompass the various causes and conditions within the nine [categories] beginning with the body.
The text consists of two parts: first, a general announcement to inform the assembly; second, from "In this place" onwards, the actual exposition. Exposition.

The middle section has two parts: first, the praise; second, the formal exposition beginning with "What is it... and so forth. Within the former [the praise], there are four parts: first, praising the difficulty of the words of recollection;
second, identifying the reasons for the difficulty; third, a further inquiry as to why this is so; fourth, revealing the distinctions of the difficulty through the phrase "It is not...

and so forth. Within the section on distinctions, there are two parts: first, a negative demonstration; second, a positive explanation beginning with "By means of the ten immeasurables... and so forth. The intent of this explanation is as follows:

This is called "inconceivable" (acintya) solely because its numerical quantity is vast and extensive; it does not refer to the nature of reality (dharmatā) being beyond words. Regarding the numerical quantity:

as previously analyzed, there are four successive layers of ten, hundred, thousand, and so forth; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly. In the subsequent formal exposition, there are three parts: first, the inquiry;
second, the actual manifestation beginning with "That is to say..."; and third, the conclusion beginning with "O Son of the Buddha...". Within the section on manifestation:
1. Because it encompasses the generation of a vast and great mind; 2. because it accomplishes a vast and pure, superior aspiration;

3. because it accomplishes vast compassion; 4. because it accomplishes vast practices and vows; 5. because it accomplishes merit and wisdom without weariness; 6. because it accomplishes vast practices for the dual benefit of self and others;
7. because it accomplishes vast skillful wisdom; 8. because it accomplishes a vast treasury of pure virtues; 9. because it accomplishes vast adornments of wisdom.
Because it is established. It is because the ten [perfections] are mostly explained as establishing the real dharma. In the section on the fetters (*saṃyojana*), it says "establishing the Tathāgata.
This refers to the causes and conditions for the manifestation [of the result], not the causes for attaining Buddhahood.
The second analogy illustrates the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Each section has three parts: first the illustration, next the application, and finally the conclusion.
As previously requested, "I pray that you provide the causes, conditions, and analogies," the preceding exposition of the Dharma constitutes the causes and conditions;
what follows below clarifies the analogies. Among these ten analogies:
The first is the analogy of the formation of a great trichiliocosm, which illustrates the Buddha’s appearance through the convergence of manifold conditions. Within this analogy, there are two parts:

first, an illustration of the causal conditions for appearance based on the characteristics of conditions; second, from "the nature of phenomena is thus" onwards, an illustration of the nature of depending on conditions for appearance.
Regarding the first part, there are three sections: first, a general enumeration of the many causes and conditions; second, "that is to say," a detailed differentiation of the many causes.
Condition. Third, the "Buddha-sons" and so forth conclude the many causes and conditions below. This section has two parts: first, a negative demonstration;

second, a positive explanation beginning with "by means of the immeasurable... Within the former, the phrase "not by a single condition" and so forth—in the Sanskrit original it is *naikena hetunā* (or *naikena pratyayena*), which here means "not by a single cause. Following this, it says "by means of the immeasurable... and so on.
*Kaṭhina* here means "not by means of a single matter or condition. If it were solely a condition, it should have been called *pātra-kaṭhiṇa*.

Since the text is not thus, we know it refers to a "matter" (*vastu*) and a "condition" (*pratyaya*). As for the later statement "by means of immeasurable [conditions]," it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Within the section on distinctions, there are two parts. First, the four wind-wheels are enumerated; second, the phrase "thus all [arise] from below" explains their cause. Within the first of these, there are two further points:
first, a general demonstration of how the four wheels depend upon one another; second, the phrase "as for those four" provides a specific analysis of the four wheels.

This means that based on clouds and rain, four wind-wheels arise. The first is named "The Able Sustainer. Through the karmic power of sentient beings, at the time of the empty kalpa, when the world was about to...
It is established. In the space above, clouds and rain first arise. If there were no wind to sustain the rain, the water would have no place to rest and would destroy other worlds;
therefore, the power of karma initiates the first wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). If the water did not diminish, there would be no means for the palaces of the various devas to arise;
therefore, the power of karma initiates the second wind-circle. Although this can evaporate the water, there is still no means for it to arise in its proper location. Thus...
Therefore, by the power of karma, the third wind-circle arises, reducing the water by one section and giving rise to a tier of celestial palaces.

In this manner, proceeding gradually downward, it reaches the arising of Mount Sumeru, the great earth, and so forth. Although these general locations arise, they cannot yet distinguish the specific categories of their adornments;
therefore, by that same karma, the fourth wind-circle arises, causing this world-system to become fully complete, beginning with the arising of the receptacle world.
The world: the subsequently arising sentient world is explained in detail as set forth in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the World" (*Lokanirdeśa*) in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

Regarding the three [types of karma] mentioned among the causes for its emergence, one should understand that there is karma that is common to both [the external environment and the internal world], karma that is common among those within [the internal world], and karma that is uncommon among those within [the internal world].
Second, that which arises from the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the bodhisattvas: this refers to the distinction between the pure and the defiled, and the purification of the defiled.

The two types of realms are explained. Why is this? Because there are no bodhisattvas within a realm that is purely defiled, and because there are no sentient beings within a realm that is purely pure;

thus, both types are observable. Within these two categories, a defiled realm may contain bodhisattvas who manifest there through the power of their compassion and vows, with the exception of the purely miserable destinies (*durgati*).
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) states: "There may be some buddha-fields where no Buddha exists..."
He manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment; or there may be buddha-fields where no phenomena exist, yet within them he manifests the preaching of the Dharma-treasury and so forth.

These three [points] collectively clarify that while the location remains the same, the various responses differ according to what is appropriate for each case. As it says in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

For example, it is like the gods eating from a single precious vessel where the colors of their food differ, and so forth. The subsequent passage, in the sixty-sixth section, has the Great Radiance King tell Sudhana:
"All the sentient beings dwelling in the City of Wondrous Light are [the children of the Buddhas]. The summary at the end can be understood accordingly.
Following this, there are three parts clarifying the manifestation of the nature of conditions; first, the single phrase "The nature of phenomena is thus" serves as the general statement.

[The text] reveals [the following]. Regarding the four lines beginning with "There is no... (二無有下四句), it clarifies that because the nature (*dharmatā*) is identical to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), arising, activity, cognition, and accomplishment do not obstruct non-arising and so forth;
and because the characteristics are identical to the nature, although there is non-arising and so forth, they do not obstruct arising and so forth.

Within the synthesis of these two dharmas, it synthesizes the three aspects each of the previously mentioned object-conditioned characteristics (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*) and the object-conditioned nature (*ālambana-dharmatā*), thereby revealing its four kinds of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

Regarding the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*): first is the wisdom that maintains without loss, which sustains the rain of the Dharma-clouds. Next are two [types of wisdom] based on the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*), accomplished through reliance on the Dharma:

first, the wisdom that extinguishes afflictions; second, the wisdom that accomplishes virtues. The final one is the wisdom accomplished through reliance on the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*).

The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. In the third section, the summary, there is both a conclusion and an exhortation; the preceding textual characteristics are easy to understand.
The second analogy, "The Great Thousandfold World System Showered by Torrential Rain," consists of three sections identical to those preceding.

Herein, the metaphor of the rain sustained by the prior wind illustrates the Buddha’s profound and vast virtues that are difficult to comprehend. This refers to the attainment of the power of inexhaustible *dhāraṇī*, whereby he preaches this teaching on the manifestation of the Tathāgata;
it is something that all followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are incapable of receiving, except for Mahāyāna bodhisattvas. Therefore...

Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva believes that the Buddha possesses unobstructed power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*), which continues until the attainment of the fruit, providing benefit and happiness without end.
Therefore, it is said: "except for those great bodhisattvas whose mental continuity possesses such power.
This treatise does not limit its scope to specific faculties, as it is distinguished by stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, those from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) downwards are not the intended recipients.

The third is the simile of the great rain having no point of origin. Herein, the great rain is as previously described: it is the power of the karma of sentient beings that evokes the clouds and rain of the nāgas.
However, there is the simile of its having neither coming nor going, which illustrates that the appearance of a Buddha is without coming or going. There are many explanations for this.

First, it responds to conditions without coming; when conditions cease, it departs without going. Second, because it manifests from causes and conditions, there is no coming at the time of manifestation.
Since there is no coming, there is no departure upon its cessation. Third, as for its initial manifestation, it has already neither come nor gone;
this is because it manifests from causes and conditions.
The fourth is the Parable of the Great Rainfall, which is also called the Parable of the Drops Counted by Maheśvara.

This is also the same as the previous Parable of the Great Rainfall during the Kalpa of Formation (*vivartakalpa*), serving as a metaphor for the Buddha’s appearance and his qualities that can be received by those of great capacity. An ancient master explained that this contains four meanings.

1. Because the teaching is vast; 2. because the practice is great; 3. because the cause is profound; and 4. because the fruit is far-reaching, it is not within the reach of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Fifth is the analogy of the great rain, which illustrates how the Buddha extinguishes afflictions and accomplishes the virtues of wisdom. Each of these has five aspects: first, the ability to extinguish the blazing fire;
second, the ability to establish the ground; third, the ability to destroy the great waters; and fourth, the ability to bring all things within the ocean to completion.
The various jewels. Fifth, they are able to adorn the locations within the great trichiliocosm. Among these dharmas, the first two eliminate delusions and accomplish merit;
the next two eliminate hindrances and accomplish wisdom; and the last one illuminates sentient beings according to their capacities through the Dharma.
The sixth [section] contains one analogy for each, illustrating how the Buddha’s single flavor conforms to the capacities of individual vessels.
The seventh [section] contains two analogies. The first establishes the analogy of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), illustrating the Buddha’s excellence in terms of conditions from the prior limit.

The second is the subsequent analogy that resolves doubts. Within these two analogies, the former first establishes that [the difference in results] arises from the power of karma, while the latter explains that the difference in phenomena arises from the diversity of the faculties of sentient beings. The remainder...

This can be further understood. Within the eighth analogy, there are three parts: first, the illustration; second, the summary beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha, like a great cloud" (Skt. *mahāmegha*); and third, the application beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha, like the Tathāgata...

The first of these [the illustration] has two sections: first, revealing the production of flowers from the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*); second, the section beginning with "At that time, within it," which clarifies the arising of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
Regarding the middle section, the third fascicle of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "For what reason is it called the 'Auspicious Aeon' (*Bhadrakalpa*)?

Ānanda, when this trichiliocosm was about to be formed, it was entirely one vast body of water. The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, observing with their divine eyes, saw that this world was but a single great expanse of water.
Within it, they saw a thousand stalks of exquisite lotus flowers; each and every lotus..."
Flowers, each with a thousand petals and golden light, shine brilliantly and universally, their fragrance wafting in all directions;
they are most delightful. Upon seeing this, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven feel joy in their hearts and even exclaim in praise: "How marvelous! How rare!
Because a thousand Buddhas constantly appear in the world throughout this kalpa, it is called the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa). [The commentary] explains: This is the name of the flowers.

The appearance of the Tathāgata is first designated by the name "summoning. Subsequently, within the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), for each successive reduction of the water, a wind-circle arises and forms a single location;
as the ten winds sequentially complete these locations, they reach fulfillment. Regarding the second point of connection:

because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) differ, the winds and the lands (*kṣetra*) are distinct, yet the rain is no different. Third, the correspondence with the Dharma: this refers to the merit of the Buddha’s accomplishment of the great task (*mahākṛtya*). [End of] Text.

The middle section has two parts: first, the actual presentation of the conjunction; second, the resolution of doubts, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, all Tathāgatas... The former [the first part] has four sections: 1) the emergence of the waters as they appear;

2) the emission of the light of wisdom and the bestowing of predictions upon the Bodhisattvas; 3) the conjunction and the production of the lotuses; 4) the symbolic representation of the number of Buddhas appearing.
3. "O Sons of the Buddha, when the Tathāgata appears... [The text] joins the ten winds below. This symbolizes that the Buddha’s virtues respond differently to various capacities.
4. "O Sons of the Buddha, through the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata... [The text] joins the upper concluding passage. Regarding the subsequent section on resolving doubts, there are three parts:

first, distinguishing the correct principle according to the preceding text and exhorting one to know it; second, "Sentient beings think thus... and so forth, which raises the doubt of biased attachment regarding the conditions of the capacity for response (*ālambana*).
Regarding the single phrase within the section on "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*), it means that it would be unreasonable for the Buddha alone to discern [the truth]; therefore, it says, "This is not so.

From "The three sons of the Buddha" onwards, the text fully reveals the accomplishment through conditions (*pratyaya-siddhi*), thereby manifesting the meaning of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). This passage consists of three parts:

first, it distinguishes how the Bodhisattva relies upon the Buddha to plant roots of goodness; later, with the words "But... and so forth, it reveals that because the Buddha possesses roots of goodness by virtue of the Bodhisattva, [the Buddha's realization] only then occurs.

By means of his majestic power, he causes them to be endowed with the virtues of a Buddha. Thirdly, the Buddha’s descent below illustrates the mutual correspondence between the faculties and their objects.

Since these conditions are established as being devoid of agency or action, there is no "accomplishment. Because there is no accomplishment, there is no destruction. Since there is neither accomplishment nor destruction, there is no differentiation.

Ninth, the analogy of the four wheels supporting one another illustrates how the Buddha’s essence and function depend upon and sustain one another; just as the water wheel is that upon which [the others] depend.
These winds have four meanings: first, they sustain water and are thus called "Abiding" (Anvaya); second, they cannot be shaken and are thus called "Immovable" (Acala);

third, they persist until the end of the kalpa and are thus called "Ultimate" (Paryanta); fourth, their substance cannot be damaged and are thus called "Firm" (Dṛḍha). Their thickness is sixteen lakṣas.
In the formal correspondence (*dharmasaṃgati*), the first four correspond to the four winds, and the latter four correspond to the four wheels. Within the former, there is one summary.
1. Gathering; 2. Bestowing the Dharma; 3. Protecting; 4. Illuminating Reality. These correspond to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four winds;

the principle is thus applicable. Within the synthesis of the four wheels: benefit and compassion correspond to the preceding earth wheel; great skillful means corresponds to water; the Tathāgata corresponds to wind;
and unimpeded wisdom-light corresponds to the jewels that mutually support one another. This is according to the commentary.

The tenth [chapter], "The Great Thousandfold World: The Parable of Benefiting Others," explains the virtue of manifesting in the world to benefit sentient beings through transformation. Regarding the benefit of the three trainings within wisdom:
first, internally attaining the true principle; second, externally employing illumination. The remainder may be understood by analogy.
In the third section, the summary and exhortation, there are eleven phrases. Each one universally summarizes the preceding ten gates:

namely, (1) one practice with many [aspects], (2) pervasiveness, (3) freedom from the transition of signs, (4) freedom from conceptual discrimination, (5) eternal quiescence, (6) being without a master or a place of lodging, (7) being inexhaustible, (8) having no rest, (9) the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha, and (10) viewing [all things] as neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither identical nor different. Ten.
The first [section] consists of the vow for the fulfillment of dedication.
In the second section, the verses of praise, there are thirty-seven verses divided into three parts. The first fourteen verses praise the profound [teaching] and grant permission for its exposition.
The first verse provides a general response. The following twenty-two verses, beginning with "For example, like the world," correspond to the ten similes mentioned above.
The third section consists of one verse praising the difficulty of explaining [the Dharma]. Regarding the first two [sections], the initial twelve verses praise the immeasurability of the Dharma;

the subsequent two verses, beginning with "Therefore," clarify the limits of verbal expression. Within the former [section], there are also two parts: first, eleven verses praising the object [of the teaching]; second, [the remaining verses praising] the speaker.
[The section on] "Knowing the Profound" follows. If one wishes to know the subsequent single verse, it praises the purity of the vessel capable of such knowledge.

Within this [section], there are also two parts: first, a single verse that generally reveals the Buddha’s virtues as profound, vast, and immeasurable; second, the ten verses beginning with "The Merit of the Ten Powers."
A separate verse sets forth ten gates of the Buddha’s qualities that are difficult to measure; each single verse reveals one specific quality of the Buddha.

The first verse generally presents the inconceivable quality of the Buddha as a whole, while the subsequent nine verses distinguish them individually, each beginning with a simile followed by the application to the Dharma. Second, the simile of the particles at the end of space illustrates the Buddha’s limitless qualities.
Third, the simile of measuring space illustrates the Buddha’s vast qualities. Fourth, the simile of counting the minds [of beings] illustrates the Buddha’s immeasurable qualities.
1. The metaphor of the five dharma-realms illustrates the Buddha’s profound virtues. 2. The metaphor of true suchness (*tathatā*) illustrates the Buddha’s virtue of being free from signs. 3.

The metaphor of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) illustrates the Buddha’s virtue of non-obstruction. 4. The metaphor of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) being like space illustrates the Buddha’s virtue of intrinsic purity. 5.

The metaphor of the nature of phenomena being beyond words illustrates the Buddha’s virtue of being beyond verbal expression. 6. The metaphor of the nature of phenomena being as quiescent as the track of a bird illustrates the state of immediate quiescence.

It employs non-color to manifest the quality of color. Next, one [verse] manifests the purity of the knower; therein, the first half provides a general exhortation, while the second half provides a specific manifestation.
Regarding the two [verses] below that which permit the teaching: the first is a warning to listen and permission to speak, while the last briefly indicates the nine gates.
In the first ten similes of the second verse, the first two verses comment on the first simile: the first verse provides the illustration, and the second verse provides the application.
The second [section] has two verses, commenting on the second simile. The third [section] has two verses, commenting on the third simile.
The fourth [section] has two verses, commenting on the fourth simile. The fifth [section] has two verses, commenting on the fifth simile—excepting only the "Lord of the World."
[The commentary] states: In the Sanskrit original, it says "except for the Lord of the World.
There are two verses for the sixth simile; seven verses for the seventh simile; four verses for the eighth simile; two verses for the ninth simile;
and twelve verses for the tenth simile. The final verse at the end of the third [section] praises the manifestation of the Dharma.

This is an explanation through analogies difficult to illustrate. Within the ten sections mentioned above, the first has concluded its clarification of the causes and conditions for the manifestation [of these dharmas].

Second, regarding the specific answers within the nine sections of the larger division concerning the dharmas that emerge, we first clarify bodily action (*kāyakarman*), as it serves as the basis for the subsequent eight.
Within the prose commentary, there are three parts: first, a general introduction; second, "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [and so forth].

One should explain the characteristics in the following section. Third, from "By means of the immeasurability of the mind" onwards, the conclusion, the exhortation, and the manifestation [of the meaning] are presented.
Within the explanation of the characteristics, there are five hundred gates of analysis: first, regarding the phenomena (*dharma*), there are five gates that collectively manifest them;

second, regarding the metaphors, there are ten bodies that are individually distinguished, which constitute fifty gates; third, the general conclusion concerning the knower also consists of ten gates, which likewise constitute...
Five hundred [verses]. Following this precedent, there should also be one thousand sections; however, they are omitted within the general summary. This consists of two parts:

first, a general indication of the vastness of the virtues; second, the explanation and establishment thereof, beginning with "What... and so forth. Within this, there are two parts: first, an indirect clarification (*paryudāsa*); second, a direct explanation (*vidhi*), beginning with "It should pervade...

and so forth. Within the former, there are five points: first, the Dharma is that upon which the matter depends; "matter" refers here to the practice of the matter. Second, the practice is that which is...

Because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). The three bodies (*trikāya*) are that which is accomplished by these phenomena; the four lands (*kṣetra*) are the basis upon which the bodies rely; and sentient beings are those to be transformed.

Since each of these extends throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, they are all immeasurable. Following this, within the detailed analysis based on analogies, the ten bodies of the Tathāgata’s manifestation are briefly elucidated:
first, the bodyless body that is omnipresent; second, the body that makes distinctions where there are none; third, the body that accomplishes benefit through great function.

Fourth, the body that accords with capacities through the fourfold equality; fifth, the body that secretly benefits those of inferior faculties; sixth, the body that transcends the inferior while responding appropriately;

seventh, the body that is neither one nor many and is without attainment; eighth, the body that accomplishes tasks without effort; ninth, the body that accomplishes benefit through its essence and function; tenth, the body that fulfills all vows.
To manifest these ten bodies, ten metaphors are presented for analysis, each of which consists of three aspects, namely:

This is the analogy, the application, and the conclusion. Regarding the first part, it clarifies the analogy of whether space is all-pervasive or not; because this space is formless, it cannot be measured.
Furthermore, precisely because it is formless, there is nowhere it does not reach. This serves as an analogy for the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).

Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it originally assumes a body for the sake of sentient beings; because it does not exist as a self-possessed entity, it is called the "non-existent body.
Furthermore, because one vows to take this [body] as the body of sentient beings rather than as one's own body, it is called the "non-self-body.
