"The treatise alone identifies five kinds of secret language: first, because they realize the profound and secret Dharma, as in the case of the name 'Tathāgata-garbha' mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*."
Second, all phenomena are expressed by a single word, as the preceding text states that the Tathāgata is equal within a single utterance.
Third, although spoken nearby, it is not heard, as in the cases of Śāriputra and Yaśas; yet although heard from afar, it is as if heard nearby, as in the cases of Indra and the striking of a gong.
Fourth, the words are near while the meaning is far, as when the three vehicles are taught as having an intentional (sandhyābhāṣya) purpose.

Fifth, there are cases where conventional expressions are used to describe ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*), such as describing awakening (*bodhi*) as "firm" when it is not actually firm, and so forth.

This present passage explains only according to the first meaning. Among the items listed: first, regarding the teaching (*śāsana*), as it is said that the mind is profound and because there is no correspondence with reality;
second, regarding places where one does not take birth, one does not say "I am now a sentient being," but says only "truly born," yet this is not false speech; third, regarding...
Manifesting the path and attaining Buddhahood are both said to be real; they are not described as mere manifestations, yet they are not false speech.

Fourth, although one knows that the karmic retributions of sentient beings are illusory, one speaks of cause and effect as being real, yet this is not false speech. Fifth, regarding the defiled and pure karma created by sentient beings, one likewise declares it to be real;
the meaning of this is the same as before. Sixth, one speaks of the dharma of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena. Seventh...

The statement that throughout the entirety of empty space in the ten directions there are worlds without interval is called "esoteric language" (saṃdhā-bhāṣya), because it is spoken as a corrective for those of inferior faculties who would otherwise fall into error.
Eighth, regarding the teaching that within a single atom there are worlds wherein Buddhas manifest the eight phases of their career.
Furthermore, it is not a limit that can be known by those of inferior faculties; thus, it is called "esoteric speech.

Ninth, although sentient beings are already in *nirvāṇa*, because they do not abandon their fundamental nature and are led to cultivate and realize it, it is said that they are "already in *nirvāṇa*"; this is esoteric speech, for it is not a falsehood.
Tenth: Although one knows that there is nothing other than the mind, one constantly speaks of them without abandoning [the conventional].

This is because virtuous friends are equal to the Buddhas in their respect, in their generation of the roots of goodness, in their dedication, in their activities, and in their renunciation. The fetters and fruits should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the third [point], the ten kinds of skillful analytical knowledge: since the preceding section already addressed skillfulness in speech, this section now reveals skillfulness of intention.

In the Jin translation, these are termed "skillful means of analytical wisdom. Among the items listed: first, entering into buddha-fields; second, entering into the inclinations and desires of sentient beings.
1. Entering into mental activities; 2. Entering into the faculties (*indriya*); 3. Entering into karmic retribution; 4. Entering into the practice of the two truths of the *śrāvaka*; 5.
Entering into the practice of dependent origination of the *pratyekabuddha*; 6. Entering into the practices of the various perfections (*pāramitā*) of the *bodhisattva*;

7. Entering into contaminated wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*); 8. Entering into uncontaminated dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). Regarding these ten dharmas above, to have clear understanding and realization through wisdom is entirely termed "entering. This concludes the section on the results.
This can be understood from the text.
Second, there are ten kinds of entering samādhi, followed by twenty phrases that clarify the universal pervasiveness of profound concentration.

Within these, the first ten clarify the essence of concentration (which is called *samyak-samāpatti-samādhi* in the Jin translation), while the latter ten clarify its functional activity; these too can be understood.

The first part clarifies profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the latter reveals its universal pervasiveness. Within the former: first, entering concentration to take the lands as the object;

second, observing the bodies of sentient beings as the object of concentration; third, taking all phenomena as the object of concentration; fourth, observing the Buddhas as the object of concentration; fifth, observing eons as the object of concentration;
sixth, arising from concentration to manifest many bodies and taking their entry into concentration as the object; seventh, observing the bodies of all Buddhas as the object of concentration.

Eighth, realizing that all sentient beings possess a single nature is taken as the object of concentration. Ninth, recollecting the successive entry into the meditative wisdom of many bodhisattvas is taken as the object of concentration.
Tenth, recollecting the subsequent fulfillment of the practices and vows of all bodhisattvas through unimpeded wisdom, entering into concentration without ceasing, is taken as the object.

The explanations for these aforementioned entries into training are the same as those previously given; the concluding summary and the fruits are easy to understand. Second, there are ten kinds [of objects].

Regarding the "Universal Entrances" (*kṛtsnāyatana*): previously, entering meditative concentration was explained; now, the process of arising from that concentration and pervading all locations is being analyzed.
In the Jin translation, these are called the "All-Bases" (*sarvatraga*). They are enumerated as follows: first, the objects of compassion as the focal point;

second, the physical basis of those [objects]; third, the essential nature of all worldly phenomena; fourth and fifth, the calamities of fire and water; sixth, the Buddha-body; seventh, the adornments of the Buddha-fields; and eighth, the merits of the Buddha.
The body. Ninth, the wisdom of various modes of teaching the Dharma. Tenth, the wisdom of making offerings to all Buddhas.

Because one understands these ten clearly and attains thorough penetration of them, it is called "entry. The remaining text is to be explained accordingly. Thus concludes the section on the universal practice of profound meditative concentration.
The third section consists of forty phrases concerning ten kinds of liberation gates, which clarify the practice of mastery over karmic functions.
Among these, the first ten follow the Sanskrit original; they are *vimukti* (liberation), specifically this supreme liberation (*vi-mukti*), so called because of mastery over what is performed.

The present mention of "liberation" alone is an abbreviation. In the Jin translation, these are termed "Dharma-gates," specifically ten in number: first, clarifying that the body pervades all buddha-fields;
second, manifesting various forms and appearances within all fields; third, entering many fields into a single field; fourth, sustaining and empowering all sentient beings;
fifth, adorning all fields by adorning the body with the Dharma-Buddha; sixth, [within] the center...

1. Seeing the basis; 2. traveling to various lands in a single moment of thought; 3. manifesting the appearance of many Buddhas within a single land; 4. a single body pervading the entire dharma-realm; 5.
manifesting the playful displays of all Buddhas in an instant of thought. These ten are explained as the gates of the functional activity of liberation;
the conclusion and so forth may be understood accordingly. Second, regarding the ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): the former [set] concerns mastery over their functional application.

Because one has attained it, there is liberation. Now, because these supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) have no attainment as their object, they are explained next. Among the list: first, knowledge of past lives; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds;

fourth, the divine eye; fifth, the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*); sixth, manifesting supernatural powers according to the minds of beings; seventh, universally manifesting many lands from a single body;
eighth, entering many lands in a single moment of thought; ninth, producing many ornaments to adorn [the lands].
[He manifests] in many lands. Tenth, he manifests many transformation bodies. Eleventh, in accordance with the minds of many beings, he manifests the attainment of enlightenment in many lands.
The summary and the results are easy to understand according to the text. Regarding the "ten kinds of clear knowledge" (vidyā), the former [chapter on] penetration is this very clear knowledge.

In the enumeration: first, knowing the karma, objects, and fruits; second, knowing that within the mind of objects there is the wisdom of no-teacher and so forth, which is fundamentally quiescent. However...
Because ordinary beings cannot observe objects, they do not appear before them; because Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas have already attained the ability to observe them, they do appear.
Therefore, it is said that "the realm of objects is known to be quiescent. This is stated in the *Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Manifestation).

Third, one knows that all objects of perception summoned through transformation are of a single nature, namely, the nature of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This nature is as firm as a diamond (*vajra*).

Fourth, vocal karma pervades the ten directions. Fifth, extinguishing the mind’s defiled attachments. Sixth, equally experiencing birth and non-birth. Seventh, the bestowing of faculties and the receiving of objects:
by means of the faculties, the mind grasps signs; by means of feeling (*vedanā*), one is established in dhyāna. Now, one abandons these two;

therefore, one does not dwell upon signs nor relish dhyāna, or alternatively, one relies on the faculties and feelings to enter the cessation concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Seventh, relinquishment. Eighth, there are four pairs. First, knowing...
All things are neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks; this means that true nature is not lost and conventional appearances are not destroyed.

Second, knowing one thing, one knows that the single nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature. Third, although one knows that all phenomena have no differentiation, one knows that this does not obstruct the existence of various phenomena.
Ninth, there are fifteen pairs: first, realizing the distant [rebirth] and receiving birth, while knowing that birth is fundamentally non-existent.
1. Arising; 2. knowing that the various phenomena of causes and conditions are themselves the fruit; 3. objective realm and practice; 4.

arising and ceasing as verbal expression—meaning verbal expression speaks of arising and ceasing, or this may be considered a separate category; 5. delusion and separation from delusion; 6. inversion and separation from inversion; 7. defilement and purity.
8. Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; 9. attainment and non-attainment; 10. grasping and non-grasping; 11. abiding and moving; 12. going and coming;
13. rising and sitting; 14. ruin and renunciation—meaning that because one has lost the roots of goodness, one does not attain renunciation.

The fifteen [qualities] consist of those achieved, the faculties to be disciplined, and the conduct by which they are disciplined; their distinct names may be understood from the subsequent summary. Regarding the ten [qualities]:

first, one does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward the Buddha-dharma, the fields, or sentient beings—this constitutes four phrases. Next, "not seeing that there are sentient beings" and so forth comprise the remaining fifteen phrases.
This means that while one does not perceive the existence of real sentient beings, one nevertheless does not abandon the work of transforming and subduing them; this is Great Compassion.

Therefore, because of their great vows; because of their preaching of the Dharma; because of their hearing of the Dharma; because of their cultivation of practice; because of their reliance on the Buddha to plant roots of goodness and offer reverent support; because of their use of spiritual power to shake the lands;
because of their knowledge of the medicinal remedies of the Dharma, their knowledge of the diseases of the faculties, and their knowledge of distinctions;

because of their knowledge of the arising and ceasing of the fruits of suffering; because of their knowledge that all conditioned phenomena are like reflections; because of their unimpeded engagement in practice; and although they have forever severed the root of rebirth, for the sake of...
Because of providing protection, one is also not obstructed by the practice of taking birth, for there is no [fixed] practice.
Because one accords with the Buddha-lineage and gives rise to the mountain-king mind, one knows that all delusive entries enter the gateway of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Thus, wisdom is vast and unshakable, enabling one to achieve equal salvation within the cycle of birth and death. The specific conclusions and fruits may be understood from the text. Fourth, there are ten kinds of liberation.

This refers to the following: previously, the skillful clarity of the great vows was distinguished; now, the liberation from the bonds of the afflictive hindrances is revealed. Within the enumeration:

first, regarding greed and so forth, one first abandons the five dull fetters (*pañca-nivaraṇa*) and subsequently abandons the five sharp fetters (*pañca-kleśa*). First, one abandons the three views (*trīṇi dṛṣṭayaḥ*), and subsequently abandons the two graspings (*dvau parāmarśau*).

Among the three categories beginning with the four aggregates (*catvāraḥ skandhāḥ*), one abandons the burden and attains the "aggregate without grasping" (*anupādāna-skandha*). Fifth, one abandons the clinging to the teachings of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna-dharma-abhiniveśa*).

1. Because of abandoning that *upadhi* (substratum) for the sake of *nirvāṇa*. 2. Because of abandoning the six dharmas by contemplating arising as non-arising. 3. Because of being free from attachment to the four kinds of objects.

4. Because of dwelling free from the two extremes. 5. Because of being free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). 6. Because of knowing the three time periods (*tryadhvan*) in a single moment of mindfulness;
this is because one is free from the delusion regarding the ripening of karma (*vipāka*) and the failure to understand the three times. [The concluding and progressive sections of the text.]
Easy. The preceding forty phrases conclude the explanation of the practice of mastery over karmic activity.
From here on, the third section—consisting of one hundred and fifty phrases beginning with "ten groves"—clarifies the practice of the fulfillment of supreme virtues.
This section contains four parts: first, the initial forty phrases clarify the practice of the perfection of virtue; second, the twenty kinds of generating the immovable [mind].
The twenty phrases following "In the mind" clarify the profound practice of dwelling in the mind.

The fifty phrases following the thirty kinds of wisdom-observation clarify the practice of the extraordinary capabilities of wise virtue. The forty phrases following the four kinds of "immeasurable" clarify the lofty and profound practice of heavy merit.
Regarding the first ten [of the thirty-two marks], they refer to strolling for pleasure in gardens and groves. The next ten refer to the main palace halls.
The following ten refer to enjoying pleasures therein. The final ten refer to being prepared with girdles; thus, they are called "adornments.

Within the first category of gardens and groves, each entry first cites the name and essence of the garden or grove, followed by an explanation of its meaning—namely, that it serves for wandering, relaxation, and delight. The first seven belong to one's own nature (*svabhāva*).

The practice of application; the subsequent three are the practices for superior progress toward the fruit. Among the former [five], the first two are practices for the benefit of others, and the latter five are practices for one's own benefit.

Regarding the five aspects—first, time; second, place; third, adversity; fourth, favorability; and fifth, cultivation—the path and so forth flow from the Buddha; thus, it is called "the realm of the compassionate father.

Within the latter three, the first is the dharma of the result of a single thought-moment, the second is the manifestation of supernatural powers, and the third is the attainment of perfect enlightenment. This concludes [the section].
And the fruition can be understood. Regarding the "ten kinds of palaces": whereas the preceding groves and gardens were for external excursions, these palaces are for internal dwelling;

thus they are explained next. Furthermore, as before, the names are first indicated and their meanings subsequently revealed. Within the enumeration, there are two parts: the first is general, and the latter nine are specific.
The general refers to the bodhicitta being the root of practice for sentient beings; if it is lost or forgotten, then the Dharma...

Because their practice is without dependence. Within the subsequent section on specific categories, the first seven concern practices for the benefit of others. Among these, the first four involve transforming sentient beings within the three realms:
first, transforming those in the realm of form; second, the four Brahma-abodes, which refer to the noble gods, Brahmās, and Buddhas.

These abide in the noble practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they abide in the celestial practices of the four dhyānas; and they abide in the Brahma-practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Furthermore, they dwell constantly performing Buddha-activities; yet this is the effortless practice of a Buddha. Second, because the five gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) have not yet severed the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the Bodhisattva is born among them in order to sever them; therefore, it is said that he is undefiled by any afflictions (*kleśa*). These five fetters are:

attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*arūpya-rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—these being the two [remaining] of the five [fetters] in the Pure Abodes. Next...

Regarding the three types of transformation within the process of conversion: first, for the sake of sentient beings in defiled lands, the Bodhisattva manifests a body that conforms to their kind in order to cause them all to sever their afflictions;
second, for the sake of converting those with whom he previously practiced together, he manifests birth in a royal palace; third, for the sake of converting those who are arrogant.
The latter two [stages] consist of the fulfillment of one’s own practice: first, the cultivation of the cause; second, the attainment of the fruit. The remaining text is clear.
Regarding the "ten kinds of desired objects": since he previously dwelt in the palace and delighted in superior benefits, these are listed.

Among them, the first eight are delights within the dharmas of the cause, while the latter two are delights within the dharmas of the fruit. Within the former group, the first six are dharmas for self-benefit; alternatively, the fifth may also be [included therein].

Benefiting others. The latter two are the methods for benefiting others. Regarding the fourth [point], which has ten kinds of adornments: because the mind has already become mature through delight, one adorns oneself with supreme qualities.

Among these, the first two are the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); the next two are the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

The next two [vows] concern the adornment through practice; the following two concern the gathering of lands and the raining down of the Dharma; the final two concern maintaining practice and manifesting transformations.
The above concludes the section on the practices for perfecting the faculties and virtues.
Second, there are twenty phrases clarifying the firm and profound practices of the abiding mind; therein, the first ten concern the arousal of the immovable resolve.

Regarding the mind: among the distinctions, first is the firmness of relinquishing all [attachments]; second, turning toward the Dharma; third, making offerings to the Buddha; fourth, contemplation of compassion; fifth, gathering [beings] through loving-kindness;

sixth, bestowing [the Dharma] upon those seeking it; seventh, constant cultivation; and eighth, firm faith that has roots, for such faith gives rise to the fruit of Buddhahood. "Without turbidity" means not being mixed with doubt.
"Pure" means not being mixed with the vehicles of the two [Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas]. "Utterly pure" refers to correct realization.
Because it is the principle. "Free from defilement" means there is no seeking in the observance of precepts. "Luminous and penetrating" means not being deluded regarding cause and effect.
"Respectfully making offerings to all Buddhas" means being directed toward the fruit. "Non-retrogressive" means the causal practices are firm. "Inexhaustible" means the mind is limitless.
"Indestructible" means being unmoved by external conditions. "Great joy" means corresponding to one's original vow.
Therefore, regarding "the immovable mind up to the path of skillful means," this refers to bringing the wisdom of the fruit to fulfillment.
Regarding "hearing of all bodhisattvas and so forth," this refers to the perfection of causal practice. Second, regarding the "ten kinds of not abandoning the profound mind":

it is said that because one's previous practices are firm and immovable, one is able to exhaustively penetrate the profound principle. Within the specific [categories], there are three: first, wisdom; second, compassion; third, manifestation.

The transformative intentions: first, cultivating a resolute mind; second, drawing near to spiritual friends; third, making offerings to the Buddhas; fourth, seeking the Dharma; fifth, upholding pure precepts; sixth, gathering those of like practice;
seventh, maintaining the Buddha-Dharma; eighth, cultivating vows and practices.
The third section below consists of ten kinds of wisdom that observe the fifty phrases below.
Regarding the "Superior Intelligence, Virtue, and Excellence" capable of practice: therein, the first ten [verses] concern not abandoning through the weight of the mind;

they present the teachings on the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), secondly the methods of practice (*caryā*), thirdly the methods of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), fourthly the skillful observation of the signified meaning (*lakṣya-artha*), and fifthly the majesty of the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*).

The former refers to function; this is the Buddha’s supernormal power (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The latter refers to essence: the Dharma-body sustains all virtues. Sixth is internal retention; seventh is external preaching of the Dharma;
eighth is contemplating the profound; ninth is contemplating the vast; tenth is contemplating the illumination of the wisdom that knows phenomena as phenomena—its function is inexhaustible.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. Regarding the second point, the ten kinds of preaching the Dharma: first comes observation, followed by the preaching of the Dharma.

Furthermore, the title of the *Jin jing* (The Scripture of the Jin) is "Discrimination. Among its sections, the first two explain the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) through one principle and one metaphor;

the next one explains that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is devoid of substance, such that there is nothing to dispute; and the final seven explain the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature):
first, the merit equal to the sands of the Ganges; second, the essence is truly without dependence; third, it is as firm as a diamond; fourth, it is this very *dharmakāya*; fifth...
The Dharma-body is quiescent. It is subsumed under the six [aspects of] the path of realization. Seventh, its essence and characteristics are of a single flavor;

the summary and so forth may be understood accordingly. Regarding the three types of tenfold purity: by means of discerning the profound Dharma, there is purity through the removal of hindrances. The Jin (Western Jin) edition reads "beginningless" (*anādikāla*).
Among these, there are eight: first, no seeking for anything else; second, no doubt; third, no wrong views; fourth, no obstructions; fifth, no lack of desire for the fruit of Buddhahood;
sixth, no stammering speech; seventh, no weak nature; and eighth, manifesting great compassion.

Because these are the dwellings of a bodhisattva, furthermore, if one dwells in wisdom, one does not dwell solely in nirvana, nor does one dwell in any single place; in both cases, there is no dwelling or attachment.
Therefore, because they are (9) free from defilement, (10) free from subtle attachment and obstruction, and free from all supreme stains, they are all called "pure.
Regarding the "fetters" and so forth, it is as in the text. As for the four kinds of ten seals (*mudrā*): they are called "seals" because their qualities of purity are firm, certain, and unchanging.
The Jin version calls them "wisdom seals" (*jñāna-mudrā*). Among the list, the ancient masters correlate them with the ten patiences (*kṣānti*). First, regarding...

"Tranquilly enduring the conditions of suffering": because patience and wisdom are unshakable, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*). At the beginning, there are ten types. First, the three primary sufferings:
namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), which refers to the sensation of suffering among the three sensations, as well as those phenomena conducive to the sensation of suffering.

Since the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) are already places followed by the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), they are termed "the suffering of suffering" with emphasis due to the addition of painful contact. Second, the suffering of objects (*viṣaya-duḥkha*), which refers to that which is associated with pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).

Furthermore, phenomena conducive to pleasant feeling are suffering because they are subject to change. Third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which refers to that which accords with neutral feeling and phenomena conducive to neutral feeling;
it is suffering because its nature is fluxional and thus opposes the abiding in bliss of the aggregates. Second, one seeks the Dharma without indolence; third, one practices without weariness;
fourth, one is not startled upon hearing profound teachings; fifth, one does not feel fear; sixth, one does not feel dread; seventh, one does not feel terror; eighth, one does not...
1. Abandoning vows. 2. Firm resolve in the practice of patience toward those who cause one harm. 3. Firm resolve in the patient acceptance of profound Buddhist teachings;
this is the *dharmānusāri-kṣānti* (patience through discernment of the Dharma). 4. Firm resolve to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings. 5.
Firm resolve regarding the various Buddha-dharmas, such as the teaching on liberation. 6. Firm resolve regarding the great desire [for enlightenment].

There are eleven phrases. The first, "wholesome desire," is the general [heading]; the remaining ten are the particulars. Seven concern the determination to seek the fruit of Buddhahood without sparing one's body or life.
Eight concerns causing roots of goodness to grow in sentient beings whose roots are not yet mature. Nine concerns leading those whose roots are already mature to enter the Dharma.
Ten concerns the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit. Within each of these aforementioned phrases, there are multiple meanings according to what is appropriate.
Commentary: The [remaining] fetters and so forth may be understood accordingly. Regarding the "ten kinds of wisdom-light illumination" within the five [categories]:

this refers to the function of causing illumination through the determination of the essence of the preceding practices, such that there is no failure in their application. In the enumeration, each instance first clarifies that which is illuminated, and subsequently manifests that which illuminates.

The first two seek the fruit and behold the Buddha; the next two perceive sentient beings and the subsequent Dharma; the next two rely on spiritual friends to reveal the Buddha; and the final two gather in sentient beings through teaching.
Dharma. In the latter two Buddhas, the common practice is fulfilled.
Below this, the fourth section contains ten kinds of peerless abodes; below that, forty gates clarify the measure of virtue, the loftiness and depth of practice.

Within these, the first ten clarify the practice of reverence; the next ten, the practice of courageous cultivation; the next ten, the practice of lofty excellence; and the final ten, the profound [practice].
Extensive Practice. Regarding the first ten [difficulties], it is said that their application is difficult to fathom because they conceal the lower [stages] while being equal [to them].

Among these: (1) the difficulty of abiding in reality without realizing [nirvāṇa]; (2) the difficulty of accomplishing goodness without grasping; (3) the difficulty of knowing the practice of transformation;

(4) the difficulty of remaining untiring throughout long kalpas; and (5) the difficulty of attaining extinction without dwelling [therein]. Furthermore, another interpretation explains four as the difficulty of not wearying of saṃsāra, and the fifth as...

1. The difficulty of abiding in nirvāṇa; 2. The difficulty of establishing the characteristics of phenomena while understanding that the characteristics of the kalpas are exhausted; 3. The difficulty of knowing that dharmas are without activity while teaching that there is activity; 4.
The difficulty of realizing that the three realms and the three periods of time are solely this one mind, yet not remaining fixed in that [realization] regarding the immeasurable and boundless;

5. The difficulty of dwelling for many kalpas to practice for the sake of each and every sentient being without giving rise to weariness or aversion; 6. The difficulty of relinquishing the fruit because the causes are fulfilled. By means of these...
This is difficult to fathom; it transcends the lower stages. Second, there are ten kinds of non-inferior mind (*an-hīna-citta*).
In the Jin translation, these are called "minds free from indolence. This is because their non-inferior conduct and application surpass those who are merely courageous and uninterrupted.

Among the items listed: the first two refute the heterodox and bestow the correct; the next one skillfully guides others to joy; the next one achieves universal practice for oneself; and the next two [cultivate] merit.

The first [of the four practices] is the practice of perfecting the fruit of wisdom through conduct. The next two are the practices of teaching the Dharma and manifesting the body to discipline and transform beings.
The next one is the practice of cultivating internal and external giving for the sake of sentient beings. The last one has five parts.

Regarding the ten gates of the Dharma to be understood, the third section, "In this way," and so forth, corresponds to the characteristics of the one who understands; within this, there are six points, namely, knowing that one should understand those natures and characteristics with focused application.

Furthermore, because one awakens to its realm, it is "enlightenment" (*jue*). Because it manifests clearly before one, it is "vision" (*jian*). Because there is no vision that does not penetrate through, it is "realization" (*zheng*).

Because there is no goodness that is not advanced, it is "cultivation" (*xiu*). Because there is no ceasing, it is "severance" (*duan*). These three points clarify, in the following section, the characteristics of the mind that acts as the cognitive subject;
ten phrases may be understood therein. Fourthly, from "non-duality" (*buer*) onwards, the text provides a further explanation. That is to say, since regarding that...
Since there is no conceptual differentiation, how can one speak of a subject, an object, and an act of cognition?

Within this context, there are twelve phrases concerning knowledge, five phrases concerning manifestation, and one phrase concerning entry; "entry" here carries the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*) and the sense of "clearly understood through wisdom.
There is one phrase concerning realization. Regarding the three [realms], there are ten types, which, like a mountain, are preeminent for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

As for "mind" (*citta*): it is said because it is accomplished through courageous practice; the great mind is resolute and directed toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), such that it cannot be shaken.
Among the list, the first is the cultivation of the decisive wisdom that realizes [the truth]. Second, one contemplates that all phenomena have been non-existent by nature from the very beginning;
because they are decisively non-existent as a nature, one realizes non-attainment, which constitutes ultimate realization. Third, the cultivation of aspiration.

Because one knows and sees through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is "pure white" (*śukla*). Fourth, having achieved the four certainties, one seeks the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
not seeking fame, profit, or honor, there is no "seeking anything else. Not hearing the Dharma from others, yet claiming "I understand it," there is no "thieving mind regarding the Dharma.
For the sake of the Dharma, one is able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish; being free from all pride, one serves those who preach the Dharma.
For this reason, because of their equanimity, they give rise to a sense of respect and a sense of wonder never before experienced.
This is the fifth great practice of patience: the practice of increasing patience when encountering adverse conditions.

Because they have attained impartial equanimity (*upekṣā*) within their discernment, it is like a lion cub who, upon hearing its mother’s roar, not only fails to fear her, but instead increases its own majestic presence. This constitutes the sixth perfection.

The Practice within the Realm of Māra. This consists of four sections. First, the accomplishment of superior retribution, which comprises ten phrases. Second, although one may later fall to a lower state, one does not cling to this superiority;

this includes five general and specific phrases. Third, regarding those who merely sink deeply, it concerns only the Dharma; there are thirteen phrases, which can be understood by referring to the explanation in the preceding "Chapter on Pure Conduct.
Fourth, the Son of the Buddha cites the causes to establish the accomplishment; herein, there are three parts: the heading, the inquiry, and the explanation.

This may be understood. Seventh is the practice of courageous diligence. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Though the fool practices for even a short time, his mind is weary and he feels as if it has been long;
the Buddha, through immeasurable eons, considers diligent courage to be but a moment. Eighth is the practice of not abandoning those who forget [the path].

Ninth is the practice of courageous cultivation without relying on companions. Tenth is the practice of the simultaneous application of the provisional and the ultimate, meaning that although all phenomena are ultimately non-existent, [one acts accordingly].

It can be attained, yet one does not abandon the diligent cultivation of virtue. Regarding the fourth point, the ten kinds of entry into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* such as the ocean-like wisdom (*sāgarajñāna*), and so forth:
previously, because the aspiration was shown to be lofty and difficult to look up to, it was described by the metaphor of a mountain;

now, because the wisdom is analyzed as being deep and unfathomable, it is named after the ocean. Among these ten types listed: first, entering the immeasurable realms of sentient beings; second, entering the world-realms; third...

Entering the realm of empty space. Fourth, regarding the excellent entry into the *dharmadhātu*, there are seven ways of entering. "Entry" (*praveśa*) refers to clear understanding and realization, as previously explained.
Fifth, entering the realm of roots of goodness associated with the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth, entering the realms of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Ninth, being able to make offerings to many Buddhas. Tenth, being able to seek many teachings. The above constitutes the general response. This is the thirtieth verse.
The section on the characteristics of practice within the stages is concluded.
From here begins the fourth major section, from the ten kinds of abiding like jewels up to the ten kinds of bodies, which consists of three hundred phrases.

These answer the previous thirty questions and clarify the characteristics of practice within the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). The ancient masters [have categorized] the ten [questions] within the inquiry...

Within the "Mastery of a Single Phrase," the first phrase serves as the general [principle], while the remaining phrases serve as the particulars. By dividing the general into particulars, there is no further general principle remaining;

thus, it is said that this answers the previous twenty-nine questions. Now, since within both the question and the answer mastery is singular and unique, the names of the remaining phrases have no functional application.
This means that the relationship between general and particular does not exist here, and thus the general may be eliminated. This is...
Therefore, in the subsequent answer, two hundred phrases respond to the thirty phrases of the preceding question, corresponding exactly to them.
Within these three hundred phrases, there are three divisions: first, one hundred and ten phrases clarify the meaning of the firmness of the essential nature of dedication;
second, from the ten masteries downward, one hundred and twenty phrases clarify the meaning of mastery without attainment.
The seventy phrases from the third section, "Ten Kinds of Play" (*daśa-vikrīḍita*) onwards, clarify the meaning of the perfection of conduct and virtue.
Within the first [section], the essence of conduct, there are two divisions. First, forty gateways clarify that the essence of conduct achieves the high tower of the further shore (*pāra*).

The second section, comprising seventy gates from "The Ten Unbreakable Non-beliefs" (*daśābhedyaprasāda*) onwards, elucidates the supreme virtues of the essence of practice, which are free from obstacles and encompass all dharmas.

Within this, first are the ten kinds of "abiding like a jewel" (*ratnasthiti*). Because one abides in the noble and precious place of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), it is called "abiding like a jewel.
Furthermore, because one abides by means of non-abiding, it is also termed "abiding like a jewel. Among these, the first is proximity to the Buddha, and the second is hearing the Dharma.

Third, mastery over taking birth. Fourth, knowing that phenomena arise from one and many, and that after passing through many they ultimately return to one; teaching that all are without attainment (*anupalambha*). Fifth, knowing mastery:

this refers to the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) of wearying detachment, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) of cessation, the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) of eradication, and the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) of protection.
The text is not in sequential order. Protection means guarding against the fear of stagnating in quiescence like the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). And...

One does not realize [nirvana]. Not realizing is the practice of a bodhisattva; not realizing is the means of skillful mastery regarding the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the limit of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
This prior non-realization while practicing is the practice of the simultaneous application of the provisional and the ultimate.
1. One who has learned well that which is to be learned: through the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), they cause the Dharma to become free from obstacles and fulfill their vows.

2. The body does not grow weary: because for the sake of sentient beings, they undergo birth and death throughout many kalpas. 3. Although the minds of the six classes of sentient beings have no location and no activity, they are said to "exist" for the purpose of taming and transforming them.

4. Knowing that both principle and phenomena are without [inherent existence], one does not fail to attain the Dharma. 5. Knowing that principle is non-existent, one does not fail to give rise [to realization].

9. They are skillful regarding emptiness, and their aspirations are never in vain. 10. Having heard the diverse teachings of many Buddhas, they are well able to synthesize and reconcile them, because they have reached a definitive understanding through the four intentions (*abhiprāya*) and the four methods of universal inclusion (*siddhānta*).
Second, there are those who give rise to the ten kinds of Mahāyāna vows as firm as a diamond; such persons are able to attain the limitless dharmas of the Mahāyāna by means of a resolute mind.
This is because they exhaust the very limits [of existence]. Within this, there are six aspects: first, knowing the dharmas that have no bounds throughout the three periods of time;
second, encouraging many bodhisattvas through self-exhortation; third, adorning boundless lands; fourth, extending blessings and wisdom to reach limitless sentient beings;
fifth, making offerings to limitless Buddhas with roots of goodness; and sixth, seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma, rejoicing without attachment to either oneself or the Buddhas.

He knows that he is not everything, yet he does not destroy anything. The commentary explains: because the Buddha does not grasp at anything as "everything," he is able to endure boundless suffering and affliction.
Taking the severing of attachments as his standard, he endures manifold sufferings throughout many kalpas without ceasing his cultivation of practice or his gathering of sentient beings.
The commentary explains: 1. Because one contemplates that phenomena have no dual characteristics. 2. One practices the bodhisattva path throughout the eight boundless times and places.

3. One resolves the mind to necessarily accomplish boundless great deeds. 4. One remains quiescent yet functions constantly. Within this, there are four points: first, non-apprehension regarding the object;

second, not abandoning the practice of activities that arise for those who are inferior or unequal; third, the section beginning with "Why is this? which cites the original vow; [and fourth, the fulfillment of that vow].
This explains the accomplishment. Regarding the fourth [point], although it is realized later, it is paired with the great vow that fuses both below.

As for the "ten kinds of great initiations" in the third [section], it is said because they cause the great tasks to be initiated and manifested. Within this, the first three are the greatness of transforming meritorious karma;

the next three are the greatness of transforming activity, which adorns the lands in order to gather in sentient beings; and the final two clarify the greatness of superior progress in gathering merit.
Ninth, attaining Buddhahood; tenth, preaching the Dharma. Regarding the four kinds of ultimate great deeds (*daśa-paryanta-mahā-kṛtya*):

whereas the previous great deeds were merely able to manifest before one, these are called "ultimate" because they clarify that what was to be done has been fully accomplished. Among them, the first is honoring and serving the Buddha.

Second, seeking help according to the capacity of beings; third, seeking the Buddha-dharma exclusively; fourth, the two [stages] following that which consist of gathering wholesome thoughts on the Dharma; next, the two [stages] consisting of the fulfillment of aspiration and practice;
and finally, the three [stages] consisting of serving a spiritual friend, approaching the Buddha, and hearing and upholding the Buddha-dharma.

The second section contains ten kinds of indestructible faith (*avetyaprasāda*). Below are seventy gates that clarify the excellence of the practice’s essence, its freedom from obstacles, and its inclusion of all dharmas.
Among these, the first forty gates clarify skillfulness in clarity and wisdom (*prajñā*), while the latter thirty gates manifest the virtues included within mental activity.
Within the former group, the initial ten clarify indestructible faith; regarding this, it refers to pure faith in the profound person and the Dharma.
The Obstacles to Faith. The first six are the conditions for the practice of faith; the latter four are the essence of the practice of faith.

Within the former, "sentient beings" refers to those who are to be transformed—the objects of compassion—and it also refers to the belief that they possess the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. Second, regarding the ten kinds of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*):
because one inwardly harbors firm faith and outwardly receives the prophetic decree, there is the bestowal of the prediction. The preceding section clarified self-knowledge.

"Bestowing Prophecy" (vyākaraṇa) refers to the Buddha’s granting of a specific prediction regarding one's future enlightenment. Among these, there are four types: first, those who possess profound understanding and realization, whose secret teachings accord with the intent of the Buddha;
second, those who, upon hearing this Great Teaching, plant roots of goodness in accordance with it, such as the sentient beings who received prophecies in the third assembly mentioned above;
third, those capable of attaining the great resolve and practicing vast deeds; and fourth, those who [attain it] through their own bodies...

1. Because of receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in the presence of the Buddha; 2. Because of receiving a prediction while still suspended [in the intermediate state]; 3. Because of realizing the truth in the first stage (*bhūmi*); 4.
Because of receiving a prediction upon attaining the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the eighth stage; 5.

Because of receiving a prediction for being able to discipline and transform others—such as the predictions given to Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa for lighting the torch of the True Dharma (*saddharma-pradīpa*), and so forth; 6. Because of completing two great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; 7. Because of attaining [the fruit] for oneself...

Regarding "because of being established": the third [section] concerning the ten kinds of dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) refers to the dedication of one's own roots of goodness in accordance with and in harmony with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Within this, the first two are the same in terms of aspiration; the next one is the same in terms of practice; the next two are the same in terms of cultivating both phenomena and principle (*tattva*);

the next two are the same in terms of livelihood, meaning that right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is able to act as an antidote; and the final one is the same in terms of purity, meaning that what is to be remedied is purified.

The same applies to the [previous] stage. Regarding the latter two, they equally attain the ultimate. Among the four types of those who attain wisdom, there are ten kinds. This is because their merit has been matured through dedication;
it is said that next comes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). In the enumeration: the first two refer to mastery and the profound understanding of the Dharma;
the third refers to entering the Buddha-wisdom, meaning to understand it with clear penetration; the fourth is the ability to dispel doubts; the fifth is entering the wisdom of the wise.
1. The sphere [of activity]. 2. Understanding the Buddha’s skillful speech in teaching the Dharma. 3. Understanding how even a small amount of merit can fulfill the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
4. Accomplishing the inconceivable stage of a bodhisattva. 5. Being able to dwell in unspeakably many lands in a single thought-moment. 6.
Awakening to the Bodhi of the Buddhas and entering all dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). 7. Hearing and retaining all the Buddha-Dharmas. 8. Entering the various adornments of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding the "Exalted Speech and Sound":
the second section, consisting of thirty gates beginning with "There are ten kinds of generating immeasurable, boundless, and vast minds," clarifies the virtues subsumed within mental activities.
Among these, the first concerns generating a mind that accords with the infinite realm; hence the statement [is made]. First.

1. Extensively recollecting that which is sought; 2. Extensively recollecting those to be saved; next, extensively recollecting that which is revealed—namely, first, the phenomena (*vastu*), and second, the revealed principle (*tattva*).
Next, the two [points] on extensively recollecting the stages of cause and effect; 7. Extensively comprehending karma and faculties; 8. Extensively adorning the buddha-fields;

9. Entering the great assemblies; 10. Contemplating the perfect sound. Regarding the ten kinds of hidden treasures (*nidhāna*): they exist because the previous great resolve was universally pervasive.
Because his virtue is exhaustive and his practice profound, he is next elucidated. Within this, there are eight points: first, knowing that all phenomena are capable of giving rise to merit;

second, knowing them as that which is contemplated; third, knowing them as that which is maintained; fourth, knowing them as that which is explained; fifth, knowing them as that which can awaken one to the ineffable truth;
sixth, knowing that the Buddha’s penetration is the demonstration of what is observed; seventh, knowing that the Dharma is the skillful production of equality; eighth...
Knowing the Dharma is the cause and condition for seeing the Buddha. Ninth, thoroughly understanding that kalpas are like illusory abodes.

Tenth, knowing that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the conditions for generating faith and joy. These ten items above all contain and accumulate [qualities], and are thus collectively termed "Treasury" (garbha).

Regarding the third, the ten kinds of discipline (*vinaya*): this refers to the accumulation of merit until it is full, making one fit for subduing; hence the name. Among these, the first is to be free from...
1. Refuting slander; 2. Dispelling doubt; 3. Abandoning pride; 4. Abandoning one's own [wrong] views; 5. Turning away from the Hīnayāna; 6. Departing from what is not firm;
7. Abandoning lack of benevolence; 8. Advancing in wholesome conduct; 9. Subduing Māra; 10. Departing from depravity. The above concludes the explanation of the firmness of the essence of practice.
Next, there are twenty kinds of mastery, followed by one hundred and twenty gates which clarify the practice of mastery without attainment.

This section has two parts. The first ten phrases clarify the practice of mastery (*vaśitā-caryā*); the latter one hundred and ten phrases clarify the practice of non-attainment (*anupalambha-caryā*).

Within the former, "mastery" refers to the fact that whatever is undertaken is accomplished with ease. Much of this section is identical to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī bhūmi*), though there are differences:

here it is called "requisites" (*pariṣkāra*), whereas there it is called "wealth" (*dhana*; *vitta*); here it is called "taking birth" (*upapatti*), whereas there it is simply called "birth. Here it says... [text continues].

Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). That is called "according with one's wish" (*yathā-icchita*); the rest is the same. However, each individual phrase contains both a heading and an explanation, which can be understood from the clarity of the text.

Regarding the subsequent lack of further utility: this is because that which was to be accomplished has already been achieved by oneself. Within this, there are three parts: first, a general heading for the ten chapters; next...
"O Son of the Buddha, how [are they categorized]? This section below explains them according to their specific chapters. The final part, "O Son of the Buddha," and so forth, provides the summary.

Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the general heading; second, the inquiry into the number, beginning with "What are they?"; and third, the formal enumeration of the names, beginning with "They are as follows.
These range from the unimpeded application regarding sentient beings up to the unimpeded application regarding power.

Following this, the middle two sections are revealed according to their respective chapters. First, there is a general inquiry; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the ten chapters are specifically revealed, which constitute ten segments.
Within each chapter, there are again four parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the enumeration; and fourth, the conclusion. Regarding the first [of these four]:

Regarding the clarification of the ten kinds of sentient beings: they are so designated because they are those to be transformed. Among these, the first two rely on the accomplishment of function through contemplation;
since the two phenomena are identical with principle, sentient beings are themselves non-existent. These two have two meanings: first, "mind-only," and second, "resolute conviction.

As for "mind-only," the faculties are the mind’s preparatory application and practice; when contemplating sentient beings, one finds them not separate from one's own mind, and thus it is said that they are merely sustained by the faculties.
Second, regarding the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): because the Bodhisattva’s power of resolute conviction definitively seals and sustains sentient beings as being non-existent.

Third, because he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings at the appropriate time. Fourth, because he is able to manifest sentient beings. Fifth, because he draws all sentient beings into his own pores.
Sixth, because he manifests the sentient beings of other lands so that they may be seen here. The latter four demonstrate the eight classes of beings.

This is because it is equal to the physical marks of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. Second, the explanation of the ten kinds of lands refers to the resultant environment upon which those to be converted depend.
Within this, there are ten points: first, many [lands] manifest as one; second, many enter into a single hair-pore; third, knowing them to be inexhaustible.

Regarding "knowing them to be inexhaustible," there are two types: first, knowing through contemplation that there are many lands; second, knowing through contemplation that the essence of the lands is identical to the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
1. Because they are inexhaustible; 2. filling all lands with the four modes of birth; 3. manifesting all lands within one's own body; 4. moving through lands without frightening sentient beings;
5. adorning many lands within a single land; 6. adorning a single land within many lands; 7. pervading all lands with a single assembly; 8.
pervading the nets of all directions with nine types of lands; and 9. manifesting these to the sentient beings who are to be delivered.

"Causing one to see" refers to the square lattices. Within each of the twenty tiers of the various realms (*kṣetra*), there are three sets of principal and attendant deities that encircle the realm in its entirety.
"Broad realms" refers to realms that are wide and long; "deep realms" refers to subtle realms. They are called "subtle" because they are difficult to know, and thus they are termed "profound.
Regarding the third point, the ten kinds of phenomena, these refer to the various [meanings] to be explained.
Because of the Dharma: therein, each and every [phenomenon] enters into many others without destroying its own original characteristics;
thus, it does not contradict the mental understandings of sentient beings. Second, through the wisdom of *prajñā*, one analytically expounds all phenomena.

Third, one knows that all phenomena are beyond words, yet causes them to be realized by means of words. Fourth, one knows that all phenomena enter into a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), yet is able to speak of them.
1. The characteristic of manifold dharmas. 2. Fifth, knowing that all dharmas transcend verbal expression, yet being able to explain them extensively.

3. Sixth, skillfully transforming the meanings of all dharmas through the wheel of syllables. 4. Seventh, subsuming all dharmas into a single dharma; though one were to speak for many eons, one would never exhaust it, yet without contradiction. 5.
Eighth, subsuming worldly dharmas into the Buddha-dharma, causing all to awaken to and understand them. 6. Ninth, knowing that all dharmas are boundless. 7. Tenth...
One knows that all phenomena are without attainment, like the various distinctions within a net of illusions. Fourth, regarding the ten kinds of bodies: these are the bodies capable of cultivation.
Among them, the first two involve the mutual entry of the other and self, self and other, many and one, and one and many.

The next two involve the mutual entry of the Buddha-bodies as many and one, and one and many, as previously described. The next one involves entry into the correct [state]. The final one is the fulfillment of the three periods of time.

Within the Dharma, there are five types of tenfold vows: first, each individual body manifests as many bodies and enters meditative concentration; second, each individual body manifests as many bodies and attains Buddhahood;
third, within one [body], one manifests as a single body among many sentient beings, and within one, one manifests as many;
fourth, within one, one manifests the Dharma-body among the bodies of many sentient beings, and the Dharma-body manifests as the bodies of many sentient beings; fifth, there are ten kinds of vows.
Within this, first, one takes the vows of others as one’s own vows; second, one takes the accomplishments of others as one’s own accomplishments;
third, the benefiting of others becomes the fulfillment of one’s own benefit; fourth, there is the vow to remain unobstructed until the end of all future kalpas;

and fifth, when consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it is attained through non-apprehension, such that both are without attachment. Nevertheless, by the power of the vow, various [manifestations] appear.
1. [The perfection of] body; 2. causing other bodies to obtain benefit; 3. causing others to hear the Dharma—these first two both involve fulfilling the vows of others through one’s own vows;
4. because of the great vows, one constantly cultivates practice without interruption; 5.

by the power of these vows, within a single pore of one’s own body, one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood pervading all Buddha-fields, just as for the sake of a single sentient being, one does so for unspeakably many worlds.

Sentient beings are also like this. Tenth, by the power of their vows, they preach a single phrase of Dharma that suffuses and pervades the realm of sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Regarding the sixty kinds of spheres, each has its own specific limits; thus, they exercise sovereign mastery over these ten kinds of superior and inferior spheres.
Because they manifest the inferior within the superior, it is called "non-attainment. [The three pairs are: first, principle and phenomenon; second, correct and erroneous; third...

1. Defilement and purity; 2. Cause and effect; 3. Tranquility and agitation; 4. Reality and delusion; 5. Ordinary beings and sages; 6. Wisdom and compassion; 7. Abiding in concentration and manifesting wisdom, etc., within the world; 8.
Abiding in the realm of the Buddha while manifesting the appearance and deportment of the Two Vehicles. Regarding the seventh [section], the clarification of the ten kinds of knowledge:
knowledge does not manifest itself; it manifests itself by means of that which is known. Within this, the first two relate to the transformer (the one who converts).
Wisdom. First, discernment; second, retention. Next, three types of wisdom for knowing those to be converted: first, knowing their faculties; second, knowing their mental activities;
third, knowing the "medicine and disease" of their inclinations and desires. Sixth, ascending to enter the powers of a Buddha. Seventh, descending to know the three periods of time.

Eighth, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood. Ninth, knowing all karmas within a single faculty. Tenth, understanding all languages through the voice of a single sentient being. These are the ten.

Among the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, manifesting many bodies from within each single body; second, hearing the Dharma in the assemblies of many Buddhas while listening to the Dharma in a single Buddha’s assembly;
third, attaining ineffable great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and awakening sentient beings within a single thought-moment;

fourth, manifesting all vocal sounds from within a single sound, causing each to understand according to their own capacity; fifth, manifesting the karma of the future limit within a single thought-moment.
1. Each causes them to see for themselves their respective fruits. 2. Causes all lands to be fully adorned. 3. Universally enters the three periods of time. 4.
Radiates the light of Dharma, manifesting the bodhi of Buddhas and the practices and vows of sentient beings. 5.

Protects all roots of goodness belonging to devas, nāgas, and others, as well as those of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgata’s ten powers. 6. According to the Jin edition: "O Son of the Buddha, this is a brief explanation of bodhi..."
The Bodhisattva impartially observes all phenomena, attaining mastery over them; this mastery allows him to act as he pleases, which is termed "non-obtaining" (anupalambha).
This brings about primordial liberation. [This should be verified. Among the ten kinds of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), the first is placing many lands within a single atom;
the second is manifesting many lands within a single atom; the third is placing the waters of the oceans within a single pore; [the fourth is the ten directions...]
1. Moving back and forth without disturbing sentient beings. 2. Manifesting supernatural powers by containing many lands within one’s own body. 3.
Binding many mountains with a single hair and carrying them through various lands without frightening sentient beings. 4. Mutually manifesting the formation and destruction of many eons.
7. Not causing sentient beings to fear; 8. Manifesting the three calamities and so forth within all lands, yet not distressing sentient beings; 9.
Protecting the necessities of life for sentient beings during the time of the three calamities in all lands, ensuring they are not damaged; 10.

Holding many lands with a single hand and casting them beyond other lands, yet not causing sentient beings to be startled or terrified; 11. Explaining that all lands are identical to space, causing sentient beings...
Awakening and Understanding. Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*): these are the functional manifestations of the power of compassion and wisdom that are beyond attainment.

Among them: first, the maturation of sentient beings; second, the adornment of the buddha-fields; third, causing the body to enter the bodiless; fourth, practicing throughout eternal kalpas; fifth, awakening sentient beings;
sixth, subsuming all practices within a single practice; seventh, delivering and liberating sentient beings; eighth, personally awakening to all dharmas; ninth, by means of...
Attaining perfect enlightenment as the Omniscient One; tenth, not abandoning sentient beings.
In the third section, the summary, there are four parts: first, a brief conclusion; second, "All possess... and below, which clarifies the benefits; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation.
Thus far, the meaning of mastery and non-attachment has been elucidated.
From here below are the thirty kinds of play and so forth, seventy gates in total, which clarify the perfection of conduct and virtue.
This section is divided into two parts: first, twenty gates that clarify the excellence of conduct and virtue; second, fifty gates that clarify the complete fulfillment of conduct and virtue.
In the first ten [verses], it is explained that one’s conduct is accomplished according to one’s own will, such that there is no obstacle to wandering and enjoying [the world]; hence the name.

Within these, the first two clarify how the defiled, the pure, and their basis act as mutual causes for one another. In the next two, in the first, the body of a Buddha manifests as the body of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, while in the latter, the body of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha* manifests as the body of a Buddha.
In the following two, the body of a Bodhisattva manifests as the body of a Buddha, and the body of a Buddha manifests as the body of a Bodhisattva. In the next two...
Within nirvāṇa he manifests birth-and-death; within birth-and-death he manifests nirvāṇa. Next, during one period of entering meditative absorption, he manifests the four modes of deportment.
Finally, while at the site of a single Buddha asking about the retention [of the teachings], his body simultaneously hears and retains them throughout the assemblies of many Buddhas.

Neither does he manifest multiple bodies, nor does he emerge from meditative concentration. In this way, though kalpas may come to an end through the continuous succession of thought-moments, the bodhisattva’s practice can never be exhausted.
Regarding the second [section], the ten kinds of "objects" (*viṣaya*): in the Jin translation these are called "superior practices" (*śreṣṭha-caryā*).

Here they are termed "objects" because they are that which is encountered during his travels. Among these, the first is to demonstrate the gateways of all dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) to cause sentient beings to enter them.

Second, manifesting the adornments of all lands to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Dharma; third, knowing that the births within the realms of sentient beings are entirely like transformations (*nirmāṇa*), and employing skillful means (*upāya*) to bring them to awakening.
Regarding the phrase "the words of the transformation [bodies] depart," the Sanskrit original must be consulted. Next, the third section clarifies the mutual emergence of three pairs:

first, the Buddha-body and the Bodhisattva-body; second, the realm of empty space and the world-realm; third, the realm of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the realm of nirvāṇa. Finally, the fourth section clarifies...
The three karmas: first, from within the conventional speech of sentient beings, one brings forth the words of all Buddha-dharmas;

second, many bodies manifest as a single body, and a single body manifests as many bodies; third, a single body fills the entire dharma-realm; fourth, in a single thought-moment, one causes sentient beings to resolve for enlightenment, each manifesting many bodies to attain Buddhahood.
The second section contains fifty gates following the Ten Powers (*daśabala*). Within the context of the perfection of the virtues of conduct and realization, first are the Ten Powers.
They are called "powers" (*bala*) because their virtuous excellence consists in the functional capacity of wisdom. Each is presented with both a heading and an explanation.

Among these, within the first seven powers which are the power of causes for one's own development (*svabhāga-hetu*), the first three concern one's own practice: first, not being entangled in worldly sentiments; second, not abandoning the Buddha-dharma; third, cultivation.

Excellent conclusion. Next are the four practices for the benefit of others: first, knowing the minds of beings; second, fulfilling the wishes of beings; third, constant transformation through cultivation; and fourth, manifesting vehicles.
The latter three are the practices of superior progress: first, manifesting pure benefits and the appearance of Buddhas within a single pore;

second, causing sentient beings to resolve their minds toward enlightenment and attain Buddhahood; and third, preaching a single phrase of Dharma that accords with the faculties, desires, and natures of all beings. (2)

Regarding the ten kinds of fearlessness: because he has previously excelled through the power of merit and wisdom, he is next without dread. Among these, the first two consist of upholding both the letter and the meaning, and thus being fearless in answering difficult challenges.
The third is the thorough knowledge of the two emptinesses, such that there is no lack of understanding regarding [the absence of] an agent or an action, as explained extensively in the treatise.
The fourth is fearlessness in having no deficiency in one's deportment (*īryāpatha*). The fifth is fearlessness in having no error in the three types of action (*trikarma*). The sixth...
1. Being free from the fear of obstacles posed by Māras and non-Buddhists; 2. Attaining the state where there is no fear regarding what cannot be heard or retained; 3.
By the power of aspiration, being free from the fear of attachment to birth and death (saṃsāra); 4. Manifesting in common with the two vehicles while remaining fearless regarding falling back; 5.
When the conditions for a response appear before one, being free from the fear of being unable to manifest a response—these are the ten types of uncommon qualities previously explained.

Fearlessness. Now, the unique [qualities] (*āveṇika*) are distinguished by two meanings: first, they are not shared with ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle; second, there is nothing else with which they could be shared.

Regarding these ten phrases, all state that "it is not through the teaching of another. Among them: first, one personally cultivates the six perfections without depending on the instruction of a teacher;

second, one is universally able to gather in sentient beings; third, skillful dedication of practice; fourth, skillful means of practice. Within this [fourth], there are seven [points], the first of which is... [not shared with others].

1. Skill in detesting worldly artifice; 2. Skill in not clinging to one’s own pleasure; 3. Skill in mastery over meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); 4. Skill in not discriminating against places of birth; 5.
Skill in being fully equipped with worldly branches of knowledge; 6. Skill in manifesting the small without losing the great; 7. Skill in manifesting the fruit without severing the cause. 5.
The dual practice of skillful means and reality (*upāya-tattva-yuganaddha*). Within this, there are ten types: 1. Manifesting *saṃsāra* within *nirvāṇa*; 2. Knowing... [text fragment ends]
1. To manifest birth while being unborn in order to exhort and transform others; 2. To enter extinction while manifesting delusions; 3. To manifest many bodies from a single body; 4.

To enter meditative concentration while manifesting the experience of desire; 5. To transcend the three realms while not abandoning the joy of rebirth; 6. To internally experience the bliss of the Dharma while externally manifesting a lack of joy;
7. To adorn the body with marks while manifesting an ugly form; 8. To accumulate merit while manifesting birth in the three evil destinies; 9. To attain the fruit while not abandoning causal wisdom.
Sixth, the three karmas follow the movement of wisdom. Seventh, one undergoes the sufferings of the three miserable realms on behalf of sentient beings.

Eighth, one never tires of beholding sentient beings. Ninth, one vows to be firm and pure oneself, and likewise to make others firm and pure. Tenth, having perfected the sphere of self-awakening, one attains spontaneous enlightenment without a teacher.

Regarding the "four kinds of tenfold activities": the preceding [section] established the uncommon virtues; now, because the activities performed are being distinguished, the next passage says: "Within this..."
The first [verse] refers to the location; the next three refer to persons; the next one refers to time; the next two refer to function—first, one's own practice, and second, bodily radiance;

the final three refer to the basis for upholding—first, protecting the Dharma, second, expounding the Dharma, and third, fulfilling vows according to aspiration. Each has its respective heading and explanation.
Regarding the "five kinds of ten-fold bodies," this is because the former are the causes consisting of past karma, while the latter are the results consisting of the body. This, too, is a dedication.

Regarding the ten bodies obtained upon the fulfillment of the stage of orientation (*mukha-avasthā*): among them, the first two concern the essence (*svabhāva*). First, the characteristic of coming is exhausted;

second, because there is fundamentally no coming and likewise no going, they cannot be apprehended through seeking. The subsequent five concern function (*vṛtti*). The first [of these five] is as if it were real.
It is not unreal. Second, because it reveals the true principle to the world, it is not false. Third, because it abides in the exhaustion of the inexhaustible.
Fourth, because it is indestructible. Fifth, because it is immovable. The latter three concern characteristics: first, the characteristic of merit; second, the characteristic of the signless.

The characteristics of the three fruits. These are found within the ninth practice; among the ten bodies, there are similarities and differences, and their mutual inclusion is as explained in the chapter.
The three hundred phrases above complete the response regarding the characteristics of the practices within the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*). The original commentary states:

"Regarding these ten karmas and ten bodies mentioned above, many ancient masters have categorized them as being included within the subsequent ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). However, according to the separately circulated version of the *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Delivering the World from Suffering)..."

Within the sixth cycle of questions and answers, this occurs at the end of the fourth cycle. Now, based on that sutra, I shall categorize and analyze this text as being included within the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).

From here begins the fifth major section. Following the ten types of bodily action, there are five hundred phrases that answer the fifty preceding questions regarding the modes of practice within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

This section is divided into four parts: first, one hundred and twenty gates clarify the distinct capabilities of the three types of action (*trikarma*) within the ten stages, which are situated in the first stage;
second, from "ten types of diligent cultivation" onwards, ninety... [the text continues].

1. The section on the ten kinds of paths of departure from birth (*daśavidha-vivarta-mārga*) comprises ninety gates, clarifying the practice of cultivation that eliminates obstacles; it is associated with the second and third stages (*bhūmi*). 2.

From the ten kinds of perfections (*daśapāramitā*) downward, there are two hundred gates, clarifying the practice of cultivation that brings maturation to fruition; it is associated with the fourth stage and those above. 3.

From the ten kinds of feet (*daśavidha-pāda*) downward, there are two hundred gates, clarifying the practice of the perfect completion of the marks of retribution (*vipākaphala-lakṣaṇa*); it is associated with the eighth stage and those above.

Regarding the first [section], it is divided into three parts. First, twenty phrases clarify the practice of bodily action (*kāyakarman*). Second, forty phrases clarify the practice of verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Finally, sixty phrases clarify the practice of mental action (*manaskarman*).
Regarding the first two of the initial ten [powers]: first, each individual body pervades all sensations; second, from a single body, all sensory faculties arise;
third, from a single body, one takes birth in all realms of existence; fourth, one travels through various lands; fifth, one approaches all Buddhas;
sixth, one covers all lands with a single hand; seventh, one crushes the vajra-mountains of all lands into atoms with a single hand; eighth, within the body...

1. Manifesting the formation and destruction of all lands; 2. Containing the realms of sentient beings within the nine bodies; 3. Manifesting pure lands and sentient beings attaining enlightenment within the ten bodies.

Regarding the ten types [of bodies] following these two: these are explained in terms of the practice of the Dharma as constituting the body, which differs from the preceding section that speaks directly of the ontological essence of the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Among them: 1. The practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); 2. The practice of the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*); 3. Substituting for the suffering [of others].

1. The practice of compassion; 2. The practice of protective kindness; 3. The practice of beneficial merit; 4. The practice of wisdom of identical essence; 5. The practice of not being subsumed by the realms of existence; 6.
The practice of responding whenever there is a sentient being to be reached; 7. The practice of manifesting supernormal powers; 8. The practice of demonstrating the attainment of Buddhahood.
The second section consists of ten types of speech and forty subsequent phrases, which clarify the essence of vocal action (*vāk-karman*).

It should properly be termed "vocal action," because speech is subsumed under the category of bodily constituents (*kāya-bhāga*). Within this [section]: first, it is called "gentle" (*mṛdu*) because it is free from harshness;

second, it is called "all-purifying nectar" (*amṛta-sarva-śītala*) because it is free from feverish affliction—that is, because divisive and disruptive speech causes the mind to burn with heat. The next two [phrases] are free from false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). The remaining six...
