Abstaining from frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*). These [explanations] are all given according to the perspective of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). If explained according to the perspective of manifestation (*vijñapti*), then each of the ten [types of speech] reveals a specific virtue.

Second, regarding the "ten kinds of pure cultivation of vocal action": this is named according to the causes of cultivation. Within this, the first two concern delighting in hearing the virtues and conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the next two concern conduct free from faults; the next two concern acts of vocal karma as offerings to the Buddhas; and the final two concern the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
1. Practice. 2. The practice of the two subsequent layers of Dharma that involves slighting the body. 3. Attaining the ten protectors:

because one’s speech is truthful, the dragons, devas, and others respectfully guard them; it should be understood that to these eight classes of beings, the Brahma kings and the Buddhas, the Kings of the Dharma, are added to make ten.
4. Being able to accomplish the ten great matters: because of the internal cause of sincerity and the addition of external conditions.
"Guarding" means causing what has been spoken to be extensively accomplished and fulfilled. Within this, there are nine aspects: first, the ability to sever all doubts;

second, the ability to reach everywhere; third, the thorough understanding of sentient beings; fourth, the purification of all resolute convictions (*adhimukti*); fifth, the ability to sever all delusions; sixth, causing one to be free from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
seventh, causing the aspiration for the Dharma to be purified; eighth, causing the cultivation of virtue to expand; and ninth, the universal surveying of phenomena according to their principle.
The Dharma-realm. Tenth, the universal realization of parinirvāṇa.
Third, there are ten kinds of mind, followed by sixty gates that clarify mental karma (*manas-karman*).

Within this, the first ten phrases clarify the essence of mental karma, while the subsequent fifty phrases clarify the function of mental karma. Regarding the former, [the first] is the expansive mind, the second is the profound mind, and the third is...
1. The superior mind; 2. the pure mind; 3. the sharp mind; 4. the firm mind; 5. the unstained mind; 6. the aspiring mind; 7. the wisdom mind; 8. the boundless mind.

These are all minds of resolute intention (*āśaya*). Regarding the second [category], there are ten kinds of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*), because it is appropriate for the essence of the mind to give rise to its superior functions once it is fully filled with principle. Among these, the first six clarify benefit (*hita*).
The mind of others. Next, two are the minds for one’s own benefit. The final two belong to the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣabhāga*) and consist of benefiting others.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific; however, it should be understood that all of them benefit others. Regarding the third [category], there are ten kinds of pervasive minds (*pariccheda-citta*):

since the aforementioned generation of the resolve has ultimately accomplished its task and pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, they are so called. Among these: first, the breadth of compassion; second, ...
1. Wisdom accords with the profound. 2. Relying on the mind, one discerns karmic functions; in a single moment of mindfulness, one knows the three periods of time through many minds. 3.
One universally perceives the realms of all Buddhas and fully understands the eight phases of enlightenment. 4. One universally knows the faculties, desires, and habitual tendencies of beings.

5. One follows the various wisdoms that realize the dharma-realm. 6. One knows that all mental activities are like an illusory net. 7. One universally knows the consciousness of those who practice the contemplation of the non-arising of all conditioned phenomena.

Regarding their essential nature: ninth, they are pervasive and without attainment, because the mind does not abide in either self or other minds; tenth, they are pervasive in all sovereign minds, because one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
Fourth, regarding the ten faculties (*indriya*): because the preceding mind is fulfilled, it is capable of serving as a vessel for the Dharma and can give rise [to further qualities];
therefore, they are called "faculties. Among these: first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of pure aspiration; third, the faculty of diligence; fourth, the faculty of concentration...
The faculties: (1) constantly abiding in cultivation; (2) the five wisdom-faculties (*pañca-prajñendriya*); (3) the continuity of the six faculties until the ultimate goal;

(4) firm and sharp realization that penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); (5) realized wisdom that illuminates and functions to reach the realm of the Buddhas; (6) illumination that all Buddhas share the same single nature.
The ten unhindered wisdoms reach the limit of non-obstruction, for this is the fundamental locus of the Buddha’s ten powers;
thus it is said, "profoundly entering," and so forth. From the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) downward, all these are wisdom, merely manifested through different names.

Regarding the five kinds of profound mind (*gambhīracitta*), which in the Jin translation are called "direct mind" (*ṛjukacitta*): here, "profound mind" has two meanings. First, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)...

Because they reach the ultimate limit of excellence; because their two minds constantly delight in cultivating all wholesome practices; therein, the first two are untainted and unmixed with those of the ordinary or the Lesser Vehicle;
the next two realize the objects and the wisdom that perceives them; the fifth is immovability amidst adversity; the sixth is the pure cultivation of perfect wisdom;

the seventh is the upholding of what has been heard; the eighth is non-attachment toward the places of rebirth; and the ninth is the possession of the wisdom regarding objects that are difficult to know. The tenth—
One cultivates goodness without weariness. The sixth [stage] has ten kinds of superior profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*).

While the Jin dynasty simply called these "profound resolves," they are now termed "superior" because their practice surpasses the preceding stages. Among them: first, firmness in advancing toward goodness; second, understanding the esoteric teachings;
third, being able to uphold the True Dharma through aspiration and practice; fourth, reaching the depths of profound meaning; fifth, mastery over the teachings; sixth, reaching all states of peace.

1. Establishing the gates of the teaching; 2. Purifying the buddha-field; 3. Maturing sentient beings; 4. Receiving empowerment from the Buddhas; 5. Attaining mastery over birth; 6. Establishing the gates of the doctrine; 7. Accomplishing all practices; 8. Excellence in meditative concentration and its application;
9. Fulfilling one's original vows; 10. Bringing the benefit of others to completion. The characteristics of the first stage (*bhūmi*) are hereby concluded.
The twentieth section below, titled "Diligent Cultivation of Universality," consists of ninety gates that clarify the characteristics of practice from the second bhūmi upward.
This is divided into three parts: first, thirty phrases clarifying the practice of diligent cultivation through wisdom;

second, thirty phrases starting from "Ten Resolute Understandings of Knowing the Realm of Sentient Beings" clarifying the practice of diligent cultivation through compassion; third, ten kinds... [text truncated].
The thirty phrases below explain the ultimate practice of compassion and wisdom.
Regarding the beginning: "Those who first diligently cultivate" attain the state of superior mental attainment precisely because they have diligently cultivated.

Within this section, the first six phrases describe the diligent cultivation of the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), while the latter four describe the diligent cultivation of the practice of gathering in sentient beings (*saṃgrahavastu*). To know that phenomena lack intrinsic nature and to teach it accordingly is called "compassion" (*maitrī*).

Knowing that the aggregates of phenomena are empty is called compassion (*karuṇā*). Substituting for suffering is called pity (*anukampā*). Demonstrating the ten powers of a Buddha and causing others to speak [of them] is called joy (*muditā*).
Turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma so that it reaches the minds of sentient beings is called equanimity (*upekṣā*), because of abandoning birth and death.

Second, there are ten kinds of resolute understanding (*adhimukti*), because one gives rise to resolute and superior resolve toward all virtuous practices: first, delighting in supreme goodness; second, delighting in various adornments; third, delighting in extensiveness.

1. Greatness; 2. Profundity of the four joys; 3. Pervasiveness of the five joys; 4. Worthy of receiving empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); 5. Joyful compassion and patience; 6. Clear understanding of karma and its results; 7.
Manifesting supernormal powers according to need; 8. Receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Third, there are ten kinds of definitive understanding regarding all worlds:
because one has already attained internal understanding and certainty, one also knows that the external vessel-worlds interpenetrate one another without obstruction.
It is an obstruction. Within this, there are eight [knowledges]: first, knowing many [realms] to enter into one; second, knowing one to enter into many;
third, knowing a single Buddha’s flower-throne to pervade all lands; fourth, knowing all lands to be like space; fifth, knowing all lands to be endowed with the adornments of Buddhas;
sixth, knowing all lands to be filled with Bodhisattvas; seventh, knowing all lands to enter into a single pore; eighth, knowing all benefits to enter into the body of a single sentient being.

next, one contemplates the nature of being free from conditioned activity; next, one establishes oneself in the joy of wholesome conduct; next, one is free from views of existence and non-existence;
finally, each single thought encompasses the entire Dharma-realm. Regarding the second [set], the ten treasuries: the former explained the belly in general, while now they are specifically revealed.
It is called a "storehouse" (*garbha*) because it is like the five internal organs. This is explained next. Here too, the meaning of "gathering and storing" is taken as the primary sense.

Within this, the first six [perfections] gather sentient beings below, while the latter four gather the fruit of Buddhahood above. Regarding the former, the first three constitute a general gathering: the first is the bestowing of understanding.
Second, it causes them to practice. Third, because they perfect their virtues and enter the wheel of non-retrogression, the latter three [aspects] are specifically subsumed.

For those among the three groups of sentient beings whose faculty of faith is already established, [the Buddha] responds to their needs simultaneously without increase or decrease, causing them to achieve perfection in a single thought-moment.

For those whose faith is not yet established, he causes their faith to continue in succession, becoming firm and non-retrogressive. For those who are fixed in error, he gives rise to compassion and acts on their behalf.
Regarding the causes and conditions for generating faith in the future, it brings sentient beings to nirvāṇa.

Although they may lack the bodhicitta, because the light of the Dharma enters their pores, it can act as a causal condition for their awakening. Among the four subsequent superior summaries: first, the summary of the Buddha’s ten powers;
second, the summary of the four fearlessnesses; third, the summary of the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); and fourth, the summary of the Buddha’s thorough knowledge of the four types of objects.

Regarding "Wisdom": there are ten recollections (*smṛty-upasthāna*). While the Path generally reveals all the internal organs, here the heart-organ (*hṛdaya*) is specifically clarified as being supreme.

Among these, the first two comprise the mind that gathers virtue: first, the mind of diligent exertion; second, the mind of extinguishing evil—the former subduing heterodoxy, the latter eliminating delusion.
The next two constitute the mind that stabilizes practice: first, non-retrogression; second, non-attachment. These six above pertain to one’s own cultivation.

The next two [verses] concern the mind that gathers and nurtures beings: one causes them to awaken, and the other involves compassionate rescue and so forth. Regarding the "mind of the Brahma-abodes," the Brahma-abodes are precisely the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

The final two concern the mind that accomplishes virtue: one is profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the other is the "mark of the proclamation" (the Sanskrit text reads *śrī-vatsa-lakṣaṇa*).
The third section, from the twenty lines beginning with "the ten kinds of donning armor," clarifies the armor of the body.

Regarding the armor: the first ten phrases concern donning the armor upon the body. Because it prevents injury from the enemy, it symbolizes that one uses compassion and so forth to protect oneself, not allowing the thieves of delusion to cause harm.
Within these, the first two are the armor of compassion; the next two are the armor of seeking through vows;
the next three are the armor of gathering sentient beings; and the final three are the armor of gathering virtues. Second, regarding the ten kinds of weapons: these are the blades of weaponry.

Generally speaking, these are designated as the "appliances" (upakaraṇa) for giving, ethical discipline, and so forth, in order to subdue stinginess and other such afflictions. Among them, the first five are appliances that accord with [the goal] to destroy impurities;

the next three are appliances that oppose [the goal] to destroy impurities—just as one uses a thief's own weapons to harm that very thief. The final two should be understood as appliances for accomplishing virtues and achieving merit.
The fourth [section] consists of seventy phrases beginning with ten "heads" (*mūla*), which clarify the functional activities of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

First, regarding the "heads": they are so called because they are situated at the top of the body. Within this section, the first clarifies the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); the second, the virtue of reverence (*gaurava-guṇa*); the third, the virtue of understanding (*prajñā-guṇa*); the fourth, the virtue of merit (*puṇya-guṇa*);
the fifth, the virtue of compassion (*karuṇā-guṇa*); the sixth, the virtue of honor (*pūjya-guṇa*); and the final four, the virtues of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). There are two [sets] of ten.

Regarding the "eye": because it practices virtue, is pure, supreme, and clearly illuminates its objects of perception, it is like an eye. Among these, the first five names are the same as those in the provisional teachings;

however, in the Mahāyāna, the essence and function are entirely distinct, as explained in a separate chapter. Regarding the latter five, the "Wisdom Eye" refers to the unimpeded discernment of phenomena;
the "Unobstructed Eye" refers to seeing the dharma-realm where principle and phenomena are unimpeded; and the "All-Knowledge Eye" refers to seeing the Indra’s Net.

Because they are objective spheres (*viṣaya*), the rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the ten types of ears: the first two hear distant sounds that accord with [reality], remaining free from attachment and aversion;
the next two abandon minor joys and embrace great [joy]; the next two take pity on empty suffering and remain detached from false pleasure;

the next two perfect virtue and practice; and the final two realize that the conventional is entirely the ultimate. Regarding the ten types of noses: they experience and smell the fragrance of practice based upon the nose.
It is called "increasing" because [the faculties] increase. Within this, the first four [powers] consist of hearing odors while the body does not follow after objects.

The next three not only do not follow after objects, but furthermore possess excellent discernment; they know the body, its requisites, and so forth, as well as their transformations, and they know those afflictions—this is the power of the Path.
Knowing the odors of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) means that these odors are perceived by Bodhisattvas of this class. The final three...

Each [benefit] corresponds to its respective advantage: first, causing [beings] to abide for a time in the Buddha-wisdom; second, causing them to enter the stage of fruition by means of the causal stage;
third, through the fragrance of unobstructed vows, attaining the fruit while not abandoning causal practice; fifth, possessing ten kinds of tongues, which clarifies mastery over verbal karma.

This is because one increases the roots of goodness by relying upon it. Within this, the first five [verses] manifest the virtues by way of analytical exposition, while the latter five manifest the virtues by way of functional application.
Regarding the "ten bodies" in the sixth [verse], this clarifies that the body of action (*kāyakarman*) is sovereign, manifesting forms in accordance with sentient beings.

Within this, the first three manifest as ordinary persons; the next five manifest as the bodies of the Three Vehicles; and the final two manifest as the body of essence and function, wherein essence and function are one.
As for the "seven with ten kinds of intention," this clarifies mastery over mental action (*manas-karman*). Among these, they are: first, merit; second, faith;

third, understanding; fourth, knowledge of joy; fifth, non-separation; sixth, detachment from dust; seventh, timeliness; eighth, the place of release; and ninth, subduing. (The tenth is implied by the context.)
The tenth [section] concerns the absence of self and what belongs to self.
The fifth [section] contains ten types of practice within sixty gates, clarifying the conduct of the four postures and movements. Regarding the first ten practices:
they refer to the initiation of movement and wandering. Among these, the first two concern being able to hear and being able to teach; the next one concerns self-discipline.
Next, two [stages] transform sentient beings, as there is one for each of the two realms. Next, one [stage] accomplishes wisdom. Next, two [stages] transform sentient beings through making offerings.
The final two involve attaining the fruit while maintaining causal practice; this is because nirvāṇa is itself saṃsāra. Thus, not severing saṃsāra is the practice of nirvāṇa.
One is that although the Buddha’s merits are fulfilled, he does not abandon the bodhisattva practices. Second, regarding the ten kinds of abodes:

Because conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*) comes to rest, the next section clarifies "abiding" (*vihāra*). Within this: first, abiding in the basis of practice; second, abiding in the characteristics of practice; third, abiding in right wisdom;

fourth, abiding in the locus of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); fifth, abiding in conduct associated with ethical discipline (*śīla*). The subsequent two [points] concern faith in the Dharma and associating with virtuous persons.
Next, two [of these] represent the perfection of knowledge and patience; the final one represents the fulfillment of abiding in the fruit.

Regarding the three types of "sitting," they correspond to the sequence of the four modes of deportment. Among them, the first four describe the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*) as a symbolic representation of the Dharma;

the latter six manifest the Dharma by relying on names and meanings: first, fearless speech; second, skillful speech according to the faculties; third, non-retrogressive speech; fourth, speech that bestows happiness; fifth...
We humbly discuss this together. Regarding the sixth [topic], "Subduing Māra and Crushing the Outsiders," there are ten kinds of "lying down.
This refers to the fourth of the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*). Among these, the first four "lying downs" signify the meaning of silent quiescence, thereby manifesting the Dharma.

The next four "lying downs" signify the meaning of peace and security, thereby manifesting the Dharma. The final two "lying downs" signify the meaning of ultimate non-action, thereby manifesting the Dharma. One should reflect upon all of these.

This is visible [in the following]. Regarding the five types having ten kinds of abodes: because wisdom has objects of focus (*ālambana*), the former [section] clarified that which dwells, while this reveals the place where it dwells.
Furthermore, the former demonstrated the dwelling of the body, whereas the present explains the state of the mind. Within this, the first four abide in the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*);
the next one abides in all the perfections (*pāramitā*); the next three abide in the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*); and the final two abide in mindfulness (*smṛti*).
"Wisdom is fulfilled and all phenomena are equal. Regarding the six [perfections] having ten types of practices, Yuan’s commentary states:

"The preceding [five] were for the benefit of others; now this is for one's own benefit. To be precise, the former clarifies the initial cultivation of skillful means, and thus practices such as 'delighting in hearing' are employed;
here, it clarifies the cultivation of mastery, and thus practices such as 'right mindfulness' are employed. The *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "The former was based on the body..."
This refers to mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*). If so, why is it that the preceding ten [categories] also involve mental wisdom-activity? The commentary states:

"This sutra explains that the external matters of a bodhisattva’s body and so forth are all presented in terms of internal practice to manifest their characteristics; since this is the case for all [subsequent categories], there is no cause for doubt.
Now, examining the various interpretations of the masters, they differ from one another precisely because the textual content of the sutra was not yet fully established at that time.
Now that this has been made clear, there is no need for further elaboration regarding the meaning of "the sphere of practice. Within this, the first four [points] concern one's own practice:

(1) preparatory application; (2) awakening to the principles of the Dharma; (3) subsequent wisdom in accordance with the Buddha; and (4) the cultivation of the perfections to the point of attaining Buddha-wisdom while remaining free from signs.
The next four concern the practice of gathering sentient beings: (1) a general summary; (2) acting in common; and (3) using the original language to demonstrate sameness.

Because greed and the other afflictions are subsequently awakened to, there are four practices of beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*). The latter two [practices] bring the two types of conduct to fulfillment.
Thus far, totaling five hundred and twenty phrases, the fifth major section—elucidating the characteristics of practice within the ten stages (*bhūmi*)—is concluded.

From here, the sixth major section, beginning from the "Tenfold Observation" and comprising five hundred and ten phrases, answers the aforementioned sixth [section] on the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results (*hetu-paripūri-phala-sampad-pratipatti*).

This is divided into two parts: first, three hundred and twenty phrases clarify the ultimate practice of the perfection of causes, which corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-mārga*);
second, there are one hundred and nine [phrases] beginning with the "Tenfold Abiding in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace."
Ten phrases: the practice of the perfection of manifest fruition is also the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Within the preceding [section], there are three parts:
first, one hundred and forty gates clarify the essential nature of causal practice; second, from "ten kinds of meanings" downward, eighty gates clarify the practice of skillful cultivation;
third, from "ten kinds of māras" downward, one hundred gates clarify the removal of obstacles within causal practice.

Regarding the preceding two sections: first, the forty phrases clarify the skillful means for initiating practice; second, from "the ten kinds of giving" onwards, they clarify the essential nature of the ten perfections.
Within the first section: the initial twenty phrases clarify the observation of mental action (*manas-karman*); the next ten phrases clarify the vigor of physical action (*kāya-karman*);
and the final ten phrases clarify the roar of vocal action (*vāk-karman*). Within the first of these, the ten kinds of observation refer to observing:

Because of the understanding of skillful means, one thoroughly masters the characteristics of what is permeable and obstructed in practice. Within this, the first three contemplations concern those to be transformed: first, knowing their karma; second, knowing their retribution;

and third, knowing their faculties. One knows these without grasping at their signs. The subsequent six contemplate the Dharma-treasure: first, the dharma of non-attainment regarding principle and phenomena;

second, the dharma of fruition; third, the dharma of teaching; fourth, practice; and fifth and sixth, the dharmas of the five stages: first, the cessation of delusions; second, [the cultivation of roots of goodness].
The accomplishment of virtue. Regarding the final [section] on the methods of transformation, there are ten kinds of "universal observation," so called because they involve thorough examination.

Among these, the first six cause sentient beings to attain the practice of the six perfections; the next one follows the instructions of spiritual friends; the next one realizes the hearing of the Dharma;
the next one uproots suffering; and the last one accomplishes wisdom. Third, there are ten kinds of "valiant strides" (*vikrīḍita*), which is a term from the Sanskrit language.
The translation says: "Sovereign Fearlessness. This means that just as the lion king attains fearlessness among the herd of beasts, moving in and out and coming and going without any obstruction;
herein, because one rides the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is said that one eclipses all others.

2. Because it tames the mind and mobilizes sentient beings; 3. Because it gives rise to the great Dharma teachings; 4. Because it extinguishes afflictions; 5. Because it subdues Māras and non-Buddhists;
6. Because it extinguishes afflictions; 7. Because it reveals the characteristics and nature of phenomena; 8. Because it teaches according to faculties; 9.
Because it speaks swiftly, according to inclinations, to bring joy; 10. Because it universally causes all to attain the fruits of the Path through mindfulness. There are ten kinds [of these].
The "Lion's Roar" (siṃhanāda) refers to being definitively fearless. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are eleven matters regarding the Lion's Roar, as fully explained therein.
Following this are: first, the bodhicitta; second, great compassion; third, repaying kindness; fourth, firm vows; fifth, upholding the precepts; sixth, seeking merit;
seventh, seeking wisdom; eighth, cultivation; ninth, the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti); and tenth, manifesting birth. These are also...

Acting according to what has been taught. Second, there are ten kinds of pure giving; the following one hundred sections clarify the practice of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). Regarding the first ten types of giving:

(1) Giving because one restrains oneself to bestow upon others; (2) Giving by bestowing each [gift] individually; (3) Giving that fulfills requests; (4) Giving that is not in vain; (5) Giving according to necessity.
1. Not clinging to the reward; 2. No non-correspondence; 3. No non-giving; 4. Giving free from extremes; 5. Not abandoning giving; 6. Giving without signs.
Second, there are ten kinds of precepts, because they guard against the ten branches. Among these, the first seven are the natural [precepts].

The latter three are categorized according to superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*). Among the former [three], the first three are the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts); the next three are the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome qualities).

Within these, the first transcends the inferior, the second turns away from the small, and the third accords with the great. The final one is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for benefiting sentient beings). Skillfully refuting the violation of prohibitions is termed "subtle.

Within the subsequent superior progress, there are likewise the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*). Regarding the three types of patience (*kṣānti*), they are as follows: in accordance with...

This is because one endures and accepts adverse conditions. Among these, the first three constitute the patience of enduring enmity and harm, as one endures the afflictions caused by the three types of action (karma) of others.
The next three constitute the patience of accepting suffering: first, abandoning base and inferior views; second, sacrificing one’s life to save others;

and third, not disparaging those who have not yet realized the truth. The final four constitute the patience of discerning the Dharma: first, seeing that the body is like an illusion and thus free from suffering, so as not to harbor anger; second, if...
Third, because one perceives that transgressions committed by oneself or others must be confessed; fourth, because one perceives that objects are not real, delusions do not arise accordingly.

Fourth, if there were a distinction between subject and object, then all phenomena would have arising. Regarding the four types of tenfold diligence, it refers to the diligent exertion that accords with principle.
Among these, the first five clarify the diligence of the three karmas: first, serving the field of honor; second, praising the Buddha.

He expounds the Dharma. There are three kinds of existence (*tri-bhava*): first, entering and emerging from various meditative concentrations; second, being free from all that is unreal; third, advancing toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
Sixth is diligence that does not pass in vain; seventh is diligence for the extinction of delusions; eighth is diligence guided by wisdom; ninth is impartial diligence;
tenth is diligence in manifesting the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] to deliver sentient beings. Fifth, there are ten kinds of dhyāna: one-pointedness of mind...

Because they are the nature of the object (*viṣaya*). Among these, the first two are explained in terms of the objects of tranquility (*śamatha*) with respect to one's own and others' bodies; the next two are explained in terms of the objects of tranquility with respect to places;

the next two are manifested by means of the mind’s cultivation and stillness (*praśrabdhi*); the next two clarify the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the final two are the functions of concentration.

The first five [of the ten] above concern the attainment of the conditions for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the next three concern the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of concentration; and the final two concern the functional activity (*kāritra*) of concentration.

Furthermore, among these, the first eight constitute the dhyānas of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); the ninth concerns benefiting sentient beings; and the tenth concerns the dhyāna that brings forth [supernormal powers].

Regarding the "six who possess ten wisdoms," this is because they engage in detailed discernment (*viniścaya*). Within this, the first three concern the understanding of phenomena (*dharma*): first, understanding the causes; second, understanding the afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, likewise understanding the results. Second, understanding...
The collection of conditions. Just as one condition leads to the arising of one dharma, so too does it lead to the arising of many.

For example, when ten conditions reach a single form-dharma (*rūpa*), those ten dharmas assemble together; each is distinct, yet one should always know that the dharmas thus assembled undergo transformation through their conditions and are individually differentiated.
As it is with form, so it should be understood for all dharmas such as sound, odor, and the rest; they are likewise produced by three conditions.

It is free from existence and non-existence. Next, the four [aspects] encompass the wisdom that gives birth to sentient beings: first, the elimination of views; second, the realization of illusion; third, the confrontation of adversaries; and fourth, the state that is neither heterodox nor limited.
The latter three [aspects] are as follows: first, seeing the characteristics to know the nature, which includes: (1) seeing the Dharma-body; (2) seeing the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
(3) the true nature of all phenomena; and (4) seeing the exhaustion of the characteristics of the lands. Second, maintaining discernment to achieve skillful means for ultimate benefit and happiness.

Third, there is the attainment of the ultimate wisdom that severs subtle obstacles and attachments. Regarding the seven types of tenfold loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because it is characterized by the intention to bestow happiness, they are:

first, equal gathering of the mind; second, conforming to joy; third, identity of essence; fourth, constant mindfulness; fifth, causing the extinction of afflictions; sixth, seeking the fruit of Buddhahood; seventh, universally illuminating the world;
eighth, universally rescuing and protecting; and ninth, realizing the nature of reality (*tathatā*). This [is not...]* *Note: The original text appears to be incomplete at the end.*

As previously stated: because ten [types of compassion] realize the true nature that is free from arising by means of non-referentiality. Regarding the eight types of compassion that possess ten aspects, they consist of the mental engagement of uprooting suffering;
therein, first is saving those who suffer without a companion, second is taking on their suffering oneself without seeking deliverance, and third is being born in places of hardship.

1. To cause those who have not yet heard [the Dharma] to hear it. 2. To cause the four types of birth to be born in the happy realms (*sugati*). 3. To cause them to cease their heedlessness (*pramāda*). 4. To cause them to generate the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). 5.

Why, throughout many eons, would one allow [this resolve] to be in vain? [This is done] to cause the four types of birth to arise. 6. To bestow happiness solely upon others. 7. To seek no recompense for one's kindness.

8. To be free from perversions (*viparyāsa*). 9. To know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure. 10. To know that all phenomena are like the tracks of a bird, having emptiness as their nature; thus, one feels compassion for sentient beings.

Because they cannot be fully understood. Regarding the nine types of joy, there are ten kinds: because one attains joy by delivering sentient beings, and gives rise to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of joy that does not depart from them.

Among these, first is the joy of personally generating the resolve for enlightenment; second is the joy of celebrating the relinquishing of all possessions; third is the joy of delivering those who have broken the precepts.

1. Rejoicing in the ability to endure those who commit evil; 2. Rejoicing in the ability to sacrifice one’s body to seek the Dharma; 3. Rejoicing in the desire and delight for the joy of the Dharma; 4.

Rejoicing in causing sentient beings to relinquish the joy of worldly possessions and instead delight in the joy of the Dharma; 5. Rejoicing in reverently making offerings to the Buddhas without weariness;
6. Rejoicing in the attainment of meditative concentration by others; 7. Rejoicing in one’s own compliance with the bodhisattva path and the realization of the Buddha’s concentration and wisdom.

There are ten kinds of relinquishment (*upekṣā*). Because the mind is free from attachment and craving, among these: first, relinquishing honor and offerings; second, not feeling anger toward those who treat one with contempt;
third, not being defiled by the eight worldly dharmas; fourth, waiting for the proper time regarding those who are vessels of the Dharma, and not disparaging those who are not vessels.

1. Not seeking the causes, practices, or fruits of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). 2. Constantly remaining far removed from the current [of saṃsāra]. 3. Not praising the vehicle that seeks weariness with birth and death. 4.

Remaining far removed from speech that obstructs the bodhisattva path through mere partial effort. 5. Waiting for the proper time to transform those whose small faculties have matured but whose great faculties are not yet mature.
6. Establishing a karmic connection with bodhisattvas; it is only when those bodhisattvas attain buddhahood that one becomes capable of being transformed. This...
Furthermore, because it also awaits the proper time, the Bodhisattva abandons [the practice] as being equal and without distinction for the two preceding types of persons.
The above concludes the explanation of the essential nature of causal practice.
Second, there are ten meanings below which comprise eighty sections, clarifying the skillful means of cultivating practice. Within this, the first four...
The ten gates clarify the practice of one’s own level (*svacaryā*). Following these ten, forty gates clarify the superior progress (*viśeṣacaryā*).
Within the former [the ten], there are ten meanings: because they are the essential purport to be realized; and because the practice is established based on those meanings.
Among them: first, practicing in accordance with the teachings; second, explaining the teachings; third, reflecting upon the principles; fourth, attaining tranquility; fifth, detachment...

Regarding the statement "there are ten kinds of phenomena": these are [the phenomena of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the path (*mārga*), sustenance (*dhṛti*), maturation (*paripāka*), and practice (*caryā*).
Among these, the first is called the "practice that accords with reality" (*tathatā-anudharma-caryā*). The next four are the phenomena for abandoning hindrances (*āvaraṇa-prahāṇa-dharma*). Next...

Third, the dharma of the characteristic of detachment. The latter two [sections] establish practice in contrast to the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) by contemplating the original self-nature. First, one abandons the remainderless nirvāṇa of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding *upadhi*, this is translated as "having suffering. According to the third fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the Two Vehicles do not attain remainderless nirvāṇa because there are three kinds of "remainder":
namely, that the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) have not yet been severed.

Because untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) has not yet been exhausted, and because the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) has not yet been abandoned—meaning that delusion, karma, and suffering still persist—it is called "Nirvana with Suffering.
There are ten kinds of requisites for merit within the three realms of existence; as these are all conditions for accomplishing merit, they are called "requisites" (*upakaraṇa*).
Among them: first, exhorting beings to give rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*); second, accordingly practicing the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Third, teaching and transforming others with right wisdom; fourth, tireless compassion; fifth, the ability to relinquish both body and wealth; sixth, diligently cultivating the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha;
seventh, not disparaging even small virtues; eighth, not looking down upon ordinary people; ninth, revering and supporting great beings; tenth, practicing vast generosity.
Regarding the "four kinds of requisites for wisdom," this refers to the causes and conditions that bring about wisdom. In...

[The middle section: First, one draws near to true and virtuous friends and does not contravene their instructions; this constitutes the attainment of "endowment with wisdom. The following points are to be understood accordingly.

Second, one disciplines oneself to be essential and compliant with the wholesome. Third, one is mindful of the good and perceives the evil. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 18) states: "The six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) are: recollection of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, ethical discipline (*śīla*), generosity (*dāna*), and the devas.

The six respects (*ṣaḍ-ārādhanā*) refer to the six ways of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-abhivādana*). [These concern] body, speech, mind, ethical discipline, views, and conduct; some also mention generosity (*dāna*)."

Some speak of "learning" (*śikṣā*), which refers to the identity of body, speech, and mind; the identity of practicing compassion; the identity of the bodhisattva precepts; and the identity of right view, because one learns the *pāramitās*.

Regarding the "six firmnesses" (*ṣaḍ-dṛḍha*), the *Benye jing* (Upāyakauśalya-sūtra), first fascicle, states: "Understanding, practice, dedication, the ten stages, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. The commentary explains:
Based on these six firmnesses, it clarifies that this sūtra extends from the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) onwards to the inconceivable state of Buddhahood.
The various chapters preceding the "Chapter on Discussing the Dharma" (Yìfǎ Pǐn) all belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Sambodhi).
Previous masters have judged that the chapters following the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are all the superior progress of the ten stages and lack the stage of Equal Enlightenment;

this is precisely because they did not see this text and the *Mūlavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Běnyè Jīng). Herein, it is now clearly established that this is indeed the stage of Equal Enlightenment. Furthermore, this...
The six firmnesses (*ṣaḍ-dṛḍha*), also known as the six types of nature, the six patiences, the six wisdoms, and the six contemplations. The six firmnesses refer to:

firm faith, firm dharma, firm cultivation, firm compliance, and firm awakening. The six types of nature refer to: the nature of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*), the nature of essence (*prakṛti-gotra*), and the nature of the path (*mārga-gotra*).

The lineage of the sages; the nature of equal enlightenment; the nature of wondrous enlightenment; the six patiences—namely, the patience of faith, the patience of dharmas, the patience of cultivation, the patience of correctness, the stainless patience, and the patience of all-knowledge;
the six wisdoms—namely, hearing, reflection, cultivation, signlessness, illumination-and-quiescence, and quiescence-and-illumination;

the six contemplations—namely, the contemplation of the ten abodes, the contemplation of the ten practices, the contemplation of the ten transferences, the contemplation of the ten stages, the contemplation of signlessness, and [the contemplation of] all...
The contemplation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is explained in detail as therein. The ten kinds of knowledge have already been explained previously.

Fourth, abandoning worldly discourse, one distances oneself from the Lesser Vehicle and enters the Great Vehicle; delighting in what is realized and the means of realization, one finds no satiety in such delight. Fifth, the mind is single-pointedly devoted to the practice of the six perfections.

As for the four Brahma-abodes, they are fully revealed as previously stated in the first chapter on the palaces. Regarding those who accord with the luminous Dharma, they respond to questions accordingly.

For the sake of penetration; the remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. Sixth, because one has already severed the three types of discursive thoughts—desire, ill-will, and harm—one realizes the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

the remainder of the text is to be known by analogy. Seventh, one contemplates the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements] as being like illusions, mirages, and so forth, neither annihilated nor eternal, and without arising or ceasing.

Eighth, one has deep faith in quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Ninth, one constantly abides in calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), wherein the nature of phenomena is equal, and this and that are free from intrinsic nature. Tenth...
Because one sees the dharma of dependent origination, one sees that all things are originally pure. This concludes the section on the practice of one's own level.

Second, there are ten kinds of "perfection of clarity" (*vidyā-vaipulya*), consisting of forty gates, which clarify superior progress. Among these, the first ten manifest the perfection of clarity. To explain in detail:
"clarity" is called "perfection" because it is all-encompassing; furthermore, it is "clarity" because the darkness of delusion has been exhausted. It is the function of wisdom.

Because they are fulfilled, they are "complete" (*pūrṇa*). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Taishō No. 374), chapter eighteen, asks: "What is meant by 'one perfected in knowledge and conduct' (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*)? 'Knowledge' (*vidyā*) refers to attaining immeasurable wholesome fruits;

'conduct' (*caraṇa*) refers to the feet. The commentary states: According to this interpretation, that "one perfected in knowledge and conduct" is precisely what is here termed "perfected in knowledge" (*vidyāsampanna*).
Furthermore, it is said that "good fruit" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Feet" refers to the vehicle of precepts and wisdom;
by relying on the feet of precepts and wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Moreover, "illumination" is another name for mantras.
"Practice" (*caryā*) is named "Auspiciousness" (*śubha*). "Sufficiency" (*pāda*) is named "Fruit" (*phala*). Furthermore, "Mantra" (*dhāraṇī*) is named "Liberation" (*vimukti*).
"Auspiciousness" is named "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Fruit" is named "Mahāparinirvāṇa. Furthermore, "Clarity" (*vidyā*) is named "Light" (*prabhā*).

"Practice" is named "Action" (*karman*). "Sufficiency" is named "Fruit. Furthermore, "Light" is named "Heedfulness" (*apramāda*). "Action" is named the "Six Pāramitās. "Fruit" is named "A... [Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi].

...anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, "clear knowledge" (vidyā) refers to the three types of clear knowledge: first, the clear knowledge of a bodhisattva; second, the clear knowledge of all Buddhas;

and third, the clear knowledge of non-illumination (avidyā-vidyā). The clear knowledge of a bodhisattva is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā. The clear knowledge of all Buddhas is precisely the Buddha-eye.
The clear knowledge of non-illumination is precisely ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā). For the sake of sentient beings, the practitioner has cultivated this throughout immeasurable kalpas.

"All wholesome karmas" refers to those who clearly perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The commentary states: "Now, this refers to being precisely in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), encompassing both cause and fruit.
Within this, the first seven phrases concern practice (*caryā*), while the final three specifically manifest the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*), which may be understood accordingly.
There are ten kinds of seekers of the Dharma, as they rely on seeking the true Dharma to accomplish supreme practice. Among these, the first two are the avoidance of faults:
first, avoiding crookedness; second, avoiding pride. Next is one [type] that values the Dharma. Next are two [types] who, for the sake of sentient beings, establish precepts and attain peace.

Next are two [types] who [seek] for the sake of Bodhi and Nirvana. Next are two [types] who cause sentient beings to resolve their minds and sever doubts. The final one is for the sake of fulfilling [the path].
Regarding the "Vehicle": there are ten kinds of factors for clarity. These are for the sake of causing those to be converted to have clarity regarding the Dharma;

thus, these ten phrases all pertain to benefiting others. Among them, the first refers to the ignorant ordinary person (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), who is one belonging to the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) and is not yet able to cultivate the practice of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-caryā*).
For now, they are led according to worldly teachings so that they may grow toward the states of humans and devas.

Due to their roots of goodness, there are two types of followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*). These are those of dull faculties who, during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), merely follow others, believing the words of another as they practice.
Third are the followers of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*). They are the same as the former in that they exist during the fifteen moments of mind;
however, being of sharp faculties, they understand the Dharma and practice in reliance upon the Dharma themselves. These two types of persons are included among the seven types of individuals and...
Among the twenty-seven noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*), these are all the first two. Regarding the "fourth, the person of the eighth stage" (*aṣṭamaka*), there are two interpretations. One says:

having departed from the eight [wrong paths] such as false views and so forth, one proceeds toward the eight [right paths] of right view; when these eight practices are perfected, they are collectively termed the "eighth.
Another says: "eight" refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*); it means being far removed from the constraints of external forms, and so on, up to being far removed from the mind.
The affliction of such slander is like an abscess or an arrow; these all constitute the removal of hindrances. To abandon and turn away from them is called "separation" (*viveka*).

To apply remedies and proceed toward liberation is called "orientation" (*niyāma*). The "eighth person" refers to one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*); alternatively, by mentioning the latter, the former is included.
Using the superior to encompass the inferior, they are collectively called the "eighth person. Fifth, the one who has attained the first fruit and extinguished the multitude of fetters:

this refers to one who has extinguished the eighty-eight fetters—the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing—and has severed the outflows of birth and death in the evil realms. Sixth, the one who has attained the second fruit and contemplates the flavors of desire as a calamity:
because they have already abandoned six grades [of afflictions], yet the remainder is not yet exhausted. Seventh, the one who has attained the third fruit does not delight in the three [realms].

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*) and so forth: because the general meaning is distinguished [from the specific], one severs the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) regarding the arising of rebirth and so on, and thus does not return to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The eight [liberations], the fourth fruit, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), and the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvid*) are all as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*. This rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha] awakens through self-reflection and cultivation by the power of past habituation.
Therefore, the ten great wisdoms, the faculties of sharp intelligence, the delight in liberation, the power, and the fearlessnesses are fulfilled; such is the Bodhisattva who has awakened.
Regarding the four types of tenfold methods of cultivation, because one cultivates according to the Dharma, therein are: first, honoring spiritual friends; second, awakening through the heavens;
third, constant shame and remorse before the Buddha; fourth, constantly remaining within the three realms of existence; and fifth, bringing the cultivation of goodness to ultimate completion.

Sixth, the bodhisattva who follows the mind of the Mahāyāna through the six recollections; seventh, abandoning heterodoxy to seek the correct path; eighth, subduing Māra as well as afflictions and karma;

ninth, knowing the faculties [of beings] to preach the Dharma, even leading them to abide in the stage of Buddhahood; tenth, abiding in the non-dual dharma-realm of principle and phenomena, causing the body of afflictions to be extinguished and purified.
Thus concludes the preceding section on the cultivation of practice.
The third section contains ten types of māras and one hundred gates, clarifying the practice of being free from hindrances. It is divided into two parts:
first, fifty gates clarify the accomplishment of practice by being free from hindrances; second, fifty gates clarify the empowerment that is free from hindrances.

In the first section, there are three parts. First, twenty verses clarify the obstacles to be abandoned. Second, ten verses clarify the skillful means for abandoning those obstacles. Third, twenty verses clarify the vision of the Buddha and the perfection of practice.

Within the first part, the initial ten concern "Māras," so called because they obstruct the Path. Among these: first, the burden of the appropriated aggregates (upādāna-skandha) hinders the cultivation of the Path;
second, the various afflictions (kleśas) can obstruct the ultimate realization of both the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga); third...
1. All unwholesome karmas can obstruct the Path. 2. The four types of pride (*māna*) are extremely obstructive because they look down upon others with arrogance.

3. Because it arises from [wrong] views. 4. It acts as a condition for sentient beings to experience pleasure within the three realms. 5. Because it involves grasping at the notion that all phenomena possess a substantial intrinsic nature.
6. It is attachment to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). 7. It is due to emotional attachment and longing for a specific individual. 8. "Dharma" refers to that which has been attained.
Dharma. Wisdom is precisely the wisdom that can realize [the truth]. To possess wisdom yet possess attachment is an obstruction to the Dharma-wisdom (*dharmajñāna*).
Second, there are ten kinds of demonic delights (*mārakrīḍā*); this is because the former is the essence and these are its functions. First, the demonic delight in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Since this involves abandoning the goodness of signlessness (*animitta*) and accumulating tainted merit (*sāsravapuṇya*), one cannot transcend birth-and-death; this is its activity. Second, giving with an evil mind.

1. These and others are all states of mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), such as seeking pleasure, abandoning [the Dharma], or having an evil nature; because they contradict the bodhicitta, they constitute karmic obstacles. 2. Seeking profit and goods through the Dharma;
obtaining a lamp without a sincere heart; and likewise losing the bodhicitta. 3. Not delighting in the signless (*animitta*); nor being diligent and earnest. 4.

Keeping far from the good and drawing near to evil; delighting in the small [vehicles] and entering into cessation (*nirvāṇa*). 5. Hating Bodhisattvas, seeking their faults, and cutting off their offerings. 6. Seven... [text fragment].

1. Slandering the Dharma and taking no pleasure in it; not honoring the preaching of the Dharma. 2. Delighting in worldly literature and rhetoric; concealing the Great [Vehicle] and expounding the Small. 3.

Bestowing the profound upon those who are not fit vessels; abiding in the heterodox while claiming to be correct. 4. Being intimate with those who are already at ease, while remaining distant from those who are not yet at ease.

5. Being self-exalting and disrespectful; being vexing, harmful, and stubbornly closed-minded. Regarding the "ten kinds of abandoning": because one practices cultivation in opposition to these obstacles, they are called "abandoning. Among them, the first is...

1. Respectfully supporting and honoring virtuous friends; 2. Refraining from self-exaltation; 3. Believing in the profound Dharma; 4. Constantly and single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha; 5. Diligently practicing without negligence;
6. Seeking the Bodhisattva teachings; 7. Preaching the Dharma without weariness; 8. Taking refuge in the Buddha’s protection; 9. Believing in the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); 10.
Sharing the same roots of goodness as all Bodhisattvas. Fourth, there are ten ways of seeing the Buddha. Regarding these...

Because the obstacles have been removed and the realm of the Buddha manifests before one, it is so stated. Within this, first, although a Buddha appears in the world and achieves [enlightenment], there is nothing that is achieved;
seeing the Buddha in this way is truly seeing the Buddha. Second, seeing the Buddha is because he responds to the invocation of vows, not merely due to his birth.
Third, for the sake of sentient beings' deep faith, he manifests as a result of past causes; seeing the Buddha in this way is truly seeing him. Fourth, in order to... [text truncated]

The Dharma left behind remains for a long time without perishing; it abides through the sustaining power of the Buddha. To know this in accordance with reality is called seeing the Buddha in the form of the *śarīra* and images.
Fifth, in order to cause sentient beings to feel sorrow, grief, longing, and devotion toward the Buddha’s roots of goodness, he manifests *nirvāṇa*.
In truth, the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished. To know this is called seeing the Buddha of *nirvāṇa*. This vision penetrates deeply.
Because it is the realm of the Buddha. Sixth, knowing that the Buddha’s body reaches everywhere, because it is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.

Seventh, for one who dwells in the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), this person sees the Buddha as not departing from this mind.
Eighth, knowing the meaning of non-reliance; this person sees the Buddha because the Buddha has realized the perfection of non-reliance. Regarding "immeasurable," [it refers to] all phenomena...
5. Because there is no basis. Ninth, the fundamental nature takes non-existence as its nature; now, clearly seeing this original nature is itself seeing the Buddha.
Tenth, the Buddha does not exist for his own sake, but acts for the sake of sentient beings; now one knows that he manifests his body in accordance with the intentions of all.
This person sees the Buddha because he universally accepts [all beings] and universally manifests himself in accordance with them. 5.
There are ten kinds of Buddha-activities. Because what preceded was the essence and this is the activity, among them: first, all Buddhas take the transformation of sentient beings as their activity;
second, they cause those who have planted seeds of wholesome karma within the Buddha-lineage to awaken to that goodness;

third, for those who have not heard the sūtras, they cause them to hear the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) so that doubts may be severed; fourth, for those who harbor doubts because they believe they have committed offenses due to a sense of self...

One regrets being unable to emerge from it oneself; this is because one can obtain [the realization that] there is fundamentally no self, and so forth. "Envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to the active manifestation of doubt and affliction that shrouds the mind.
Regarding the fifth, "for the sake of the stains of various delusions and the small mind," etc.: it is to adorn the body with auspicious marks, thereby increasing merit and extinguishing obstacles.

Regarding the sixth, when the Dharma is difficult to hear, it causes one to hear it and be universally able to receive great benefit. Regarding the seventh, it removes demonic obstacles through skillful means, and...
8. For the sake of benefiting others, he does not speak of the state of self-realization to those whose faculties are not yet matured and who have not realized the two types of selflessness.

9. Although his afflictions and capacities are exhausted, he does not abandon the bodhisattva practices. 10. He realizes that both himself and all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning;

nevertheless, he encourages others to practice without weariness. He knows there is no volitional construction, yet volitional construction is not lost; he knows there are no marks, yet he observes marks; he knows there is no teacher, yet...
Yet they seek to manifest [enlightenment]. They know that lands are empty yet adorn and purify them; they know there is no birth yet manifest through transformation-birth.

Without moving, they display supernatural powers; having perfected the fruit, they cultivate the causes. They know that dharmas transcend words yet constantly preach them; they manifest extinction yet are born again. These are all practices of the dual operation of the provisional and the real.
The following fifty phrases clarify the practice of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that is free from obstacles.

Within this, the first twenty phrases establish the practice of becoming free from obstacles, while the latter thirty phrases clarify the practice of external sustaining power. Regarding the former [the first twenty], the initial ten cite the obstacles, and the subsequent ten manifest their virtues.
Regarding the ten types of pride among the [twenty] karmas of the former [section]: their nature is to exalt oneself by relying upon [certain qualities] while holding others in contempt;

their function is to produce suffering. Among these: first, because the mind does not pay homage toward those who are venerable or possess virtue; second, because one does not show respect toward those who possess virtue or the Dharma;
third, because one does not verbally praise the sublime Dharma one has heard. These three, along with the subsequent six [types of pride], [constitute the ten].
8. According to the eight types of pride (*māna*), this is the eighth, *mada* (arrogance), also called *tīrṇa-māna* (pervasive pride).

This is because one is unwilling to pay respect or prostrate before objects of veneration. 4. The fourth is *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride), which is characterized by the nature of a haughty mind that considers oneself superior to those who are equal.
This is simply a variation of *mānātimāna*. 6. Not praising those with virtue. 7. Seeking for oneself arrogance.

Regarding "high seats" and so forth: this refers to one who actually lacks virtue yet claims to possess it; this is false pride (*mithyāmāna*). Regarding "seeing a person of virtue frowning" and so forth:
this is the same as the sixth [type of pride] mentioned previously. Regarding "seeing one who is wise" and so forth: this arises from clinging to the self as having a real, sovereign master;
being unwilling to yield even for a moment to accept what leads to long-term peace, one is swallowed up and destroyed by the pride of self (*asmimāna*).

It is for this reason. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there are sentient beings who... and so forth: this is because their minds are shrouded by pride (*māna*). Due to this, regarding the supreme Dharma (*adhyātma-dharma*), they claim to have attained what they have not yet attained.

Consequently, even if they encounter the era of a Buddha, they are unable to draw near to him. Thus far, if one considers the inclusion of the seven and nine [categories], the respective assignments can be understood.
Second, regarding the "ten types of wisdom-action" (*daśa-jñāna-karman*): this reveals the practice of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). As for the preceding...
This is because one now applies the remedies once the afflictions have been recognized. Among these: first, believing that cause and effect do not perish;

second, recollecting the Buddha based on the bodhicitta; third, reverently supporting and honoring virtuous friends; fourth, demonstrating the relationship between the signifier and the signified, reconciling with what is correct and opposing what is erroneous;

fifth, abandoning the notion of self-importance toward external objects; and sixth, the three types of action—wherein the Bodhisattva acts as a Buddha, cherishing the Dharma as his own body and protecting the Buddha as his own life.

Constantly virtuous. Seventh, knowing both principle and phenomena; because one attains the facts, one does not destroy dependent origination and remains free from false views and the like. Eighth, one accords with the cultivation of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*);
perceiving all the perfections as being without marks, one takes them as the mother, while skillful means and faith are the father, entering deeply into straightforward compassion.
Ninth, diligently accumulating generosity, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, meditative concentration, and so forth; tenth, diligently cultivating all dharmas praised by the Buddhas.
Second, there are ten kinds of demonic influences that sustain [the practitioner]; the following thirty phrases distinguish the practice of external empowerment. Within this:
Regarding the first ten points on being "held by Māra": these all constitute the sustaining power of hostile obstacles, for they prevent one from attaining liberation.
Among them: 1. Laziness is contrary to diligence; since diligence can spur all practices to reach Bodhi, laziness is held by Māra. 2.
A narrow and inferior resolve is the mind of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha); as this contradicts Great Bodhi, it is held by Māra. 3. Cultivating few practices...
5. Because they do not reach the fulfillment of the ocean of the Buddha’s virtues. This minor practice contradicts the ocean of the practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

it is encompassed by Māra. 4. As for "only one and not the others," the Sanskrit original states: because one can endure [the suffering] in only one instance and cannot endure it throughout all instances. 5.
Because they do not give rise to the vow to extensively deliver sentient beings and seek great enlightenment. 6.
Because they are shown to be the same as the two vehicles; because they enter nirvāṇa too quickly; because they cannot practice asceticism for the sake of sentient beings;

because they cannot remain in saṃsāra for a long time to transform sentient beings; and because they would truly harm the Mahāyāna if they were to doubt it. Second, regarding being sustained by the Buddhas:
since they have already departed from the sustenance of heterodox paths, they are sustained by the Buddhas. Within this, the first two points concern bodhi.

Regarding the mind: first, it is difficult to initiate [the resolve] for the first time; second, it is to develop it deeply through repeated practice. The next two concern the arousal of conduct. The next two pertain to compassion and wisdom.

The next two follow along with the transformation of others, realizing that [the Buddha] is neither identical to nor separate from them. The final two involve the simultaneous application of the provisional and the real.
As for the "three things sustained by ten kinds of dharmas," this is because one abandons oneself to follow the Dharma. Within these, the first four are the four seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).

In the Sanskrit language, it is *udāna*; here it is called "seal" (*mudrā*), and also "distinctive mark. This means that impermanence is the distinctive mark of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
suffering is the distinctive mark of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); selflessness is the distinctive mark of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*);

and peaceful nirvāṇa is the distinctive mark of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). A detailed explanation is as found in the *Caturodāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*. Next, [the following] two...

One knows the twelvefold dependent origination: first, through the contemplation of general characteristics; second, through the contemplation of the reverse and direct orders. Next, two [knowledges] concern the emergence of the Three Vehicles:

the small [knowledge] brings forth the Two Vehicles through the three liberations, while the great [knowledge] brings forth the Mahāyāna by encompassing all beings. Finally, two [knowledges] concern bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Altogether, these comprise three hundred and twenty sections, elucidating the teaching of the perfect and ultimate.
The second section, "The Deeds of the Gods Dwelling in Bliss," consists of one hundred and ninety gates. It elucidates the perfection of the Buddha’s activity through its fruits.

This is largely based on the manifestation of the eight aspects to clarify the Buddha’s function. This is divided into six parts: first, twenty phrases elucidate the practice accomplished while dwelling among the gods;
second, from the twenty phrases beginning with "the ten kinds of manifestations in entering the womb" below, it elucidates the subtle details of dwelling in the womb.
1. Approaching and proceeding; 2. From "The Ten Kinds of Birth" downward, clarifying the conduct of emerging from the womb; 3.

From "The Ten Kinds of Great Adornments" downward, forty phrases clarifying the conduct of living as a layperson in common with the world; 4. From "The Ten Kinds of Leaving Home" downward, sixty phrases clarifying the conduct of leaving home to seek the Way;
5. From "The Ten Kinds of Accomplishing the Power of a Tathāgata" downward, forty phrases clarifying the attainment of Buddhahood.
Regarding the conduct of fruition:
concerning the first [of the two parts], the first ten [deeds] are those performed while remaining in the heavens; the latter ten are those performed when about to descend from the heavens.

Within the first ten: first, transforming the gods of the desire realm; second, transforming the gods of the form realm; third, transforming the sentient beings of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system; fourth, with...
1. Bodhisattvas of similar class from the ten directions discourse together from afar on the Dharma of the eight manifestations of descending to birth;

2. [The Buddha] teaches the Dharma appropriately to the bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions to bring them to excellence; 3. Skillful subduing of Māra; 4. Skillful means for teaching and transforming the devaputras of the desire realm;

5. Visiting the Buddhas of the ten directions to hear the Dharma; 6. Making offerings to many Buddhas; 7. [The Buddha] makes offerings to many Buddhas; 8. [The Buddha] makes offerings to many Buddhas.
The second [point] concerns the benefit arising from the body. When the Bodhisattva was about to descend from heaven, he explained the affairs of his time in heaven and the reasons for his descent;
therefore, this is clarified next. Thus, the *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states:

"The Bodhisattva, in accordance with his original vow, dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven palace and is able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of Dharma; it is not that he is incapable. The Bodhisattva reflects upon Jambudvīpa..."
The people of Jambudvīpa do not go up to the Tuṣita Heaven to hear and receive the teachings of the Dharma; however, the beings of the Tuṣita Heaven can descend to Jambudvīpa to hear the Dharma.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva relinquishes the Tuṣita Heaven and attains Buddhahood in Jambudvīpa. Within this, there are ten kinds [of manifestations]:

first, the light from his foot extinguishes [the darkness] and touches those beings so that they may know [the truth]; second, the light from the tuft of hair between his brows awakens those who have resided [in the past].

The Causes and Conditions of the Palace: 1. The light from the three hands adorns the realm, establishing those who were not yet vessels for the Dharma. 2. The light from the knees awakens beings to their duties, causing them to follow and provide offerings.
3. From within the śrīvatsa mark on the chest, light is emitted to awaken all the Mallas. 4. Light is emitted from the pores to awaken all those who assist in the transformation of beings. 5.
The light from the palace shines down upon the place of birth, so that his kinsmen may be born together with him. 6. The light from the pavilion... [text ends]
1. The light from the palace and other sources illuminates the mother’s womb. 2. The light from the nine feet extends his lifespan. 3. Within the minor marks, the light manifests the eight signs. 4.
Regarding the second [topic], the manifestation of dwelling in the womb, there are ten matters; in the following twenty phrases, the first ten clarify the location.

The womb. The subsequent ten phrases clarify the extremely subtle modes of rebirth. Regarding the ten types of entering the womb mentioned therein: first, because he transforms [beings] with small faculties; second, because he gathers his retinue;
third, because his mindfulness is undisturbed at the times of entering, abiding, and emerging; fourth, because he manifests extensively to benefit sentient beings;

fifth, because he transforms the masses according to his vows; sixth, because he conforms to human beings by entering the womb; and seventh, because he causes those with whom he has a karmic connection to see him.

1. Like gazing at a reflection in a mirror; 2. All those of the same class who are to receive subsequent bodies gather together; 3. Within the womb, a magnificent and adorned palace appears; 4. Making offerings to the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma.

Regarding the second [section], the ten types of extremely subtle courses (*sūkṣma-gati*): this clarifies that within the womb there is a vast gathering of profound and secret matters that are difficult to know; thus they are called "subtle courses.

Because they are the objects of the sphere of wisdom and the destination of the mental factors (*caitta*), among these, the first is: [The text continues with the specific details of the subtle courses.]

The first [verse] manifests the practice of past causes; the next eight manifest the eight phases; and the final one manifests supernormal powers. These are all constantly manifested while within the womb.
Regarding the third point, the ten kinds of birth: when emerging from the right side of the mother’s flank, these ten types occur. First, he is free from delusion and confusion.
1. Emitting radiance; 2. This is the final limit, as there will be no further rebirth in the future; 3. Arising through the integration of principle; 4. Arising like an illusion; 5.
