Constant Following at the Site of Enlightenment; 7. Cultivation of Merit and Adornments with Hidden Treasuries on the Left and Right; 8.
Offering to the Buddhas and the Flow of Goodness with Adorned Treasuries Emerging from Between the Trees; 9. All World Rulers Raining Down Offerings; 10. [The tenth virtue].

When the Buddhas of the ten directions are about to preach the Dharma, they first emit light that illuminates their bodies and enters the crown of their heads; the subsequent [mudrās] may be understood accordingly. Third, from the passage beginning "Then all the bhikṣus...

down to the end, it clarifies how six thousand [monks] heard the praise of Mañjuśrī’s virtues and obtained benefits, which is divided into two parts: first, the narration; second, from "Those monks...
onwards, the manifestation of the benefits. Within these benefits, there are sixteen phrases: 1. purity of mind; 2. firmness of faith; 3. attainment of joy; 4. [purity of] body...
1. Suppleness; 2. Delight of the five faculties; 3. Elimination of the six types of sorrow and suffering; 4. Exhaustion of defilements; 5. Constantly seeing the Buddha; 6. Seeking the True Dharma; 7.
Possessing the powers of a bodhisattva; 8. Arousing great compassion; 9. Arousing great vows; 10. Entering into vast and profound realms.
Fifteen: The ocean of Buddhas constantly appears. Sixteen: Deeply believing in and delighting in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Four:
This refers to the fifth among the superior conditions for the various views from this point downward. One: The White Honored One requests that he be led to see [the Buddha]. Two:
At that time, Śāriputra and others are instructed regarding the six thousand [monks]. Three: At that time, Mañjuśrī and others; Mañjuśrī observes those six thousand. Four: At that time...

The section beginning with "All the bhikṣus" below clarifies the making of vows by six thousand [bodhisattvas]. The section beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī" below clarifies the exhortation to accomplish ten dharmas.

The first two passages can be understood through their textual observation. Regarding the third passage, Mañjuśrī’s observation of the six thousand [bodhisattvas] reveals that their spiritual faculties (*indriya*) are capable of entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The expression "like the turning of an elephant king" means that both body and head turn together, signifying the gravity of the matter before them and their being gathered under his care.

Because of their characteristics. Question: Are these six thousand [beings] not originally of the Mahāyāna? Answer: Originally they were of the Hīnayāna, yet they possess the nature capable of entering the Great Vehicle, just like those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
This can also be understood from the four types among them who have made vows; specifically, four out of the five.

First, regarding those who are exhorted to accomplish the ten kinds of practices for entering the Mahāyāna: because they turn toward the mind of the True Teaching (*saddharma*) without weariness. Within this, the first is the accumulation of merit.
1. Seeing the assembly of Buddhas; 2. Seeking the Dharma; 3. Cultivating the detachment from the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*); 4. Fulfilling all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*); 5.

Entering the three periods of time—this entry constitutes clear understanding; 6. Universally adorning the buddha-fields; 7. Taming and transforming all beings; 8. Accomplishing the bodhisattva practices throughout all lands and eons; 9.
For the sake of bringing a single sentient being to accomplishment, cultivating practices equal in number to the atoms of a buddha-field until attaining Buddhahood.
First, the single power. Thus, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, one accomplishes all the powers of the Tathāgata.
Second, the two bhikṣus—or, as the text below states, "if any good man"—clearly demonstrates that by deeply generating the aforementioned ten minds, one attains benefit:

first, nurturing the roots of goodness; second, abandoning birth and death; third, transcending worldly dispositions; fourth, not falling into the stages of the Two Vehicles; and fifth, being born into the family of the Buddhas.
1. The household; 2. Possessing the five bodhisattva vows; 3. Cultivating the merits of a Buddha; 4. Practicing the various conducts of a bodhisattva; 5.
Attaining the ten powers of a Buddha to crush Māra and subdue outsiders; 6. Extirpating delusions; 7. Entering the stage of a bodhisattva and drawing near to the fruit of Buddhahood.
At the three times, the bhikṣus below clarify that six thousand [monks], as before, were encouraged to advance and obtained the benefit of samādhi.

By attaining this concentration, they attained the unobstructed eye. Because they attained this eye, they were able to accomplish twenty-five kinds of benefits: first, they were able to see the realm of all Buddhas;
second, they saw the Buddha’s places of enlightenment in immeasurable lands; third, they saw those various realms of existence; fourth, they saw...
1. To perceive the distinctions between those various lands; 2. to perceive the atoms within those various lands; 3. to perceive the palaces of the sentient beings therein; 4.
to hear the various sounds of the Buddhas’ speech and their preaching of the Dharma within those lands; 5. to observe the faculties, inclinations, and minds of the sentient beings within those lands;
6. to be able to recollect the ten successive births of the sentient beings therein; 7. to recollect the past events within those lands.
11. Recalling the ten past-life stories (*jātaka*) of that Buddha; 12. Attaining perfect enlightenment; 13. Turning the wheel of Dharma; 14. The ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
15. The ten ways of teaching the Dharma; 16. The ten forms of instruction; 17. The ten types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*); 18.
Establishing ten thousand bodhisattvas in the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*); 19. Ten thousand meditative absorptions (*samādhi*); 20. [The twenty-first...]
20. Purification of the three wheels in ten thousand ways; 21. Attainment of great wisdom; 22. Perfection of radiance; 23.
Attainment of the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva; 24. Because the body and mind are harmonized and tranquil, it is called "supple and subtle."
Twenty-fifth is the firm stabilization of the bodhisattva mind.
Fourth, at that time, Mañjuśrī concludes the preceding section and exhorts the six thousand [bodhisattvas] toward their ultimate attainment, which consists of eight parts:

first, abiding in the practices of Samantabhadra; second, entering the ocean of vows; third, accomplishing the ocean of great vows; fourth, the purification of the mind; fifth, the purification of the body...

1. Purity; 2. sharpness of the six sense organs; 3. attainment of supernatural powers (abhijñā); 4. by virtue of these great supernatural powers, although he remains in the presence of Mañjuśrī, he manifests bodies throughout the ten directions to accomplish the Buddha-dharma.

The second [section], the Assembly for Gathering the Nāgas, consists of four parts. First, the connection between the preceding and the following may be understood. Second, the gradual descent to the subsequent place of transformation;

herein are two parts: first, the designation of the name; second, the praise of its excellence from "In the past" onwards. Within this, there are three parts: first, where the Buddhas of the past once resided;
second, the place where the present Buddha formerly practiced his conduct; third, the constant offerings made by the three divisions [of the community] and others. Finally, Mañjuśrī.

The following clarifies the teaching of the Dharma. Within this, first the title of the sutra is revealed; subsequently, from "this below," the benefits are explained. Regarding the former, the title of the sutra is *The Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu*.

This is because it explains how the ten eyes are perfectly clear and bright, suddenly perceiving the dharmadhātu in which phenomena and principle, as well as phenomena and phenomena, are mutually unimpeded.
The explanation of the term *dharmadhātu* is fully detailed as set forth in the separate *Xuánfú Chapter*. Regarding the subsequent revelation of the benefits, first [the benefits] are revealed...

Regarding the category: this refers to the various hosts of nāgas. In the subsequent explanation of the benefits, there are two parts. First, hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas renounce their nāga bodies and are reborn among humans and devas.
Second, ten thousand nāgas do not regress from bodhicitta.

The third [section] concerns the causes and conditions for gathering the assembly and gradually advancing toward entry into the Real Teaching (*saddharma*), as explained in detail in the section on "Teachings Adapted to Capacities.
Other specific divisions may be understood as usual.
The fourth section, the *Sudhana-saṃgraha-parivarta*, consists of two parts: first, a preliminary analysis of its meaning; second, the formal explanation of the text.

Within the former, there is a brief analysis according to eight gates: (1) the number and combination of assemblies; (2) the manner in which the teaching and the listeners arise and engage; (3) the classification into five aspects.
1. The four categories of assembly leaders; 2. The five indefinite southern practices; 3. Praising and questioning existence and non-existence; 4. Deferring to those who are superior; 5.
Distinguishing through questions and answers.
Within the first section, there are two parts: first, an account based on the Jin translation; second, reliance on the Tang translation.

Regarding the former, according to Master Guangtong and others, there are forty-four individuals in total as "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) herein. Of these, the first, Mañjuśrī alone, corresponds to the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The subsequent forty individuals correspond to the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), and the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*). The next two individuals correspond to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*). The final one...

Some assign these to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue-wei*). However, according to the *Wutai Shan Lun* (Treatise on Mount Wutai) and masters such as Master Yi, they do not assign them to stages at all, nor do they provide any formal structural divisions;
rather, they offer a free exegesis following the text according to each assembly.

Later, those who relied on the Tang dynasty translation categorized them from Mañjuśrī down to Samantabhadra, totaling fifty-three assemblies; since the boys and girls share a single dialogue, they are treated as one throughout.
If there is a question but no answer from a companion, the assembly cannot be established; for although Mañjuśrī is the same person before and after, the two assemblies are distinct.

Regarding the arising of the listeners' understanding based on the speaker, there are three types: first, that which arises through the power of the transformer, who abides in the practice of great compassion.

Because they are friends who do not need to be requested [to teach]: Mañjuśrī, Samantagāmin, and others listen and transform beings spontaneously. Second, because it causes those to be transformed to practice the conduct of reverence toward the Dharma;
for one must wait for them to come and request before speaking. Sāgaramegha, Sāgaranātha, and others speak only when they have sought out and questioned [the teacher].
Third, because they possess both of the aforementioned practices: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the Earth Goddess Anantā, and so forth, as well as Sudhana.
Without having heard [the teaching], one immediately offers praise; this is like an uninvited friend (*aprārthita-mitra*). Furthermore, there are those who request that it be explained;
this is like the practice of honoring the Dharma (*dharmapūjā*). Maitreya, as well as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and others later on, all likewise act in this manner.
Regarding the three categories as five aspects: herein there are fifty-five positions in total.

According to the original commentary (*benshu*), the first forty-one persons clarify the aspect of practicing by relying on assigned stages (*jìwèi*). Next, from below Māyā, there are nine assemblies and eleven persons.

1. One person, Maitreya, clarifies the entry into the true reality (*tathatā*) through the convergence of conditions. 2. One person, Maitreya, clarifies the characteristics of the stages of attainment and the formation of causes.
3. One person, Mañjuśrī, clarifies the wisdom that illuminates the non-dual characteristic. 4. One person, Samantabhadra, clarifies the characteristic of the vastness of manifest causes.
If one relies on the current edition, there is generally no difference. The few minor variations in the middle sections are as follows:

from Mañjuśrī up to the forty-first, Gopa, these are collectively titled "The Stages of Cultivation by Borrowing Positions," because they manifest the practice of cultivation by borrowing and traversing various positions.
Second, from Māyā up to the boys and girls who equally attain the liberation of illusory abiding, these are collectively titled "Entering Reality by Conjoining Conditions."

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to distinguishing between male and female characteristics by means of the principle of "dwelling as an illusion," thereby realizing their differences and entering the reality-nature of equality;

thus is the name. If judged according to the stages, this is the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) of the tenth bhūmi, while the latter three characteristics belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

However, because the initial traversal of the stages is more extensive, it is designated by the larger number [of ten] rather than the smaller. Third, one enters through the station of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
The liberation called "the adornment of wisdom that does not forget any object of the three periods of time" is termed the "causal characteristic of gathering virtuous qualities.

This refers to the wisdom that gathers the objects of the three periods of time within mindfulness without loss or forgetfulness, thereby serving as the cause for accomplishing the virtues of a Buddha who manifests through transformation.
Fourth, subsequently, Mañjuśrī attains immeasurable great wisdom, light, dhāraṇīs, great vows, samādhis, supernormal powers, and insight.
He enters the bodhimaṇḍa of Samantabhadra and dwells where Mañjuśrī dwells; this is called the non-dual wisdom of insight.
This means that when Sudhana arrives here, he enters what Samantabhadra has entered and dwells where Mañjuśrī dwells, shining together with these two sages.

Because they share a single objective realm, these five attain the ocean of all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva at the station of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. They become equal to Samantabhadra;
they become equal to all Buddhas; their single body fills all lands; their practice is equal to that of perfect enlightenment; and their supernormal powers are equal [to those of the Buddhas].

The turning of the Dharma, eloquence, speech, voice, powers, fearlessnesses, the abodes of a Buddha, great compassion, and the inconceivable mastery of liberation—all these are entirely equal. This is called the manifestation of the characteristic of the vastness of the cause;
that is to say, because the causes for those future great fruits are now being established, and because those causes bring about such vast fruits.
Regarding the classification of the four assemblies, there are twenty categories in total: first, bhikṣus; second, physicians; third, householders;
fourth, upāsikās; fifth, ṛṣis; sixth, brāhmaṇas; seventh, maidens; eighth, boys;
ninth, lay devotees; tenth, kings; eleventh, non-Buddhists; twelfth, boatmen; thirteenth, bhikṣuṇīs; fourteenth, women; [fifteenth, ... ten.
Fifth, the bodhisattvas; sixteenth, the celestial deities; seventeenth, the earth deities; eighteenth, the night deities; nineteenth, the forest deities;
twentieth, the elder beings.

Fifth, regarding the uncertainty of "southward movement": the Sanskrit term for south is *dakṣiṇā*. According to the etymological explanations of the Western Regions (India), "south" (*dakṣiṇa*) carries the meaning of "right.
"Right" carries the meaning of "conformity" (*anuloma*). Since the cities, palaces, gardens, dwellings, and Bodhi trees all face east, the south is to their right.
People generally find the right side stable; stability constitutes conformity. This applies to practices such as circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
All matters stem from these words; therefore, within this context, it is revealed that Mañjuśrī’s gradual transformation and Sudhana’s gradual seeking both involve traveling southward.
An ancient commentator explained: "Sudhana’s journey south symbolizes the Middle Way Dharma-realm, which is free from the two extremes of east and west.
Furthermore, it symbolizes the teaching of the true direction. If this were so, then even if the teaching had originated from here [the north], [it would still have been appropriate].

One may take the "south" (nan) from the *zhinan* (指南, south-pointing compass) as the correct usage. Regarding the meaning of "south-pointing," all instructions begin from the west; why then not rely on that explanation for the meaning of "south"?
It is because one knows it is not so; rather, one should adopt the sense of "conformity. As the *Jingxing pin* (Chapter on Pure Conduct) of this sutra states:

"When circumambulating a stupa to the right, one should wish that all sentient beings act without opposition and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). The Jin translation [of the *Lotus Sutra*] reads "li" (離, separation).
The *Lokadhātu-parivarta* states: "To embrace the right Dharma is to not contradict what has been taught by all Buddhas. The current edition reads "to accord with" (*su-anunaya*).
This is because it does not exhaustively cover all the instructions of the Venerable One. According to the term "to accord with," its Sanskrit equivalent is *deśanā*.
This refers to "right" (dakṣiṇa). The *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* by Yaśomitra also explains it in this same way.
This signifies that Sudhana’s seeking of spiritual friends was entirely in accordance with them; he did not fail to follow their instructions, and for this reason, he traveled southward.
Since traveling to the right signifies the meaning of "conformity," even when he subsequently went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or the Bodhimaṇḍa, all of these were likewise [acts of conformity].
This does not contradict the meaning of "southern course," for all such instances are practices that accord with the teachings.
Regarding the sixth point, the praise or questioning of existence and non-existence, there are two meanings.

First, because bodhi is that which all bodhisattvas revere, upon hearing that it can be generated, there are none who do not offer praise. Second, due to specific conditions, there may be no such praise. These specific [conditions are as follows]:...
There are three conditions: first, because Sudhana encounters a spiritual friend at a time when he is in right reception, as in the cases of the householder Vimukta and the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja.

Second, after Sudhana has spoken of his own resolve for enlightenment to a spiritual friend, that friend does not immediately respond with praise, but instead describes what they themselves have attained;
this section mostly involves omissions or abbreviations. Third, because the spiritual friend demonstrates the contrary.

This is a transformation through signs. If one were to praise someone immediately upon hearing them resolve their mind [for enlightenment], it would contradict the characteristic of "opposition," as seen in the cases of King Anala, the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the woman Vasumitrā, and other such virtuous friends.
Because they lacked these three conditions, they all offered such exhortations.

Regarding the seventh point, "deferring to those superior in rank": among these various positions, only the final Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas have no one else to whom they defer for superiority;
this reveals that their status is most exalted. Aside from these, all others involve such deferral.
If there is none provided in a particular instance, it is due to omission; there is no other underlying reason.
Regarding the eighth section, the "Analysis through Questions and Answers": Question: These various assemblies were not spoken by the Buddha; how can they be considered sūtras? Answer:
These are all accounts of the activities of various bodhisattvas who sought and taught the Dharma at the time of the compilation.
They are similar to the teachings on the *Vaiśravaṇa* (Self-Mastery) and other dharmas revealed in the original assembly at the Jeta Grove, which were intended for that great multitude.
Having seen it, one enters the Dharma. Although there is no word of the Buddha, how could it not be a sutra? Question:
In the previous original assembly, although the Buddha did not speak, all the matters revealed were within the Buddha’s assembly. Now, this [text] is in a distant place and a different location;

furthermore, it was not spoken by the Buddha, and later it does not face the Buddha. How can this be taken as an example? Answer: Although it is in a distant place, it does not depart from the original assembly.

Therefore, he is always present before the Buddha. As stated above regarding each individual scene within the Jeta Grove, it should be understood that these encompass all Buddha-fields of the ten directions; why then would this location not be included?

For this reason, these fifty-three assemblies do not depart from the fundamental assembly, and are thus called "a single assembly," namely, the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter. Since all these locations are situated therein...
Śrīvatā. In the subsequent text, Sudhana should see Samantabhadra and the Buddha’s great assembly in this land.

Why, then, does he later see them at the Vajra-maṇḍala? The answer is that because the Bodhi tree and the vajra constitute the basis for the nine assemblies, the immovable Bodhi tree pervades all places of assembly.
Thus, by seeking the branches, one finds the root; it remains right here. Furthermore, at the beginning of this assembly...
Samantabhadra and the Buddha remain in the Jeta Grove without ever moving; that which is seen at the Bodhi tree is itself the Jeta Grove, and they likewise dwell beneath the tree.
Reflect upon this. The brief analysis above is hereby concluded.
Regarding the subsequent formal explanation of the text: it is explained according to the five preceding characteristics.
Within the first characteristic, there are forty-one individuals; among them, the first, Mañjuśrī alone, corresponds to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The Manifestation of Faith (*Śraddhābhūmi*) is not a formal stage; therefore, it consists of only one [chapter]. Second, from the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī to the Maiden Maitreyacāritrā, these correspond to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Third, from the Bhikṣu Sudarśana to the Wanderer Samantagupta, these correspond to the ten practices (*daśacaryā*).
Fourth, from the Merchant Dhūpāyudha to the Earth Deity Sthāvarā, these correspond to the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*). Fifth, from the Yakṣiṇī Vidyutprabhā...

The deities reach Gopa and take their stations upon the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the first point, concerning the single individual Mañjuśrī who takes his station among the spiritual friends of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts), upper scroll, states:
"Before ascending to the [ten] abodes (*vihāra*), there are bodhisattvas by name who possess the ten minds; they constantly practice these ten minds, namely:
the mind of faith, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of diligence, the mind of wisdom, the mind of concentration, the mind of non-retrogression, and the mind of dedication."

The protective mind, the ethical mind, and the aspirational mind. The commentary states: Although "faith" (śraddhā) is the same for both [the sūtra and the treatise], its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its object (*ālambana*) differ entirely in the two scriptures, as has already been clarified in the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) and elsewhere. In this present text, there are six sections: first, the section on assembling the assembly;
second, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta... onwards, the section on observing the capacities of the audience and bestowing the teaching; third, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards...
1. The Section on the Exposition Following the Contemplation; 2. At that time, Mañjuśrī turned like an elephant king and so forth, the Section on the Praise, Contemplation, and Reception;
3. "Good son, in this [place]... and so forth, the Section on Pointing Out the Subsequent Friends; 4. At that time, Sudhana... and so forth, the Section on Reflection, Departure, and Transformation.

Regarding the first [of these four], there are two parts: first, a general enumeration; second, from "At that time... onwards, a specific exposition. Within the specific exposition, there are four assemblies.

First, laymen (*upāsaka*); second, laywomen (*upāsikā*); third, young men; and fourth, young women—each group numbering five hundred. Among these, the first two groups are collectively referred to as *upāsaka* and so forth;
this is a term from the Sanskrit language, which here translates as "male lay devotee" (*upāsaka*) and "female lay devotee" (*upāsikā*).
This means that men draw near to and serve the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*), while women draw near to and serve the monks.
Because they are nuns, they may be distinguished by their enumeration.

Second, regarding the analysis according to capacity, there are two parts. First, the general indication of the intent of the teaching may be understood. Second, subsequently, Mañjuśrī specifically observes Sudhana.
Within this, there are two parts: first, he clarifies his present state; second, "furthermore, he knows" and below, he clarifies his past lives. Regarding the former:
Four. First, it clarifies the manifestation of extraordinary jewels at the time of entering the womb; next, from "Then Sudhana" onwards, it clarifies the perfection of his physical marks;

next, from "His seven... onwards, it fully displays the precious objects; finally, from "By this... onwards, it summarizes and establishes the name. Second, it clarifies his previous lives, briefly displaying ten virtues:
first, having previously made offerings to Buddhas; second, the vastness of his faith and understanding; third, delighting in spiritual friends; fourth, the three karmas...

There is no fault. Fifth is the purification of the bodhisattva practices; sixth is the seeking of the Buddha’s wisdom; seventh is becoming a vessel for the Dharma; eighth is purifying the mind so that it is like space;
ninth is the practice of dedication; tenth is attaining the gate of non-obstruction.
The third [section], the "Section on Teaching," consists of two parts. First, it clarifies the teaching given; second, from "At that time, Sudhana...

onwards, it clarifies the request for salvation through the recitation of verses. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the observation of Sudhana, his consolation, and his inspiration;

second, from "And he taught him... onwards, the actual teaching given; third, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards, the conclusion of the teaching and the exhortation to advance. Regarding the teaching:

Within the Dharma, there are two parts: first, a general indication; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words "namely. Within this detailed exposition, there are ten points: first, extensive practice and study; second, non-interruption;

third, explaining the periods before and after the Buddha’s appearance; fourth, explaining the purity of the Buddha’s assemblies; fifth, explaining the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma and his transformative guidance;
sixth, explaining the Buddha’s physical marks and secondary characteristics; seventh, explaining the Buddha’s Dharma-body; eighth, explaining the Buddha’s verbal teachings; ninth...
The first ten explain the illumination of the Buddha’s light; the third section on the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) can be understood from the middle [portion].
Regarding the subsequent section where Sudhana speaks verses seeking salvation, there are two parts: first, the prose account of his intent, which can be understood;
second, the actual verses, totaling thirty-four, divided into two sections. First, four verses describe his state while still entangled in afflictions; second, thirty verses offer praise.

One seeks deliverance through the virtue of Mañjuśrī. In the first verse of the preceding section, it is clarified that by relying on the three realms with arrogance and haughtiness, one enters and exits without leaving the gates of the five destinies;
this is because one is submerged by deep attachment. The next verse explains how the three poisons cover and burn, causing one to cycle through birth and death like a subject serving a king.
The following verse describes how the rope of greed binds and the bridle of flattery and deception obstruct the eye of wisdom.
[They] enter the path of evil. The final verse [describes how], due to stinginess, envy, and pride, they enter the three evil realms and undergo the eight sufferings.
Within the subsequent thirty verses, each [section] is divided into two parts: the first three lines praise the virtues of Mañjuśrī, while the last line seeks his deliverance and protection.
Regarding the former: 1) wisdom-sun and compassion-moon; 2) wisdom-moon and kindness-sun; 3) the Dharma-realm Wheel-Turning King traversing the Dharma.
1. The Dharma-jewel of the true emptiness of the realms leads the way. 2. The merchant-lords of merit and wisdom courageously seek the Buddha-jewel to benefit all beings.

3. Through the patience of the five wisdoms, they subdue Māra. 4. Through meditative concentration and wisdom, they realize the summit of the Dharma. 5. By extinguishing the causes of hell, they purify the effects of the three realms of existence. 6.

By departing from the fruits of the three evil destinies, they accomplish pure and virtuous causes. 7. Seeing the eight inversions, they practice the eightfold right path. 8. They thoroughly understand that there is no distinction between the false and the correct.
11. Dispelling doubt; dwelling in the vision of the Buddha and following the Buddha’s tree-walks. 12. Like the sun of the Buddhas of the three periods appearing. 13.
Wisdom decisively determining the karma of defilement and purity and the practices of the three vehicles. 14. Taking compassion, vows, faith, and patience as the hub, spokes, and axle-pins. 15.
Holding the box of the Dharma, the canopy of loving-kindness, and the ringing of the bell of discernment. 16. The drum of the Dharma for pure conduct and samādhi.
17. The Jewel of the Virtues of the Four Means of Integration, along with Shame and Awe; 18. The Wheel of Giving, the Fragrance of Precepts, and the Flower of Forbearance;
19. Dhyāna and Skillful Means leading to Non-retrogression; 20. Vows, Sustenance, Firmness, Power, and the Accomplishment of Wisdom;
21. Universal Practice of Compassion without any Stinginess; 22. Firmness, Skillfulness, and Unobstructedness; 23. Bestowing upon Beings Utmost Purity.
24. Equal to space and bliss; severing the delusions of the twenty-four pure karmas and crushing the suffering of conditioned existence through the subduing of Māras and externalists.
25. Filling wisdom to universally adorn the lands, so that good vows may reach all beings. 26. Eliminating craving and views, becoming pure like space and benefiting all. 27.
Abiding in meditative concentration, universally directing the power of vows with swiftness. 28. Moving and being born like water and earth, remaining unshakable.
Twenty-nine: The Sunlight of the Dhāraṇī of the Four Means of Integration. Thirty: Entering the City of Dharma, donning the Crown of Wisdom, and binding the Silken Band of Dharma.

Within the third section, "The Section on Praising, Exhorting, and Receiving," there are three parts: first, praising and describing the arousal of the mind; second, from "Sudhana said" onwards, the repeated request for liberation;
and third, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards, the formal answer to the questions asked. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, praising the arousal of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "the mind turns like an elephant king," this was already briefly explained previously. This is because, while internally possessing the measure of thorough investigation, one externally lacks superficial or hurried gestures;
rather, one turns the face toward the disciple to manifest the aspect of receiving them. Subsequently, wishing to state the underlying intention and offer encouragement, there are two parts:
first, the statement, and second, the exhortation. Within the statement, there are three points: first, associating with a spiritual friend; second, seeking understanding; and third...
Cultivation. The two lines in the middle of the latter section on "the good man" first cite the preceding point that relying [on a teacher] is the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, chapter twenty, states: "For all sentient beings who attain the conditions for the proximate cause of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, none is more fundamental than the virtuous friend," and so forth, as explained at length.
In the subsequent conclusion of the exhortation, it is stated that for the sake of attaining Buddhahood, one must abandon weariness, slander, and indolence.
Furthermore, within the second set of repeated requests, the questions are identical to those in the subsequent teaching. According to the Sanskrit original, there are twelve points:

first, the question concerning training; second, the question concerning faith and acceptance; third, regarding orientation; fourth, regarding cultivation; fifth, regarding accomplishment; sixth, regarding purification; seventh, regarding entry; eighth, regarding emergence; ninth...
Conformity; tenth, recollection; eleventh, expansion; twelfth, the fulfillment of the conduct of Samantabhadra. Regarding the second question, "How does one practice the bodhisattva path?
the Sanskrit text reads *pratipatti-mārga-yan-mīlanam*, which here is translated as "practice," also termed "faithful acceptance.
This passage consists of eleven phrases divided into three parts: the first concerns the cultivation of understanding through study, and the subsequent nine...
Right Cultivation. Finally, the ultimate consummation. Within right cultivation: first, a general inquiry regarding the departure from evil; second, exclusive orientation toward practice;
third, advancing in goodness; fourth, the elimination of signs; fifth, clear understanding and realization regarding practice; sixth, the complete possession of meditative concentration;

seventh, non-contradiction between principle and phenomena; eighth, recollecting and maintaining prior cultivation; ninth, practicing the previous [stages] to make them expansive; tenth, exhorting skillfulness for swift perfection.
In Mañjuśrī’s direct response, there are two parts: first, the verses; second, the prose section beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī...

which further praises the arousal of the bodhicitta and instructs on seeking a spiritual friend. Within the former, the ten verses are divided into two sections: the first verse is a general praise of Sudhana for possessing merit and compassion, and seeking the Buddha-Tathāgata;
the subsequent nine verses praise Sudhana for having already perfected great vows and great practices. Among these, the first [verse]...
One makes vows and practices cultivation for the sake of extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings. Second, Mañjuśrī exhorts him, saying:

"If you do not weary of saṃsāra, this is the firmness of possessing the conduct of Samantabhadra for the sake of sentient beings. Third, in the first half [of the verse], it praises Sudhana’s merit as being able to extinguish suffering;

it is called "light" because merit can destroy obstacles, and it is called "power" because the place of birth reveals jewels; it is called the "place of merit," and its characteristics are extinguished.

"Merit vast" refers to the ocean of purity. The second half of the verse concludes this as the vow and practice for the sake of sentient beings. Among the four [verses], the first half of the fifth shows the seeing of many Buddhas;

the second half shows hearing the Dharma and not forgetting it. In the fifth [verse], the first half shows the seeing of many Buddhas; the second half shows the fulfillment of the ocean of vows through the cultivation of practice.
In the sixth [verse], the first half clarifies that within the stage of abiding, one skillfully cultivates practices that encompass the same fruit as a Buddha. Thus says the text.

It says that at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one is equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time; this is explained at length. The second half of the verse further clarifies the first half:
because the Buddha-fruit is eternally attained, the original state remains indestructible. It says that one follows and learns from those of the future.

Seventh, it praises how Sudhana has perfected the practice of Samantabhadra’s path by traversing as many lands as there are atoms in a kalpa. Eighth, it praises Sudhana for [traversing] many lands and kalpas.

The universal vows have been fulfilled through cultivation. Among the nine [sections], this describes how many beings, having heard of Sudhana’s vows, resolve their minds on the Great Vehicle and aspire to study the Great Dharma.
It is asked: at what stage of spiritual attainment is Sudhana? The answer is that the sutra contains no explicit statement;

since human judgment is difficult to rely upon, although there have been many ancient explanations, they are not worth recording. If one follows the subsequent passage concerning the goddess Anuvartinī dwelling among the assembly of goddesses, it says:
Regarding the statement that "this person has already been born into the lineage of the Dharma King," this text may be taken as definitive; however, there are differing interpretations.

One view holds that this refers to one who, through wisdom in accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is born into the family of the Buddha, and is thus said to have "been born into the lineage of the Dharma King"; this refers to a Bodhisattva who has already entered the Great Stages (*mahābhūmi*).
Another view holds that this refers to one who, through the cultivation of extensive learning and the accomplishment of true resolve (*adhimukti*) regarding the true nature, has achieved Buddhahood.
"Born into the lineage of the Dharma King": this refers to the bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) within the stage of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śukla*).
Question: If they are subsumed under faith, how should one reconcile this with the vast vision, hearing, vows, and practices described in this verse?
Answer: This mention of "faith" is not the same as the faith described in the *Karmanirdeśa-sūtra*.

In the subsequent prose section, there are four parts concerning the repeated praise of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the instruction to seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). First, the repeated praise of the arousal of the mind and the instruction to seek a true friend.
Second, from "Good son, in this regard... onwards, the pointing out of the subsequent friend. Third, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the longing...
He thought of withdrawing. He turned toward the four directions and, following the instructions, sought out the superior bliss.

Within the first of these gates, there are three parts: first, praising the ability to generate the resolve; second, because seeking the practice thereafter is the most difficult among difficulties, it is called "faith";

third, the noble son’s formal instruction on seeking a spiritual friend, which constitutes the attainment of the Dharma. This section has two parts: first, the instruction on seeking, and second, the admonition and exhortation.

Regarding the two types mentioned previously: first, because one delights in attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "the knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*). Second, one must seek a true friend;

that which is called a "true spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) refers to one who can cause one to know wholesome dharmas not yet known and to recognize unwholesome dharmas not yet recognized—such a person is termed a "spiritual friend.
As for the term "true," there are briefly four kinds [of qualities] manifested: first, causing one to recognize the three... [text fragment ends].

First, they cause one to escape from evil suffering and lead one to know that the bliss of humans and devas can be attained; though such a person is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are not the true one.

Second, they cause one to recognize the suffering of birth and death as something to be loathed and lead one to know the bliss of *nirvāṇa* as something to be rejoiced in; though such a person is a spiritual friend, they are not the true one.

Third, they cause one to recognize conditioned and out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena as something to be abandoned and lead one to know unconditioned and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) phenomena as [something to be realized].

"Delightful. Although this is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is not yet the true one. Fourth, [the true friend] causes one to know that birth and death are not [necessarily] free from defilement and that *nirvāṇa* is not [necessarily] quiescent;

yet, they themselves always remain far removed from defilement and constantly cultivate practices that are free from signs (*animitta*). One who causes others to know in this way is a true spiritual friend.
For a detailed analysis, see what is explained in the separate chapter on Spiritual Friends (*Kalyāṇamitra-paṭala*) within the section on Exhortations and Admonitions.

Fourth: (1) Although he undergoes many hardships, because he values the Dharma, his body and mind never grow weary; (2) although he remains in close attendance day and night, because he values the Dharma, his affection never reaches satiety;
(3) regarding all instructions and admonitions, he hears them and certainly puts them into practice;

(4) as for those who act contrary to the path, he uses skillful means to discern that they are not within his sphere of influence—what fault could there be in this? Second, regarding the instruction on future companions, there are four points: (1) the country...

"Victorious Bliss" (Jinle) refers to a stage superior to the preceding one, because it is a state worthy of joy and delight. "The Wondrous Peak of the Two Mountains" means that the aforementioned mind has transcended faults and stands at a high level;

thus, it is a "Wondrous Peak. Regarding the bhikṣu named Meghaśrī: there are three meanings of "bhikṣu": first, a mendicant (*bhikṣu*); second, one who destroys evil; and third, one who terrifies Māra.
Here, having newly resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), the palaces of Māra tremble; thus his virtue is like a cloud that contains [rain].
Because of the rain of the Dharma; because the palaces of the four teachings trembled; and because the eleven phrases in the question are the same as before, it says "up to.

Regarding the three reflections on the words of longing and attachment, there are two parts: first, one rejoices because of hearing the Dharma; second, one weeps with sorrow because of being separated from the sound of the Dharma.
[The Buddha] asked Mañjuśrī to observe Sudhana’s consciousness, faculties, desires, and so forth, having already seen all that was necessary.

It is possible to explain all Buddha-dharmas; why then do many people cause [the teaching] to be turned toward different questions? The answer is that this is not without purpose; there are briefly five reasons.
First, to serve as a model for the present and the future. Second, to reveal that in practicing the myriad paths of conduct, one must first seek a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Third, to clarify that in the practice of cultivation, one does not rely on oneself alone. Fourth, to reveal that by relying on a virtuous friend...
Because it is focused on a single point. The fifth [chapter] reveals that there is no selection in seeking a friend. Question:

Since Sudhana seeks the Dharma by measuring his practice against his capacity, why must he travel extensively and seek out many matters and much knowledge? Answer: The Bodhisattva seeks extensive learning (bahuśruta) for the sake of saving sentient beings.
One must not begrudge one’s own body or life. If one does not study and practice exhaustively, the ocean of virtue will remain unfilled; how then could one act in accordance with what is appropriate?
Regarding this passage on the qualities of a virtuous friend from the works of ancient masters, some have divided it into three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten sections and so forth.
Now, however, it shall not be done thus; rather, the divisions shall follow the text itself, as it is improper to impose fixed limits. Above.

Within the twenty-five aspects of the [Avataṃsaka] Sūtra, the first concerns the aspect of cultivation based on the stages of practice (*avasthā*). First, it clarifies that Mañjuśrī is established within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Following this, secondly, among the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the ten stages of faith, the first is the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, who is established as representing the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
Abiding with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Among these, there are six [sections].

First, regarding the seeking [of the path] based on the instructions, there are two [sub-sections]. The first is the explanation according to the teachings on searching for the country and the mountain.

Regarding the phrase "having passed seven days," the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "First, one purifies the seven limbs [of the prostration] and then beholds the virtuous friend. As for "proceeding slowly along the path," it refers to the companion’s reflection.
Because of their practice. Second, having seen [the Buddha], they approach him; this clarifies the inquiry. Within this, there are four parts: first, the performance of respectful etiquette;

second, "In this way," etc., describing their own arousal of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); third, "But I do not yet know," etc., which explicitly presents the question (the question being the same as before);
fourth, "I have heard," etc., concluding the question and requesting the teaching.
In the section "The Clouds of Virtue of the Three Times" (*Sāndhāyika-guṇamegha*), the actual answer is clarified. This consists of two parts: first, praising the aspiration to seek the Dharma;

second, from "Good son, I have attained... onwards, clarifying the Dharma he himself has realized. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, praising the aspiration; second, from "He is able...

onwards, praising the inquiry into the methods of practice. This praise consists of eleven phrases, all containing the word "seek" (*paryeṣate*). The first is the general inquiry seeking the methods of practice.
1. The limit of what is practiced; 2. The cause that serves as an antidote to practice; 3. The cause for transcendence through practice (which is also the fruit);
4. The already purified great mind; 5. The attainment of sovereign mastery; 6. The demonstration of the skillful means of liberation;

7. The demonstration of shared activities; 8. Knowledge of the minds of others; 9. Practice that does not abide [in extremes]; 10. Seeking that which is both conditioned and unconditioned, neither one nor different; 11. [The second category].

Regarding the two aspects of the dharmas attained by oneself: first, the essence of the attained dharmas is clarified; second, from "proceeding to the ten directions" onwards, their functional activity is clarified.

Within the former, there are two parts: first, the essence is indicated; second, from "the power of faith" onwards, the characteristics are explained. Regarding the former, "sovereignty" refers to the absence of obstruction in one's activities.
"The power of decisive resolve" (*adhimukti*)—here, "resolve" means *adhimukti*—refers to the force of definitive apprehension; it is so named because of this.

Power (*bala*) refers to the unimpeded determination, retention, and transformation regarding objects. There are three subsequent explanations of its characteristics: first, faith; second, wisdom; and third, the concluding explanation.
First, by means of pure faith, there is the unimpeded determination, retention, and transformation of both the eye and the object.
Second, because the light of wisdom universally illumines objects without obstruction, there is mastery. Third, the concluding explanation: by means of...

This knowledge consists of the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*), which is certain and sovereign because it is endowed with external skillful observation, internal clarity, and pure conduct.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of its functional activity, there are two parts: first, a brief presentation of the four activities; second, a detailed explanation of the fourth activity, beginning with the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*). Within the first part:

(1) the activity of traveling to the lands of the ten directions to reverently serve and support the Buddhas; (2) the activity of constantly practicing mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*); (3) ... [the third activity].

The karma of upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas; fourth, the karma of constantly seeing all Buddhas as present. Regarding the latter, within the extensive explanation of the fourth karma, there are two parts:
first, a general statement on seeing the Buddhas; second, under each respective direction, a detailed explanation of the various matters of seeing the Buddhas individually.

The first and middle [sections] consist of two parts. First, the eastern direction is explained in detail, beginning from seeing one Buddha up to seeing Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. The subsequent nine directions follow the first; they can be understood through a brief explanation.

Regarding the mention in the middle section of "seeing Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm" and "Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field," the Sanskrit original states: *Namo...* (Homage...).
*Śubhatara-pramāṇu-rajaḥ*. This is translated as "the number of atoms in ten buddha-fields. The Chinese version omits the character for "ten" (*śata*).
Hereafter, various matters concerning the Buddhas will be seen separately. Of the two [sections], the former and the middle, first is the Buddha’s capacity to respond.

Following this, the subsequent section clarifies what is to be accomplished for sentient beings. Within the preceding [section], there are ten types, which can be understood as beginning from physical appearance and extending up to lifespan.
Within the subsequent "what is to be accomplished," there are three: first, according to the inclinations of beings; second, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood; and third, preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the four ways of humbling oneself and deferring to others' excellence, there are two [sections]. First, one humbles oneself by acknowledging knowledge of only a single dharma;
this refers back to the previously mentioned "Gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha. Second, one defers to the excellence of others through the phrase "how could I... and so forth.

Within the first section, the phrase "recalling all objective spheres" (*viṣaya*) refers to the numerical limits and divisions of the Buddhas of the ten directions, as the Buddhas are the objects of contemplation. "Wisdom-light" (*jñānāloka*) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Because it is that which illuminates. "Universally seeing" means illuminating and seeing exhaustively. "Dharma-gate" refers to the summary and its attribution.

Regarding the phrase "the light of the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, wherein one broadly sees the Buddhas upon first entering the stage of abiding": this is because the Buddha is taken as the fundamental basis.

Therefore, within the description of the first abiding, it says, "This bodhisattva sees the physical forms and features of the Buddhas," and so forth. There are three parts to the subsequent "inferring the excellence": first, a single sentence as a general summary; next...
Regarding what is called "distinct manifestation," the final phrase, "and I... serves as the conclusion. Within the general section, the "boundless wisdom" and so forth refer to:
illuminating the inexhaustible realm of the Buddhas and practicing the boundless conduct of the Buddhas. Within the distinct section, there are twenty-one phrases;

each first presents the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), followed by an explanation of the specific distinctions of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). Of these, the first ten concern the Buddha’s supreme virtues being perfectly complete, while the latter eleven [concern...]

The wondrous function of mindfulness of the Buddha is sovereign. Regarding the preceding section: first, because it possesses the merit of seeing all Buddhas together with their retinues, it says, "constantly seeing the lands of all Buddhas," and so forth.
Second, because mindfulness of the Buddha causes sentient beings to depart from perversions, it says, "pure.

Third, because mindfulness of the Buddha possesses merits such as the ten powers—including the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), and so forth—it [is so described]. Fourth, because mindfulness of the Buddha is able to remain non-perversion regarding the Dharma...

It is said that this is capable of bestowing [realization], because the bodhisattva’s mind is unerring regarding the Dharma. Thus, one is able to recollect having seen the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and received and upheld it.
Fifth, having already reached the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, one perceives that all buddha-fields are without difference.

Sixth, one recollects the Buddha within the subtle realm and perceives the Buddha’s sovereign activity therein. Seventh, one recollects seeing the Buddhas continuously throughout all kalpas. Eighth, one recollects all...
1. At all times, one contemplates the Buddha as being ever-present and never departing. 2. One contemplates that within all lands, the Buddhas everywhere manifest their supremely excellent bodies. 3.

One contemplates that throughout all worlds, the Buddhas are universally perceived according to the inclinations of beings' minds. Following this, the section clarifies the mastery of wondrous functions: 1.
One contemplates the Buddha appearing sequentially within all various differentiated realms. 2. One contemplates the Buddha manifesting the appearance of *nirvāṇa*. 3. One contemplates...
1. Contemplating that the Buddha emerges from his own dwelling place without interval throughout the course of a single day; 2. Contemplating that the Buddha’s body fills all dharma-realms; 3.
Contemplating that many Buddhas appear upon a single hair-tip, all of whom one serves; 4. Contemplating that the Buddha manifests in all places, attaining Buddhahood and displaying sovereign mastery;
5. Contemplating that the Buddha appears and emits the light of wisdom to turn the wheel of Dharma; 6. Contemplating that it is mind-only.

1. Contemplating the Buddha as appearing according to the mind’s inclination: one knows that the Buddha manifests forms in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings. 2. Contemplating the Buddha as manifesting according to the inclination for joy:

one knows that according to the karma of sentient beings, he manifests auspicious forms gathered through that very karma. 3. Contemplating the Buddha’s supernatural power: he manifests his body sitting upon a lotus flower, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
4. Contemplating the Buddha’s true virtue: like the void, his body adorns the emptiness of the Dharma-realm. The conclusion at the end may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the five points of instruction for the subsequent friend (*mitra*): first, there is the instruction on seeing the person;

second, the instruction on attaining the Dharma, beginning with the passage "Good son, Sāgaramegha... Within the former [section], there are five parts: first, pointing out the direction, which accords with what preceded;

second, indicating the country called Samudramukha—this is termed "Sea Gate" because it is the means (*upāya*) for cultivating the ocean of the virtuous mind, and because this country is situated precisely at the mouth of the Southern Sea; third, the bhikṣu...
Regarding "Sāgaramegha" (Sea-Cloud): the meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. "Sāgaramegha" means that this bhikṣu internally contains the water of the Dharma, deep and vast like the ocean;
externally, he preaches in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, like clouds raining down. Fourth is the exhortation to go and inquire about the Dharma.

Fifth, from "the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha" onwards, there is praise for his skillful preaching, which is easy to understand. Within his instruction on attaining the Dharma, there are nine phrases. The first is "causing one to attain reality."
1. To provide instruction for the path of practice, as taught in the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra Sūtra*. 2. To attain the cause for achieving omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). 3.
To serve as the cause for generating the great resolve (*mahācitta*) upon hearing the teaching. 4. To attain the wisdom and vision that arise from the true teaching. 5.

To attain the ability to cultivate practices that accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). 6. To be able to practice the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct. 7. To achieve the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s vows. 8. To attain purity.
The skillful means of the vow; ninth, attaining the power of great compassion that is without object;
sixth, observing the difficulty of abandoning those who have shown kindness and then taking leave. The first dwelling is concluded.
Second, regarding the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha’s dwelling in the stage of "Purifying the Ground" (*bhūmi-pariśodhana*) among the "Spiritual Friends," there are seven sections:

1. From "At that time, as previously described... up to the end of the first section. 2. From "Gradually descending... down to "seeking according to the teaching. 3. From "He spoke these words... down to "having seen him, he asked about the Dharma. 4. From "Then the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha said...
down to the "correct response. 5. From "Good son, I only know this much... down to "humble oneself and defer to the superior. 6. Good... [text fragment].
The youth proceeded south from this point, as indicated below. Regarding the section on Sudhana’s contemplation of virtues and his withdrawal from the initial [vision], there are eleven phrases:
the first phrase is general, while the remaining phrases are specific. Within the specific section: 1. the function of wisdom-illumination; 2. the skillful means of unimpeded function; 3.
the skillful means of meditative concentration; 4. the assembly of bodhisattvas; 5. the vision of the Buddha appearing before one; 6. the vision... [of the Dharma].
The Buddha’s dwelling. Seventh, observing the standards of others' conduct; eighth, observing the vastness of the Buddha-realm; ninth, observing the sequence of the Buddha’s manifestations;
tenth, observing the Buddha’s entry into skillful transformations. These ten topical sections all pertain to the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*).

Second, within the section on seeking according to the teachings, there are three parts: first, arriving at the location; second, approaching Samudramegha; third, prostrating and below, the inquiry into the Dharma. Within this [third part], there are three sections:
first, the performance of respectful etiquette; second, from "Thus having... onwards, the description of having already resolved upon the mind [of enlightenment];

third, from "But I do not yet know... onwards, the actual words of the inquiry. Within this [third section], there are ten phrases: first, abandoning the mundane and arising in the supramundane; second, transcending... [and so forth].

1. Entering the clarity of wisdom from the darkness of ignorance; 2. Departing from the three realms of ordinary beings to enter the state of the noble ones; 3. Severing the stream that follows worldly currents to enter the stream that flows against them; 4.

Shattering the wheel of transmigration within the three realms of existence and accomplishing the wheel of the vow of great compassion; 5. Extinguishing the defilements of attachment to pleasure and practicing the conduct free from defilement;

6. Drying up the ocean of craving and increasing the ocean of great compassion; 7. Blocking the three evil paths and the eight difficulties while opening the gates to the human and celestial realms and to nirvāṇa; 8. Nine...
Leaving the city of the triple world, one enters the city of Buddha-wisdom. The ten abandonments of all playthings entirely benefit sentient beings.
Among the four correct answers, there are three: first, the fundamental and thorough generation of the mind; second, the statement by Sāgaramegha praising the difficulty of generating that mind.

"Third, 'Good son, I abide here'—below this, I shall explain the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the first [section], there is first a formal inquiry, followed by Sudhana’s reply, 'Yes, sir.
Second, within the praise of its rarity, there are three parts: first, the counter-objection; second, the affirmative objection;

and third, the specific explanation beginning with 'One who has generated the bodhicitta... The initial counter-objection states: 'If one does not plant roots of goodness, one cannot generate the bodhicitta.'"
Next, regarding the eleven phrases within the "Conformity to Objections," the first ten phrases provide specific explanations, while the final phrase serves as a summary. Within the former:
First, it says that one must obtain the light of the roots of goodness of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). This means that practicing a single practice is equivalent to all practices;
because wisdom is clear and lucid during each individual practice, it is called "light. Second, it is to possess the light of wisdom of the samādhi of the true path. This accords with...

1. Through the cultivation of meditative concentration on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one generates the light of wisdom. 2. Third, one extensively produces merit. 3. Fourth, because one increases untainted (*anāsrava*) states without interruption, it is called "freedom from indolence.
4. Fifth, out of reverence for the Dharma, one serves spiritual friends without weariness. 6. Sixth, out of reverence for the Dharma, one does not begrudge anything one possesses.
7. Seventh, one universally vows to bear the burden [of others]. 8. Eighth, one universally desires to eliminate suffering. 9. Ninth, one bestows happiness and does not abandon those to be rescued.

"Uprooting. The ten [verses] consist of contemplating the realm of the Buddha; the concluding phrase at the end may be understood as the summary. In the subsequent detailed explanation, there are two parts: first, a general heading;
second, the specific exposition beginning with "That is to say," which contains eleven phrases. Within each phrase, there is both a heading and an explanation. The first is "uprooting suffering.

The second, "benefiting," is the bestowing of happiness, for through merit one is assisted and protected so that one does not depart from happiness. The third is "extinguishing suffering. The fourth...

1. To remain free from unwholesome dharmas; 2. to guard the five [faculties] so as not to allow them to be terrified; 3. to be free from all obstacles; 4. to attain [realization]; 5. to fulfill the dharma-realm; 6.
to be equal to the realm of space; 7. to see many Buddhas throughout the far reaches; 8. to know all objects of the three periods of time in accordance with reality;
9. to universally illumine all spheres and enter the ocean of wisdom.
Third, within the analysis of practice, there are four parts: 1. Contemplating the ocean as the skillful means for expression; 2.

"Good son, when I was reflecting," and so forth, which describes attaining the vision of the dharma-realm where there is no distinction between the environment and its inhabitants; 3. "At that time, this Tathāgata," and so forth, which describes receiving the boundless teachings that flow from it;
4. "If there are sentient beings from the ten directions," and so forth, which describes transmitting [the teachings] to sentient beings so that they may enter the Dharma together.
Regarding the "Dhātu" (Realm/Element), within the first two [sections], there is first a general heading, followed by a specific analysis beginning with the words "That is to say.

The general statement, "He dwelt here for twelve years," has been explained by ancient masters as follows: some say it refers to his contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*);
others explain it as dwelling in the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; and yet others explain it as referring specifically to the second of these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Thus it is said.
Twelfth: Because one constantly takes the ocean as the object of contemplation, it is called the "sphere" (*viṣaya*). Within the subsequent distinct section, there are ten phrases:
first, the vast teaching; second, the profound principle; third, abiding in gradual stages; fourth, adorned with many jewels of the Dharma; fifth, accumulated waters of great compassion.

Sixth, the extraction of differences according to individual capacities. Seventh, the manifold types of those to be transformed. Eighth, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contained within the ocean of the teaching.

Ninth, the principles and meanings expounded as contained within the ocean of the teaching. Tenth, the profound stillness of the ocean of the teaching: though many sentient beings in the realms of birth-and-death are transformed and enter extinction, the realm of birth-and-death does not diminish;

though many sentient beings are not transformed and remain in extinction, the realm of birth-and-death does not increase. Second, attaining the vision of the Dharma-realm, which is non-acquisitive and abides in the center.

Two. First, the vision of the dependent fruit (*niśraya-phala*) is explained; later, when it is extinguished, the vision of that [fruit] follows—this explains the vision of the direct fruit (*sākṣāt-phala*).
Within the former, there are two parts: first, the present fruit is explained; second, from "This great... onwards, the past causes are explained. Within the former, there are two parts:

first, the causes for the manifestation of the flowers are explained, which contains four points that can be understood. Second, within the actual explanation of the dependent fruit that is manifested, there are two parts: first, the mental reflection is restated; second...

This section below clearly elucidates the fruits that manifest. Within the manifestation of these fruits, there are two parts. First, it distinguishes the source and the temporal and spatial dimensions of the flowers' emergence;
that is to say, within the great ocean, at the very moment of forming a thought, they suddenly appear.

Second, from "Because nothing can surpass them" onwards, it elucidates the adornments. Within the adornments, there are two parts: first, it elucidates the adornment of the essential body itself; second, from "One million asuras... onwards, it elucidates the external adornments. Regarding the former:

Five [parts]: first, the stalk; second, the flower; third, the petals; fourth, the pedestal; fifth, the crest. Regarding the subsequent external adornments of the interior, there are twenty-two types.
Among these, eleven phrases describe various adornments held by sentient beings who are kings, and eleven phrases describe adornments consisting of non-sentient objects;
both may be understood accordingly. In the subsequent section clarifying past causes, there are ten phrases: the first nine phrases refer to specific times, while the final phrase is general.
The conclusion of the virtues is inexhaustible. Within the preceding section: first, the cause of outflow-free [wisdom]; second, the sympathetic joy of all bodhisattvas;

third, the cause arising from contemplative practices such as viewing things as like illusions and dreams; fourth, pure karma; fifth, the cause of the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*); sixth, contemplating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); seventh, abiding in sovereign function;
eighth, contemplating the profound realm of the Buddha; ninth, the conclusion; tenth, the twenty phrases clarifying the vision of the true fruit. First:

1. Seeing the Buddha atop the flower; 2. the two lotus seats; 3. the three sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); 4. the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*); 5. the secondary refinements (*anuvyañjana*); 6. supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*); 7. purity of physical appearance; 8.
the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣaśiraskatā*); 9. the mark of the broad and long tongue (*prabhūtajihvatā*); 10. skillful exposition; 11. the perfect voice (*brahmasvara*).
10. The twenty powers; 11. The four fearlessnesses; 12. Eloquence; 13. Past causes; 14. Manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood; 15. Expounding the Dharma; 16.
Universally manifesting all adornments; 17. Appearing differently according to those who see; 18. Fulfiling all benefits.
Regarding the third [section], receiving the teaching, there are two parts. First, it clarifies extending the right hand to stroke the Sea-Cloud [Bodhisattva].

[The Buddha] touched [his] head. Subsequently, for my sake, he correctly expounded the sutra. Regarding the first part, his right hand touching the head is the sign of the empowerment of physical action (*kāyakarman*) through sympathetic reception.
Regarding the subsequent exposition of the sutra, there are three sections: first, clarifying the functional efficacy (*karman*) of the sutra;
second, from "I, from that Tathāgata... onwards, hearing the sutra and receiving it into memory; third, from "Good son, when I, at the Buddha’s... onwards, the time of receiving and maintaining it.
Regarding the extent of the Dharma, there are two parts within the first section. First, the title of the sutra is revealed:
it is called the "Universal Eye" because, based on what is expounded therein, one achieves the Universal Eye—namely, by illuminating and seeing the single, equal Dharma-realm.

Second, the function of the sutra is shown below; herein there are ten phrases: first, the realm of the Buddha; second, the practice of the Bodhisattva; third, the gathering of the Wheel of Dharma; fourth, the ability to purify the Buddha... [text continues].

1. It is like the earth. 2. It can destroy the heterodox. 3. It can annihilate the armies of Māra. 4. It causes sentient beings to rejoice. 5. It can illuminate the minds of beings. 6. It can discern the faculties of beings. 7.
It enables them to attain awakening according to their minds. Regarding the second [section], "Hearing the Sūtra and Receiving and Maintaining it," there are two parts:

first, clarifying the accomplishment of the six dharmas; second, the comparison of the quantity [of merit] starting from "Even if... Within the former: 1. Because one internalizes the Dharma within the mind; 2. Each...
1. Because it is not lost; 2. because one proclaims it in accordance with the text; 3. because one expounds it by reciting against the text; 4. because one recalls it without forgetting; 5.
because one contemplates it with clarity and precision. Regarding the subsequent evaluation:

the statement that even writing out a single verse from within a single chapter using many pens and ink does not yield even a small portion [of the merit] is intended to manifest the vastness of this Dharma-gate. (3) Receiving.

Regarding the method for maintaining [the teachings] during the intermediate period of two thousand years: the first line is general, while the subsequent section beginning with "day by day" is specific.

Within the former, the phrase "those who maintain it for twelve hundred years" indicates a single division (one *piṭaka*). In the latter, specific section, there are ten phrases that apply identically every day;
since each one consists of countless chapters (*aneka-paryāya*), we know that a single division contains ten such countless sections. First, hearing.
1. Because of the light of upholding *dhāraṇīs*, one receives countless chapters. 2. Because of the light of tranquility, one enters. 3. Because of the light of revolving, one universally enters. 4.
Because of the light of following the stages (*bhūmi*), one discerns. 5. Because of the light of majestic power, one universally gathers.
6. Because of the light of the lotus, one brings forth. 7. Because of the light of pure sound, one expounds. 8. Because of the light of empty flowers, one reveals. 9.
Because it is the radiance of the mass of light, it increases and expands. Because it is the light of the *dhāraṇī* of the ten ocean-treasuries, it discerns and analyzes countless chapters.
Regarding the second part of the fourfold transmission to sentient beings: first, it is understood that the ten classes of kings and the common people come to listen;

subsequently, from the words "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, it correctly explains the preaching of the Dharma. Within this, there are two parts: first, it reveals that the speaker possesses four attributes, the first of which is joy (*rati*).
I. Indicating; II. Explaining; III. Proclaiming; IV. Praising. Following this, the section beginning with "all cause" clarifies the benefiting of others through three phrases:
I. Delight; II. Entry; III. Abiding.

Regarding the five points on humbling oneself and deferring to the superior, there are two sections. First, humbling oneself and knowing [the Dharma] as one; this explains the name of the *dharmaparyāya* as before.

Second, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior by knowing that [others] are many; this consists of eleven phrases. The first ten phrases explain individually, while the final phrase provides a summary.
In the preceding section: first, awakening to and understanding the ocean of practices, making vows, and engaging in cultivation—this is the meaning of "entering the letter" (入字), as explained below;
second, awakening to and understanding the great vows to remain in the world for many eons; third, awakening to and understanding the benefit of sentient beings according to their inclinations;

fourth, awakening to and understanding the power and light of wisdom arising from the ocean of the mind; fifth, awakening to and understanding the taming and transformation of the faculties of beings; sixth, awakening to and understanding the adornment of buddha-fields; seventh, awakening to and understanding [the state of] indolence.

1. To understand the Buddha’s body as eternally present and to make offerings to it; 2. To clearly understand and awaken to the teachings of the Dharma; 3. To clearly understand and awaken to the perfection of meritorious deeds; 4.

To clearly understand and awaken to the sounds of words and speech used in preaching the Dharma. The final phrase concludes that the superior objects of knowledge are not something one can sever by one's own power.

Sixth, regarding the six points indicated for the subsequent friend: first, "going south" is to be understood as before. Second, "six thousand *yojanas*"—the ancient masters explain that this is because one has cultivated the practice of the six *pāramitās*.
Third, "at the edge of the Laṅkā path" refers to the vicinity of the road leading toward that mountain.
Fourth, "there is a village" refers to a place inhabited by a multitude of people. Fifth, "named Seashore" refers to the Southern Sea.
On its northern bank was a bhikṣu named Supratiṣṭhita. His body dwelt in the void, signifying that his inner mind dwelt in true nature.
At that time, Sudhana descended from his aerial vehicle, paid homage, withdrew, and departed—so it should be understood. The second dwelling is concluded.

Within the third dwelling, the Dwelling of Cultivation by the Bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita, among the six [sections] concerning spiritual friends: first, seeking according to the instructions; second, the good...
1. From "Sudhana" onwards, the actual inquiry regarding the Dharma is clarified. 2. From "The bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita" onwards, the actual response is clarified. 3.

Within the section on humbling oneself and deferring to the superior, from "Good son, I only... onwards. 4. From "Good son, from here... onwards, the subsequent spiritual friends are indicated. 5. From "At that time, Sudhana...
onwards, he honors the virtues [of his teacher] and takes his leave.

Regarding the first of these two [sections], one first recollects the ten phrases previously heard: first, recollecting the instruction that points out; second, recollecting the Dharma taught; third, recollecting the Buddha’s empowerment;
fourth, recollecting the retention of the Dharma phrases; and fifth, clearly and distinctly awakening to and understanding the gateway to the ocean of Dharma.
Sixth, the differentiation of the six modes of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-dharma*). Seventh, awakening to and understanding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to its deepest extent.

Eighth, suddenly awakening to and understanding that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness (*sarva-dharma-śūnyatā*). Ninth, purifying attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*). Tenth, contemplating the source from which the emptiness of phenomena arises.

Regarding the subsequent explicit clarification of seeking [the goal], there are two parts: first, distinguishing the destination toward which one proceeds, which is clear; second, beginning with "seeing this bhikṣu," clarifying the vision of that which is proceeded toward.
Among these, there were two [visions]. First, he saw bhikṣus walking back and forth in mid-air.
