Subsequently, various classes of devas from the formless realm descended with radiance, and each of the different types of beings offered their respective acts of worship. Among these, there were ten categories: first, devas; second, nāgas; third, kiṃnaras; fourth, mahoragas;
fifth, asuras; sixth, garuḍas; seventh, rākṣasas; eighth, yakṣas; ninth, Brahmā kings; and tenth, Śuddhāvāsa devas.
The second part, explaining Sudhana’s formal inquiry, has two sections: first, recapitulating what was previously seen; second, from "In this way... onwards, initiating the subsequent section.

Within the initiation of the subsequent section, there are two parts: first, personally recounting that he has already resolved upon the Great Mind; second, from "But I do not yet know... onwards, formally presenting the questions he wishes to ask.
In the questions, there are two parts. First, eleven phrases concerning hearing the Buddha’s Dharma; second, ten phrases concerning not abandoning the various dharmas.
Within the first part, the initial ten phrases pose specific questions, while the final phrase summarizes the preceding inquiries. Furthermore, within the first part: (1) initiating practice;
(2) gathering [the teachings] so as not to let them be lost; (3) striving to achieve completeness; (4) repeatedly hearing the Dharma from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); (5) gradually...

[The practice] becomes increasingly extensive. Sixth, it is summarized and grasped. Seventh, one ensures it reaches its conclusion. Eighth, one purifies that which is defiled. Ninth, one examines it minutely and treats it again.
Tenth, one exhausts all obstructions. The final phrase concludes the preceding questions. The word "furthermore" (*fu*) serves to connect the two sets of ten questions.
As for the statement in each of the latter ten phrases that one "does not abandon," it means that regarding those ten dharmas, there is not even a momentary separation from the mind [of cultivation].
First, because one constantly and diligently cultivates upon seeing the Buddha; second, because bodhisattvas share the same roots of goodness; third, because the Buddha-dharma is clearly realized;
fourth, because the great vows universally benefit and increase life; fifth, because there is no weariness in various practices; and sixth, because buddha-fields are universally adorned and purified.

Seventh, because of seeing the Buddha’s mastery through the power of the seven Buddhas; eighth, not abandoning the conditioned while not dwelling in existence, thereby manifesting transformation bodies;
ninth, because of hearing the Dharma and receiving the correct teaching; tenth, because of awakening to and understanding that the three periods of time are one through the light of wisdom.
Within the threefold correct response, there are two parts. First, the inquiry into Sudhana’s arousal of the bodhicitta and the nature of the Dharma he asks about can be understood [from the text].

Second, from "Good son, I have already... onwards, there is the actual description of what [the teacher] has attained, which consists of three sections: first, the manifestation of the liberation achieved; second, from "If [they] come...
onwards, the clarification of the skillful means that bring about this liberation; and third, from "Knowing all... onwards, the manifestation of the functional activity of that liberation.
Regarding the preceding section, "the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded liberation": that which is attained during the causal stage is termed "the Bodhisattva’s activity.

Mastery is termed "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*). Within the section on skillful means, there are two parts: first, the clarification of cultivation; second, from "at that very moment" onwards, the manifestation of attaining liberation.
This "light of wisdom" is precisely another name for the unimpeded liberation. Regarding the application of the three karmas:
Three. First, the twelve phrases of unimpeded knowledge are explained individually; second, there is an inquiry followed by an explanation. Regarding the first [section], there are ten:

(1) knowing the mental activities of beings; (2) knowing the death and rebirth of beings; (3) knowing past lives; (4) knowing the events of future kalpas; (5) knowing present events; (6) knowing speech and sounds;
(7) resolving doubts and questions; (8) knowing the various faculties; (9) responding appropriately to the time for transformation; (10) knowing all things.

Regarding time-periods (*kāla-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the *kṣaṇa* and so forth. As for the *kṣaṇa* and so forth, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) states: "Nine hundred arisings and ceasings constitute one *kṣaṇa*;
ninety *kṣaṇas* constitute one thought-moment (*tatkṣaṇa*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts, the smallest unit of time is called one *kṣaṇa*.
One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tat-kṣaṇa*, and sixty *tat-kṣaṇas* constitute one [lava].
Thirty *lava*s constitute one *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrta*s make one day and night.
Eleventh, he knows the transmigration through the three periods of time; twelfth, his body travels everywhere throughout the ten directions. Next, the commentary on the meaning states:
How is this attained? Because there is no obstruction among all phenomena. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the meaning, there are two parts.
First, it is shown that by means of this liberation, one possesses the power of non-abiding and so forth, which makes it known [as such].

Second, from "Good son" onwards, it further explains the various functions manifested within emptiness. Within this, there are two parts: first, the general indication, which can be understood; second, regarding the void...
Within the section on "Manifestations in the Air," there are twenty distinct manifestations: first, unimpeded movement through a single path; second, unimpeded concealment and manifestation;

third, manifesting the body as one or many; fourth, passing through solid objects; fifth, coming and going while sitting cross-legged; sixth, entering into the earth and water; seventh, emitting smoke and flames from the body;
eighth, shaking the earth; ninth, touching the sun and moon with the hand; tenth, ascending to great heights; eleventh, manifesting fragrances and so forth.
12. In a single thought-moment, he traverses one buddha-field, up to as many fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.

13. He hears the Dharma taught by the Buddhas within all those fields previously traversed. 14. In the presence of each of those Buddhas, he manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable buddha-fields.
15. Each of those bodies, in turn, manifests as many [bodies] as there are atoms in immeasurable buddha-fields.
Clouds of offerings as numerous as atoms of dust—specifically, the ten types listed below should be understood.

(16) "Each and every Tathāgata" and so forth refers to hearing and receiving the teachings spoken by those various Buddhas. (17) "Each and every land" and so forth refers to recollecting all the adornments present in those various lands.
(18) The conclusion regarding the ten directions summarizes this supernormal power (*abhijñā*). (19) "In this way, all... and so forth clarifies the above.

All sentient beings in all lands who behold his body will certainly attain bodhi. Twenty: he manifests bodies identical to those of various sentient beings to transform them. Four: regarding the humility of oneself and the deference to others, there are two [sections].
First, it clarifies the humility of knowing only one’s own [limited] knowledge; second, as in the passage "like all [others]," it defers to the excellence [of others].

"Knowing much. Regarding the phrase "universally and swiftly, etc. in the preceding section: it means that for the sake of accomplishing the practice, understanding, and realization of sentient beings, one swiftly and universally makes offerings at the presence of all Buddhas throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Within the extensive explanation of "knowing much," twenty-one phrases are briefly elucidated.

The first twenty phrases specifically manifest the upholding of the Bodhisattva precepts, beginning from Great Compassion and ending with Freedom from Defilement; all of these are categorized according to their upholding.
The mental activity (*citta-carita*) serves as its name; this may be understood according to the explanation. The final phrase, "In this way," and so forth, reveals that it was not known by himself.
Among the five indications regarding the subsequent friend, four are presented. First, the name of the country is *Darīṇasa*; this means "Dissolving" (*saṃyoga*). That is to say:
Dissolving erroneous interpretations and attaining correct knowledge in accordance with the teachings, which arises from the sacred doctrine, is called the "Abode of Noble Birth.
Second, the city is named "Mastery" (*Vaśavartin*); having attained noble birth, it is termed "mastery. Third, the spiritual friend is named Megha;
this translates as "Cloud," signifying that his wisdom contains the water of the Dharma to extensively benefit sentient beings. Fourth, he instructs you to go there and inquire about the Dharma.

Sixth: At this time, the youth Sudhana, having reflected upon the virtues [of his teacher], took his leave. This concludes the section on the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who dwells in the practice of cultivation. Fourth:

Among the seven [sections] concerning the spiritual friend Maitreya, the physician born of noble lineage, who dwells in the stage of "Birth in a Noble Lineage" (jātigotrasthiti), there are: first, a reflection on what was previously heard;
second, gradually descending to seek the friend and obtaining a vision of him; third, at this time, the youth Sudhana properly clarifies his inquiry into the Dharma; fourth, at that time...
1. Megha’s reply, which clearly elucidates the answer; 2. "Good son, I only..."—humble self-deprecation and referral to a superior;
3. "Good son, from here..."—pointing out the subsequent spiritual friend; 4. "At that time, Sudhana..."—the friend’s sorrowful parting words.
The first ten phrases are as follows: First, through the contemplation of the dharma-gate of a single thought-moment, one gives rise to superior resolve and attains clear understanding.

Second, one recollects that the power of the Buddha and the Three Jewels are eternally present. Third, one praises the reality manifested through [the overcoming of] greed. Fourth, one recollects the kindness of spiritual friends.

Fifth, one illuminates the equality of the three periods of time. Sixth, one recalls the vow to save sentient beings. Seventh, because one knows the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Eighth, one contemplates all...
I. Nature; II. Adorning the lands; III. Not being attached to the Buddha’s assembly. Regarding the second [section], "Seeking Friends":
within the middle two [subsections], first is the clarification of seeking and searching, and subsequently, from "yet I... onwards, is the clarification of seeing. This may be understood.

Within the third [section], "Correctly Clarifying the Questions," there are two parts: first, the clarification of recounting one's own resolve for enlightenment; second, from "but I... onwards, the actual posing of the questions. Within the questions...
There are twelve phrases. The first two are general: the former phrase refers to "learning" (*śikṣā*), and the latter to "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). Within the subsequent specific section:
(1) although the body undergoes superior transformation, the mind does not follow in that transformation; (2) attaining the single nature; (3) attaining a firm mind free from defilement;

(4) uprooting suffering without weariness; (5) clear awakening to the dhāraṇīs; (6) giving rise to the function of great wisdom; (7) manifesting power to resolve and clarify profound meanings; (8) ... [and so forth].

1. Through the power of mindfulness, one realizes the various and distinct wheels of Dharma. 2. One preaches the Dharma to those in the nine realms of existence. 3. Through the power of wisdom, one definitively discerns the meanings and principles of all dharmas.

4. Regarding the four types of correct and clear answers, there are seven [points]: first, the inquiry into the arousal of the mind; second, Sudhana says "Only... and below, he answers what has already been [asked].

1. The arousal [of the mind]. 2. Megha immediately descends from his seat, praises the arousal of the mind, and prostrates to Sudhana, offering flowers, incense, and hymns of praise for the arousal of the mind.
3. "Good son, if there be... and so forth; this praises the benefits of the arousal of the mind. 4. "Good son, you should know... and so forth;
this praises the difficulty of the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas. 5. "Megha, having praised thus... and so forth; this explains that Megha emits light.
He summoned the assembly to preach the Dharma. Then, Māṭhara answered from below regarding the Dharma he himself had attained.

As for the initial inquiry, it was intended to praise and manifest that the arousal of the bodhicitta is no ordinary matter; if one were truly able to arouse it, it would be something extraordinary in the world, and thus [the question] sought to manifest respect.
He asks these questions in order to cause Samantabhadra to hear them. Regarding the second [point], because he answers directly and straightforwardly, the word "only" (*kevalam*) is used.
Third, out of a mind of respectful devotion, he immediately descends from his seat to pay homage to Sudhana, scattering various flowers and incense as offerings and praise.

Fourth, regarding the praise of the benefits of generating the bodhicitta, there are two parts: first, praising the accomplishment of those benefits; second, the section beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*), which explains the aforementioned "peaceful security. Within the first of these, there are twenty [subsections].

There are two phrases. The first phrase is general; the remaining phrases are specific. It should be understood that the eleven characters beginning with "arousing *anuttara*... apply throughout all the phrases.
Because the bodhicitta possesses the three types of mind, the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. Because it possesses the profound and upright mind (*ṛjukacitta*), the buddha-fields are adorned.
Because of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇācitta*), sentient beings are brought to maturity. Because of the upright mind, one penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Because of the profound and upright mind, one awakens to and understands the characteristics and nature of the seeds of karma. Because of the profound mind, one fulfills all practices. Because of the three minds, great vows are never interrupted.

Because of the upright mind, one accords with the true nature and is free from greed. Because of the profound and upright mind, one perceives the characteristics and nature of the three periods of time.

It is likewise for attaining resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) regarding all phenomena. Because they possess these three minds, they are protected and sustained by all Buddhas; the Buddhas keep them in mind.

Mindfulness is likewise so; the bodhisattva’s equanimity is likewise so. Because one possesses these three minds and serves as a refuge for the world, one is protected by the noble ones, saluted by the Brahma King, honored by the Lord of Devas, guarded by yakṣas, attended by rākṣasas, welcomed by nāga kings, praised by kiṃnaras, and extolled by the lords of the world.
This brings universal peace to all beings. Next, the commentary explains the eleven phrases concerning "peace" mentioned previously: first, abandoning the four evil destinies; second, ...

1. To escape the eight difficulties; 2. To sever the causes of poverty among humans; 3. To create the causes for rebirth in the heavens; 4. To encounter virtuous friends; 5. To hear and uphold the True Dharma; 6.
To give rise to the great resolve (bodhicitta); 7. To give rise to the great resolve that is free from signs; 8. To behold the path traversed by Bodhisattvas.
Tenth, [the bodhisattva] possesses clear understanding through the wisdom of a bodhisattva. Eleventh, they abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the five praises of the bodhisattva’s difficulties, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation beginning with "They are the refuge for all sentient beings. Within the former, there are four phrases:

first, the difficulty of what is to be done, meaning that they arise as a basis for all things; second, the difficulty of appearing, meaning that they wait for the resonance of sentient beings' capacities; third, the difficulty of encountering [them], meaning...
Because those of little merit cannot encounter it, the four visions are doubly difficult. This refers to seeing the place where the Bodhisattva dwells.

In the subsequent explanation, there are seventeen phrases; each phrase contains the aforementioned four difficulties, or they may be divided into four groups. The first seven phrases explain the difficulty of what has been performed.
The next three phrases explain the difficulty of emergence, meaning that the light of wisdom emerges surpassing the lamps of all the stars, both large and small.
Light. His virtue rises above all mountains; the comparison of the Bodhisattva’s virtue with that of the two vehicles is likewise. The next two lines explain the difficulty of encountering [him]:

because those of meager merit have not yet met with the conditions for receiving glory, they are unable to see the King or his generals; yet if they encounter a Bodhisattva, they will surely accomplish the virtues of practice.
The final five lines explain that what one sees when seeing a Bodhisattva is necessarily the hearing of the Dharma and the arising of faith, thereby escaping the drifting through existence (*bhava*).
...and so forth. Within the second section on the emission of light from the six *mī* syllables, there are two parts: first, clarifying the emission of light to assemble the assembly;

second, from the passage on the Mahāsattva Megha onwards, clarifying that he preaches the Dharma so that those who hear it do not regress from Bodhi. Regarding the "Chapter on the Wheel-Syllable" (*Cakrākṣara-parivarta*), the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states:

"The Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman explains that the 'wheel' has many meanings; briefly, three interpretations are presented. First, regarding the form of the letter: in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the letter..."

First, because the wheel is complete, like the footprint of an elephant; second, regarding that which is expressed, it exhausts the principle and is all-encompassing, like a wheel that is fully perfected;
third, regarding its functional activity, what is spoken is not in vain—as can be understood from the text. Seventh, in the response concerning what has been attained, there are two parts.
First, he immediately ascends the seat because he reveres the Dharma and the person; then he immediately descends the seat and bows again to Sudhana, thereby making [his own attainment] manifest.

Regarding the etiquette between teacher and disciple: revering the Dharma is the reason for ascending the seat before preaching. Following the passage "Afterward, good sons... and so forth, the text correctly clarifies the attainment of the Dharma.

Within this section on attaining the Dharma, there are two parts: first, the designation of the Dharma’s name, namely, the *Sūkṣmasvara-dhāraṇī*; second, the formal explanation beginning with "Able to discern and know...

and so forth, which means that being able to discern and know is called "wondrous" (*sūkṣma*), while the languages of the various devas and others are called "sounds" (*svara*); thus it is the *Sūkṣmasvara-dhāraṇī*.
Because Megha possesses this dhāraṇī within his wisdom, the rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the fifth section, "Humbling Oneself and Recommending the Superior," there are two parts: first, humbling oneself to acknowledge one's own limited knowledge; second, recommending the superiority of others to acknowledge their vast knowledge, as indicated by the passage beginning with "Just as [the Buddhas]... and so forth.
Of the fourteen phrases in the preceding section, the first thirteen are explained individually, while the final phrase concludes that [the matter] is not known by oneself.

Regarding the individual explanations: "provisioning" (*prajñapti*) refers to deportment (*īryāpatha*); "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) means completion; "superior phrase" (*uttara-pada*) means an excellent statement;

"superior-superior phrase" (*uttarottara-pada*) refers to that which is superior even among the superior; and "the limit of the wheel of syllables" (*akṣara-cakra-paryanta*)—the "wheel" is as explained previously, and "limit" (*paryanta*) refers to the boundary.
Because it is the ultimate limit of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*).

Among the six gestures indicating the subsequent friend, there are two parts: first, the manifestation of the name and so forth; second, the exhortation "Go to him" and the instruction to inquire about the Dharma.

Within the former, the meaning of "village" (*grāma*) is as explained previously. "Dwelling in the forest" (*vana-vāsin*) means one who possesses a multitude of virtues because they have established them. "Elder" (*sthavira*) refers to one of advanced age.

Because those of venerable virtue and long-standing experience are superior to others; and because those who have attained liberation are unimpeded in the functional application of the dharma-gates they have realized themselves.
The four phrases in the subsequent exhortation to inquire may be understood accordingly.
The seventh [type of] profound and heavy spiritual friend departs with lingering affection. This concludes the section on the "noble-born spiritual friend.

Within the fifth [category], the "spiritual friend who dwells in the perfection of the skillful means of liberation," there are seven [types]. The first is the friend who [reminds one of] the Dharma previously attained.
1. "Second, 'Gradually traveling on' and below explains seeking according to the instructions. 2. "Third, 'Having already seen him' and below correctly explains the inquiry. 4.

"Fourth, 'At that time, the householder Vimukta immediately entered' and below correctly explains the response. 5. "Fifth, 'Good son, as for me alone' and below is the humbling of oneself and the referral to a superior.
6. "Sixth, 'Good son, from here to the south, in the land of... and below points out the subsequent friend. 7. "Seventh, 'At that time, the good... [The text ends here.]

In the section on the Bodhisattva Sudhana’s expression of longing for virtue and his words of departure, the first part consists of forty-one sentences divided into two sections. The first eleven sentences correctly recollect the Dharma previously attained;
the subsequent thirty sentences, beginning with the vow, exhort his own mind to rely upon what has been taught. Within the former section, the first sentence is general.
The names of the preceding dharma-gates are indicated; the subsequent ten phrases are distinct. Within these distinctions: first, profound awakening and understanding of language;

second, mindfulness and knowledge of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for conduct difficult to know; third, contemplation of the mind free from faults; fourth, the accomplishment of wholesome roots that illuminate and benefit;
fifth, the ability to give rise to pure resolve; sixth, the sharpening of the wisdom that gathers sentient beings; seventh, firm and vast aspiration and joy; eighth, the sustaining of excellence.
Aspiration and delight; ninth, the faith-understanding of the nine pure virtues; tenth, the mind of the bodhisattva’s practice. Within the subsequent section on self-exertion:
the first ten phrases concern firm resolve and protective maintenance; the next ten phrases clarify that differentiated objects are non-differentiated;
the final ten phrases clarify that body and mind enter the realm, and the realm enters body and mind.

Regarding the second point, "seeking by relying on the teachings," as for the twelve years, ancient commentators explain that this is because one practices the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) for six years each in both the cultivation of one's own level (*svabhāga*) and the cultivation of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
The explanations for the names of the cities and so forth are all as previously clarified.

Third, the explicit explanation of the inquiry has four parts. First, within the setting forth of the ritual of respect, there are three sections: first, attaining benefit through self-deliverance; second, the interrogation; and third, the explanation.
Within the explanation, there is the heading, the manifestation, and the conclusion. The conclusion is easily understood. Regarding the ten phrases in the manifestation:
"difficult to appear" means that those who understand the Bodhisattva path are rare in the world. "Receiving and welcoming" means to sustain and accept those who draw near. "Joyful."
This is because one always accords with the instructions and commands; the rest may be understood by analogy. Second, regarding the description of the mind already generated, there are three parts:

first, the formal description of the initial generation of the mind; second, "For the sake of [accomplishing] deeds," etc., which clarifies the purpose for which the mind is generated; third, "O Noble One, I now...

and so forth, which clarifies the mental activities such as attention directed toward that which was previously intended. Third, "I have heard from the Noble One... and so forth, which praises the ability to provide guidance and instruction.
Bodhisattva. Fourth, the formal request for the teaching to be proclaimed, which consists of four parts. The first and the third can be understood from the preceding context.

Second, regarding the purpose for which the resolve is generated, there are thirty-one phrases. Within these, they are divided into four sections: first, the thirteen preceding phrases are for the sake of exhausting the sphere of the Buddha-jewel;
second, the five phrases beginning with "for the sake of wishing to hear" are for the sake of exhausting... [the Dharma-jewel].
Because it is the realm of the Dharma Jewel. Third, "desiring to bestow upon all" and the following five phrases are for the purpose of exhausting the practices and vows of the Saṃgha Jewel.
Fourth, "desiring to obtain" and the following eight phrases clarify the desire to exhaust the ten treasuries (*daśakośa*). Each of these should be understood according to the preceding explanations.
Of the three [sets of] phrases, there are ten phrases within the first [set]; the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. All of these are likewise [to be understood].

This can be understood. Regarding the third section, which praises the ability to provide guidance and instruction, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "indicating the path" (*śāsana-mārga*).
The detailed explanation consists of twenty-seven phrases divided into three sections: 1. The first three phrases indicate the essential methods for the means of practice (*prayoga-upāya*). 2.

From "causing [them] to eliminate" (*apanayati*) onwards, thirteen phrases instruct on the removal of faults and afflictions (*doṣa*). 3. From "causing them to quickly" (*kṣipram*) onwards, eleven phrases instruct on the attainment [of results].

The benefits should be understood according to the respective explanations. Among the four correct expositions, there are two parts: first, a single line indicating the topic; second, four lines briefly requesting [instruction].

Within the four correct clarifications of the answer, there are three sections: first, clarifying the entry into meditative concentration; second, at that time, the householder Vimukta [arose] from samādhi...

The following clarifies the emergence from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). First, he addresses Sudhana and subsequently describes the Dharma-gate he has attained. This section consists of three parts.

First, it clarifies that there are three causes and conditions upon which the meditative absorption relies: (1) one’s own past roots of goodness as the cause; (2) the Buddha’s spiritual power as the condition;

and (3) Mañjuśrī’s power of mindfulness as the condition. Second, [the text] "immediately enters" and below clarifies the name of the meditative absorption, which is called "Universally Encompassing All."
Regarding the "Dhāraṇī of Boundless Revolutions of Buddha-fields": this means that many fields are gathered and maintained according to wisdom;

that which is transformed and gathered resides within the transforming wisdom, and is thus called *saṃdhāraṇī* (total retention). From the passage beginning "Third, having entered this samādhi," below, the functional application of meditative concentration (*samādhi-karma-prayoga*) is clarified.

Within this, first, it is clarified that the Buddha’s body manifests within his own body as the bodies of the three worlds. Second, it is clarified that he may manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment in a single world-system at a lower level.
Third, it is clarified that the youth Sudhana is able to enter the lands manifested within that body and hear the Dharma from the Buddha therein.
Regarding the second point, the clarification of emerging from meditative absorption: because the matters of the meditative state are concluded, he is about to preach the Dharma.

Therefore, because there is certainly no verbal expression [of it]. Third, the description of the dharma-gate attained by oneself has three parts: first, clarifying the name and essence of liberation;

second, from "Good son, my entering and exiting... onwards, clarifying its functional activity; third, from "Good son, you should know that a bodhisattva... onwards, exhorting cultivation so as to enter [it].
Regarding the first, the name "Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Adornment" refers to the certainty of manifesting the merit of fruition.
Therefore, he is named Tathāgata. Regarding "unimpeded," the original commentary provides four meanings: first, because every Tathāgata is individually endowed with unimpeded adornments;
second, because each and every Tathāgata mutually pervades one another without obstruction;
third, because the adornments of all Tathāgatas entirely enter within the body of this elder; and fourth, because the elder perceives clearly the ocean of Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

Now, I shall provide another explanation. It is said that the power of this samādhi enables the practitioner to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, along with their lands and assemblies, entering and emerging [from the samādhi] without any obstruction.
Second, within the explanation of the functional application of the concentration, there are two parts: first, explaining the vision of one Buddha in each of the ten directions;
second, from "Good son" onwards, summarizing the vision of ten Buddha-lands as numerous as atoms in each of the ten directions.
Regarding the enumeration of the Buddhas: in the first part, the initial section provides a general heading for the time of entering and emerging from this samādhi;

the subsequent section specifically clarifies the vision of the Buddhas of the ten directions and their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment. In the final summary of the vision of many Buddhas, there are four points: first, a general heading for the number of Buddhas; second, the section beginning with "Those various...
which indicates that seeing the Buddhas does not require going or coming; third, the section beginning with "If I wish... which clarifies the desire to see [the Buddhas]; and fourth, the conclusion.
If the Buddhas wish to be seen, they are seen immediately; as before, there is no waiting for them to come or go. Briefly, nine Buddhas are listed.

Fourth, the explanation of why seeing [the Buddhas] does not depend on coming or going: it is because one knows that the Buddhas and one’s own mind are like a dream, like a reflection in water, like an illusion, and like an echo;
for that which is seen arises from the mind. Third, the exhortation to practice and enter [the path], which consists of two parts. First, the presentation of what is to be done.
Attaining the Dharma. Hereafter, the following clarifies the causes for what is to be accomplished. Within the preceding section, there are eleven points:

the first single phrase provides a general summary, while the subsequent ten phrases beginning with "purifying all" provide specific explanations. In the latter section clarifying the causes for attaining [the result], there are two parts:

first, the single phrase "all arise from the mind" serves as a general heading; second, the section beginning with "therefore" provides a detailed analysis. Within this analysis, there are ten phrases, the first of which states: [The first phrase: "All arise from the mind."
"Assisting" means they support one another. "Da-tang" (怛蕩) means broad and level. "Knowing and realizing purity for oneself" means being firm and penetrating.
"Dull yet pure and unmixed" is easy to understand.
Regarding the five ways of humbling oneself and deferring to others who are superior, there are two parts. First, humbling oneself through the knowledge of one’s own [limited] nature;

second, deferring to those who are inferior by acknowledging the multitude of their superior qualities, which consists of thirteen phrases. Of these, the first twelve specifically manifest [the qualities], while the final phrase—beginning with "Such sublime conduct"—summarizes that these are beyond one's own knowledge.

Regarding the six instructions, there are three parts within the section concerning the subsequent friend (*mitra*). First, the location is revealed; second, from "He exists there" onwards, the friend is identified;

third, from "Go to him" onwards, the method for sending the inquiry is clarified. Regarding the first of these, the term "Jambūpānta" refers to the southern extremity of this continent (Jambudvīpa); it is the name of a country in the Sanskrit language.
This has not been explained in detail. As for the second spiritual friend, Sāgaradhvaja: his wisdom is profound and vast, and thus he is like the ocean;
his practice and realization are loftily eminent such that all turn to him for refuge, and thus he is like a banner.

At the seventh stage, Sudhana, out of affection for the Virtuous One’s qualities and with a heart moved by compassion, takes leave of his friend. This consists of nine points: first, mindfulness of his station; second, service; third, reverence;
fourth, [the realization] that he has attained the Buddha-wisdom; fifth, not turning back; sixth, being without flattery or deception;
seventh, constant compliance; eighth, regarding him as a compassionate mother; ninth, regarding him as a compassionate father. The fifth dwelling, concerning the Good Friend, is concluded.

The sixth bhikṣu, Sāgaradhvaja, dwells in the stage of the "Rightly Established Mind" (samyak-citta-vihāra) among the nine [stages] of spiritual friends: 1. From "At that time, the elder... onwards, the instruction by the elder; 2. From "Gradually...
onwards, following the instruction to seek him out; 3. From "Searching everywhere... onwards, Sāgaradhvaja entering meditative absorption (samādhi); 4. From "Sudhana said in praise...
onwards, praising the functional activity (karmavastu) of the samādhi; 5. From "O Noble One... onwards, inquiring about the name of the samādhi; 6. "Sudhana the youth said... [and so forth].
1. The inquiry regarding the realm of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya*). 2. "Good son, I only..."—this expresses humility and defers to a superior. 3.
"Good son, from here..."—this indicates the subsequent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). 4. "At that time, Sudhana..."—this describes his departure out of longing for the virtues [of the teacher].
Within the first enumeration, there are thirteen items: (1) correctly recollecting that teaching; (2) observation; (3) mindfulness; (4) reflection;
(5) deep penetration, meaning profound understanding and realization; (6) inclination; (7) clear vision; (8) comprehension; (9) discernment;
(10) contemplation, meaning re-examining the underlying causes; (11) thorough mastery; (12) cultivation; and (13).
The initiation [of the practice] can likewise be understood from the manifest teaching.
Regarding the second point, "seeking according to the instruction," one arrives at the border of that country, which is also the southern limit of this continent, as explained previously.
An ancient commentator explained: "The reason it is called *prajñā* (wisdom) is because it is the final stage among the six perfections; thus, it is called a 'limit' (*pāra*)."

The section on Samudrareṇu entering meditative absorption consists of five parts: first, the name of the samādhi; second, from "From beneath his feet," clarifying the functional application of the samādhi;
third, from "The bhikṣu Samudrareṇu," describing the emission of nets of light from the pores of his body and so forth;
fourth, from "Sudhana with single-mindedness," reflecting upon his entry into absorption; and fifth, from "Thus remaining established," clarifying his emergence from absorption.

Because the initial and middle stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are named "entering the cessation of sensation and perception" (*nirodha-saṃjñā-vedayita*), it is said that apart from the inhalation and exhalation of breath, there is no other volition or awareness, and the body is peaceful and unmoving.
Regarding the karmic function of this single concentration: all of these arise through the power of vows made during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of concentration.

As for what manifests in the body, there are fourteen locations. First, from beneath the feet, long figures and so forth emerge; this clarifies that at the beginning of practice, one should employ giving (*dāna*).
First, from his two knees emerge the kṣatriyas and other classes of beings; they gather and sustain living beings through kind speech and shared activities.

Third, from his waist emerge the rishis. Because these beings do not believe in past causes but instead gain faith through guidance by means of medicinal herbs that temporarily extend their lifespan—taking this as the Way—they have already developed faith in intermediate conditions while remaining faithless toward their fundamental cause; therefore, the rishis emerge from the waist.
This indicates that because he is free from defiled desire, one should teach him the Dharma of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) as appropriate.
According to the Sanskrit original, this refers to the "nābhi-cakra" (navel-wheel) of the rishi. Thus, the Sanskrit sūtra says *nābhi-maṇḍala*, which is translated here as "navel-wheel."
If it were the waist, one would have said "kaṭi"; therefore, [the former reading] is an error. Fourth, as for the dragons emerging from the ribs:
because the activity of dragons is mostly performed by the strength of their shoulders and ribs, they now manifest through transformations that accord with their habitual actions to provide guidance;
thus, they rain down various fragrant flowers and the like. Fifth, as for the asuras emerging from the *śrīvatsa* on the chest: *Śrī*... [text fragment]
The *li-ma-cuo* (liṃba-ja) are supreme among those who transcend the world. The asuras are supreme among those of mixed classes, for they are able to manifest illusory arts.
This demonstrates the subduing of Māra through great power, such as by shaking mountains and seas.
Sixth, "those of the two vehicles emerge from the back" because they turn their backs on the Mahāyāna. Seventh, "yakṣas and others emerge from the shoulders" manifests the Great...
As for "sinews and strength," this refers to the back, shoulders, and biceps. Because he now wishes to manifest such physical power in order to transform beings, it issues forth from his shoulders.
Although he manifests various terrifying forms, these are mostly for the purpose of protecting sentient beings and the various worthy sages.
Eighth, from his abdomen issue the kings of the *kiṃnara* and *gandharva*, each according to their respective abilities, playing music as an offering.
They praised the Triple Gem with songs. From the ninth [face], a multitude of wheel-turning kings emerged from the mouth-entrance, practicing the transformation of the ten wholesome paths.
They asked: "Why is it that female beauty is not bestowed? They replied: "This refers to the ten wholesome paths; it merely prohibits illicit sexual conduct.

This applies to laypeople who observe the five precepts, not to those in monastic robes who have entered the Way. From the tenth [face], sun-disks emerged from the eyes; for the eye’s power of illumination is identical to the light of the sun.

Therefore, according to its illuminating function, it brings about various benefits: namely, by illuminating the hells so they may leave suffering behind, by bringing light to those in darkness, and by causing them to abandon ignorance and obscurity.
Eleventh, from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the assembly of Śakra emerges;

this symbolizes that within the Buddha’s True Dharma there is pure faith and clarity, and that one should always transform the celestial hosts of one's own heaven through the True Dharma, or manifest the power of merit and the power of wisdom.
...up to manifesting the activities for the benefit of sentient beings. Twelfth, the assembly of Brahmā kings emerges from the forehead;

because the forehead is a high place on the body, and because the Brahmā kings dwell in the first dhyāna of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), they benefit the world through their physical marks, majestic deportment, and beautiful voices, exhorting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma and so forth.
Thirteenth, the bodhisattvas emerge from the head, expounding the Dharma-gates of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) according to [the needs of beings].
Regarding those who are to be transformed: the emergence of the Buddha’s body from the fourteen crests signifies that he is most supreme and exalted.

Within this, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of the three types of action (*trikarma*); second, for the sake of all [beings], a specific explanation of the verbal action (*vākkarman*). Within the former, there are two further sections.

The first line provides a general heading; the subsequent section, beginning with "his body," specifically clarifies the three karmas. Within the three karmas, the first—bodily karma—consists of three points:

first, adornment by the marks and signs; second, the blazing intensity of majestic radiance; and third, light illuminating the ten directions. Second, vocal karma consists of one point: wondrous sound filling the dharma-realm.
Third, mental karma manifests supernatural powers. Finally, within the specific explanation of vocal karma, there are two [points].
The first line provides a general heading; the subsequent thirty-two lines provide a detailed exposition;
and the final line provides a concluding summary of its pervasiveness. The initial heading is self-evident. Within the detailed exposition, there are two parts:

the first twelve lines explain the Dharma for all bodhisattvas, and the latter twenty lines explain the Dharma for all sentient beings. Within the former, the first point is "universal knowledge of equality."

As for the Dharma: it is because Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) contemplate the equality of the single nature of all phenomena and thereby swiftly achieve wondrous enlightenment.

Second, as for entering the Dharma of the Universal Gate: it is to exhort Bodhisattvas who have received the consecration (abhiṣeka) to study the ten kinds of Buddha-wisdom, which are equal throughout the three periods of time.
This means that regarding the objects of wisdom, one universally awakens to and understands them with clarity. Third, the Dharma of Universal Adornment:

it encourages the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes to study and know the skillful means of the Dharma King’s domain and the Dharma King’s station, as well as the vehicles of mastery (*yāna*) and so forth;
because they universally study and know those realms, it serves as an adornment. Fourth, the Dharma of the Firm Mountain: it encourages the *kumārabhūta* (Crown Prince) Bodhisattvas...

It refers to learning to know the Buddha-fields, even to the extent of making offerings to many Buddhas within a single *kṣaṇa*. Because this knowledge and vision cannot be altered, it is called "firm.

The sublime height of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is metaphorically named a "mountain. Regarding the "five ocean-treasury dharmas," these are the exhortations for non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas to study ten kinds of vast dharmas;
that is, regarding each and every object within the qualities and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu*.

The inclusion of form, mind, and so forth—whether large or small, one or many—is due to their equality and non-attainment (*aprāpti*), which is inexhaustible. Thus, the Dharma of the Ocean-Treasury is further named the "Vast Great Ocean.
Regarding the sixth, the Dharma of the Universal Realm: it exhorts Bodhisattvas of right mind to study and know that all dharmas are without marks (*animitta*) and without essence (*anātman*), etc.
Ten items are cited to manifest their inexhaustibility, as this is the universal realm. Seventh is the Gate of Self-Nature.

The Dharma consists of: (1) encouraging the perfection of skillful means so that bodhisattvas may know that the self-nature of sentient beings is boundless and immeasurable, up to knowing that sentient beings have no self-nature;
(2) the eight dharmas that accord with the world, which consist of understanding and teaching in accordance with the actions and fruits of both sentient beings and their environment;
and (3) the dharma of universal compassion, which encourages practicing bodhisattvas to train in observing sentient beings.
Regarding birth, the dharma-realm, the four great elements, and the three realms, one universally gives rise to compassion within them.

As for the tenth, the "Treasury of Accumulation" (saṃbhāra-kośa), it refers to encouraging bodhisattvas on the stage of virtue (*guṇavatī*) to study, recite, and practice extensive learning, up to the point of being far removed from delusion and immovable.

Within this, because practices such as recitation all possess the sense of cultivating and generating virtuous qualities, they are called the "Treasury of Accumulation. This refers to those who are newly trained.
First is the cultivation of the ground of the mind, which involves generating the ten minds, such as the mind of benefiting others. Second, the method for gathering sentient beings:

this refers to exhorting bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds to study [the path], encouraging them to make offerings to the Buddhas, and delighting in dwelling within saṃsāra to lead the world; thus, it is called the method for gathering sentient beings.
Third, the method for the inexhaustible realm appearing universally before one: this refers to exhorting bodhisattvas of faith and understanding toward excellence.

Because one advances in the practice of the ten kinds of faith, contemplating those realms so that they become increasingly superior and distinct, it is called "faith-understanding" (*adhimukti*), for this faith serves as the requisite for understanding.

Question: According to the text in this section, after the completion of the Ten Abodes, one immediately reaches the stage of the Bodhisattva at the site of enlightenment, the position of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If this were not so, why would the Ten Practices and so forth not be mentioned?

Answer: This reveals the great principle of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), specifically the meaning of the mutual integration and inclusion of the upper and lower stages. This is explained in detail above in the ninth section, "The Gate of Manifesting the Meaning," of the *Xuántán* (Preliminary Discourse).
Regarding the subsequent twenty phrases for preaching the Dharma to sentient beings, as for preaching the Universal Gate Dharma to those of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are attached to—
First, regarding the physical body as being superior: this is now to cause universal contemplation of formless dharmas. Second, regarding the universal treasury of dharmas:

although compassion arises in the Brahma-world and one has long practiced much compassion, such pity is not universal, being restricted only to one's own kin; now, for their sake, it is taught universally, so that universal compassion may produce vast merit.
Third, regarding the teaching of the dharma of the power of birth for the sake of Mahesvara: this refers to the wisdom of this Heavenly King.
Regarding the mastery of power: in a single thought-moment, one can know the number of raindrops within a great trichiliocosm; there is none superior to this.
Now, because it exhorts the seeking of the Buddha’s power of wisdom, it is called "the arising of power. Fourth, as for preaching the Dharma of the Mind-Banner to the hosts of Māras:

this is subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This means that the compassionate mind is like a banner, for it subdues all the hosts of Māras; thus, compassion is named the "banner."
It is a banner. Fifth, for the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), he taught the Dharma of pure mindfulness;

this means that while those gods themselves emanate objects of enjoyment, they now instead teach them the Dharma of their own pure mindfulness. Sixth, for the gods of Tuṣita, he taught the Dharma of generating certainty;
this means that regarding supramundane dharmas, they generate a sense of joyful contentment. Seventh, for the gods of Yāma, he taught the Dharma of joy; this was taught for the sake of...

The Dharma appropriate to their capacities and suited to the occasion is taught in order to bring them joy. Eighth, for the sake of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he teaches the Dharma of swiftly adorning the realm of space;
this is because those dwelling in heaven take the adornment of the realm of space as a marvel, and thus he teaches the Dharma of adorning the emptiness of the dharma-nature through merit and wisdom.
Ninth, for the sake of the yakṣas, he teaches the Dharma of joy; this is because yakṣas and rākṣasas frequently manifest as...
Regarding the fear of terrifying forms: now I shall explain for sentient beings the Dharma that brings joy upon seeing these forms.
Tenth, as for the teaching of the Vajra-Wheel Dharma for the gandharvas: this class of beings cannot rejoice on their own;
for them, I shall explain the Dharma of attaining mastery, namely, that the mantra-practitioner constructs a vajra-maṇḍala, or whatever rites they wish to perform, all shall be attained.
It is sovereign; this [teaching] is likewise so named. Eleventh, for the sake of the asuras, he teaches the Dharma of the Great Realm (*mahāviṣaya*).
This means that these beings, relying on their own physical stature and great size, give rise to arrogance;

now, for their sake, he teaches that the marks of the Buddha’s body pervade the entire dharma-realm, and thus it is called the Dharma of the Great Realm. Twelfth, for the sake of the garuḍas, he teaches the Boundless...
Regarding the "Dharma of Radiance": it is said that these birds can only observe one continent and the four great oceans; they perceive the various nāgas and know when their lives are ending.
Now, for their sake, the radiance of the Buddha’s wisdom is explained, which illuminates all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*, fully knowing their faculties, desires, and dispositions.
Thirteen: for the sake of the *kiṃnaras*, [he speaks of] those with supreme wisdom regarding all worlds. This class, by means of the world...
Singing and music are their preeminent skill; now, in accordance with their faculties, the supreme supramundane wisdom is taught.

Fourteenth, for the sake of human kings, the teaching on the dharma of non-attachment to pleasure is given; for most worldly kings are deeply attached to sensual pleasures, and thus, according to their affliction, the teaching on non-attachment is proclaimed.
Fifteenth, for the sake of the nāgas, the teaching on the Dharma of the Banner of Joy is given; for most nāgas suffer from the oppression of the three types of suffering.
Now, because he teaches the Dharma for leaving behind sorrow and suffering, it is called the "Banner of Joy. Sixteenth, regarding the teaching of the Dharma of Great Rest to the Mahoragas:
this class of beings has the nature of poisonous serpents; it is said that he now teaches according to their ailment to cause them to cease their evil poison.
Seventeenth, regarding the teaching of the Dharma of Adornment through Right Mindfulness to the sentient beings in the hells.

It means that when those sentient beings see instruments of suffering with their eyes and their bodies are oppressed by pain, they become terrified and their minds are distracted, leaving them no leisure for right mindfulness.

Now, the Dharma is taught so that their minds may be settled in correctness; this is what constitutes adornment. Eighteenth, regarding the teaching of the Dharma of the Treasury of Wisdom for animals:
it is because the Dharma is taught so that they may abandon their afflictions and give rise to wisdom. This is the Dharma thus taught.
This is precisely what is called a "repository" (*pitaka*). Nineteenth, for those in the realm of Yama, he preaches the Dharma of fearlessness;
this refers to how that world constantly uses molten iron and copper as food, and it is said because he now preaches for them the Dharma that allows them to be free from the terror of those flames.
Twentieth, for sentient beings in distress, he preaches the Dharma of universal consolation; this means that for all those in distress, whether in body or mind—
Day and night there is sorrow and suffering; now, it is for the sake of explaining the dharma of peace and bliss within his body that this name is given.
The final phrase summarizes the entirety, which may be understood as such.
Regarding the sixth [section] on the light-nets emerging from the pores of the body of Samudra-ketu: first, the pores capable of manifesting light; second, the light-nets.

1. Enumeration; 2. The characteristics of the colors of the three lights; 3. The adornments of the lights; 4. The spheres of the lights; 5. The activities of the lights; 6. The fulfillment of the light-activities throughout the dharma-realm.

the two [powers] pertaining to the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) while emerging from concentration. Regarding the first of these, it first clarifies the duration of time spent in the analytical investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*) while established in meditative concentration;

Because each of the preceding ten [benefits] arises from these causes, they are described as "profound" and so forth. First, one is freed from the suffering of poverty; second, one is freed from the suffering of the hells;
and so on, up to being able to establish others within the sphere of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). These points are easily understood from the text. Among them:

Regarding the five questions on the names of the samādhis, there are two parts: first, the questions; second, the answer beginning with "Ocean Banner. Within the answer, there are two sections: first, the answer regarding the names of the samādhis;

The third category consists of two phrases concerning unimpededness toward sentient beings: 8. Gathering in sentient beings through great compassion; 9. Great compassion [itself].

Fifth, there are three phrases: regarding the realm of sentient beings, one is unimpeded—first, entering the ocean of sentient beings; second, knowing the ocean of the faculties of sentient beings; third, the wisdom that knows the distinctions among the various faculties of sentient beings.

Regarding the seven [verses] on humbling oneself and deferring to others' excellence, there are two parts. First, humbling oneself regarding one's own knowledge; second, like those below, deferring to others' excellence regarding the vastness of what is known.

It serves as a basis for all things. Hereafter, the section beginning with "I" and ending with "below" reveals that [the knowledge] within the intermediate state is not one's own;

it contains eleven phrases. First, "excellent practice" refers to skillfulness in benefiting others. Third, "that which is practiced" refers to what one cultivates oneself. Sixth, "entering the essential gate" refers to the locus where the meaning of the revolving flow is realized and understood.

This is because it concerns the state of mind; the rest may be understood accordingly.

By virtue of this vow, thirdly, it is intended that the hearing of the Dharma may be understood.

The eighth, the rishi Vimalaghoṣa, dwelt among good friends during his stage as a youth. In a single thought-moment, he followed the instruction of his former friend through mental attention (*manasikāra*). Within this, there are twelve phrases: the first two accord with the preceding methods of practice, while the latter ten concern the arising of progressive states of mind, such as merit and wisdom.
